The Harivaṃśa,
Chapter One [1]
Now follows the eulogy of the author:
Victorious are the twice-born (Brahmins) born from the manifest lotus of the Lord of Lakṣmī, who emerged as rivers flowing from the tips of His feet, and who are the saviors of the three worlds.
Victorious is that very sage named Viśva, the crest-jewel among those whose inner light flashes forth due to their freedom from defects such as passion, hatred, and pride. || 1 ||
In his lineage was born Nivāsudeva, the foremost among those who bore a stainless series of virtues, a treasure-house of learning, conduct, discernment, and eloquence;
by whose fame the three worlds were whitened, [surpassing] even Śrīkaṇṭha and Vaikuṇṭha.
Our dwelling is within the home that is the domain of Mount Kailāsa and the Ocean of Milk. || 2 ||
Having gladdened the world of living beings with various acts of charity,
and having established his fame throughout the ends of the world and beyond,
there was one known by the name Kāmadeva.
Through his meritorious conduct, he was indeed Dharma incarnate.
There was a teacher named Hemādri, known as Kāmadeva, who possessed incomparable splendor and was a mine of jewels of stainless virtues;
he was the remover of the mire of fear caused by the stains of the entire Kali age.
Like the current of the celestial river, it flows from the foot of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
We know that even in the past, Śrī Kāmadeva performed an incalculable merit,
by which he was able to make the world free from poverty.
Hemādri also descended into his house. || 5 ||
By whom can the wonderful life-story of that Hemādri be described,
for whose progeny, when requested, attains the nature of a wish-fulfilling tree?
Merely upon seeing him, the three worlds, experts in the circle of fame, thought,
"He will surely possess such vast artistic skill as that of the Moon."
The Creator became lax in his effort to fashion [the world]. || 7 ||
This boundless majesty of the Lord of the Golden Mountain surpasses the Himalayas,
which remain inaccessible from afar to those with fawn-like eyes.
By which he maintains a mind that is indeed not inert. || 8 ||
He bears the entire collection of arts and sciences,
he always bestows thousands of cows,
and he possesses the status of the king of the twice-born, renowned throughout the world.
Nevertheless, he who possesses the power of delivering [others] from [samsara]. || 9 ||
All his enemies were indeed utterly destroyed by that supreme scholar Hemādri, who was like a moon increasing the ocean of ghee and milk for the great lord of the earth, Mahādeva;
for it was he who, having attained the position of chief minister (*śrīkaraṇādhipatya*), [attained] learning as well.
Prosperity and Sarasvatī have been deposited by the wise both in their homes and in their bodies.
A few here engage in the inquiry into Dharma;
others know it already through their composition of all the scriptures. Furthermore, on this earth, [the work] of Hemādri-sūri is declared by us to be superior to all others.
Indeed, no one in the past nor anyone hereafter will ever be able to comprehend or traverse [it]. || 11 ||
Now, that noble-minded one composes the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* in order to dispel the world's fear of darkness. (12)
That beautiful wish-fulfilling gem of immeasurable qualities, which Mandara Mountain previously extracted from the ocean and bestowed almost entirely upon those who requested it many times—
having now reflected upon all the oceans of Smṛti, Nigama, Purāṇa, and Itihāsa— [this work is produced].
Hemādri, as if out of rivalry with him, has revealed the Caturvargacintāmaṇi. || 13 ||
Having reflected that this very Cintāmaṇi jewel wards off blinding darkness and remains far away, let the wise not exert themselves elsewhere for the fulfillment of their desires. 14.
May this very Cintāmaṇi, worshipped with undistracted mind, always bestow upon you the entirety of all that is desired, even beyond the power of thought. (15)
In this work, there are sections (khaṇḍa) named Vrata, Dāna, Tīrtha, and Mokṣa in successive order;
that which is the fifth is the Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa.
Wherein the Dharma shines forth unimpaired. || 16 ||
Dharma triumphs, the sole cause of prosperity,
whose six varieties they enumerate as distinct types through their association with specific particularities.
Others also [are called by the same name] when many exist in a given place. || 17 ||
Even Vācaspati himself is incapable of declaring all the various divisions of this [work],
and even the great-souled sages are so in their treatises.
They establish one part of that. || 18 ||
Therefore, the wise Hemādri stated in his own treatise the common characteristic of dharma,
based on the distinction between the desire for arts and the desire for liberation.
And that which they declare to be both optional (kāmya) and obligatory (nitya). || 19 ||
As Hārīta said:
"By performing these ascetic practices for the sake of specific desires, they return again from the heavenly world to birth."
"Those who are liberated from desires reach the worlds of truth, along with their sacrifices;
they go to the imperishable worlds established in austerity. Thus [it is said]. 20.

Now, what are those six types of *dharma*, and what is that specific category of *dharma* called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) which is to be explained in this treatise? It is said: in that regard, while the term *dharma* continues to apply, the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* states: "The *dharma* of the social classes (*varṇadharma*) is remembered as one; after that, the *dharma* of the stages of life (*āśrama*); the third is the *dharma* of both class and stage (*varṇāśrama*); and likewise the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the occasional (*naimittika*)."
O King, that dharma which proceeds by depending upon a single caste is called the dharma of caste, such as the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
And that dharma which proceeds by relying upon a stage of life (āśrama) is indeed the dharma of the stages of life, such as the alms-bowl, the staff, and so forth.
That which operates with reference to both caste and stage of life is indeed the dharma of caste and stage of life, just as the girdle of muñja grass [is the specific dharma] of the student.
That which proceeds by virtue of its quality is called a "quality-dharma," such as the protection of subjects by one who has been consecrated as a sovereign.
Whatever phenomenon proceeds by depending upon a single cause is to be understood as "caused," just like the rule for penance.

Regarding the phrase "relying on a single *varṇa*-status": the word "single" (*eka*) is intended to exclude both causes that will be mentioned later, because the property to be discussed here is a property of *varṇa*. However, since this [act] is based on *varṇa*-status without depending on *āśrama*-status, there is no contradiction with the word "single," even though the initiation (*upanayana*) does depend on factors such as being eight years of age. Alternatively, the word "single" (*eka*) may be used in a distributive sense (*vīpsā*). Thus, whatever is enjoined with reference to each individual *varṇa*-status is a *varṇa*-dharma. For this very reason, the initiation enjoined with reference to multiple *varṇas* by means of sentences such as "eight years old," etc., is cited as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). In the phrase "relying on a single cause" (*nimittam ekam āśritya*), the status of being "occasional" (*naimittika*) for the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is established merely by its difference from the obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites; it is not like the bath prescribed upon seeing Rāhu (an eclipse), which is for the purpose of removing the fault produced by non-performance. Rather, its injunction is justified solely for the purpose of removing the demerit (*adharma*) arising from performing a prohibited act. Furthermore, it does not have a dual purpose like the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice, because in that case the result and the cause possess a dual nature, whereas here it is not so.
The common duties, however, are stated in the Mahābhārata:
"The performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), austerity, truthfulness, freedom from anger,
contentment with one's own wife, purity, and constant absence of malice."
Knowledge of the self and forbearance, O King, are the common duties for all.
The phrase "of the four castes" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Austerity (*tapas*) refers to the *cāndrāyaṇa* and other such practices. As Devala says:
"O King, austerity is the heating of the body through vows, fasts, and observances."

In this context, the word *vrata* refers to bathing, giving gifts, recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), worship, fasting, and so forth; by this, it is indicated that the duties taught in the *Vrata-khaṇḍa* are also common [to all]. By the phrase "knowledge of the Self" (*ātmajñāna*), it is further indicated that even the duties taught in the *Mokṣa-khaṇḍa* are common. Nor should it be argued that because Śūdras lack the qualification for knowledge according to the logic of the *Śūdrādhikaraṇa*, how could the duties of liberation be common to them? For their lack of qualification applies only to the investigation of Vedic sentences due to the impossibility of study resulting from the absence of initiation (*upanayana*). However, regarding non-Vedic matters, there is the injunction: "One should cause the four castes to hear [it]," and since we see the instruction of knowledge as set forth in the Purāṇas and Smṛtis—even for Śūdras—just like the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) and other such practices, [the duties of liberation are indeed common].

If it is asked: "Even so, how can Śūdras have the qualification for the dharma of liberation (*mokṣadharma*) in the absence of knowledge produced by the inquiry into Vedānta texts?"—do not say so. For it is established that knowledge, which is the means to liberation, has that [inquiry] as its sole means. Thus, scripture declares the attainment of liberation to be accomplished through the knowledge of the Self: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow; he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself; the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; through knowledge he enjoys immortality. Furthermore, since the knowledge of the Self is possible even through familiarity with the inquiry into the collection of statements from the Purāṇas and other sources, we do not accept that the scriptural injunctions such as "It should be heard" (*śrotavya*) are restrictive rules (*niyamavidhi*) regarding inquiry. Or, if they were accepted as such, then because that [inquiry] is restricted to the twice-born (*dvijāti*), let the injunction found in Purāṇic statements such as "One should cause the four castes to hear" also extend as far as inquiry, just like the injunction for formal study (*adhyayanavidhi*). Consequently, just as there is no difference in the fact that sacrifices are accomplished by means of material substances (*dravya*), yet those sacrifices must be accomplished by substances acquired through the specific means prescribed for each respective caste, so too, although there is no difference in the fact that liberation is accomplished by the knowledge of the Self, it is accomplished by the knowledge produced by those specific means [of inquiry]. Thus, everything is faultless.
Furthermore, it is said in the Bhāgavata:
"The three Vedas were not within the range of hearing for women, Śūdras, and the low-born among the twice-born;
thus, the sage composed the narrative of the Mahābhārata out of compassion."
Also in the Mahābhārata: "O Kaunteya, even those who may be of low birth— women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras— even they attain the supreme goal by taking refuge in me."
Viṣṇu said: Forbearance, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, charity,
control of the senses, non-violence, service to the teacher, visiting sacred fords, and compassion.
"Sincerity, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins,
and likewise absence of malice— this is said to be the common dharma."

In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: "Knowledge, compassion, self-restraint, purity, truthfulness, non-stealing, austerity, mastery over the senses, freedom from anger, and modesty— this is remembered as dharma."
[8] In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Its gates are sacrifice, austerity, charity, compassion, forbearance, celibacy, as well as truthfulness, and the auspicious visiting of sacred fords (*tīrtha*)."
The study of one's own sacred texts, association with the virtuous, worship of the gods,
service to one's teachers, and the honoring of Brahmins.
Restraint of the senses, celibacy, freedom from envy, bathing in the Gaṅgā, Lord Śiva, worship of Brahmins, contemplation of the Self,
and meditation upon Nārāyaṇa— this, in brief, is the definition of Dharma.

By the term "giving" (*dāna*), those matters set forth in the *Dānakhaṇḍa* are indicated; by the term "visiting sacred fords" (*tīrtha-anusaraṇa*), those set forth in the *Tīrthakhaṇḍa* are indicated; and by the term "worship of gods and Brahmins," the commonality of the duties such as the worship of deities set forth in the remaining sections (*pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*) is shown. Bṛhaspati says:
"Compassion, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, and auspiciousness..."
Freedom from miserliness, lack of covetousness, and that which is common to all beings.
Whether toward an enemy, a circle of kinsmen, or even a friend who always hates, one must protect them when they are in distress; this is proclaimed as compassion.
Whether toward external or internal suffering, or even toward occasional portents of misfortune, one who does not become angry nor strike back— that is proclaimed as patience (kṣamā).
One does not destroy the virtues of the virtuous, praises even those of meager merit, and does not delight in the faults of others; this is proclaimed as *anasūyā* (freedom from envy).
Avoidance of forbidden food, association with blameless people,
and remaining established in one's own duty— this is proclaimed as purity.
Whatever action, even if most auspicious, causes the body to suffer, one should not perform it to excess; that is called non-exertion.
The constant practice of what is commendable and the avoidance of what is blameworthy—
this indeed has been declared as auspiciousness by the seers who perceive the truth.
One should provide assistance, however small, with an undepressed inner self;
for whatever is done day after day, even if slight, is remembered as being free from miserliness.
One should practice contentment with whatever meager things have arisen;
thinking of the welfare of others is proclaimed as being free from craving.
Thus, the sixfold categories known as *dharma* have been defined. Now, that which is to be established is stated in due order:
first, in this section on observances (*vrata-khaṇḍa*), there is the definition of *dharma*;
thereafter follows the technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*) of the observances and their praise.
The vows for the primary lunar days beginning with the first day (pratipad), followed by the various collections of vows for different lunar days,
as well as the vows for the weekdays and the constellations (tārā).
And thereafter follows the compendium of the vows for yoga, karaṇa, saṃkrānti, and the months; from this point, the vows pertain to various months, seasons, and years.
"Herein are the miscellaneous vows (*prakīrṇaka-vrata*), followed by rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and prosperity (*pauṣṭika*). Thus ends the summary of the subject matter.
Now follows the determination of the dharma that serves as the means for engaging the listener. Regarding this, there is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
[10] Dharma is the breath of the world and its foundation; in this world, people approach that which is most righteous.
By means of dharma they dispel evil, for everything is established in dharma; therefore, they declare dharma to be supreme.
Thus it is said in the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa.
Dharma is declared to be the highest good; the highest good is characterized by worldly prosperity.

Here, by the term "first welfare" (*prathama-śreyaḥ*), the means to welfare is indicated, because the word "welfare" (*śreyaḥ*) has the sense of "prosperity" (*abhyudaya*), as in the phrase "welfare characterized by prosperity. Manu says:
"Learn that dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous who are always free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart."

"By those free from hatred and passion," meaning by those who are devoid of unobstructed attachment and aversion. "Approved by the heart" means accepted through a state of being free from doubt. Āpastamba says: "We two do not personally determine what is dharma and what is adharma; neither the gods, nor the Gandharvas, nor the ancestors declare, 'This is dharma' or 'This is adharma. Rather, that which the noble ones (āryas) praise when it is being performed is dharma, and that which they censure is adharma. Viśvāmitra says:
For those who know the scriptures praise that which is done in accordance with reality;
that which they censure is called unrighteousness (adharma).
Bhṛgu said:
Vedic action is of two kinds— active and renounced—
and it was created by Brahmā, in the form of the Vedas, while bringing forth heaven and the other realms.
The dharma known as active (pravṛtta) is threefold according to its qualities:
it is distinguished as being sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic.
And that action which is performed here, O twice-born one, even for the sake of liberation, without attachment and devoid of desire for fruit, is declared to be sāttvika.
That action which is performed after forming the resolve, "I do this for the sake of liberation," should be known as rajasic; it does not directly bring about liberation.
O best of the twice-born, that action which is performed here without regard for the resulting effect and without dependence on scriptural injunctions is declared to be tāmasa.
In the Varāha Purāṇa,
Mahātapa said:
"Now, O King, I shall proclaim the great origin of Dharma."
Endowed with greatness, O lord of men, [I shall relate it] in detail.
In the beginning, Brahmā was imperishable, pure, and designated as both the higher and the lower;
desiring to create subjects, he first contemplated their protection.
As he was thus reflecting, from his right side there emerged a person adorned with earrings, wearing white garlands and anointed with unguents.
Seeing him in the form of a four-footed bull, the Blessed One said:
"O son, protect these subjects; become the eldest of the world."
Thus addressed, he arose with four feet in the Kṛta Yuga;
in the Tretā, he existed with three feet, and indeed with two in the Dvāpara.
In the Kali age, the Lord protects his subjects with but a single foot;
he is established in three ways among the Brahmins through their six divisions, and in three ways among the Kṣatriyas.
The Self-born Lord of the world [manifested] in two ways among the Vaiśyas and in one way among the Śūdras,
throughout all the netherworlds during the Dvāpara ages.
[12] Having four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands, bound in three ways, he dwells in the mouth of the Brahmins, protecting all creatures.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Toward cows, Brahmins, the Vedas, fires, and virtuous people;
toward friends and those who are abodes of fortune (Śrīnivāsa)—toward these, he is especially so."
While virtuous and truthful people, as well as those established in generosity and morality,
exist, he— the glorious one, composed of pure essence and the refuge of the seven worlds—
will never be surpassed among men.
Now follows the determination of phenomena by way of their results:
In the phenomenon designated as "active," the result is considered to be worldly prosperity;
in the phenomenon designated as "ceased," the result is considered to be the supreme good.
In the Mahābhārata: Learning, wealth, physical form, valor, birth in a noble family, freedom from disease,
and the cause for the cessation of saṃsāra— all these are proclaimed to arise from dharma alone.
O Bhārata, a living being attains mastery over sound, touch, form, taste, and smell through dharma; the wise know this to be its fruit.
Likewise: "One who desires the supreme accomplishment of one's goals should practice dharma from the very beginning;
for without dharma, there is no sovereignty, nor the heavenly world and so forth, even after death."
[13] Even if one who is reflecting upon the Dharma should be deprived of life, he thereby attains heaven; the wise know this to be the fruit of the Dharma.
Those who act according to the Dharma are true; woe to those who act contrary to the Dharma! For in this eternal world, one should not abandon the Dharma out of a desire for wealth.
With arms upraised, he cries out, yet no one heeds me;
since both wealth and pleasure arise from righteousness, why is it not practiced?
Those who are faithful, peaceful, wealthy, and performers of auspicious deeds go from festival to festival, from heaven to heaven, and from happiness to happiness.
Dharma, when practiced again and again, increases wisdom;
then, with increased wisdom, a person constantly undertakes meritorious deeds.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Since from dharma one obtains both happiness and knowledge,
therefore a wise person, having abandoned everything else, should practice dharma."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "From dharma, indeed, wealth is born; from dharma, desire is produced;
from dharma alone comes the supreme Brahman; therefore, one should take refuge in dharma."
Vedavyāsa said:
One who desires pleasure and wealth, while seeking them, should practice dharma from the very beginning;
for it is my conviction that nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain apart from dharma.
Just as frogs come to a water-hole or birds to a pond full of water,
all forms of prosperity come helplessly to one who performs auspicious deeds.
[14] In the *Skandapurāṇa*: "From righteousness come sovereignty, wealth, and happiness; from unrighteousness arises suffering.
Therefore, for the sake of happiness, one should practice righteousness and avoid evil."
Since whatever happiness exists in both worlds is obtained from dharma,
one should therefore practice dharma alone for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims.
Whoever should even mentally contemplate an action conjoined with Dharma,
he increases like the wind, or like the lord of stars during the bright fortnight.
For those whose sins have been shaken off by dharma through the practice of austerity for a long time in the forest of penance, their heart's desires are fully realized.
When righteousness increases, all beings always prosper;
when it is absent, they decline. Therefore, one should cause righteousness to increase.
Manu:
For a human being who practices the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even unto death;
for everything else indeed goes to destruction along with the body.
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate Dharma for the sake of a companion;
for with Dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Dharma is indeed one's mother and father; Dharma is likewise one's kinsman and friend.
Dharma is one's brother and companion; O scorcher of foes, Dharma is one's master."
There is no kinsman equal to the Dharma; there is no friend equal to the Dharma.
There is no gain equal to the Dharma; there is no destination equal to the Dharma.
Therefore, Dharma should always be cultivated as a companion by men;
for Dharma is the refuge of the virtuous, and Dharma alone is the support of the good.
Dharma is the foundation of the worlds, and from it proceeds all that is moving and unmoving.
Yājñavalkya: One should practice dharma through action, mind, and speech. Manu: [Thus it is said.]
Dharma alone, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when protected, protects.
Therefore, Dharma must not be violated, lest violated Dharma destroy us.
In the Mahābhārata: One should practice dharma even as a youth, since life is impermanent;
for just as with ripe fruits, there is constant fear of falling.
One should not abandon the Dharma out of desire, nor out of passion, nor out of agitation;
for Dharma alone is the refuge of the virtuous in this world and in the world beyond.
Likewise,
O dear one, I shall tell you this other matter, which bestows merit and is most distinguished.
One should never abandon the Dharma out of desire, fear, or greed, even for the sake of one's life.
Vyāsa says: Even if an action should be of great fruit, if it is devoid of dharma,
a wise man should not practice it, just as one who is pure would not handle kusha grass or sesame seeds.

Having obtained this human state, which is so difficult to find and the world itself is unstable, one should not fail to act for one's own welfare; otherwise, one will be deceived by it for a long time.
O Brahmins, since life and wealth are as fickle as a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass, one should therefore practice righteousness.
[16] In the *Mahābhārata*: "When even a single day has passed devoid of righteousness,
it is fitting to lament for a long time, like one who has been plundered by bandits."
A wise person should contemplate knowledge and wealth as if they were free from old age and death;
yet, as if seized by the hair by Death itself, one should practice the Dharma.
He whose days come and go devoid of the three aims of life does not truly live, even though he breathes, like the bellows of a blacksmith.
Therefore, one should always practice dharma with all one's being;
lest, turning away from dharma, one fall into blind darkness after death.
If one’s dharma does not decline even while living by means of a skull, one should consider oneself truly wealthy; for the virtuous are those who possess the wealth of dharma.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Since life is impermanent and wealth is exceedingly fickle,
one should practice dharma as if seized by the hair by Death."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "He who, having attained human birth— which bestows both heaven and liberation—
does not accomplish one of these two, suffers for a long time after death."
As long as one possesses a healthy body, so long should one practice the Dharma;
when one is unwell, being urged by others, one will not have the strength to perform anything else.
Viṣṇu:
One should seek dharma while still young, since life is impermanent;
when dharma is practiced, there will be fame in this world and indeed happiness after death.
Just as one who waters sugarcane for its sake also sprinkles upon the grasses and the creepers,
so too does a person proceeding by the path of Dharma.
He enjoys happiness, sensual pleasures, and riches.
Now follows the definition of Dharma according to its authoritative sources. On this matter, Manu says:
"The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛtis and the conduct of those who know it, the practice of the virtuous, and also the satisfaction of one's own self."

Injunction (*vidhi*), that which is enjoined (*vidheya*), reasoning (*tarka*), and the six auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*)—these constitute the Veda. Injunction is that portion of the Veda which makes known what was previously unknown. That which is enjoined is the *mantra*. Reasoning is *mīmāṃsā*. Regarding the auxiliary limbs, Devala says: phonetics (*śikṣā*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), etymology (*nirukta*), prosody (*chandas*), ritual procedure (*kalpa*), and astronomy (*jyotiṣa*) are the auxiliary limbs of the Veda.

Regarding the statement, "Virtuous conduct (*śīla*) is pure behavior," since conduct itself is designated as virtue, why is it mentioned separately? It is not so; for conduct consists of actions characterized by the performance of traditional precepts (*ācāryānuṣṭhāna*), whereas virtue is a specific quality of one's essential nature (*svarūpa*). Thus, the distinction between them is manifest. As for the phrase "virtuous conduct is pure behavior," the term "behavior" is used figuratively for virtue because virtue is the cause of a particular kind of behavior. Now, what does virtue establish as its own inherent nature (*dharmatā*)? Virtue, being the specific character of a person that would otherwise be inexplicable, makes known its own status as a means to the highest good (*śreyas*). Accordingly, in the statement of Hārīta beginning with "the state of being a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇyatā*), the use of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) indicates that virtue is inseparable from action, thereby making known its very nature. As Hārīta says: [The text continues with Hārīta’s definition of *brāhmaṇyatā* as the performance of prescribed duties and avoidance of prohibited ones.]

Reverence for Brahmins, devotion to gods and ancestors, gentleness, non-inflicting of pain upon others, absence of vulgarity, mildness, lack of harshness, friendliness, pleasant speech, compassion, gratitude, providing refuge, and tranquility—this is the thirteenfold morality (*śīla*). Regarding conduct (*ācāra*), such as the performance of marriage rites and the binding of the marriage-thread (*kaṅkaṇabandhana*), "self-satisfaction" refers here to the mental contentment of virtuous people whose inner faculties are permeated by Vedic consecrations when faced with a doubt regarding Dharma; that is, their minds being satisfied on one particular side [of the dilemma]. Yājñavalkya says:
"The Śruti, the Smṛti, the conduct of the good, and what is dear to oneself."
Desire born of right resolve is remembered as this root of Dharma.
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras along with the auxiliary sciences (Aṅgas)—
these fourteen are the repositories of knowledge and of Dharma.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "The four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the expansion of Nyāya,
Dharmaśāstra, and Purāṇa— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge."
The science of longevity, the science of archery, and the science of music— these three,
along with the science of polity as the fourth, constitute the eighteen branches of knowledge.

Even among those four [scriptures] whose objects are perceptible, there exists the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the Dharma, because they sometimes establish supramundane matters. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"The Smṛtis are the Dharmaśāstras. Their authors are Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, Dakṣa, Aṅgiras, Atri, Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Āpastamba, Vaśiṣṭha, Kātyāyana, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Saṃvarta, Gautama, Śātātapa, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Prācetasa, and others. [19] Yama says:
Manu, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Dakṣa, Viṣṇu, as well as Aṅgiras,
Uśanas, Vākpati, Vyāsa, Āpastamba, and Gautama.
Kātyāyana, Nārada, Yājñavalkya, Parāśara, Saṃvarta, Śaṅkha, Hārīta, and likewise Likhita.
Those treatises on Dharma which were indeed composed by them in ancient times are the supreme authorities; they must not be undermined by mere reasoning.

The word "and others" (*ādi*) includes Budha, Devala, Soma, Jamadagni, Prajāpati, Viśvāmitra, Vṛddha-Śātātapa, Paiṭhīnasi, Pitāmaha, Bodhāyana, Chāgaleya, Jābāli, Cyavana, Marīci, and Kaśyapa. For it is said in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"O mighty-armed son, having examined those statements which are found in the eighteen Purāṇas, as well as in other Smṛtis..."
"I shall speak to you after having examined, in due order, the statements of those twenty-six Smṛtis which have been proclaimed [beginning with] Manu and the others.

Thus, the number of Smṛtis beginning with Manu is stated as twenty-six; and that number is fulfilled precisely by those [Smṛtis] mentioned immediately above. Furthermore, those works such as the Mahābhārata, the Rāmāyaṇa, the Viṣṇudharma, the Śivadharma, and so forth, as well as the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭas, are included by the very phrase "and in other Smṛtis. And so it has been said in the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa:
The eighteen Purāṇas, as well as the life-story of Rāma,
the Viṣṇudharma scriptures, and the Śivadharma texts, O Bhārata.
[20] And the fifth Veda is the Black One (Kārṣṇya), which is remembered as the Mahābhārata;
and the solar duties (saurā dharmāḥ), O Indra among kings, were spoken by Manu, O lord of the earth.

"The wise indeed proclaim their name as 'Jaya'. This [text] should also be understood as being included by the phrase "and also in other Smṛtis. Likewise, whatever else is accepted by great men and is not contradicted [by scripture], that too should be understood as being included by the very same phrase "and also in other Smṛtis. Vasiṣṭha says:

Dharma is that which is ordained by the Śruti and Smṛti; when those are unavailable, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is the authority. Likewise: "Those whose Veda has come down through tradition along with its supplements (paribṛṃhaṇa), those distinguished Brāhmaṇas should be known as the causes for the direct perception of the Śruti."
The definition of a Purāṇa is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Cosmic creation, secondary creation, genealogies, the periods of the Manus,
and the history of the dynasties— these are the five characteristics of a Purāṇa."
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "Those who know the Purāṇas declare that there are eighteen Purāṇas:
the Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata."
Likewise, the Nāradīya is another, and the Mārkaṇḍeya is the seventh;
the Āgneya is the eighth, and the Bhaviṣya is remembered as the ninth.
The tenth is the Brahmavaivarta, the Laiṅga is remembered as the eleventh,
the Vārāha is the twelfth, and the Skānda is the thirteenth.
The fourteenth is the Vāmana, and the fifteenth is remembered as the Kaurma;
then follow the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and after that, the Brahmāṇḍa.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Other Upapurāṇas have indeed been narrated by the sages;
the first is that spoken by Sanatkumāra, and after that, the Nārasiṃha is supreme."
The third is designated as Nānda and was spoken by Kumāra;
the fourth, known as Śivadharma, was spoken directly by Nandīśa.
The wonderful account spoken by Durvāsas, that which was spoken by Nārada thereafter, as well as the teachings of Kapila, Manu, and likewise those set forth by Uśanas.
The Brahmāṇḍa, the Vāruṇa, and that which is called the Kāpila,
as well as the Māheśvara, the Śāmba, and the Saura, which contains the collection of all subjects.
The first is that spoken by Parāśara, as well as the two Bāgavatas;
this is declared to be the eighteenfold Purāṇa, the excellent Kaurma.
That which was ordained of old by the sages, the foremost knowers of the meaning of the Vedas, should be known as the supreme dharma; it is not established in other scriptures.
Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all those are fruitless after death, for they are declared to be grounded in darkness.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"That description of Narasiṃha which was proclaimed in the Padma Purāṇa is here called the Nārasiṃha [Purāṇa], consisting of eighteen thousand verses."
[22] That Purāṇa in which the majesty of Nandī is described by Kārttikeya is celebrated in the world as the Nandīpurāṇa, known by the name of Nandā.
Wherever there shall be a narrative with Sāmba placed at its forefront,
that is further proclaimed in the world as "Sāmba" itself, O you of pure vows.
In this very way, it is also designated there as the "perception of the sun."
But whatever is seen in the Purāṇa as distinct from these eighteen,
know that, O best of the twice-born, it has emerged from among these.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"That which was proclaimed by Vāyu as the Śaiva, the Vairiñca, and the Saura;
that which is called the Kālikā, and that which is remembered as the Mūla-Bhāgavata."
Devala says:
Itihāsa consists of ancient accounts concerning the deeds of ṛṣis, which have the fruit of providing guidance for conduct.
Manu says:
One who desires the purification of dharma must thoroughly understand the triad of direct perception, inference, and verbal testimony consisting of various scriptures.

Manu says: "He who, by means of reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures, harmonizes the traditional teachings of the sages with the instruction on Dharma— he, and no other, knows Dharma."

By means of reasoning, such as Mīmāṃsā and other systems. Vyāsa says: "For those desiring the purification of dharma, nothing other than the Veda is sought as the pure cause of dharma; any other is proclaimed to be mixed."
Therefore, that which is understood from the Veda is the supreme dharma;
however, that which is established in the Purāṇas and other such texts should be known as inferior.
Know that whatever else besides these expresses the Dharma is even further removed; delusion is considered its basis.
[23] Śaṅkha and Likhita say:
For those burned by the fires of passion and hatred and submerged in the waters of the sense-objects,
all the scriptures are a remedy, just as medicine is for diseases.
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa, Sumantu said:
"Listen, O mighty-armed one, to this Bhaviṣyat [Purāṇa] characterized by five marks."
Having heard which, O King, a person is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Those five which were indeed proclaimed in various places by the Self-Existent One are as follows:
the first is declared to be Brāhma, and the second is remembered as Vaiṣṇava.
The third, pertaining to Tvaṣṭṛ, has been explained; now the fourth, Bhāvya, is being described, as well as the fifth, Pratibhāvya, which is honored throughout all the worlds.
Hārīta says:
For those blinded by the darkness of ignorance and led astray by various views,
this lamp of the Dharma-śāstra is the instructor of the path of Dharma.
Śātātapa says:
"The Śruti and the Smṛti are proclaimed to be the two eyes of the Brahmins;
one who lacks one of them is called one-eyed, while one who lacks both is proclaimed to be blind."
In the *Yamapurāṇa*:
"Because of the great number of scriptures here, the root of dharma is the Śruti and Smṛti, as well as the Itihāsas and Purāṇas; therefore, fix your mind upon them."
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The Vedas, because they are scattered, are difficult to understand as a means for accomplishing dharma;
therefore, the Śruti was indeed ordained by Brahmā to be accessible and capable of that purpose."
Men who perform those various duties proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti shall attain merit; otherwise, their destination is hell.
He who, relying on false scriptures, would subvert with fallacious arguments the Vedic and Smṛti injunctions regarding ritual actions and speech, should be known as one censured by the learned.
In the Mahābhārata:
"One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'He will deceive me.'"
O lord of men, the treatises on dharma, the Vedas, and the six auxiliary sciences are prescribed for the benefit of a man whose actions are untainted.
Vyāsa says:
For the twice-born, the Śruti and Smṛti are the means of accomplishing the goals of human life;
likewise, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are authoritative for the determination of Dharma.
Yama says: The Vedas are authoritative; the Smṛtis are authoritative;
and speech endowed with righteousness and purpose is authoritative.
Who would take as authoritative the word of one for whom even authority itself is not authoritative?
He for whom the Vedas, the treatises on Dharma, and the words of the elders are not authoritative in this world— that evil-souled man is destroyed by his own religious duties.
Even that [cognition] would not be a valid means of knowledge for him in this case.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Know that Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—
these five are the means for the thorough investigation of Brahman."
It bestows the destruction of saṃsāra and serves as a bridge toward the requisites for attaining heaven;
indeed, this Vaiṣṇava dharma is proclaimed to be the very essence.
This much alone is declared to be the entire path of the Veda;
from these, hundreds and thousands of other [texts] have also been praised.

Now follows the determination of dharma by way of its constituent factors (*nimitta*). Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In this regard, the characteristics of dharma are: place, time, means, substance, faith, recipient, and renunciation. When all these are present, there is the arising of dharma; this is the common rule, otherwise it is the reverse. Dharma perfected by faith and a worthy recipient is [the result]; time consists of the transits of the sun and so forth; faith is the production of the substance; time is the root of that [substance]; and place is rooted in that [time]. Place refers to Brahmāvarta and other such regions.

"Means" (*upāya*) refers to the duty to be performed; "substance" (*dravya*) is that acquired through one's own occupation; "faith" (*śraddhā*) is the conviction in the existence of the Dharma; and the "recipient" (*pātra*) is one endowed with the threefold knowledge (*vidyā*). In these, there arises the production of common merit (*sādhāraṇadharma*). Otherwise, there is no arising of merit. Faith, substance, and the time of their production—this too is a time for Dharma in acts such as giving, just like the transit of the sun (*saṃkrānti*) and so forth. "The place is rooted in that" means that a place endowed with such a time is also a producer of Dharma. Now, the determination of the place is introduced. Regarding this, in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
O Blessed One, this Jambudvīpa has been described by you in brief;
as for that which was spoken by you, [it is such that] action elsewhere does not bestow merit.
O Great King, having avoided the wicked and the deceitful in this land of Bhārata,
from here one goes to heaven, liberation, the intermediate state, and the end.
Indeed, human activity is not ordained here upon this earth;
for this continent extends for a thousand yojanas from south to north.
The Kirātas are known to dwell on its eastern edge, and the Yavanas on its western;
Malaya lies to its south, and likewise Himavat to its north.
This very land of Bhārata, O best of the twice-born, contains all seeds;
even the state of Brahmā, the lordship of the immortals, and divinity itself are difficult to attain there.

O Brahmin, one who gives [the earth] enjoys the fruit of that gift through the wombs of beasts, birds, and medicinal herbs, as well as all stationary beings; therefore, [the earth] is both auspicious and inauspicious.
O Brahmin, they go to the land of action; it does not exist in other worlds.
Likewise, the attainment of heaven and liberation, as well as merit and sin, [occur there].
[27] O brahmin-sage, even for the gods this is a constant longing:
"May we, having fallen from our divine state, attain human birth upon the earth.
Whatever a human being accomplishes cannot be achieved by the gods or the asuras.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "That region which lies north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains is named Bhārata, where the lineage of the Bhāratas resides."
In this regard, O best of beings, a living creature may perhaps attain human birth through the accumulation of merit even after thousands upon thousands of births.
Indeed, the gods sing songs of praise for those who dwell upon the portion of the land of Bhārata,
which serves as the path to the abodes of heaven and liberation.
Men become [beings] once again due to their state of being *suratva*.
Having renounced actions along with their unanticipated fruits in Viṣṇu, who is the form of the Supreme Self,
one attains that infinite realm of action.
But those who are stainless attain dissolution in that.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"The region beyond Brahmāvarta is the land of the sages (Ṛṣideśa);
the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) is inferior to that, and the Land of the Āryas (Āryāvarta) follows after."
When the negative particle *nañ* is used in the sense of "slight," it means "slightly deficient. Manu says:
"The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, that land created by the gods they call Brahmāvarta."
[28] Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasenika—this is indeed the land of the Brahman-sages (brahmarṣideśa), immediately following Brahmāvarta.
Matsya is the country of Virāṭa; Pañcāla refers to the countries of Kānyakubja and others; Śūrasenika is the country of Mathurā.
That region which lies between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is celebrated as Madhyadeśa.
Vinaśana is Kurukṣetra.
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean,
between those very two mountains, the wise know the land to be Āryāvarta.
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature is to be known as the land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
however, a Śūdra, when distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.
This source of Dharma has indeed been declared to you from its very root;
it is meritorious, the remover of all sins, and the means for accomplishing all rites.

Vasiṣṭha: In Āryāvarta—east of the Adarśa mountain, west of the Lokācala mountain, north of the Kumārikā river, and south of the Himavat mountains—whatever duties and customs exist, all those are to be accepted, but not others that are contrary to the law. Some call this region Āryāvarta; others say it is the area between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers, or as far as the black antelope roams, for so far extends the luster of Vedic knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). Paiṭhīnasi: [29]

From the Himalayas to Kumārī, from the river Sindhu to the Vaitaraṇī, and as far as the northern course of the sun, or wherever the black antelope roams—therein Dharma exists with its four feet. Thus says Saṃvarta:
"Wherever the black antelope, that natural creature, always roams..."
That should be known as the teaching of the Dharma, the means for accomplishing the dharma of the twice-born.
Vyāsa says: All mountains are meritorious, as are the oceans and the rivers;
likewise, forests are meritorious, and Naimiṣa especially so.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "The sacred places are the rivers, Gayā, the mountains, the Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, Puṣkara, Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and Jambukeśvara."
Kedāra, Bhīmanāda, Kuṇḍaka, the one called Puṣkara,
the highly meritorious Someśvara, and likewise Amarakaṇṭaka.
Likewise, Kāliñjara and Vindhya, where the cave of Vāmīguha is located—
all these are meritorious hermitages of Śiva, and all rivers there bestow auspiciousness.
Indeed, charity, ritual bathing, and fasting always yield fruit for human beings.
Viṣṇu:
One should know that country to be a land of Mlecchas in which the establishment of the four castes does not exist; beyond that is Āryāvarta.
Baudhāyana says: The Ānartakas, Aṅgas, Magadhas, Surāṣṭras, the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha),
as well as the Sindhus and Sauvīras— these are of mixed origin.
[30] Ānartaka is the region where the Yāskas dwell. Likewise: "He who enters the Kaliṅgas commits sin with his feet."
The sages have declared that the expiation for this is an oblation of ghee in the fire.
Now follows the exposition of *śrāddha*. The venerable Śruti declares:
"By faith the fire is kindled; by faith the oblation is offered.
Faith is at the head of fortune—we proclaim this with our speech," and so forth.
Manu says:
The gift of a generous person is purified by faith; that which is otherwise is destroyed by a lack of faith.
One should always perform sacrifices and works of public utility with faith, exerting oneself diligently.
In the Vahnipurāṇa: All dharmas are preceded by faith; they abide in faith as their middle and their end;
faith is their conclusion and their foundation; indeed, faith alone is proclaimed as dharma.
Subtle are Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara, whose essence consists solely of being heard;
they are grasped by faith alone, neither by the hand nor by the eye.
The subtle Dharma is not attained through many bodily hardships nor by heaps of wealth, even by gods who are devoid of faith.
Faith is the supreme, subtle Dharma; faith is the highest knowledge and the highest austerity. Faith is heaven and liberation; faith is this entire world.
[31] Even if one were to give away all one's possessions or even one's very life without faith, one would not obtain anything at all; therefore, one should possess faith.
Vyāsa said: O King, that goddess Śraddhā is indeed of the nature of goodness (sāttvikī); she is the daughter of the Sun, the progenitress Sāvitrī, and likewise the one who gives life to the universe.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Faith is like a mother, the progenitor of both knowledge and merit;
therefore, having generated faith, one should acquire knowledge and merit.
In the Mahābhārata:
Faith is the daughter of Dharma, a goddess, purifying, and the sustainer of the universe.
Through faith dharma is accomplished by the great, not by heaps of wealth.
For sages who possess nothing, purified by faith, have gone to heaven;
faith is the supreme cause of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
For men lacking faith, there is neither dharma nor its fruit.
Likewise, one who has faith in action, who is generous, wise, free from malice,
and who knows the distinction between dharma and adharma, crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
We shall discuss time and the other factors in the section on giving (*dānakhaṇḍa*), as they are most essential therein.
Now, the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). In the *Bhavaiṣya Purāṇa*: "An action must be properly accomplished by one who is qualified."
O Great Hero, it is practiced by one free from desire, and by one possessed of desires for the sake of attaining desired objects.
[32] One who is endowed with right conduct, possessed of faith, a knower of the Vedas, the best among those who know the inner self,
and who possesses wealth acquired by righteous means, attains the fruit of his actions.

"Correctly" means by means of the first ritual manual (*kalpa*) and so forth; "accomplishment" (*saṃsādhana*) refers to the performance according to the prescribed rules. It is performed by one who is qualified—an aspirant, capable, and learned—and who is the best among those possessing inner knowledge (*adhyātmavid*), having firm conviction in the self that partakes in the fruits of the next world. "One whose wealth is earned by righteous means" means one whose wealth is acquired through his own proper occupation. Āpastamba states: "The instigator, the consenter, and the doer are sharers in the fruits of heaven and hell; whichever of these exerts himself more, to him belongs the greater portion of the fruit. Yājñavalkya says: [and so forth].
But he who performs an action prescribed by rule according to an improper method obtains no fruit at all; for that [action] of his results in nothing but suffering.
Manu says: "He who, being capable of following the primary rule, conducts himself according to a secondary rule— no fruit pertaining to the next world exists for that person of perverted intellect."
Kātyāyana, in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*, states:
"The learned have declared that there are three kinds of non-performance for those who act according to their own whims:
non-performance itself, that which is called performance by another [in error], and thirdly, improper performance."
That fool who, having abandoned what remains of his own branch, desires to perform [rites] based on another's branch, his fruit shall be in vain.
That which is not prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, provided it is not contradictory,
should be performed by the learned, just like the Agnihotra and other such rites.
Just as the Agnihotra sacrifice is prescribed in the branches of the Yajurveda.
[33] It is performed by the Chandogas and others. In the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"Whether it be much or little, whatever rite is proclaimed in one's own *gṛhya* [sūtra], when the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled to that extent, everything is considered done."
Likewise:
"If one should perform in some way what has been commenced otherwise due to delusion,
one should complete it from that very point at which it became otherwise."
That which has proceeded, having been commenced, and has become otherwise—that is, that which has reached a state of reversal through a change in its sequence.
If, upon completion, one should realize, "I have done this otherwise," one should do it again at that very moment; there is no repetition of all ritual acts.
This, however, concerns the knowledge of performing otherwise at the completion of the ritual action.
Where there is the non-performance of the principal act, that [act] together with its subsidiaries is performed again;
but upon the non-performance of a subsidiary, there is neither repetition nor the performance of that [principal act].

Where there is a non-performance of the principal rite (*pradhāna-karman*), that must be performed again together with all its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*). However, if a subsidiary is omitted, there is neither a repetition of the principal rite along with its subsidiaries, nor is there a performance of only that specific subsidiary; rather, only an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is to be performed. Thus says Hārīta.

The line to the north of the thumb is the *brahmatīrtha*; behind the little finger is the *prājāpatya*; the tips of the fingers are the *daiva*; between the thumb and the forefinger is the *pitrya* (or *pitṛtīrtha*); and the middle is the *āgneya*. One should perform the ritual rinsing (*upasparśana*) with the *brahma* tīrtha; the sipping of water (*ācamana*), oblations (*homa*), and libations (*tarpaṇa*) with the *prājāpatya*; cleansing (*mārjana*), worship (*arcana*), the offering of bali, and eating with the *daiva*; rites for the ancestors (*pitr-artha*) with the *pitrya*; and one should accept gifts with the *āgneya*. Thus says Chāgaleya. The *brahmatīrtha* is in the middle of the hand, but it is used for receiving gifts from the right.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "The wise perform the rites of rice-balls and water for the Nāndīmukhas by means of the Prājāpatya tīrtha; and whatever else is produced [by this]."

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "O Brahmin, the *prājāpatya*—the great sacred ford (*tīrtha*)—is located at the root lines of the fingers, at the base of the thumb, and at the wrist; with that, one should always perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*)."
If the lines for wealth, longevity, and wife intersect at the *somatīrtha*, it is middling;
therefore, one should perform the oblation of parched grain and other offerings, as well as the shaving of the head.
Shaving refers to the pouring out of rice and other grains. In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"O King of the Raghus, a wise man should always perform the touching of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and the consumption of curd by means of the *Soma-tīrtha*."
Vasiṣṭha says: One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors,
as well as for the recitation of purificatory texts and for giving gifts prescribed by rule.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"The atheist who performs a ritual act here out of delusion without having sipped water—his entire ritual action becomes fruitless; of this there is no doubt."
Kātyāyana says: One should not perform giving, sipping water, fire-offerings, eating, worship of the deities, Vedic study, or libations to the ancestors while sitting with the feet raised.
He who has his feet placed upon a seat, with his hands in the añjali gesture between his knees,
and sits with his thighs crossed, is called *prauḍhapāda*.
Vasiṣṭha says: During the recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, and fasts, one should wear clean garments;
being adorned, pure, silent, full of faith, and having conquered the senses.
Baudhāyana says: One who performs recitations, burnt offerings, or accepts gifts while wearing saffron-colored garments—
his oblation to the gods, his offering to the ancestors, his *svadhā*, and his sacrificial gift do not reach their destination.
Vyāsa says: Whatever recitations, fire-offerings, or acceptance of gifts one performs while wearing wet clothes,
as well as whatever is performed with the knees outside [the knees of the garment], all that should be known as demonic.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "One should not engage in rituals such as fire-offerings and the worship of deities, nor likewise in sipping water (ācamana),
nor in the recitation of the words of the twice-born, while wearing only a single garment."
Regarding the recitation by Brahmins, such as the *dvija-svastivācana* and other rites, Śātātapa states:

"One should know that garment which has slipped from the left shoulder and remains at the waist to be 'single-clothed' (*ekavastra*); one should avoid it in rites for the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*)."
Yājñavalkya says:
A garment with the waist-knot tied outside is indeed asuric;
it should be diligently avoided by the learned in all religious rites.

"Bahiḥkakṣā" means that which has gone outside the armpit (the outer part). Kātyāyana states in the *Chandoga-pariśiṣṭa*: "In cases where an action is prescribed but the body-part of the agent is not specified, it should be understood that the right hand is the one that brings the rites to completion."

In those rites such as recitation and fire-offerings where no restriction of direction exists, three directions are prescribed: the eastern (Aindrī), the northern (Saumyā), and the unconquered (Aparājitā).

The eastern direction belongs to Indra, the northern to Soma, and the northeast to Aparājita (the Unconquered). Where no specific rule regarding posture— whether sitting, standing, or bowing— is prescribed, then it should be performed while sitting, and not while bowing or standing.
*Prahvaḥ* means with knees bent forward; *pravaṇena* means by one who is bowed; *tiṣṭhatā* means by one who is standing upright. Regarding the term *oṃkāra*, Āpastamba says in continuation:
"Therefore, having uttered 'Om', the sacrificial, charitable, and ascetic acts prescribed by the rules proceed constantly for those who discourse on Brahman."
[37] However, a duration of three *mātrās* should be employed in all undertakings of ritual actions;
those who contemplate the meaning of reality should perform them with three and a half *mātrās*.
But at the time of meditating on the deity, one should perform the prolated vowel (pluta); of this there is no doubt.

Kaśyapa states: Rites for prosperity (*bhūtikarma*) consist of such high-pitched utterances as "May it be an auspicious day! May there be great abundance! and so forth; these rites for prosperity bring about success. They begin with the syllable *oṃ* and include the recitation of benedictions (*svasti*) and similar formulas.
Yama says: O Goddess, the recitation of the Puṇyāha (the auspicious day) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa;
one should perform this very same rite for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, but without the syllable *oṃ*.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Without the rising of the sun, rites such as bathing and giving gifts do not take place;
likewise, the ritual tending of the fire and the performance of sacrifices are observed [to be impossible]."
By the term "sunrise," the time of dawn is understood; therefore, the intended meaning is that one should not perform [these acts] at night. Dakṣa says:
"Rites for the gods should be performed in the forenoon, but those for humans in the midday."
And it is the settled rule that the rites for the ancestors should be performed in the afternoon.
Aṅgiras: At both twilights during the recitation of prayers, while eating, when cleaning the teeth,
during rites for the ancestors and the gods, and likewise after voiding urine or excrement;
Especially when giving gifts or performing sacrifices in the presence of gurus,
a person who maintains silence on these occasions attains heaven.
Yājñavalkya: If, in any way, there should be a lapse of silence during the recitation of *japa* and other rites,
one should utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Whatever may fall away during sacrifices through ignorance or delusion, that becomes complete simply by the remembrance of Viṣṇu; such is the Vedic revelation.
Likewise, there is the scriptural passage concerning oaths:

"Now, whatever one who has restrained his speech utters, from that the sacrifice, once released, turns back; therefore, one should mutter a verse or a formula addressed to Viṣṇu," and so forth. Manu [states]:
One should not cause pain to anyone by deed, thought, or word;
however, while performing the ritual ablution, one may perform other rites.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, eating, and even the offering of oblations—these must always be performed with the thumb; otherwise, they belong to the Asuras."

"With the thumb" means with the thumb joined to the fingers. O King, these very acts—giving and so forth—should especially be performed with the hands between the knees; the same applies to the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
In the same manner, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed. Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"One should always wear the sacred thread (upavīta) and always have one's topknot tied.
Whatever one performs without the topknot or without the sacred thread is as if it were not done at all."
[39] In the *Nigama-pariśiṣṭa*:

On the left shoulder, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is worn for rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva*); it is worn as the *prācīnāvīta* for ancestral sacrifices (*pitṛyajña*), otherwise. When suspended from both shoulders, it is the *nivīta* at the time of ritual dismissal (*utsarga*). When hanging down along the back, it is used during sexual intercourse (*grāmyadharma*). Sexual intercourse refers to union with a woman. — Bodhāyana.
One engaged in ritual action should avoid touching the area below the navel.
Yājñavalkya says: [One should avoid] mantras dedicated to Rudra, the Pitṛs, and the Asuras, as well as those addressed to the gods and those intended for malevolent magic.
Having recited the *vyāhṛtis* and touched himself, and having touched water, he may perform other [rites].

Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*: "During the recitation of ancestral mantras (*pitṛmantra*), the selection of the lineage (*pravaraṇa*), the touching of oneself (*ātmalambha*), the looking [at the food],
the downward emission of wind (flatulence), laughing, and speaking untruth."
Upon touching a cat or a mouse, when reviled, when anger arises, or upon any such other occasions— on all these occasions, one should touch water like an elephant.

Regarding "touching oneself" (*ātmālambha*), it refers to touching the heart; regarding "in a rite such as a sacrifice" (*yajñādau vihite*), one should understand that only water prescribed for sacrifices and the like is to be taken.
Laghu-Hārīta says:
"In recitation (*japa*), in fire-offerings (*homa*), likewise in giving (*dāna*), in Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), and in the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*)."
One should, however, make the hand non-empty with gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass.
[40] But that twilight devotion which is devoid of darbha grass, that gift which is without water,
and that recitation which is uncounted— all that is useless.
Likewise: "One should avoid six types of *kuśa* grass: those used on a funeral pyre, those found on a path, those from sacrificial grounds, and those used for spreading, as seats, or for *piṇḍas*."
The darbha grass used for the sake of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), those by whom the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) has been performed,
and those smeared with urine or food remnants— their disposal is prescribed [as follows].
One should know those darbha grasses which are placed within the *nivī* and those which are made into the *brahmasūtra* as sacred; as is the body, so are the *kuśa* blades.
In the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa: "Darbha grass, the black antelope skin, the mantras, Brāhmaṇas, the sacrificial oblation, and the fires—
these are not exhausted by use and may be employed again and again."
Marīci says: On the new moon day of the month of Nabhas, the collection of darbha grass is prescribed;
those darbha blades, being of undiminished potency, may be employed again and again.
In the *Chandopariśiṣṭa*, Kātyāyana states:
"Green *darbha* grasses are for the *yajña*; yellow ones are for the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*);
those with roots are for the ancestors (*pitṛdaivata*); and speckled ones are for the Viśvedevas."

The *kuśa* grasses for the *pravaraṇa* should be short, and those for the *barhis* should be long. Those intended for the five sacrifices are for the purpose of the five sacrifices; "fit for the *pravaraṇa*" means fit for the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), and thus they are called *pravaraṇīya*. It should be without an inner core, with its tip intact, made of *kauśa* grass, and indeed double-folded.
It should be understood that the purifier is the size of a span wherever it may be found.
That very same characteristic of a bunch of darbha grass has been declared for the purpose of purifying the clarified butter; it is indeed just as much as that.
Āpastamba: [One should not study] in a temple, at a śrāddha, in a cow-pen, at a sacrifice, during the two twilights, at a crossroads, or in the presence of a teacher.
In the fire-sanctuary, at a wedding, during Vedic study, and likewise while eating—
on these occasions of Brahminical ritual practice, one should raise the right hand.
"Regarding 'the right': having placed the garment on the left shoulder, one should expose the right arm from the upper robe; this is the meaning.
When the prescribed substance is unavailable, that which resembles it should be accepted—just as wheat is accepted in place of barley, or rice in place of paddy."
When no specific substance is prescribed for oblations, clarified butter (ājya) is ordained;
as for the mantra and the deity, Prajāpati is the established rule.
"In the absence of instruction" means in the absence of a specific rule.
When there is no instruction regarding a mantra or a deity, Prajāpati is the deity;
the indicators of that [deity] are the mantras and the collective Vyāhṛtis.
[42] In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa: "O King, regarding the number of materials not explicitly mentioned for images of deities: they may be made of gold, silver, copper, wood, or likewise of clay."
They should be known as made of clay or made of flour, according to one's own wealth;
they should be prepared by those free from deceit, ranging in size from an *āmaṣa* up to a *pala*.

Paiṭhīnasi states: "In the case of stalks, roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, and sprouts, one may provide a substitute for the fragrant substances and so forth based on their similarity; if nothing at all is available, barley becomes the substitute. This is from the *Matirāyaṇīyapariśiṣṭa*.

One gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as the characteristic mark of those rites rooted in the acquisition of the fee. And one should not sacrifice here [if the materials are lacking]; in the absence of *darbha* grass, *kāśa* grass is the substitute. Now, regarding the fuel (*idhma*), it should be from the *pālāśa*, *aśvattha*, *khadira*, red *udumbara*, or green *udumbara* trees; in their absence, from any forest tree. One must exclude the *bilva*, *nīpa*, *nimba*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *śālmalī*, *kakubha*, *kapittha*, *kovidāra*, *vibhītaka*, *śleṣmātaka*, and all thorny trees. Ghee is the substitute for other substances; in its absence, curd or milk. Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* states:
"An offering made with the hand consists of twelve finger-joints' fullness."
With the ladle filled by means of the *rasa* and other substances,
the oblation is offered into the fire by the divine *tīrtha*,
into that fire which possesses bright embers and a clear flame.
The man who offers oblations into the fire when it is not recently kindled and when its embers have vanished,
is born with weak digestion, prone to illness, and indeed destitute.
Therefore, one who desires health, long life, and ultimate prosperity should offer oblations only when the fire is well-kindled, and never when it is not kindled.

While offering oblations and when the oblation has been offered with the *sruva* and other ladles held in the hand, one should not blow on the fire; rather, one should fan it with a fan or similar means.
"One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for the defect arises from the mouth"—
as for the statement "one should not [blow] on the fire with the mouth," that applies to the worldly fire.
Now, in the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa:
"Pṛṣadājya" is said to be the pair consisting of curd and clarified butter;
when curd is added to milk that has been heated until warm, it is called "āmikṣā," which arises from two ingredients.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "With equal parts of cinnamon bark, leaf, and filaments, it is remembered by the sages as 'Trisama'."
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"Clarified butter, milk, and honey are called the 'three sweets' (*madhuratraya*).
Cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and saffron constitute the 'four equals' (*catuḥsama*)."
In the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
"Two parts of musk, four of sandalwood,
three of saffron, and one of camphor— this is the 'fourfold equal' [mixture]."
Camphor, sandalwood, *darbha* grass, and saffron— these four in equal parts are declared to be "all-fragrance" (*sarvagandha*), beloved by all the gods.
Vṛddhagarga states: Saffron, sandalwood, uśīra, musta, lāmajjaka, keśara, camphor,
and the three fragrances (trisugandha) are proclaimed as "all-fragrance" (sarvagandha).
The "three aromatics" (trisugandhi) is proclaimed to consist of equal parts of cinnamon bark, cardamom, and cinnamon leaves.
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Camphor, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, and *kakkola*—
with these five ingredients, *yakṣakardama* is prepared."
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "O King, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are curd, milk, sugar, honey, and ghee.
In the *Skandapurāṇa*:
One should collect, in due order, the urine, dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter from cows that are respectively copper-colored, reddish-brown, white, black, and blue-black.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara: [One should take] water from a cow of golden color, ghee from a blue one,
curd from a black one, and cow dung from a white one.
One should employ the urine of a copper-colored cow in the preparation of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
[45] In the Skanda Purāṇa,
Viṣṇu says: "Likewise, those presided over by Agni, Indra, Vāyu, and Arka [the Sun] follow in due order."
Know these to be Kuśoda and Pitṛrāja as their presiding deities.
In the absence of those previously mentioned, however, one should prepare these from a Kapila cow:
one part of cow urine, half of that [part] of dung, and three parts of milk.
Two [handfuls] of curd and one of ghee; one [handful] each of kuśa grass and lotus;
cow's urine with the Gāyatrī mantra, and cow dung with the "gandhadvārā" mantra.
One should offer milk with the mantra "āpyāyasva," curd with "dadhikrāvṇo,” clarified butter with "tejo ’si śukram," and water with kuśa grass with "devasya tvā."
When these five are combined, they are called the "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya);
this very substance is of great merit and is traditionally known as the "Brahma-spoon" (brahmakūrca).
The characteristics of the *brahmakūrca* rite are from the *Brahma Purāṇa*. Vyāsa says:
"In cow's urine of a copper-colored cow, [one should take] this quantity measured by one *māṣaka*."
It is meritorious, has Varuṇa as its presiding deity, and is consecrated with a verse in the Gāyatrī meter.
One should slowly take four *māṣaka* measures of the white-colored cow dung, dedicated to the deity Agni, with the mantra beginning "Gandhadvārām."
The milk of a golden-colored cow, dedicated to the deity Soma,
measured at twelve māṣas, [should be offered] with the mantra "āpyāyasva."
One should take curd produced from black-colored [cow's milk], which has Vāyu as its presiding deity,
measuring exactly ten māṣakas, while recollecting the mantra "Dadhikrāvṇo."
Into the clarified butter, they take five māṣakas from the blue-colored [cow], reciting in sequence the mantra: "Thou art the splendor whose deity is the Sun."
One should take three hundred and forty-five measures of Kuśa-water while reciting the mantra "devasya tvā."
Having mixed that [substance] in a copper vessel or a vessel made of palāśa leaves,
they stir it with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and drink it while reciting the syllable Om (praṇava).
Facing north, having sipped water three times, he should then go to that house;
there too, for the sake of the fire-oblation, he should first place his body [in the proper posture] and offer the sacrificial fee to the south.
For a Brahmin, however, it should be beautiful and pleasing according to his capacity;
as for the colors of the cows, such as white and so forth, they may not exist in certain regions.
In that regard, one should collect the five products of the cow without discrimination of color;
there is no fault if their colors cannot be obtained, but one should avoid them if they are deficient in quantity.
And curd, urine, and milk from those who are defiled must be abandoned;
likewise, semen from those who are excessively attached and blood from those who act out of ignorance.
It is inauspicious for those who eat the hair or bones of monks, for those who consume forbidden foods,
for those afflicted by disease, and for those who have died from the pain of lice or from eggs.
Those whose offspring have died, those whose fetuses have perished;

those who are barren due to their lack of generative power, as well as those cut by worms; meat that has not been weighed out, that which has been given back, and that produced by a cow in milk while still pregnant.
When various [alms] have fallen upon the ground in a clean and pleasant vessel, they should be accepted; one should not cause them distress on account of those [alms].
This Brahmakūrca vow destroys all sins;
it grants all desires to men and bestows beauty, health, and fame.
It is the destroyer even of great sins and the increaser of prosperity. [47] In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The tender leaves of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, Cūta, and Nyagrodha trees..."
These are declared to be the five auspicious combinations (pañcabhaṅga) that are favorable for all ritual activities.
In the Ādityapurāṇa:
"Gold, silver, pearl, rājāvarta, and coral—these are declared the five gems; I shall now describe the remaining objects."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Pearl, gold, lapis lazuli,
ruby, topaz, emerald, sapphire, and likewise the emerald-gem (*gārutmata*)."

Coral, pearls, and so forth have been mentioned. In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* it is said: "Sweet, sour, salty, astringent, bitter, and pungent—O King of Kings, this is declared to be the sixfold group of tastes."

The characteristics of *śāka* (vegetables) have been stated by Kṣīrasvāmin: "Roots, leaves, stalks, tips, fruits, stems, bark, flowers, and mushrooms— these are remembered as the ten kinds of *śāka*."
*Karīra* is a bamboo sprout; *agra* refers to young shoots; *kāṇḍa* is a stalk; and *kavaka* is a mushroom. Furthermore, in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Barley, wheat, grains, sesame, and likewise *kaṅgu* [grain],"...
Śyāmāka and cīnaka are declared to be among the seven grains.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: Gold, silver, copper, brass,
iron, tin, and lead— these are proclaimed as the seven metals (dhātavaḥ).
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, curd, unbroken rice,
sesame seeds, barley, and white mustard— thus the eightfold *argha* offering is proclaimed.
From the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: Flowers, fruit, barley, milk, curd, water, kuśa grass, sesame seeds,
and rice mixed with sesame seeds— this is called the eight-limbed offering (aṣṭāṅga-argha).
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "When the worlds— Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahas, and the rest— had thus been consumed by fire,
the good fortune of all the worlds then became concentrated in one place."
It reaches the heavens and the surface of the earth;
when thrown up by the wise son of Brahmā, Dakṣa, it stays in the intermediate space,
and as soon as it is drunk, it produces beauty and charm.
The strength and splendor born from the oblation of Dakṣa Parameṣṭhin fell as a remainder upon the earth; it was born there in eightfold form.
Sugarcane, the king of trees (mango), niṣpāva beans, sacrificial grain,
the products of barley and cow’s milk, safflower, and likewise saffron.
And salt is the eighth therein; this is called the "Eightfold Saubhāgya" (Eight Substances of Good Fortune).
The Vātulāgama states:
Ghee, curd, honey, milk, the king of trees (the coconut), coriander, goats, sheep, and flat beans— this is called the eightfold auspiciousness (maṅgalāṣṭaka).
In the Āditya Purāṇa: Midday, a vessel of rhinoceros horn, as well as a Nepalese blanket, silver, darbha grass,
sesame seeds, a cow, a daughter’s son, and a kutapa woolen cloth— these are the eight [auspicious items].
Likewise: dūrvā grass, barley sprouts, bālaka, mango shoots,
the two types of turmeric, white mustard, peacock feathers, and snake-skins.
These nine medicinal herbs, known as the *kaṅkaṇa*, are traditionally taught as the *kautuka*.
In the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"Kuṣṭha, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, murā, śaileya, candana, vacā, campaka, and musta— these are remembered as the ten universal herbs (*sarvauṣadhyaḥ*)."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
These seeds, both those known as cultivated and those known as wild,
are recorded as one hundred and seventeen medicinal plants whose life ends with the ripening of their fruit.
Rice, barley, wheat, millet, mustard, panic seed,
kovidāra, koradūṣa, and chickpeas.
Māṣas, mudgas, masūras, niṣpāvas, along with kulatthas,
āḍhakīs, and caṇakas— these are the sixteen types of cultivated and wild grains.
[50] Thus, these are recorded as the species of cultivated plants;
one should know that there are fourteen types of sacrificial plants, both cultivated and wild.
Rice, barley, wheat, millet, and mustard;
beans, mung beans as the seventh, and horse gram as the eighth.
Śyāmāka, nīvāra, jartila, gavedhuka,
kovidāra, and likewise those which are bamboo-seeds—
these are the fourteen plants belonging to both cultivated and wild varieties.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"Aguru, sandalwood, mustā, sihla, and vṛṣaṇa—these should be made in equal parts; this incense is called Amṛta."
Likewise: one should burn white sandalwood with knots, agallochum, storax, nut-grass,
and sugar for three days on the lunar day of the Moon (the first day).
Thus, O best of gods, this Anantadhūpa has been described.
Likewise: black agallochum, sihlaka, vālaka, and vṛṣaṇa,
as well as sandalwood, tagara, mustā, and prabodha, combined with sugar.
Camphor, sandalwood, costus, uśīra, and likewise silhaka;
Granthika, vṛṣaṇa, bīja, kuṅkuma, gṛñjana,
as well as harītakī and uśīra, are declared to be yakṣadhūpa.
Likewise: one-sixth part of kuṣṭha, double that amount of jaggery (guḍa),
three parts of lac (lākṣā), and five parts of the "five-clawed" (pañcanakha) substances.
One part each of harītakī, sarjarasa, and māṃsī, and three parts of śilājatu.
[51] Four types of incense for wealth and one ten-ingredient incense for the city have been taught by the lords of sages.
Likewise, O Brahmin, [use] vṛṣaṇa, sihlaka, śrīkhaṇḍa, and likewise aguru;
as well as karpūra, mustā, sugar, and the bark, O twice-born one.
Thus, this Vijaya incense was personally created by the Lord himself:
camphor, sandalwood, spikenard, cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves.
They declare that aloe-wood, frankincense, and incense constitute the Prājāpatya offering.
