Now, the description of measures; then, the names. In the Āditya Purāṇa: "The minute particle of dust that is seen when the sun shines through a lattice window—that is declared to be the first among measures of length, the *trasareṇu*."
A trasareṇu should be known as consisting of eight atoms (paramāṇu);
eight such trasareṇus are considered to constitute one rathareṇu.
Eight of those chariot-dust particles are known by the wise as a single hair-tip;
eight lice are said to be one barley-corn, and eight barley-corns constitute one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
Twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula) are indeed proclaimed to be a span (vitasti);
the distance from the thumb to the forefinger is called a prādeśa.
A tāla is said to be measured by the middle finger, and a gokarṇa by the ring finger;
a vitasti, however, is said to consist of twelve finger-breadths when measured by the little finger.
A *ratni* should be known as twenty-one finger-joints;
furthermore, there are exactly twenty-four finger-joints for the hands and feet.
A *kiṣku* is recorded as being thirty-two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height;
a bow-staff (*dhanur-daṇḍa*) is proclaimed to be ninety-six finger-breadths.
A bow, a pair of staffs, and a nāli should be known by their respective measures in yavas and aṅgulas;
those who know the reckoning say that thirty bows make one nalva.
Two thousand bows are taught to be one *gavyūti*,
while eight thousand bows are proclaimed to be one *yojana*.

In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: the atom (paramāṇu), the subtle particle (paraṃ sūkṣmaṃ), the mote in a sunbeam (trasareṇu), the dust of the earth (mahīrajaḥ), the tip of a hair (vālāgra), the nit (likṣā), the louse-egg (yūkā), and then the barley-corn and the finger-breadth (yavāṅgula).
They say that eight *yavas* successively make one *aṅgula*;
six *aṅgulas* are said to be a *pada*, and a *vitasti* is recorded as being twice that.
Two *vitastis* make one *hasta*; with two circumferences [of the hand], it is the *brahmatīrtha*;
four *hastas* make a *dhanus*, a *daṇḍa*, or a *nālikā*, which is equal to two of those.
Two thousand bows make one *krośa*, and four times that is a *gavyūti*;
from that, a *yojana* is declared to be double [the *gavyūti*] by those skilled in calculation.
Bṛhaspati says: A *nivartana* consists of thirty *daṇḍas*, where a *daṇḍa* is ten cubits long.
One who gives ten such *gocarmas* to Brāhmaṇas [attains great merit].
Vasiṣṭha says: A bamboo staff ten cubits long, with a width of ten such staffs at its base,
and extending five more [cubits] beyond that— this is called a *gocarma*.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O twice-born ones, if a man eats [only what is obtained] as it arises for the duration of a year,
this is declared by the wise to be equivalent to a *gocarma* (cow-hide) area of land."
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Thirty daṇḍas, each seven cubits long, constitute a nivartana;
Prajāpati has declared that three-quarters of a nivartana is the measure of a gocarma."
Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says:
Where a hundred cows and one bull may stand unconfined,
those who know the Vedas call this the measure of a *gocarma*.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Those designations which have been recorded by the sages in the treatises on Dharma for the purpose of measurement— all of them must be understood according to tradition for the sake of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*)."
Manu says:
I shall explain in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold which are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.
When the sun has moved into another mansion [of the zodiac], that subtle dust which is seen is called a *trasareṇu*, the ultimate among atoms.
Eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* in terms of measure;
three of those are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*.
Six mustard seeds make one middle-sized yava; three yavas make one kṛṣṇala.
Five kṛṣṇalas make one māṣa, and sixteen of those make one suvarṇa.
Four suvarṇas make one pala; ten palas make one dharaṇa.
Two kṛṣṇalas weighed together should be known as one silver māṣaka.
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute one *purāṇa*;
furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*, also called a *paṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one silver *śatamāna*;
a *niṣka* should be understood by its measure to consist of four *sauvarṇikas*.
Yājñavalkya says: A mote of dust seen in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*. Eight of those are a *liṣka*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*.
Three of those [white] are a *gaura*; six of those are a *yava*; three of those middle-sized [yavas] are a *kṛṣṇala*; five of those are a *māṣa*; and sixteen of those are a *suvarṇa*.
Four or five suvarṇas are proclaimed to be one pala;
two kṛṣṇalas are one silver māṣa, and sixteen of those are one dharaṇa.
Ten *dharaṇas* make one *śatamāna*, and also one *pala*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *niṣka*; a copper coin weighing one *kārṣika* is called a *paṇa*.

Viṣṇu: Eight particles of dust situated in a window-beam, which are known as *trasareṇus*, constitute one *likṣā*. Three of those make one *rājasarṣapa*; three of those make one *gaurasarṣapa*; six of those make one *yava*; three of those make one *kṛṣṇala*; five of those make one *māṣa*; twelve of those make half an *akṣa*; four *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*; four *suvarṇas* make one *niṣka*. Two *kṛṣṇalas* make one silver *māṣa*; sixteen of those make one *dharaṇa*. A copper coin is a *kārṣāpaṇa*. [55] Kātyāyana:
A māṣa should be known as one-twentieth of a kārṣāpaṇa;
a kākinī, however, is one-fourth of a māṣaka or a paṇa.
In the region of the Five Rivers, however, this is the conventional designation;
and its measure is fixed here by a single *kārṣāpaṇa*.
One [māṣaka] is to be known as one kārṣāpaṇa, and four of those [kārṣāpaṇas] are a dhānaka.
Also in the work proclaimed by Agasti:
"Six mustard seeds make one barleycorn (*yava*); three barleycorns make one *guñjā*;
and five *guñjās* are declared to be one *māṣaka*."
A suvarṇa is traditionally said to consist of sixteen māṣas;
four of those [suvarṇas] make one pala, and they know a tenth part of a pala to be a dharaṇa.
A *taṇḍula* consists of eight distinct white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*);
a barley grain (*yava*) is said to consist of eight of those, while others have declared that it consists of wheat (*godhūma*).
Viṣṇugupta: Five guñjas make one māṣa, and with four times as many mustard seeds;
those sages expert in the measurement of gems call this a dharaṇa.
They know that one *majjāṭikā*—a specific variety of *kaṇaja*—is equal in weight to two *guñjās*;
twenty *majjāṭikās*, according to the opinion of those who know, constitute a *dharaṇa*.

It is recorded that for rubies (padmarāga) and other gems such as sapphires (indranīla), the value is determined by māṣakas according to whether they are large, medium, very fine, or even extremely fine.
Three *hastas* should be employed where no specific measurement has been stated;
a *dīnāra* is proclaimed to be equivalent to twenty-eight silver coins (*raupyaka*).
A silver māṣaka is considered to be the seventieth part of a suvarṇa.
He [Varāhamihira] himself states another method:

"Just as in a fertile field, when the grain has ripened at the proper time in the middle of the season, ten *māṣa* beans constitute a *suvarṇa*; or five *guñjā* seeds constitute a *suvarṇa-māṣaka*. Sixteen of these make a *suvarṇa*. This is the second name for that quantity established by measure, namely *karṣa*. Four *karṣa* make a *pala*; one hundred *pala* make a *tulā*; twenty *tulā* make a *bhāra*. This same *bhāra* has a second name, *udataulika*, as stated in the *Brahmaprokta*."
Twenty *palas* are considered a *vīśa*; five *vīśas* are held to be a *tulā*.
That same [measure] is an *udataulika*, and twenty *tulās* constitute a *bhāra*.
Viṣṇugupta states:

The measurement for silver is declared to be distinct from that of gold. Twenty-eight white mustard seeds constitute one *rūpyamāṣaka*; sixteen of those [make] a *dharaṇa*, or twenty *niṣpāva* beans make a *rūpyamāṣaka*. Ten *dharaṇas* make a *pala*, and one hundred *palas* make a *tulā*. Twenty *tulās* make a *bhāra*.
Twenty grains of rice, when weighed on a scale, constitute one *dharaṇa* of this diamond jewel.
One should calculate a grain of rice as being equal to eight white mustard seeds.
Thus [it is stated] in the *Nighaṇṭu* by the author of the *Kapardibhāṣya*. Likewise:
"Weight is measured by scales, finger-breadths, and *prastha*s; five *guñjā*s and so forth constitute a *māṣaka*."
Sixteen of those [ratis] are one akṣa; four karṣas are one pala.
A *suvarṇa* is a weight of gold; a *hemnokṣa* is the same; a *kuruvista*, however, is one *pala* of that [gold].
A *tulā* (feminine) is one hundred *palas*; twenty *tulās* would be a *bhāra*.
Ten bhāras would constitute an ācita; a cartload is an ācita bhāra.
A kārṣāpaṇa is equivalent to a kārṣika, and a kārṣika is a copper paṇa.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "Two palas constitute a prasṛti; double that is considered a kuḍava.
Four kuḍavas make a prastha, and four prasthas make an āḍhaka."
Four of those *āḍhakas* are said by the wise to be one *droṇa*;
two *droṇas* are a *kumbha*; a *śūrpa* is [the same]; and sixteen *droṇas* are a *khārī*.
In the Varāha Purāṇa: Two palas are called a prasṛta; one pala is known as a muṣṭi.
Eight muṣṭis make a kuñci, and eight kuñcis make a puṣkala.
Four *puṣkala*s are proclaimed to be one *āḍhaka*;
four *āḍhaka*s make one *droṇa*—this is the definition of measurement.
Four *setikās* are proclaimed to constitute one *prastha*.
The *setikā* consists of *kuṣavas*. Some say it is a handful for the sacrificer;
one handful is recorded in the *Pādma* as being equal to one *pala*. Thus it has been stated. [58]
Two *pala*s make one *prasṛta*, and twice that is considered a *kuḍava*.
Four *kuḍava*s make a *prastha*, and four *prastha*s make an *āḍhaka*.
Four *āḍhaka*s constitute a *droṇa*; such is the measure of a *droṇa*.
In the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa: five kṛṣṇalas make one māṣa; sixty-four of those make one pala;
thirty-two palas are proclaimed as one prastha among the Māgadhas.
Four of those [āḍhakas] make one āḍhaka, and four āḍhakas make one droṇa.

Now, the characteristics of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and so forth. In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "Ghana, Ghoṣa, Virāja, Kāñcana, Kāmarāmaka, Sughoṣa, Gharghara, Dakṣa—these are considered the nine pavilions."
There are four supporting pillars at the corners, two at each of the doors, and two on the sides; furthermore, there may be other supporting pillars as required for the sake of beauty and stability.
The eastern and subsequent archways (toraṇas) should be made of Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa wood;
they should measure five, six, or seven cubits, and from that point on, each subsequent one may be smaller.
For a cloth, the increase is by two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) up to a maximum of eight cubits (karas) along with a half;
know that the first trident is nine aṅgulas, and from there, each subsequent one increases by two aṅgulas.
Its width at the two horns is such that the entry is two finger-breadths long.
In this regard, it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Having left two cubits outside, one should install the arches (*toraṇa*). The length of the spear (*śūla*) shall be nine finger-breadths, and its width shall be one-fourth of that."
The central horn should indeed be straight, while those on the sides are slightly curved;
that is declared to be the first type, and one should then plant it at a depth of two finger-breadths.
For the remaining [types], the increase is two finger-breadths (aṅgula) and the entry is by an increase of one finger-breadth;
the shaft has a circumference of eight finger-breadths, and the maximum length is sixteen finger-breadths.
The breadth at the forehead and the two sides is six finger-breadths;
this is declared as another [measurement], while for the remainder, there is an increase of eight finger-breadths.
The Svastika or Śrīkañjaka design, or one with arches on all sides, bestows all desired fruits;
the width of the arches should be half of that [height], or half of that again.
The supporting pillars are equal to the arches; the altar-pillars are six units in height.
Their depth is five parts, or according to the requirements of the ground portion.
The altar is four cubits in size, with four pillars at its center and corners;
these are eight finger-breadths high, increasing by one finger-breadth for each subsequent pillar.
Neither in width nor in height should there be a knot-like constriction within;
the goddess Mahotkā is yellow and equal in length and breadth to the liṅga.

According to some views, having divided the width of the pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) into nine parts, the altar (*vedī*) for the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) should be situated in the center by one part; this is the extent [of the altar].
Above the hand-span, in some cases, the altar increases by six finger-breadths;
leaving a space greater than one-quarter of the altar, there are nine or five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Those Vedas would indeed be those very same ones, or perhaps they might be circular in some places.
And it is said in the *Śaucācārapaddhati*:
"Those auspicious sites should always be circular or square;
for the purpose of burning in fire, they should be in the shape of a vulva; in the rite of hatred, they should be in the form of one's own [face], facing south and north."
A five-pointed [triangle] is intended for destruction in the southwest, while a six-pointed one is prescribed for the northwest;
here, a circular pit is declared to be beneficial for rites of pacification in the west.
The Vṛddhiśivāgama states that a lotus-shaped pit in the north increases prosperity;
an eight-cornered pit in the northeast brings fear;
and for the rite of immobilization (stambhana), a four-cornered pit is prescribed in the east.

Likewise, in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "In the rite of destruction, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in all directions should be quadrangular; in the rite of installation, it should be that same shape or circular; and likewise in rites for specific desires, it should be as prescribed in the ritual manual."
In the east, it should be square, auspicious, and the bestower of all desires;
in the southeast, it should resemble a bodhi leaf, always increasing one's lineage.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a half-moon in the southern direction is for the purpose of inciting hatred among men;
one should fashion a triangular pit in the southwestern quarter for the purpose of killing.
The excellent pit located in the west is used for constant nourishment;
the hexagonal pit situated in the northwest is intended for eradication.

The fire-pit (kuṇḍa) should be lotus-shaped in the north for the accomplishment of nourishment (puṣṭi). Alternatively, it may be octagonal in the northeast, which brings about extreme fear. This pit is always for optional rites (kāmya); one should avoid it in ceremonies such as the installation of deities.
In the Svāyambhuva [Kalpa],
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be either square or circular, measuring one cubit;
this applies to rites performed daily, for occasional purposes, or for desired results, as prescribed by the ritual manual.
It should be square in the east,
shaped like a triangle in the southeast, half-moon-shaped in the south, and triangular in the southwest.
A circular pit is for the western direction (Vāruṇī), a five-cornered one for the north-west (Vāyavyā);
a lotus-shaped one for the northern direction (Saumyā), and an eight-cornered one for the north-east (Aiśānī).
For the urine of animals belonging to Varuṇa, however, the shape of a water-pot is prescribed.
The [mandala] of the Vāyavyas is like a banner; that of the Māhendras is like a vajra;
and that of the Āgneyas is said by the best of gurus to have the form of the seven-tongued [fire].
For those of middling or superior vigor, it should be four finger-breadths square;
for those of little vigor, it should be triangular; and for those of female form, it should be shaped like a vulva.
The crescent moon is for the fierce deities, while the circle is indeed for the gentle ones;
the pentagon is for the female messengers (dūtīs) and likewise for the kinnaras.
The creation of enmity through knowledge is considered beneficial when it takes the form of a lotus;
thus, for all weapons, their shape should be such that it fulfills every desire.
Therefore, people who know the scriptures of ritual procedure perform their conduct accordingly.
As it is stated in the *Kālottara*:
"In the ritual installation (*nyāsa*) consisting of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*), one should fashion nine sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*);
in that consisting of the five forms (*pañcamūrti*), one should fashion five [pits] shaped like a *veda* (triangle)."

O Six-faced One, one should fashion sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) measuring one cubit in the Hāstika [mandala]; thereafter, for the remaining [mandalas], they should be increased sequentially by two finger-breadths each.
One should construct eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the eight directions according to the specifications for the feet of the altar;
one should cause a ninth pit to be made in the center of the altar, which is quadrangular.
And there are four in the four directions, while the fifth is in the northeast corner.
Likewise:
"Furthermore, the altar-base (vedi-pāda) and so forth, starting from the cardinal directions of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
are made respectively outside [the pit] for those [fires] ranging from the largest to the smallest."
Having established that two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) are equivalent to one part,
one should determine the cubit (hasta) of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) by those same number of finger-breadths.
One should dig one cubit deep horizontally, together with the girdle, upwards;
outside the excavation, the neck shall be one finger-breadth wide—this is the rule for all fire-pits.
Three girdles should be made with corners measuring five finger-breadths;
the navel should be twelve finger-breadths in length and three finger-breadths in width.
That pedestal, likewise within the base, should be one finger-breadth high;
it is considered to be joined with two *kumbha* sections and shaped like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
The ring finger is joined with the thumb-girdle, while the middle finger likewise holds the clarified butter;
the forefinger is situated on the right (south), the south-eastern direction, while the ring finger is situated in the west and north.
The womb of the other *kuṇḍa* is situated on the right petal;
[the lines] extend toward the cardinal directions, while the fifth is in the region of Īśa (the northeast).
"On its right, on the petal of the navel, that which is desired is prescribed;
a pentad of fire-pits (kuṇḍas) should be made, situated toward the east.
Thus it is said, and as follows in the first [chapter]:
The pit is one *jināṅgula* in width and height, together with the girdle;
for others, there is an increase of two *aṅgulas*, provided with the [other] parts of the body.
[63] Above twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) is one māṃsaka; by that measure, the dimensions of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are prescribed according to the parts of the body.
Outside the neck-finger measurement, one girdle should be made six finger-breadths wide;
alternatively, three [girdles] of four, three, or two finger-breadths are auspicious in all cases.
The girdle is in the middle; the womb (yoni) should be made with a width of one-third of half the pit (kuṇḍa), having a lip the size of a thumb, or shaped like a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha).
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) located in the east, southeast, and south are said to have their openings facing north;
the remaining ones are recorded as facing east, arranged according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "One should examine what has been described regarding the pit (kuṇḍa) drawn with the hand and so forth;
the rim (oṣṭha) should be made one finger-breadth wide and twelve parts in length."
The lip is auspicious when it resembles the lip of an elephant due to its width;
the first girdle (mekhalā) should be four finger-breadths in measure.
A pit that is one finger less than two fingers [in depth] thus brings about auspiciousness;
it should be square, starting from the east, and equal in size to a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
In the northeast direction, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be made either five or eight cubits in size, circular, or shaped like an elephant,
or in the form of a lotus.
As it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*:
"Since the installation (*āsthāpana*) is the primary entrance for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the stabilization (*sthāpana*), and so forth,
one should construct two pavilions after leaving aside the northern pavilion."
Having left one sacred space for another, the sacrificial pavilion (yajñamaṇḍapa) is situated at the front of the sacred space;
it should be ten or twelve cubits in size, increasing by two cubits each time thereafter in sequence.
[64] Having divided that middle portion into nine parts, the altar (vedikā) should be made with the central part;
it may be constructed with eight, twelve, or nine finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
In the same way, leaving aside the northern direction and measuring ten cubits,
the peace pavilion (śāntimaṇḍapa) should be constructed either in the eastern or the northern part.
In the center of that, upon the altar-lotus, the worship of the planets (graha-pūjana) should be performed;
there too, one should arrange nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the purpose of the peace-offering (śānti-homa).
In the rite of installation, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) located outside the base of the altar,
in every direction within the center of the sacrificial pavilion, should be quadrangular.
That very same [structure] may be made circular, or constructed with a different shape;
it should be above twenty-four finger-breadths, increasing by two finger-breadths and so forth.
The width of the pit is said to be one-fourth of its depth, while the bottom is [one] finger-breadth lower than that.
Outside the pit, there is a neck one finger-breadth wide, and outside of that, the tiers (mekhalā) follow in sequence.
From the first [line], it is nine finger-breadths high with a width of one finger;
from the middle, it is two finger-breadths on the outside; but the third is three finger-breadths.
Alternatively, five girdles (mekhalās) should be made according to the options of six, five, two, or three;
having determined the height of the five or three girdles, one should dig the remaining depth below.
If the pit is too deep, there will be disease; if it is too shallow, there is loss of cattle and wealth.
In the case of a circular pit (cakrakuṇḍa), there is suffering, while if the boundary line (mekhalā) is broken, death occurs.
In the absence of a girdle, there is excessive grief; in the absence of wealth, there is loss of property;
and a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) fashioned without a womb (yoni) is said to cause the destruction of one's wife.
"It is declared that a *kuṇḍa* devoid of a neck (*kaṇṭha*) causes the destruction of one's offspring;
for the installation of all *kuṇḍas*, the tip of the banner (*dhvajāgra*) grants all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
Thus, in the *Kālottara*, banners and other such items are prescribed for each individual *kuṇḍa*."
The banners should be seven cubits long and one-seventh as wide.
The world-protectors are golden; the ninth [flag] has the luster of snow;
and those of yellow, red, and other colors are known as the five-handled banners.
Those made of bamboo are considered to be joined with ten-twice-five (ten) staffs;
the *viṣṭara* seats consist of twenty-seven sections and are of great measure.
Fuel sticks of half a cubit are praised here, and furthermore, in the northern [direction],
those of twice-born [brahmins] should be made five cubits long and two cubits in width.
The banners should be seven cubits long and twenty finger-breadths wide;
they should be inserted into the five-cubit flagstaffs to the extent of one-fifth of their length.
The staffs for ten hand-length banners have been inserted;
they are vermilion, variegated, smoky, grey, and resembling clouds.
Green, pale yellow, and white—these are the colors for the banners in order from the east onwards;
such colored banners should be made, O Pākaśāsana.

The origin and characteristics of the ritual water-pot (*kalaśa*). From the *Devīpurāṇa*: "One should make the water-pots very firm; I shall describe their characteristics to you. O Sage, I shall tell you their origin, characteristics, and measurements."
It is by him that the *vārakas* and *kalaśas* are proclaimed in the world,
when the nectar was being churned by all the gods assembled together.
[66] Having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope,
the nectar of immortality, endowed with great heroism and prowess, was produced there.
This jar is proclaimed to be for the very purpose of holding that [nectar],
having been fashioned by Viśvakarman after taking a portion from each of the gods.
Since this jar was fashioned by the gods, it is called *kalaśa*;
likewise, since it wards off various planetary influences as well as [other] human [calamities].
And because they were thus struck by the wicked-hearted ones, they are known as the *vārakas* (obstructors).
Brahmā is at the mouth of the jar, while Maheśvara is at its neck.
Viṣṇu is established at the base, the hosts of Mothers are situated in the middle,
and all the deities surround [the fire] in the four directions from the tips of the flames.
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth truly reside within this jar;
in the home, there shall be peace, nourishment, joy, and the satisfaction of the ancestors.
The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and likewise the Sāmaveda,
together with the Atharvaveda— all of them are situated within the water-pot.
They are entirely supported by water that is full of nectar—
whether it be from rivers, lakes, dug-out wells, or ponds.
Bringing happiness through divine ponds, wells, and oceans,
they are the most auspicious of all auspicious things and the destroyers of all sins.
Such auspicious jars should always be taken for consecration,
whether at the time of a procession, a wedding, an installation ceremony, or a sacrificial rite.
These should be specifically applied as accomplishers of all rites;
they are fifty finger-breadths in width and sixteen finger-breadths in height.
The measurement of the jars (*kalaśa*) is such that their mouth should be eight finger-breadths wide.
Next is the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij-varaṇa*). Regarding that, it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* concerning the gift of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍa-dāna*).
Having honored a Brahmin who maintains the perpetual sacred fire (agnihotrī), who is handsome and endowed with virtues,
together with his wife, and having adorned him with ornaments;
Having invited the preceptor as the foremost, along with other twice-born men endowed with the twenty-four qualities, together with their wives.
One should cause those clothed in unwashed garments, wearing garlands and adorned with ornaments,
to be given rings as well as earrings.
Having thus inspired confidence and honored them, he himself stood before them and prostrated again and again with the eight-limbed salutation.
Having repeatedly joined their palms in reverence toward the domestic priest, they said:
"Indeed, you are Brāhmaṇas, favored by the Creator for the sake of friendship."
By your gracious countenance here, a man shall himself become purified;
through the union of your affection, the Grandfather himself becomes pleased.
Regarding the *tulāpuruṣa* (weighing against a person), it is stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"That which exceeds one hundred *niṣkas* is considered the best; half of that is remembered as the middling;
half of even that is the lowest. Thus, three types are prescribed therein."
A pair of garments, a turban, earrings, a neck ornament,
a finger-ring, and an ornament for the wrist.
[68] And all of these, at the commencement of every ritual act,
one should first give to the domestic priest and then cause them to be presented to the officiating priests.
The wise one should give all the previously mentioned ornaments, together with the turban and the garments, as well as this covering cloth to the practitioners.

Having appointed twenty-four other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), twenty-five Brahmins are to be invited, according to the statement "having made [them] so. Furthermore, with reference to the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), they are mentioned separately in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"In that [rite], there are eight auspicious Hotṛs and likewise eight gatekeepers."
Furthermore, eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas should be appointed as chanters.
All of them should be endowed with the auspicious marks, possessed of the mantras, and have conquered their senses;
they should be reciters of the scriptures, O best of the twice-born, and be possessed of noble lineage and virtuous conduct.
"Twenty-five officiating priests (ṛtvij) should be adorned with golden ornaments;
the preceptor (ācārya) should initiate them all together and receive double [the fee].

Starting from one *niṣka* up to a hundred, or twenty-five, the value of the garments and ornaments should be understood accordingly. This is the formula for the selection (*varaṇa*) of the performers: "Oṃ, today I shall sacrifice with such-and-such a sacrifice; for the sake of such-and-such a rite which is a constituent part thereof, I choose you, named so-and-so, of such-and-such a lineage, whose tutelary deity is so-and-so, as my preceptor. The response is: "I am chosen."
And the division of the ritual duties is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having adorned the door-keepers on all sides with perfumes and flowers,
he should say to them, 'Read [the texts],' and he should worship the Ācārya."
[69] "One should say to those Hotṛ priests, 'Sacrifice!
and to the Jāpaka priests, 'Remain with the recitation of the most excellent mantras.

Because of this statement in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*—"at the commencement of all rites"—this [procedure] is common to all religious observances (*vrata*) and the like that are to be accomplished by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Now, regarding the honey-mixture (madhuparka), Jābāli says:
"One should honor with the honey-mixture a Brāhmaṇa, a sacrificial priest, a learned scholar who has come to one's house, a Snātaka, and likewise a dear friend."
Viśvāmitra says: Having honored the officiating priests with the madhuparka offering, one should have them perform the ritual;
for by having them perform the ritual without honoring them, one is defiled by sin alone.
Now follows the procedure for the fire oblation (*homa*). In the *Devīpurāṇa*:

Having swept around [the site], smeared it, scraped it, and turned over the soil, one should establish the fire, spread out a seat for the *brahmán* to the south, lead forward the water, and strew grass around it. Having placed the necessary items there, having prepared two strainers (*pavitra*) and consecrated the sprinkling-water (*prokṣaṇī*), and having again consecrated the sprinkling-water and placed the necessary items there, one should pour out the sprinkling-water, place the clarified butter (*ājya*) on the fire, perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagni-karaṇa*), heat the *sruva*-ladle, wipe it with *darbha* grass, sprinkle it, heat it again, and sprinkle it again. One should add the clarified butter, remove it from the fire, lift it up, purify it, inspect it, and take up the *kuśa* blades used as a support (*upayamana*) as before. Having added fuel-sticks and sprinkled water around the fire, one should offer the oblation. This same procedure applies wherever there is an oblation; the sweeping is done with the verse "Mā naḥ stokāḥ," and the smearing is performed with that [same verse].
Having scraped it with the formula, "Thee, the breaker of the enclosure," and having lifted it up with the formula, "Go to the fold; thee for the god," with the mantra *devasya tvā*.

Having sprinkled water around the fire with the mantra *ūrdhvā asya*, and having established the fire, he should place a fuel-stick upon the kindled fire with the mantra *samidhāgniṃ devasya tvā*. Having performed the sprinkling of the fire with the mantra *api gṛhṇāmi*, the Brahman priest should sit to the south with the *Hiraṇyagarbha* hymns, and the *praṇītā* waters to the north with the mantra *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. The spreading out of the *praṇītā* waters is performed with the mantra *kayā naścitraḥ*. The preparation of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is done with the mantra *pavitre stho vaiṣṇavyau savitre dveṣṭṛn*. Having heated the offering-ladle (*sruc*) with the mantra *trātāram*, he performs the wiping (*saṃmārjana*) with the mantra *aniśito ’si sa patrakṣit*. He performs the heating again with *pratyuṣṭa rakṣaḥ*. He heats it once more with *savitur vaḥ prasava utpunāmi*. The purification (*utpavana*) is performed with the mantra *tad evāgniḥ*. The sprinkling around (*paryukṣaṇa*) is done with the mantra *dhūsaro ’si*. The root-offerings (*mūlahoma*) are made with the oblation *prajāpataye svāhā*. In this manner, the Vedic fire becomes consecrated.
Thus, this sacrificial procedure, endowed with these characteristics,
was ordained for all sacrifices by Brahmā of immeasurable splendor.
Otherwise, those who perform [the rite] relying solely on the sūtra go there without hope; all the gods are certain of this.
Now, therefore, the deities of the ritual strewing are described.

For the sweeping, the Karapayas; for the smearing, the Viśvedevas; for the scraping, Mitra and Varuṇa; for the lifting up, the Earth; for the sprinkling, the Gandharvas; for the placing of the fire, Sarva; for the placing of the sacrificial fee, Brahmā; for the Praṇītā water on the north, the Ocean; for the setting aside of the materials, Śatakratu; for the binding of the strainers, the Pitṛs; for the consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, the Mothers; for the *juhū*, *sruc*, and *sruva* ladles, likewise Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; for the heating of the clarified butter, the Vasus; [71] for the placing upon the fire, Vaivasvata; for the circumambulation with fire, the Maruts; for the removal from the fire, Skanda; for the purifying and re-purifying, the Moon and Sun; for the inspection of the clarified butter, all the Directions; for the placement of the strainers, the goddess Umā; for the fuel, Lakṣmī; and for the entire rite, all beings.
O great sage, having understood the ritual procedure, one should take one of the aforementioned fires and perform the rite of oblation.
These deities have indeed been proclaimed for the benefit of the Brahmins in sacrifices involving animal offerings, as well as in all ritual acts.
Brahmā said: O best of kings, I shall describe the supreme procedure for the sacred fire, which brings ease to all ritual actions, according to its various names, distinctions, and rites.
The formal acceptance of the sacred fire (parigraha) must be performed by those who have mastered the meaning of all the scriptures,
as well as those who are experts in the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa Siddhāntas and have reached the further shore of their own Gṛhya-sūtras.
The fire must be maintained by those who desire all prosperity;
otherwise, it becomes an obstacle to their wealth and lifespan.
Whether one is chronically ill, unfortunate, or despised by all the world,
once he has understood that [reality] exactly as it is, the knower of it experiences every happiness.
Therefore, with every effort, the ritual for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) is considered essential;
I have thus described to you the eight types of fire-pits (kuṇḍa) along with their threefold divisions.

The ritual procedure may be of many kinds, or it may be performed with a single offering according to the circumstances; however, women, children, and śūdras should perform the oblation in accordance with their own conviction.
Neither in the assembly hall nor in the kitchen, nor ever in the sacrificial pit,
should one [speak] while protecting the fire by means of refined names and designations.
[71] Those who desire the results of ritual action should offer oblations while being skilled in the meaning of the great vidyās.
And it is heard, O child, that in ancient times, O son, one did so without knowing them.
But one who holds the refined language (Sanskrit) in high esteem shall suffer the loss of his kingdom;
likewise, Vāraṇihotra met his death after a long time.
Therefore, one who is unlearned should not offer oblations into an unstable fire;
I shall explain to you that knowledge by which accomplishment is produced.
O Madhusūdana,
Rudra, who is saluted by all the gods, resides in a square pit and a mandala, as well as in one shaped like a bow.
In a square mandala, Agni is present;
in a circle, he is Hutāśana; and in a half-moon, he is Anala—thus is Agni established.
The seven deities of the twice-born are the Preceptor, Yoga, the Divinity,
Udaka, the god Varuṇa, and the great serpents within the Darbha grass.
The Great Goddess resides in the *sruva* ladle, while the three-eyed God resides in the *sruk* ladle;
through their union, there arises the Supreme All, who is saluted by all the gods.

Know that the earth is the most excellent for great sacrifices within its own domain; know that meritorious rites are the best among virtuous acts, and the great ocean is the best among worthy recipients.
In the center of the altar stands Gāyatrī, composed of Sāman hymns;
in the fuel is Maṇibhadra, likewise holding a vajra as his crest-lock.
The Hotṛ priests should recognize the mountains in the cups and other vessels;
Rudra is the deity in the saline soil, and the winds are in the palm-leaf fan.
O Śaṅkara, all the mantras are in the feet; even the ashes are there. The world-protectors are in the corners, and all the deities are in the syllable Oṃ.
The Mothers reside in the portion of the oblation, while sparks such as the Putanas and others are present;
the Sun presides over the radiance, and at the time of dissolution, the Supreme God Śiva is the locus of absorption.
The morning oblation for the gods, performed at half a watch [after sunrise], bestows prosperity;
that for humans is at midday; and for the sake of liberation, it is performed during the three watches of the night.
In the afternoon, one should worship the ancestors; at twilight, the elemental deities;
at night, for the destruction of sins; and during the day, for the accomplishment of spiritual attainments.
It should be offered at the half-watch [of the day], and likewise the rectum at midnight;
O child, [the offering] at dawn bestows sons, and for the rectum, it fulfills all desires.

In rites for the attainment of all goals, such as those performed at auspicious moments (*kṣaṇa*), one should offer the first three oblations, with a minimum of three, to the deities presiding over those moments. This bestows the attainment of everything.
Otherwise, O Brahmin, that oblation becomes fruitless;
for the pleasure of Gauri, O bull among men, the homa must be performed using materials made of wood or clay.
And there is a tenfold increase in merit through offerings, ablutions,
and meals [performed] by those who bear the marks of the trident and lotus, and whose faces are auspicious with the conch and discus.
The wise one should take clarified butter, milk, meat-broth,
and other such substances for the sacrificial rite of installing the Goddess, which are empowered by the extraction of the *vasu* mantras.

The fire sacrifice (homa) must be performed with ritual substances; for otherwise, by not following the injunctions, those deities will grant you satisfaction and nourishment during the watches of the night.
And for the groups of mantras belonging to the Velās, there is a fruit in the Daivatage;
this has been told to you, O child, which brings happiness to all the worlds.
If the *hotṛ* priest is devoid of the mantras, he is always impure;
therefore, no oblation should be offered by those outside the Vedic fold into a consecrated fire.
For the Hotṛ priests who know the mantras indeed sacrifice to the deities;
but the Hotṛ priests who are ignorant of the Vedas do not at all gratify the gods.
From the fire-oblation, the attainment of all fruits arises for everyone;
therefore, by means of the ritual application of mantras, it bestows auspiciousness even at dawn.
In the east Agni is the deity; Viṣṇu is remembered as the deity in the south;
Brahmā is situated in the west—these indeed are the deities of the fires.
One should know Rudra as the presiding deity for splendor, or likewise for water-related matters;
however, for the longevity of ritual actions of Brahmins, Lakṣmī is the presiding deity therein.
When the oblation has been thus established, the three fires likewise,
the three gods, the three times, and the three fires abide as the three qualities.
The Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇāgni, and Āhavanīya—
these three, O best of the twice-born, have arisen from one and the same source, yet possess many divisions.

The four branches are those of the Śrīparṇī, Śucī, Vikaṅkata, and likewise Khadira, Aśvattha, Bilva, and so forth; the sacrificial ladles (sruk) and the like vary in length according to the hand and other measures.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be richly endowed with the circumference of a thumb and adorned with a water-pot (kumbhaka);
indeed, there are two lotuses (puṣkara), situated upon the central line.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be fashioned with handles that are well-proportioned and beautiful;
they should have a circumference of six finger-breadths and be constructed using the earth-measuring technique.
One should know that the bulbous base at the root is two finger-breadths wide;
the pill [of the vessel] should be known as one-third of that, while the opening is one-third of the pill.
The altar should be made seven finger-breadths high and fashioned with five colors;
it should have three equal furrows, and its tip should be six finger-breadths long, made of kuśa grass.
Adorned with the beauty of the shape of a cow’s ear, reaching to the hollow of the little finger,
it should be made so that clarified butter flows out when pressed by three barley grains.
Having thus fashioned the *sruva* and the *sruk*, the oblation performed with them brings happiness.
The lower fire-drill (*araṇī*) should be made from the heartwood of the *śamī* tree, measuring one cubit in length according to the span of the Goddess’s hand.
The middle part, rich with a span (vitasti) and a hand’s breadth (pāṇi), is sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) in length;
it is circular, provided with two hands, and grants a beautiful circumference of ten finger-breadths.
The head-ornament (āpīḍa) should be made very even, with a middle part pierced by iron;
for the purpose of the ghaṭikā and aṅkura-yāga, its measurement is one finger-breadth (śamā) using a hair-cord.
Having worshipped it with the fire-mantra, one should cause it to fall;
in its absence, one may use sun-crystals, or in their absence, those made from dried cow-dung.
One should bring it into a common chamber and place it in a copper vessel,
or in a bowl, an earthenware dish, a metal cup, or a sacrificial pit provided with worship.
One should construct the fire-wheel according to the ritual rules for all rites,
using gold, silver, copper, wood, stone, or even clay.

One should prepare vessels made of precious materials and marked with auspicious signs for the purpose of offering water (argha), food offerings (naivedya), and worship, as well as for the presentation of sacrificial oblations (bali). Thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the prescribed rules and ritual procedure.

Marīci: Fuel-sticks for oblations should be taken with their tips pointing eastward, being neither stunted nor split. In rites for specific desires, such as those for subjugation and the like, they should be the opposite for one who wishes to strike down an enemy.
Those that are shattered, split, withered, crooked, many-headed,
thin, long, thick, or infested by woodworms cause the destruction of the success of one's undertakings.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, following the word "fuel-stick" (*samit*), it is said:
[76] Those produced from *śamī*, *palāśa*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, and *vaikaṅkata*;
likewise the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *bilva*, *candana*, and *sarala*.
The *śāla*, the *devadāru*, and the *khadira*—these are the sacrificial woods, according to the ritualists.
In the *Chandopariśiṣṭa*, Kātyāyana states:
"The sacrificial fuel-stick (*samidh*) should never be thicker than a thumb;
it must not be stripped of its bark, nor infested with insects, nor split."
A fuel-stick used in fire-offering rituals by one who knows the tradition should not be longer than a span, nor shorter; it should not have two forks, nor should it have leaves attached.
Kātyāyana states in the Chandogapariśiṣṭa:
"An offering made with the hand consists of twelve mouthfuls; and that [offering] should be made into a fire that has no glowing embers and possesses clear flames."
The man who offers oblations into a fire that has no flames or whose coals are extinguished is born with a weak digestion, afflicted by disease, and indeed becomes poor.
Therefore, one should offer oblations only when the fire is well-kindled, and never otherwise,
if one desires health, long life, and ultimate prosperity.
Having offered oblations and having completed the sacrifice with the hands, winnowing baskets, ladles, and other implements,
[the author] now speaks of the forms of the deities, because those forms are to be worshipped during the vows concerning lunar days and so forth which will be described hereafter.
[This is stated] in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Vināyaka, however, should be made with the face of an elephant and four arms;
in his two right hands, there should be a lotus stalk and a rosary of beads.
O destroyer of enemies, a water-filled vessel and an axe should be placed to his left;
however, a tooth must not be depicted on his left side.
One foot should be placed upon a footstool while the other remains on the seat;
and when the water-vessel is full, one should cause the tips of his hands to touch it.
Likewise, O Yādava, Lambodara and Karṇa should be made;
he [Lambodara] wears a tiger-skin garment and has a snake as his sacred thread.
The pedestal for Gaṇeśa should be shaped like an elephant’s tusk.
Goddess Sarasvatī should be fashioned adorned with all ornaments;
she should be made four-armed and likewise standing upright.
She is risen up;
in her two right hands there should be a book and a rosary,
and likewise in her two left hands a flute and a water-pot should be depicted.
The lute is made of bamboo;
she should be established with feet together and have a gentle face—
thus is Sarasvatī.
O King, Lakṣmī should be fashioned near Hari with two arms,
wearing divine forms and garments, and adorned with all ornaments.
The goddess Gaurī, clad in white garments, peerless in beauty upon the earth, should be fashioned separately with four arms; the auspicious goddess is seated upon a lion-throne.
Seated upon a lion-throne, one should fashion a beautiful lotus with eight petals and a lovely pericarp; O highly fortunate one, she is situated within that pericarp.
The goddess should be depicted seated like Vināyaka, with large arms;
in her hand, a lotus with a thick stalk should be made, auspicious for her.
O best of the Yādavas, a bracelet should be placed at the edge on the right,
and likewise, O King, a jar of nectar and a beautiful necklace should be fashioned on the left.
And her two hands, O twice-born one, should be made holding a bilva fruit and a conch;
behind her, two elephants should be made carrying a water-pot.
And upon the head of the Goddess, a beautiful lotus should likewise be fashioned.
Lakṣmī: In the collection of [deities associated with] water— Śrī resides upon a lotus, holds a lotus in her hand, is bathed by a jar poured forth by an elephant,
wears a garland of lotuses, and possesses the form of Kālikā.
Śrī. In the Viśvakarmaśāstra: When Mahālakṣmī is to be represented in a site other than Kolāpura, she should then be fashioned like Lakṣmī, adorned with [her characteristic] forms and ornaments.
In his lower right hand he holds a bowl, and above it the Kaumodakī mace;
in his upper left hand he holds a shield, and in the hand below that, a bilva fruit.
Bearing a liṅga upon her head, she is to be worshipped for the sake of prosperity.
Mahālakṣmī. In the Viṣṇudharmottara: Bhadrakālī should be depicted as captivating with eighteen arms, standing in the ālīḍha posture upon a chariot drawn by four lions.
O Yādava, the rosary, the trident, the sword, and the moon must be fashioned,
as well as the arrow and the bow, and likewise the conch and the lotus.
Likewise, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be fashioned, as well as the water-pitcher;
the staff and the spear should be made, along with the black antelope skin and the sacrificial fire.
Among the hands of Bhadrakālī, one hand shall be beautiful and radiant;
and yet another, O highly fortunate one, shall hold a vessel of jewels.
Bhadrakālī. According to the Viśvakarma-śāstra, Caṇḍī is thus described: she is golden-hued and beautiful in form;
she has three eyes, is in the prime of youth, is wrathful, and is considered to be standing upright.
She had a slender waist, large eyes, and beautiful, full breasts;
she had one face, a handsome neck, and was endowed with twenty arms.
In his right hands, he holds a trident, a sword, a conch, a discus, arrows, a spear, a thunderbolt, as well as the gesture of fearlessness, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a small parasol.
Always auspicious, she holds, by means of the sequential order starting from the top,
a serpent-noose, a shield, an axe, a goad, and a bow.
In the left hands, he holds a bell, a banner, a mace, a mirror, and a mallet;
beneath him is a buffalo with its head severed and fallen.
A man with his hand raised holding a weapon,
stiff-necked, pierced by a trident, vomiting blood, with blood-stained eyebrows, head, hair, and eyes.
Being devoured by a lion, yet firmly bound by a noose around his neck;
with his right foot treading upon the lion and his left foot trampling the demon Ghasmari.
This [goddess] has a fierce, raised weapon and is the destroyer of all enemies without exception.
Pavī is the thunderbolt; [it is held] by Mahiṣa among the Asuras.
Caṇḍikā holds a spear, an arrow, a trident, a sword, and a discus in her right hands.
The lunar disc is below on the left, and a skull is above.
Bearing a trident and a discus, mounted upon a lion, and possessing ten arms—
this goddess is designated as Durgā, the deliverer from difficulties.
Digbhujā has ten arms;
she is Durgā, the goddess Nandā Bahavatī, born from the joy of Bhāradvāja.
And she has four arms, holding a boon-granting gesture, a noose, and a goad.
Nandā is fair-complexioned, mounted upon an elephant, and holds a sword, a shield, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness.
Ambā has the luster of a white water-lily and holds a noose, a lotus, and the gestures of fearlessness and protection.
The Mother should be fashioned with four arms, seated upon a lion, and bestowing all auspiciousness;
she holds a rosary and a lotus in her right hands, and carries a trident and a water-pot in her left.
Sarvamaṅgalā,
Ekavīṇā, Jayā, Karṇapūrā, Nagnā,
Kharasthitā, Vaṅgotthā, Karṇikākarṇī, and Tailābhyaktaśarīriṇī.
In her left foot she wears ornaments of iron thorns that shine;
pulling her hair upward, she increases [her stature] as the terrifying Kālarātri.
Kālarātri holds a conch, a head, and a sword in her hands on her left side;
in her right hand she holds a fruit and añjana; she is gracefully poised with her upper body and beautifully adorned.
Lalitā has a prominent nose, drooping lips, and sagging breasts and belly;
she is known as Ālohitā, the elder Lakṣmī, for the sake of prosperity.
Holding a blue lotus and the gesture of fearlessness, she has two arms and is praised by heroes.
Jyeṣṭhā is red and blue,
with her feet touching the ground; she touches the earth with both arms, has two arms, and is worshipped by heroes.
Nīlajyeṣṭhā is fair-complexioned and has the form of a maiden; meditated upon by the Maheśvaras,
she has two arms, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and always bestows prosperity.
She holds a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and a lotus, and below that, a water-pot;
or her form may be made with four arms, seated upon a lotus, and white in complexion.
Gaurī is dark-complexioned, large-eyed, with a face resembling milk and dawn;
she has two arms and holds a *liṅga*, armor, and a weapon in her right hands.
Seated upon a lion-throne, her hair adorned with pearl ornaments,
she is especially attended by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and other such beings.
And by the Indrarakṣasas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others,
the Goddess is also renowned as Bhūtamātā beneath the Aśvattha tree.
Bhūtamātā;
the goddess Surabhi, who has a cow’s face, is beautiful and adorned with all ornaments;
she holds a handful of fodder and a water-pot, bestowing prosperity and nourishment.
Surabhi is to be known as having two arms; she is seated upon a bed, very gentle, with eyes like buds, and holding a drinking vessel. She is thus described.
Yoganidrā: Now, therefore, O Jaya, I shall fully describe to you the forms of the Mothers.
Among them, Brāhmī has four faces, six arms, and is seated upon a swan.
Piṅgalā is adorned with ornaments and wears a deer skin as an upper garment;
she holds a sacrificial thread, a cord, and a wooden ladle in her three right hands in succession.
On the left, however, she holds a book and a water-pot, and bestows fearlessness;
Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull, has five faces, and three eyes.
White, with matted locks as white as the *indubara* flower, she bestows all happiness;
she has six arms, and among her right hands, she holds a rosary and a *ḍamaru* drum while granting boons.
That same goddess of great arms holds a trident, a bell, and the gesture of fear in her left hands;
Kaumārī shall be red in color, six-faced, and possessed of twelve eyes.
Ravibāhu is seated upon a peacock, bestows boons, and holds a spear;
she carries a banner, a staff, a bow, and an arrow in her right hands.
In her left hands she holds a bow, a bell, a lotus, and below that a sharp axe; beneath those, she displays the gesture of fearlessness.
Vaiṣṇavī is mounted upon Tārkṣya, dark-complexioned, six-armed, and adorned with a garland of forest flowers;
she bestows boons and holds a mace in her right hands, as well as a lotus garland.
Holding a conch, a discus, and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, she is this Vārāhī with radiant arms,
dark-complexioned, boar-faced, and pot-bellied.

She is the bestower of boons, always holding a staff and a sword in her right hands, while in her left she holds a shield, a noose, and displays the gesture of fearlessness; thus she shines with her resplendent arms.
Aindrī has a thousand eyes, is gentle, golden-hued, and seated upon an elephant;
she bestows boons, holds a thread, and carries a thunderbolt raised upward in her right hand.

In her left [hand] she holds a water-pot and a vessel, while below that hand is the gesture of fearlessness; Cāmuṇḍā rides upon a corpse, is red in color, has a distorted face, and is adorned with snakes.
Daṃṣṭrāgra, Kṣīṇadehā, Gartākṣī, Bhīmarūpiṇī,
Digbāhu, Kṣāmakukṣi, Muśala, Kavaca, and Śara.
Holding a goad and a sword in her right hands,
she holds a shield, a noose, a bow, a staff, and an axe in her left hands.
Caṇḍīkā should be white in color, mounted upon a corpse, and possess six arms;
she has matted hair, three round eyes, bestows boons, and holds a trident.
Holding a pericarp in her right hand, and from that [hand] a drinking vessel and the gesture of fearlessness—
thus has the Mother been described according to the arrangement of her various forms.
Thus ends the description of the forms of the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī.
The Mothers beginning with Gaurī, however, are described in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā..."
Devamātā, Svadhā, Svāhā, and likewise other Mothers of the World (Lokamātṛkā).
Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi, together with Ātmadevatā,
should be worshipped either in a painting or in an image, with their hands granting boons and fearlessness.

The Nāndīmukha Mothers are to be worshipped in a place adorned with nine lotuses; Durgā herself is to be worshipped in her own form at the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the end, according to the sequence of the syllables of the nine principles (tattvas).
She has eighteen arms, one face, and full breasts and hips;
she is adorned with all ornaments and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
With their left hands, they hold a hair-tuft, a shield, a bell, a mirror, a threatening gesture, a bow, a banner, a hand-drum, and a noose.
Holding in her right hands a spear, a mallet, a trident, a thunderbolt, a conch, a goad, an arrow, and a discus.
These [goddesses] should be worshipped by high-souled ones desiring victory;
the remaining sixteen-armed ones are mere sticks without a target.
Rudracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā,
Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, and Aticaṇḍikā.
The ninth is Ugradaṇḍā, situated in the middle and resembling fire;
then Rocanā, Vāruṇā, Kṛṣṇā, Nīlā, Śuklā, and Dhūmrikā.
She should be known as yellow and pale-white, seated upon a lion within her nest; she stands upon a buffalo, holding weapons, grasping the hair on the head of a Daitya,
lotus-shaped, and stationed in a chariot— thus it is stated in the Skandayāmala.
Thus [is the description] of Navadurgā.
She stands in a circle, wears matted hair, and holds dice; she possesses a radiance equal to the flames of fire.
Terrible with a skull and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands, she is the Auspicious One who bestows auspicious fruits.
This [goddess] should be fashioned with two arms and one face by the wise man.
Vāmā is pale-red in hue, holding a vessel of eight sacrificial cakes;
she is fierce, the great Brālā for prosperity, the slayer of enemies, and the first-born of Śeṣa.
Jyeṣṭhā is clad in red garments and is likewise fierce; she holds a skull-cup and a chowrie in her hands.
She should be known as following the previous [deity], with a black face and very terrifying.
Raudrī is dark blue like a rain-cloud; thereafter Kālī, whose face has the luster of copper-red,
should be known as the destroyer of fear, holding a skull at her ear with her hand.
[86] Kālī,
the great goddess who is blue and white, whose ears are distorted, and who is preceded by Kalapūrvikā;
she holds a skull and a spear in her hands, removes fear, and bestows auspiciousness.
Kalavikarṇī is brown-hued, large-eyed, and wears a garland of skulls; she bestows peace for the sake of prosperity, and as Vikarṇikā, she is full of power.
Balavikarṇikā has a coppery luster and is white in color; Balapramathanī is auspicious.
This [goddess] holds a skull and a noose, and she brings about the destruction of all enemies.
Balapramathanī;
Jayā, who has the luster of the finest flowers, possesses fangs, and has a large belly;
she holds a skull and a vajra, is the subduer of spirits, and is foremost among all.
The subduer of all beings,
with a complexion of dark blue, copper, and crimson, large-faced, and transcending the mind;
bearing a skull and a sword, she increases the fear of enemies for the sake of prosperity.
From the *Viśvakarma-śāstra* regarding Manonmanī:
"She should hold a rosary and a water-pot at the center of her chest with palms joined in *añjali*,
and she should bear a dark complexion while standing in the midst of the five sacrificial fires."
Kṛṣṇā holds a rosary, a lotus, a mirror, and a water-pot in her hands; she is Umā, who is worshipped even by the gods.
Umā [beheld] the rosary, Śiva, the presiding lord of the hosts of gods, the water-pot,
and two fire-pits at his sides; Pārvatī was born from the mountain.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, Pārvatī is described as follows:
"She became a woman with a slender waist and large eyes, resembling crushed collyrium, her beautiful face marked by fangs."
Adorned with four arms holding a sword, a bowl, a severed head, and a shield,
she wears a necklace of headless trunks and bears a garland of heads.
Mahākālī is indeed Śivarātri, according to the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Lambodarī should be depicted with red garments and breasts,
holding a trident in her hand, highly auspicious, and likewise having weapons in her arms."
The goddess Vāruṇī should be made very beautiful, turbid with cotton,
with large nails, and likewise with many arms.
Cāmuṇḍā has indeed been described as the one who brings all sentient beings under her control.
Vāruṇī is Cāmuṇḍā;
likewise she has a distressed face, is withered, and especially has a withered body.
The goddess possesses many arms and is entwined by serpents.
The formidable Śivadūtī should be depicted wearing a garland of skulls, bearing a khaṭvāṅga staff, and possessing an auspicious jackal-like face. [88]
O King, the goddess stands in the ālīḍha posture, four-armed,
holding a vessel of blood, as well as a sword and a trident.
But her fourth hand should likewise be made with meat;
thus says Śivadūtī in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"I shall describe the form of Kātyāyanī, who likewise has ten arms."
She was an imitator of the three gods, following them in their very likeness.
She was endowed with a mass of matted hair, marked by the crescent moon,
possessed three eyes, and had a face like the full moon.
Resembling the flax flower, well-established, with beautiful eyes,
endowed with fresh youth, and adorned with all ornaments.
Likewise, [he saw] Mahiṣāsura-mardini, who is beautiful to behold, with full and elevated breasts, and whose three parts are perfectly proportioned and situated.
One should place a trident, a sword, and likewise a discus on the right;
understand that a sharp arrow and a spear are on the left.
One should place the shield, the full vessel, the noose, and the goad,
as well as the bell, the axe, and the fly-whisk.
One should perceive a buffalo standing below, depicted as headless;
likewise, one should see a Dānava there, arisen from the severing of the head, with a sword in his hand.
Pierced in the heart by a spear, adorned with a horizontal girdle,
his limbs were stained deep red, and his eyes were wide with blood.
One should visualize the lion of the Goddess as being ensnared by the serpent-noose, its face terrifying with a frown, and its mouth vomiting blood.
Thus says Kātyāyanī. In the Mayadīpikā:
"Ambikā is mounted upon a lion, three-eyed, adorned, and bearing a mirror."

[The description] that she holds a mirror in her left hand and has the "boon-granting" (varada) gesture in her right is incorrect; for it is said that in the *Niśā-yuddha* [tantra], the "boon-granting" gesture is always considered common to all hands,
as is the "fearlessness" (abhaya) gesture.
She should be depicted with four arms, holding a sword and a shield in two [hands],
according to the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya* of Ambikā;
she has ten arms and three eyes, and holds weapons, a spear, a sword, and a drum.
Holding a bell and a shield in her right hand,
and a khaṭvāṅga staff and a trident in her left, the goddess is considered to be Yogeśvarī.

Such is the form of Yogeśvarī; another [form] may be of this same nature, but red in color and joined with a noose and a goad. If the one called Bhairavī is desired, she should be endowed with twelve arms.
From the *Viśvakarma-śāstra* of Bhairavī:
[90] Holding a water-pot and a rosary, bearing a thunderbolt and a goad,
seated upon an elephant, Rambhā is beautiful and the granter of all desires.
Regarding Rambhā, the Devīpurāṇa states:
"Śivā should be depicted seated upon a bull, three-eyed, with hands granting boons,
wearing two serpents, and bestowing the trident and the gesture of fearlessness."
For Śivā:
One should have Kīrti fashioned with a slender waist, seated upon a blue lotus,
her limbs adorned with all ornaments, and holding a water-pot and a lotus.
She whose fragrance was like that of wine and cooked rice, and who was adorned with ornaments of precious jewels.
Contentment is the goddess Siddhi, who should be visualized as bestowing boons and accomplished goals;
she has the fragrance of white sandalwood and is adorned with white lotuses.
The goddess Siddhi is seated upon a white throne and adorned by female door-keepers;
one should likewise cause Ṛddhi to be depicted as beautiful, seated in the paryanka posture.
[He saw her] with a mirror, light, and flowers, adorned with the dark mark of a tilaka,
enriched by the beauty of garlands and chowries, and always fond of the flute and lute.
Riddhi is to be depicted with a pleasant countenance, wearing a yogapaṭṭa as her upper garment,
seated upon a lotus posture (padmāsana), and with one hand raised in the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā).
Equipped with a trident and a girdle, she is tranquil and established in yoga.
Kṣamā is indeed well-established; she should be fashioned as Vaiṣṇavī, holding a sword, a discus, a mace, and a lotus,
adorned with a garland of forest flowers, wearing yellow garments, and beautifully radiant.
[91] Vaiṣṇavī; Aindrī, the presiding deity of the best of gods, seated upon the king of elephants,
the goddess holding a thunderbolt and a goad, adorned with necklaces and armlets.
The Aindrī and the Vaivasvatī are to be fashioned; Durdharā stands upon a buffalo,
with the face of a boar, drinking blood from a skull-cup and holding a staff.
She belongs to Yama;
she should be made preeminent in brilliance, radiant, and seated upon the moon-throne.
She is radiant; she should be depicted as lovely Rati, resplendent with ornaments suited to the spring season, dancing, auspicious, and endowed with all her divine jewelry.
She was habituated to playing the lute, anointed with musk and camphor,
holding a staff and a rosary, established in her vows, and absorbed in yoga.
Rati is white, resembling the full moon, and seated upon a white lotus.
Śvetā is to be made auspicious and very auspicious, seated upon a throne;
she holds a blue lotus and a fruit in her hands, and carries a trident, a thread, and a rosary.
The auspicious goddess is seated upon a lion throne, adorned with a crown of matted locks;
she holds a trident and a rosary, and displays the gestures of granting boons and dispelling fear while wielding a bow.
Śivā holds a mirror, an arrow, a club, a sword, and the moon;
she is beautiful, endowed with auspicious marks, possessed of lovely breasts, and sweet-spoken.
Her limbs are adorned with every ornament, and she is seated upon a throne of universal splendor.
One should worship Maṅgalā, as well as Jayā and Vijayā, who bear the trident and lotus seeds,
are ready to grant boons, are seated upon a lion, and are the accomplishers of all rites.
Vijayā;
Kālī, who has the form of a hand-drum and holds aloft a fierce noose—she is Kālī. [92]
Ghaṇṭākarṇī should be fashioned holding a bell and a trident;
Ghaṇṭākarṇī. Jayantī, the beautiful one, should be made holding a spear, a trident, and a sword.
And she, with her hand occupied by a shield, should be worshipped by those endowed with auspiciousness.
O great sage, when the goddess Diti, honored by the Daityas, is to be worshipped on Jayantī,
she should be visualized seated on a staff-throne (daṇḍāsana), auspicious and adorned with all ornaments.
Her hand holds a blue lotus, and she is adorned with a child on her lap.
Diti is free from anger; the goddess Ruṇḍhatī wears white garments and stands upon a wheel,
holding leaves, flowers, and water in her hands, and is beautifully anointed with sandalwood paste.
Arundhatī and Aparājitā should also be fashioned, both of great strength and mounted upon lions; Arundhatī holds a Pināka bow in her hand, while Aparājitā carries a sword and a shield.
She has three eyes, bears a mass of matted hair adorned with the moon, and wears Vāsuki as a bracelet.
Aparājitā and Kaumārī should also be fashioned; [the former] seated upon a peacock and bearing a spear,
while [the latter] has the form of Kāla, holds a triple staff, wears red garlands, and is accompanied by a cock.
In the *Kaumārī-mayadīpikā*, there are sixty-four forms of the *rogiṇīs*:
"One should fashion [the goddess] Vajrasthā in the south, holding the gesture of fearlessness and then holding a shield; she should be adorned with golden ornaments and seated upon an elephant."
Akṣobhyā (1).
Akṣakarṇī, however, has a fair complexion; she holds a conch, an arrow, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
O gentle one, she holds a bow and a skull-cup, stands upon a bear, and is poised with her index finger raised in the *tarjanī* gesture.
Ṛkṣakarṇī (2):
The Rākṣasī Hemavarṇā should have beautiful limbs and be mounted upon a bull;
she holds an axe and a thunderbolt in her right hands, and is endowed with a noose and a goad in her left.
The Rākṣasī Kṣapaṇā,
who has the shade of a Campaka tree, holds a mallet and a goad in her right hands,
and a skull-cup and a fruit in her left; she is seated upon the bones of a forest thicket.
Kṣapaṇā (4):
Kṣayā is established in the form of a tortoise; she is Gaurī, engaged in recitation, and accompanied by a water-pot.
She holds a skull and a lump of food in her left hands and is adorned with all ornaments. || 5 ||
She has tawny eyes, a brownish complexion, and three eyes;
she is mounted on a horse, holds a silken noose in her right hand, and carries a goad and a shield in her left hands.
Piṅgākṣī (6):
She is of inexhaustible [merit], golden-hued, with beautiful limbs, and seated upon a wolf;
she holds an axe and a sword in her right hands, and is endowed with a noose and a goad in her left.
[94] Akṣayā is yellow; she holds a skull-bowl, a spear, and a bow in her hands.
In the southern direction, she holds a hand-drum and a trident, carries a bladder, and is seated upon a deer.
Kṣayā (8):
holding a spear and a sword, three-eyed, carrying a shield, a noose, and a skull-cup;
she is red, stands outside, and is a young girl playing with fires.
Vālā (9): Līlā is red in color, adorned with a victorious lotus in her right hand; she holds a spear and a noose in her left hands, and bears the half-moon and a lotus.
(10) Līlā:
Jayā, red in color and mounted upon a bull, stands in the south;
she holds a staff and a sword in her right hands, while in her left she carries a pair of scissors and a half-moon, with a ball of rice attached to her index finger.
(11) [The goddess] Layā; [the goddess] Kartarī; [the goddess] Mārjanī; in the south, Samyā; Piḍanakaṅkarā;
and Lolā Sāradā, who holds a trident joined with a human corpse in her two hands.
The restless one (12).
On the left is a head of a buffalo, and Raktikā drinks its blood;
Laṅkā stands upon the chest, devouring the flesh of Dhanam.
[95] Laṅkā; Triphalā, Śākakhoṭā, Āmodakāśī in the south; Śoṇā, Laṅkeśvarī, Kumbhā, and Ḍimbhābhū, who bears the earth.
Laṅkeśvarī (14):
She holds a boon-granting wheel in her right hand and a bracelet on her left hand;
she stands upon a boar, is red in color, and is considered to be intensely longing for raw flesh.
Lālasā (15):
Standing on a leopard, she is stainless and red, adorned with ornaments and three eyes;
in her right hand she holds a knife and a jar, and in her left a noose and a skull-cup.
Vimalā (16):
Kṛṣṇā is stationed on the fire-altar; Jvālinī is auspicious on the right;
on the left, however, she should have her hand in the gesture of fearlessness and be provided with a vessel of clarified butter.
Hutāśanā (17):

Śūkarāsyā has wide eyes; she holds [a skull] at the three junctions [of the day], and in her left hand she holds a bell, while in her right she holds a small knife and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
Viśālākṣī (18):
She should have the sound "huṃ" as her mantra; she has the face of a fish and holds a rosary of beads.
In her left hand she carries a pestle, while in her right she holds fruit and sprouts.
Huṅkārā (19):
Vaḍavāmukhī, bearing two children on her limbs, sits upon a couch;
she holds a fish and a tortoise on her right side, because she wears dark blue garments.
Vaḍavāmukhī (20):
In the north, she holds the gesture of fearlessness with her index finger; in the south, she carries a staff and a skull-cup.
She is dark-complexioned, makes the sound "hā hā," is cruel, and is mounted upon a donkey.

Hāhāravā (21): she has the face of a buffalo, stands upon a buffalo, is exceedingly cruel, and is black. In her left hand she holds a noose and a *melā* flower; in her right, a staff and a writing brush.
Mahākrūrā (22):
Asitā, wrathful, is in the south, devouring a ball of meat;
Vidyujjihvā, cruel, is on the left, while Sīrakapālinī is on the right.
Standing upon a wheel, she carries wine in her ear; she is seated upon a jackal.
Krodhanā (23). Kṛṣṇā, Bhayānanā, Gṛdhrī, Daṃṣṭrogrā, and Asthibhūṣaṇā;
in the southern direction there should be Śikhara, Śūla, Gharghara, and Lelihāna.
Bhayānanā (24):

Carrying a trident on her back, she holds a skull-cup and a *ḍamaru* drum in her left hands, and with two [right] hands she holds a vessel; she rides upon a corpse, is all-knowing, and is white in color.
Sarvajñā (25):
Having placed her hands upon her knees, she rises and trembles;
holding a trident and a *ḍamaru* drum in her hands, Godhāṅgataralā is white.
[97] Taralā (26): Tārā is endowed with the qualities of crossing over; she is white and resides in the north-west.
She holds a trident and a mallet on her gentle left side, and something else on the other.
Tārā (27):
She is black, seated upon a lotus; in her right hands she holds the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*) and a rosary; in her left hands she holds the *Ṛgveda*, a book, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
Kṛṣṇā (28):
Raudrā is black, horse-faced, seated upon a headless torso, and has the face of a horse;
she holds a skull and a winnowing basket in her left hands, and bears the mark of Saṃhārikā on her right.
Hayānanā (29):
with severed hands, dragging corpses, essential, stout, and wearing matted hair;
she then holds a skull-topped staff and a hand-drum in her gentle [aspect], and thereafter a trident and a torch.
Standing upon a corpse, she gathers the essences; she dances, has matted hair, and is white.
She carries grain-baskets, wheels, and skeletons, and is clothed in skin.
The youngest [consort] is the Śabarāli, who holds the essence (rasa), is devoted to the gods and the twice-born,
and carries a sword with her left hand resting on her lap, directed toward those who bear torches.
[98] Śabarā (31):
Having the luster of crystal, seated upon Garuḍa, and very beautiful, she has a palate and tongue;
with the tips of her hands holding a conch and a shield, she bears a svastika and a sword in the southern direction.
Tālujihvikā (32):
She has red eyes, is mounted upon a vehicle, drinks blood, and possesses the luster of the moon;
she holds a mace and a sword in her right hands, and carries a noose and a skull-cup in her left.
Raktākṣī (33): Vidyujjihvā is white and fierce; she holds a plow and a skull-cup in her left hand, and she holds a wheel, a bell, and a chisel in her right hand.
Vidyujjihvā (34), Grāhasthā, Cāmarachatrabhṛt, she who is joined with two leather bags,
Kumbhapāśadharā, Śvetā, Krodhaputrā, and Karaṅkinī.
Karaṅkiṇī (35);
Meghanādā, however, has the luster of the moon and carries a sword and a shield;
she is surrounded by lattices, mounted upon a cloud, and resembles a circle of lightning.
Meghanādā (36) is fierce and terrible, situated upon a crocodile; she should be in the south, bearing the fruit of the *kartarī*.
Elsewhere, she holds a skull and a severed head; she is the slayer of enemies and possesses the luster of crystal.
Pracaṇḍogrā (37) is fierce, seated upon a white bull, and terrible; she holds a rosary of rudrākṣa beads. She is world-renowned as Kālakarṇī, adorned with earrings of black iron.
Kālakarṇī (38) holds a pair of scissors; Śvetā grants fearlessness and bestows boons in the south,
as she is mounted upon a cat and holds a vessel full to the brim.
Varadā (39):
Gaurī stands with a candrahāsa sword; she has four faces and holds in her two pairs of arms, respectively, a water-pot and a goad, as well as a rosary of mantras and a sacrificial ladle.

Candravālī is golden-hued and seated upon a golden lion-throne; she holds a rosary and a garland in her right hands, while in the remaining [left] hands she bears a lotus and a banner. Candrāvalī (41): She who is endowed with a garland of fruits, from whom [proceed] those who bear spears and water-pots in the south; she possesses a golden garland, is manifold in her manifestation, is fair-complexioned, and is the manifestor of the universe. (42)
A fair-limbed woman with the face of a monkey, bearing the name Markaṭasthāpraśākhā on her two hands, joyfully eats a mango fruit.
Prapañcikā (43):
Picuvaktrā, Mṛgavyālī, and Piṅgākṣī are situated between the southern and northern [directions],
and they are equipped with a bhindipāla and a shield, as well as a noose and a sword.
[100] Picuvaktrā (44),
Kākāsyā, Śyenagā, Gaurī, Piśācī, and Raktamaṇḍitā;
Kaṅkālakartarī, who bears a sword, [is located] between the southern and northern [directions].
The Piśācī (45): She holds a cotton-fruit in her left hand and carries a sword as a weapon;
she stands upon a sword, is brownish in color, a consumer of flesh, and extremely emaciated.
The flesh-eater (46),
dancing, greedy, corpulent, and mounted upon a donkey, stands between the southern and northern [directions],
bearing a sword, a hand-drum, a knife, and a noose.
Lolupā (47);
Vamanī shall be situated in Puṣpaka, accompanied by the host of Yakṣas;
she holds a mace and a spear, and is gentle; thereafter [is] Sthūlatomarīṇī.
Vamanī (48), Tapanī, Sarpagā, Gaurī, Varāṅgī, and Pannagānanā—
she who has a fierce form, with her hands placed upon the coils of these two [serpents] at her own ears.
Tapanī (49):
She is yellow in color, possesses large breasts, and is short in stature;
she holds an axe and a club in her left hands, and then a rosary and a jackfruit.
[101] Vāmanī (50): She has the face of a boar pierced by a spear, her body is dragged by a lion, she possesses two tongues, and her faces are distorted in four ways. || 51 ||
Śaṅkhapūraṇikā holds two conchs; Vṛkābhayadharā holds two [weapons] in two [hands];
Dvisiṃharathasaṃsthā should be [yellow] like a palmyra fruit; and Vāyuvegikā is [blue] like the wind.
Established in Bhāsa, she has a large belly; in Saumya, she carries a skull and a severed head;
in Gaurī, she is massive-bodied; and in Śaurya, she is a devourer of elephant-hide garments.
(53) Bṛhatkukṣi; the camel-riding Gaurī is deformed and has a face distorted by eating raw flesh;
she holds a quiver and a hand-drum in the southern direction, and a sword and a severed head in the northern direction.
Vikṛtā (54):
She holds a shield and a sword in her left hands, and from there she holds a mace, a discus, and a sword;
she wears a garland of forest flowers, is yellow in color, and stands upon Tārkṣya in her universal form.
Viśvarūpikā (55). Holding a pestle, a mallet, an axe,
and a noose, Yamajihvā should be depicted as fierce and mounted upon a buffalo.
Yamajihvā (56):
White, dancing, moving on a donkey, she stands in the southern direction holding a hand-drum and cotton;
