on the mountain of the Daityas, she is fierce with a severed head, and in her two left hands she holds Jayantī.
[102] Jayantī (57):
Mounted upon a dog, invincible, white, fierce, surrounded by hosts of spirits,
with sword and spear raised in her hands, she dwells in difficult forests.
Durjayā (58):
She who repeatedly holds a spear and an arrow in her right arms toward the southern and northern directions,
and a bow and a javelin in her left hands.
Yamāṅkikā (59):
Yamāntikā, who has an extremely terrible mouth and is the color of milk, stands upon a cart;
and Viḍālī, who stands upon a cat, should be white with eyes like those of a cat.
Bilālinī (60): Carrying a quiver, a skull-topped staff, a trident, and a chisel in her left hands, Revatī is emaciated, fierce with the face of a Piśāca, and holds a skull-cup.

Revatī (61): Pūtanā, who resembles a cauldron, has three eyes and a distorted face; she stands upon a corpse, holding a granary-staff in her left hand, and carrying a skull-topped staff and a skull-bowl.
Pūtanā (62):
Holding a scissor and a trident, she is on the southern side; on the left is Muṇḍakapālinī.
White in color and mounted upon a bull, Vijayā bestows victory.
Vijayantikā (63). From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The wise man should have an image of the god Brahmā made, who is gentle and four-armed."
Seated in the bound lotus posture, joyful, and likewise clothed in a black antelope skin.
He wears matted locks, has four arms, and is seated upon a chariot drawn by seven swans;
one pair of his arms should have the other hand placed upon the left thigh.
In this right hand is a beautiful rosary, and in the second [hand] a water-pot; he wears all the ornaments.

O King, one should have the deity fashioned for worship, in a painting, or for the laying of a foundation— with a face endowed with all the auspicious marks, possessing the form of tranquility, with eyes closed in meditation, and with a luster like the tip of a lotus petal.
Brahmā:
Brahmā, seated upon a lotus-leaf throne, should be depicted with four faces;
likewise, Sāvitrī should be made to occupy his left lap.

In the Ādityapurāṇa: "Having the color of the sun, knowing the Dharma, and likewise holding a rosary in her hand—her form should be made as previously described; such is the other form of the Lord of the World."
Prajāpati [is as follows]:
on the swan-vehicle, he should be made with one face, and not four-faced;
the other form called Brahmā, which is entirely Prajāpati, should be made.
Holding a rosary, a book, a lotus,
and a water-pot, Sāvitrī, endowed with four powers, is beneficial in the homes of those learned in the Vedas.
[104] The world-protector Brahmā is to be fashioned; the lord Viśvakarman, however, should be made assuming the form of a deity,
with two arms, holding tongs in his hand, possessing a great embodiment of splendor.
Viśvakarman:
Dharma should be depicted by the wise as having four faces, four feet, and four arms; he wears white garments, is adorned with all ornaments, and is white in color.
In his right hand there is a rosary, and in his left a book;
the personified Embodiment of Resolve (Vyavasāya) should be depicted on the right side.
Then, on the left side, a bull of supreme beauty should be made;
likewise, their two hands should be placed upon the head with palms marked by lotuses.
Dharma [is derived] from the Viśvakarmaśāstra.
The Ṛgveda should be white in color, two-armed, with the face of a donkey;
he holds a rosary, is gentle, pleased, and intent upon study.
The Rigveda has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus; the Samaveda is horse-faced,
depicted as holding a rosary in his right hand and a conch in his left.
The Sāmaveda has a goat for its face and is yellow in color; the Yajurveda holds a rosary of beads.
With a thunderbolt in his left hand, he is the bestower of prosperity and the granter of auspiciousness.
The Yajurveda;
the Atharvaveda, white in color with a monkey's face,
holding a rosary and a skull-topped staff— this one is fond of victory.
The Atharvaveda: Śikṣā is auspicious, bestowing beauty and fearlessness, endowed with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā),
holding a rosary and a water-pot (kuṇḍikā), two-armed, and bearing a staff and a lotus.
Śikṣā: Kalpa is radiant like a white water-lily, with a face like a crow, and a large belly;
he holds a staff and a water-pot, stands upon a lotus, and is adorned with a girdle and earrings.
The ritual manual states: The white grammar [Vaiśravaṇa] is to be known as having the face of a peacock and a protruding belly;
he is divine, endowed with a lute and a water-jar, and adorned with celestial garments.
Regarding the description [of Vyākaraṇa]: it should be as stainless and peaceful as the moon, with the face of a crane, a slender belly,
a noose and a lotus in its hands, and holding a rosary and a book.
The Nirukta has been determined; now the Vedic meters are being determined.
The Nirukta:
The wise one should know that the meter resembles a hibiscus flower;
it has the face of a cakora bird, possesses a japā-rod (China rose) color, bears a spear, and is endowed with a crest.
Adorned with earrings made of iron and earrings fashioned from coral.
Chanda holds in his right and left hands a rosary of lotus seeds, auspicious, resembling an *indragopa* insect, and shaped like a cat's face, as well as a *jyotiṣa* gem.
Jyotiṣa;
the supreme Mīmāṃsā-śāstra with a luster like the brilliance of the moon;
holding a rosary of beads in his right hand and a jar filled with nectar in his [other] hand.
Mīmāṃsā is like the flax flower; Nyāya should be known by the wise as having the face of a lion, holding a thread in his right hand and a banner in his left hand.
The Nyāya [deity] is white, wears a turban, has the face of a blue jay, and sits upon a lotus throne. He holds a string of pearls in his right hand, while his left hand holds a balance scale.
The Dharmaśāstra is like the hue of a campaka flower; it has four petals and the face of a parrot.
It should be known as having three rosaries and adorned with various ornaments.
Itihāsa has the luster of a lotus, a boar’s face, and a large belly;
he holds a rosary and a jar, and is adorned with lotus ornaments.
[107] Itihāsa: yellow in color, possessing a lute, with a face like that of a cuckoo and a large body;
he wears a garland of jewels, and his matted locks are adorned with mantras.
The science of archery (Dhanurveda) is yellowish like turmeric; he has the face of a monkey and large eyes,
and holding a rosary and a jar of nectar, he bestows perfect health.
Āyurveda; and the white, beautiful Nṛtyaśāstra, who has the face of a deer, wears matted hair,
and bears a rosary, a trident, and has three eyes.
The *Nṛtyaśāstra*:
The scripture known as the *Pañcaśāstra* is white and has the face of a bull;
it holds a rosary and a plow, and is adorned with a forest garland.
The Five Treatises:
the Pāśupata scripture is radiant, with the face of a serpent and a slender belly;
it is formidable, holding a staff and a vessel, and is clothed in a tiger skin.
The Pāśupata [form] is red, known as Pātañjala, with a serpent face and great luster;
it wears earrings and is tearing apart a snake and a rosary.

[108] A *pṛdāku* is a serpent. The *Pātañjala* [is as follows]: Sāṅkhya is that which belongs to Kapila; it is tawny-brown, with a prominent belly, long, bearing a rosary and a staff, and possessing long nails, hair, and matted locks.
The Sāṅkhya system; the Arthaśāstra shall be white; the auspicious Sārikā-candana;
holding a rosary, fruit, food, and a water-pot.
The science of polity (arthaśāstra) is a branch of knowledge (vidyā). 33.
From the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Brahmā is traditionally held to be the Ṛgveda; the Vasus are the Yajurveda;
likewise, Viṣṇu is the Sāmaveda, and Śambhu is the Atharvaveda."
The Kalpa is to be known as Prajāpati’s Śikṣā; Brahmā is proclaimed as Vyākaraṇa, and the Lord Varuṇa as Nirukta.
Chandas is Viṣṇu, and likewise Agni; the Lord Ravi is Jyotiṣa;
Mīmāṃsā is the Lord Soma, and Nyāyamārga is Samīraṇa.
Dharma, the Dharmaśāstras, the Purāṇas, and likewise Manu;
Itihāsa, Prajādhyakṣa, the Dhanurveda, and Śatakratu.
Likewise, the Lord Dhanvantari is the personification of Āyurveda;
the Goddess Earth is the science of arts (Kalāveda), and Maheśvara is the science of dance (Nṛtyaśāstra).
Saṅkarṣaṇa [revealed] the Pañcarātra, Rudra likewise the Pāśupata,
Ananta the Pātañjala, and the sage Kapila [revealed] the Sāṅkhya along with its auxiliary branches.
He who knows the science of wealth is proclaimed as the Knower of the Banner of Wealth; he who knows all the arts is Kāmadeva, the Teacher of the World.
Whatever other scriptures and whatever rituals they proclaim, that alone is their deity; the scripture and the ritual are like a god to them.
The presiding deities: Now, regarding the forms of the sages in the *Nayasaṃgraha*:
they are indifferent, wearing sacred threads, carrying water-pots and rosaries; with matted hair and beards, they are peaceful, seated and intent on meditation.
The seven ṛṣis— Vasiṣṭha accompanied by his wife Karyā,
Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Kaśyapa, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, and Atri— [flourished] during the Vaivasvata interval.
The sages: Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.
Ten sages with matted hair and beards, peaceful, emaciated, and covered in dust,
holding safflower and rosaries, should be depicted with two arms.
Nārada, the celestial Gandharva, bearing a rosary and a water-pot,
is indeed to be served with his lute cradled in the crook of his left arm.
Of Nārada; from the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*; the sages; Agastya:
"Having caused it to be fashioned out of gold by nature, one should adorn it according to one's means."
Having the form of a man, tranquil, and wearing beautiful matted locks.
With a water-pot in hand, surrounded by disciples and deer, the excellent sage held darbha grass in his hand; he was the conqueror of death and the endurer of all things.
Of Agastya:
the deities named Bhṛgu are to be fashioned in the form of Śakra;
likewise Bhuvana, Bhāvana, Sujanya, and Sujana.
Kratu, Svaḥ, Svasṛ, Nāman, Vyaja, and likewise Vyaṃuna;
Prasava, Avyaya, and Dakṣa as the twelfth.
The twelve gods worthy of sacrifice are designated as the Bhṛgus.
The Bṛgu-s should be made as the form of living beings, and likewise the Aṅgiras-s as the gods;
[the others are] Ātman, Abhi, Āyu, Manas, Dakṣa, Pada, and Prāṇa.
Haviṣya, Gaviṣṭha, Ṛta, Satya, and Tejas.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara* by Aṅgiras:
One should likewise have the God of gods, Viṣṇu, fashioned as seated upon Garuḍa,
his chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, and wearing all ornaments.
He should likewise have four faces, which are like water-laden clouds and possess a beautiful luster, and eight arms, adorned with divine yellow garments.
The face on the east is like the gentle moon, the southern is that of Narasimha,
the western face is tawny, and the excellent one on the west is that of Varaha.
In his right hands, he holds a rising sun, a mace, the gesture of fearlessness, a shield, a plow, and a boon-granting hand;
and in his left, he wears a garland of forest flowers.
O knower of dharma, the activities of Viṣṇu [should be assigned] to the left hands in successive order.
The sun is the discus and the moon is the conch;
he is Viṣṇu, the Lord who has one face and two arms, bearing the mace and the discus.
Lokapālaviṣṇu has one face and four arms; he is of gentle form, beautiful to behold,
clad in yellow garments, cloud-like in hue, and adorned with all ornaments.
The neck shone with its auspicious region, resembling a conch shell,
adorned with excellent ornaments and graced by exquisite earrings.
Wearing armlets and bound bracelets, adorned with a forest garland,
he bore the Kaustubha gem upon his chest and likewise a crown upon his head.
His head should likewise be fashioned with a beautiful lotus-shaped crown;
he has full, well-knit, and long arms, and his body is slender with copper-colored nails and fingers.
The Earth, assuming the form of a woman, should be made to stand between his feet, her waist beautifully adorned with the three folds of skin.
The god Janārdana should be depicted with his two feet placed upon that [object],
his steps set at intervals of one tāla, and his right foot slightly extended.
The earth should be gazed upon with wonder at what has been shown by the god;
and the god should be made to appear as if reaching down to the knees with his garment tied around his waist.
A forest garland (vanamālā) should be fashioned reaching down to the knees of the deity;
a sacred thread (yajñopavīta) should be fashioned reaching as far as the region of the navel.
One should place a full-blown lotus in the right hand of the deity;
the conch held in the left hand should be fashioned in the shape of a conch.
To the south, however, was the goddess Gadā, slender-waisted and fair-eyed;
she assumed the form of a woman, charming and adorned with every ornament.
Beholding the Lord of the gods, she should hold a chowrie;
she should place that right hand of the god upon his head.
On the left side, Cakra should likewise be made with a protruding belly,
adorned with all ornaments, and with wide-open, rolling eyes.
He should be depicted with a fly-whisk in hand, intent on gazing at the god;
and Rāma, making the gesture of a deity, should be placed upon his head.
Vasudeva said:
"The Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa should be fashioned in the form of Vāsudeva;
however, that best of the Yadus should be made with a white body and blue garments."
In the place of the mace, a pestle should be made, and in the place of the discus, a plow;
however, in the middle of the body, they should be fashioned in human form, endowed with beautiful features.
Saṅkarṣaṇa;
and Pradyumna likewise exists in the form of Vāsudeva.
He (Pradyumna) is prescribed as being dark like a blade of dūrvā grass and clad in white garments.
In the place of the discus there should be a bow, and likewise in the place of the mace, an arrow;
those two should be fashioned in such a way that they resemble a pestle and a plough.
Pradyumna said:
"One should likewise fashion the form of Aniruddha with a body having the luster of a lotus petal and wearing red garments."
In the place of the discus there should be a shield, and in the place of the mace there should indeed be a sword;
the shield may take the form of a discus, and a long sword is prescribed [for the other].
O Yādava, one should first clearly show the beautiful forms of the weapons, such as the discus and others, in their true nature.
O King, the excellent banners of the gods should be placed on the left side,
mounted upon poles and adorned with beautiful streamers, just as has been prescribed.
Aniruddha [states], according to the Viśvakarma-śāstra:
"Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa should be fashioned together, possessing divine forms;
the form of the Lord is situated on the right, while the form of Lakṣmī is on the left."
Her right hand is placed against his neck, while her left hand holds a lotus;
the Lord’s left hand always rests upon the region of Lakṣmī’s belly.
Her every limb was perfectly formed, adorned with all ornaments;
her eyes, cheeks, and face were exquisite, and she was endowed with beauty and youth.
The auspicious Siddhi should be depicted standing nearby, holding a chowrie;
the vehicle should always be placed on the right side, situated below the deity.
Two men bearing conchs and discs should be placed before him—
dwarfish in stature, and adorned with necklaces, armlets, crowns, and jewels.

[114] Two lay devotees (upāsakas), whose nature was that of Brahmā and Śiva, stood near the Lord; they held their tongues and wore their meditation-bands (yogapaṭṭa), with their topknots bound and their hands joined in the añjali gesture.
Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa:
Seated upon a lotus throne, with his eyes slightly closed and his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose,
he rests upon a white lotus.
The left and right hands are turned upward and placed together;
on the sides of those two hands are a lotus and a great sword.
In his two raised hands are the Pāñcajanya conch and the Sudarśana discus;
he should be known as the Lord of Yoga, to be worshipped by yogins seeking liberation.
The Lord of Yoga. In the *Siddhārthasaṃhitā*:
"Vāsudeva is considered to bear the mace, conch, discus, and lotus;
Nārāyaṇa holds the lotus, conch, mace, and discus in sequence."
Mādhava bears the mace, the discus, as well as the conch and the lotus;
Puruṣottama likewise bears the discus, the lotus, the conch, and the mace.
Adhokṣaja bears the lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, the conch, and the discus;
Śaṅkarṣaṇa is traditionally described as bearing the mace, the conch, the lotus, and the discus.
Govinda bears the discus, the mace, the lotus, and the conch with his arms;
Viṣṇu likewise bears the mace, the lotus, the conch, and the discus.
Madhusūdana holds the discus, the conch, the lotus, and the mace;
Acyuta always bears the mace, the lotus, the discus, and the conch.
Upendra should bear the lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, the discus, and the conch.
Pradyumna is said to be the bearer of the discus, the conch, the mace, and the lotus.
Trivikrama bears the lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, the conch, and the discus;
Vāmana always carries the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Śrīdhara holds a lotus, a discus, a mace, and a conch with his arms;
Narasiṃha likewise bears a discus, a lotus, and a conch.
Janārdana holds the lotus, the Sudarśana discus, the conch, and the mace;
Aniruddha has arms resplendent with the discus, the mace, the conch, and the lotus.
Hṛṣīkeśa should hold a mace, a discus, a lotus, and a conch; Padmanābha likewise carries a conch, a lotus, a discus, and a mace.
Likewise, Dāmodara holds the lotus, the discus, the mace, and the conch;
and Hari likewise bears the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace.
Viṣṇu bears the conch, the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, and the discus;
these forms are to be known according to the sequence of the hands starting from the lower right.
The syllables beginning with *vā* and *su* are six each; these likewise serve as the bases for the twenty-four forms (*mūrti*) [of Viṣṇu]. In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The Haṃsa, the Matsya, and the Kūrma—these are the ones who assume those forms."
Janārdana, the God of gods, should be depicted with horns and fish.
The Fish and the Tortoise;
and Aniruddha as Sovereignty, and the Lord Hari as the Boar,
who by the power of sovereignty lifted up the earth with the tip of his tusk.
Alternatively, the Lord may be depicted as a boar, the best among men, standing upon Śeṣa;
and Śeṣa should be made four-armed, endowed with beautiful jewel-adorned hoods.
O Yādava, with eyes wide open in wonder and intent upon gazing at the god,
the plow and the pestle should be placed in his two hands.
One should assume the posture of a coiled serpent with palms joined in añjali;
standing in the ālīḍha stance, the Blessed One should be positioned behind him.
The auspicious Earth, in the form of a woman with two arms, is situated upon his left jewel; she should be worshipped by him with prostrations.
On the arm upon which the goddess Earth rests, there should be a conch;
his other hands should be made to hold a lotus, a discus, and a mace.
Alternatively, the Blessed One may appear with his hand raised in wrath at the severing of Hiraṇyākṣa’s head,
or as Sumukha, having rescued Hiraṇyākṣa from death.
The wise know Hiraṇyākṣa to be embodied powerlessness;
that crusher of enemies was cast out by power that is indestructible.
Alternatively, he should be made as a Nṛvarāha, situated in meditation like a mass of clouds;
or else he should be made with two arms, intent on offering the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍa).
In the form of a complete boar, standing amidst many demons,
the best of men, Varāha, should be depicted as tearing apart the earth.
Of Varāha: That very method of meditation upon the Blessed Viṣṇu, who assumed the form of Narasiṃha, has been declared as that which increases supreme knowledge.
With thick shoulders, hips, and neck, a slender waist and a lean belly,
he has the face of a lion, a human body, wears blue garments, and is endowed with radiance.
Standing in the ālīḍha posture, adorned with all ornaments,
his face surrounded by garlands of flames, and his circle of hair like a mass of fire.
Since Hiraṇyakaśipu’s chest was not rent even by extremely sharp claws,
Devajāmātṛ should likewise be made to resemble a blue lotus.
The wise know that Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was ignorance itself.
The Narasiṃha [form] is to be fashioned; the god Vāmana should be made with limbs and joints that are slightly bent, with stout limbs, holding a staff, and intent upon his studies.
He should be made dark-green like dūrvā grass and likewise wear a black antelope skin.
Regarding Vāmana: Trivikrama should likewise be depicted resembling a water-laden cloud;
he should be shown holding a staff and a noose, as well as a conch, a discus, and a mace.
The conch, discus, mace, and lotus of that beautiful-formed [deity] should be fashioned; they must not be made bodiless. The remainder, however, should be executed as previously described.
The deity should be depicted with one face turned upward and with wide-open eyes.
Trivikrama said:
"But Bhārgava Rāma must be depicted as having matted locks that are difficult to behold;
he should hold an axe in his hand and wear a black antelope skin."
Paraśurāma:
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, must be established as king, protected by the marks of royalty;
so too shall be Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and the highly illustrious Śatrughna.
In the same manner, all [the rites] should be performed, but they are to be devoid of the head.
Rāma and the others;
Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the discus, should be depicted with the complexion of a blue lotus petal,
and his [consort] should be made to appear as if she were the personified Indīvarā herself.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Balarāma should be depicted holding a plow, carrying a club, and wearing earrings;
he should be white, dressed in deep blue garments, and have eyes rolling with intoxication.
Balabhadra should be depicted holding a bow and arrows; and Pradyumna, O King,
should be handsome, dark as an Indra-maṇi gem, dressed in white garments, and intoxicated with passion.
Pradyumna: Kāmadeva, however, should be fashioned as peerless in beauty on earth;
he should be made with eight arms, adorned with a conch and a lotus.
Holding a bow and arrows in his hand, with eyes anointed by passion,
he is Rati, Prīti, Śakti, Madaśakti, and Ujjvalā.
He should have four wives, enchanting in their beauty;
and he should have four arrows that reach the breasts of his wives.
And Ketu should be made as a great Makara with five arrow-faces;
he is Kāma. And the lord Aniruddha must also be made, bearing a sword and a shield.
Sāmba should be made with a mace in his hand and especially handsome in form;
Sāmba and Aniruddha should both be depicted as lotus-colored and wearing red garments.
Aniruddha and Sāmba [should be depicted];
likewise, Devakī should be made with a complexion as fair as the tip of a lotus petal.
May Yaśodā also always possess the luster of the Madhūka flower.
Yaśodā: One should fashion an image of Gopālaka, intent upon playing the flute,
adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, dark as a rain cloud, two-armed, and standing upright.
Of Gopāla: clad in saffron-colored robes, with his monastic garment draped over one shoulder,
seated upon a lotus and sun disc, two-armed, and meditative— such is the Buddha as he is proclaimed.
The Buddha is proclaimed as Kalkī, who has two arms, is mounted on a horse, possesses great strength, is wrathful with a sword raised in his hand, and effects the destruction of the Mlecchas.
Kalkī should be depicted as a man dark-green like dūrvā grass, with two arms and great strength; Nārāyaṇa has four arms and the complexion of a blue lotus petal.
Between those two, however, a jujube tree adorned with fruit should be made;
on the ground beneath the jujube tree, both [deities] should be made holding rosaries.
They stood upon a delightful vehicle equipped with eight wheels and yoked with living beings;
they wore black antelope skins, were self-controlled, and bore circles of matted hair.
In this case, Hari should be made equal to Nara, with one foot standing on the chariot and the other foot resting upon the knee.
Kṛṣṇa, too, possessed a form equal to that of Nārāyaṇa.

Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa. The god [Hayagrīva] should be depicted with a white complexion, wearing blue garments, bearing a horse's head, and with his feet placed upon the hands of the personified Earth.
One should know that the Lord who bears the horse-head is a portion of Saṅkarṣaṇa;
that eight-armed deity should be fashioned with four hands [held] from the fourth [hand].
The wise one should cause the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus to be fashioned in their own forms;
and four hands should be made, embodying the Vedas.
Placed upon the head by the god, they were adorned with all ornaments.
Hayagrīva; know Pradyumna as having assumed the body of Kapila through dispassion;
in the center, however, Karaka is to be made, with the other [deity] seated upon his lap.
His other pair of arms should hold a conch and a discus;
he is seated in the lotus posture with his eyes closed in meditation.
The god Kapila should be visualized, consecrated by the circle of matted locks,
his shoulders made full by the restraint of breath, and his two feet marked with lotuses.
O King, the Lord, the Master, wearing a deerskin, with a beard and a sacred thread,
was seated within the great lotus bud of the mantra.
With a state of dispassion, the Great-Souled One, established in meditation, remains thus meditating upon his own supreme station,
the protector of the world.
The ancient Puruṣa is the proclaimer of Sāṅkhya.
Kapila, Kṛśa, Vyāsa of dark body, Piṅgala who wears exceedingly matted locks,
Sumantu, Jaimini, Paila, and Vaiśampāyana as well.
And he should have four disciples appointed as his attendants.
Vyāsa says: Vālmīki should be made fair-complexioned, with a halo of radiance difficult to behold;
devoted to austerity and peaceful, he should be neither emaciated nor corpulent.
Vālmīki: One should represent Vālmīki in the full form of Dattātreya. Dhanvantari should be well-executed, handsome, and pleasing to behold.
And in his two hands there should be a jar containing nectar;
[he is] Dhanvantari.
He should be depicted standing in the midst of water, with the serpent Śeṣa visible.
His neck was adorned with a mass of hoods, its crests made difficult to behold due to the great jewels.
There, the God of gods should be made secret and four-armed;
likewise, another should be made, seated upon the coils of the serpent Śeṣa.
One foot of this Lord should be made resting upon the lap of Lakṣmī;
likewise, the other [foot] should be made positioned there upon his knee.
Another hand of his should likewise be placed at the region of the navel;
in the same manner, another hand of the deity should be made to rest upon the neck.
Likewise, O Yādava, another [lotus] shall arise for him from the lotus born in the lake of his navel, bearing a cluster of blossoms upon its stalk.
The god Pitāmaha (Brahmā) is to be fashioned as before, consisting of the entire earth;
and Madhu and Kaiṭabha are to be depicted clinging to the stalk of the lotus.
O serpent, his weapons, which assume human form, are likewise stationed nearby for his tasks;
this is the secret of the best of the Yadus before you.
The form of that supreme deity.
He is reclining upon the waters.
Tārkṣya has the appearance of an emerald, with a nose shaped like that of an owl;
he should be depicted with four arms, and likewise with round eyes and face.
With thighs, knees, and feet like those of a vulture, adorned with two wings,
he shines, resplendent with a golden plumage arranged in the *prabhāsa* formation.
One should cause an umbrella and a full water-pot to be placed in his two hands;
likewise, his two hands should be fashioned in the gesture of joined palms (añjali).

When the Blessed One’s hands are placed behind his back holding a parasol and a water-pot, they should not be depicted there; rather, the auspicious hands supporting the feet of the deity should be depicted.
He should be depicted with a slightly protruding belly and adorned with all ornaments.
Garuḍa [says], from the Viṣṇudharmottara: "O delighter of the Yādavas, one should have the God of gods, Mahādeva, fashioned as mounted upon a bull;
his faces should be made five."
All the gentle forms have a southern face that is deformed;
it wears a garland of skulls, is terrifying, and is the cause of the destruction of the world.
All [the faces] have three eyes, except for the northern face;
upon his great mass of matted hair there shall be a digit of the moon.
Above that, a fifth face is prescribed;
one should likewise fashion for him the sacred thread and Vāsuki.
The Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods, should likewise be fashioned with ten arms,
holding a rosary, a trident, a shield, a staff, and a blue lotus.
O mighty-armed one, in his right hands these should be depicted,
and in the left, a plantain tree, a bow, a mirror, and a water-pot.
Likewise, the skin of the trident-bearing God of gods must be fashioned;
its color should likewise be made with a luster resembling the rays of the moon.
[124] Rudra, Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, and Aghora— according to the sequence of their birth from the left—
are proclaimed to have four colors: white, yellow, black, and red.
All are remembered as having five faces and being adorned with ten staff-like arms;
they carry a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, a water-pot, and a rosary.
They are endowed with hands granting boons and fearlessness, holding tridents and lotuses in their hands.

Vāma is Vāmadeva; Sadyojāta is he who is born; these are the five forms beginning with Īśāna. Sarva, Bhīma, Mahādeva, Rudra, Paśupati, Bhava, Ugra, and Īśāna—these are the eight forms that resemble Śiva.
They have the moon as their crest-jewel, are adorned with circles of matted hair,
possess three eyes, and hold excellent khaṭvāṅgas and tridents in their hands.
The Eightfold Form:
Half of the deity shall be made as a woman endowed with auspicious marks,
while the other half shall be made as a man adorned with all the characteristic marks.
On the half belonging to Īśvara, a mass of matted hair adorned with the moon should be fashioned;
on the half belonging to Umā, a tilaka mark and likewise beautiful locks of hair should be made.
One half is smeared with ashes, while the other half is adorned with saffron;
one half wears a snake as a sacred thread, while the other half is decorated with necklaces.
On the left half, one should fashion a breast that is dense, full, and well-proportioned;
on the other half, it should be made with Umā, adorned and wrapped in beautiful garments.
There, one should cause a girdle adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli to be offered;
it should have an upward-pointing linga, half of which is the Great Lord (Maheśvara), and be decorated with a serpent-girdle.
And one should remember the foot of the God of gods, resting upon an even lotus,
marked with lac-dye and adorned with collyrium.
A trident and a rosary are prescribed for the two right arms;
a mirror and a blue lotus should be fashioned for the two left arms.
Ardhanārīśvara; likewise Dikpāleśāna,
bestowing the southern mudrā and holding a white rosary in his upper portion.
And in his left [hand] he holds a book containing all the Āgamas and other scriptures,
and upon his head he bears the bearer of nectar (the moon).
The Lord, white in complexion, seated upon a white lotus, clad in white garments and white unguents, with the moon upon his crest,
imparting knowledge to the sages.
He who proclaims that Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Dakṣiṇāmūrti:
A pair consisting of a woman and a man should be fashioned— Umā and Īśa, possessing divine forms—
as well as the Lord of Gods with eight faces, adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon.
One should visualize the goddess as having two hands and two arms, with a beautiful waist and lovely breasts;
one should place the left hand of the goddess upon the shoulder of the god.
"The right hand of Śambhu, adorned with a blue lotus,
should be placed by the Goddess upon the shoulder of the God; likewise, she should cause a moon-like mirror to be held in her left hand."
Umā and Maheśvara;
Sadāśiva is the right half of Hari-Hara,
while Hṛṣīkeśa is the left half, appearing respectively white and blue in form.
"In the right [hands] are, in order, the excellent trident, the discus, and the lotus;
on the right side is the bull, and on the left side is the king of birds. Thus is the form of Hari-Hara.
They have the colors of the directions, wear matted hair, possess three eyes, and hold tridents in their hands;
all of them are lords of the universe, each with a single face and palms joined in reverence.
Ananta, Trimūrti, Sūkṣma, Śrīkaṇṭha, Śiva,
Śikhaṇḍin, Ekanetra, and Ekarudra— these are [the lords] in order.
The Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) [are described] from the Viśvakarma-śāstra:
"Now I shall describe the Rudras, endowed with sixteen arms:
the great Rudra named Aja bears a trident and a goad."
In his eight right hands, he holds a skull-cup, a hand-drum, a snake, a mallet, and the Sudarśana discus, as well as a rosary; likewise in his eight left hands.
There, the threatening gesture (tarjanī) is at the top, with the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) below it in the hand;
[the other hands hold] a mace (gadā), a sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa), a bell (ghaṇṭā), a javelin (śakti), an axe (paraśu), and a water-pot (kuṇḍikā).
[127] Ajekapadaḥ || 1 ||
The one known as Ekapāda, holding an arrow outside the twelve [fingers],
a discus, a hand-drum, a trident, and a mallet below that, and a boon-granting gesture.
In the lower left hand is a rosary, and in the upper hand is a khaṭvāṅga;
[in the others are] a bow, a bell, a skull-cup, the Kaumudī lute, and a water-pot held in the threatening gesture (tarjanī).
He holds the axe in sequence and holds it in his eight arms;
through sacrifice, he always brings about the attainment of manifold enjoyments.
One-footed. || 2 ||
Ahibudhnya holds a mace and a discus; Caṇḍa holds a hand-drum and a mallet; and [the others hold] a trident, a goad, and a rosary, respectively, in their right and left hands.
He holds in his left hands a trident, a spear, a shield, a skull-bowl, a threatening gesture, and a javelin; he holds a battle-axe in his right hand just as he does the others.
Ahirbudhnya. 3.
Then Virūpākṣa, bearing in his eight hands a sword, a trident, a hand-drum, a goad, a serpent, a discus, a mace, and a rosary.
In the eight hands beginning with the left half [of the body], he holds a shield, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga),
a spear, an axe, a raised index finger, a jar, a bell, and two cheeks.
Virūpākaḥ || 4 ||
Revata holds in his right hands a bow, a sword, a trident, a mace, and the earth;
and from the top downwards, he holds a discus, a goad, and a rosary.

Then, on the left arms, like the sun [in position], he holds a bow, a shield, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a bell, a threatening gesture (tarjanī), an axe, a sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa), and a vessel.
This [deity] brings about all prosperity; indeed, one is born [to it] abundantly through worship.
Revataḥ || 5 ||
In the hand called *hara*, he holds a mallet, a hand-drum, a trident, and a goad;
and from the upper right, he tears asunder a club, a serpent, and a rosary.
A spear, a javelin, a trident, an axe, a threatening gesture,
and a skull-bowl— these are held in the left hands, starting from the uppermost and proceeding in order.
Hara. || 6 ||
Bahurūpa bears a *ḍamaru* drum and the *sudarśana* discus in his right hands,
while he holds a winnowing basket, a trident, a goad, the *kaumudī* lute, and a rosary for recitation.
In the eight hands beginning with the left half [of the body], he holds a bell, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a threatening gesture, a water-pot, a bow, an axe, and a paṭṭiśa weapon.
He is multiform. || 7 ||
Ambaka also holds a discus, a hand-drum, a mallet, an arrow,
a trident, a goad, and a snake in his right hands, starting from the upper right and proceeding in order.
In the eight hands beginning with the left half [of the body], there are a mace, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a vessel, a bow, a threatening gesture,
two jars, an axe, and a sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa).
The one with eyes like lotuses. || 8 ||
Indeed, the lord of the gods holds in his eight right arms the ḍamaru, the discus, the trident, the goad, the arrow,
the mallet, and the bow.
One should cause a lotus, an axe, a bell, a sharp-edged spear, a threatening gesture, a bow, a skull-topped staff,
and an alms-bowl to be depicted on the eight sprouts in the left [hands].
Sureśvara || 9 ||
Jayanta, the tenth Rudra, likewise holds a goad, a discus, a mallet, a trident,
a hand-drum, an arrow, and a rosary, saying, "Go to Yama!"
He holds in his eight left arms a mace, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), an axe, a skull-cup, a spear, a threatening gesture, a bow, a water-pot, and a sacrificial ladle.
Jayanta || 10 ||
Then Aparājita holds, in order from the right, a lance, a sword, a goad,
a trident, a snake, a wheel, a ḍamaru drum, and a rosary of beads.
Holding a spear, a shield, a mace, a vessel, a threatening finger, a battle-axe, a conch, and a bell— starting from the top and moving downwards— from the north.
The Unconquered. || 11 ||
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, Raivata, Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka,
Sureśvara, Jayanta, and Aparājita— these are declared to be the eleven Rudras.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
Kumāra should be depicted with six faces, adorned with a crest-lock,
wearing red garments, and mounted upon a noble peacock.
A cock and a bell should be depicted in his two right hands,
and a Vaijayantī banner and a spear should be made for his two left hands.
[130] Skanda said: Now, therefore, I shall describe the manifestation of the form of Bhairava.
He should be made pot-bellied, with round, tawny eyes.
With a face made terrifying by its fangs and nostrils thus dilated,
he was fierce, wearing a garland of skulls and adorned everywhere with serpents.
He was terrifying the goddess Parvatinandini with a serpent,
resembling a water-laden cloud, and wearing an elephant hide as an upper garment.
Pervaded by many arms, adorned with all kinds of weapons,
resembling massive *śāla* trees, and possessing sharp, beautiful claws—
this form of Bhairava is proclaimed as being turned slightly sideways.
Bhairava said: "This indeed is the Bhairava face of Mahākāla;
a terrifying goddess should be depicted [at his side], and a serpent should be held in his hand."
And the goddess Parvatanandinī should not be placed before him.
Neither white nor red garments should be used for him in the presence of the principal group of Mothers; likewise,
his retinue should be prepared accordingly.
And groups should be formed, appearing in many different forms.
Mahākāla;
Nandin should be depicted with three eyes, four arms, and mighty limbs,
resembling the hue of vermilion and clad in a tiger skin.
One should have a trident and a bhindipāla made for his two hands;
the third, however, should be placed upon his head, while another likewise threatens [with it].
One should look out from afar for people approaching from a distance.
Nandī:
But the wise know Vīrabhadra by this very form.
Vīrabhadra said:
"The Fever [deity] should be made with three feet, three eyes, and three faces;
Rudra has ashes as his weapon, three arms, and agitated eyes."
Fever.
From the Viśvakarma-śāstra:
Now, therefore, O Jaya, I shall fully describe to you the forms of the Vasus.
In his two hands, right and left, there is a rosary of lotus seeds.
This first Vasu, named Dharā, bearing a plough and a spear,
holds a garland made of lotus seeds, a discus, a spear, and a water-pot.
He whose [hands] hold a water-pot and so forth on the right and a rosary and so forth on the left is considered Dhruva;
his attributes are a pearl necklace, a lotus, a spear, and a goad.
O dear one, that Vasu is indeed celebrated by the wise by the name Soma;
his two hands, which extend upward to the left and right, are joined with the Śakti.
And with a plow and a goad held below, he would be known as Āpa;
with a rosary and a sacred thread above, and holding a spade and a spear in his hands below.

He who possesses these two is named Anila; he is the fifth Vasu, the bestower of auspiciousness, holding a sacrificial ladle and a rosary in his right hands, and bearing a spear and a skull-cup in his left.
That Vasu known as Nala, who is situated in the sequence beginning from the upper right,
holds a skull-topped staff and a goad in his right hands, and carries a spear and a shield in the others.
This seventh is proclaimed as Vasu, named Pratyūṣa;
he holds a staff and a skull-bowl in his right hands, while in his left hands he carries a goad and a spear.
This eighth Vasu, Prabhāsa, is proclaimed as the bestower of auspiciousness;
all these are declared to be like gold in their brilliance.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Thus ends the manifestation of the form of Vasu.
Listen, my child, O Jaya, for I shall explain to you the divisions of the Sun,
and how the illuminating Sun arises through his various forms.
In her right hand she holds a lotus garland and in her left a water-pot;
with her hands adorned by two lotuses, she is known as the first Dhātrī.
In her left hand is a trident, and in her right is the moon;
she is named Mitrā, three-eyed, and adorned with a lotus.
In the first [form], there is a discus in the right hand and likewise the Kaumudī moon in the left;
this form is to be known as being made of jewels, with hands like lotuses.
[133] With a rosary in her right hand and a discus established in her left,
she is to be known as the form of Raudrī, the principal one, adorned with a lotus.
She who has a discus in her right hand and a beautiful noose in her left,
with both hands occupied by a lotus, is the Vāruṇī form.
To the right, there should be a water-pot and a rosary made of rudrākṣa;
that [image] is considered excellent, being the form of the Sun adorned with a lotus.
She who has a trident at her right side and the Sudarśana discus in her left hand is known as Bhagamūrti; she is auspicious, holds a lotus in her hand, and is Jaya.
Alternatively, it is taught that she holds a rosary in her left hand and a trident in her right;
her form is indeed that of Vivasvat, marked by the insignia of a lotus.
The form known as Pūṣan should be understood as having two arms, marked with a lotus,
removing all sins, and endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
In the right [hand] is the mace, and in the left is the Sudarśana;
Sāvitrī holds a lotus in her hand—this is the form that accomplishes all aims.
He holds a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) in his right hand and the ritual peg (*kīlaka*) produced from the fire-oblation in his left;
his form is that of Tvaṣṭṛ, with both hands joined by a lotus.
Holding the Sudarśana discus in her right hand and a lotus in her left,
this is the twelfth form of Viṣṇu, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Rudra, Varuṇa, and Sūrya;
Bhaga, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Savitṛ is remembered as the tenth.
[134] "The eleventh is Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu is called the twelfth.
Thus ends the manifestation of the twelve Ādityas.
Now, therefore, I shall describe to you the forms of the Maruts.
In his right hand he holds a rosary and a lotus, and in his left he is endowed with a water-pot and a banner.
Thus, the one called Śvasana bestows excellent accomplishment upon practitioners;
it consists of the eyes, the rosary, the vessel, and the banner, and is named Sparśana.
The one named Vāyu holds a skull-topped banner, a noose, and a lotus;
Mārari is considered to have a skull, a lotus, a banner, and a bowl in his hands.
Sadāgati should hold a banner, a rosary, and a lotus vessel;
Mahābala, however, should bear a banner, a sword, a shield, and vessels.
Adorned with a banner, a noose, a skull, and a serpent, he is the increaser of strength;
holding an alms-bowl, a rosary, a noose, and a lotus, he has spotted deer as his steeds.
The one named Gandhavaha holds a rosary, a mace, a conch, and a banner;
Gandhavahaka has a skull-topped banner, a vessel, a lotus, and a hand [in his four hands].
He is considered blue in color, with hands holding the wisdom-mudrā, a rosary, a lotus, and a banner;
while the Swift One (Aśuga) holds a rosary, a deep-blue lotus, a banner, and a conch.
Sumukha should be depicted holding a banner, an arrow, a bow, and a water-pot;
the one named Karkara should hold the mudrās of a banner, a lotus, and a vessel.
Samīraṇa has a lotus, a rosary, a bowl, and a banner in his hands; Samīraka, however, bears a banner, a bowl, a cloud, and a lotus.
The unsurpassed one bears a rosary, a banner, and a lotus, as well as a shaven head;
the one named Māruta likewise holds a rosary, a banner, and a lotus.
The head is *kaṃ*.
Born from the womb of a serpent (*nāgayonija*), he is joined with a thunderbolt, an eye, a thread, a noose, and a lotus;
he should possess a banner, a severed head, and an eye-vessel, and is known by the name Jagatprāṇa.
The one named Pāvana is endowed with a banner, a cord, and a lotus;
the one known as Vāta bears a skull-topped staff, a banner, and a trident.
Prabhañjana, however, should be depicted holding a banner, an axle, and a vessel;
he is named after his hand-holding of a rosary, a banner, a lotus, and a serpent.
Nabhasvān is considered to hold a trident, a lotus, a banner, and a vessel;
Atibala is regarded as bearing a banner, a goad, an eye, and a severed head.
The one marked with the emblem of a lotus on a banner is proclaimed as Tarasvin;
the one bearing a staff, a severed head, a banner, and a lotus is considered Drāvaṇa.
The deity of the Yakṣas has a banner, a threatening forefinger, and two hands holding a vessel; the deity of the Apsarases holds a rosary, an axe, a lotus, and a pair of banners.
Holding a bell, an axle, a banner, and a severed head, he is named Adhara; his hands hold a sprout of enlightenment, a thread, a lotus, and a banner, and his gaze is eternally directed upwards.
One who possesses a rosary, a banner, an aśoka branch, and a bowl is known as Matirodhana;
one who possesses a rosary, a banner, and a shaven head is to be known as Pāṇika.
The practitioner is considered [perfected] when he holds the banner, the rosary, the jar, and the vessel;
joined with the citron, the banner, and the lotus-rosary, he is the fulfiller of the universe.
The refuge of the world is joined with bells, eyes, banners, and garlands;
he is named Viśvātiriktaka (Exceeding the Universe), endowed with the banner-mark and the noose.
When the lotus-born [Brahmā] holds a bell and a banner, he is Kajāgara;
when he holds a conch, a trident, a jar, and a banner, he becomes Viśvodara.
The one named Agraja is to be known as holding a yakṣa-arrow, a bow, and a water-pot;
he who holds a bilva fruit, a lotus, a rosary, and a vessel is considered Tīvraka.
This one, holding a conch, a skull, a banner, and a noose, is proclaimed as Suvaha;
while Bījavardhana is endowed with a rosary, a banner, a noose, and a vessel.
The one known as Bhadrajava is endowed with a banner, a noose, a skull, and a lotus;
while Puṣkarodbhava bears an axe, a noose, a banner, and a lotus.
The Lord of the Lotus-Lake has in his hands a *palāśa* leaf, a noose, a lotus, and a banner;
he possesses a manifest form, with hands joined by a rose-apple seed, a banner, a lotus, and an *akṣa* bead.
Holding a club, an eye, a banner, and a lotus, he is considered Viśvaga;
all [these deities] should be known as four-armed, youthful, and having curved eyebrows.
Holding weapons in the sequence from the topmost upward to the end of the uppermost,
they have red eyes, possess great heroism, and are adorned with all ornaments.
Smoke-colored, mounted upon deer, and all wearing variegated garments—
thus have those auspicious hosts of Maruts been described here to you.
The number is forty-nine for the removal of all diseases;
there are forty-nine Maruts,
according to the Skanda Purāṇa.
The sons of Dharma are the great-souled ones to be accomplished; they are seated upon lotus-thrones, holding water-pots and rosaries, and are twelve in number, worshipped by the immortals.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "Mano, Anumantṛ, Prāṇa, Narayāna, the heroic Vīryavān,
Vittis, Harya, Naya, Haṃsa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa."
Prabhava, Viṣṇu, and Viśva were born as the twelve Sādhyas.

Regarding the Sādhyas, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states: "The two divine physicians should be depicted with bodies, possessing the luster of a lotus petal and gold, wearing garments resembling lotus petals, and having two arms."
Adorned with all ornaments and especially possessing beautiful eyes,
divine medicinal herbs should be placed in their right hands.
O twice-born one, two books should be made and displayed in the two left hands;
O Yadava, one should be on the right side of one [image] and on the left side of the other.
A pair of women should be fashioned, beautiful in form and lovely to behold;
their names, as well as their perfection of beauty and their physical appearance, are now declared.

The perfection of form (*rūpa-saṃpad*) is proclaimed as resembling the *madhūka* flower; likewise, its shape in the world is said to be like a stalk of reed (*śara-kāṇḍa*). Furthermore, it should be depicted with jewel-ornaments in the hands and clad in garments white as the moon.
The two Aśvins;
Revanta, the lord, should be depicted like Sūrya, seated upon a chariot.
[The description] of Revanta:

[138] In the *Mayasaṃgraha*: The forms of the yakṣas are as follows. They should be depicted with protruding bellies, two arms, and treasures in their hands; they are intoxicated with pride. Vaiśravaṇa holds a mace and is most beloved; Nṛpāla is the eighth and most excellent.
Siddhārtha, Maṇibhadra, Sumanas, Nandana, Yaśas, Kaṇḍūti, Pāñcaka, Śaṅkha, Maṇimān, Padma, and Rāmakau.
Eating everywhere, tawny-eyed, clever, and taking refuge on Mount Mandara;
Śubhadra, Candrapradyota, Meghavarṇa, and Jayāvaha.
Dyutimān, Ketumān, Śveta, Maulimān, Vijayākṛti,
Padmavarṇa, Mahāghāsa, Puṣpadanta, and Sudarśana.
Pūrṇamāsa, Hiraṇyākṣa, Śatajihva, Balāhaka,
Valāka, Vipula, Padmanābha, Kumuda, and Vīraka.
These Yakṣas are called Sugandhas; their king is Dhanādhipa.
The manifestation of the form of a yakṣa; and the form of a rākṣasa in the *Mayadīpikā*:
"Wearing red garments, black in color, with long nails and prominent fangs, and holding in their hands axes and swords—such are the rākṣasas of terrible appearance."
Heti, Praheti, Yajñaghna, Śaṅku, and Sanabandhana;
Vidyut, Sarjama, Nṛmāṇa, Apauruṣeya, and Sukeśin.
These are said to be the principal Rākṣasas, namely the Ugras, Mālins, Bhūtas, Dānas, Dīrghavaktras, and Piśācakas.
[139] Thus is the manifestation in the forms of rākṣasas, bhūtas, and piśācas.

Bestowing boons upon the world of devotees, he wears a crown, earrings, and carries a mace. Furthermore, for specific purposes, he takes the form of a gandharva, delighting in the playing of the lute.
The *Gandharvas*. Viśvakarman describes the forms of the *Nāgas*:
Ananta has a red body and wears a garland of white lotuses;
he is a serpent with a hundred thousand coils, his head adorned with blue water-lilies.
Vāsuki is to be made with a white body, resembling shimmering pearls;
the great Takṣaka has red limbs, is endowed with the svastika mark, and possesses great luster.
Kṛṣṇa is Karkoṭaka, marked on the neck with three white lines;
he resembles a red lotus, has lotus-like veins, and possesses coral-red tips at the white parts.
Śaṅkhavarṇa is of the color of a great lotus and holds a black trident upon his head;
Śaṅkhapāla should be golden-hued with a white streak on his neck.
The Kulika has a red body, his head is shaped like a half-moon,
he has two tongues, seven arms, and is endowed with the jewels on his hoods.
All of them held rosaries and were equipped with water-pots and tail-fans;
they had either one wife or three wives, and likewise sons and other offspring.
Thus ends the creation of the forms of the Nāgas. Maya said:
"The ancestors, who carry the *piṇḍas* as their vessels, sit upon seats of *kuśa* grass and lotuses.
This is from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Prabhākaras, the Barhiṣads, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas;
the Kravyādas, the Ājyapas, and the Sukālins.
The Pitṛs. According to the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Ṛtu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kālaka, Dhuri, Ulocana, Purūravas, and Mādravas—these are remembered as the ten Viśvedevas."
The *videhas*, however, should be placed on the right side with their left hands raised;
those devoted to the bow should be placed on the left side.

The Viśvedevas and Viśvakarman. Regarding the weapons: the sword and the spear are considered to be thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long, while the trident, the noose, the lotus, and the conch are proclaimed to be one tāla in length.
The mace and the noose are two tālas in length, as is the gīla-staff;
the arrow is two tālas, while the staff is double that, measuring twelve aṅkusas.
The skull-cup, the lotus, the shield, and the sword marked with five [blades] are prescribed;
likewise the hand-drum, the resonant bell, and the knife sixteen finger-breadths long.
That Vajra is a man, gross, harsh, exceedingly firm, and powerful;
Śakti, however, has the form of a woman, with red limbs, and is supported by a wolf.
The Staff-man was also terrible, with blood-red eyes;
and the Sword-man was dark-complexioned and beautiful, with angry eyes.
The noose is a seven-hooded serpent-man joined with a tail;
the banner is a yellow man of great strength with a face turned away.
The mace was a girl with a yellow luster and very full hips;
the trident was a divine man with beautiful eyebrows and a dark-complexioned body.
Śaṅkha is also a divine person, white-limbed and with auspicious eyes;
Heti is mentioned many times in the scripture, as is Bhīma, who possesses divine vision.
The arrow should be a divine man with red limbs and divine eyes;
the bow is a woman with the luster of a red lotus, holding a drawn bow above her head.
In this way, one should know the weapons to be purified in the Supreme Lord;
and upon the head of all those mentioned, there is the mark of His own weapon.
The two arms, however, should always be made by the wise to be joined to the shoulders.
Thus concludes the section on the names of the weapons. Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya are likewise proclaimed to have the forms of a white, red, yellow, and black lion, respectively.
[She possesses] knowledge of the Dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty.
The Earth should be depicted as white in color, adorned with divine ornaments,
four-armed, with a gentle form, and wearing garments resembling the rays of the moon.
O delighter of the Yadavas, a jewel-vessel, a vessel of grain, a vessel filled with medicinal herbs,
and a lotus should be depicted in his hand.
Likewise, she should be depicted on the backs of the four elephants of the quarters;
the goddess is then traditionally described as being white in color and endowed with all medicinal herbs.
The Earth and the Salt Ocean are to be fashioned with two arms for the sake of all-enlightenment;
she holds a lotus garland in her right hand and a vessel filled with jewels in her left.
Wearing an upper garment and a sacred thread, having the hue of the *pāṭala* flower, and clad in fine clothing;
with the *pavitra* held outside the hand, he bestows gain and is adorned with prosperity.
Lavaṇoda;
Kṣīroda is white in color, two-armed, and adorned with jeweled earrings.
Seated upon a makara, he holds a lotus in his right hand and a vase in his left.
The Ocean of Milk;
here, the Ocean of Curd-Whey (Dadhimaṇḍoda) is to be understood as the lotus-seated one (Brahmā),
who possesses matted hair and has two arms, bearing a staff and a conch.
There is the Dadhimaṇḍoda ocean; Ghṛtoda is to be known as Kapila, who stands upon a crab and wears matted hair.
He holds a vessel of yellow kaśeru grass and a jar in his two hands.
The Sea of Ghee; here the Sea of Sugarcane-Juice should be fashioned, having a complexion like cow's urine,
standing upon a tortoise, holding a jar and a staff, and wearing blue earrings.
Ikṣūda;
Suroda, situated within Gaṇṭakānta, should be known as resembling a *gomedaka* gem;
he holds a mallet and a water-pot, has two arms, and is the increaser of prosperity.
Suroda is sweet-tasting, resembling pearls, residing in a frog, and wearing fine attire; he holds a vessel half-filled with a string of pearls and is adorned with serpents.
All [the deities] should be fashioned resembling lapis lazuli, two-armed, and holding water-pots;
they should be seated upon lotuses for the purpose of the deities' ritual bathing.
The ocean; all the islands, continents, and mountains, since they assume any form at will— these men should be depicted as holding their most beloved weapons and bearing their respective emblems.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
The eastern direction is the color of a young elephant, red in hue;
she should be known as seated upon a lotus, with her hand resting on a female elephant.
The southern [direction] has a large mouth and a large body, with the luster of a lotus;
she stands upon a chariot, is yellow in color, and likewise appears as one who has reached youth.
The southern-western [direction] is mounted by a camel, black and yellow, and youthful;
the western [direction] is mounted by a horse, black and past her youth.
The blue [line] has grey hair nearby; immediately following that is the deer-goer;
then the white, the man-rower, and likewise the old woman comes last.
Exceedingly large, situated upon a bull, and white, it should be in the northeast;
it is like the earth below and established in the sky above.
O King, the Lord of the Gods (Indra) should be depicted as white and mounted upon a four-tusked elephant;
his wife Śacī should be portrayed seated on his left lap.
Wearing blue garments, with a golden luster, and adorned with all ornaments, Tārkṣya should likewise be depicted, decorated and with [his gaze] directed sideways toward the forehead.
Śakra should be depicted with four arms, and Śacī likewise with two;
a lotus and a goad are to be held in his left and right hands respectively.
The second [hand] on the left, positioned behind Śacī, should be joined with a vajra;
in the hand of the consort on the left, a cluster of *santāna* flowers should be fashioned.
One should cause the right [hand] of the King of Gods to be placed upon his back.
Indra [should visualize] Agni as red, wearing matted hair, clad in smoky-colored garments,
surrounded by garlands of flames, gentle, three-eyed, and possessing a beard.
He saw the Lord of Gods with four arms and four tusks, having Vāyu as his charioteer,
seated upon a smoke-bannered chariot yoked to four parrots.
Svāhā, like Śacī to Śakra, should be on the left lap;
the goddess, with a jewel-bowl in her hand, is in the two right hands of Agni.
A flaming trident should be fashioned [therein], and a rosary of beads on the left.
Agni;
and Yama, who has the luster of a water-laden cloud, whose garment is a heated yak-tail whisk, mounted upon a buffalo, and adorned with all ornaments, should be depicted. [145]
One should place Dhūmorṇā, who has the luster of a blue lotus, upon the left lap;
Dhūmorṇā should be made with two arms, and Yama should be made with four arms.
Both a staff and a sword should be placed in his right hands,
while a flaming trident and a rosary should be made for his left hands.
The face should be made upon the staff, adorned with garlands of flames;
with a smoky beard in his right hand, he should be positioned on the back of Yama.
In her left hand, a beautiful mātulāṅga fruit should be depicted;
on his right side, one should likewise have Citragupta made.
One should have him depicted in northern attire, with his own characteristic form, two arms, and a serene appearance;
one should place a pen in his right hand and a leaf in his left.
Kāla, of fierce appearance, should be depicted holding a noose in his left hand.
Yama is three-eyed, with a wide-open mouth, long fangs, and a blazing face;
his hair stands erect, his beard is green, he has two arms, and his countenance is terrifying.
In appearance, his limbs are blackish-red, and he likewise wears black garments;
he is adorned with all ornaments, and holds a camel-whip and reins in his hands.
Four wives are to be made:
Devī, Nirṛti, Kṛṣṇāṅgī, and Kṛṣṇavadanā; the dwarf [Vāmana] has a noose in his hand.
Nirṛti is on a chariot drawn by seven swans; Varuṇī, the mistress of aquatic creatures,
is likewise there, resembling smooth vaidūrya gem and wearing white garments.
[146] O King, Mahādeva has four arms, a slightly protruding belly, is adorned with pearl necklaces, and wears all ornaments.
One should have a dolphin made as his banner on the left side;
above his head is a well-polished umbrella, and his wife is beautiful in all her limbs.
O King, she should be placed on the left lap; in the center, however, she should have two arms.
One should cause an utpala lotus to be made in her left hand, while the right hand is behind the deity.
One should fashion a lotus and a noose in the two right hands of the deity,
and one should fashion a conch and a jewel-vessel in his two left hands.
In the southern portion, however, the goddess Gaṅgā should be depicted seated upon a crocodile, holding a chowrie and a lotus in her hands, fair as the moon and possessing a beautiful countenance.
On the left, however, Yamunā should be depicted seated upon a tortoise, holding a chowrie;
she is gentle, with a blue lotus in her hand, and resembles a dark blue water-lily in complexion.
Varuṇa;
Vāyu, however, has the color of the sky and should have garments of that same form;
he stands in his embodied form with two arms, his wheel filled within his chest.
The desire to go is his auspicious wife, and she should be placed on his left;
O twice-born one, the wind should be made to hold the interior of his mouth with both hands.
In that very same way, the goddess Śivā should be made most beautiful;
likewise, her face should be turned away, and the hair on the goddess's head should be disheveled.
Vāyu [should be visualized]: he should be made to resemble a lotus petal, granting boons, and having men as his vehicle;
he is golden-hued, a granter of boons, and adorned with all ornaments.
Hara had a protruding belly, four arms, and tawny eyes as wide as a fathom;
he was dressed in northern attire, wore armor, and was adorned with a heavy burden of necklaces.
And two fangs should be made upon the face of that [deity] who bears a beard;
O crusher of enemies, his crest-jewel should be fashioned with the left [hand] representing his sovereign power.
The goddess Buddhi, the bestower of boons, should be depicted seated on the left lap;
her right hand, however, is placed behind the neck of the deity, as she has only two arms.
O destroyer of enemies, he should be depicted holding a jewel-bowl in his left hand,
and a mace and a spear should be placed in his two right hands.
One should place a banner marked with a lion and a sun upon his feet,
and two beautiful treasure-vases (nidhis), Śaṅkha and Padma, situated within their respective treasures.
On both sides of his face, there should be the conch and the lotus held in the añjali gesture.
The Giver of Wealth (Dhanada). From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:

"He should be made with two arms and a gentle appearance, resembling the sky in the luster of a blue lotus, possessing that same color, holding excellent [attributes], and having the moon and sun in his hands."
The space [is] square; O mighty-armed one, the base should be square, and from that, it becomes circular.
And a square equal to that, situated like Mount Meru, is auspicious.
The third part, the space of the sky, is said to consist of an auspicious pedestal;
and the middle part is proclaimed to be square, like a pillar.
[148] Furthermore, one should offer another lotus there, like a noble seat (bhadrapīṭha);
it has eight auspicious petals, and in its center, within the pericarp (karṇikā), is the Sun.
One should place the guardians of the directions upon its eight petals in all directions. Dhruva, the lord of the host of planets, should be fashioned as Vyoman, assuming the form of Viṣṇu.
The glorious one, with two arms and a gentle appearance, emits rays of light from his wheel.
Dhruva says: The Sun should be depicted with a handsome beard, possessing a beautiful luster red as vermilion;
dressed in northern attire, well-proportioned in form, and adorned with all ornaments.
He should have four arms and great splendor, and be completely covered by armor;
his girdle should be fashioned with those known as the *pātīyāṅga* [mantras].
His rays should be fashioned upon the left and right hands;
above, they are auspicious, arranged in the form of a flower garland and filled with all kinds of blossoms.
His staff, which is his own form and possesses his own aspect, should be placed on his left side;
on the right, in the Piṅgalā portion, it should be made exceedingly tawny.
O Yādava, both of them should be depicted in the attire of northerners;
moreover, the two hands of the Fire-god should be placed upon their heads.
The two scribes, Piṅgala and Atipiṅgala, should be depicted;
likewise, the god bearing a shield and a spear must be fashioned with great care.
A lion and a flame should be made, likewise to the left of the Sun;
and four sons should be made on his two sides.
Revanta, Yama, and the two Manus,
as well as Ravi, the king of the planets, should be depicted either surrounded by the planets or alone.
The queen Savarṇā, Chāyā, and likewise the goddess Suvarcasā—
these four should be made as his attendants on both sides.
The god whose charioteer is Aruṇa should be depicted seated upon an excellent chariot that has either one wheel with seven horses, or six horses.
From the Matsya Purāṇa: He whose seat is a lotus, whose hands hold lotuses, whose splendor is like the petals within a lotus,
who is stationed upon a chariot drawn by seven horses, who has two arms, and who is the eternal movement (the wind).
The Sun; and the Moon, the Lord, should be depicted with a white body, wearing white garments,
possessing four arms, great splendor, and adorned with all ornaments.
Two white lilies should be placed in the hands of that deity;
and Kānti (Beauty), personified, should be depicted at his right side.
On the left, a splendor should likewise be fashioned, peerless in form upon the earth;
its emblem, marked by a lion, should appear on the left side like the sun.
On the chariot drawn by ten horses, two wheels and two excellent charioteers should be fashioned.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Śiva should be depicted as white, wearing white garments, with white horses and white ornaments;
two-armed, holding a mace in his hand, bestowing boons, and possessing the moon."
Candra [is described] from the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Bhauma (Mars) should be made equal to fire, and Tvaṣṭṛ [should be placed] upon his own golden chariot.
[This is] from the Matsyapurāṇa.
Wearing red garlands and garments, holding a spear, a trident, and a mace,
four-armed and mounted upon a ram, the son of Varuṇa shall be the bestower of boons.
Bhauma (Mars): From the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"In the balance and likewise in the chariot for Bhauma, the wise man should be made equal to Viṣṇu."
Budha [is] of the appearance of molten gold; Bṛhaspati has two arms,
and one should have a book and a rosary fashioned in his hands.
And likewise, the Guru should be adorned with all ornaments and clad in yellow garments.
The Guru says:
In a divine golden chariot drawn by eight horses, beautiful to behold,
Śukra should be depicted with a white body and likewise clad in white garments.
His two hands are said to be joined with a treasure and a book;
the son of Bhṛgu should be depicted as shining upon a chariot drawn by ten horses.
[151] Venus; likewise, Saturn should be depicted as dark-complexioned, dressed in black garments, with a white face,
adorned with two hands joined by a staff and a rosary.
A chariot made of black iron should likewise be prepared, equipped with eight horses.
Saturn [is to be placed] on a silver chariot likewise drawn by eight horses; Rāhu, O wise one,
should be made with one arm joined to a woolen blanket and a book.
One hand should indeed be made ready; the right hand, however, should be empty.
Rāhu:
"One who understands [the matter] should fashion Ketu with a form similar to that of Mars;
however, for him, ten horses should be made, O King."
The Banner (Ketu) [is described] according to the Viśvakarma-śāstra.

Now the lunar days (tithis) are indeed being stated: the first day, Pratipad, is reddish-brown with two arms; situated in Aries, she holds a spear and a vessel, and is considered the first of the bright fortnight (sitapakṣa).
The Pratipadā:
the second [tithi] is white, moving on a swan, and holding a vessel and a book.
This is for the second [tithi].
The third is Gaurī, riding a bull and considered to bear a trident and a vessel;
she belongs to the third lunar day.
The fourth has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus and stands upon a boar.
Indeed, she is joined with a yellow garment, bearing an axe and a vessel.
The fourth [form] is seated upon a lotus, has the luster of coral, and is adorned with the tips of hoods;
the fifth is considered to bear a conch, a mudrā, and likewise a noose.
Of the fifth.
The sixth [is] peacock-colored and red, holding a bowl and a cock;
[this is] of the sixth.
The seventh [form] is considered to be mounted on a horse, holding a copper-colored lotus vessel;
of the seventh [form].
The eighth is mounted on a cow, holding a bell and a vessel, and is white as cow’s milk.
Of the eighth [day]:
the ninth is indeed Himsagā, white, holding a vessel, and auspicious.
Of the ninth [day].
The tenth [deity] is black in color, seated upon a buffalo (lulāpa), and holds a staff and a vessel;
"lulāpa" means a buffalo. Of the tenth:
the eleventh [deity] is seated upon a deer and a lotus, and is endowed with a balance scale and a razor.
She has the face of a lion, a red throat, a protruding belly, and is supremely graceful.
The eleventh [tithi] is Garuḍa-ridden, cloud-colored, and holding an alms-bowl.
The wheel is Ara; she belongs to the twelfth [tithi].
Gaurī, holding a bow and arrows and seated upon a crocodile, is Trayodaśī;
she belongs to the thirteenth [tithi].
Seated upon a lotus, pale-red in hue, holding a vessel of wine, and with eyes like a blue-throated peacock or an indragopa insect— such is this goddess of the fourteenth day.
On the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], there is the full moon, white and adorned with pearl ornaments;
O wise one, her left and right hands hold a jar filled with nectar.

On the full moon day, she is smoke-colored; at the beginning of the dark fortnight, she is established in Māra and has four faces. With four arms, she holds a rosary, a *sruva* ladle, a book, and a vessel.
The first day of the dark fortnight: on the second day, there is the appearance of a white water-lily (*kumuda*), situated upon a tree, with a staff and a water-pot.
[154] This is for the second day of the dark fortnight.

The third [form] is blue, mounted on Tārkṣya, and holds a conch-vessel in her two hands; this is for the third day of the dark fortnight. The fourth is the color of collyrium, mounted on a buffalo, and possesses four arms.
The fanged goddess bears the rosary of patience, the staff, the noose, and the bowl.
On the fourth day of the dark fortnight:
Grāhasthā, with the luster of the moon, holds a staff and a water-pot on the fifth day;
[this is] from the fifth day of the dark fortnight.
Three-eyed and riding upon a peacock, she is red in color and holds a spear and a cock.
She has one face and two arms; as the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, she wears red garments and is beautifully adorned.
Her neck is encircled by dark blue locks of hair, and she is decorated with matted locks and a crescent moon.
Of the sixth day of the dark fortnight:
the seventh [day] is mounted on an elephant, fair-complexioned, two-armed, and holding a vajra-vessel;
this is for the seventh day of the dark fortnight.
Pretagā is red, has a black neck, and wears white garments;
she holds a rosary, a sword, a shield, and a bowl in her four arms.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight: Sarpagā is blue, fanged, and holding a bowl and making a threatening gesture. [155] On the ninth day of the dark fortnight: Kṛṣṇanavamyā.
Seated upon a throne, radiant white, with yellow earrings on the tenth day, she holds a vessel of wisdom; clad in yellow garments, she is garlanded with lotuses.
Of Kṛṣṇadaśmī:
the eleventh [tithi] is Vṛṣasthā, bearing a lotus, blue, white, and a trident.
Of Kṛṣṇaikādaśī.
Copper-colored, mounted upon a chariot, holding an alms-bowl, a shield, a sword, and a lotus;
this Dvādaśī is adorned with auspicious garments and blue earrings.
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight [she is] Kṛṣṇadvādaśī. On the thirteenth day [she is] Trayodaśī, holding an aśoka bud, an arrow, a bow, and a vessel;
she is seated upon a dark blue lotus, dark-complexioned, dressed in yellow garments, and languid with passion.
Or the thirteenth lunar day may be white-complexioned, holding a mace and a bowl, and standing upon a treasure.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight:
she is two-armed, mounted on a horse, black in color, and [appears] on the fourteenth day.
She holds a sword and a spear, has blue earrings, and is adorned with parrots.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
she should be represented on the new moon day as having the luster of a polished emerald,
seated upon a seat of *darbha* grass, holding a bundle of *darbha*, and appearing emaciated.
[This concludes the section] on the new moon.
Now, I shall describe the forms of the lunar mansions in brief.
Among them, first, Aśvinī is to be known as auspicious, resembling the petals of a lotus.
Mounted upon a horse-faced lotus, she has two arms and wears white garments;
in her right hand she holds a vessel of divine medicine, and in her other hand a book.
Of Aśvinī:
Bharaṇī is proclaimed to be mounted upon a buffalo, elephant-faced, with the luster of collyrium,
holding a staff and a noose, extremely fierce, and red-eyed.
[The goddess] Bharaṇī:
seated upon a goat, with the face of a goat, with tawny eyebrows, hair, and eyes;
holding a thread and a spear, with stout limbs and a reddish belly.
And she is celebrated as Kīrtikā, adorned with a garland of gold.
Kṛttikā; Rohiṇī, who has the luster of snow, whose face is like a serpent, who rides upon a swan,
who holds a thread and a water-pot, and who is adorned with necklaces— thus is the goddess celebrated.
Of Rohiṇī:
she has the face of a deer or the face of a horse; she has the face of a serpent; she is the seizer;
[157] she stands upon a vulture; she is as white as the moon; she holds a water-pot; she wears a garland of victory.
Of Mṛgaśīrṣā:
Śvamukhī is black in color, with blood-stained [garments], holding a trident in her hand;
she wears blue clothing, is mounted upon a bull, and is adorned with a garland of bones.
[The deity] of Ārdrā has the face of a boar and stands upon a cat; Punarvasu is white in color and is described as holding a thread, a vajra, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness.
In Punarvasu:
mounted upon a goat, cloud-colored; in this Puṣya: possessing a honey-yellow hue, four-armed, holding dice, a fierce trident, and a water-pot.
Of Puṣya:
Maghā has the face of a monkey, is dark-complexioned, thin-limbed, and large-bellied;
she holds a bundle of darbha grass and stands upon a lotus, and is described as having two arms.
Of Maghā:
the eastern [face] is elephant-faced, standing on a lotus, with two parrot-like hands, and red;
[the syllable] *ska* (or *spha*) is a wheel.
The first [deity] has the face of a tiger,
stands upon a bull, possesses an auspicious complexion, and is four-armed;
she is proclaimed to have two eyes and to hold a thread and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
Of Uttarā:
he is fair-complexioned and reddish, with the face of a buffalo, mounted upon a horse named Hastin;
possessing two arms holding a die and a thunderbolt, he is proclaimed as the bestower of prosperity.
Of Hasta:
Vyāghrāsyā is mounted upon a buffalo, variegated and fair-complexioned, with four arms;
she holds a rosary, a water-pot, a book, and is endowed with a jar filled with nectar.
Of Citrā:
she is considered to be mounted upon a buffalo or a deer, fair or dark in complexion,
plump, four-armed, and holding a snake, an axe, a banner, and a vessel.
Of Svāti:
she has the face of a lion, is red in color, and her navel and the area down to her feet have the luster of gold;
seated upon a ram or a goat, she holds a goad and a vajra in her hands—this is Viśākhā.
In her left [hands], she holds a spear and a vessel below, adorned with golden ornaments.
Of Viśākhā:
Haristhā has a feline face, possesses two arms, and holds a lotus and a vajra;
she is dark from the head down to the navel and fair from there to the feet, respectively.
Anurādhā is to be fully understood as being adorned with rubies.
Of Anurādhā:
yellow in color, mounted upon an elephant, with the face of either a spear or a deer;
she holds a rosary and a lotus in her left hands, while in her right she holds a goad and rests upon a couch.
For Jyeṣṭhā:
her primary form should be fashioned as dark-complexioned,
mounted upon a corpse, fierce, holding a sword and a shield, two-armed, and having the face of a wolf.

Of the Root [Mantra]: she who dwells in a jar, who has the roar of a crocodile, who is blue, who stands upon a monkey, and who always bears a rosary, a lotus, a noose, and a vessel, and has four arms.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā is described as wearing yellow garments and adorned with a lotus.
Of Pūrvāṣāḍhā [the following is said]:
Uttarāṣāḍhā moves through the serpents; she is cow-colored, beautiful in form, adorned with a mass of matted hair bound by a serpent and decorated with golden earrings.
She holds an eye and a snake in her right hands, and a book and a water-pot in her left.
Of Uttarāṣāḍhā:

Abhijit has the luster of a white water-lily; she rides upon a swan, has the face of a crocodile, and is four-armed, endowed with a boon-granting gesture, a rosary, a book, and the gesture of fearlessness.
[The deities of] Abhijit:
Nīraruḍ, mounted on a horse; Śravaṇī, with the face of a monkey;
and [the deity] bearing a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, adorned with golden ornaments.
Of Śravaṇa: she has the luster of molten gold; she resides in a treasure-trove; she is seated upon a lotus;
her lower lip is like the ripe bimba fruit; she is slender, with full and elevated breasts.
She has a long braid adorned with flowers and endowed with pearl ornaments;
she possesses beautiful eyes, is richly dressed, has two arms, and wears crimson garments.
Dhaniṣṭhā is proclaimed to be gentle and endowed with an excellent abode.
Regarding Dhaniṣṭhā:
she is radiant, seated upon a sea-monster, dark-hued like a horse, two-armed, and holding a noose and a vessel.
Pāṭalā, when combined with Vastrasaṃyuktā, is proclaimed as Śatatārakā.
The hundred stars; Pūrvā Bhādrapadā has the face of a white cow and the gait of a goat;
she bears the head of a ram and carries a vessel of spirituous liquor.
Of Pūrvabhādrapadā:
[The deity] of Uttarabhādrapadā is white, has the face of a donkey, and is mounted upon a bull;
