she holds a vessel and a *ḍamaru* drum, and is described as having two arms.
[161] Of Uttarabhādrapadā:
Revatī has the face of a camel, possesses two arms, and moves with the gait of an elephant;
she holds a lotus and a water-pot, is white in color, and has a great voice.
[The mantra] of Revatī. Now, [the mantras] of the yogas: Viṣkumbha is to be known as the first; he is yellow in color and has six arms.
He had a red face, a blue throat, round eyes, and was most terrifying.
He had a broad forehead, long limbs, and a slender nose;
he wore matted locks and golden jewel-encrusted earrings made of sapphire.
Clad in garments resembling white and blue indragopa insects, adorned with golden ornaments,
he holds a mallet in his first right hand and a pair of scissors here in the second.
In the third [hand] is a vajra; in the first left [hand] is an axe, and in the second a white-tailed [animal];
and in the third is a vessel of nectar.
This venerable one, when honored with fragrant yellow flowers, will surely bring about the accomplishment of the task; otherwise, he would be a giver of obstacles.
Of Viṣkumbha:
the second, named Prīti, resembles a hibiscus flower;
he has a white face, large eyes, long ears, and wears moon-shaped earrings.
Adorned with a tilaka on his forehead, gentle, decorated with pearls,
clad in white garments, wearing matted locks as a crown, he has eight arms and a large belly.
In the first watch of the night, one should offer jasmine, Bandhūka, Puṣpāñjana, Jīvottha, and Mallikā flowers;
in the second, a sweetmeat (modaka) in the hand; and in the third, a plantain fruit.
In the fourth [hand] there is a lotus, and in the first left hand an amṛta-pitcher;
in the second [left hand] there is indeed a beautiful vessel filled with soma.
In the third [hand] he holds a vajra, and in the fourth here indeed a banner;
bearing these for the sake of prosperity, for the sake of joy, and for the cessation of all suffering.
From Prīti [was born]:
"But this third one, Āyuṣmat, has the luster of a pearl, with a reddish interior;
he is clothed in linen garments and adorned with ornaments of pearl and gold."
Two-armed, in the first [hand] on the right is a rosary of pearls;
in the second, indeed, is dūrvā grass; and in the third, a mango sprout.
In the fourth [hand] there is a lotus, and in the fifth an umbrella;
in the first left hand there is a jar of nectar, covered by a citron.
In the second sprout-like hand, he holds a vessel filled with curd and unbroken rice;
in the third hand, a bilva fruit; and in the fourth, a trident.
And in his fifth hand, he should hold a white and auspicious yak-tail whisk with a golden handle;
indeed, he is to be worshipped for the increase of enjoyments and longevity.
Of the Venerable One:
here, the fourth is named Saubhāgya; he has the luster of crystal, possesses three eyes, has reddish shoulders, is a great being, is handsome, and has the sky as his garment.
This ten-armed deity holds a *śrīphala* fruit in his first hand,
and a rosary made of coral in his second sprout-like hand.
In the third [hand] is a lotus, in the fourth a sword;
in the fifth is a spear, and right here in the first left [hand] is a vessel.
In the second [hand] he holds an amṛta-pitcher, in the third a fly-whisk;
in the fourth a mirror in his hand, and in the fifth a sugarcane staff.
Bearing a gentle, auspicious, and fortunate appearance for the sake of prosperity, longevity, and splendor—
this beautiful fifth yoga is called Saubhāgya; it is white-faced, self-controlled, and powerful.
His remaining limbs were reddish and emaciated, and he wore earrings made of coral.
Clad in red and white garments and adorned with ornaments of pearls and coral,
he holds a rosary made of fine gold in his first right hand.
In the second [hand] there is a lotus in the hand; in the third, a bilva fruit;
in the fourth, a spear in the lotus-hand; and in the first left [hand], indeed, a water-pot.
In the second [hand] he holds a vessel made of gold, and in the third a mirror;
in the fourth hand he holds a fly-whisk, thus possessing eight arms.
He should be worshipped with great devotion for the increase of happiness and good fortune. Now, the sixth yoga, known as Atigaṇḍa, is recognized [as follows] for Śobhana.
He has cheeks that are reddish-white, he is fierce, his face is black, and the sun is his ornament.
Stout, with large ears, a prominent nose, and reddish ornaments;
with a tawny beard, hair, and a crown of matted locks; six-armed and wearing a waist-thread.
One should place a rosary made of iron in the hand-bud of Āditya;
in the second [digit] an ena deer, and in the third a lotus.
In his left hand he holds a vessel, and in the second [right hand] a spear;
indeed, in the third he bears a banner, colored black and red.
He should be worshipped with great devotion for the sake of averting fear from the wicked.
Of Atigaṇḍa:
He indeed has four arms, is of virtuous deeds, with white arms, belly, and ears;
he is endowed with blue and white garments and adorned with golden and blue ornaments.
On the first sprout-like hand, [he placed] a rosary of rudrākṣa beads;
on the second hand, a lotus; and on the left hand, first, a staff.
Carrying a banner in his second, beautiful hand,
he bestows auspiciousness upon the commencement of human undertakings for the sake of great prosperity.
Of Sukarman:
the eighth yoga is called Dhṛti, known as Vasuvāhuka;
Bhālāruṇa, however, has a white complexion on all his limbs and wears reddish garments.
Abounding in gold, pearls, and sapphires, with ornaments set with coral,
he holds a rosary of pearls in his first right hand and two jeweled rings.
In the second [hand] he holds a *śrīphala* fruit; in the third, an *aśoka* sprout;
in the fourth, a golden staff; and in the first left hand, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
In the second [hand] he holds a vessel of nectar, in the third a lotus in his hand,
and in the fourth he bears a banner for the increase of prosperity.
From the portion of Vyakta, the ninth, named Śūla, is now described:
he has a neck that is coppery-red, is white in complexion, and has a slender belly.
He has three lines on his forehead, three matted locks, and dark-blue hair;
when the sun is in the hands of Yama and the other [planets], he holds an exceedingly terrifying trident.
In the second [hand] a mallet, in the third a rosary,
in the fourth a chain, and in the fifth a staff.
In the sixth hand there is a lotus, and in the uppermost [hand] a skull;
in the second is a chisel, and in the third indeed a water-pot.
Holding a pair of tongs in his fourth hand, a mirror in the fifth,
and a banner in the sixth, he is thus worshipped.
It shall lead to the destruction of misfortune and the total defeat of enemies for men.
Regarding Śūla: this tenth yoga here is called Gaṇḍa.
Gaṇḍa has a white and reddish body, six arms, and dark blue garments.
Adorned with ornaments of emerald and wearing blue coral earrings,
he holds a rosary in his hand positioned at the first [digit] and a sword named Candrahāsa in the second.
In the third [hand] is a blue lotus; in the first left hand is indeed a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu);
in the second is a shield, and in the third is a banner.
This is the procedure for the satisfaction of the sacrificer and for the cessation of diseases and misfortunes.
Of Gaṇḍa:
the eleventh is called Vṛddhi, occurring when the [sum of] the planets is sixty-one;
it is characterized by a red foot, a secondary white horse, a forehead mark, and a crossed mandala.
Adorned with variegated garments and decorated with ornaments of pearl and gold,
he holds a rosary in his hand placed on the first [finger], and an amṛta-pitcher on the second.
In the third [hand] he holds the Nandaka sword, and in the fourth the arrow;
in the fifth the mallet, and in the sixth the pair of tongs.
In the seventh [position] there is a conch, and right here in the eighth, a lotus;
in the first position on the left there is a water-pot, and in the second, a leaf.
In the third [hand] he holds a shield, and in the fourth a bow;
in the fifth a chisel, and in the sixth a flute and a horn.
Holding a bow in his seventh hand and a banner in his eighth,
he brings about the increase of welfare and the prosperity of the wealth of the two arms.
(The word *vṛddheḥ* means "for the sake of increase.")
The twelfth is indeed named Dhruva, and the Yoga is described right here;
likewise Dakṣasthālāruṇa and Śvetasarvāṅga.
Clad in crimson garments and adorned with golden earrings, he possesses fourteen arms; in his first right hand is a rosary.
In the second [hand] he holds a lotus, in the third a sword,
in the fourth a mallet, in the fifth an arrow, and in the sixth a lotus.
In the sixth [hand] he holds a captivating conch, and in the seventh a fly-whisk while reclining;
in the first left hand there is a vessel, and in the second a shield.
In the third hand he holds a ṭaṅka, and in the fourth a bow;
in the fifth hand, which possesses excellent characteristics, he holds a banner.
Holding the mirror of Manoharā in the sixth [hand] and [the gesture of] bestowing in the seventh,
he should be worshipped with great devotion for the sake of the stability of prosperity and other benefits.
[167] Now the thirteenth yoga, called Vyāghāta, is being described for Dhruva:
this one has red above the navel, is preceded by white, and is three-eyed.
Wearing a garment that was white within and reddish at the edges, with earrings of the sun,
he had a crystal rosary around his neck and was adorned with rudrākṣa beads.
Maṇibandhālivarṇa, however, has six arms and a curved face;
he holds a lotus in his first right hand and an axe in the second.
And here, in the first [hand], there is indeed a noose on the left and a vessel;
in the second, an ambrosia jar; and in the third, he rests upon a goad.
This highly venerable one, bearing [this burden], acts to prevent the failure of his duty.
Regarding the contradiction: now the fourteenth conjunction called Harṣaṇa is described;
this one is red above the knee, and white immediately prior to that.
Clad in garments the color of the *pāṭala* flower, adorned with pearls and lapis lazuli,
he possesses twelve arms, long ears, and large eyes.
In the first right hand he holds the Kaustubha gem, in the second a rosary of beads,
in the third a lotus, and in the fourth an arrow.
In the fifth [hand], a conch; right here in the sixth lotus-hand, a noose;
in the first left hand, a vessel; and in the second, a jar of nectar.
In the third [hand] he holds an axe, and in the fourth a bow;
in the fifth hand a discus, and in the sixth he rests an elephant goad.
Bearing [this] for the sake of excellence, prosperity, the increase of honor, and happiness—
[this is] of Harṣaṇa. Now, the fifteenth yoga is described, known as Vajra.
Wearing a white snake as a girdle, he has a black neck and a reddish face.
Clad in yellow robes, with pierced ears and three eyes,
he is richly adorned with ornaments of diamond and beryl, and equipped with a waistband.
Wearing matted hair in three coils, possessing eight arms on all sides and endowed with strength,
he holds a rosary in the first pair of hands directed toward Yama and Āditya, and likewise an arrow in the second.
In the third [right] hand he holds a lotus, in the fourth a vajra, in the fifth an axe;
and in the first left hand he holds a jar of nectar.
In the second [hand] there is a bow, in the third an excellent vessel,
in the fourth a thunderbolt, and in the fifth a noose.
Bearing [these] for the sake of the happiness of victory and for the increase of the lineage of prosperity—
now the sixteenth yoga, named Siddhi, of Vajra is being described.
His feet and shanks are reddish, while his upper body is white in color and possesses a beautiful face.
With arms reaching to his knees, a red neck, and garments dyed red,
he is adorned with pearl necklaces, gems, and gold ornaments, and wears earrings made of moonstones.
In the first right hand he holds a bilva fruit, in the second a lotus,
in the third a book in his hand, and in the fourth a shaft.
In the fifth [hand], however, there is a banner in the hand; here, in the first left [hand], there is a bowl;
in the second, an ambrosia jar; and in the third, a fly-whisk.
Holding a bow in the fourth and a banner here in the fifth,
he grants the fulfillment of desired goals for the sake of men's success.
And here, the seventeenth yoga is indeed called Vyatīpāta;
he has a red throat, a white neck, and a face like that of a bee.
Clad in white and madder-dyed garments, adorned with ornaments of blue sapphire and gold,
the god has eighteen arms and a face contorted with a frown.
In his first hand is a sickle, in the second a stone-cutter;
in the third is a rosary, and in the fourth an enchanting arrow.
In the fifth [hand] he holds an iron chain, in the sixth a breastplate;
in the seventh hand a mallet, and in the eighth hand a lotus.
A spade in the ninth hand, a horn in the first of the upper hands,
a vessel in the second, and a golden jar in the third.
In the fourth hand he holds a bow, in the fifth here a knife;
in the sixth a pestle, and in the seventh an adze.
In the eighth [digit] he holds a banner in his hand, and in the ninth he lies with a raised staff,
for the destruction and even the death of the host of enemies.
For the sacrificer, it is for the sake of the continuity of his lineage, and for the enjoyment of prosperity and happiness.
Regarding Vyatīpāta:
the eighteenth is called the most excellent and supreme yoga.
It has a neck-deep white color and a red throat.
White-faced, large-eyed, with long ears and sun-like earrings,
he was richly adorned with golden ornaments and endowed with many auspicious marks.
Clad in white garments with reddish borders, endowed with thirty-two arms,
he holds a rosary in his [first] pair of hands toward Yamāditya, and a citron in the second.
In the third [hand] he holds the Candrahāsa sword, while in the fourth lotus-hand he holds an arrow;
in the fifth he holds a conch, and in the sixth right hand he holds a battle-axe.
In the seventh [hand] there is a mallet, and in the eighth a sickle;
in the ninth there is indeed a horn, and in the tenth hand a lotus.
In the eleventh [hand] he holds a thunderbolt, and in the twelfth a plow;
in the thirteenth hand a staff, and in the fourteenth the spear weapon.
In the fifteenth hand is a lotus, and in the sixteenth a trident;
in the first left hand is a skull-cup, and in the second a leaf.
In the third [hand] he holds a shield, and in the fourth a bow;
in the fifth hand a discus, and in the sixth an axe.
In the seventh [digit] there is a ṭaṅka, and in the eighth, a chowrie;
in the ninth, a ḍamaru, and in the tenth, a lute.
In the eleventh [month] he holds a goad, and in the twelfth he lies with a mace;
in the thirteenth he holds a noose, and here in the fourteenth a club.
Holding a mirror in the hand of the son of Tithi (Mars) and a banner in this very sixteenth [hand],
one attains welfare, prosperity, and the happiness of all enjoyments.
The most excellent one;
and here the nineteenth is called Parighāsana.
He has beautiful feet and knees, a white face, and wears matted hair.
With a dark-blue streak upon his reddish-maroon belly, he was clad in blue garments; a being of great courage, he wore earrings made of gold and jewels.
Adorned with golden ornaments, six-armed and fierce in appearance,
he holds a mace in his first hand and a club in the second.
In the third [hand] is a lotus;
in the first left hand is a bowl, in the second hand a paṭṭiśa, and in the third here indeed a banner.
Bearing [this] for the destruction of enemies and for the cessation of fear from the wicked.
Of Parigha.
Now, the twentieth yoga here is called Śiva;
he is white in color, has three eyes, and is adorned with ornaments of pearl.
In the first right hand is a beautiful citron;
in the second, a rosary; and in the third, a conch shell.
In the fourth hand he holds an arrow, in the fifth a sword (candrahāsa),
in the sixth hand a mallet, and in the seventh he rests upon an axe.
In the eighth hand he holds a spade, in the ninth a sickle,
in the tenth a horn, and here in the eleventh a thunderbolt.
In the twelfth [year], he should indeed draw a five-fingered hand and the breaking of a clod of earth;
in the thirteenth, a plow; and in the fourteenth, a spear as a weapon.
In the fifteenth [finger] he holds a staff, and in the sixteenth here an ambuja;
in the seventeenth (municandra) a trident, and in the eighteenth (vasucandra) a tomara.
In the first left hand she holds a vessel; in the second, a jar of nectar;
in the third, a discus; and in the fourth, indeed, a bow.
In the fifth [hand] she holds a shield, in the sixth lotus-hand an axe,
in the seventh hand an axe (kuṭhāra), and here in the eighth a prāṅkuṭa.
In the ninth [hand] he holds a white chowrie, in the tenth a hand-drum (ḍamaru),
in the eleventh hand a trident, and in the twelfth a mirror.
In the eighteenth [digit], he lies bearing a spear for the increase of peace.
Of Śobhana: Now the twenty-first yoga, named Siddhi, is described. It resembles the Javā flower and has three white lines within its belly.
His crown, adorned with eight matted locks and joined by a crescent moon,
is endowed with red and white silken garments and furnished with crystal ornaments.
He has eight arms, is gentle, pot-bellied, and possesses all auspicious marks;
he holds a lance in the first right hand and a trident in the second.
In the third hand he holds a lotus, in the fourth a staff made of gold;
in the fifth hand he holds a spear, and in the sixth indeed a plough, O Śayyā.
In the seventh [house] there is a vajra in the hand; here itself, in the eighth, a horn;
in the ninth, a sickle; and here itself, in the tenth, a battle-axe.
Indeed, the mallet is in the hand of Rudra; the sword Candrahāsa is in the twelfth;
the arrow is in the thirteenth hand; and here, the conch is in the fourteenth.
In the first hand she holds a water-pot, and in the second a hand-drum;
in the ninth hand she holds a vessel, and in the tenth indeed an axe.
In the eleventh hand is a ṭaṅka, and in the twelfth a shield;
in the thirteenth is a bow, and here in the fourteenth is a discus.
Tearing [the enemy], he is worthy of worship for the sake of victory in the glory of wealth and happiness.
Because of its accomplishment,
that very yoga is said to be the twenty-second [chapter] to be accomplished;
it is white in color, large-eyed, with a flame-like line upon its neck and face.
Clad in saffron-colored garments, with earrings of diamond and lapis lazuli,
possessing arms like those of a celestial deity or fire, and adorned with a girdle set with many jewels.
In the second [mandala] of Yamāditya, there is a rosary;
in the third, a citron; in this very same [fourth], a spear; and in the fourth, a trident.
In the fifth hand he holds an arrow, in the sixth lotus-hand a vajra;
in the seventh hand a lotus, and in the eighth right hand a staff.
In the ninth [hand] he holds a tomara, in the tenth a spear,
in the eleventh a plow in his hand, and in the twelfth a horn.
In the thirteenth hand he holds a sword, and in the fourteenth a battle-axe;
in the beautiful fifteenth hand, which has firm fingers, he holds a mallet.
In the sixteenth [hand], there is a sickle; right here, in the seventeenth, there is a conch shell.
In the first left hand is a water-pot, and in the second, a bowl.
In the third hand he holds the gesture of fearlessness, and in the fourth a *ḍamaru* drum;
in the fifth hand he holds a bow, and in the sixth he rests upon a goad.
In the seventh [house] there is a divine banner, and in the eighth a noose;
in the ninth there is a spear, and in the tenth here a mace.
Indeed, a pestle is in the hand of Rudra; in the twelfth [hand] is a chowrie;
in the thirteenth hand is a shield, and in the fourteenth is an axe.
Holding a ṭaṅka in the fifteenth hand, a mirror in the sixteenth,
and a discus in the seventeenth hand, he grants the increase of prosperity.
Of the one to be accomplished:
here too is described the twenty-third yoga, named Śubha;
he is dark-blue and red, yet has the luster of a pearl and possesses three eyes.
His neck was marked with red streaks; he was draped in a crimson and white silken garment;
he was adorned with ornaments of pearls, coral, and rubies, and wore golden earrings.
Endowed with thirty-two arms, his circle of matted hair is tawny;
he holds a boon-granting gesture in his first hand and a rosary in the second.
In the third [hand] there is indeed a trident, in the fourth lotus-hand an arrow;
in the fifth a lotus, and in the sixth a thunderbolt.
In the seventh [hand] she holds a spear, and indeed a staff in the eighth hand;
in the ninth hand a javelin, and here in the tenth a horn-bow.
In the eleventh [hand] there is a plow, and in the twelfth a sword;
in the thirteenth hand there is a discus, and in the fourteenth a mallet.
In the fifteenth [hand] he holds a conch shell, and in the sixteenth a battle-axe;
in the first left hand he holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and in the second a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
In the third [hand] he holds a bowl, in the fourth likewise a bow;
in the fifth hand a *ḍamaru* drum, and in the sixth a goad.
In the seventh [hand] there is indeed a citron, and in the eighth hand a banner;
in the ninth a drinking vessel, and in the tenth a spear.
A mace in the eleventh hand, and a shield in the twelfth;
a fly-whisk in the thirteenth hand, and a drum here in the fourteenth.
Bearing a discus in the fifteenth [hand] and an axe in the sixteenth,
he should be worshipped for the sake of enjoyment, beauty, and happiness.
Of the auspicious one; now, twenty-four [units] here are called Śukla.
This one at the chin is Lohita, pale-white as the moon and three-eyed.
He has matted locks adorned with a crescent moon and a streak of sapphire blue; he is three-eyed, his face is smeared with vermilion, and he is marked by a beautiful tilaka on his forehead.
Adorned with ornaments of coral, pearl, and gold, with the Kaustubha gem upon his neck,
joined by the sky, fire, and arms, and endowed with the jewel-seal (ratnamudrā).
In the southern direction, on the first sprout-like hand, she holds a winnowing basket and a rosary;
on the second, a trident; and on the third, an arrow.
In the fourth [finger] one should place the supreme weapon, the mace; in the fifth, the conch;
here in the sixth, the hammer; and in the seventh, the sickle.
In the eighth hand, however, he holds a sword; in the ninth, a plow; in the tenth, a horn;
and in the eleventh, a javelin.
In the twelfth hand he holds a staff, in the thirteenth a spear;
in the fourteenth hand he holds a sword, and in the fifteenth hand a lotus.
In the first left hand is a citron, in the second a vessel,
in the third hand a bow, and in the fourth indeed an axe.
In the fifth [hand] is a discus; here itself, in the sixth lotus-hand, is a chisel;
in the seventh hand is a fly-whisk, and in the eighth [hand] resting on the lap is a shield.
In the ninth [digit], however, there is a mace here; in the tenth, an ambrosia jar;
in the eleventh hand, a spear; and in the twelfth, a vessel indeed.
In the thirteenth [hand] he holds a goad, and in the fourteenth a mirror;
in the fifteenth hand, he bears a banner for the sake of great glory.
Of the white [deity],
the twenty-fifth yoga is recognized as named Brahmā;
he is red, yellow, and entirely white, as bright as the moon, and three-eyed.
He is dark blue and red in color, with a golden neck marked by three lines; he has three matted locks hanging down, is gentle, and has a smiling face.
Clad in garments of copper-colored silk, with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads around his neck,
adorned with ornaments made of pearls, rubies, and gold, and wearing earrings of moonstone;
Adorned with a sky-blue lotus for an armlet and a girdle of tinkling bells,
[he holds] a gentle rosary in his first right hand, which is beautiful at its base.
In the second [hand], however, there is a boon; in this thirteenth [hand], a sword;
in the fourteenth hand, a plow; and here in the fifteenth, a horn.
In the sixteenth [pore], he holds a sword of iron; in the seventeenth, a javelin;
in the eighteenth, a staff; and in the nineteenth, a spear.
In the twentieth [digit] there is a discus; in the twenty-first, a lotus lies in the hand;
in the twenty-second, a cup; and in the twenty-third, an arbuda lies in the hand.
In the twenty-fourth hand, there is a well-seen iron-cutter;
in the first left hand, however, is the weapon of protection (Rakṣāstra), and indeed in the second left hand, a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
In the second [hand] there is the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and in the third here indeed the *dhruva* [staff];
in the fourth is the *khaṭvāṅga*, and in the fifth the spade.
In the sixth [hand] he holds a bow; in the seventh, armor rests upon his arm;
in the eighth, a spear is in his hand; and in the ninth, indeed, the Sudarśana discus.
In the tenth [hand] she indeed holds a citron, in the eleventh hand a noose;
and here in the twelfth she holds a chisel, while in the thirteenth she holds a shield.
In the fourteenth [finger] is the one called the axe; in the one named after the lunar day (fifteenth) is the hand-drum;
in the sixteenth hand is the fly-whisk; and here, in the seventeenth, is the water-pot.
In the eighteenth [finger], one should place a mace (gadā) here; in the nineteenth, a pestle (muśala);
in the twentieth hand, a goad (aṅkuśa); and in the twenty-first, a noose (pāśa).
In the twenty-second [tattva] is a white banner; in the one born from three sides is Vīrabhadra;
in the Jina is a perfectly pure mirror; and in the twenty-fifth, the Ajina lies upon a bed.
Bestowing upon the sacrificer the supreme longevity of the cow-pen for the sake of its increase.
Of Brahmā. Now, O Indra, the twenty-sixfold [Vidhi] is being described to you here:
this Śeṣa has hands and feet that are ruddy, and his eyes are white.
Adorned with garlands of *dharmilla* jasmine and *mallika*, and anointed with sandalwood paste and other unguents;
his forehead was graced with a tilaka mark, and his ears were darkened by earrings.
With a radiant pearl necklace upon his chest and adorned with ornaments of every kind of gem,
he wears garments with the luster of white moonstones and sapphires, and is endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Endowed with eight arms and eyes slightly reddish,
he holds a spear in his first hand and a pearl necklace in the second.
In the third [hand] there is a lotus; here, in the fourth, a conch shell;
in the fifth hand, a water-pot; and in the sixth, a trident.
In the seventh [hand] he holds a warrior’s sword, and in the eighth hand a spade;
in the ninth he holds a leafy branch, and in the tenth a crescent-shaped sword (candrahāsa).
In the eleventh [hand] he holds a plow, in the twelfth a horn;
in the thirteenth hand a javelin, and in the fourteenth a staff.
In the fifteenth [hand] he holds a spear, in the sixteenth a thunderbolt resting on his lap,
in the seventeenth a discus, and in the eighteenth a battle-axe.
In the nineteenth [day] there is a pestle; in the twentieth, a book;
in the twenty-first, a seat; and in the twenty-second, a mallet.
In the twenty-third [chapter], however, is the Camasa; in the twenty-fourth, Arbuda;
and in the twenty-fifth, Haste and Loṣṭabhedana.

In the twenty-sixth [hand], he holds a Turuṣka weapon; in the first left hand, he displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), in the second a water-pot (kuṇḍikā), and in the third a citron (bījapūraka).
In the fourth left hand is a vessel of ghee; in the fifth, indeed, a *sruva* ladle;
in the sixth, a *khaṭvāṅga* staff; and in the seventh, he holds a *ḍamaru* drum.
In the eighth [hand] he holds a goad, in the ninth a bow,
in the tenth hand a shield, and in the [eleventh] hand of Rudra an axe.
In the twelfth [digit] there is a chowrie in the hand; here, in the thirteenth, a spear;
and in the fourteenth, a mace; and in the fifteenth, a pestle.
An elephant goad in the sixteenth hand, a noose in the seventeenth hand,
a paṭṭiśa in the eighteenth, and a wheel in the nineteenth.
The armor is indeed in the twentieth, and the sickle in the twenty-first;
in the twenty-second is the chisel, and here in the twenty-third is the banner.
In the twenty-fourth [chapter] Vīrabhadra, and in the twenty-fifth the mirror;
in the twenty-sixth, he bears a deer-skin for the increase of prosperity.
Of Indra:
the yoga known as Vaidhṛti is the twenty-seventh here;
it is white in color, extremely fierce, with a red neck and a white face.
With five matted locks hanging down, wearing dark and reddish earrings,
adorned with ornaments made of blue, red, and gold, and clad in dark garments;
Endowed with arms as long as the arrows of the Vedas, with a large belly and slow gait,
he held a rosary in his hand on the second day of the fortnight of Yama, and likewise a boon.
In the third [hand] he holds a pair of tongs, in the fourth a conch shell born of the ocean;
in the fifth hand a lotus, and likewise in the sixth a sacrificial ladle (śruva).
In the seventh [hand] is an arrow; in this eighth [hand] is knowledge as a sword;
in the ninth is a spade, and in the tenth is a trident.
In the eleventh hand is a horn, and in the twelfth a plow;
in the thirteenth is a sword, and in the fourteenth a lance.
In the fifteenth hand he holds a staff, and in the sixteenth a spear;
in the seventeenth hand he holds a thunderbolt, and in the eighteenth (the Vasu-candraja) a breastplate.
When the moon rises in the constellation Nanda, one should give an axe; in the twentieth [nakṣatra], an arbuda;
in the hand [nakṣatra], and likewise in the twenty-first, when it is in Śaya, a clod-breaker.
In the twenty-second [chapter] is indeed the Turuṣka weapon; in the twenty-third, the conch;
in the twenty-fourth, the book; and in the twenty-fifth, the seat.
In the twenty-sixth [hand] he holds a mallet in his hand, and in the twenty-seventh a sacrificial cup;
in the first left hand he holds a water-pot, and in the second the gesture of fearlessness.
A fish in the third hand, a citron in the fourth,
a vessel in the fifth, and likewise a *śruva* ladle in the sixth.
In the seventh [hand] he holds a bow, and in the eighth hand a hand-drum;
in the ninth hand a goad, and in the tenth direction-hand a skull-topped staff.
A fly-whisk in the Rudra [eleventh] and a battle-axe here in the twelfth;
a shield in the thirteenth and a spear here in the fourteenth.
In the fifteenth hand he holds a mace, and here in the sixteenth a pestle;
in the seventeenth hand a goad, and in the eighteenth hand a noose.
In the twenty-first [day] from the rising of Nanda and Candra, one holds a spear (paṭṭiśa); in the twentieth, Vīrabhadra;
in the twenty-first, a sickle (śaya); and in the twenty-second, a hatchet (ṭaṅka) and a deer-skin (ajina) in the hand.
In the twenty-third [chapter], indeed, the wheel and the armor are in the hand of the Jina;
in the twenty-fifth, the bowl; and in the twenty-sixth, the auspicious mirror.
In the twenty-seventh [year], holding a banner in his hand, he becomes a slayer of the wicked.
[This concludes the section] on Vaidhṛti.
Thus are the forms of the yogas.
Now, I shall describe the characteristics related to the forms of the karaṇas.
Indeed, he was named Vava, yellow-complexioned, with matted hair and jeweled earrings.
He wears blue garments, is adorned with rudrākṣa beads, and has a pale neck;
he is endowed with fourteen arms and possesses three tawny eyebrows and eyes.
In the first hand he holds a boon-granting gesture, and in the second a bow;
in the third hand a thunderbolt, and in the fourth indeed a lotus.
In the fifth [digit] he holds a mallet, and in the sixth a pair of tongs;
in the seventh, on his five-fingered, large belly, is a divine goad.
In the first [hand] on the left there is the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), in the second a bow,
in the third a book in the hand, and in the fourth she rests upon a mirror.
Holding a ṭaṅka in his fifth hand, a small knife in the sixth here,
and a serpent-noose in the seventh hand, he bestows prosperity.
Of Bava:
that which is called Vāla is indeed red, with a blue neck and a large belly;
he wears white garments, has a mass of matted hair, is tawny, and has a prominent nose.
He had a rosary of rudrākṣa beads around his neck, was radiant with ashes white as time itself, possessed the nectar-like rays of the moon, and carried a small casket tucked under his arm.
In the first beautiful right hand, she holds a sweetmeat;
in the second, a ketaki leaf; and in the third, a spear.
In the fourth [hand] there is a lotus; in the fifth, indeed, the Sudarśana discus;
in the sixth, an arrow made entirely of iron; and in the seventh hand, a thunderbolt.
In the eighth hand he holds a pair of tongs; here, in the first left hand, he holds a bowl; in the second, a water-pot; and in the third, a spear (paṭṭiśa).
In the fourth hand he holds a *bījapūra* fruit, and in the fifth a conch;
here, in the sixth, a bow, and in the seventh hand a thunderbolt.
Bearing the eighth book for the sake of subjugation and victory.
The third [day] is named Kaulava, belonging to Vālava; it has the luster of the pericarp of a white lotus,
a red throat, and a parrot-like face, and its garments are blue, white, and reddish.
Adorned with ornaments of pearls, rudrākṣa beads, and gold, as well as sapphire,
he is endowed with eighteen arms and possesses small bells and a waist-cord.
In the first hand, let there be the boon-granting gesture (vara-mudrā); in the second, a rosary;
in the third, a golden staff; and in the fourth, a book.
In the fifth [hand] she holds a sweetmeat (modaka), and in the sixth a pair of tongs (saṃdaṃśa);
in the seventh hand she holds a hand-drum (ḍamaru), and in the eighth right here a thunderbolt (vajra).
In the ninth [finger], she holds here a horned creature; in the first left [hand], a red guñjā seed and so forth, and in the second, a water-pot.
In the third [hand] is the Vāsava vessel; in the fourth, an excellent lotus;
in the fifth, a bright chowrie; and in the sixth lotus-hand, a sickle.
Holding a lute in the seventh hand, an elephant-goad in the eighth,
and a plantain leaf in the ninth, he bestows prosperity and happiness.
Of Kaulava:
the fourth is named Taitila, dark-complexioned with a slender belly,
wearing red garments, adorned with a garland of hibiscus flowers, and having the face of a partridge.
He is endowed with wings and arms like those of Garuda, possesses a waist adorned with a bell,
and holds a most beautiful *śrīphala* fruit in his first right hand.
In the second [hand] he indeed holds a sword, and in the third a book;
in the fourth hand an rosary, and in the fifth an arrow.
In the sixth [hand] is the divine Sudarśana; in the seventh here is the thunderbolt (kuliśa);
in the eighth hand is the sacrificial ladle (sruva), and in the ninth is the mallet (mudgara).
In the tenth [hand] there is a goad; in the first left hand a vessel, in the second a shield, and in the third an auspicious lotus.
In the fourth [position] is a water-pot; here, in the fifth, a bow;
in the sixth, a charming conch; and in the seventh, a white fly-whisk.
Holding a *sruva* ladle in his eighth hand and a chisel in his ninth,
he bears a noose in his tenth hand for the prosperity of the sacrificer.
[184] Of Taitila: here the fifth karaṇa is to be known as named Garā;
it has a cow's face, a variegated neck, is smoke-colored, and wears red garments.
Endowed with wings and arms, and adorned with lotus-seed beads,
he holds a spear in his first right hand and a discus in the second.
In the third [hand] she holds a *śrīphala* fruit; in the fourth, a lotus;
in the fifth, a beautiful manuscript; and in the sixth, a charming arrow.
In the seventh [hand] is a bull's horn, and in the eighth hand is a thunderbolt;
in the ninth is a lute, and here in the tenth is Vīrabhadra.
In the eleventh [digit], however, there is the *saṃdaṃśa* (tongs) on the beautiful five-fingered hand;
in the second [digit] located at the north, there is the gesture of fearlessness (*abhīti*), and here indeed is the conch.
In this [form], he holds a vessel in the third hand and a fly-whisk in the fourth;
in the fifth hand he holds a ḍamaru drum, and in the sixth, a bow.
In the seventh [birth], he holds a water-pot; in the eighth, a ten-spoked wheel;
in the ninth, a bamboo flute in his hand; and in the tenth, a mirror.
In the eleventh [chapter], however, he bears the Rudra-weapon for the sake of fame, happiness, and prosperity.
Of Garuḍa: the monkey-faced merchant, smoke-colored, wearing yellow garments, seated upon a bull,
endowed with four arms, and adorned with golden ornaments— this is the sixth.
In the first hand, a mirror is excellent; in the second, a rosary;
in the third, a conch shell; and in the fourth, a sweetmeat.
In the fifth [hand] is a vajra; in the sixth lotus-hand is a spear;
in the seventh is a bamboo staff; and right here in the eighth is a sword.
In the ninth [section] he should place a noose, and in the tenth a banner;
in the eleventh the Turuṣka weapon, and in the twelfth the Sudarśana.
In the first hand of this gentle one is the gesture of fearlessness, in the second a water-pot,
in the third a citron, and in the fourth a drinking vessel.
In the fifth [hand] he holds what is called the five-faced [thunderbolt], and in the sixth a spear;
in the seventh hand he holds a fly-whisk, and in the eighth a shield.
In the ninth hand he holds a goad, and in the tenth a plow;
in the eleventh hand is a beautiful, exceedingly stainless mirror.
Holding a conch in the twelfth [hand], for the increase of fortune and good luck.
The merchants [saw] Bhadrā, who was clothed in tiger-skin garments, white-complexioned, with the face of a donkey,
endowed with seven arms, three feet, and adorned with iron ornaments.
In the first [hand] on the right, he holds a *kartṛkā*; in the second, a mace;
in the third, an arrow in his hand; and in the fourth, a *candrahāsa* sword.
In her left upper hand she holds a shield, and below that, a bow;
beneath that, she carries a vessel in her left hand while inspiring fear in her enemies.
Of Bhadrā:
the eighth karaṇa is named Śakuni; it has a green luster, is adorned with coral ornaments, and its garment resembles the color of a red insect (śakragopa). [186]
One endowed with six arms and a jackal face, possessing a voracious appetite;
in the first [position] there is a discus, and in the second, a boon-granting gesture.
In the third [hand] he holds a rosary, and in the fourth a lotus;
in the fifth hand he holds a sweetmeat, and in the sixth lotus-hand a vajra.
In the seventh [hand] he holds a tomara-spear, and in the eighth a śakti;
in the ninth a tusk of an elephant, and in the tenth a candrahāsa sword.
In the eleventh hand he holds an arrow, in the twelfth a goad, and in the thirteenth a mace;
here, in the first left hand, he holds a conch shell.
In the second [hand] there is the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and in the third a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu);
in the fourth hand a citron (bījapūra), and in the fifth a bowl (pātra).
In the sixth lotus-hand is a horn, in the seventh a spear,
in the eighth hand an iron club, and in the ninth a staff.
A shield is in the tenth hand, a bow rests in the eleventh;
a vessel is in the twelfth, and a trident is in the thirteenth.
Wearing it for the sake of excellence, prosperity, victory, and happiness,
and especially for the torment of one's enemies, it is highly honored.
Śakuni said:
"O Jaya, the ninth [figure] here is called Catuṣpada;
it is black in color, four-footed, four-faced, and endowed with matted locks."
Its eastern face is indeed human, its southern face is that of a cow,
its western face is that of a goat, and its northern face is that of a boar.
Having the form of a human, with everything emerging from the three-pronged tail;
wearing yellow garments, possessing a large belly, and adorned with blue pearls.
He is endowed with eight arms, makes a long sound, and possesses great speed;
he holds a spear in his first right hand and a rosary in the second.
In the third [digit] there is the Sudarśana discus, and in the fourth the lotus;
in the fifth the mallet, and in the sixth the water-vessel.
In the seventh hand he holds a mace, and in the eighth a goad;
in the ninth hand an arrow, and in the tenth a sword.
In the eleventh hand he holds a tooth, in the twelfth a spear;
here indeed, in the thirteenth, he holds a firm and auspicious javelin.
In the fourteenth [digit], however, there is indeed the vajra in the first left [hand], and likewise the bell;
in the second, the water-pot, and in the third, the conch shell.
In the fourth [hand] there is indeed a citron; in the fifth, a ṭaṅka;
in the sixth, a vessel filled with nectar; and in the seventh, a trident.
In the eighth [digit], a bowl; right here in the ninth, a bow;
in the tenth, a shield in the hand; and in the eleventh hand, a staff.
In his twelfth hand he holds a spear, and here in the thirteenth a lance;
in the fourteenth he bears a horn, highly honored for the increase of the lineage.
The tenth, named Nāga, is red in color, wears blue garments, and has matted hair;
it is human in form, with its head resting upon that fruit.
Endowed with arms possessing the qualities of space, adorned with pearls and rudrākṣa beads,
he holds a sweetmeat in his first [right] hand and a lotus in the second.
In the third [hand] here, he holds a rosary; in the fourth lotus-hand, a boon-granting gesture;
in the fifth hand, a wheel; and in the sixth, a thunderbolt upon a corpse.
In the seventh [hand] he holds a tomara, and in the eighth right hand a spear;
in the ninth he holds a radiant tusk, and in the tenth a candrahāsa sword.
In the eleventh hand he holds an arrow, in the twelfth a goad;
in the thirteenth a mace, and in the fourteenth the Turuṣka weapon.
In the first [hand] on the right is a sickle, and in the first on the left is a bowl;
here, in the second [left hand] is a citron, and in the third, indeed, a water-pot.
In the fourth hand there is the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and in the fifth there is a conch;
in the sixth lotus-hand there is a horn, and in the seventh there is an excellent kuta.
In the eighth hand he holds a spear (paṭṭiśa), and here in the ninth a staff (daṇḍa);
in the tenth he holds a shield (kheṭaka), and in the eleventh hand a bow (dhanus).
In the twelfth [hand] is a noose; right here in the thirteenth is a trident;
in the fourteenth is indeed a ten-faced [head]; and in the fifteenth hand is Arbuda.
Bestowing victory and health, it shall grant fearlessness to men.
Of the Nāga;
now the eleventh karaṇa is called Kiṃstughna. It is white as cow’s milk, wears yellow garments, and has the face of a horse.
Adorned with all ornaments and possessing thirty-two arms,
he holds a boon-granting gesture in the first right hand and a rosary in the second.
In his third lotus-hand he holds a radiant discus, in the fourth a lotus;
in the fifth hand he holds a sweetmeat, and in the sixth he rests upon a thunderbolt.
In the seventh [digit] is a javelin in his hand, and in the eighth is a spear;
in the ninth is an elephant-goad, and in the tenth is an excellent sword.
In the eleventh [digit], however, he holds Bāṇa; in the twelfth, Śṛṇi;
in the thirteenth, a mace; and in the fourteenth, a hand-drum (ḍamaru).
In the fifteenth [hand] she holds a book, and in the sixteenth a battle-axe;
in the first left [hand] she displays the gesture of fearlessness, and in the second a water-pot.
In this [rite], a conch shell is indeed for the third [day], a citron for the fourth;
in the fifth, a vessel of liquor, and in the sixth, a horn pleasing to the mind.
In the seventh [house], a spear; right here in the eighth, a battle-axe lying down;
in the ninth, a bamboo staff; and in the tenth, a shield.
In the eleventh hand there is a bow, and in the twelfth a vessel;
in the thirteenth there is indeed a trident, and in the fourteenth a chisel.
In the sixteenth [digit], one should hold a lute and an arrow in the hand, as well as a banner;
it should be worshipped by the wise for the destruction of enemies.
For one seeking the attainment of knowledge, contentment, victory, and other forms of happiness—
this is for Kintughna. These are the forms of the instrumental case.
[190] Now, the forms of the zodiac signs:
A man with the face of a ram, red in color, with two arms, seated upon a lotus,
marked with the *jñānamudrā*, wearing yellow garments, and adorned with golden armlets.
Of Aries:
A man with the face of a bull, white in color, wearing red garments, and possessing eyes like those of a water-jar. Of Taurus:
A man holding a mace or a woman holding a lute constitutes a white couple. Of this couple:
a man who is tawny, with a dog-like face, and bearing the tortoise-mudrā.
[The mantra] of Karkaṭaka:
Siṃhavaktra is red, seated upon a lotus, with two arms, and joined with the gesture of fearlessness and a vessel.
[This is] for Siṃha.
The maiden [Kanyā] holds a white sword, is white in complexion, two-armed, and seated upon a lotus.
Of the maiden:
the man [Tulādhara] holds a balance, is fair-complexioned, has tawny eyes, and is seated upon a lotus.
Of Tula:
A man situated in Scorpio is tawny, two-armed, and has the face of a monkey;
he holds a garland of scorpions in his right hand and a vessel filled with wine in his left.
[191] Of Scorpio: A man with the face of a horse, his right hand drawing the bowstring;
the bow.
The one who holds dice and a water-pot is Nīla; he is a man with the face of a deer.
[This is] for Makara.
The one with the face of a crocodile is white, situated in a fish, a man with an empty pitcher, and a jar.
Of Kumbha: dark-complexioned, seated upon a pair of fish, holding a fish in his hand, pot-bellied,
with the face of a fish, silent, and adorned with emeralds.

Regarding Mauna [Muni]: from the Viṣṇudharmottara—He should be depicted with a terrifying face, ever-moving, and fearsome; he should have a noose in his hand and hair consisting of snakes and scorpions.
Regarding the time [of the ritual], according to the Viśvakarma-śāstra:
here, his eye should be dark blue like a deep sapphire;
he holds a rosary in his right hand and the gesture of knowledge (jñāna-mudrā) in the left.
Wearing [these] for the sake of perfecting yoga, he is to be worshipped by the wise. Of the *nimeṣa*,
the *kāṣṭhā* shall be blue in color, wearing yellow garments, and three-eyed.
She is endowed with eighteen arms and holds a book of wisdom.
Of the *kāṣṭhā* [the North]:
she should be known as white in color, wearing blue garments, and having three eyes;
she wears a garland of sky-vajras, sprouts, and rudrākṣa beads suspended around her neck.
Holding a rosary of pearls and the sun, and joined with a lotus in her left hand,
she should be worshipped especially for the sake of attaining knowledge and wisdom.
Of the *kalā*: he is named Kṣaṇa, yellow in color, with the pearls of the sages' wings as his crest-ornament,
endowed with the three pearls of matted locks, and white as sandalwood paste.
In her left [hand] she holds a pearl necklace, a sun, and an elephant, while a golden water-pot is held in the other.
Now I shall speak of the Muhūrtas of the Kṣaṇa, each distinguished by a hundred thousand names and their respective fruits.
Among them, let the first be Raudrākṣa, possessing a complexion that is dark, white, and reddish.
Clad in white garments and very tall,
he holds a serpent in his right hand and a vessel filled with nectar in his left for the accomplishment of minor rites.
Of Raudra:
the second is named Sita, white in color and of great splendor;
his garments have the luster of white and red, and he is adorned with white pearls.
Holding a pure white lotus in his right hand and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in his left,
he who bestows two fortunes should be worshipped for the increase of yoga and for happiness.
Of the white one: the third is called Ajapa; he is black, brilliant, and large-bodied.
In his right hand is a blue lotus, and in his left is a serpent with a great hood.
Possessing vast enjoyments, he is worthy of worship by one of great intelligence.
Of Ajapa:
Turya, and the one named Āryabhaṭa, Nīla, Śubhra, and Mahodara;
in the right hand is a book, and in the left hand indeed a trident.
Maintaining this for the sake of excellence, prosperity, victory, and happiness.
From Āryabhaṭa:
And now, O Jaya, the fifth [sun], that of Savitṛ, is described;
he is white in color, has a horse for his vehicle, and is clothed in dark garments.
Holding a book in his right hand and a flawless sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in his left,
he should be worshipped day and night for the destruction of diseases.
This is the form of Sāvitra. Here, the sixth [deity] is indeed Vairāja, dark-complexioned and wearing matted locks;
in his right hand he holds a staff, and in his left hand a sacrificial ladle (sruva).
Bearing these for the sake of increase and happiness, he should be worshipped with supreme devotion.
[194] Here, the seventh Gandharva of Vairāja is Tāmra-varṇa, who has a slender waist.
One should hold a lute in the right hand and a spear in the left;
he should be worshipped by the wise for the increase of happiness and the increase of fame.
Now the eighth, named Abhijit, is described as auspicious:
he is yellowish in color, very short, copper-colored, and has a large belly.
Equipped with two hands holding cotton, he should be worshipped for the attainment of happiness.
The *abhijit* [nakṣatra] is to be understood by the wise as being that very same one called *kutapa*;
it is indeed very dear to the ancestors, as is this [time] when one holds the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) in hand.
O Jaya, the ninth muhūrta of Kutapa is said to be named Rauhiṇyeya;
he is white in color, large-eyed, wears blue garments, and has cloud-shaped earrings.
Holding a lotus in his right hand and a sweetmeat (modaka) in his left,
he bestows the attainment of happiness and the increase of victory and prosperity.
[This was] of Rauhineya.
Now, my child, the tenth [incarnation] named Bala is described:
he is fair-complexioned, with garments reddish-white, and adorned with golden earrings.
Holding a conch in his right hand and a lotus in his left.
[195] Of Vala: golden-hued, with large limbs, wearing black, white, and reddish garments;
holding a rosary in his right hand and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in his left.
Bestowing supreme happiness upon living beings and worthy of worship by the wise,
the eleventh Muhūrta, now known as Vijaya, should be understood.
Of Vijaya: now the twelfth muhūrta is to be known as named Nairṛta;
he has a blue lotus on his head, yellow garments, and great strength.
Holding a wheel in his right hand and displaying the gesture of fearlessness in his left.
Of Nairṛta:
here the thirteenth day shall be; he is red in color, named Satamasa, wearing copper-colored garments, possessed of great majesty, and adorned with earrings of jewels and gold.
His right hand holds a red lotus, while his left is endowed with a water-pot.
And here, the fourteenth muhūrta of the month of Śrāvaṇa is said to be named Varuṇa;
he resembles a pearl and is adorned with a pearl necklace.
And one who bears a bow and arrows should also be honored for the attainment of happiness.
[This is] of Varuṇa.
Now, the fifteenth should be known as Subhaga, who has a green luster.
[This is] of Subhaga.
Now we shall describe the night-wandering Muhūrtas, equal in number to the lunar days (tithis).
Among them, the first is named Atiraudra, black in color and wearing crimson garments.
Four-armed and exceedingly fierce, consisting solely of a collection of bones,
he holds in his first right hand a most terrifying owl.
In his second hand he holds a snake, while in the left hand he holds a pair of tongs;
below that, he holds a vessel, destroying all obstacles.
Of Atiraudra,
there is indeed a second [son] there named Mahāgandharvarāja;
he has a neck that is black, white, and reddish, wears blue garments, and possesses great strength.
Four-armed, large-eyed, fair-complexioned, and wearing matted locks;
in his first right hand he holds a conch, and in the second, a lotus.
Holding a lute in his upper left hand and a bowl in the one below it,
he should be worshipped by the wise for the attainment of their desires.
Now, the third [son] of the great Gandharva king is described as Draviṇa, born of Night;
he has the luster of molten gold and wears garments that are black, blue, and reddish-brown.
In the first right hand is an exceedingly beautiful lotus made of gold;
in the second right hand is a lute, and in the upper left hand is a citron.
May it be for the increase of all prosperity, happiness, longevity, and glory.
[197] Of Draviṇa: the fourth is named Śrāvaṇa; he is blue in color, wears earrings of the sun, is clothed in blue and reddish garments, and wears a garland of blue lotuses around his neck.
Holding a sword in his first right hand and a lotus in the second,
and carrying a lute in his upper left hand and a vessel below it,
he— thus established— is to be worshipped for the sake of attaining knowledge and wisdom.
Now, the fifth muhūrta of Śrāvaṇa is described; it is named Vāyu.
He is green in color, with ears like hibiscus flowers, clad in white garments, and possessed of great strength.
In her first right hand she holds a parrot, and in the second a banner;
in her upper left hand she holds a plough, and in the second a vessel.
[The mantra] of Vāyu;
then the sixth, named Agni, resembling a javā flower,
endowed with black-blue garments, and joined with a crest and rudrākṣa beads.
Holding a vessel in his first right hand and a spear in the second,
and holding a parrot in his first left hand and a plough in the second—
[one should meditate on him] for the sake of renown, worldly enjoyment, and the increase of victory and longevity.
Of Agni.
Now it is told, O child, that the seventh is named Rākṣasa;
he has dark blue color and fierce fangs, and wears garments that are blue, white, and reddish-brown.
Holding a lotus in his first right hand and a trident in the second,
a khaṭvāṅga in his first left hand and a bowl in the one below it,
he who destroys enmity should be worshipped by practitioners.
Of the Rākṣasa: And Dhātṛ is the eighth, yellow in color, wearing saffron-colored garments,
with golden earrings set with sphoṭika gems, and possessing a neck like a conch shell.
Holding a pustī-mark and other items in his first right hand, and a seat (viṣṭara) in the second;
holding a rice-ball (piṇḍa) in his first left hand and a golden earring in the second—
he is thus for the sake of pleasure, enjoyment, victory, and happiness.
The ninth is named Saumya; he is white in color, large-eyed,
wears yellow garments, possesses great majesty, and has all his limbs adorned with pearls.
Holding a conch in the first right hand and a lotus in the second,
and a bowl in the first left hand and a plow in the second—
thus worshipped for the sake of contentment and worldly enjoyment, he is the bestower of liberation.
Of Saumya,
the tenth muhūrta here is to be known as Brahman;
it is yellow in color, wears white garments, and is endowed with matted hair and a crown.
This man has a rosary of rudrākṣa beads around his neck, white sandalwood paste on his forehead,
is adorned with golden earrings, and wears a waist-thread and an upper garment.
In the first hand [on the right], he holds a rosary; in the second, a lotus;
in the upper left hand, a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*); and in the hand below that, a book.
Bearing these, he grants the attainment of gold and pearls, as well as victory.
Of Brahmā: now the eleventh is to be known by the name Vākpati;
he is golden-hued and clad in black and white garments.
In his first right hand he holds a water-pot (*kuṇḍī*) and in the second a plow (*sīra*);
in his first left hand he holds grain (*kīra*) and in the second a lotus (*nīraja*).
He bestows progeny and brings about the accomplishment of one's tasks.
Vākpati is the twelfth deity here; he is known by the name Pauṣṇa, and is deep red in color.
He wears yellow garments, has matted hair and a crown, and his ears are adorned with sage-flowers.
Pot-bellied and wearing a sacred thread, he is white like a blue sacrificial post;
in his first hand, beginning with the right, he holds a bright yellow citron fruit.
In the second [hand] he holds a lotus, and in the first left hand a bowl;
holding a pair of tongs in the second [left hand], he is the remover of the calamities of enemies.
Now, regarding Pauṣṇa: here indeed is to be told the thirteenth [chapter], named Vaikuṇṭha;
this [deity] is white from the feet to the knees, with a neck of youthful color.
He is golden-colored, with earrings made of many jewels at the ends of his hair;
in his first right hand he holds a book, and in the second a lotus.
Holding a peacock feather in his first left hand and a parasol in the second,
he should be worshipped with white lotuses for the sake of renown and worldly enjoyment.
Of Vaikuṇṭha,
the fourteenth is now to be known by the name Samīraṇa;
he resembles the color of water-lilies and possesses the luster of beautiful emeralds.
Wearing garments with white, blue, and reddish borders, and possessing tender eyes,
he holds a palm leaf in the second hand and a blue lotus in the presence of the sun.
Holding a vessel in his first left hand and a blue lotus in the second,
he brings prosperity to the sacrificer, as well as growth of progeny and happiness.
Of the wind [deity].
Now, the fifteenth muhūrta is to be known as Nairṛta-Aruṇa;
he has the luster of a dark cloud, possesses three eyes, has fangs, and wears reddish garments.
Holding an arrow in the first right hand and a lotus in the second,
and a bow in the first left hand and likewise a water-lily in the second—
bearing these for the sake of peace, excellent enjoyment, strength, and victory.
These are all the night-roaming *muhūrtas* known to you, beginning with Nairṛta; and here,
the one called *Ahorātra* has black neck and hair at the crown of his head.
This [deity] is white from the neck down to the feet, has two arms, and long fingers;
he wears a crown of matted hair with a full moon, and his beard and eyes are tawny.
Adorned with a garland of human skulls and clothed in black and white garments,
he should be worshipped by the wise for the sake of attaining the fruits of their sacrifices and charitable works.
Of the day and night, the bright fortnight is the man: he is white-complexioned, endowed with a crown of matted locks,
wearing crimson garments, large-eyed, and adorned with a tilaka upon his forehead.
Holding the sun upon the sun-disk and the lunar orb in his left hand,
he is to be worshipped with great devotion on every bright first day of the fortnight.
Its twelve divisions should be understood according to the distinction of colors;
it is to be worshipped with great force, distinguished by each month.
The bright fortnight is white;
the dark fortnight, however, is dark-hued. The powerful one wears white and red garments, holds the solar disc in his right hand, and a radiant island in his left.
He is to be worshipped with great power according to the distinctions of each month;
thus, there are various divisions of this [deity] known by the names of the lunar mansions, fortnights, and so forth.
Of the dark fortnight;
by its own name, however, it shall be the month; it has two colors and two eyes.
He whose hair is not above [the head], who is white and black, who has tawny eyes, and whose hair grows upward—[he is the one].
This very [deity], accompanied by the sun and moon, is worshipped every month with mantras preceded by his own name and concluding with fire offerings (homa) and ritual worship.
[202] Of the month;
furthermore, we shall describe the six seasons by their characteristic names and distinct fruits.
Among them, the first is called Hemanta (winter), whose deity is Kapila, who has reddish-brown earrings.
Clad in yellow garments, he had three matted locks and wore a black lizard as an amulet.
The forehead is the cow’s head.
The grain [vessel], however, is rich with *añjarikā* and serves as the lid for the left bowl;
it should be worshipped for the sake of prosperity and for the increase of the abundance of grain.
Of the winter season: the second, however, is named Śiśira; it resembles green, yellow, and reddish-brown;
it has yellow earrings on its ears and a necklace of coral upon its neck.
Holding a vessel marked with the blossoms of the honey-tree in his right lotus-hand,
and a bowl of grain in his left, he brings about the increase of one's desires.
[The ritual] for Śiśira.
However, that which was stated in the section on Viṣṇu should be understood here as [the ritual] for Vasantaka.
[The ritual] for Vasanta.
The fourth, named Grīṣma, is smoke-colored with a rough body;
he holds a rosary and the sun in his right hands and carries a white parasol in his left.
He, the destroyer of the enemy faction, should be worshipped for the destruction of the torment of disease.
Of the summer season:
the fifth [deity] of that season is yellowish-green in color with reddish-brown eyes,
clad in garments of copper hue, and wearing earrings of black coral.
When the Sun is in Pisces, one should worship him holding a fish in his hand and a water-filled jar in the other;
he is surrounded by a garland of clouds and possesses the blazing radiance of lightning and fire.
He is to be worshipped with plates of yellow orpiment for the sake of nourishment, contentment, and prosperity.
Then follows the autumn season, the sixth, white as the moon, with beautiful eyes,
wearing a pearl necklace upon his neck and crescent-moon earrings upon his ears.
Holding the lunar disc in his right hand and a jar of nectar in his left,
he should be worshipped for the increase of longevity and for happiness.
Autumn;
then the one known as the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), who is dark-complexioned, with eyes like those of Soma and Indra,
wearing yellow garments, possessing a large snout, and ears like the petals of the karṇikāra flower.
The seed, the sprout, the bowl, the sun, the shovel, and the raised hand— these,
when constantly worshipped, lead to accomplishment and the abundance of wealth and grain.
Then, for the southern course,
there is one known as the northern course: auspicious in appearance, large-eyed,
clad in madder-dyed garments, and adorned with gold and pearls.
Holding a book in his right hand and the solar disc in his left,
he should be worshipped for the sake of enjoyment, joy, and indeed for fame.
Of the northern course [of the sun].
[204] Now we shall describe the years beginning from Lakṣa-phala:
the first is named Prabhava, yellow in color and large-bellied.
Clad in blue garments and adorned with golden earrings on his right ear,
he has the color of crystal on his left side and three matted locks hanging down from his back.
In his first right hand he holds a spear, and in the second a lotus;
in the first left lotus-hand he holds a shallow bowl filled with seeds,
and in the second he holds a pair of tongs, for the sake of increasing nourishment.
The second [deity] of Prabhava is named Vibhava; he has a complexion of blue, yellow,
and reddish hues, wears yellow and white garments at the ends, and holds a rosary of lotus seeds around his neck.
Holding an arrow in his first right hand, a blue lotus in the second,
a pair of tongs in the one situated in the upper left, and a bow in the second [left],
he should always be worshipped by the wise for the sake of prosperity.
Of Vibhava:
the third, named Śukla, resembles one who is white and tawny;
he holds a lotus and a rosary at his neck, and wears garments with bright borders and bees.
Holding a shallow vessel (śarāva) in the first [hand] facing south and an arrow in the second;
a mirror in the first facing north and a bow in the second— he,
for the welfare of mortals, should be worshipped by those of perfected self.
Of the White [Family]:
the fourth is named Pramoda; he has a blue neck and a large belly, wears white garments, resembles a lotus, and has a yogapaṭṭa as an upper cloth.
Holding a pair of tongs in the first right hand and a plow in the second;
and holding a shallow bowl in the first left hand and a blue lotus in the second—
he brings about happiness, enjoyment, victory, and greatness.
Of Pramoda: here, the fifth is indeed named Prajāpati; he resembles gold, is richly adorned with red ornaments and garments, is pot-bellied, and is fair-pale in complexion.
If situated in the direction of Yama (the south), he holds a rosary in his second hand;
if situated in the northern direction, he holds a book in his second hand while seated upon a corpse.
He should be worshipped by one who knows [the truth] for the increase of progeny and for prosperity.
From Prajāpati came the one named Aṅgiras; he was the sixth [son], fair-complexioned, with very fine body hair,
wearing copper-colored garments, possessed of great splendor, twelve-limbed, and adorned with sandalwood paste.
With purificatory darbha grass in his hand and his head adorned with matted locks,
he holds the sword of knowledge in his right hand and sacrificial fuel in his second hand.
Holding a shallow vessel in her first left hand and the staff of Brahma in the second,
she, being well-worshipped, bestows prosperity, excellence, and happiness.
The seventh [son] of Aṅgiras is named Śrīmukha; he is yellow in color, large-eyed,
clothed in pale-red garments, and possesses long ears and beautiful curls.
Abounding in ornaments of gold and jewels, it brings about the destruction of all misfortunes;
the *śrīphala* is situated in the south, and the lotus (*paṅkaja*) is in the second [direction].
Holding a lotus in his upper left hand and a water-jug below it,
he is worshipped with sandalwood paste and other offerings for the sake of nourishment and prosperity.
Of Śrīmukha: the eighth therein is named Bhāva, possessing a complexion that is blue, white, and reddish;
his garment is yellow with black and red borders, and he wears variegated earrings.
This [deity] has a garland of pearls and coral, and his matted locks are tawny-eyed;
in the first right hand he holds a book, and in the second a garment.
Holding a trident in his upper left hand and a vessel of liquor below it,
he is indeed to be worshipped for the attainment of grain and for prosperity.
Of Bhāva: here the ninth is called Yuvan, with the hue of a trumpet-flower (pāṭala), with reddish eyes,
wearing blue garments, with matted hair rising high, and adorned with dark jewel-earrings.
Holding a conch in his first right hand and the Sudarśana discus in the second,
and a vessel in his first left hand and a blue lotus in the second—
bearing these for the sake of splendor, he should be worshipped for the increase of prosperity and good fortune.
Of the one called Yuvākhya:
Dhātṛ alone is to be recognized as the tenth, with tawny eyes,
wearing garments that are white at the center and reddish at the edges, and adorned with white earrings.
In the first right hand she holds a shallow bowl, in the second a citron;
in the upper left hand a book, and in the one below it a blue water-lily.
[207] For the sake of victory and the attainment of sons, he should be worshipped with sincere devotion.
Of the one called Dhātṛ,
this eleventh [form] is to be known here as indeed named Īśvara;
he has the luster of a white water-lily, possesses three eyes, and bears on his crest a mass of matted hair with a crescent moon.
Adorned with ornaments of pearls, crystal, and rudrākṣa beads, and possessing a prominent nose,
he holds a trident in his first right hand and a plow in the second.
Holding a shallow bowl in his first left hand and a book in the second,
he should be worshipped for the sake of happiness, the increase of yoga, and the attainment of sons.
Of Īśvara:
the twelfth is named Bahudhānya; he has a yellow, blue, and reddish luster, wears yellow garments, has large eyes, a protruding belly, and long fingers.
This [deity] wears a garland of Java flowers, is clad in armor, and possesses armlets;
in his right hand he holds a golden pitcher filled with all kinds of grain.
In his first hand is a hero’s skull-cup with a lid studded with many jewels;
in his second hand is a ḍamaru drum, and above that, a blue lotus.
In his second hand, however, he holds a plough that bears all kinds of grain;
for the sake of accomplishment, he should be worshipped daily, consecrated with his own name and the initial syllables [of the mantra].
Of Bahudhanya:
the first is named Pramāthin; he is white in color, possesses mighty arms, is endowed with three matted locks, bears a long burden, and wears earrings of the sun.
Clad in red and blue garments, adorned with many golden rings,
he holds a cuckoo and a sun-disk in his first hand, and a water-pot in the second.
Holding a noose in his upper left hand and a water-vessel beneath it,
he acts for the destruction of enemies and for the nourishment of his own followers.
The [first] is Pramāthin;
the second, however, is named Vikrama, who is dark-blue and white,
has a large belly, wears yellow garments, possesses a great garland, and wears a necklace of pearls around his neck.
In the first right hand is a conch, and in the second, a lotus;
in the first left hand is a bowl, and in the second here, a noose.
Even though he possesses excessive power, he must nevertheless be honored with great effort.
Of Vikrama:
the third, named Vṛṣa, is white-grey with large eyes, thick hair, and is exceedingly joyful; he has a ketaki leaf as an ear-ornament.
Wearing garments with yellow borders and red accents, and a girdle-bell at his waist;
he holds a noose in his first right hand and a conch shell in the second.
In her left hand she holds a vessel, and in the second, a deer;
for the sake of the increase of wealth and grain, she should be worshipped with great reverence.
Of Vṛṣa:
the fourth is named Citrabhānu; he has a variegated neck, wears crimson garments, resembles the interior of a pearl, is a granter of boons, and wears golden earrings.
Holding a garland of pearls in his first right hand and a rosary in the second;
and holding a conch in his first left hand and an auspicious lotus in the second—
he should be worshipped for the attainment of bliss and for the increase of all desired objects.
Of Citrabhānu:
the fifth is named Śubhānvā, auspicious with a brilliant crimson luster;
his throat is marked by three red lines, and his matted locks resemble gold.
Holding a lotus in his first right hand and a radiant conch in the second;
in his upper left hand he holds a noose, and in the one below it a goad— bearing these,
he bestows peace upon the three factions of enemies.
Of Subhānu: here the sixth year is called Tāraṇa;
he is clad in white garments, and is white, blue, and reddish-brown, adorned with golden earrings.
Holding a water-pot in his first right hand and a lotus in the second,
and holding a noose in his first left hand and a conch in the second,
he exists for the destruction of manifold miserable rebirths, and for prosperity and victory.
Of Tāraṇa:
the seventh is indeed named Pārthiva; he resembles molten gold, wears yellow and red garments, has a black neck, and is exceedingly handsome.
Richly adorned with all kinds of jewel ornaments and having a *ketakī* petal as his crest,
he holds a shaft in his first right hand and a lotus in the second.
Holding a bow when situated in the second house from the North (Uttarā), and likewise a conch shell,
he should be worshipped with great effort for the attainment of sovereignty and other blessings.
[210] Of the Pārthiva: the eighth is called Avyaya; he resembles the white and red water-lily (kairava), wears garments that are black, blue, reddish, and white, and possesses variegated earrings.
Holding a goad and other implements in his first right hand, and a plow in the second;
and holding a conch in his first left hand, and a noose in the second—
he is for the constant prosperity, growth, longevity, and glory of the sacrificer.
Of the Imperishable One:
here, the ninth among all the Victors is white-blue with black radiance;
he has blue garments and high matted locks, and wears earrings of black lotuses.
Holding an arrow in his first right hand and a book in the second,
and holding a vessel in his first left hand and another vessel in the second—
this one, thus depicted, should be worshipped for victory and happiness.
O child, the tenth, Sarvadhāraka, is now described:
he resembles a heron’s feather and is clothed in garments of pale red.
Having the color of a blue lotus and adorned with pearl necklaces,
he holds a noose in his first hand and a ketaki petal in the second.
Holding a conch shell when situated in the north and a book in the second [position],
he brings about victory, health, and prosperity for the sacrificer.
[He is] the Sustainer of All.
Now the eleventh year should be known as Virodhin;
his body is black and pale, he is the Bestower of Boons, and he wears blue earrings.
With a border black and a fringe red, adorned with the edge of his garment;
first, the bimba fruit, and second, the white lotus at the beginning of the sun [and other signs].
Holding a serpent in his first left hand and a noose in the second,
he should be worshipped for the destruction of enemies and for the increase of the strength of the sacrificer.
The twelfth, known as Vikṛta, is hostile; he is smoky-colored with tawny eyes,
clad in blue and white garments, and wears earrings made from the horns of rams.
Holding a noose in his first right hand and a goat horn in the second,
and holding a conch in his upper left hand and a noose in the hand below it,
he brings about the destruction of disease and the subjugation of wicked enemies.
From Vikṛti [arose] Kharābhidhāna; he was the first [of them], red in color, with a large belly,
wearing blue garments, possessing a massive forehead, and having thick, matted hair.
Holding a spear in his first right hand and a sword in the second,
and holding a vessel in his first left hand and a fly-whisk in the second—
this [deity] is to be worshipped for the tormenting of enemies and for the victory of the sacrificer.
Of Kharas: the second, named Nandana, is powerful, with a face that is yellowish-red,
clad in white garments, with matted hair hanging down, long ears, and seated upon a lotus.
In the second hand located at the beginning of Yama (the south), there is a lotus;
in the second hand at the beginning of Indra (the east), there is a spear, a vajra, and a goad.
Bestowing excellence and prosperity, he is worthy of worship and possesses great fortune.
Of Nandana:
the third, however, named Vijaya, has a complexion white, yellow, and reddish;
he wears black garments, has thin and lofty matted locks, and carries a rosary of rudrākṣa beads.
Holding a rosary in his first right hand and a thunderbolt in the second,
and holding a spear in his first left hand and a lotus in the second—
thus worshipped, he brings about victory, health, and prosperity.
Of Vijaya: the fourth here is named Jaya; he is yellowish-red, pure, and happy.
He wears yellow garments, has a single lock of matted hair, and is encircled by a yellow-colored halo.
Holding a book in his first right hand and a blue lotus in the second,
and holding a vajra in his first left hand and a spear (śakti) in the second,
he is worshipped for the sake of auspiciousness and the increase of prosperity.
Of Jaya:
the fifth is named Manmatha; he is blue and red, pure and auspicious, adorned with golden earrings, and his garment resembles the wings of a parrot.
Mallikādhanvabāṇa, however, has a garland made of mūrvā flowers;
he holds a staff in his right hand and a lotus in the second.
Holding a book in his first left hand and a spear in the second,
he grants success, prosperity, and the power to bring women under one's control.
[213] Of Manmatha: And the sixth year here is to be known as named Durmukha;
he has a crest like a parrot’s beak and wears blue earrings.
In her first right hand she holds a spear, and in the second a thunderbolt;
in her first left hand she holds a parrot, and in the second a serpent.
He whose face is curved with a frown should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite for the destruction of wicked enemies and for the pacification of all diseases.
Of Durmukha:
the seventh is named Hemalamba, with a complexion resembling red and yellow;
he has vulture wings and a goad, and is adorned with jeweled earrings.
O Victorious One, for the sake of enjoyment, you hold a golden lotus in your first right sprout-like hand,
a thunderbolt in the second, and a supreme vessel in your first left hand,
while holding a spear in the second.
Of Hemalamba: the eighth, however, is named Vilamba, with the hue of a trumpet-flower (pāṭala), slender-waisted,
wearing yellow garments and a large garland, adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon.
Holding a serpent in his first right hand and a spear in the second,
and holding a vessel in his first left hand and a lotus in the second— thus bearing these for the destruction of enemies, he should be worshipped with special care.
Of Vilamba:
the ninth is Vikārī, possessing a dark-blue and reddish luster;
he is adorned with copper earrings and fine garments, and has three red lines upon his neck.
Holding an arrow in his first right hand and a book in the second,
and holding a bow in his first left hand and a spear in the second—
he should be worshipped especially for the pacification of all diseases.
They were subject to transformation.
The tenth resembled the night of the new moon, with a complexion that was black, white, and reddish;
he wore crimson garments, possessed exceedingly long limbs, and had coarse, thick hair on his head.
Holding a serpent in his first right hand and a *śālmalī* leaf in the second,
and holding a *kauśika* in his first left hand and a spear (*śakti*) in the second—
when worshipped, he brings fame, nourishment, and the destruction of enemies.
The Śārvarins:
the eleventh is named Plava, whose complexion resembles the ear of a hare,
who is endowed with a garment like the color of a frog, and is equipped with earrings of copper.
In his first right hand he holds a water-jar joined with a jewel;
in the second [right] hand a spear; in the first left hand a vessel;
and in the second [left] hand he bears a lotus. Thus bearing these, the slayer of enemies is to be worshipped.
Of Plava:
Śubhakṛt is also the twelfth here; he resembles an elephant, has beautiful eyes, is clothed in pale-red garments, and is adorned with black earrings.
In her first right hand she holds a terrifying spear,
in the second a golden lotus; in her first left hand she holds a mirror,
and in the second a thunderbolt— she who bestows happiness and prosperity.
Śubhakṛt;
Śobhakṛt is yellowish-brown, while the first [is] clad in blue garments,
adorned with blue ornaments, and has fingers marked with jewel-seals.
Holding a water-pot in his first right hand and a book in the second,
and a bowl in his first left hand and a banner in the second—
he, being worshipped, leads to prosperity, nourishment, and victory.
Śobhakṛt; the second, however, is named Krodhin, blue and white, with a lean belly, clad in dark blue garments,
and possessing a prominent nose and a pale complexion.
Holding a lotus and a sun-disk in his first right hand, and a banner in the second; and holding a lotus in his first left hand, and a plough in the second— he,
being well-worshipped with black substances, brings about the destruction of enemies.
The wrathful ones:
Viśvāvasu is the third; he has a black neck, very restless eyes, wears garments that are black, white, and reddish at the edges, and possesses variegated earrings.
Holding a banner in his first hand, a thunderbolt in the second, and a conch,
