he grants enjoyment, pleasure, and the attainment of fruits consisting of various delights.
Of Viśvāvasu:
Parābhava was the fourth; then Dhūmara, Aruṇajāmbra, Nīlotpalaśruti, and Kṣudraghaṇṭikamekhala. [216]
In his first right hand he holds a blue lotus, and in the second, a banner;
in his first left hand he holds a vessel, and in the second, a pair of tongs. He who destroys the enemies should be worshipped by the wise in this form.
Regarding defeat:
the fifth, however, is named Plavaṅga; it resembles a deer skin, has the appearance of a sheep's belly, and possesses joined black cavities.
Holding a banner in his first right hand and a ram’s horn in the second,
and holding a vessel in his first left hand and a noose in the second—
he who bestows prosperity should always be worshipped by men for their well-being.
Then the sixth [son] of Plavaṅga is named Kila; he is black in color, exceedingly tall,
wears blue garments, has a mass of matted hair, and is adorned with black earrings.
Holding a *kīlaka* (stake) in his second hand on the right side, and likewise a banner (*dhvaja*) in the first left hand, and a noose (*pāśa*) in the second [left hand]—
he who is thus worshipped brings about victory, health, and prosperity.
Next, the seventh auspicious year, named Saumya, is proclaimed for the Kīlaka [year]. He possesses blue and yellow matted locks and wears garments resembling the petals of a plantain tree.
He has ears like golden leaves, a garland upon his lotus-like neck,
the moon and sun in his first hand, and a ketaki petal in the second.
Holding a banner in his first left hand and a beautiful lotus in the second,
he should be worshipped with great devotion for the attainment of good fortune.
Of Saumya:
the eighth [form] is to be known as common, with a complexion that is blue, white, and reddish;
he wears yellow and red garments at the ends, and is adorned with golden earrings and jewels.
Holding the Candrahāsa sword in his first [right] hand, the Kīlaka in the second,
the Dhvaja in the left hand, and the Saṃsaṃśa in the fourth,
he should be worshipped with white lotuses for the increase of wealth and the attainment of happiness.
And the ninth year, Jaya, should be known as causing obstacles for one who is common [to both].
He has the luster of a cuckoo, wears white garments, and has tawny eyebrows and eyes.
Holding a conch in his first right hand and a banner in the second,
and a sword in his first left hand and an axe in the second,
may he who brings torment to enemies grant victory for the destruction of disease.
The tenth year is to be known as Paridhāvī;
it has the hue of a blue lotus, is reddish-white, and its garments appear black and yellow.
Brahmaprasavakarṇa, however, has a garland of lotuses upon his neck;
he holds a cuckoo in his first hand and a banner in the second.
Holding a bell in his first left hand and a mallet in the second,
he bestows increase in prosperity, well-being, happiness, and longevity.
[218] One who runs about should also be known as negligent, even if he has completed eleven years [of practice]. He resembles the flax flower and wears garments that are greenish-blue and reddish.
With eyes rolling from intoxication, as if overcome by drowsiness and sluggish,
he held a staff in his first hand and another staff in the second.
Holding a vessel in his first left hand and a lotus petal in the second,
the sacrificer [is worshipped] for the alleviation of disease and the destruction of enemies.
For those who are heedless,
the twelfth [deity] here is indeed named Ānanda; he is white, wears yellow garments,
is adorned with pearls, sapphires, and gold, and has blue earrings.

In the second [digit] starting from the south, there is a lotus; in the upper left hand, a ketaki petal; and in the one below it, a banner and a sweetmeat (modaka). He should be worshipped with scents, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings for the subjugation of women.
Of Ānanda:
the first year of those under the influence of tamas shall be named Rākṣasa;
he will have the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, wear golden garments, and be adorned with the sun.
Holding a sun-disc in his first right hand and a sickle in the second,
and a blue lotus in his first left hand and a vajra resting upon his lap in the second—
he, who bestows the destruction of diseases and other afflictions, is to be worshipped by the Sthāṇus themselves.
Of the Rākṣasa: the second, however, is named Anala, possessing a complexion that is dark blue, auspiciously reddish, and yellow at the edges;
he is clothed in garments like bees and adorned with earrings of diamonds.
Holding the Candrahāsa sword in his hand positioned toward the east, the discus in the second (south),
the flesh (of enemies) in the direction of the north, and the supreme axe in the other (west),
he grants great prosperity to the sacrificer and leads him surely to victory over his foes.
Of Anala:
the third here is named Piṅgala, resembling a white lotus and red;
he wears garments that are white at the edges, reddish, and blue, and is adorned with golden ornaments.
In the first [hand] he holds flesh, in the second to the south a plow, and in the first to the left a thunderbolt;
in the second [left hand] he holds the syllable *saṃsaṃśaṃ*.
Thus worshipped, he brings about victory, health, and prosperity.
Of Piṅgala:
the fourth is named Kālayukta; he is Nīlakaṇṭha, Vṛkodara, clothed in yellowish-red garments, and adorned with ornaments made of blue and gold.
In his first right hand he holds a serpent, and in the second a plow;
in his first left hand a vessel of liquor, and in the second a stake.
He should be worshipped especially by the sacrificer for the death of his enemies.
For one joined with the [proper] time;
now, O child, the fifth [deity] named Siddhārtha is proclaimed:
he resembles molten gold and wears garments that are blue, white, and reddish-brown.
Adorned with blue earrings and decorated with pearls and coral,
he holds a golden pitcher in his first right hand.
Holding a blue lotus and a vajra in the upper right and left hands respectively,
and a citron below them, he brings about welfare and joy.
Of Siddhārtha:
then the sixth is named Raudra, who is tawny, dark-red,
clad in pale-red garments, and has short, curly hair.
In the first hand he holds a parrot, in the second a plow;
in the third hand a water-pot, and in the fourth a fuel-basket; in the remaining [hands] he rests upon a conch-shell.
This one should be worshipped against adversaries for the destruction of disease and for the attainment of enjoyment.
Of Raudra:
this seventh [form] is described as having the luster of a dark-blue cloud and being very evil-minded;
he holds a conch shell, the sun, and so forth in his hands, and possesses a golden girdle and jewels.
In this second [form], he indeed lies upon Indra and others with a small water-pot;
holding a book in his second hand, he causes enmity among enemies.
Of the evil-minded one:
in the eighth [birth], he is like a drum, with a blue neck and large eyes;
moon-colored, wearing white lotuses as garments, and having black lizards for skin.
On the forehead of this [deity] adorned with a crown of matted locks, there is an auspicious mark with the luster of a golden leaf;
on the second [hand], there is a plantain fruit, and on the first, a conch shell.
Holding a citron in his first left hand and a cluster of grain in his second,
he should always be worshipped by men for the sake of wealth and food.
Of Dundubhi:
the ninth is Rudhirodgārī, joined by the deity Nīlaśoṇāli;
he wears garments that are black-edged, reddish, and white, and is adorned with blue ornaments.
Red-eyed, with matted hair of tawny hue, and anointed with red sandalwood paste;
he holds a red lotus in the second hand positioned at the northeast, and a thunderbolt in the one resting on his lap.
Holding meat in his first hand and a goad in his second,
he should be worshipped when situated in the north for the destruction of enemies, and indeed for the increase of the sacrificer's hair.
Vomiting blood;
and the tenth is Raktākṣī, Nīlakaṇṭha, Kṛśodara,
Pītanīlatanu, and Nīlaśoṇālikāmbara.
Holding an arrow in his first hand and a lotus in the second,
and a plow in his first hand and a knife in the second,
he who bestows the destruction of enemies should be worshipped with great effort.
Raktākṣī.
Now, my child, the eleventh, named Krodhana, is described:
he resembles a water-laden cloud and is clothed in yellow and red garments.
Adorned with iron ornaments, with a lotus situated in the midst of his hair,
he holds a trident in his right hand, which is joined with a dried piece of meat at its tip.
In the second [hand], she holds a pair of scissors; in the first left hand, a vessel of liquor;
and in the second [left hand], she indeed holds a pair of tongs for the death of her enemies.
For the wrathful one,
there shall be the twelfth year here called Kṣaya;
he has a black neck, a very blue body, red eyes, and wears matted hair.
Wearing garments of variegated and reddish-brown, with blue and reddish-brown side-panels,
he holds a serpent in his first right hand and a noose in the second.
Holding a jar of poison in his first left hand and deceit in the second,
and bearing a black flower, he is the destroyer of enemies.
Of destruction.
Thus end the forms of the deities.
Now follows the procedure for the installation of the planets, according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
One should know Bhāskara (the Sun) to be in the center; Lohita (Mars) to the south;
Guru (Jupiter) to the north; and Soma (the Moon) to the southeast.
One should know Śani to be in the west, Rāhu in the southwest,
and one should place Ketu in the northwest using white rice grains.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: One should place Śambhu to the north of the Sun, Umā to the south of the Moon,
and Skanda to the south of Aṅgāraka (Mars).
Know that Viṣṇu is to the southwest, Brahmā to the east of Jīva, Indra in the eastern direction from Śita, and Yama in front of Mandāgni.
One should place Kāla, who brings fear to all beings, in the north-eastern direction from Rāhu;
and one should install Citragupta in the south-western quarter from Ketu.
Having installed Gaṇādhipa, who is saluted by all the gods, to the north of Saturn and the Sun, and to the south of Jupiter and Ketu.
Having established the presiding deities of the locations and their respective counter-deities,
one should place Vināyaka and others, as well as Durgā and others, between the planets and the gods.
In another Smṛti:
"Having established Indra in the east, likewise Yama, the Lord of the Dead, in the south;
Varuṇa in the western quarter, and Kubera in the north."
One should place Agni and the other world-protectors in the corner regions;
the wise practitioner should invoke the Vasus on the right side of Indra.
Between Deveśa and Īśāna is the path of the Ādityas;
they know the path of the Rudras to be in the western part of Agni.
One should designate the station of the Mothers between the Lord of the Dead (Yama) and the Rākṣasas;
they know the abode of Gaṇeśa to be in the northern part of Nairṛta.
The abode of Kubera and the Maruts is thus described. Now follows the origin and the characteristics of the *kalaśa* (vase). In the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"One should make the *kalaśas* very firm; I shall tell you their characteristics.
O Sage, I shall explain their origin, characteristics, and measurements."
These were proclaimed in the world as the *vārikas* and *kalaśas*,
[the vessels] for the purpose of drinking by all the deities while the nectar was being churned.
Having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope,
the nectar of great heroism and prowess was produced there.
This jar is proclaimed for the purpose of containing that [nectar],
having been fashioned by Viśvakarman from taking a portion of each of the portions of the gods.
Because this vessel was fashioned by the gods, it is called a *kalaśa*;
likewise, because it wards off various planetary influences as well as the *mātṛ*s.
And because they likewise ward off misfortunes and terrors, they are known as *vārakas*.
Brahmā is at the mouth of the jar, while Maheśvara is at its neck.
Viṣṇu is established at the root, the hosts of Mothers are situated in the middle,
and all the deities surround [the tree] on the branches in the four directions.
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth, they indeed reside within the water-pot;
likewise, peace, prosperity, and affection with one's kinsmen abide in the home.
The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and likewise the Sāmaveda,
as well as the Saṃhitās of the Atharvaveda— all are situated within the pitcher.
Those golden lotuses are filled with nectar-like water,
whether it be from rivers, lakes, autumnal waters, or the water of ponds and the like.
Bringing happiness through divine ponds, wells, and oceans,
they are the most auspicious of all auspicious things and the destroyers of all sins.
Such auspicious jars as these should always be taken for consecration,
or at the time of a procession, a wedding, an installation, or a sacrificial rite.
[225] These should be applied specifically as accomplishing all ritual actions.
The width of the jars should be fifty finger-breadths, their height sixteen finger-breadths,
and the mouth of the jars should be eight finger-breadths.
From the Nṛsiṃhakhaṇḍa of the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
Bhṛgu said:
"Tuṅgā and Bhadrā are two sister rivers born from the Sahya mountain."
O child, having established Keśava on the bank of those two [rivers], Bhadrā—
Having propitiated that Lord of the World with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order,
one should place the collection of senses within the heart and restrain the mind with effort.
O child, meditating with one-pointed mind upon the Lord of Gods in the heart-lotus, who holds the conch, discus, and mace, one should practice the twelve-syllable mantra.
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva!
For one who recites this mantra of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the Soul of the Universe becomes pleased; by that, death is pacified.
Thus ends the twelve-syllable mantra from the Nāradīya-Nṛsiṃha-Khaṇḍa. Śuka said:
"O father, what should one who is constantly devoted to Viṣṇu recite to be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra? Tell me, O father, for the benefit of all."
Vyāsa said:
I shall proclaim the eight-syllabled mantra, the supreme among all mantras;
by reciting which, a living being is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra.
Having meditated with one-pointed mind upon Viṣṇu, who stands in the center of the heart-lotus and holds the conch, discus, and mace, a person should perform the recitation.
With a one-pointed mind, in a solitary place, before an image of Viṣṇu, or near water,
one should mutter the eight-syllable mantra while fixing Viṣṇu in the heart.
For this eight-syllable mantra, Nārāyaṇa is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi);
its meter (chandas) is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deity (devatā) is the Supreme Self (paramātman).
The syllable Oṃ is white in color, while the syllable Na is said to be red;
the syllable Mo is black in color, and the syllable Nā is indeed red.
The syllable *rā* has the luster of saffron; the syllable *ya* is said to be yellow.
The syllable *ṇā* has the hue of collyrium, while the syllable *ya* is multicolored.
"Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" is the mantra that accomplishes all aims.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, everything is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa;
O twice-born one, I do not see anything here that is superior to Nārāyaṇa."
All this—visible and invisible, moving and unmoving—is pervaded by him;
one should remember Nārāyaṇa, meditate upon him, and place him within one's hands and body.
In the remaining [fingers], one should place [the letters] up to the palm on the index fingers and so forth;
one should place the syllable *oṃ* on the left foot and the syllable *na* on the right.
The syllable *mo* is on the left hip, and likewise the syllable *nā* on the right;
the syllable *rā* is at the region of the navel, and the syllable *ya* on the left arm.
One should place the syllable *ṇa* on the right hand and the syllable *ya* on the head;
[likewise] below, above, in the field of perception, on the sides, behind, and in front.
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, one should again perform the armor-rite:
"May Govinda protect me in the east; may Madhusūdana protect me in the south."
May the god Śrīdhara protect you in the west, and Keśava likewise in the north;
may Viṣṇu protect you in front, and the imperishable Mādhava in the southwest.
May Hṛṣīkeśa protect [me] in the northwest, and likewise Vāmana in the northeast;
may Vārāha protect [me] upon the surface of the earth, and likewise Trivikrama above.
Having thus performed the armor-rite (*kavaca*), the person should thereafter contemplate himself:
"I am the divine Nārāyaṇa, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Having meditated upon himself in this way, he should then utter this mantra.
Thus ends the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa. In the Agni Purāṇa:
"Hara is the direct cause of liberation; he is omniscient and the source of knowledge."
This is its mantra of expression, and that which is expressed is likewise remembered.
Because he is both the designator and the designated, Hara grants success through the mantra;
therefore, O best of sages, the supreme six-syllabled mantra resides in the Veda.
What need has he for many mantras or for scriptures of great extent,
if this mantra "namo harāya" is established in his heart?
By him everything has been studied and heard, and by him all that has been prescribed— whatever are the stations of dharma and whatever are the stations of ritual rule— has been fully practiced.
[228] The meditations upon the six-syllable mantra are, in brief, as follows.
Thus ends the six-syllabled mantra.
This is the five-syllabled knowledge (vidyā) of Śiva. In the Vāyusaṃhitā: Now, the essential nature of the supreme knowledge is being described.
First, "namaḥ" should be employed, and after that, "śivāya."
The five-syllabled Śaiva Vidyā, situated upon the head of the fivefold audition,
is in brief the seed of the entire collection of sounds.
First, she who resembles molten gold, with full and elevated breasts, spoke her own words in brief, as they issued from my mouth.
Four-armed and three-eyed, with the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, she holds a lotus and a blue water-lily; gentle in appearance, her hands bestow boons and grant fearlessness.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament,
seated upon a white lotus throne, with dark and curly hair.
Her fivefold colors, from which circles of shimmering rays emanate,
are yellow, black, smoke-colored, and likewise red.
These five, when employed separately, are adorned with the *bindu* and the *nāda*.
The *bindu* has the form of a half-moon; the *nāda* has the form of a lamp-flame.
O fair-faced one, the second seed among these seeds of the mantra is the long [vowel] of the fourth [consonant]; one should assign the fifth as the śakti.
The seer is named Vāmadeva, the metre is declared to be Paṅkti,
and the deity of this mantra, O fair-faced one, is I myself, Śiva.
[229] O beautiful woman, Gautama, Viśvāmitra, Aṅgiras,
and Bharadvāja are recorded as the sages of the social classes in their respective order.
The meters are Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Virāj;
their deities are Indra, Rudra, Hari, Brahmā, and Skanda.
O fair-faced one, they say my five faces are their abode;
beginning from the east and ending with the zenith, they correspond in order to the syllables beginning with *na*.
The first letter is acute (udātta), the fourth is circumflex (svarita), and the second is grave (nihata);
the fifth is also circumflex, while the middle one is considered grave.
Without the Mūla-vidyā, Śiva, the Śaiva-sūtra, and the five-syllabled mantra,
one should know that even this common [practice] is my heart-intent, considered to be Śaiva.
The syllable *na* is said to be Śiva; the syllable *ma* is called the crest (*śikhā*). Likewise, the syllable *śi* is the armor (*kavaca*), and the syllable *vā* is called the eye (*netra*).

The syllable *ya* is the weapon; when the five syllables *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* are each protracted (*pluta*), they constitute the limbs of the mantra whenever they are employed.
Even then, this is the root mantra due to its slight variation;
here, its fifth syllable is adorned with the twelfth vowel.
Therefore, with this mantra, one should perform the worship of us two through the divisions of mind, speech, and body, as well as by means of recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth.
Thus ends the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva.
Now follows the six-syllabled mantra of Sūrya, as stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
[230] Now I shall describe the procedure for worship; learn from me the extraction of the mantra, which is meritorious, removes all sins, and destroys all diseases.
Oṃ, homage to Khakholka. This is the root mantra.
Oṃ viṭhiṭhiṭhaṭha, [homage to] the head.
Oṃ jvala jvala ṭhaṭha, [the mantra for] the crest-lock (śikhā).
Oṃ sahasra sū ṭhaṭhaḥ, [the mantra for] the armor (kavaca).
Oṃ sarvatejo’dhipataye ṭhaṭha, [the mantra for] the weapon (astra).
Oṃ, to the one blazing with a thousand rays, ṭhaṭha—this is the binding above (ūrdhvabandhaḥ). To the Earth, the source of the world, ṭhaṭha—this is the binding of the elements (bhūtabandhaḥ).
In the flame, blaze forth, ṭhaṭha—this is the fire-rampart (agniprākāraḥ).
We know the Āditya; we meditate upon the creator of all.
May that Sūrya inspire us.
The Gāyatrī.
This is the Saṅkalīkaraṇa.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Self of Dharma in the east.
Homage to Yama from the south;
homage to Daṇḍanātha from the west;
homage to Raivata from the north.
Oṃ, homage to Śyāmapiṅgala in the northeast;
Oṃ, homage to Dīkṣita; Oṃ, homage to Lakṣmī, the Vajra-holder Viśvajaya, in the southwest.
Oṃ, to Āditya, Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, obeisance in the northwest;
to Candra, the lord of the moon, obeisance in the east;
Oṃ, to Kāraka, the son of the Earth (Mars), obeisance in the southeast.
Oṃ, homage to Budha, the son of Soma, in the south;
Oṃ, homage to Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras, in the southwest;
Oṃ, homage to Śukra, the great seer and son of Bhṛgu, in the west.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śanaiścara, the son of Ravi;

[in the northwest]. Oṃ, O Blessed One, garlanded with immeasurable rays, Lord of the entire world, whose vehicle is the seven horses, four-armed, bestower of supreme accomplishment, bearing the mark of Viṣṇu, O Bhānu, protect, protect this one!
"Accept the *arghya* that has come upon my head; O you of fierce splendor, blaze eternally! *Ṭhaṭha*.
This is the mantra for the invocation of the *arghya*. *Oṃ namo bhagavate ādityāya sahasrakiraṇāya gaccha gaccha.* (Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One Āditya, the thousand-rayed one; go, go!)
For the sake of returning once more to the city of the best of gods.
The mantra for dismissal: Listen, O Aho! I shall proclaim the entire ritual procedure in its proper sequence.
Thus ends the six-syllabled mantra dedicated to Sūrya.
Now, the Gāyatrīs according to the different deities:
for that Varuṇa we have known; for Mahādeva we meditate.
May Rudra impel that for us.
We know Gaṇāmbikā; we meditate upon Karmasiddhi;
may that Gaurī inspire us.
Let us know that Being; let us meditate upon Him whose face is fire.
May Skanda inspire us.
We know that Being; we meditate upon the one with the curved trunk;
may He, the Tusked One, inspire us.
We know the one whose army is swans; we meditate upon the one whose mouth is fire;
may that Skanda inspire us.
We know him of the sharp horns; we meditate upon him whose feet are fire;
may that Bull inspire us.
We know him whose face is like that of Hari; we meditate upon him who carries Rudra as his vehicle;
may that Nandin inspire us.
We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva;
may that Viṣṇu inspire us.
We know Mahāmbikā; we meditate upon her who grants the perfection of action;
may that Lakṣmī inspire us.
We know her who has been uplifted; we meditate upon her through Viṣṇu alone;
may that Dharā inspire us.
Let us know the son of Vinatā; let us meditate upon the one with beautiful wings;
may that Garuḍa inspire us.
We know him who was born from the lotus; we meditate upon him whose mouth is divine;
may that Creator inspire us.
We know the auspicious garland; we meditate upon the auspicious garland;
may she inspire our speech.
We know the King of the Gods; we meditate upon him who holds the thunderbolt in his hand.
May Śakra impel us toward that.
We know Vaiśvānara; we meditate upon him whose play is flame.
May that Agni inspire us.
We know Vaivasvata; we meditate upon him who holds a staff in his hand.
May Yama inspire us.
We know the night-walker; we meditate upon him who holds a sword in his hand;
may Nirṛti impel us toward that.
We know him whose hand is pure; we meditate upon him whose hand holds the noose;
may that Varuṇa inspire us.
We know the one who is all life; we meditate upon the one whose hand is creation;
may that Vāyu inspire us.
We know the Lord of Yakṣas; we meditate upon him who holds a mace in his hand;
may that Hand inspire us.
We know the Lord of All; we meditate upon the one who holds the trident in his hand;
may that Rudra inspire us.
We know Kātyāyanī; we meditate upon Kanyākumārī;
may that Durgā inspire us.
We know her as the Fortunate One; we meditate upon her who wears a garland of desire;
may that Gaurī inspire us.
We know the one whose self is the gods; we meditate upon Hiraṇyagarbha;
may that Six-faced One inspire us.
We know Bhāskara; we meditate upon the thousand-rayed one.
May that Sūrya inspire us.
We know the one who holds the hand of Rudra; we meditate upon the one who holds the spear in her hand.
May that Goddess inspire us.

"Having thus divided the Gāyatrī according to each respective deity, one should worship and establish them; their seat is said to be the Praṇava. Thus ends the divisions of the Gāyatrī in the Liṅga Purāṇa.
O Śivadharmiṇī! Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of kalpas,
all that is consumed by a bath of ghee, just as fire consumes fuel.

A practitioner of yoga who has mastered the Vedas should give ten thousand milch cows adorned with garments, gold, and other ornaments to one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas; that is the fruit for one who bathes in the Kṣīra-saras.
That man who bathes the Liṅga with curd even once with devotion,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
That man who, having bathed with honey even once out of devotion,
casts off the cloak of sin, is glorified in the world of Fire.
Whoever performs even a single bath with sugarcane juice upon the linga shall attain the world of the Vidyādharas, endowed with all objects of desire.
Having bathed [the image] in succession with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and other substances,
while reciting the mantras beginning with "Iśa," one shall attain the world of Śiva.
That man who performs the consecration of Śiva with sesame oil and oil produced from a hand-press shall attain the state of Śiva.
The measurement for these is stated in that very same source:
"A bath is to be known as one hundred palas, while an oil massage is twenty-five palas;
however, a great bath (mahāsnāna) is proclaimed to consist of two thousand palas."
From the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"O observer of noble vows, he who performs the great bath (*mahāsnāna*) with ghee and honey thereafter attains union (*sāyujya*) with me through these baths."
A bath is known to require one hundred palas, while an anointing requires twenty-five;
however, a great bath (mahāsnāna) is proclaimed to require two thousand palas.
Having bathed my liṅga with cow-products or indeed with clarified butter,
and having purified it with all ritual substances, one should consecrate it by sprinkling it with water.
When the great bath (mahāsnāna) is undertaken, it is traditionally held that the bath performed with water alone or with scented water out of devotion possesses eightfold merit.
One should indeed sprinkle all that with twenty-five palas [of liquid];
and according to the prescribed rite, one should offer *śamī* leaves, *bilva* leaves, and *campaka* flowers,
as well as other leaves, but one must never abandon the *bilva* leaf.
An offering of ten *droṇas*, or even eight *droṇas*,
is ordained to yield merit equal to that of one hundred *droṇas* by means of a single *āḍhaka*.
For a mortal devoid of wealth, there is no need for deliberation here regarding [the sounds of] kettledrums,
clay drums, Muraja drums, hand-clapping, Paṭaha drums, and so forth.
With various musical instruments and likewise with diverse kinds of swings,
one should cause a vigil to be held there and offer prayers in the proper sequence.
Together with his own servants, sons, wives, as well as relatives and kinsmen,
he should perform a circumambulation and pray to the divine Liṅga.
Having thus spoken to Rudra and Śānti with haste,
he likewise spoke of the mantra as the great seed-syllable of the five syllables.
Thus is the Great Bath (mahāsnāna),
according to the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"On the full moon day of Kārttika or Vaiśākha, on the solstices and other festival days..."
Having offered lamps and kindled them, one should then present the bali offering before the deity.
Among all beings, one who is wise regarding the God of gods among Brahmā and the others should,
having observed the vow and addressed the Lord, sleep on the ground while remembering Hari.

Having smeared himself with [ashes] and gone home, he should sleep at night without food. On the following day, in the forenoon, having gone to that very temple, he should perform the great ablution for Hara according to the prescribed rite; listen.
Then, one should have an anointing performed with exactly twenty-five palas;
indeed, the bathing of Śiva with clarified butter is prescribed to be with one hundred palas.
A great ablution (mahāsnāna) is prescribed with two thousand palas of honey and likewise with an equal amount of curd. Then, once again—
From that very milk, indeed from cow's milk alone,
there shall then arise again an inexhaustible yield of one thousand five hundred fruits.
Then, the knower of mantras should perform the bath with the essence (rasa) with devotion, and thereafter with water containing flowers;
then again, having offered water filtered through a cloth, he should bathe with cold water.
One should bathe [the image] on the ground with devotion using [water] contained in a vessel of fragrant substances;
having bathed it according to the rite, one should then smear it with gorocanā and bāṇa.
Having smeared it with a thick and auspicious paste composed of black saffron, camphor, sandalwood, agallochum,
and black musk,
one should then [worship] the Liṅga up to the top of the fillet (āpīḍa).
Having bound a garland with a thousand blue lotuses, one should worship [it].
If one does not obtain a thousand, one should worship with half of that amount, or even half of that again;
if blue lotuses are unavailable, one should instead worship with the leaves of the *śrītara* tree.
Whether with lotuses, or even with campaka flowers, or with jasmine and apālata, or with punnāgas, karṇikāras, or even those born from white mandāra trees.
With *madana* flowers, desert blossoms, or *śamī*, white *arka*, and *nāgara*;
or with whatever leaves are available that are odorless, pure, and unblemished.
Having worshipped with devotion, one should cause a pavilion of fragrant flowers to be made;
one should burn guggulu mixed with clarified butter and scented agaru.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gaurī with songs, musical instruments, and auspicious rites,
[he offered] radiant lamps made from prepared flour of śāli rice and filled with ghee.
Then one should perform the *nīrājana* rite with twenty-six lamps,
using mustard seeds mixed with curd, along with *dūrvā* grass, *gorocanā*, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
One should offer water with perfumes and flowers, meditating upon Śaṅkara for the sake of incense;
then, [one should visualize] a golden eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
Having meditated, one should offer upon the head of the *liṅga* flowers along with a pair of fine garments— either white or resembling a lotus— accompanied by song.
One should cause the chowrie, the mirror, and the lamp-wick to be offered; likewise, the incense-bearer and the attendant for times of distress should be provided beforehand.
One should offer two banners of Vināyaka, provided with the sound of tinkling bells;
then, with devotion, one should prostrate like a staff upon the earth with its eight limbs.
Then one should recite aloud the hymn of Śaṅkara, which is dear to Śiva;
thereafter, avoiding the remains of offerings, one should perform the circumambulation slowly.
Having bowed down once more, he should thereafter present the food offering (naivedya) to those who have arrived—
the poor, the blind, the wretched, and those initiated by Śiva.
One who knows the Dharma, out of respect for those mentioned, should satisfy them all with food and drink; he should perform this great ablution according to the prescribed rule.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who has it made with devotion to Śiva:
having delivered one hundred and fifty generations of his lineage, he shall be freed from sin.
Having enjoyed all pleasures without exception throughout the world up to the realm of Brahmā,
he shall go and sport there, seated in a celestial chariot together with the immortals.
Having enjoyed pleasures as desired, one shall attain union with Śiva;
and having cast off that Māyā, one shall ultimately obtain Yoga.
Then, with clarified butter alone, or with cow's curd, or with milk,
or with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or with honey, or with sugarcane juice;
Whoever should cause a great ablution to be performed according to this rite and with the recitation of mantras,
he too shall go by that very path to the supreme state.
But he who dies in the interval, whether his practice was incomplete or lacking in regularity,
shall also go to that very state, provided he is unwearied in his devotion to Śiva.
By this rite, one who has no property of his own should cause twenty men to perform the bath with water; he shall go to the supreme state.
In this very way, although a Śūdra is excluded from the touch and the mantras,
he who worships with the application of mantras shall become even more meritorious than that.
[240] Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the Great Worship (*mahāpūjāvidhi*),
according to the *Vāstusaṃhitā*.
The eternal Mahādeva, whose form is the Liṅga, is worthy of worship;
there is a golden eight-petaled lotus adorned with the nine gems.
One should imagine a seat covered with a pericarp and filaments;
it may be made of silver, or in its absence, red or white.
In the absence of even that lotus, however, one should create a mere lotus consisting of meditative visualization;
having placed a small liṅga in the center of the pericarp of that lotus, [one should proceed].
Alternatively, having consecrated that liṅga according to the prescribed rite and performed its purification, one should worship it, provided with crystal, according to the extensive procedure.
One should imagine a seat for the form [of the deity] in the manner of five faces,
[purifying it] with the five products of the cow and other meritorious substances, according to one's available means.
One should bathe Śambhu with full jars numbering a thousand or more,
using fragrant substances such as sandalwood mixed with camphor and saffron.
Having smeared the pedestal and adorned the liṅga with ornaments,
[one should worship] with bilva leaves, lotuses, and red and white water-lilies.
With blue lotuses and other such meritorious, fragrant flowers;
with auspicious, praiseworthy, and variegated leaves, as well as dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and so forth.
Having thus performed worship and obtained the gains, one should perform the great worship according to the ritual injunctions;
likewise, one should offer incense, lamps, and especially the food offering (*naivedya*).
Having reported one's wealth, one should perform auspicious deeds;
and those things that are desired, distinguished, and acquired through righteous means.
[241] All substances should be given as offerings during that vow,
especially the fruit of the *śrīpatra*, the *utpala*, and so forth, as well as *bilva* leaves of the same measure.
One should offer flowers according to what is available, following the prescribed rule;
the eightfold offering is thus indicated, with incense and lamps being especially important.
Black aloe-wood is in the face called Aghora; realgar is in the right [face];
sandalwood is in the face called Vāmadeva, and black aloe-wood again [is in the left].
One should specifically offer incense: guggulu in the southeast, saugandhika in the northeast, and īśānī in the north. One should also offer it in the mouth.
One should offer guggulu mixed with aguru and combined with clarified butter;
however, they declare that sandalwood, aguru, kuṣṭha, and so forth constitute the general [offering].
Then a lamp made of camphor should be offered, followed by an oblation of ghee;
thereafter, water for the guest-offering (argha) and water for sipping (ācamana) should be given for each face.
In the first enclosure, sesame seeds are indeed offered; in the first enclosure they are worshipped. In the second enclosure, the Vidyādharas and Cakravartins are to be honored.
In the third enclosure, behind [the central deity], is Maheśvara with his eight forms;
likewise, Mahādeva and the others are there with their eleven forms.
In the fourth enclosure, all the lords of the Gaṇas are to be worshipped;
however, outside of the lotus, according to the sequence of the fifth enclosure.
The lords of the ten directions, along with their followers, as well as all the hosts of luminaries who are the mind-born sons of Brahmā, are to be worshipped according to the scriptures.
All the gods and goddesses, all the sky-dwellers,
the other inhabitants of the netherworld, and even all the hosts of sages.
The five winds of the yogin, as well as the five mothers of the cows,
the guardians of the fields with their retinues, and indeed all that is moving and unmoving.
Then, having performed the worship of the enclosure,
he should fully worship the Supreme Lord and offer to Hari delightful food accompanied by ghee and various side dishes.
Having given a residence such as Sukhāvatī, along with betel-leaf and its accompaniments,
and having adorned him once more with various flowers and ornaments;
Having performed the rites up to the end of the lustration (nīrājanā), one should complete the remainder of the worship;
then one should provide a comfortable bed along with offerings for the deity.
Whatever food has been cooked that is pleasing to the heart— all that, having prepared it and caused it to be prepared, and having offered oblations and performed worship, in due order.
Having recited the hymn that causes delusion, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī-vidyā).
Having offered the arghya water and eight flowers, one should dismiss the deity from the liṅga.
The characteristics of betel (*tāmbūla*) and mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*) are stated in the *Ratnakośa*:
"The leaves of the *mahāpippala* tree and the fruits of the *kramuka* tree,
combined with the lye of oyster shells, are designated as 'betel'."
A white leaf, a full betel nut, areca nuts,
along with coconut fruit and citron,
together with cardamom, kakkola, and camphor, are declared to be mouth-perfumes.
"But if even these are not available, the wise one should call to mind each respective substance;
having mentally conceived that substance, he should offer it even with flowers.
Thus ends the procedure for the Great Worship according to another method.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
[243] A great lamp should always be offered, which yields great fruit for the protector of the earth;
especially during the dark fortnight, and particularly on that [lunar day].
The new moon day and the twelfth day are also specified as yielding great fruit;
this refers to whichever occurs in the dark fortnight after the month of Āśvayuja has passed.
O King, on the new moon day— which is greatly meritorious— and especially on the twelfth day,
a measure of oil should be offered at the right side of the deity.
O King, one should prepare a wick there, joined with eight leaves,
using a cloth entirely dyed with saffron.
O King, on the left side of the deity, a balance of ghee should be offered;
one should also cause to be given a meritorious white wick measuring eight palas.
Having fasted and subdued his senses,
O lord of the earth, he should thus offer this pair of wicks once with an entire garment.
Having enjoyed the heavenly realm for a long time, when he is born again upon the earth,
he becomes endowed with fortune, beauty, and good luck.
O tiger among kings, in that kingdom, in that country, and likewise in that city and family, there shall be radiance like that of a lamp.
He becomes exceedingly brilliant in battles and in quarrels;
he always attains renown in the world as one possessing the excellent qualities of the virtuous.
Or else, one might give even a single desired gift to these two;
O sinless one, one thereby obtains everything in the human state that has been described by me to you.
O King, the gift of even an ordinary lamp yields great fruit;
how much more so for a large one—for its fruit has no end.
The gift of a lamp is certainly of great merit even for another deity;
how much more so for the God of gods, the infinite and great-souled one?
It should be given on mountain peaks, on the sandy banks of rivers,
at crossroads, on main roads, and in the dwellings of Brahmins.
By giving lamps at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, and in the depths of forests, one enjoys the great fruit of this supreme mantra.
Thus ends the procedure for the Great Lamp-offering. Now, the time for commencing a vow: regarding this, Satyavrata states:
"That lunar day which is situated in the water (the *udavasthā*) shall not fall in the middle of the day."
"That [day] shall not be 'unbroken' (akhaṇḍā) at the commencement or the conclusion of the vows.
Regarding the unbroken day distinct from this, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states the following:
"If the lunar day (tithi) should be unbroken, such that the sun traverses its own segment [of the sky]."
"The commencement of the vow should take place on that [lunar day] when Jupiter and Venus are not set.

This means that if the lunar day (tithi) is joined with Jupiter and Venus who have not set—that is, joined with Jupiter and Venus who have not gone down—then the vow should be commenced on that day. This is an illustrative indication; the meaning is that the vow should not be commenced even when Jupiter and Venus are in their infancy or old age. And so it is stated by Vṛddhamanu and Bṛhaspati:

One should avoid the installation of the sacred fires, consecrations, sacrifices, gifts, and vows; Vedic observances, the ritual release of a bull, the tonsure ceremony, the investiture of the girdle, auspicious rites, and royal ablutions during the intercalary month (malamāsa).

"Whether in childhood or in old age, when Venus or Jupiter has entered retrogression (vātagata), one should avoid visiting a deity during these times, just as during an intercalary month. Thus says Gārgya as well.

The naming ceremony, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, the marriage, the tying of the girdle, the first outing, the birth rite, and the optional rite of releasing a bull— these [are the sacraments].
"When Jupiter and Venus have set, when [the Moon] is in its infancy or old age, or during the intercalary month (malimluca),
one should by no means perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) or the commencement of vows. Thus says Laṇṇa.

If [the Moon] is situated in a debilitated sign, even if it is retrograde, or is in an Abhicaraṇa state, or is a child, old, or set, then renunciation, a pilgrimage to a deity, the performance of vows, the piercing of the ears, initiation,
the tying of the sacred girdle, the tonsure ceremony, the rite of marriage, or the consecration of a temple deity [should not be undertaken].

"The wise should avoid [these] with effort when Jupiter, the preceptor of the thirty gods, is situated in a sign of its fall. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the definition of the exaltation (*ucca*) in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) is as follows: "For the planets beginning with the Sun, the exaltations are respectively Aries, Taurus, Cancer, and Capricorn."
"A woman [is auspicious] in Capricorn, Pisces, and Libra, as well as in the eleventh and seventh houses;

the seventh from the exaltation sign is the fall (nīca). This means that the seventh house from the sign of exaltation is the fall. Thus, when Jupiter is in its fall, it means Jupiter is situated in Capricorn. So says Śaunaka.
One should know [the auspicious times for] fame, building a house, marriage, sacrifice, travel, drinking milk and so forth, piercing the ears, learning, beholding deities, initiation (*upanayana*),
consecration (*dīkṣā*), examination, vows, bathing, visiting sacred sites (*tīrtha*), battle, entering a city, great gifts, and the consecration of temples.
When the Sun is situated in Leo, which is honored by the gods, it does not bestow auspiciousness upon the performer; likewise when it is in Aries.
The eight characteristics [of planetary states] are given in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"The conjunction of the other planets with the Sun is called 'setting' (*asta*).
The duration for these two has been shown in various ways in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*):

"Venus is a child for ten days and an old man for five; thereafter, when risen, it is [in its state of] *tryaha* for three days; and when set, it is in a state of *mauḍhya* (dullness) for a fortnight in due order."

"The *jīva* [period] is ten days for those who are aged, while others say it is seven nights; even for a child, it is always ten days, and for both the aged and the child, it is said by some to be ten days.
The application of these various views depends on the specific region or upon times of distress (*āpad*). Thus says Gārgya:
When Venus and Jupiter are in the eastern quarter, they are in their childhood state for ten nights in Vindhya and Avanti,
and for six and five nights respectively in Vaṅga and Hūṇa.
"And they say that in the remaining region, it lasts for three days. Thus [says Varāhamihira]; Varāhamihira also says:
"Many times have these periods been shown, both in childhood and in old age."
"In that [context], the remaining [fingers] are to be grasped more prominently due to the difference in location, or as the occasion demands.
Now, the characteristics of the mudrās:
having brought the two hands face-to-face, with the fingers slightly contracted...
She is indeed proclaimed as Mukuṭī, for she has emerged from the lotus.
[247] There are the *mukulinī* and the *paṅkaja* mudrās. The *mukulinī* is that which is turned forward with the fingers extended at the tip;
the *vyākośa* mudrā is the *mukula*, and one should display the *padma* mudrā.
Regarding the lotus mudrā:
the two thumbs are bent and wrapped by their own fingers;
having joined both hands facing one another, it is the *niṣṭhurā*.
For Niṣṭhurā:
having bent the two index fingers and likewise the little finger,
with the [other] fingers facing downward and the nails visible, they are positioned in the middle of the hand.
Raise four fingers on the back and join the two thumbs together;
when these two are thus positioned, it is proclaimed as the Vyoma-mudrā.

[This concludes] the Vyomamudrā. Now, regarding the seers (*ṛṣi*), deities (*daivata*), and meters (*chandas*) of the Vedic mantras, Yājñavalkya states their purpose: "The seer, the meter, the deity, and likewise the ritual application (*viniyoga*)."
This should be understood with diligent effort, especially by a brahmin.
But he who performs officiating at sacrifices, teaching, recitation, burnt offerings, chanting within the water, or giving gifts without knowing [the rules], shall obtain only meager fruit from them.
Likewise:
"He who knows the seer, the meter, and the deity of the mantras;
their application, the Brāhmaṇa, the meaning of the mantra, and the ritual action [performed with it]."
Even for each individual seer, he shall indeed be like a guest who brings no fruit;
and as for the deities, he attains union with them—of this there is no doubt.
That twice-born one who knows the seers and so forth in the manner previously described shall possess the qualification for the secret rites and others.
That by which a seer perceived [the mantra], that by which he indeed attained perfection,
and whatever was proclaimed by him as his mantra— the nature of that seer constitutes its "seer-attribute" (ārṣaka).
Desire was designated as sandalwood paste, and form as clothing;
in ancient times, the Self was indeed covered by the gods out of fear of death.
By means of the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras, those very Vedic meters are indeed [constituted].
Whichever deity is specified for whichever mantra, that mantra shall take the form of that deity; its divinity is said to consist in that very divinity.
In ancient times, the mantras were produced by the gods solely for the purpose of ritual action;
that which must be performed with this [mantra] is called its application (viniyoga).
That which provides the etymological explanation of a mantra, its application and purpose,
its ritual installation, and its praise— that is what is called a Brāhmaṇa here.

"In this way, one should indeed recollect the fivefold yoga at the time of recitation (*japa*), as well as during fire-offerings (*homa*), internal water-rites (*antarjala*), yoga, self-study (*svādhyāya*), and officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*).

Thus [it is said]. Therein, first are the mantras of the *Ṛgveda*: for the hymn beginning with "agnim īle," Madhucchandas, Viśvāmitra, Agni, and the Gāyatrī meter [are the seer, deity, and meter, respectively]. For the seven verses beginning with "vāyavāyāhi," Madhucchandas is the seer; for the first three, Vāyu is the deity; for the following [four], Indra and Vāyu; for the seventh, Mitra and Varuṇa. For all seven, the Gāyatrī is the meter.
For the mantra beginning with *sadasaspatim*, Kāṇva Medhātithi is the seer, Sadasaspati is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter.
For the mantra beginning with *ambayo yanty adhvan*, Kāṇva Medhātithi is the seer, the Waters are the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter.
For the mantra beginning with *yat siddhi satyasomapāḥ*, Ājīgarti Śunaḥśepa is the seer, and Indra is the deity.
The *paṅkti* meter for the seven verses beginning with "adyā," the *gāyatrī* for the nine verses beginning with "yuvānā";
Medhātithi Kāṇva is the seer for "yuvānā" and the *Ṛbhus*, and the *gāyatrī* meter;
Medhātithi Kāṇva is the seer for "syonā pṛthivī" and the Earth, and the *gāyatrī* meter.
For the two verses beginning with "ato devā," the seer is Medhātithi, the deity is Viṣṇu, and the metre is Gāyatrī.
For the fifteen-verse hymn beginning with "kasya nūnam," the seer is either Ājīgarti Vaiśvāmitra or Śunaḥśepha; for the first verse, the deity is Prajāpati and the metre is Triṣṭubh.

For the second [verse], Agni is the deity and the Triṣṭubh is the meter. In the three verses beginning with "abhi tvā," Savitṛ is the deity; in this [verse] beginning with "bhagasya," Bhaga is the deity and the Gāyatrī is the meter.
The ten verses beginning with "nahi te" are dedicated to Varuṇa and are in the Triṣṭubh meter.

“O Agni, you are the first Aṅgiras,” etc., consists of eighteen verses; the eighth, sixteenth, and eighteenth are *triṣṭubh*s. “Come hither,” etc., consists of fifteen verses; [the seer is] Āṅgirasa Hiraṇyastūpa, [the deity is] Indra, and the meter is *triṣṭubh*.
*Kadudroya*—nine verses; Ghorakāṇva is the seer, Rudra is the deity.
In the third verse, Rudra and Mitra-Varuṇa are the deities; in the three verses beginning with the seventh, Soma is the deity; the meter is Gāyatrī.
*Yās te* is the final verse, which is Anuṣṭubh.
[250] “ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam” consists of thirteen verses; the last is a *triṣṭubh*. [The hymn] is recited by one who has vomited.
The first nine are *gāyatrīs*;
the four beginning with the tenth are *anuṣṭubhs*. The final triplet of verses is a destroyer of disease.
The final half-verse is Śatrughna; the tenth verse of the [hymn] beginning with "paśvā" is by Śāktya Pārāśara, addressed to Agni, in the Dvipadā Virāj meter;
according to the opinion of Śaunaka, it consists of five Paṅkti verses in the Virāj meter.
The *Rapiḥ* hymn consists of eleven verses; its seer is Śakti, its deity is Pārāśara-Agni, and its metre is the two-footed *virāj*.

In the opinion of Śaunaka, *pañca paṅkti* is *virāṭ*. In *vaneṣu jātāḥ*, there are ten; in the opinion of Śaunaka, five. In *śrīṇan*, there are eleven; in the opinion of Śaunaka, five. In *vane apūrvyaḥ*, there are eleven verses; in the opinion of Śaunaka, six. For the ten-verse hymn beginning with *upa prajinvan*, the seer is Śāktya Pārāśara, the deity is Agni, and the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For *nikāvyā vedhasaḥ*, there are ten verses by Śāktya; the deity is Agni, the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the ten-verse hymn beginning with *rapir nayaḥ pitṛvittaḥ*, the seer is Pārāśara, the deity is Agni, and the meter is *triṣṭubh*. The nine verses beginning with *upa prayantaḥ* have Rāhūgaṇa Gautama as the seer, Agni as the deity, and the meter is *gāyatrī*. For the twelve-verse hymn beginning with *hiraṇyakeśo rajasaḥ*, Gautama is the seer and Agni is the deity; the first three verses are *triṣṭubh*. In these, the middle verse is either the intermediate Agni (*madhyasthāna*) or the pure Agni (*śuddha*). The fourth through the sixth verses are *uṣṇih*. Following that, there are six *gāyatrī* verses.

"O Soma, you have become aware through our wisdom"—this [hymn] consists of twenty-three verses. Gautama is the seer; Soma is the deity. Of the first four verses, the meter is *triṣṭubh*; then for twelve verses, it is *gāyatrī*; the seventh is *uṣṇih*; and then for six verses, it is *triṣṭubh*.

[251] Regarding the hymn of eleven verses beginning with *prapaṇdine*: Kutsa, a descendant of Aṅgiras, is the seer; Indra accompanied by the Maruts is the deity. The first seven verses are in the Jagatī meter; the first is a secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) concerning the miscarriage of the fetus. Then follow four verses in the Triṣṭubh meter. Regarding the hymn of eleven verses beginning with *imā rudrāya tapase*: Kutsa is the seer; Rudra is the deity. Nine verses are in the Jagatī meter; the tenth and eleventh are in the Triṣṭubh meter. Regarding the hymn of seven verses beginning with *ubhe punāmi*: Pārukṣepa is the seer; Indra is the deity. The first verse is in the Triṣṭubh meter; the second through fourth are in the Anuṣṭubh meter; the fifth is in the Gāyatrī meter; the sixth is in the Dhṛti meter; the seventh is in the Uṣṇih meter. Regarding *ye devāsaḥ*: Pārukṣepa is the seer; the Viśvedevas are the deities; the meter is Triṣṭubh. Regarding the hymn of eleven verses beginning with *pitunnustoṣam*: Agastya is the seer; Soma is the deity. The first verse is in the Anuṣṭubh meter; the second is in the Garbha-Uṣṇih meter; the second and fourth verses are in the Gāyatrī meter; the third is in the Anuṣṭubh meter; the fifth through seventh are in the Anuṣṭubh meter; then three verses are in the Gāyatrī meter; the final two are in the Bṛhatī and Anuṣṭubh meters respectively. Regarding the hymn of eight verses beginning with *agne naya*: Agastya is the seer; Agni is the deity; the meter is Triṣṭubh. Regarding the hymn of eight verses beginning with *anarvāṇaṃ vṛṣabham*: Agastya is the seer; Bṛhaspati is the deity; the meter is Triṣṭubh. Regarding the hymn of fifteen verses beginning with *upemasṛkṣi*: Gṛtsamada is the seer; Apām Napāt is the deity. It consists of Triṣṭubhs. Regarding the triplet beginning with *karikradaj januṣam*: Gṛtsamada is the seer; Śakunta is the deity; Indra is the deity; the meter is Triṣṭubh. Regarding the hymn of twenty-four verses beginning with *ilāparvatā*: In the first verse, Indra and Parvata are the deities. From there until the fourteenth, Indra is the deity. In the following two verses, Sarasvatī is the deity. In the four verses beginning with the seventeenth, the parts of the chariot and Indra are the deities. In the final four verses, Indra is the deity. [252] The first nine verses are in the Triṣṭubh meter; the tenth is in the Jagatī meter; the eleventh is in the Triṣṭubh meter; the twelfth is in the Anuṣṭubh meter; the thirteenth is in the Gāyatrī meter; then two verses are in the Triṣṭubh meter; the sixteenth is in the Jagatī meter; the seventeenth is in the Triṣṭubh meter; the eighteenth is in the Bṛhatī meter; the nineteenth is in the Triṣṭubh meter; the twentieth and twenty-second are in the Anuṣṭubh meter; the twenty-first, twenty-third, and twenty-fourth are in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Regarding the hymn consisting of twenty-four verses beginning with "agninendreṇa":
Śyāvāśva Ātreya is the seer; the Aśvins are the deities; it belongs to the Upariṣṭāj-jyotis class.
The twenty-second and twenty-fourth verses are Paṅktis, and the twenty-third is a Mahābṛhatī.
The seer of the seven-verse hymn beginning with "avitāsi" is Śyāvāśva; the deity is Indra; the meter is Śakvarī.

The final [verse] is a *mahāpaṅkti*. Of the ten-verse hymn beginning with "toṣi" (*stoṣīti*), Nābhāka Kāṇva is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the meter is *mahāpaṅkti*. Of the thirty-three-verse hymn beginning with "ime viprasya," Virūpa Āṅgirasa is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the meter is *gāyatrī*. Of the thirty-verse hymn beginning with "samidhāgnim," Virūpa Āṅgirasa is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the meter is *gāyatrī*. Of the forty-two-verse hymn beginning with "ādyāya," Triśoka Kāṇva is the seer, Indra is the deity, and the meter is *gāyatrī*. Of the eighteen-verse hymn beginning with "mahivṛdhaḥ," Trita Āptya is the seer and the Ādityas are the deities. The last five verses are *upastha-mahāpaṅkti*s; they destroy bad dreams. Of the five-verse hymn beginning with "pratite," Pṛṣadhra Kāṇva is the seer; it is addressed to Indra, is in the *gāyatrī* meter, and the final verse is a *paṅkti* addressed to Agni and Sūrya. Of the twelve-verse hymn beginning with "pro asmai," Pragātha Kāṇva is the seer; it is addressed to Indra and is in the *pāṅkta* meter.

[253] The seventh, eighth, and ninth verses are *bṛhatī*s; they belong to those Kṣatriyas. For the hymn of twenty-one verses, the seers are Matsya Sāmmada and Agastya. Many fish that swim in nets and the seers are the deities; for the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth verses, Āditya is the deity. The metre is *gāyatrī*. The hymn "Yo rājā" consists of fifteen verses. Puruhanman Āṅgirasa is the seer; it is addressed to Indra and is in the *bārhata* style. The second, fourth, and sixth verses are *sato bṛhatī*s; the thirteenth is *uṣṇih*; the fourteenth is *anuṣṭubh*; the fifteenth is *pura-uṣṇih*. Regarding the hymn of fifteen verses beginning with "Tvan no agne mahobhiḥ," Sudīti Puramiḍāvanya is one of the seers. Agni is the deity; the metre is *gāyatrī*. The first ten verses are all *bṛhatī*s; the eleven and subsequent verses are uneven *sato bṛhatī*s. Regarding the seven-verse hymn beginning with "Kanyāvāḥ," Atri is the seer; Indra is the deity; the metre is *anuṣṭubh*, and the first two verses are *paṅkti*s. Regarding "Udved abhi," there are thirty-four verses. Indrakṣa is the seer; Indra is the deity; the metre is *gāyatrī*; another verse is addressed to Indra and Agni. Regarding the nine-verse hymn beginning with "Āpo hiṣṭhā," Ambarīṣa Sindhudvīpa is the seer; the Waters (*āpas*) are the deity; the metre is *gāyatrī*. The fifth is *vardhamānā*, the seventh is *pratiṣṭhā*, and the last two are *anuṣṭubh*s. Regarding the sixteen-verse hymn beginning with "Parepivāṃsam," Vaivasvata Yama is the seer; Yama is the deity. The sixth verse has its deity indicated by its characteristic marks. The three verses beginning with the seventh are either ancestral (*pitrya*) or addressed to Yama (*yāmya*). In the three verses beginning with the tenth, the metre is *triṣṭubh* with *śvāna* as the deity. The thirteenth and fourteenth are *anuṣṭubh*s; the fifteenth is *bṛhatī*. Regarding the fourteen-verse hymn beginning with "Paramṛtyau," Saṅkusuko Yama is the seer. For the first four verses, Mṛtyu is the deity. In the fifth, Dhātṛ; in the sixth, Tvaṣṭṛ. The remaining verses have the Pitṛyajña deities as their object; the final verse is addressed to Prajāpati or is *triṣṭubh*. The eleventh is *prastārapaṅkti*; the thirteenth is *jagatī*; the final verse is *anuṣṭubh*. Regarding the ten-verse hymn beginning with "Bhadraṃ naḥ," Vimada is the seer, addressed to Indra, or to Prajāpati, or to Vasukṛt. Agni is the deity; the metre is *gāyatrī*. The first verse is a single word for the sake of peace; the second is *anuṣṭubh*; the ninth is *virāṭ*; the final verses are *triṣṭubh*s. Regarding the fifteen-verse hymn beginning with "Pradevatre," Pṛlūṣa Kaṃṣava is the seer; the Waters or the Son of the Waters (*āponaptṛ*) are the deity; the metre is *triṣṭubh*. Regarding the fourteen-verse hymn beginning with "Prāvepāmām," Maujavān Akṣa or the Seers (*kavayaḥ*) are the seers. In the first, seventh, and ninth verses, there is praise of agriculture; in the twelfth, praise of dice; in the remainder, a censure of dice. Regarding the fourteen-verse hymn beginning with "Traiṣṭubham ambughnam," Dhānākolūṣa is the seer; the Viśvedevas are the deity; the metre is *jagatī*, and the last two are *triṣṭubh*s. Regarding the twelve-verse hymn beginning with "Namo mitrasya," the deity is Sūrya; the metre is *jagatī*, and the tenth is *triṣṭubh*. Regarding the twelve-verse hymn beginning with "Divas pari," Vatsapri Agni is the seer; the metre is *triṣṭubh*; the final verse has its deity indicated by its characteristic marks. Regarding the six-verse hymn beginning with "Ā pragāma," Bandhu, Subandhu, Śrutabandhu, and Viprabandhu are the seers; Indra is the deity; the metre is *gāyatrī*. Regarding the twelve-verse hymn beginning with "Yatte yamaḥ," the four seers are Bandhu and the others; the deities are Yama and the others; the turning of the mind is the subject; the metre is *anuṣṭubh*. Regarding the twenty-seven-verse hymn beginning with "Idam irtyāḥ," Nābhānediṣṭha Māmateya is the seer; the Viśvedevas are the deity; the metre is *triṣṭubh*. Regarding the eleven-verse hymn beginning with "Bṛhaspate," Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa is the seer; the Supreme Self is the deity; the metre is *triṣṭubh*; the ninth is *jagatī*. Regarding the seven-verse hymn beginning with "Ya te manyo," Manu Tāpasa is the seer; Manyu is the deity; the metre is *triṣṭubh*; the first verse is *jagatī*. Regarding the twenty-five-verse hymn beginning with "Rakṣohaṇam," Vāyu Bharadvāja is the seer; Agni is the deity; the metre is *triṣṭubh*.

The last four are *anuṣṭubh* verses. For the hymn of nineteen verses beginning with *haviṣyantam*, the seer is either Āṅgirasa or Vāmadevya; the deity is Murdhanvan Sūrya Vaiśvānara; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of sixteen verses beginning with *sahasraśīrṣā*, the seer is Nārāyaṇa Paramātman; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. [255] For the hymn of twenty-three verses beginning with *yā oṣadhīḥ*, the seer is the Atharvan physician; the deity is the plants; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. For the hymn of twelve verses beginning with *bṛhaspate pratima*, the seer is Devāpi Rāṣṭiṣeṇa; the deity is the Viśvedevas; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of twelve verses beginning with *ayāścitraṃ*, the seer is Vaikhānasi; the deity is Indra; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of thirteen verses beginning with *āśuḥ śiśānaḥ*, the seer is Indrapratiratha; the deity is Indra; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. The fourth verse is addressed to Bṛhaspati, the penultimate and the final verses are addressed to the Maruts, and the final one is an *anuṣṭubh*. For the hymn of seven verses beginning with *vaiśvāgnim*, the seers in order for the seven verses are Aṅgūti, Vātajūti, Viprajūti, Vṛṣaṇaka, Karikrata, Etaśa, and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga; the deity is Keśin; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. For the hymn of seven verses beginning with *utadevāḥ*, the seers in order are Bharadvāja, Kaśyapa, Gotama, Atri, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha; the deity is the Viśvedevas; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. For the hymn of six verses beginning with *agne accha*, the seer is Tāpasa Agni; the deity is the Viśvedevas; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. For the hymn of six verses beginning with *imāṃ khanāmi*, the seer is Indrāṇī; the deity is the Upaniṣad; the subject is the destruction of co-wives; the meter is *anuṣṭubh* for the first five and *paṅkti* for the last. For the hymn of five verses beginning with *śāsaḥ*, the seer is Bharadvāja; the deity is Indra; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. For the hymn of five verses beginning with *muñcāmi*, the seer is Yakṣmanāśana Prajāpati; the deities are Indra and Agni, or Indra alone; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. The final verse is a *bṛhatī*. For the hymn of six verses beginning with *brahmaṇāgnisaṃvidānaḥ*, the seer is Rakṣohā Brāhma; the deity is Agni who establishes the embryo; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. For the hymn of five verses beginning with *apehi*, the seer is Pracetas Āṅgirasa; the deity is the Viśvedevas; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*, with the third verse being *triṣṭubh* and the final verse being *paṅkti*; it destroys bad dreams. For the hymn of five verses beginning with *devāḥ kapotaḥ*, the seer is Kapota Nairṛta; the deity is the Viśvedevas; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. It is a rite of expiation when a dove enters the house. For the hymn of four verses beginning with *mayobhūḥ*, the seer is Śabara Kākṣīvata; the deity is Gau; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of three verses beginning with *pataṅgam*, the seer is Pataṅga Prājāpatya; the deity is Māyabhedas; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of three verses beginning with *apaśyan tvā*, the seer is Prajāvān Prājāpatya; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of three verses beginning with *viṣṇur yonim*, the seer is Garbhakartṛ Tvaṣṭṛ Prājāpatya, or Viṣṇu or the Viśvedevas; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. According to some, the hymn *viṣṇur yonim* consists of five verses. For the hymn of three verses beginning with *mahitrīṇām*, the seer is Satyadhṛti Vāruṇi; the meter is *gāyatrī*. For the hymn of three verses beginning with *āyaṅgauḥ*, the seer is Sārparājnī; the deity is the Self or Sūrya; the meter is *gāyatrī*. For the hymn of four verses beginning with *saṃsamit*, the seer is Saṃvanana Āṅgirasa; the deity is Saṃjñāna; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*, with the third verse being *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of three verses beginning with *vāstoṣpate*, the seers are Maitrāvaruṇa or Vasiṣṭha; the deity is Vāstoṣpati; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of nine verses beginning with *tat savituḥ*, the seer is Śyāvāśva; the deity is Savitṛ; the meter is *gāyatrī* for the first verse and *anuṣṭubh* for the rest. For the mantra beginning with *mātā rudrāṇām*, the seer is Jamadagni Bhārgava; the deity is the Cows; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of the *Śanno devīḥ* (*śannodevī*), the seer is Vasiṣṭha; the deity is the Viśvedevas; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of seven verses beginning with *yuvaṃ vastrāṇi*, the seer is Dīrghatamas; the deity is Mitra and Varuṇa; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the hymn of eleven verses beginning with *samudrād ūrmiḥ*, the seer is Vāmadeva; the deities are Agni, Sūrya, the Cows, or Ghee; the final verse is *triṣṭubh*, the penultimate is *jagatī*. For the hymn beginning with *svastidā viśaspatiḥ*, the seer is Śāsa Bharadvāja; the deity is Indra; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. For the hymn beginning with *sudevaḥ*, the seer is Priyamedha; the deity is Indra; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. For the hymn of twenty-one verses beginning with *vāyo ete*, the seer is Gṛtsamada; the deity of the first two verses is Vāyu, of the third is Indra and Vāyu, of the next three is Mitra and Varuṇa, of the next three is Mitra and Varu

In the order of the *ṛc*s: Samiddha, Tanūnapāt, Īḷa, Barhis, Devyo-dhāra, Uṣāsānaktā, the two divine Hotṛs, the three goddesses, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vanaspati, and the Svāhākṛtis; the metre is *gāyatrī*, while the last four are *anuṣṭubh*.

*mandrayā* (9 verses): Asita or Devala is the seer; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *asṛgram* (9 verses): Devala Kāśyapa or Soma is the seer; Gāyatrī is the meter. *ete somāḥ* (9 verses): Ata or Devala is the seer; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *paripriyā divaḥ* (9 verses); *prasvānāsaḥ* (9 verses); *upāsmai* (9 verses); *somā asṛgram* (9 verses); *somaḥ punāno arṣati* (9 verses).

*pariprāsiṣṭi* is a hymn of ten verses; *eṣadhiṣa* is a hymn of eight verses; *ete setāraḥ* is a hymn of eight verses; *pranisneneva* consists of eight verses; *perisuvānaḥ* is a hymn of seven verses;
*yat soma* is a hymn of seven verses; *prakaviḥ* is a hymn of seven verses; and *ete dhāvanti* is a hymn of seven verses.

[259] These *somāsaḥ* hymns consist of seven verses each: *somā asṛgram*, *pra somāsaḥ*, and *ete somāḥ*. Thus for all these six-verse hymns. *Dṛḍhacyuta* of the lineage of Agastya; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *tam ṛkṣanta*. For the six-verse hymn, *dārḍhacyuta*; *idhmavāha*; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *eṣa kaviḥ* for the six [verses]. *Nṛmedha* of the lineage of Aṅgiras; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *eṣa vājīnām*. *Priyamedha* of the lineage of Aṅgiras; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *prāsyadhāvāḥ* for the six [verses]; *sāmadham* of the lineage of Aṅgiras; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *prāsyadhārāḥ*. For the six [verses], *nṛmedha* of the lineage of Aṅgiras; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *pradhārāḥ*. For the six [verses], *bindu* of the lineage of Aṅgiras; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *prasomāsaḥ*. For the six [verses], *śyāvāśva* of the lineage of Agni; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *prasomāsaḥ*. For the six [verses], *trita āsya*; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *prasuvānaḥ*. For the six [verses], *gotama rāhūgaṇa*; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. *trita ānapavasya*. For the six [verses], *prabhavasuḥ*. *asarjirathyaḥ*. [37] For the six [verses], *prabhūvasuḥ*. *sasasutaḥ*. For the six [verses], *rāhūgaṇa*. *eṣa utsyaḥ*. For the six [verses], *rāhūgaṇa*. *āsurarṣaḥ*. For the six [verses], *bṛhanmati* of the lineage of Aṅgiras; *punānaḥ*. For the six [verses], *bṛhaspati*. *prayegāvaḥ*. For the six [verses]. *janayat*. For the six [verses]. *yo atya iva*. And for the six [verses], *medhātithi*; Soma is the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter throughout. [260] *prayā indraḥ* for the six [verses], *ayāsya*. *sayavasvaḥ* for the six [verses], *mayāsya* of the lineage of Aṅgiras. *asṛgram* for the six [verses], *ayāsya*. *ayāsomaḥ* for five [verses], *kavi* of the lineage of Bhṛgu. *tat tvā yāmi* for five [verses]. *pavasva svavṛṣṭim* and for five [verses], *kavi*. *utte śuṣmāsaḥ* for five [verses]. *utathya* of the lineage of Aṅgiras; *adhvaryo* for five [verses]. *paridyukṣaḥ* and for five [verses], *utathya*. *utte* for four [verses]. *asya pra snām* for four [verses]. *vayaṃ vayaṃ* and for four [verses], *avatsāra*; *parisomaḥ*. For four [verses], *avatsāra* of the lineage of Kaśyapa. *prate dhārāḥ* for four [verses]. *taratsamandī* for four [verses]. *pavasvaḥ*. [60] And for four [verses], *avatsāra*. Śukrajyotis (is the seer). 18|7|1. Parameṣṭhī Mātura [is the seer]; the meter is Uṣṇih.

*Sūryasthā*: Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati; Sūrya. For the *vyāhṛtis*, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati; Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati. *Upaprayanto bṛhaddevāgniḥ*: Gāyatrī. *Tanūnapād agne bṛhaddevāgniḥ*: Gāyatrī. Regarding the two *yajus* beginning with *eṣa te rudrabhāgaḥ*: for the first, Prajāpati and Rudra; Bṛhatī or Sāma-Paṅkti. For the second, Yajus-Bṛhatī. *Adas tena tvā parameṣṭhī prajāpatiḥ*: Ājyam; Prajāpati; Rudra; Kakup. Regarding the two beginning with *ambakam*: for the first, Vasiṣṭha; for the second, Prajāpati; for both, Rudra; Anuṣṭubh. *Ākūtyai, prayuje, medhāyai; dīkṣāyai, svarasvatyai*: for these four Maudgalya verses, Prajāpati, Agni, and Āsuri; Triṣṭubh; or Yajus-Paṅkti. *Cid asi manāsi*: Prajāpati; the cow for purchasing Soma; Brāhmī Paṅkti or Atiśakkarī. *Agnestanūpāḥ parameṣṭhī prajāpatiḥ*: Havis; or Deva Viṣṇu; Prajāpati Viṣṇu; Anuṣṭubh. *Viṣṇor nukam*, *divo vā*, *pratadviṣṇuḥ*: for these three, Prajāpati Viṣṇu; Triṣṭubh; Yajus at the end of the first. *Viṣṇor arāṭam*: for these five *yajus* formulas, Prajāpati Viṣṇu; for the first, Daivī Jagatī; for the following four, Daivī Paṅkti. *Agnervrata-pāḥ*: Prajāpati Agni; Brahmā; Triṣṭubh. *Ayaṃ naḥ prajāpatir agniḥ*: Yajus; Triṣṭubh. *Idam āpaḥ*: Prajāpati Āpas; Mahāpaṅkti ending in Triṣṭubh, being a *pāvamāna* verse. *Devās tvā śukrapāḥ*; *devās tvā manthipāḥ*: for these two, Prajāpati; respectively Śukra and Manthin; the two *havirdhāna* carts; Agni; Yajus-Paṅkti. *Ādityayā kuvaktyai*: Manu; Sato-Bṛhatī. *Yukṣvā hi keśinā*: Madhucchandas; Indra; Anuṣṭubh. *Agne pavasva*: Vaikhānasa Agni; Gāyatrī. *Ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam*: Devas; Sūrya; Gāyatrī. *Ud u tyaṃ praskaṇvaḥ*: Sūrya; Gāyatrī. *Citraṃ devānām*: Kutsa Āṅgirasa; Sūrya; Triṣṭubh. *Catvāri śṛṅgā*: Parameṣṭhin; Yajñapuruṣa; Triṣṭubh. *Devo yajñaṃ prajāpatiḥ sarasvatyaḥ*: Liṅgoktā; Anuṣṭubh. *Pitṛbhyaḥ prajāpatyaḥ sarasvatyaḥ pitaraḥ*. *Vasena kratunā prajāpatiḥ sarasvatī*: Liṅgoktā; Anuṣṭubh. *Senā prajāpatiḥ*: Anuṣṭubh. *Agnaye śeṣapataye*: Dakṣiṇāgni; Āsurī Paṅkti. *Agneryatte śukram*: Prajāpati Agni; Gāyatrī. *Suparṇo ‘si garutmān*: Prajāpati Garutmān; Kṛti. *Drupadād iva*: Kokila Rājaputra or Drupada; Āpas; Anuṣṭubh. *Śatavantaḥ*: Ātharvaṇa; Oṣadhīs; Anuṣṭubh. For the twenty-seven verses beginning with *yā oṣadhīḥ* and ending with *yo asmābhidāsati*, the son of Ātharvaṇa, the physician; Oṣadhīs; Āpas; Anuṣṭubh. *Aśvāvatīr gomatīḥ*: Vasiṣṭha; Uṣas; Triṣṭubh. *Sīrā yuñjanti*: Prajāpati Sārpi Agni; Prajāpati; Anuṣṭubh. *Kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ*: for these five, Devas Vāmadeva; Agni; Triṣṭubh. *Kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt*: for these two, Agni iṣṭikā; Anuṣṭubh. *Apāṅgam bhan*: Prajāpati Varuṇa; Paṅkti. *Imaṃ me varuṇa śrudhi*: for these five verses, Prajāpati Agni; Triṣṭubh. *Apātvā oṣadhīr āpaḥ*: Agni; Anuṣṭubh. For the Rudrādhyāya beginning with *namas te rudra manyave*, the seers are Prajāpati or Vāmadeva. The first section (*anuvāka*) consists of sixteen verses, having Rudra as its deity. The first is Gāyatrī; then the three beginning with *yā te rudra* are Anuṣṭubhs; the three beginning with *asau yas tāmra* are Paṅktis; the seven beginning with *namo astu nīlagrīvāya* are Anuṣṭubhs; then the two are Jagatīs. *Manomantaṃ mānastoke*: Kutsa; the rest as before. In the section ending with *dvāpe andhasaspate*, there are seven verses. There, the first is Upariṣṭād-Bṛhatī; the second, seen by the seer Kutsa, is Jagatī; the third is Anuṣṭubh. *Parito rudrasya*, *mīḍhuṣṭama*: these two are Triṣṭubhs. Then two Anuṣṭubhs beginning with *asaṃkhyātā sahasrāṇi* and ending with *ya etāvantaḥ* are called the *daśāvatāna* mantras, having Bahurudra as their deity and Anuṣṭubh meter. Then the final three *yajus* beginning with *namostu rudrebhyo ye divi* are called *pratyavaroha*, having Bahurudra as their deity and Ghṛti meter. Between the first and last sections, all the *yajus* beginning with *namo hiraṇyavāhave* and ending with *nama ānirhatebhyaḥ
Now follow the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.

Regarding the verses beginning with *yad devāsti*, *yadi divā*, and *yadi jāgrad*: for these three, Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*); their deities (*devatā*) are respectively Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya; and the meter (*chandaḥ*) for all is Anuṣṭubh. The Yajus formula *yad grāme* has its deity indicated by its characteristic marks (*liṅga*). The verse *samudre te* is a Dvipadā Virāj, non-divine (*adaivī*). *Drupadād iva*: Prajāpati is the seer, the Waters (*āpaḥ*) are the deity, and the meter is Anuṣṭubh. *Ud vayaṃ tam*: Praskaṇva is the seer, Sūrya is the deity, and the meter is Anuṣṭubh. *Āpo adyānvacāriṣam*: Prajāpati is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the meter is Paṅkti. *Edho ’si* and *Samid asi*: these two Yajus formulas have Śamī wood as their deity. *Samāvavarti*: for this verse, Agni is the deity, it is addressed (*abhiruktā*), and the meter is Gāyatrī. *Vaiśvānara jyotiḥ*: this is a Yajus addressed to Vaiśvānara. *Abhyādadhāmi*: for this triplet of verses, Āśvatarāśvi is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the meter is Anuṣṭubh. *Aṃśunā*: for this verse, Sūrya is the deity and the meter is Anuṣṭubh. *Siñcati pariṣiñcati*: for this verse, Sūrya or Indra is the deity and the meter is Anuṣṭubh. *Dhānāvantam*: for this verse, Viśvāmitra is the seer, Indra is the deity, and the meter is Gāyatrī. *Bṛhadindrāya nṛmedha purumedhasā*: these two are addressed to Indra, the seers are Nṛmedha and Purumedha, and the meter is Bṛhatī. *Naye māyāvakānaḥ sarasvatī*: for this triplet of verses, Madhucchandas is the seer, Sarasvatī is the deity, and the meter is Gāyatrī. *Āmandor*: Viśvāmitra is the seer, Indra is the deity, and the meter is Bṛhatī. *Ā no viśāsuhavyam*: Śvāvāśva is the seer, Indra is the deity, and the meter is Bṛhatī. *Prasenānīḥ sakuśaskandhaḥ*: Skanda is the seer, and the meter is Triṣṭubh. *Pavitraṃ te*: for these two verses, Arkapṛṣṭhaskandha is the seer and the meter is Jagatī. This is known as the *Skandhasaṃhitā*. *Yad vā upaviṃśati*: Agastya is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the meter is Gāyatrī. *Sanād agne śrutir*: Yātudhāna is the seer, the meter is Gāyatrī. *Akṣaṇnamīmadantaḥ*: Yama is the seer, Indra is the deity, and the meter is Pañcapadā Paṅkti. *Avipṛṣṭhaḥ śaṃyur varuṇas*: Śaṃyu Varuṇa is the seer, the meter is Triṣṭubh. *Akrāt samudraḥ*: Vaikhānasa is the seer, Soma is the deity, and the meter is Triṣṭubh. This is known as the *Amityā Saṃhitā*. *Ye te panthā ajitasya jityantā*: the meter is Gāyatrī. *Etontv indraśuddhiyaḥ*: Indra is the deity, the meter is Virāj. *Śukraṃ te anyat*: Pūṣan and Agni are the deities, the meter is Triṣṭubh. *Mahatas somā vaśiṣṭhaḥ pavamānas*: Vasiṣṭha is the seer, Pavamāna is the deity, and the meter is Triṣṭubh. *Agnisti agninā*: Vāmadeva is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the meter is Gāyatrī. *Paritoṣiñcitā sutam acchidraḥ somo bṛhatī*: Soma is the deity, the meter is Bṛhatī. *Pavasva soma*: Dharma and Indra are the deities, the meter is Akṣarapaṅkti. *Cakraṃ yad asya*: Bhāradvāja is the seer, Indra is the deity, and the meter is Bṛhatī. *Ghṛtavatīti varuṇo dyāvāpṛthivyāvavir jagatī*: Varuṇa, Heaven and Earth, and Avidhi are the deities, the meter is Jagatī. *Adyā no devasavitaḥ sa ukṣa savitā gāyatrī*: Savitṛ is the deity, the meter is Gāyatrī. *Trātāram indram*: Maitra is the seer, Indra is the deity, and the meter is Bṛhatī. *Mahitrīṇāṃ paṣṭhohaḥ*: Indra is the deity, the meter is Gāyatrī. *Viśvāmitrasya bṛhadindrāya*: the meter is Bṛhatī. *Yo bhūtānām*: for this verse, Nārāyaṇīya Kauṇḍilya is the seer; the deity is Gṛdhyamāṇagraha; the meter is Paṅkti. This is the form of the Self (*ātman*) in the nature of discourse during the regulation of breath (*prāṇayāma*). *Aśinakṛtasyeti dve*: these two are Anuṣṭubhs; the following two are Bṛhatīs, with deities indicated by their characteristic marks. *Samiddha indra ity ekādaśānām āprī saṃjñakānām*: for these eleven verses known as the *Āprīs*, Aṅgiras is the seer in sequence.
