The deities are: Indhān, Tanūpāt, Nārāśaṃsī, Iḍas, Barhis, Dvāras, Uṣasānaktā, Daivyā, Rātiḥ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vanaspati, and Svāhākṛtis. Here, the first is *Urūpathāḥ prathamānam*; the *vyūha* consists of twelve verses beginning with *Suvīrāvīram*, and another set of twelve beginning with *Acchinnam*.
Thus ends the injunction regarding the Yajus formulas. Now follow the seers, deities, and meters of the Sāmans.

This [hymn] belongs to Viṣṇu; it is the inspired speech (*prakāvya*) of the inquiring Viṣṇu, like Uśanas speaking with his brows. It is called *Vaiṣṇavī*, for it pertains to the vow of Puruṣa. In that [hymn], "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" (Viṣṇu here) has Prajāpati as its seer and Gāyatrī as its meter. "vṛkṣasya viṣṇo" (of the tree, O Viṣṇu) has Viṣṇu as its deity and Jagatī as its meter. "prakāvyaṃ uśaneva bhruvāṇaḥ" (the inspired speech, as if speaking with his brows) has Varohe Viṣṇu as its deity and Triṣṭubh as its meter. "puruṣavrate" (in the vow of Puruṣa) has the two Puruṣas, Nārāyaṇa and [Viṣṇu], as its deities and Anuṣṭubh as its meter. "idaṃ oṃ hyatvojaseti" (this, Oṃ, indeed, by strength) is the first [verse]; therein Madhucchandas is the seer, Indra is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter. For the seven [verses] beginning with "vyomaghonāṃ" (of those possessing the celestial waters), Madhucchandas is the seer, the Vimeda gods are the deities, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter. For "purāsindhuḥ" (formerly the ocean), Kavi is the seer, the Maruts are the deities, and Indra is the deity with Anuṣṭubh as the meter. "tavasva somam" (be strong, O Soma); Madhucchandas is the seer, Pavamāna is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. "surūpakṛt nu" (the maker of beautiful forms, now); Madhucchandas is the seer and Gāyatrī is the meter. "ud uttamaṃ varuṇapāśam" (up the highest bond of Varuṇa); Gautama is the seer, Varuṇa is the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter. "śukraṃ candro" (the bright moon); Śukra Candramas is the deity and Gāyatrī is the meter. "śuddhāśuddhā" (pure and impure); Śuddha is the deity, Indra is the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter. "nṛtasūktaṃcaḥ" (the hymn of the manly one); Agni is the deity, Śyena is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. "indrastridhātu" (Indra, three-layered); in the verse "indre," Indra is the deity and Bṛhatī is the meter. "viśā pṛtanā" (with the people, the army); Triśoka Indu is the deity and Jagatī is the meter. "somaṃ rājānaṃ" (King Soma); Bṛhaspati, Agni, Āditya, Varuṇa, and Viṣṇu are the deities. "caruṣaṇī ghṛtaṃ" (the ghee for the eater of food); Vārhakṣṇa is the seer, Sarpa is the deity, Prasarpā is the deity, and Jagatī is the meter. "saminyāyanti janidhānam" (they come together to the place of birth); Ayāṃ Garbha is the deity, Āpas (Waters) are the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. "indrāho nṛpam" (O Indra, the protector of men); Agni is the deity and Gāyatrī is the meter. "sante payāṃsi" (may the milks be yours); in the "Somavrate," Soma is the deity, Soma is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. In the "Somavrate," likewise in the "Daivavrate," the "Ṛṣivrate," Rudra is the deity. In the third [section], the Viśvedevas are the deities. "yajñapad indro ‘nayadane" (Indra led us to the place of sacrifice); Pūṣan is the deity, Pūṣan is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter. "bhago na citra" (Bhaga, like the bright one); Sāntanika Agni is the deity and Virāṭ is the meter. This applies to both [sections] of the Sāman. "imam indreti" (this Indra); for the two sections, Vasiṣṭha is the seer, Indra is the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter. "paripriyā kavir" (the wise one, dear on all sides); Karṇāpava Kavi is the seer and Gāyatrī is the meter. In the Rathantara [Sāman], Vasiṣṭha is the seer. "īśāna" (the lord); Indra is the deity and Bṛhatī is the meter. In the Vāmadevya [Sāman], Vāmadeva is the seer, the All-Gods are the deities, and Gāyatrī is the meter. "yaśaḥ sameti" (glory comes together); Yaśas Indra is the deity and Bṛhatī is the meter. "indramihāsināh" (bring Indra here with the sword); Kaṇva is the seer, Indra is the deity, and Bṛhatī is the meter.

[281] *Rathantara* is as before; *gīrvāṇā*, *pāhi naḥ sutam*—*hariḥ*, *śrīḥ* is the *nidhana*; *indraḥ*, *gāyatrī*. *Attrāviśantv indavaḥ*, *āśita indraḥ*, *gāyatrī*; *indro himat sindhavaḥ*, *pūṣā*, *indraḥ*, *gāyatrī*. *Āyantīha trāyanti ye*, *indraḥ*, *bṛhatī*. *Gavyeṣu godvaye*, *śyāvāśvaḥ*, *indraḥ*, *gāyatrī*. *Idaṃ moghaṃ tu*, *madhuchandāḥ*, *indraḥ*, *gāyatrī*. *Bhadro no agnir āhutaḥ*, *gautamaḥ*, *bhagaḥ*, *indraḥ*, *gāyatrī*. In the *vairūpyāṣṭaka*, *virūpaḥ*, *indraḥ*, *bṛhatī*. In this *aṣṭaka*, the seers (*ṛṣis*) follow in order: for the first two, *śikhaṇḍī*; for the next two, *atriḥ*; for the next two, *mahāstravetasaḥ*; for the next two, *śirīṣaḥ*. In all these cases, *indraḥ* is the deity and *jagatī* is the meter. *Agne vivasvad uṣasaḥ*, *iḍimāṇḍavyaḥ*, *jātavedāḥ*, *anuṣṭup*. *Evaspate soma indras*, *triṣṭup*. *Trir asmai marutāṃ dhanvan dhenavaḥ*, *jagatī*. *Svātvāhitveti oṃ sahasra iti*, *indraḥ*, *yajus*. *Dhānāvantaṃ karayanbhaṇam iti*, *abhiṣavaḥ*, *indraḥ*, *gāyatrī*. *Vāstoṣpate iti*, *prajāpatiḥ*, *vāstu*, *yajus*. *Abhrātuvya iti*, *abhrātuvya indraḥ*, *kakup*. *Vāta āvātu bheṣajam*, *kāśinaḥ*, *vāyuḥ*, *gāyatrī*, with five *nidhanas*; *vāmdevyaḥ*, *vāmadevyaḥ*. *Rāhuḥ*, *gāyatrī*. *Asitvā pūrvapītaya iti*, *vaṣṭkāraḥ*, *prajāpatiḥ*, *indraḥ*, *bṛhatī*. *Abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ*, by means of the secret word *hi*, *indraḥ*, *bṛhatī*. *Indram id devatātaye*, *krasuvaḥ*, *indraḥ*, *bṛhatī*. *Gavāvrate*, *prajāpatiḥ*, *gāvaḥ*, *triṣṭup*. *Puruṣavrate*, *puruṣo nārāyaṇaḥ*, *anuṣṭup*. *Rātrer vrate*, *prajāpatiḥ*, *rātriḥ*, *anuṣṭup*. *Indra sānasiṃ rohit*, *kulāyaḥ*, *indraḥ*, *gāyatrī*. *Bhāruṇḍasāmani*, *bhāruṇḍaḥ*, *vrātavedāgniḥ*, *jagatī*. *Gāyatram sā pauṣkalam*, *āgneyagāyatrī*. *Revata kumbhavaraivataḥ*, *indraḥ*, *gāyatrī*. *Trisuparṇe*, *trisuparṇaḥ*, *sūryaḥ*, *gāyatrī*. *Mahāvaiśvānaravrate*, *vaiśvānaraḥ*, *ambis*.
[282] The *triṣṭubh* meter; *āniṣaṅgaḥ* (the quiver); *indraḥ*; various meters (*nānāchandāṃsi*). The *bṛhatsāman*s; Bhāradvāja; Indra; the *bṛhatī* meter—thus is the *Sāmavidhāna*.

Now, the seers (*ṛṣi*), deities (*devatā*), and meters (*chandas*) of the *Atharvamantra*s: for the *Śāntātīya* group, the seer is Śāntātīva-aśva, the deity is Indra, and all meters apply. For the *Bhaiṣajya* group, the seer is Bhaiṣajya, the deity is Āyu, and the meter is *uṣṇih*. For the *Raudra* group, the seer is Brahmā Raudra, and all meters apply.

Now, the ten groups (*daśagaṇa*). 1. Of the *Śāntigaṇa*: the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Soma; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. 2. Of the *Kūtpādūṣaṇagaṇa*: the seer is Śukra Kūtpādūṣaṇa; the deities are all the meters (*chandāṃsi*). 3. Of the *Dhātanagaṇa*: the seer is Dhātāgaṇa; the deity is Agni; the meters are all the meters. 4. Of the *Mātṛṇām gaṇa*: the seer is Mātṛnāman; the deity is Mātṛnāman; the meter is *uṣṇih*. 5. Of the *Vāstoṣpatigaṇa*: the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Vāstoṣpati; the meters are all the meters. 6. Of the *Pāpmana gaṇa*: the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Pāpmahan; the meters are *gāyatrī*, *uṣṇih*, *kakubh*, and *anuṣṭubh*. 7. Of the *Yakṣmanāśanagaṇa*: the seer is Mātṛnāman; the deity is Yakṣmanāśana; the meters are all the meters. 8. Of the *Duḥsvapnanāśanagaṇa*: the seer is Yama; the deity is Duḥsvapnanāśana; the meters are all the meters. 9. Of the *Āyuṣyagaṇa*: the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Āyuḥ; the meters are the seven beginning with *gāyatrī*. 10. Of the *Sarvasya gaṇa*: the seer is Atharvan; the deity is Bṛhaspati; the meters are *anuṣṭubh*, *bṛhatī*, *paṅkti*, and *anuṣṭubh*. Of the eighteen groups: the seer is Atharvan; the deity is Candra; the meters are all the meters. *Śanno devīḥ* (Hymn of the Goddesses): the seer is Sindhudvīpa; the deity is the Waters (*āpaḥ*); the meter is *gāyatrī*. *Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ* (The golden-colored, pure ones): spoken by Atharvan; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. For the *Atharvāṇānuvākādi* (Atharvan’s recitations, etc.): the seer is Atharvan; the deity is Candra; the meters are all the meters. *Yā oṣadhīḥ* (Those which are herbs): the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Bṛhaspati; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. For the fourteen hymns beginning with *Mamāgne varcaḥ*: the seer is Kubera; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. *Nadīpaṃ tv apsarovādarāyaṇīr apsaraḥ*: the seer is Apsaras; the meter is *jagatī*. *Sodakrāmat sā devānām aparivrata indraḥ*: the deity is Indra; the meter is *aticchandas*. *Suparṇo ‘si sauparṇo garutmān*: the seer is Suparṇa; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. *Indra jīva* (O Indra, live): for the *Hṛdayasūkta* (Heart Hymn), the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Indra; the meter is *gāyatrī*. *Yat svam mṛtpur abhyatsva*: the seer is Bṛhaspati; the deity is Mṛtpur; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. *Yaś cedam śūnyam aśītisūktam* (This hymn of eighty verses on emptiness): the seer is Atharvan; the deity is Bhūmi; the meter is *paṅkti*. In the mantra *Pṛthivyām* (On the earth): the deities are Agni, Earth, Atmosphere, Sky, and Moon; the meters are *paṅkti* and *atijagatī*. *Uttamo ‘si* (Thou art the highest): for this mantra, the deities are Pratisara, Indra, Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, Rudra, and Agni Prajāpati; the first meter is *paṅkti*, and for the seven following, it is *anuṣṭubh*. *Udumbareti maṇineti sūktam* (The hymn beginning with "On the udumbara tree" and "With the amulet"): the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Kubera; for the three beginning with the fifth verse, the meter is *triṣṭubh*; for the remaining thirteen, it is *anuṣṭubh*. *Yonasva* (From the womb): the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Īśvara; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. *Indreṇa vṛttam*: the seer is Varuṇa; the deity is Indra; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. *Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*: the seer is Brahmā; the deity is the Waters; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. *Iyam vediḥ*: the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Indra; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. *Abhitavyam etātasya*: the seer is Atharvan; the deity is the Waters; the meter is *paṅkti*. *Sarasvatī vrateṣu te*: this is the *Sūkta*; the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Sarasvatī; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. The *Saurasāmans* beginning with *Viṣāsahi sahamānam*: the seer is Ātharvaṇa; the deity is Āditya; the meter is *jagatī*. *Piśācakṣayo gamaśiyātanaḥ piśācakṣaśau*: the seer is Piśācakṣa; the meter is *gāyatrī*. *Yamasya lokād adhyā*: the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Yama; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. *Agnir vaiśanāyadavāya*: the seer is Agni; the deity is Indra; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. *Ūrdho bhavet agnikṛtyā pratiharaṇaḥ*: the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. *Indra vaya vāṇijam*: the seer is Atharvan; the deity is Īśāna; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. *Kamomerājantv iti*: the seer is Brahmā; the deity is Kāma; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. *Bhadrāyakarṇadarvyeti*: the seers are Kauśika and the Aśvins; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. *Tubhyam eva janisantv iti*: the seer is Śāṃyu; the deity is Jarimā; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. *Āyātu mitra*: the seers are Mitra and Varuṇa; the deities are the Waters and the Fires; the meter is *triṣ
Such is the ritual injunction of the Atharvans.

Now, regarding the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and *devatā* of the syllable *Oṃ*: according to the *Yājuṣa-sarvānukrama*, for the syllable *Oṃ*—which is the supreme imperishable (*paramākṣara*), the support for yogins, known as the *praṇava*, the supreme Brahman, and endowed with qualities such as grossness (*sthūla*) and so forth—the *ṛṣi* is Brahmā, the *chandas* is *Gāyatrī*, and the *devatā* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is at the beginning and conclusion of Vedic study (*brahmārambha*), in sacrifices, oblations, and other rites, in peaceful ceremonies, and in all other obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rituals. Thus says Śāṭyāyana: "In acts of giving, sacrifice, austerity, Vedic study, recitation, meditation, twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), oblation, and the chanting of mantras dedicated to the gods or ancestors, as well as at the commencement of Vedic study—one should maintain the *praṇava*. One should set it in motion. This establishes the necessity of knowing the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and *devatā* of mantras. Having described the nature of the *ṛṣis*, deities, and meters in the *Yājuṣa-sarvānukrama*, [the text] states: "He who studies, recites, mutters, offers oblations, sacrifices, or officiates at sacrifices without knowing these, his Vedic merit does not endure long; he perishes like a withered stump, or is consumed by fire, or becomes worse off. As stated in the *Chandoga-brāhmaṇa*: "He who..."

[287] Or, if one officiates at a sacrifice or teaches with a mantra whose *ṛṣi* and *brāhmaṇa* are unknown, he strikes against a wooden post or falls into a pit; he becomes worse off and his meters become exhausted. Therefore, one should know these [details] for every mantra. Now follow the mantras for the giving of various substances. Among those, the mantras for the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the nine planets are as stated in the *Mātsya*:
O Kapilā Rohiṇī, you are worthy of worship by all beings because you embody all sacred fords; therefore, grant me peace.
O Kapila, you are meritorious; you are the merit of all things meritorious and the most auspicious among auspicious things. Since you are eternally held by Viṣṇu, grant me peace.
O Gaṅgā,
you are Dharma in the form of a bull, the bringer of joy to the world;
as the abode of the eightfold form [of Śiva], grant me peace.
Of the red bull:
"The golden seed of the sun, residing within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha, bestows the fruit of infinite merit; therefore, grant me peace."
Of gold:
Since a pair of yellow garments is dear to Vāsudeva,
may Viṣṇu grant me peace through the gift of that.
O you who wear a pair of yellow garments,
since you are the very form of Viṣṇu and since you are born from the nectar of immortality,
and since your vehicle is eternally the moon and the sun, therefore grant me peace.
Of Śvetāśva: Since you are the entire earth, a cow resembling Keśava,
and the eternal remover of all sins, therefore grant me peace.
O black-colored bull,
since all iron works, such as the plow and other weapons, are always dependent upon you, therefore grant me peace.
O Iron,
since you are established as an auxiliary to the goat sacrifices and are the constant vehicle of Vibhāvasu (Fire), therefore grant me peace.
O goat,
you are the refuge of all the worlds and the supreme protector of modesty;
since you wear such beautiful attire, grant me peace.
For one who wears white garments,
a pair of red garments is always dear to the Sun;
therefore, by the gift of these to me, may Sūrya grant me peace.
Of the pair of red garments:
"The most beautiful black garment was worn by Dharmarāja;
for the destruction of all afflictions, I offer this black garment."
Of the one clad in black garments:
"Since food alone is Lakṣmī, and food alone is Janārdana,
may food, which is the Brahman that protects all, be mine in birth after birth."
[289] Of food: Seated upon the lunar disc, with a radiance equal to the moon and the lotus,
may Vāmana be pleased by my gift of curd-rice.
May the King of Dharma always be pleased with me through this gift of curd-rice with side-dishes, which embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Of rice with curd and side-dishes;
this vessel of rice with curd, accompanied by water—
when honored, it becomes fruitful along with the ritual fee.
Take this bowl of curd-rice from me.
May Nārāyaṇa—
the soul of all, the lord of all worlds, the eternal, and the all-pervading—
be pleased by the gift of this rice-and-pulse dish accompanied by water.
Of the kṛsarānnam:
May milk-rice (pāyasa) and fine rice (paramānna), the most excellent among all gifts,
worthy of all deities, bestow prosperity and nourishment.
Of the milk-rice:
"This food, through the splendor of the Sun, brings about the highest excellence of birth;
that food is dear to me—accept this most excellent cake."
Of the cake-food:
Since flour-meal (śaktavaḥ) has been declared to belong to Prajāpati in the sacrificial rite, therefore I offer this flour-meal; may Prajāpati be pleased with me.
[290] Of the barley-meal: Silver, which arose among the Asuras and is dear to the ancestors,
may Rudra be well-pleased with me through the offering of this.
May the copper vessel purify that silver [offering] and whatever sin has arisen from slandering others, calumny, and the eating of forbidden food.
Of the copper vessel:
"Whatever sinful deeds have been committed through desire, arising from desire,
may they always perish for me by the gift of this bell-metal vessel."
[This is] for the bell-metal vessel:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, bestower of the fruits of desired objects!
I shall offer a vessel of sesame seeds, as I abide upon your body."

O mirror, by your very sight you are the bestower of auspiciousness upon men; may you grant them valor, good fortune, noble fame, and stainless knowledge. Regarding the vessel for gold, sesame seeds, and so forth: [the same applies].
Of the mirror:
May the pearls produced from the Tāmraparṇī river, those arising from oyster shells, and those described in the Purāṇas as being born of the ocean— may they grant me worldly enjoyment and liberation.

O you who are born from the golden lotus of the Creator Brahmā, the progenitor of the world; O you who were born from the navel of Hari, the dweller in the lotus—protect me always! O you who are liberated!
[291] Of the Golden Lotus: In wildernesses, forest fastnesses, and on paths infested with thieves and beasts of prey,
may the harmful ones not cause harm, through the power of the lion’s gift.
Of Siṃha:
"I offer this golden ring, produced from the Golden Womb (Hiraṇyagarbha), which bestows righteousness; may the Lord of Kamalā be pleased."
Of the ring:
"I shall give a golden bracelet, which bestows beauty, luster, and happiness; this ornament always adorns me."
Of the bracelet: "The pair of earrings that first emerged during the churning of the Ocean of Milk,
which emerged together with Śrī— may Śrī be pleased with me as she gives them."
A pair of earrings,
flowers of gems and gold, and those made of jewels and pearls,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of offering a *tulasī* leaf.
Through the offering of a Tulasī leaf, may the sins born from the body of Brahmā be pacified, and may all desires be fulfilled.
The Mantra for the Gift of Tulasī:
"May it constantly remove misfortune and constantly increase good fortune;
it is auspicious, life-prolonging, and bestows peace—therefore, grant these to me."
I shall offer butter produced from the milk of the wish-fulfilling cow, which is supremely pleasing to Viṣṇu;
grant me strength and nourishment.
Of butter:
May this clarified butter, produced from the wish-fulfilling cow, the supreme oblation of the gods,
which increases the lifespan of the giver, protect me forever.
Of clarified butter:
Oil is always nourishing, life-prolonging, and a destroyer of sin;
it removes inauspiciousness and is meritorious; therefore, grant me peace.
"For the sake of warding off thorns, leftover food scraps, stones, scorpions, and the like,
I shall bestow these sandals; please accept them out of affection for the Brahmin."
The mantra of the sandals:
O you who resemble the rays of the moon, white as snow and sea-foam,
beloved by the gods and immortals, quickly dispel all misfortune!
O sandalwood tree,
friend of the mandāra tree that is the abode of the yakṣas, honored by the gods—
by your grace, O sandalwood, be the bestower of intense bliss upon me.
Of a piece of sandalwood:
"I offer this unguent, blended with *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *kāṇḍa*, camphor, musk, and saffron; may it grant me constant happiness."
[293] O you who are praised by all beings, including gods and asuras, and who are anointed with sandalwood and other unguents—
may musk applied to your limbs always grant me happiness.
Since camphor bestows the pride of the god of love and satisfies the vital breaths, O you who take pride in the Śrāddha rite, let the torment of worldly existence depart through your gift of musk.
Of camphor:
that saffron and other unguents which had adhered to the bodies of the Gopīs during their water-sports in Dvāravatī were cast into the water.
Gopīcandana has been described by the lords of sages as the destroyer of sins;
therefore, by the offering of this, may Viṣṇu grant one's desire.
Regarding Gopīcandana:
since you, having prepared the nectar for the gods, transformed it into the Hālāhala poison.
Likewise, O Lord, the triple city of the gods was burnt by a single arrow for the sake of the welfare of the world.
Through your gift, I too shall be faultless;
indeed, freed from faults, I shall attain the Gaṇas.
Act accordingly; I seek refuge in you.
O Lord, best of gods, be gracious toward me.
Of the image of Śiva:
May Bhava, the Great Lord clad in an elephant hide, be forever gracious—the God who, together with Pārvatī, is the cause of the world's creation. [294]
Of Umā and Maheśvara:
Since this entire world, both moving and unmoving, consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti,
may the Blessed One therefore grant me all auspiciousness through this.
May the Lord who dwells on Kailāsa, the consort of Gaurī, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes,
the soul of all that is moving and unmoving, who exists in the form of the Liṅga, grant our desire. [Salutation] to the Liṅga.
This emerald *liṅga*, together with a silver pedestal,
accompanied by twelve types of grain and eleven fruits,
I offer according to the prescribed rite; may the fruit as described be mine.
Regarding the *marakata* linga;
however, in the case of the Kāśmīra linga, one should say it is born from the *indrakāśmīra*.
Regarding the Kāśmīra linga.
The earth, the refuge of all beings, was lifted up by the Boar;
she who bestows infinite crops and fruits—therefore, grant me peace.
[The wool] produced from sheep and rams [is used for] the land of crops; since it removes the fear of cold winds and acts as a remover of frost,
therefore grant me peace.
O Lord, may your woolen footprint, which is the golden seed, be meditated upon;
O Lord of Gods, accept what is offered and swiftly destroy my sin.
O Lord of the Ūrṇā hair-tuft! You bestow grain upon the donor both in this world and in the next;
therefore, let grain be given, and through this, grant me peace.
Of grain: Since Jambūdvīpa consists of food, is the source of wheat,
and bestows the wealth of happiness upon the Gandharvas, therefore grant me peace.
Since mung beans are indeed dear to Parameṣṭhin,
may my satisfaction be eternally accomplished through the offering of these.
Of mung beans:
"In ancient times, at the moment Govardhana was lifted up, these chickpeas were eaten by Hari;
they destroy all sins, so grant me peace."
Of all pulses, salt is the first-born and best among juices; it increases strength and was created by Brahmā himself. Therefore, may it grant peace.
Of salt:
"And barley, the king of grains, auspicious and pleasing to the twice-born;
therefore, by the gift of these, may my desired fruit be attained."
[296] Of barley:
"Sesame seeds always remove sin; they are born from the body of Viṣṇu.
O Keśava, through the gift of sesame seeds, destroy all my sin."
Of sesame seeds:
Born of the lineage of nectar, O Night of the Excessive Flow of Sugarcane, you who are eternally pleasing to the Sun; therefore, grant me peace.
Of sugar:
"Sugar has arisen from the middle of the bow of the Mind-born [God of Love].
Therefore, by the offering of this, may my heart's desires be fulfilled.
The *praṇava* is always the foremost of all mantras, as Pārvatī is among women;
likewise, sugarcane juice is always considered the best of all juices.
Therefore, O Guḍa, grant me prosperity and haste at all times.
O molasses, since you were drunk by the ancestors at the *śrāddha* as honey born of nectar,
therefore, by your offering, protect me from the ocean of suffering.
Madana said:
"Since it contains a jar filled with water and embodies three deities, may Dharmarāja be pleased; may there be merit through this gift."
[297] Of the water-jar: "I shall offer these sandals for warding off thorns and the like;
since they grant comfort in all places, bestow peace upon me."
O pair of sandals,
you who bring coolness and bliss to all living beings,
auspicious and eternally bestowing satisfaction upon the ancestors; therefore, grant me peace.
Of the fan:
Adorned with wheels and other ornaments by its dwelling in a great treasury;
through this gift to the deity, may my heart's desires be fulfilled.
O Śālagrāma, you are the dweller in the great treasury; you are Mahādeva, the Great Lord. May he be pleased by this gift of yours, and therefore grant me peace.
Of Śivanābha: At the most terrible gate of Yama, there is that river Vaitaraṇī;
desiring to cross it, I give this—please ferry me across with ease.
O Vaitaraṇī!
Since you are the entire earth, like a cow belonging to Viṣṇu,
and are eternally the remover of all sins, therefore grant me peace.
To you, who have obtained a cow and have set out for the transition of death in order to increase the transition into happiness, I offer this cow known by the name Samutkrānti.
Of the cow of departure:
Whatever evil deed has been committed by me through speech, mind, or body— may all that go to dissolution, being countered by the gift of you.
The verses of Meṣī:
"O Blessed One, Lord with the trident in hand, destroyer of Dakṣa and other enemies! By the granting of your weapon, may my trident be forever destroyed."
Of the trident:
"Whatever numerous sins have been committed by me out of desire,
may they be destroyed forever by the gift of this iron vessel."
May these [sins]— the eating from a copper vessel, approaching those who should not be approached, and violating the wives of others—
always perish for me through the gift of a silver vessel.
Of the silver vessel:
All sesame seeds, when combined together, cause the destruction of misfortune and constantly bring pleasure to Viṣṇu; therefore, grant me peace.
Regarding the gifts of gold and sesame seeds: Sesame seeds are meritorious, purifying, auspicious, and fulfillers of all desires;
they are both white and black, having originated from the body of Viṣṇu.
Whatever sins there may be, even those equal to the murder of a Brahmin,
may they always be destroyed for me by the gift of a vessel of sesame seeds.

This vessel of sesame seeds along with gold destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; it was created by Brahmā in ancient times from the essence of the many-seeded Kushmanda. Therefore, grant me peace.
Of the Kushmanda:
"O Brahmin, this abundant fruit is offered by me before you;
by means of it, may I attain success in every birth."
Born from the splendor of the sun, effecting all auspiciousness,
and destroying all sins— O Maṇḍakas, grant me peace!
Of the *maṇḍakas*:
Whatever evil I have committed throughout thousands of other births,
may there be some peace for me here through this gift of a golden vessel.
Of the *vyatīpāta*:
Whatever prosperity (*lakṣmī*) is established in every limb by means of this [offering] to your body— may you pacify all that which is to be pacified, and increase both prosperity and nourishment.
For the sake of health, clarified butter (ājya) is used;
clarified butter is declared to be splendor, and clarified butter is remembered as the remover of sin.
Clarified butter is the food of the gods; the gods are established in clarified butter.
For the sake of destroying evil, [I offer] this clarified butter.
You are the protector of the gods and of men; for you are indeed my weapon. Therefore, through every effort, may there be peace at all times.
May these various kinds of cakes, which grant pleasure to Keśava when offered with devotion and bring satisfaction to Śambhu, Brahmā, and the Sun, bestow innate strength upon the weapon.
Of all foods,
the wood produced from the *soma* plant is most dear to Jātavedas;
therefore, O Vibhāvasu, grant prosperity through the offering of these.
Of the wooden sticks: those named Agnivarṇodbhavā increase strength and fame;
Kulattha destroys all sins; therefore, grant me peace.
Of the horse gram seeds:
"The seeds always sprout upon the surface of the earth when it has been ploughed at the proper time;
by your gift, may all my heart's desires be fulfilled."
O Lord of all planets, constellations, and stars; O Bhāskara, you are indeed the Lord of all!
O Divākara, ward off for me the affliction of the "thorn" (śūla) caused by the transition of the sun (saṃkrānti).
For one afflicted by the pain of transmigration,
I bestow this book, which produces all branches of knowledge and consists of graceful syllables; thus, the goddess Sarasvatī becomes dear to him.
By this [book], the protection of the lives of all living beings in the world is achieved;
for those grains which become rice through cooking belong to the Vaiśvadeva deities.
They are purifying in all sacrifices and highly praised in the rite of oblation;
therefore, may the Viśvadevas be pleased by this gift of rice.
Because the mind takes refuge in them, they are known as *sumanas* (flowers).
"May those given grant me constantly joy, virtue, and true prosperity."
Since the mandala for auspicious rites arises from flowers and cumin,
may Girijā be pleased with me through the gift of cumin.
Of cumin: Betel is auspicious, bestowing prosperity, and consists of the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
by the offering of this, may Brahmā and the other gods grant abundant well-being.
Of the betel:
accompanied by rice mixed with *nārāvalī* and filled to overflowing;
and with a full bowl of lime-powder (*cūrṇa*) containing camphor.
O Kaṇṭaka, you who are free from attachment, by your grace grant me forgiveness— this divine betel-chewing along with areca nut, which is so dear to the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Of the betel-bearer: May turmeric,
which is dear to Lakṣmī, the giver of Lakṣmī, which like Lakṣmī is fond of garments,
and which bestows good fortune upon excellent women— may it be glorious for me.
With turmeric,
pairs of bodice-cloths, as well as earrings,
necklaces, and ornaments, may Nirmāndinī be pleased.
Of the pair of auspicious substances:
"O illustrious wife of Rāma, O embodiment of merit, O one free from ailment!
O Jānakī, accept these winnowing baskets given by me."
Of the winnowing basket: A water-pot, filled with water, containing gold within, and possessing auspicious marks, is offered to you, O Mahāsena; may you be forever gracious.
"O Lord, this great and divine sacred thread (brahmasūtra) has been fashioned by me with great effort for the water-pot;
by the offering of this sacred thread, may I attain birth as a Brahmin."
Regarding the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*):
"This [thread], joined by me with twenty-eight Rudrākṣa beads, has been offered into your hand; accept it, O leader of the divine hosts!"
To Akṣamālā.
O Vidhuntuda, son of Siṃhikā, imperishable one, homage to you!
By this gift of the elephant, protect me from the calamity of being born as an outcaste.
O Svarṇanāga, I shall give you this sugarcane stalk, which is of great merit, full of juice, and the granter of all desires; by this, may the Supreme Lord be quickly pleased with you.
Of the sugarcane stalk:
camphor becomes like a plantain tree, O God, always dear to the gods;
it is the highest fortune of kings, and through its gift, one enjoys happiness.
O Goddess, born from the ocean through churning, I shall offer this jar made of flesh with devotion; may my heart's desires be fulfilled.
To the one who desires fragrance, the Sun grants all necessary implements;
may Bhāskara grant me the attainment of my heart's desire.
The embodiment of the Sun;
whom all praise as the Lord of the Universe, the Protector of the World, the Son of Umā,
and the Lord of Obstacles— O Swift One, I shall grant you that which bestows all desired things.
[304] Of the image of Gaṇeśa:
Since the fourteen worlds abide within the limbs of cows,
may there be auspiciousness for me in this world and in the next.
The mantra for the gift of a bed: "Since the bed of Keśava and of Śiva is never empty,
may my own bed likewise be never empty in birth after birth."
Just as all the gods are established within all the jewels,
so may the deities grant peace to me through this gift of jewels.
This is the Jewel Mantra:
Just as other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of land,
may peace for me arise here from the gift of land.
The mantra for the gift of land:
"O Śrīvatsa, this female slave is bestowed by me upon you;
therefore, she is to be enjoyed as a servant according to your wish. May there be prosperity for me."
The mantra for the female servant: Homage to the chariot, homage to the lord of the chariot; homage to you, Viśvakarman;
homage and homage to the lord who is all beings, to Aruṇa.
[305] Regarding the chariot: "O Lord Keśava, grant me protection here, there, and in both worlds!
For your pleasure, this auspicious umbrella has been given by me to a brahmin."
The mantra for the parasol:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, Soul of the universe!
O Lord Janārdana, be pleased by this palanquin which has been offered."
The Śivikā-mantra:
"O Brahmin, accept this house, complete with all its furnishings; through your grace, may my desired fruit be attained."
The House Mantra:
"O Treasure of the World, for the sake of my pleasure, grant me a dwelling.
This is the Dwelling Mantra.
O Brahmin, this fair-complexioned maiden, adorned according to your means, I offer to you of the Śarman lineage; O Brahmin, please accept her.
The Mantra of the Virgin:
"May the greatness of the gift of this queen— the auspicious chief consort of the world-protectors such as Candra— grant all my desires."
May she, whose son is established in the service of Dharmarāja and who is the mother of Mahiṣāsura, grant all my desires.
[306] Regarding the buffalo-cow:
A man shall conquer death by giving a buffalo-cow that is well-behaved, full of milk, accompanied by its calf, and adorned with jewels, cloth, and flowers.
O auspicious one, you have been bestowed upon the world with all your resources— your passion, skin, flesh, marrow, and so forth— as the queen of Death; therefore, I pray for your welfare.
Of the Ram:
"He who is the mouth of the gods, the bearer of oblations, honored by all—
of him you are the worshipful vehicle, revered by the gods including Indra and by the great seers."
Whatever digestive fire I have previously produced as a result of the ripening of past karma— destroy all that quickly and increase my internal fire.
Formerly you were created by Brahmā as the supreme, pure one;
since the sacrifice has arisen from your progeny, therefore become a bringer of peace.
The mantra for the unborn [Brahmā].

Now follows the procedure for the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others. Regarding that, it is stated in the *Padmapurāṇa* concerning the gift of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍa-dāna*):
"A Brahmin who maintains the perpetual fire (*agnihotrī*), who is handsome and endowed with virtuous qualities..."
And having honored him along with his wife, and having adorned them with ornaments.
Having invited the preeminent domestic priest and other officiating priests, all endowed with twenty-four qualities and accompanied by their wives; [307]
One should cause to be given new garments, garlands, and pure ornaments,
as well as rings and earrings.
Having thus honored them and standing before them,
he prostrated himself again and again with the eight-limbed salutation.
Placing their joined palms before the family priest, they said:
"O Brahmins, you have indeed been favored by the Creator as our friends."
By your gracious countenance here, a man shall himself become purified;
through the union of your affection, the Grandfather himself becomes pleased.
Regarding the *tulāpuruṣa* (weighing against gold), it is stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"That which exceeds one hundred *niṣkas* is considered best; half of that is remembered as middling;
half of that again is the lowest; thus it is prescribed there as being of three kinds."
Then [he gave] a pair of garments, a turban, earrings, a neck ornament,
a finger-ring, and an ornament for the wrist.
And at the commencement of all these rites, one should cause half of all these [fees] to be given to the domestic priest (purohita) and the other half to the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
One should give all the aforementioned ornaments, together with the turban and the garments,
as well as this covering cloth, to those who perform the rite.

In that regard, having appointed twenty-four other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), twenty Brahmins are to be chosen elsewhere as well. Regarding their installation, they are described with specific distinctions in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"In that rite, eight auspicious Hotṛ-priests and likewise eight gatekeepers should be appointed;
furthermore, eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas should be made reciters (*jāpaka*)."

The best of the twice-born who are endowed with all auspicious marks, possessed of the power of mantras, masters of their senses, and belonging to the two [eligible] lineages, shall be the consecrators.
Twenty-five officiating priests (ṛtvij) adorned with golden ornaments should be appointed;
one should honor them all equally, but the preceptor (ācārya) should receive double.

In this context, the value of items such as gold coins (*niṣka*) should be understood as one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five; this applies to the garments and ornaments for the officiants and the members of the assembly (*sadasya*). The formula for the invitation is: "Today, with such-and-such a sacrifice, I shall perform a rite; for the sake of that subsidiary act, I invite you, named so-and-so, of such-and-such a lineage, a student of such-and-such a Veda. The response is: "I am invited. The distinction between the various rites is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Having adorned the door-keepers on all sides with perfumes and flowers..."
The teacher should say to them, "Sacrifice," and he should honor them in return.
He should say "Sacrifice! to those who are the Hotṛ priests after honoring them;
and he should say "Remain [in meditation]! to the reciters (jāpaka), for they have already performed their duty through the muttering of mantras.

Based on the statement "at the commencement of religious rites," it should be understood that this [madhuparka] is common to all religious acts accomplished by officiating priests, such as universal giving, worship, and fire-oblations (*homa*). Now, Jābāla describes the *madhuparka* for those who have been chosen [as officiants]: "One should honor with the *madhuparka* the one related by marriage, the officiating priest, a *śrotriya* who has come to the house, a *snātaka*, and likewise a dear friend."
Viśvāmitra says: Having honored the officiating priests with the madhuparka offering, one should have them perform the ritual;
by having them perform the ritual without honoring them, one is joined with sin alone.
Now follows the procedure for the fire oblation (*homa*). In the *Devīpurāṇa*:

Having swept around [the site], smeared it, scraped it, dug it out, sprinkled it with water, and established the fire; having spread a seat for Brahmā to the south, led forward the water, strewn grass around it, placed the ritual implements according to their purpose, prepared two strainers (*pavitra*), consecrated the sprinkling-water (*prokṣaṇī*), sprinkled the implements as required, poured out the clarified butter (*ājya*), melted it, and carried fire around it; having heated the *sruva* ladle, wiped it, sprinkled it, heated it again, and set it down; having poured out the clarified butter, purified it, inspected it, and likewise prepared the sprinkling-water; having taken the *upayamana* grass-blades, added fuel-sticks, and sprinkled water around the fire, he should offer the oblation. This same procedure applies wherever there is a fire-oblation. Now we shall explain the mantras for the distribution of deities in the rites beginning with the sweeping around.

With the verse, "Whatever offense against the gods," he sweeps around [the site]. With the hymn, "May the mind protect us," he anoints [himself]. Having scratched [the ground] with the verse, "Thee, O Indra, lord of the virtuous, with the Vṛtras," and having lifted [the soil] with "Go to the fold," he sprinkles [it] with water while reciting, "Of the god thee. Having established the fire with the verse, "Agni is the head," he should place a fuel-stick upon it with the verse, "With fuel, O Agni, do ye honor."

Having sprinkled water toward the fire with the mantra *api gṛhṇāmi*, the Brahman priest sits to the south with *kiraṇyagarbha*. The *praṇītā* waters are placed to the north with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. The spreading of the *praṇītā* grass is performed with *kayā naś citraḥ*. The two strainers (*pavitre*) are consecrated with *pavitre stho vaiṣṇavye*. The clarified butter (*ājya*) is set out with *iṣe tvā*. Having heated the *sruva* ladle with *trātāram indram*, the cleansing (*mārjana*) is performed with *atiśino ’si sapatnīn*. It is heated again with *pratyuṣṇarakṣaḥ*. The purification (*utpavana*) is done with *saśinur vaḥ prasava utpunāmi*. The stirring upward (*udiṅgana*) is performed with *tad evāgniḥ*. The sprinkling around (*paryukṣaṇa*) is done with *bhūr asi*. Then the root-offering oblations (*mūlahomāhutayaḥ*) are made: *prajāpataye svāhā*, *indrāya svāhā*, *agnaye svāhā*, *antarikṣāya svāhā*, *oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*. In this way, the Vedic fire becomes consecrated.
Thus, this sacrificial procedure endowed with these characteristics has been ordained there for all fire-offerings by Brahmā of immeasurable splendor.
Otherwise, those who act while relying solely on the ritual manual (sūtra) will undoubtedly all depart from there without hope; so it is for all the gods.
Now, therefore, the deities of the ritual strewing are described.

Kāśyapa is present during the sweeping; the Viśvedevas during the smearing; Mitra and Varuṇa during the scraping; the Earth during the removal [of debris]; the Gandharvas during the sprinkling; Sarva during the placing of the fire; Brahmā during the preparation of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); the Āparas during the carrying forward of the water to the north; Śatakratu during the purposeful placement of the vessels; the Pitṛs during the binding of the strainers (pavitra); the Mothers during the consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* waters; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara during the *juhū*, *sruva*, and *sruvā* ladles; the Vasus during the placing of the clarified butter (*ājya*); Vaivasvata during the heating over the fire; the Maruts during the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*); Skanda during the removal [of the fire]; the Moon and Sun during the purification and re-purification; all the Directions during the inspection of the clarified butter; Umādevī during the placing of the *praṇītā* waters; Lakṣmī during the fuel-sticks (*idhma*); and all beings of the universe [are present] in the entire ritual.
O great sage, having understood the ritual procedure, one should take one of the excellent fires mentioned previously and perform the rite of oblation.
These deities have indeed been proclaimed for the benefit of the Brāhmaṇas,
both in sacrifices and in animal-binding rites, as well as in all ritual performances.
Brahmā said: O best of kings, I shall describe the supreme procedure for the fire-sacrifice, which accomplishes all ritual acts, according to its various names, distinctions, and rites.
The formal acceptance of the sacred fire must be performed by those who know the meaning of all the scriptures,
who have mastered the Siddhāntas of both the left and right traditions, the Vedānta, and the Gṛhya-sūtras.
The maintenance of the sacred fire must be undertaken by those who know how to ensure all prosperity;
otherwise, obstacles will arise to one's wealth and lifespan.
Whether one is chronically ill, unfortunate, or despised by all the world,
by knowing things as they truly are and not otherwise, one attains all happiness.
Therefore, with every effort, the rites to be performed upon the fire are considered essential;
thus, the eightfold group of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), divided into three types, has been described by me to you.
And although there are many types of fire-rituals prescribed, they may be performed as a single rite by means of figurative application;
thus, women, children, Śūdras, and the ignorant may offer oblations every day as follows.
Likewise, one should never [place it] in the kitchen or in a water-jar;
rather, having protected the sacrificial fire with consecrated mantras and various names.
[312] Those who desire the fruit should offer oblations while being skilled in the great ritual methods.
It is heard, O child, that in ancient times the sons of Vasu offered them without knowing [the proper procedure].
Those who invoked [the gods] with refined offerings met with the loss of their kingdom;
likewise, both the sacrificer and the priest soon met their death.
Therefore, one should not offer oblations nor perform the ritual on an unstable fire;
I shall explain to you that knowledge by which accomplishment is produced.
In a square-shaped fire-pit, Madhusūdana resides; in a circular pit, Kuṇḍala;
and in one shaped like a bow, Rudra, who is saluted by all the gods.
In a square mandala, Agni is present; in a circular mandala, the consumer of oblations (Hutāśana);
and in a half-moon mandala, Nala is indeed Agni—thus is Agni established.
For the twice-born, truth is the deity; the preceptor is the deity of the yogis;
Varuna is the deity in water; and the great serpents are the deities in the *darbha* grass.
In the *sruva* ladle is Mahādeva, and in the *sruva* spoon is the three-eyed God;
in their union is the Supreme God, who is saluted by all the gods.
Know that the refined waters (praṇītā) are the earth; in the utterance of "svāhā" are the great sacrifices.
Know that the seasonal sacrifices (kratavaḥ) reside in the flowers, and the great ocean in the vessels.
Gāyatrī is situated in the middle of the altar, while Soma stands at the sprinkling;
Maṇimadra is at the cooking, and likewise Vajradhara is at the crest.
One should know that the Hotṛ priests reside in the mountain-like cups and other vessels;
Rudra is the deity in the dawn; and the winds are in the palm-leaf fans.
And Śaṅkara is present even in the ashes within all the mantras;
likewise, all the world-protectors and all the deities are in all the corners.
In the portions of the oblation, the Mothers are the sparks such as Pūtanā and others;
in the brilliance, the Sun is presided over, and in dissolution, the supreme deity Śiva.
The morning oblation for the gods, performed at half a watch [after sunrise], bestows prosperity;
that for humans at midday, lasting three watches, is for the sake of liberation.
In the afternoon, one should perform the rite for the ancestors; at twilight, the rite for secret spirits;
at night, for the destruction of sins; and during the day, for the accomplishment of spiritual attainments.
If offered at half a watch, it bestows long life; at midnight, it grants longevity;
at dawn, O child, it bestows sons; and at sunrise, it fulfills all desires.
In all rites at the beginning of a moment (kṣaṇa) and so forth, which bestow the attainment of all goals,
the presiding deity of the moment should be offered the first moving oblation (carāhuti).
Otherwise, O Brahmin, your oblation becomes fruitless,
whether it be offered with vessels made of wood, clay, copper, silver, gold, or gems.
The increase of merit is tenfold through offerings, ablutions,
and meals [given to those] marked with divine signs— the trident, the lotus, the conch, and the discus— upon their auspicious faces.
A wise person should take clarified butter, milk, meat broth, and so forth;

having established the deities, a fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with sacrificial substances heated by the stream of clarified butter (vasordhārā), or otherwise according to the prescribed rule.
The deities grant satisfaction and nourishment during their respective periods;
likewise, the fruit arising from the presiding deities of the groups of mantras is obtained during their specific times.
This has been told to you, dear child, which brings happiness to all the worlds;
yet if the Hotṛ priest should be devoid of mantras, he remains perpetually impure.
Therefore, one should not offer oblations into an unrefined fire by those who are non-Vedic;
for the officiating priests, through the mantras and the deities, nourish the gods.
But non-Vedic priests do not indeed please the gods;
from the Vedic oblation (homa), however, the attainment of all fruits arises for everyone.
Therefore, one who knows the ritual application of mantras and bestows auspiciousness should perform it at dawn alone:
in the east resides the deity Agni, in the south Viṣṇu, and Hara is situated in the south.
Brahmā stands in the west; these indeed have Agni as their deity.
One should know that Rudra is the essence of their splendor, while Carcikā has the flame as her purpose.
For the longevity of the three [ages] of the Brahmins, Lakṣmī is the presiding deity there;
thus, when the fire-sacrifice is established, the three fires are present.
The three gods, the three worlds, the three fires, and the three qualities are established;
those three are the Gārhapatya, the Dakṣiṇāgni, and the Āhavanīya.
O best of the twice-born, many varieties arise from a single [pit] that is dug level,
made even, and marked with hands and other measures.
The lip should be made one finger-breadth thick, and the navel twelve fingers in length;
it is auspicious when its width is equal to that of the lip and resembles the lip of an elephant.
The first girdle should be four finger-breadths in measure;
the second is one [unit] less than half, and the third is likewise; thus the sacrificial pit brings auspiciousness.
It is square in the east and other directions, resembling the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree;
half of it has the shape of a cock, and there are five or eight circles.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be fashioned in the shape of a lotus in the northeastern direction;
likewise, [the wood for the ladles] should be from the branches of the Aśvattha, Āmra, Śrīparṇī, Sucivṛkṣa, and Vaikaṅkata trees.
The *sruva* ladle is made from *khadira*, *āsana*, *bilva*, or other such woods;
its handle is as long as the hand and so forth, enriched with a girth of one finger-breadth, and adorned with a bulbous knob (*kumbhaka*).
The *puṣkara* (spout) and the two *puṣkaras* should be marked as extending from the central line;
the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should have handles half a cubit long,
with a beautifully rounded shaft six finger-breadths in circumference, emerging from the base-mechanism.
One should know that the vessel (kumbha) at the base is two finger-breadths wide, extending to the root of the lotus;
likewise, one should understand the joint (gaṇḍikā) and the lotus-petal (puṣkarā) according to their respective divisions.
The altar (vedī) should be made seven finger-breadths high; one should fashion five circular tiers.
The excavation should be made three [finger-breadths deep] and level, and then one should make it six finger-breadths [in total].
It should be richly adorned with the shape of a cow's ear, having an opening for the little finger,
designed for the pouring out of clarified butter, and marked with three barley-grains.

Having thus prepared the *sruva* ladle, the oblation (*homa*) performed with those two brings happiness. A fire-drill (*araṇi*) made from the heartwood of the *śamī* tree should be one cubit (*hasta*) in length.

Its width and circumference are such that it is sixteen finger-breadths at the middle; it is adorned with the beauty of the shape of a cow’s ear. It is circular, provided with two hands, and possesses a perfect roundness of ten finger-breadths.
The binding of the middle iron ring should be made as even as a floral crest;
it should be of the same length as a young rope for the purpose of the fire-oblation for the sprouts of the branches.
Having worshipped it well with the fire-mantra, one should cause it to fall;
in its absence, one may use a sun-crystal (sūryakānta), or in the absence of that, one made from dried cow-dung (karīṣa).
One should bring it to a common dwelling-house and place it in a copper vessel,
or in a vessel made of tin or clay, or in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) provided with worship.
One should perform all rites according to the prescribed method for the fire-wheel,
using [vessels] made of gold, silver, or copper, or even those made of wood or stone.

One should prepare jewels, vessels marked with auspicious deities, and offerings for the purpose of the *argha*, *naivedya*, and worship, as well as the ritual oblation (*balidāna*). Thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) according to the prescribed rule and in accordance with the injunctions.

Thus ends the section on general rules (*paribhāṣāprakaraṇa*) in the *Vrata-kāṇḍa* of the *Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri, the sovereign lord of all sciences, under the illustrious Great King, the supreme monarch.
[318] Having fasted according to the prescribed rites, the gods attained the third heaven.
And the seers attained supreme perfection through fasts.
He who conquers hunger, the perception of phenomena, the vital breaths, and even fortitude—
those which are difficult to conquer— by him heaven is won.
Likewise:
One who maintains the sacred fire does not go to hell; nor does one who has a virtuous son, nor one who possesses a virtuous wife;
nor one who performs sacrifices such as the Medha; nor one who bestows a thousand cows.
O best of sages, those endowed with auspicious merit who observe fasts according to the prescribed rules do not go to the terrifying and dreadful hells.

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O tiger among sages, those men by whom Viṣṇu was not propitiated through vows and fasts in another birth are afflicted by planetary influences, diseases, and other such troubles."
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"By those who have not worshipped the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati) in the past, nor observed vows, nor spoken the truth..."
Generally, it is those very mortals who are consumed by the sufferings of poverty, hunger, and passion who lament.
In this world, mortals— whose minds are seized by the planet of greed— are tormented by the desire for cattle, land, houses, fields, wives, servants, sons, and wealth.
They worship the god, yet they do not observe the virtuous vows.
And having abandoned those enjoyments from him— which are like poison, delusive, and impermanent—
the steadfast one is one whose passion is destroyed and who is free from intoxication.
One should practice one's own auspicious dharma and observe its vows.
One who is devoted to the duties of his own caste, though fearful, and who observes the vow of Śiva and worships Tryambaka,
shall certainly attain that supreme state.
That which the virtuous call the state free from affliction.
One attains a kingdom, prosperity that may be enjoyed by virtuous people in this world, as well as the realm of Śiva or even immortality;
there is nothing in the worlds unattainable for those of firm vows.
Therefore, a man should always be devoted to his vows.
The messengers of Yama, who cause great terror and carry nooses in their hands, do not even come within the range of vision of those who are always devoted to their vows and remember Śiva.
"Her face is formidable with fangs, and her appearance is hideous and fierce.
Likewise, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, there is a statement by Pārvatī addressed to Śiva:
"If I am worthy of your grace, and if you have affection for me..."
O Mahādeva, tell me truly that which I ask of you.
Whatever observances Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas may perform,
as well as whatever other observances there may be— tell me indeed what their fruit is.
Niyama is a vow; for the successful attainment of fruits is seen from observances, O sinless one, whereas from transgressions, terrible calamities arise. [320]
Īśvara said:
O fair-eyed one, this very same rule is observed by those established in discipline;
it is performed in many ways by men as a supreme cause of physical austerity.
In that matter, a rule must be established: whatever indeed pleases anyone, O Goddess, by performing even what is difficult to do, one enjoys a thousandfold fruit.
For human life, with its impermanent wealth and pleasures, is like a bubble;
therefore, having fallen into delusion, the wise man breaks the rule.
It is difficult for a human being to carry out a complete restraint in its entirety;
for men are overcome by passion and greed, and they harbor doubts regarding the Dharma.
Fools, attached to present pleasures and delighting in unrighteousness, do not exert themselves; yet a man of great mind observes restraint from the very outset.
He indeed enjoys abundant fruit for many thousands of years;
just like the vow of the sword’s edge, so too is the practice of self-restraint.
By that virtue of steadfastness, there is the observance of restraint;
through restraints, O lady endowed with restraint, the deities attained their divine state.
O lady rich in asceticism, these stars shine by virtue of their fixed law;
O lady of noble hips, by that same law the ocean does not overstep its shores.
By discipline the fire blazes, by discipline the sun gives heat;
by discipline the wind increases, and by discipline the world is sustained.
"O auspicious one, having performed stainless austerity and observed the rules exactly as prescribed, you have reached me through this immersion; of this there is no doubt."
But that man who, intent on Me, observes the vow for a year,
indeed rejoices happily like a god among the world of the deities.
In the Varāha Purāṇa: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from blemish—
these, O observer of vows, are said to be the mental vows."
Whether it be eating once a day, eating only at night, fasting, or whatever else there may be— all that constitutes a physical vow for men, and not otherwise.

In this context, fasting (*upavāsa*) means abstaining from food for a day and a night; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [practices such as] eating only what is unasked-for (*ayācita*) are included. Likewise: "O Three-eyed One, whatever vow (*vrata*) is performed or worship is offered, and whatever is given to the Brahmins—all this yields fruit beginning from the moment of birth."
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Austerity is indeed the refuge of all beings; austerity alone is their ultimate resort.
By austerity the worlds are conquered; by austerity comes the liberation of the virtuous."
Those whose sins have been purified by austerity have attained supreme nirvāṇa;
through austerity one may likewise obtain a supreme lifespan or even peace.
Through austerity, a person attains all worlds;
through austerity, they seek even the supreme, eternal Nirvana.
Through austerity, one attains even vast success in this world;
moreover, those of mortal birth obtain sons and other blessings through austerity.
And they say that inexhaustible wealth belongs to those men on earth who practice austerity;
austerity is the heating of the body through vows, fasts, and restraints.
Having risen, one should remain standing during the day, and likewise seated at night;
this is declared to be the vīrāsana posture, which destroys even the greatest sins.
Eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating only what is unasked for, and fasting for one day— this is proclaimed as the Pādakṛcchra penance.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Having propitiated the Great Yogi residing within the heart through vows, fasts, observances, fire-offerings, and the gratification of Brahmins."
Likewise: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras as well, O best of the twice-born,
worship Mahādeva through sacrifices, gifts, and meditative concentrations."
Through vows, fasts, observances, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations,
union with Rudra and proximity to him— which are indeed extremely difficult to attain— belong to them.
And through his grace, one attains residence in the same world and a form similar to his.
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa: "In ancient times, the royal sage Dhundhumāra obtained a hundred sons through charity, observance of rules, austerity, and religious vows."
There was a royal sage named Sagara, renowned in all directions;
that high-souled king obtained a hundred sons.
Likewise, King Daśaratha, who was always devoted to his vows and satisfied through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, and yoga— that supreme person—
himself attained the state of being the son of that high-souled king.
The royal sage named Janaka, himself a treasury of asceticism and vows,
having attained incomparable sovereignty, reached the goal of the yogins.
In this very way, O Great King, kings as well as brahmins attained the characteristics of sovereignty and their respective destinies through the power of their vows.
Therefore, O best of kings, being self-possessed, constantly perform austerity and restraint; be devoted to vows and fasting, and visit sacred fords.
Likewise,
one who is self-controlled and observant of restraints should effect the restraint of the senses through fasting,
recitation, meditation, bathing at sacred fords, and other such practices.
Through vows, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and service at sacred fords,
the twice-born man destroys his sin and attains perfection over the course of many births.

Since it is stated that vows and other such practices are common to all four social classes (*cāturvarṇya*), the mention here of "twice-born" (*dvija*) is intended as an indication for the classes in general. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the term "sacrifice" (*yajña*) because the Śūdra lacks the entitlement to perform sacrifices; for "sacrifice" has multiple meanings, and its sense can include the worship of deities and so forth. Listen to me as I speak of sacrifice, charity, and austerity, which are considered to be threefold: physical, mental, and verbal.
Non-violence, the practice of vows, and austerity are said to be physical [austerity]; verbal [austerity] is truthful speech free from malice toward living beings;
and mental [austerity] is peace of mind characterized by complete detachment.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Indeed, he who observes vows and fasts quickly shatters the snare of poverty."
Those who know the truth say that for a man devoted to vows and fasts, even calamities are pacified.
Thus ends the section on the Praise of Vows within the Vrata-kāṇḍa of the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi composed by Śrī Hemādri.
Now begins the third chapter. Next, the general duties of vows and their qualified practitioners are described. In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One who is devoted to the conduct of his own caste and stage of life, and whose mind is pure..."
O King, one is authorized for the vows; otherwise, the exertion is fruitless.
O King, one who is free from greed, truthful in speech, and devoted to the welfare of all beings is qualified for the vows; otherwise, such effort is fruitless.
O King, one who possesses faith, who fears injustice, and is free from pride and deceit is qualified for these duties; otherwise, one's effort is fruitless.
O King, one who is impartial toward all beings, a devotee of Śiva with senses subdued, is authorized for these vows; otherwise, the effort is fruitless.

Having first correctly ascertained the meaning of the scriptures, the wise performer of ritual actions— who does not gamble and does not drink intoxicants— is qualified for the observances and other such rites.
In the Mahābhārata: "The performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha), austerity, truthfulness, freedom from anger,
contentment with one's own wife, purity, and constant absence of malice."
Knowledge of the self and forbearance, O King, are the common duties for all.
Devala also says:
"By means of vows, fasts, and observances, as well as by the mortification of the body,
all social classes are undoubtedly liberated from sins."

Thus, by means of this arrangement of statements, it is established that all four castes, who possess the aforementioned restraints, have the right to the vows (vratas) in common with both women and men. And so it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"O son of Kuntī, even those of sinful birth—women, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—who take refuge in me, they too attain the supreme goal."
In this regard, there is this further distinction: that women have no independent entitlement to vows and the like without the command of their husband. Thus it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
indeed, by service to their husbands alone do they go to the desired worlds."
Whatever worship and hospitality the husband performs for the gods, the ancestors, and others,
half of that fruit indeed belongs to her, and not through any other wealth.
A woman enjoys [the fruits of her life] solely through service to her husband.
She shall become a companion to her husband for the complete attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
she who serves her husband is exalted in heaven because of that."
A woman should not observe a fast or a vow that exceeds those of her husband;
O best of the twice-born, it is said that such an act shortens the lifespan of her husband.
The best of Brahmins may perform the propitiation of the deity according to his desire;
likewise, a woman known as devoted to her husband (pativratā) may do so after obtaining permission from her husband.
If a woman performs funeral rites for the deceased without being authorized by her father, husband, or son,
that act of hers shall be fruitless.

"By 'father' is meant her state as a maiden; by 'husband' is meant her period of conjugal fortune; by 'son' is meant her period of widowhood. [She should perform] funeral rites and religious vows. Or else, having renounced everything, a virtuous woman, O bull among men, should be intent on the worship of her husband and perform the propitiation of Keśava."

Whatever a woman desires in her mind, she obtains even without [her husband's] effort; yet everything performed without the husband’s permission would be entirely fruitless. Nevertheless, for a woman, the worship of Keśava remains fruitful.
Likewise, in the *Harivaṃśa*, there are the words of Pārvatī addressed to Arundhatī:
"The performance of the dharma of wifely fidelity, which is eternally unbroken for her—
her ritual of meritorious deeds is proclaimed in the Purāṇas."
O Arundhatī, even meritorious deeds such as giving and fasting, though well-performed, are fruitless for unchaste women; so it is with all virtuous acts, O auspicious lady.
Vows are meritorious;
yet those women who are corrupt in their womb (who have sexual misconduct with their husbands) do not enjoy the fruit of merit due to that defect of the womb, as they are destined for hell.
Virtuous women, possessing excellent character and regarding their husbands as deities, sustain the world; they are ever devoted to no other duty and have taken refuge in the path of the righteous.
Free from verbal faults, endowed with purity, possessed of fortitude, and observant of pure vows, these women who always speak what is virtuous truly sustain the world.
Whether he be diseased, fallen, or even destitute in any way whatsoever, a wife must not abandon her husband; this is the eternal dharma.
O lady of auspicious countenance, even a virtuous wife saves her husband— even if he has committed improper acts or is devoid of merit— and likewise saves herself.
For women corrupted by their sexual organs, there is no atonement; she is as good as dead.
For those corrupted by speech, atonement has been prescribed by the ancient sages.
A woman must always perform her religious observances according to the will of her husband;
even fasting may be done by one who desires a blessed destiny, O Satī.
For thousands of other eons, that woman does not attain a [favorable] rebirth;
due to the confusion of her womb, she is cooked within thousands of animal births.
Even if a woman, though unchaste, should somehow obtain human birth,
she will be born of low intelligence in a caṇḍāla womb with the face of a dog.
In the eternal law, the husband is always seen by women as a god;
for she whose husband is pleased is a virtuous woman who walks the path of dharma.
For women whose minds are struck by curiosity, the world is not beautiful; but for those whose hearts are established in their husbands alone through true devotion, it is so.
Those women who do not transgress against their husband in deed, thought, or word—
their meritorious fruit, O gentle one, has been proclaimed by those who possess merit.
O beautiful one, learn the entire procedure for meritorious acts regarding all the worlds;
for indeed, I have seen it all through my ascetic power.
Having bathed and risen early in the morning, a virtuous woman should request her husband for the purpose of fasting or for the performance of a vow, such as the Ghee-vow (ghṛtavrate),
by constantly touching the feet of that most excellent man with both her hands.
Taking a vessel of udumbara wood together with kuśa grass and unbroken grains of rice,
and having sprinkled the right horn of a cow, he should receive that water.
Then the virtuous wife, having bathed and purified herself, should offer that water to her husband;
thereafter, she should pour that water over her own head.
This is declared to be equivalent to bathing at all the sacred fords in the three worlds;
indeed, it should be performed during fasts and religious observances.
O beautiful lady, this bath is indeed common to both women and men;
it was seen by me, O Arundhatī, through my ascetic penance as that which pleases Hara.
Know that the bed and likewise the seat are not empty;
washing one's own feet is also prescribed as a duty.
"Anuśabdita" means spoken for the purpose of a vow.
When there is the shedding of tears and anger, it constitutes the act of quarreling;
even from fasting or from a group [of ascetics], this immediately kills a woman.
For one born under the lunar mansion Śravaṇā, white clothing alone is always praised;
likewise, during the vow of fasting, both an inner garment and another [outer garment] are recommended.
When a vow is undertaken, sandals should always be made of grass;
this same rule is proclaimed for the fast as well.
One should always avoid collyrium, yellow pigment (rocana), perfumes, and jasmine flowers during vows and fasts.
Anointing with saffron and the like serves to brighten the face.
A tooth-stick, bathing the head, or even anointment with unguents— indeed,
all [these] are prescribed for the purpose of purification, provided they are devoid of clay.
One should always perform the cleansing with sesame seeds, *āmalaka* fruits, and *bilva* fruits;
and one should always wash the head with water mixed with clay.
Anointing the head with oil on a Monday is not praised in this way; it is the established rule in the Smṛti that one should not anoint the feet or the body with oil on that day.
One should by no means employ a vehicle drawn by oxen or camels,
nor ever a vehicle drawn by donkeys while observing a vow or fasting.
O Somanandinī, river water originating from springs is indeed praised;
likewise, water from an auspicious pond or a large reservoir overflowing with aquatic plants is excellent.
Having gone [to the water], bathing is indeed always and in every way recommended;
however, if it cannot be obtained, a woman who is confined should perform a bath with a jar of water.
One should bathe with nine jars; this is the eternal rule.
Having bathed, one should perform the ritual with the head [of the jar]; thus one shall obtain the fruit of austerity.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: forbearance, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, restraint of the senses,
carrying the sacred fire for the gods, contentment, and the avoidance of theft.
This tenth rule stands as common to all vows.

[331] In this context, the description of forbearance (*kṣamā*) and the other virtues—which are prescribed as independent means for accomplishing the four aims of human life—as being constituent parts of the vow (*vrata*) is justified by the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), just as in the case of the rule "one desiring vigor [should use] a *khādira* [wooden ladle].
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Therefore, having observed the fast, one should perform a bath preceded by an oil massage..."
O King, that which destroys one's beauty must be avoided with great effort.
As for that which is stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Perfumes, ornaments, garments, flower garlands, and ointments—
these do not cause a fault during a fast, nor do the cleaning of the teeth and the application of collyrium."
And as it was stated by Vyāsa:
"Even during a vow, the use of a tooth-stick and flowers does not constitute a fault."
This refers to the case of fasting while accompanied by her husband. As stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"Even while observing a fast, she may wear collyrium, betel with its accompaniments, vermilion, and red garments; this is the supreme means for ensuring she does not become a widow."
A widow [should proceed] by the path of the ascetic, or a maiden according to her own will.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "When a woman who is pregnant, one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), a maiden, or one who is ill is impure,
then another person should perform the rite on her behalf, while she herself remains restrained."

When a fast is to be observed, one who is pregnant and so forth should perform the *nakta* (eating at night) instead. Those who are impure due to childbirth or other causes should have another person perform the vow for them. One who is self-restrained and pure should perform it herself; this same rule applies even to men, since the gender is not intended to be significant. Thus it is established that women have the right to undertake vows only under these conditions: in the state of maidenhood by the command of the father or others, as married women by the command of the husband, and as widows by the command of the son or others, and not otherwise.
In the *Agnipurāṇa*: "Rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans, peas, water, and milk..."
Śyāmāka, nīvāra, wheat, and other such grains are beneficial for a vow.
One should avoid the *kūṣmāṇḍa*, the bottle-gourd (*alābu*), the eggplant (*vārtākī*), the *pālaṅkyā*, and the *jyotsnikā*.
As for food, one may eat sacrificial porridge (*caru*), parched grain flour (*śaktu*), rice-grains (*kaṇā*), vegetables, curd, ghee, and honey.
Śyāmāka, śāli, nīvāra, barley,
and the roots and grains of yava are beneficial for the performance of fire-rituals and other rites during vows such as the *haviṣya* or *naktā*.
Having abandoned honey and meat, other things are said to be beneficial for the vow.
*Jyotsnikā* is *kośatakī*. Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"Among sacrificial grains (*haviṣya*), barley is the foremost; others are considered rice.
One should avoid mung beans, *kodrava*, millet, and the like, even when all [other grains] are unavailable."
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "Winter rice that has been steamed while white, grains, mung beans, barley, sesame seeds, peas, *kaṅgu*, *nīvāra* millet, *vāstūka* (spinach), and *hilamocikā*."
Sixty-day rice, black pot-herbs, radish, and varieties of *kemuka* other than that; bulbs, rock salt, sea salt, honey, and clarified butter.
Milk from which the cream has not been removed, jackfruit, mango, harītakī,
long pepper, cumin, orange, and tamarind;
Sages declare that plantains, *lavala* fruits, and *dhātrī* fruits, along with jaggery and sugarcane products, when not fried in oil, constitute *haviṣya* (fit for sacrificial offerings).
In this context, "ghee" and "milk" refer to those produced from cows; the phrase "not fried in oil" is a qualification specifically for the aforementioned *haviṣya* foods.
As stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Eating *haviṣya* food, bathing, truthfulness, and moderation in diet."
One should perform the fire-ritual, sleep on the ground, and eat only at night for six days.
In this context, the fire-rite consists of an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*) performed with the *mahāvyāhṛti* mantras. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"These eight do not break a vow: water, roots, fruits, milk, sacrificial food (*havis*), the desire of a Brahmin, the word of a guru, and medicine."
The drinking of milk and similar acts do not constitute a violation of a vow when they concern women, children, or those who are extremely afflicted.
Furthermore, according to the scriptures, these are declared to be non-violations of a vow even if committed once: fear of all living beings, negligence, and the instruction of a teacher.
"Fear from all beings" means fear for the performer of the vow arising from the presence of all living creatures.
If, through delusion, negligence, or greed, a breach of the vow should occur,
then one should not eat for three nights, or else one should have one's hair shaved.
Having performed this expiation, one shall become a practitioner of vows once again.

Thus ends the section titled "The Determination of the Qualifications for Vows and Their Duties" within the Vrata-kāṇḍa (Book on Vows) of the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi, composed by Śrī Hemādri, the sovereign lord of all sciences, under the patronage of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Mahādeva.
[335] Now begins the fourth chapter:
The Support of Virtues, the Friend of Those Who Anoint Themselves with Sandalwood Paste.
The renowned Hemādri, an abode of the shimmering and stainless meaning of the scriptures,
in order to provide assistance to those skilled in virtuous deeds,
describes the entire collection of vows according to the sequence of lunar days.
He now speaks for the sake of correct understanding,
a work esteemed even by the learned among the virtuous,
which brings glory to the collection of all religious observances.
It is the yielder of desires for those who rely on the path and those who rely on the state.

Now, the religious observances (*vratas*) are being described. In that regard, within the section on lunar-day observances (*tithivrataprakaraṇa*), the observances for the first lunar day (*pratipad*) are first stated.
Śatānīka said:
"O twice-born one, these lunar days have been declared by you in brief, but not in detail."
"Tell me again in detail, O best among the foremost of the twice-born."
The secret concerning the lunar days and the activities of the deities,
as well as the preferred offerings for the gods and their respective observances.
Tell me those, O knower of dharma, by which I may become purified,
and how even a poor man, O brahmin, may obtain the fruits of his desired rites.
Sumantu said:
"I shall explain the secret concerning the lunar days (tithis), as well as their respective foods and fruits,
the extent of the specific observances for each, and particularly those for women."
Understand from me this entire secret narrative;
it was previously told by Padmāsana to his own beloved in some manner.
I shall explain that to you: which lunar day belongs to which deity, as well as the secrets of the deities, their vows, and likewise their observances.
Listen to them as I speak, O illustrious one, O giver of honor:
Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa were both intent upon performing the act of creation.
Then, by means of those two, he fashioned the entire heaven and earth,
as well as the cardinal and intermediate directions, surrounded by the eight guardians of the world.
O King, the Lord himself established this first lunar day (tithi),
