because it was declared by Brahmā to be the most excellent of all lunar days.
Because it was established in the first quarter of the lunar month, it is called the *pratipad*;
at its conclusion, I shall explain the supreme procedure for the fast (*upavāsa*).
On the full moon day of Kārttika, or on the seventh lunar day, or on the Vaiśākha full moon, or on the Yugādi days,
the knower of the ritual rules should first cause the disciple to undertake the vow of fasting and restraint.

The commencement of the vow for the first lunar day (*pratipad*) is in either the month of Kārttika or Vaiśākha; that of the seventh-day vow (*saptamī-vrata*) is in Māgha; and the commencement of the vow for the anniversary days of the Yugas (*yugādi-tithi*) is in any one of the months of Māgha, Vaiśākha, Bhādrapada, or Kārttika—whichever lunar day one is able to observe with the required discipline. O lord of men, learn now the procedure for that specific lunar day.
[337] A man should first cause another to undertake the fast with its restrictive observances according to the prescribed rule;
O King, when the first lunar day (pratipad) arrives, he should indeed take up the vow.
Having taken food on the fourteenth day, one should make a formal resolve;
on the new moon day, one should not eat and should perform ablutions at the three times of day.
One should daily recite the purificatory mantras (pavitrāṇi) along with the Gāyatrī and its head (śiras).
Hereafter, I shall describe the Vedic purificatory mantras.
Those who are shrouded in darkness are purified by the recitation and the fire-offerings of the Aghamarṣaṇa,
the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs,
the Taratsamās, the Kūṣmāṇḍyas, the Pāvamānī verses, the Durgā-sūkta, and the Sāvitrī.
The Bhāruṇḍa Sāmans, as well as the Gāyatra and Raivata,
the Śataparva, the Atharvaśiras, the Trisuparṇa, and the Mahāvrata.
The Abhiṣaṅga, the Āpadastobha, the Sāmans, the Vyāhṛtis,
the Abliṅgas, the Bārhaspatya, the Vāksūkta, and likewise the Madhu and Ṛta.
Likewise: the Puruṣasūkta, the Aghanāśana, the Devavratas,
the Gosūkta, the Aśvasūkta, and the two Sāmans known as Aindraśuddha.
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agnivratam, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat.
When these are recited, they purify living beings;
one who so desires attains the memory of past lives.

Having honored the best of the twice-born according to the prescribed rite with perfumes and garlands, one should offer milk according to one's ability, saying: "May the all-pervading Brahmā be pleased with me."
Then, O King, one should consume cow's milk according to this procedure;
this very rule, O King, is declared for all lunar days.
[338] On all lunar days, beginning with the first day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
his vow is completed over the course of a year.
O lord of men, learn now what the fruit is for each person at the conclusion of the vow.
To that embodied being who is purified by the liberation from sin and possesses a divine body,
Brahmā, being well-pleased, grants a celestial chariot of immeasurable splendor.
Having enjoyed himself there for a very long time like a god, together with the deities, surrounded by apsarases and kinnaras, he attained a divine state of unimpeded movement.
Having come here, he shall obtain the status of a Brahmin for ten births;
he shall be a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, a performer of sacrifices, a scholar, and long-lived.
In the Kṛta Yuga, he is born as an enjoyer of pleasures, a lord of wealth, and a donor;
whether he be a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, he attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
The Haihayas, Tālajaṅghas, Turuṣkas, Yavanas, and Śakas,
having fasted right here in this very place, attain the status of Brāhmaṇas.
Thus ends the vow of Kṣīrapratipad in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now listen to the ritual for the first lunar day (pratipad), a vow that brings about prosperity.
By performing which one may obtain prosperity that is difficult for humans to attain here.
In a square mandala prepared with polished rice grains,
one should invoke Śrīśa and Śrī, and worship them along with their attendants.
One should worship him with ten thousand lotuses whose petals are not hidden.
With thousands of blossomed petals that are not hidden,
according to the requirements, with milk and milk-rice (pāyasa),
and having then worshipped according to the ritual, one should place the goddess Sarasvatī at the side.
Then, with undistracted mind, one should worship the Moon and afterwards the Guru;
then, by means of the assignment of the retinue, one should likewise honor them.
The prayer mantra:
May the Lord Hari, the Master of Speech, grant me knowledge;
may the Goddess Indirā, the presiding deity of knowledge, bestow knowledge upon me.
May Sarasvatī bestow upon me an exceedingly radiant increase of speech;
and may even the Moon grant me nourishment that fulfills all enjoyments.
The worship should be performed using only the name-mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Thus, the Guru, being pleased and having been worshipped, should cause the *sādhya*— that is,
the disciple who is to be instructed— to perform [the rite].
And one should cause the fast to be observed according to the prescribed rite, accompanied by the necessary restraints.
Having worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Śrī, on the second lunar day, one should,
being pure and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), eat food with milk in His presence.
The word "to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Having given a gift (*vara*) to the teacher, one should again perform an act of pleasing him. By the word "gift," gold is intended.
One should indeed begin at that time what has not been studied or commenced;
for the teacher who bestows knowledge and vows is to be regarded as a constant deity.
The word "he would think" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
For from his mouth, at that time, [he would hear] his attainment of *niḥśreyasa*;
*niḥśreyasa* means the highest good (*atiśayitaṃ śreyaḥ*).
Then one should act according to what has been said by him, and should not transgress his instruction.
One should stand while the teachers are standing, and one should not sit before them;
one should not lie down while they are sitting, and one should even carry out their commands.
One should not disregard the word of the teacher even when fallen into distress;
having informed the teacher of everything, one should first perform what is beneficial or harmful.
Thus, one who is devoted to the teacher, wise, and esteemed by the learned,
having attained knowledge and dispassion, shall obtain a long life.
Having attained vast renown and promoted the practice of virtuous conduct, one—
endowed with the prosperity of sons and grandsons— shall attain a meritorious destination.
Thus the wise man of noble intellect should conclude the vow of knowledge;
then he should give many excellent fruits to the brahmins.
Those made from plantain, mango, and breadfruit are pure;
the wise man who thus performs this vow of knowledge with undivided mind,
becoming proficient in all branches of learning, attains the station of Viṣṇu.
[341] The Vidyāpratipad-vrata as declared in the Garuḍa Purāṇa.
Puṣkara said:
Having fasted on the fifteenth day at the end of the year, one should,
with single-minded devotion, bathe in the morning on the first day of the lunar fortnight and perform the vow.
One should worship the god Bhāskara with colored powders upon a lotus that has been fashioned.
The meaning is that one should worship after fashioning a lotus with various colors upon a clean, leveled spot of ground and meditating upon the Sun-god there.
O Bhārgava, [one should worship] with white perfumes and garlands, white sandalwood,
as well as with *kunduru* incense and incense of clarified butter.
*Kunduru* is the resin of the *sallakī* tree. With cakes, with sand-like substances, with curd, and with abundant *paramānna*; "sand-like substances" refers to preparations of sugar.
And with white, pure rice, together with salted ghee.
Having worshipped the Abode of the World with the finest ghee, milk, white fruits, and offerings that satisfy the fire and the Brahmins, during the fourth part of the day.
O best of men, one should first take food accompanied by ghee;
O most excellent of men, one should avoid everything that is devoid of ghee.
Having eaten the food once, he should take his meal;
then, with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, he may drink water again.

The first meal refers to the very first morsel. Having eaten all food—both the first and the non-first—at once, that is, having consumed only a single morsel, one should discard the remaining food. The meaning is that with the permission of a Brāhmaṇa, one may again take food—that is, eat the remaining food—and drink water. Even while eating with the permission of a Brāhmaṇa, one should eat it without clarified butter, because of the prohibition: "One should avoid eating [food] devoid of clarified butter. Having performed this for a year, thereafter, directly, the thirteenth [year].
O Bhārgava, on that day there is the worship of the God of gods.

"Then, having performed [the vow] for one year, month by month, on the first day of the bright fortnight, [one should conclude] with the thirteenth [day], as is seen from the indicative mark (liṅga). One should complete the meritorious vow, O Rāma—this is what is declared in the scripture; such is the meaning."
O best of the twice-born, he should likewise give gold along with clothing.
The remainder [of the mantra] is "to Sūrya.
O knower of dharma, by means of this vow one thus dispels disease;
one attains health as well as the highest state.
Furthermore,
whether it be a man or a woman who, through their vows, perfectly honors the Foremost One in the world, they shall obtain fame as well as vast and supreme enjoyments.
[343] Thus concludes the vow for the first day of the lunar fortnight dedicated to health (*ārogya-pratipad-vrata*), together with its concluding rite (*sodyāpana*), from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with auspicious colors;
one should then worship the omnipresent Lord Brahmā within its pericarp.
Of that lotus:
the *Ṛgveda* on the eastern petal, the *Yajurveda* on the southern,
the *Sāmaveda* on the western, and likewise the *Atharvaveda* on the northern.
Likewise, the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) are in the southeast, the Dharmaśāstras in the southwest,
the Purāṇas in the northwest, and the extensive systems of logic (nyāyavistara) in the northeast.
Having thus performed the ritual placement, the knower of Dharma,
observing a fast and having subdued his senses, should perform worship beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra while remaining fasting.
O Yādava, O highly fortunate one, having undertaken this on every single day of the bright fortnight for a full year, [one should worship] with white fragrant unguents.
At the end of the year, having performed the vow with diligence, that best of men should offer abundant supreme food, incense, and lamps, and give a cow as a gift.
O King, he who performs this vow shall become a knower of the Vedas and one firmly established in dharma on earth,
having performed it for twelve years.
The person goes three times to the triple world.
[344] Thus ends the Vidyāvrata, together with its concluding rite (udyāpana), as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The entire universe is known as one alone—both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
At the commencement of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should observe a fast and subdue the senses.

At the commencement, that is, at the beginning of the rainy season, one should observe a fast on the fifteenth day as previously described. One should worship Puruṣa Viṣṇu, whether on land or in water,
with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food offerings.
A man should likewise recite the *Puruṣasūkta* while submerged in water;
the meaning is that, meditating on Viṣṇu in pure water, he should worship Him with perfumes and other offerings.
Furthermore, for each verse of the hymn, he should offer incense and join his palms in reverence.
Likewise, O knower of dharma, O mighty-armed one, having offered incense, fruits,
and the food offering (naivedya), one should likewise recite [the mantra] according to one's ability.
One should likewise offer oblations with clarified butter, give gold to a twice-born man,
and provide food with milk at the time of night, O Bhārgava.
O hero, having undertaken this as a constant vow for a year, one who is unwearied and performs it during both fortnights is liberated from all sins.
And having obtained grace from Vāsudeva—
the Lord of all, the omnipresent, the inconceivable,
and the Lord of the world— one attains the supreme state.
To that very perfection the perfected ones return once again.

[345] Thus ends the vow of Pauruṣapratipad in the Viṣṇudharmottara. The mantra for instruction is as before. O Lord of Men, that man who, having observed a fast on the full moon day, worships Viriñci with devotion according to this rite—

The mention of the full moon day (paurṇamāsī) is an elliptical indication for the preceding day; therefore, when the vow is performed on the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad), the fast is observed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā). This is according to what will be stated hereafter:
"O mighty-armed one, having bathed and being composed on the full moon day, Agni is especially the deity, or Viriñci is the deity in this case."
The chariot procession of the Lord is proclaimed for the month of Kārttika;
the man who performs it with devotion attains residence in the same world as Brahmā.
O King of kings, on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika,
one should joyfully [worship] the Four-faced One (Brahmā) along with all his various abodes by means of the Mārga path.
O King, having caused the people of the village and the city to settle there,
and having fed the Brāhmaṇas and worshipped Śāṇḍileya, one should establish it.
Śāṇḍileya Vaiśvānara should cause the God of gods to rejoice with the sounds of Vedic musical instruments;
having worshipped the son of Śāṇḍilī at the front of the chariot according to the prescribed rites.
Having honored the Brahmins and performed the auspicious *puṇyāha* ceremony,
one should place the deity upon the vehicle and keep a vigil (*prajāgara*) during the night.
O King, having performed various kinds of offerings and abundant Vedic recitations so that all creatures might thus come together, [he should address] the Brahmins at dawn.
Having worshipped him according to one's ability with various kinds of foods and edibles,
O hero, O King, having worshipped the artisan Vajra according to the prescribed rite.
O mighty-armed one, with *vāja*, milk, and *pāyasa*;
for *vajra* is clarified butter (*ājya*) and *vāja* is food.
O King, one should cause the Brahmins to recite [mantras] at night according to the ritual procedure involving the Nāga.
Having performed the rite with the proclamation of "an auspicious day," one should then cause the chariot to be circumambulated once more.
O hero, a Brāhmaṇa should cause the chariot to be circumambulated by Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the four Vedas—
the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and likewise the Atharvaveda.
One should cause that chariot of the God of gods, the most auspicious of the auspicious,
to circumambulate the entire city by way of a well-constructed path.
O hero, O King, a Śūdra who desires prosperity may mount the chariot;
however, a wise man should not allow a Mukta or a Bhojaka to mount the chariot.
O King, one should place Sāvitrī on the right side of Brahmā;
the Bhojaka, however, should place a lotus in front of Brahmā’s side.
Having thus paraded the chariot through the entire city, O hero, amidst such clamor and the abundant sounds of conchs, he circumambulated it clockwise.
The wise hero, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), should install [the image];
likewise, he who performs this procession with devotion, or even he who merely beholds it.
Whether one should draw a chariot, or cause a lamp to be offered,
or a Brahmin should perform [the rites] in the hall— he shall desire the supreme state.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), one should also worship Brahmā with offerings mixed with jaggery and with unwashed garments; such a person shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
And he who worships himself with perfumes, flowers, and new garments on that first day of the lunar fortnight shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
This lunar day is of great merit, extensive, and the promoter of sovereignty;
it is eternally dear to Brahmā and is proclaimed as the Bāleyī.
He who honors the Brahmins on this [day], and especially himself,
goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable.
O mighty-armed King, on the auspicious and excellent first day of the month of Caitra,
whatever man should see the horse's footprint and perform a ritual bath there, O ruler of men.
O tiger among the Kurus, for such a person there are no misfortunes whatsoever, nor mental afflictions, nor physical diseases; therefore, one should indeed bathe with oil.
O King, there should be a ceremonial lustration of women (*nārī-nīrājana*) which wards off all diseases;
and whatever there may be, such as cows, buffaloes, and so forth—all that he should adorn.
O scion of the Kuru lineage, one should first construct archways with flowers, oils, cloths, and other offerings,
and likewise provide a meal for the Brāhmaṇas.
For three lunar days have been declared as the foremost from of old, O joy of the Kurus;
one should observe them in the month of Kārttika, in the month of Āśvayuja, and in the month of Caitra.
O King, on whichever lunar day occurs in the month of Kārttika, bathing and giving gifts yield a hundredfold merit;
that day, known as Bali, bestows auspiciousness through the offering of clarified butter and destroys all inauspiciousness rooted in the past.
"Rooted in impurity...
Thus ends the vow of the chariot procession on the first day of the lunar fortnight for the Bali offering in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Madhusūdana, [tell me] the vows of Brahmā, Īśa, Keśava, and others, as well as those of Gaṇapati, and the vows of Durgā, Soma, Agni, and Sūrya.
O God of gods, O son of Devakī, may all those things seen in other scriptures and those that have entered my intellect be [revealed] to me.
Tell me in its entirety: for which deity and on which lunar day a specific rite is ordained according to the sequence of the ritual path.
Kṛṣṇa said: In the spring, on the first day of the bright fortnight, which is adorned by *kiṃśuka* and *aśoka* trees,
one should perform a ritual bath while established in religious observances.

O Indra among kings, whether a woman or a man, having gratified the ancestors and the deities on the bank of a river, at a pond, or in the home— in the absence of these locations— [attains the highest merit].
One should smear the image with *piṣṭātaka* for a year to effect its consecration (*puruṣkṛti*).
*Piṣṭātaka* is a specific mixture of cloth, saffron, and powdered fragrant substances.
Thereafter, one should worship it with sandalwood powder, flowers, incense, and so forth.

Subsequently, with the names of the months and seasons joined at the end with the word "namas," the learned Brāhmaṇa should worship using the auspicious mantras proclaimed in the Vedas— namely, the names of the months and seasons such as Caitra, Vasanta, and so forth.

With the *yajus* mantras beginning "Thou art the Saṃvatsara," the twice-born Brāhmaṇa is the officiant here. The mantra is as follows: "Thou art the Saṃvatsara; thou art the Parivatsara; thou art the Idāvatsara; thou art the Anuvatsara; thou art the Udāvatsara. May thy dawns be auspicious; may thy days and nights be auspicious; may thy half-months be auspicious; may thy months be auspicious; may thy seasons be auspicious; may thy years be auspicious.
Reciting this mantra revealed in the Veda, "Thou art the Saṃvatsara," the twice-born one performs the rite;
even a Śūdra, however, may worship thee with the mantra of salutation (*namaskāra*).
With the mantra beginning with "namaskāreṇa" and "saṃvatsaro ’īti," and having thus worshipped him, one should subsequently envelop him with garments,
seasonal offerings, roots and fruits, and food offerings such as sweetmeats (*modaka*).
Then, standing before him with palms joined in reverence, he should thereafter entreat him:
"By your grace, may greatness be mine at the end of the year."
"May the calamities of the year perish for me without remainder.
Having spoken thus, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin according to one's ability,
and should apply a tilaka mark made of sandalwood paste upon the forehead.
Sandalwood rubbed with sandalwood paste;
from that time forward, the forehead should be adorned daily with a sectarian mark (tilaka) for as long as a year, like the sky by the moon.
In this way, whether a man or a woman, one should observe this vow;
O tiger among men, such a person always enjoys pleasures upon this earth.
Spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and other such beings, as well as irresistible hostile grahas—
all these become rendered powerless the very moment they behold this tilaka.
Formerly there was a victorious protector of the earth named Śatruñjaya;
he had a wife named Citralekhā, who was adorned by her virtuous conduct.
In the month of Caitra, she undertook this vow in the presence of a brahmin;
for one year, she worshipped and meditated upon Janārdana within her heart.
A man who approaches her with the desire to strike or revile her,
upon seeing her *tilaka*, becomes her benefactor and departs.
Having humbled the pride of her co-wives and brought the surface of the earth under her control,
she sat there unperturbed, her heart rejoicing upon seeing her husband’s face.
Meanwhile, the husband was overcome by an elephant; the son was in pain;
and the benefactor of his friends was seized by a headache.
Afflicted with a headache, possessed by a pain in the head,
and having arrived from the city of Dharmarāja, the servants of Yama, who carry away all living beings,
came there at that very moment, O great king.
Reaching his gate, they entered the house directly,
preceded by Time and Death, in order to bring Śatruñjaya back.
Seeing Citralekhā standing by his side, her face adorned with a tilaka mark,
they lost their resolve and turned back again.
Once they had departed, O Bhārata, that king, free from disease, enjoyed with his son those auspicious pleasures acquired through his former desires and actions.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this was previously related to me by Akrūra:
this meritorious vow, known as the Tilaka of the three worlds, is a supreme ornament that removes all evils.
The mortal who practices this with desire, having lived happily, goes to the imperishable abode of the Moon-crested Lord.
[351] Thus ends the description of the Tilaka-vrata prescribed for the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja, at the rising of the sun,
one should worship an aśoka tree that has put forth auspicious, fully developed sprouts.
With sprouted grains of the seven types of cereal, auspicious *guṇaka* beans, and sweetmeats; with divine fruits produced in season, such as coconuts and pomegranates.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, one should worship that supreme tree, the Aśoka, there with incense, lamps, and other offerings; thus, one never encounters sorrow anywhere.
May you, the remover of sorrow and grief, be present everywhere within our family— among fathers, brothers, husbands, mothers-in-law, sons, and sons-in-law.
Having recited this, one should then offer the *arghya* with full faith,
having adorned [the deity] with banners and covered [it] with a fine cloth.
Just as Damayantī, as Svāhā, and as the goddess Jānakī,
so shall she become beloved by her husband through this vow of grief.
While dwelling in the forest,
he displayed his affection for Sītā upon seeing an aśoka tree in the woods adorned with young shoots, O Pārtha.
Having placed her husband and brother-in-law nearby, she should worship them with sesame seeds and unbroken rice,
lamps, red lac, food offerings, incense, sacred threads, and fruits.
Having been honored and entreated by Yudhiṣṭhira, O Rāghava, that red aśoka tree,
while Rāghava was listening, spoke with Maithilī standing with palms joined in reverence.
With his hands joined in *añjali*, he said:
"May my aged father-in-law, the lord of Kośala, live long!"
"May my husband and my brothers-in-law, Bharata and the others, live;
and may Kausalyā live, she for whose sake this Maithilī lives."
Having circumambulated this most fortunate one, the ornament of the forest, she then departed for her home.
In the same way, any other woman who should worship the Lord of the Earth with sesame,
rice, barley, wheat, and mustard seeds mixed together;
Having asked for forgiveness, one should sprinkle at the root a tree with red shoots;
or, in its absence, one made of gold or silver according to one's means.
Then, having either painted [the image] with pigments or worshipped it according to the rules,
whichever devoted wife bows down with this mantra shall [attain her goal].
O Great Bull, O Great Branch, O Abode of the Makara-bannered One!
O highly fortunate one, grant all desires to me, the earthly king.
Having thus addressed that tree and given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin,
and having given that fashioned tree together with a pair of garments;
It is made of gold or other such materials;
accompanied by her female friends, that virtuous woman, observing celibacy, should eat.
O Pārtha, those young women who worship the Aśoka tree— the destroyer of grief— with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, incense, and lamps,
shall enjoy incomparable happiness on earth arising from their husbands.
The joyful ones attain once again the state of Gaurī.
[353] Thus, in the *Bhaviṣyottara*, regarding the "Vow of the First Day of Śoka," the Blessed One said:
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the auspicious fortnight, on the first day at the break of dawn,
one should worship the charming karavīra flower born in the divine garden.
Clad in red thread, and adorned with perfumes, incense, and unguents,
[the altar] is further graced by sprouted grains of the seven types of grain, as well as by oranges and citron fruits.
Having sprinkled the jujube fruits, edible items, and beautiful coconuts with water containing unbroken rice grains while reciting the mantra, one should thus ask for forgiveness.
O Karavīra, abode of poison, salutations to you, beloved of the Sun;
O ornament of the crowns of gods such as Durgā, you who are eternally dear to them.
Having worshipped with devotion using the Vedic mantra beginning with "ākṛṣṇena," and having thus worshipped with such devotion, he gave a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the brāhmaṇa.
Then one should perform a circumambulation and thereafter go to one's own home;
this vow was formerly observed, O Pārtha, with the desire to propitiate the Sun.
It was likewise practiced by Damayantī, Sarasvatī, Gāyatrī, Gaṅgā,
and other women, even in the world of mortals.
O Pārtha, the Karavīra vow bestows the fruit of all happiness;
having worshipped the Karavīra tree, whose every branch is honored with red flowers and whose body is spread over with dark-blue leaves.
Having enjoyed on earth all desirable pleasures according to their merit,
they finally depart for the abode of the Sun, the foremost of the luminaries.
[354] Thus ends the Karavīra-pratipad-vrata from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
It is recorded in the Smṛti that by worshipping and offering oblations to Agni, one obtains all kinds of grain; through the sacrificial oblation, one shall attain immortality and wealth.

"Having sacrificed" means having worshipped. "On the first day" means on the first lunar day (pratipad). "Thus remembered" means known as Hiraṇyaretas according to one's desires. "With oblation" means with clarified butter (ghṛta). The grammatical connection is: "having offered all grains.
The root mantras are proclaimed by their own names, and the limb mantras (aṅgamantra) are likewise mentioned.
As before, the Lord of the Lunar Days (Tithīśvara) should be visualized seated upon a lotus petal.

The *mūlamantras* are the principal mantras; the *aṅgamantras* are the mantras of the retinue deities, such as "Oṃ, obeisance to Agni’s heart," and so forth. By their own designations, they are used in worship as "Oṃ, obeisance to Agni," and so on; in the fire-oblation (*homa*), they are used as "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni," and so on, as previously described in the context of the Sūryavrata. He stands in his own form within the pericarp at the center of the lotus, and in his retinue forms upon the petals. Here, Vahni (Fire) is the Lord of the lunar days (*tithīśvara*). He has matted hair and a beard, three eyes, a red body, and four arms; in his right [hand] he holds a trident, and in the other, a flame. His left arm is placed upon the shoulder of Svāhā, who sits upon his lap with a vessel of food in her hand. Four parrots are the carriers of his chariot, and Vāyu is the charioteer; this is to be understood as stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Worship performed with offerings of perfumes and flowers according to one's ability—
even if performed with deceit or hypocrisy— bestows its fruit.
"Without guile, without deceit"— this and so forth is praise.
[355] A fire-oblation performed with a peaceful mind, using streams of clarified butter, fuel-sticks, curd, milk, rice, and honey, is ordained to bestow the previously mentioned fruits.

A sacrifice performed separately with the six [substances] beginning with the stream of clarified butter (*ājyadhārā*) bestows wealth and grants the previously mentioned fruits. *Mākṣika* is honey. First comes worship, then the sacrifice of grains smeared with ghee, and thereafter the sacrifice of the stream of clarified butter and so forth. Thus is the Vaiśvānara-vrata in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Agastya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the unsurpassed Dhanya-vrata,
by which even one who is unfortunate may indeed immediately become fortunate.
On the first lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should observe the *nakta* fast and worship Viṣṇu during the night.
First to Vaiśvānara, and likewise to Agni;
then to Haviḥbhuj, and then to the vast Draviṇodas-bhuj.
Having thus worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, according to this ritual procedure, [reciting] "to Samvarta" for the head and "to Jvalana" on all sides.
Having had a sacrificial pit constructed before him according to the prescribed rules,
the wise practitioner should perform the vow at the conclusion of the fire-oblation with these mantras.
With these previously mentioned mantras beginning with "vaiśvānarāya," he should then eat barley-gruel mixed with clarified butter;
likewise during the dark fortnight, and specifically the barley-gruel during the Cāturmāsya period.
In the months beginning with Caitra, the wise man should eat milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with ghee;
in those beginning with Śrāvaṇa, he should eat barley meal (*saktu*), and then it is concluded.
And when the vow is completed, O King, the monarch should have an image of Agni fashioned out of gold; its form is as previously described,
covered with a pair of red garments, and adorned with red flowers and unguents.
In the same manner, one should likewise smear a Brahmin with saffron—
one who is complete in all his limbs, virtuous, and pleasing to behold.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual with a pair of red garments,
the mantra-possessor should thereafter offer that [gift] to him with this mantra.
You are blessed and possessed of blessed qualities; I am blessed and you are one who possesses blessings.
By means of this blessed vow that has been practiced, may I always be happy.
Having thus uttered it and deposited that [mantra] within himself like a treasure-chest,
even one who is devoid of fortune immediately attains blessedness.
In this very life, good fortune, wealth, and abundant grain are produced by the mere performance of this; of this there is no doubt.
The fire indeed burns away the evil accumulated through speech and mind;
with his evil burnt away, that pure-souled one attains [bliss] both here and in the hereafter.
Thus ends the Dhanya-vrata as declared in the Varāha Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
On the first lunar day (pratipad), one who eats only a single meal and, at the end of the year, gifts a tawny cow (kapilā).
One goes to Vaiśvānarapura; this indeed is the Vaiśvānara vow.
In the *Padmapurāṇa*, regarding the Vaiśvānara-vrata:
"He who, making the earth his vessel, eats during the junctions of the fortnights,
obtains the fruit of a three-night fast by means of a single day and night."
Thus ends the vow for the junction of the fortnights (*pakṣasaṃdhivratam*) in the *Padmapurāṇa*.
Nandikeśvara said:
"By means of the Vedic injunction, this most excellent and meritorious vow [is performed]."
On which lunar day, however, should this rite be performed? Tell that to me.
Skanda said: In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight on the first lunar day (pratipad),
one who observes silence should cook sixteen times three offerings of food (naivedya).
One should give sixteen fruits cooked with flour to a Brahmin;
these sixteen should be offered with diligence to the deity as well.
Likewise, sixteen [priests] partake [of the offerings] by relying on the observances of the vow;
one should have an image of the deity made of gold, consisting of refined metal, according to one's capacity.
A golden *karṣa* [weight] fashioned according to one's ability,
endowed with three eyes, adorned with a circle of matted locks (*jaṭāmaṇḍala*),
possessing five faces and four arms, situated in the center of a six-spoked wheel.
[358] Carrying a trident and a rosary in his right hand.
Holding a skull-cup and a water-pot in his left hands and bearing the crescent moon upon his crest,
one should bathe him with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then install him.
Upon the water-pot, the Lord of Gods, clothed in a pair of white garments,
should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and likewise with various kinds of fruits.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Teacher of the world of moving and unmoving beings! O Bull-bannered Mahādeva, salutations again and again to the Three-eyed One!
This is the mantra for worship.
One should also give a milch cow as a garment for the deity.
Whoever performs this supreme vow according to this procedure [shall attain the desired fruit].
That king, O God, likewise obtains long life and,
being completely liberated from all evil, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
"Having enjoyed various pleasures, one shall thereafter go to the city of Śiva.
Thus concludes the Mahattama-vrata with its concluding rite (udyāpana) as described in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The Blessed Lord said:
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, during the dark fortnight, on the first day,
Śaṅkara [struck him] with an arrow that had three joints, three points, and three faces.
He cut off the three heads of the sacrifice in the form of a deer;
with those heads, he performed austerities and then obtained a boon from Śaṅkara.

"With three darts" means with a three-faced one whose form is that of a dart; "of the deer-form" means of the three-faced one who has the form of a deer. "Those are to be worshipped by women, never by men.
Then, having fashioned a clay linga in the shape of the head of a deer (Mṛgaśīrṣa)...
Indeed, the golden image should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite with milk, along with water for the guest-offering (arghya),
flowers, incense, and various kinds of food offerings (naivedya).
The meal should be prepared with vegetables and auspicious cakes made from flour mixed with *sauvarcala* salt;
it should also include preparations of *atasī* seeds mixed with *sauvarcala* salt.
Furthermore, the meal should be accompanied by the playing of musical instruments from bronze vessels.
Thus ends the Mṛgaśīrṣa-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa, within the section on the Pratipad-vratas in the Vrata-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Hemādri.
[360] Now begins the fifth chapter.
The Blessed One said:
In the month of Caitra, on the first day of the bright fortnight, when the sun had risen, Brahmā created the entire world.
He likewise established the calculation of time:
the planets, the *nāgas*, the seasons, the months, the years, and the lords of the years.
Then that Blessed One, Brahmā, in the assembly of all the gods,
within the hall of Brahmā, bestowed his own form upon Brahmā.
As described, they attend upon you while bowing and praising you;
then, having performed service for them, you shall go to your own abode.
Then, O King, being thus appointed, they each performed their respective duties; at that time, the assembly hall of Brahmā was especially capable of assuming any form at will.
They maintain this ultimate form, which is inexpressible and captivating;
and from that time forth, the Dharma was practiced by those of former and even more ancient times.
Even now, this [rite] must be performed with great effort, as it is firmly established;
therein one should perform a great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) which destroys all impurities.
It pacifies all calamities, destroys the evil dreams of the Kali age,
bestows long life, provides nourishment, and increases wealth and good fortune.
Auspicious and purifying, bringing happiness to both worlds,
at its beginning Brahmā, born from the lotus, is to be worshipped.
And with water for the feet and other offerings, with incenses, garments, ornaments, and food; with burnt offerings, oblations, and gifts, as well as with the satiation of Brahmins.
Thereafter, worship should be performed for each of the deities individually in due order,
having performed the utterance of *oṃ* and the salutation with *kuśa* grass, water, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains.
With flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as with foods, in their proper sequence.

Having performed the salutation with the syllable *oṃ*, one should touch and recite the mantra for the purpose of worship, beginning with "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā" (*oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*) and so forth. The meaning is that one should touch and recite the manifold forms of the mantra. Thus, starting from "obeisance to Brahmā" (*brahmaṇe namaḥ*) and ending with "obeisance to Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self" (*viṣṇave paramātmane namaḥ*), the names of the deities contained in this collection of sentences—preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending in the dative case followed by *namaḥ*—are to be understood as the mantra. *Oṃ, obeisance to you, O Brahmā, and to Kāma, the Great Soul;
obeisance to Nimeṣa, and let there be obeisance to you, O Triṭaya.*
Homage to you for the *lava*, homage be to you for the *kṣaṇa*;
homage, homage to you for the *kāṣṭhā* and for the *kalā* at all times.
Salutations again and again to the extremely subtle Nābhikāyī and to Muhūrtā;
salutations eternally to the nights and to the auspicious days.
And always from the two fortnights, from the months, from the six seasons,
from the two solstices, and from the five years.
Having paid homage to the Lords of the Yugas, and salutations again and again to the planets;
salutations to the Purandaras and salutations again and again to their friends.
Salutations eternally to the fifty daughters of Dakṣa;
salutations always to the goddess Suprabhā and to Japā.
Salutations to you, the wielder of false weapons, and to the progenitor of all weapons;
salutations to you who have many sons, together with your wives.
Homage to Buddhi, likewise to Vṛddhi, to Nidrā, and to Dhanada;
homage to Nalakūbara, to Yajña, and to the Lord of the Guhyakas.
May there be constant homage to the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma;
homage always to Bhadrakālī, and repeated homage to Surabhī.
Salutations indeed to the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, the Vedānta, the sciences, and arithmetic; and salutations to the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Suparṇas, and to Garuḍa.
And always from the seven seas and the oceans,
and from the Northern Kurus, [I offer] salutation to Hairaṇyatas.
Salutations to Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla everywhere and at all times;
salutations indeed to Ilāvṛta and to Harivarṣa as well.
Homage to the Kimpuruṣas and repeated homage to Bhārata;
homage always to the nine regions of the land of Bhārata.
Salutations again and again to the seven netherworlds and the hells;
salutations to Kālāgnirudra and Śeṣa, and to Hari in the form of Wrath.
Homage to you from the seven worlds and indeed from the great elements;
likewise, homage to your awakening and homage to primordial nature.
Homage be to Puruṣa, the conceited one, whose form is unmanifest;
and likewise, homage to the mountains, headed by Himavat.
Salutations again and again to the seven ancient Gaṅgās;
and let there always be salutations to the seven primordial sages.
[363] Homage be repeatedly paid to the sacred fords, beginning with Puṣkara;
and homage be constantly offered to the rivers, such as the Vitastā and others.
Homage again and again to the fourteen long-sustaining ones;
homage to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and repeated homage to the meters.
Salutations to Surabhī and to the two Rāvaṇas; salutations again and again to Bhūti.
Likewise, salutations to Uccaiḥśravas and to Dhruva; salutations again and again.
Homage be to Dhanvantari; homage again and again to the sword and the missile;
and constant homage to Vināyaka and Kumāra, and to the obstacles.
Salutations indeed to Śākhā, Viśākha, and Nigameśa;
salutations to the Skanda-grahas and to the Mothers of Skanda as well.
Salutations always to Jvara, the lord of diseases, who has ashes as his weapon; and salutations always to the Vālakhilya sages and to Kaśyapa.
Salutations again and again to Agastya, Nārada, Vyāsa, and the others;
likewise, salutations to the Apsarases and to the gods who drink the Soma juice.
Homage to the Asomapas and homage always to the Tuṣitas;
homage eternally to all twelve Ādityas in every way.
Salutations again and again to the eleven Rudras, the practitioners of austerity;
and salutations indeed always to the two Aśvins, Nāsatya and Dasra.
Salutations again and again to the twelve Sādhyas, to the Paurāṇas at all times, and to the forty-nine Maruts.
Salutations to you, the divine Viśvakarman, the teacher of the arts;
and always to the eight guardians of the world, together with their followers.
Homage always to the weapons, to the vehicles, and to the dharmas;
homage always to the seats, to the drums, and to the gods.
Salutations again and again to the Daityas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, and Piśācas; and constantly to the Pitṛs of the seven classes, and to the Pretas.
And from the most subtle gods, and indeed from those who are accessible only through meditative realization—
salutations to you, the manifold-formed Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self.
Now, what is the use of much speaking? One should worship the Brahmins facing east or north with this mantra, as before, for the sake of the gods.

Alternatively, what is the use of elaborate mantras? The meaning is that one should worship the Brahmins themselves with the deities in mind. "As before" means according to the sequence prescribed by the mantras.

With *argha* offerings, flowers, incense, garments, and garlands, "with joy"—that is, with hair standing on end—one should worship; the meaning is that one should worship while being thrilled, with the hair of the body bristling.
Always [endowed] with wealth, grain, food, prosperity, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
[He should honor] the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, as well as the best of the twice-born who recite them— the meaning being by means of gifting the books of those Itihāsas and Purāṇas—
as well as servants who know the proper times and are learned in the Vedas, along with his kinsmen and relatives.
With this very mantra, ending with "svāhā," a separate oblation for Agni Yaviṣṭha should be performed for the satisfaction of all.

When the two eyes— the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*)— have been placed in their primary position by one who knows the Vedas, that is, one who knows the rites prescribed in the Vedas; and when Agni, the specific fire, has become the presiding deity at the primary position, namely at the commencement of the principal oblations— at the start of the sacrifice,
the man should then perform the touching of auspicious objects.
Having fed all the twice-born, as well as friends, relations, and kinsmen,
one should especially eat and hold a great festival;
for this is the commencement of the new year, which brings about the attainment of all success.
Thus concludes the ritual for the water-offering at the end of the year as declared in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.

Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable scholar Hemādri, the preeminent king of great kings, the illustrious Mahādeva, the sovereign of all faculties, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, within the section on Vows (*vratakāṇḍa*), the vows of the first lunar day (*pratipad-vratāni*).
[366] Now begins the sixth chapter.
Now, the second set of vows:
His divine splendor, rivaling the rays of the sun, increasing and fully matured,
shines forth on all sides throughout heaven and earth, never ceasing.
The tall lineage of that man, named Hemādri, which is victorious in the world,
clearly proclaims the sequence of the second vows as they have been received.
Śatānīka said:
"O Sage, O Blessed One, I ask you this: tell me that vow by the power of which a human being attains heaven."
This vow, which requires little effort yet yields great fruit, is the supreme among all vows.
O God, grant me your grace so that I may perform this vow.
The sage said:
"O King, there is a most meritorious vow called Aśūnyaśayana;
at the rising of the moon, one should offer arghya and worship Janārdana."
Śatānīka said:
In which month should it be performed, and what are the lunar fortnight and the lunar day?
What is the gift and what is the food? Tell me, O Great Lord.
The sage said:
O King, during the four-month period of the rains, there is an excellent vow;
it begins on the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, O lord of men.
One should perform that supreme vow from the month of Śrāvaṇa until the end of Kārttika,
especially offering flowers, incense, food offerings, and rows of lamps.
Various fruits along with an offering of food endowed with various flavors,
as well as pearls, silver, and a conch shell accompanied by milk.
It should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, for Janārdana is to be worshipped;
thereafter, in the month of Bhādrapada, one gives an offering of barley.
One should give milk to the Brahmin, and especially a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
as well as curd and fruit together with a citron.
O lord of men, Janārdana is to be worshipped with supreme devotion;
O King, he who acts in this manner attains the highest state.
Furthermore, on the second day of the lunar fortnight, the gift of a bed is especially meritorious;
his bed shall never be empty, and that man shall not be childless.
Viṣṇu, Janārdana, situated in the midst of the water,
is to be worshipped with white flowers, fruits, and garments, along with betel-leaf and a monetary gift (dakṣiṇā).
One should give food to a brahmin; hear the fruit of this, O lord of men:
he who acts thus, O King, attains the city of gold.
And then, O lord of men, on the second day of the month of Kārttika,
[one should offer] pieces of sugar-candy and the like, as well as curd, milk, and ghee.
One should offer an oblation to the Blessed One with every effort:
flowers, fruits, along with food offerings, accompanied by song and instrumental music.
One should give an umbrella, a water-pot, and especially sandals;
likewise, both men and women should observe the four-year vow.
O King, for one who thus performs the Aśūnyaśayana vow,
there shall never be suffering, poverty, or hardship anywhere.
His bed shall never be empty, nor shall that man be childless;
grief, disease, fear, and suffering shall never befall him.
A woman shall never become a widow, nor shall she ever be destitute;
by the power of this vow, a human being attains heaven.
Śatānīka said: "O Kṛṣṇa, this most wonderful vow, which is proclaimed for men and women as 'Aśūnyaśayana' (the vow of the non-empty bed), has neither been seen nor heard by me."
By whom was this practiced in the past and manifested in the world of mortals?
What kind of fruit was obtained? Tell me all of that.
The seer said:
"O King, there was one named Rūkmāṅgada, a speaker of truth who had conquered his senses. Once, while hunting deer, he went into a dense forest."
A beautiful lake was seen, filled with water and most enchanting,
crowded with swans and cranes, and adorned by ruddy geese.
Having performed his ablutions there in that playful place, which was filled with bubbles of various shapes and inhabited by many sages, he departed from the forest thicket.
Having joined his two hands in the gesture of reverence, he went to the hermitage of Vāmana;
performing a severe vow, the sage honored him with offerings of water for the feet and guest-offerings.
Having quickly performed his salutation, he stood before Vāmana.
Vāmadeva said: "What business has arisen for you that you have come here to this dense forest of mine, a place so difficult of access, even a mountain?"
O King, for what purpose have you come into my presence?
Rūkmāṅgada said:
"O Blessed One, I ask you about one matter that causes me wonder:
by the power of what merit was the son Dharmāṅgada obtained?"
My wife Sandhyāvalī is as dear to me as my own life;
my son is a king who rules over the seven continents and nine divisions of the earth.
By what power of karma did this come to be? Tell me truly, O Great Sage.
Vāmadeva said:
"O best among the foremost of kings, you are a speaker of truth who has conquered his senses;
you have asked a profound question that is difficult for those lacking intelligence to comprehend."
A wife who is pleasing to the mind and a son of the same nature—
these are never obtained anywhere by men of little merit, O Indra among kings.
O King, hear all that merit by which everything on earth is obtained by men, just as you have obtained this kingdom.
"In a previous birth you were a Śūdra; you never spoke the truth, nor did you know what is an offering to the gods or an offering to the ancestors, though your wife was devoted to her husband."
In your presence are four Brahmins, masters of the Vedas,
devoted to virtuous deeds, patient, learned, and self-controlled.
Your four neighbors are knowers of the Vedas and the Dharma;
they have performed this Aśūnyaśayana vow for you.
Having heard of its great fruit and having seen it, you too have performed this:
by offering the *arghya* to the moon on the second day at its rising.
Having given water and ghee— specifically excluding black gram and alkaline substances—
to a Brāhmaṇa, you have performed the ritual consumption.
O King, by the power of this vow observed during the four months of Cāturmāsya for four years, a desired son was obtained.
A wife equal to Saṃdhyāvalī and a son equal to Dharmāṅgada—
whatever others may do, they shall all obtain the fruit thereof.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, and filled with wealth and grain,
a human being attains heaven through the power of this vow.
Go, O tiger among kings; you shall enjoy the entire earth together with your wife and son, and you shall go to heaven—there is no other way.
Śatānīka said:
O Lord, please describe the vow together with its proper procedure;
how should one perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) when this most excellent vow is fully completed?
The sage said:
O King, one should observe this vow for four years beginning at the rising of the moon;
then, one should choose a preceptor who is learned in the Vedas and knows the dharma.
He was accompanied by officiating priests and Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas,
and provided with a sacred thread, a garment, and sandals.
Having fashioned a Vaiṣṇava image out of gold or silver,
one should likewise prepare a golden image of Viṣṇu accompanied by Rukmiṇī-Lakṣmī.
A man who is authorized [to perform this rite] should give a bed and a cotton mattress, together with the seven kinds of grain, as well as the gift of a cow.
One should give food to the Brahmins along with ghee-filled cakes mixed with sugar;
he who acts in this way, O Pārtha, attains the supreme state.
Thus ends the Aśūnyaśayana-dvitīyā-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa. From the Bhaviṣyottara:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

O Blessed One, you have declared that the excellent means for achieving dharma, wealth, and the other aims of life is the state of householdership; and that indeed exists when a husband and wife remain in love with one another.
A man without a wife, and a wife separated from her husband, cannot achieve the fulfillment of dharma, artha, and kāma; therefore, O Madhusūdana.
I shall hear that, O Lord of the gods of gods, by which vow, O Govinda, a woman does not become a widow, nor a man remains separated from his wife.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Bhārata, listen to the account of the second lunar day known as Aśūnyaśayanā,
by fasting on which, O lord of men, a woman does not fall into widowhood.
And a man separated from his wife is never able to procreate;
for it is stated further on that on this day of fasting, one should not eat again at night.
O King, when Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Universe, lies down together with Śrī...
Then that lunar day should be observed as the "Aśūnyaśayanā" (the Unempty Bed);
it should be spent through fasting, eating only at night, or likewise by eating only what is unsolicited.
O Bhārata, on the second day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, when [Viṣṇu] sleeps, this [day] should be observed;

the meaning is that it should be observed as being in close proximity to the day of his sleeping. Therefore, the month of Śrāvaṇa here should be understood according to the system where the full moon marks the end of the month.
One who is self-restrained should perform the ritual bath in a river, a pond, or at home.
Then, one should have a square altar made of clay;
there, with devotion, one should worship Śrīdhara, the Lord of Śrī, together with Śrī.
Having offered food offerings, flowers, incense, and other auspicious fruits produced in season,
one should bow down to the Lord of the World and recite this mantra:
O bearer of the Śrīvatsa, beloved of Śrī, abode of Śrī, Lord of Śrī, immutable one!
May my household life, until its very end, be productive of dharma, artha, and kāma.
May the pure ones not perish; may the gods not perish;
and may those who go to Yama’s realm not perish through the separation of my marriage from me.
The fires are pure, the gods are free from decay, and the ancestors dwell in the realm of Yama;
yet, O Lord, they are never separated from prosperity as you are.
Therefore, O Lord, let this bond with my wife not be severed for me.
O Giver of Boons, O Madhusūdana, just as your bed is never empty of Lakṣmī,
so too may my bed here never be empty.
Furthermore, these are the mantras from the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"Act in such a way that husband and wife do not experience the suffering arising from a husband's separation from his wife, nor a wife's separation from her husband."
Just as you are never separated from Śrī, O Lord, and just as Lakṣmī is never separated from you,
so may it be that we two remain steadfast through your grace, O Lord of Gods.
May our sons perish, but let there be no loss of wealth and no end to our family lineage;
may the sacred fires not be extinguished, and let there be no ruin of our home.

The remainder of the text has a meaning equivalent to that of the *Bhaviṣyottara*. Having thus propitiated and performed worship for Lakṣmī as well as for Hari, one should offer upon the bed whatever fruits are desired by the Lord of the World.
Having prostrated before Hari in the temple at night, one should eat while restraining one's speech;
at the rising of the moon, preceded by a bath, [one should consume] the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

The grammatical connection is as follows: having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin according to one’s own capacity along with the fruit, and having bowed to Hari, one should eat at night.
By this procedure, O King, for a period of four months.
On the second day of the dark fortnight, one should perform worship according to the previously mentioned procedure.
When the month of Kārttika has arrived, one should give to a twice-born man a bed joined with the Beloved of Śrī, accompanied by household utensils, a water-pot, and food.
And for Soma, one should offer a respectful oblation (argha) consisting of meat resembling that of the image, accompanied by mantras,
along with curd, unbroken grains, roots, fruits, jewels, and golden vessels.
O younger brother of Lakṣmī, who arose from the churning of the milk ocean that appeared in the courtyard of the sky,
and who illumines the expanse of the quarters with your radiance— homage be to you!
On the second day, O mighty-armed one, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the brahmin according to one's ability,
as well as whatever fruits are available at that time.

By the general statement "one should give fruits upon the bed," the specific details are then set forth with the words "which... and so on: "O best of kings, O monarch, sweet fruits—neither pungent nor bitter—should be given upon the bed according to one's own ability."
By giving sweet things, one attains the state of being beloved by the mind;
therefore, one should avoid pungent, bitter, and feminine words.
O King, taking dates and citrons along with your head, you shall carry these fruits to the bedchamber; thus, take your share of the sacrifice.

One should discard the coconut exactly as it is, together with its stalk. One should offer the inner kernel (*antargola*) as a sacrificial portion to Hara and avoid [the rest]. The meaning is that for the sake of pleasing Rudra, one should leave some portions remaining and discard the rest from all sides.
O Bhārata, these very items, along with the *gāṅgeya* (the coconut water), should be given with devotion according to one's capacity to a Brahmin on the second day.
Likewise, the gift of clothing, accompanied by the gift of grain and fruit—
these very same things which were given at the time of his lying down, as well as gold from the Ganges;
the man who performs this correctly for four months [attains the aforementioned rewards].
O Hero, for such a person, the destruction of the home does not occur throughout three lifetimes.
The phrase "for four months" implies on the second days of the dark fortnights; the meaning is that the vow concludes on the second day immediately following the Bodhinī (Bodhi-pūrṇimā).
For him, no destruction of the household occurs for three lifetimes;
he shall indeed have his bed never empty and shall accomplish virtue, pleasure, and wealth.
A man becomes one whose sovereignty is unimpeded; there is no doubt in this matter.
And so too, O Pārtha, does a woman who knows the dharma, by performing the vow according to the prescribed rule.
O best of men, she who acts [in this way] does not become an object of grief for her circle of kinsmen, nor does she suffer widowhood, misfortune, or abandonment by her husband.
O scion of the Pāṇḍu lineage, she does not undergo rebirth for three lifetimes.
O King, this second lunar day is known as Aśūnyaśayanā; it is the second [tithi] that removes all impurities.
Any man or woman who always observes this [day], [attains great merit].
He attains a bed of the foremost and most noble enjoyments.
Śaṅkara said:
One should cause the sound of singing and musical instruments to be made for the God of gods;
for one capable of ringing the bell, [the mantra] "Obeisance to the one who consists of all the gods."
Having thus worshipped Govinda, one should eat food devoid of oil at night,
avoiding pungent and salty flavors, for as long as that period of four [days] lasts.
Having observed this fast by abstaining from oil and other such substances and by refraining from eating during the day,
then when morning has dawned, the wise man should offer a bed accompanied by the Lord of Lakṣmī (Viṣṇu) and provided with lamps and food.
It should be provided with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, and a seat,
as well as adorned with ornaments and grains according to one's capacity.

[376] It should be given to a Brahmin who has no physical defects, who is a devotee of Viṣṇu, who maintains a family, and who is learned in the Vedas; it must never be given to one who practices the "heron-vow" (hypocrisy).
Having seated the couple there and adorned them according to the prescribed rite,
he should provide a meal for the wife consisting of various kinds of food and edibles.
The Brahmin should also present a golden image of the God of gods, complete with ritual implements and accompanied by a water-pot.
Thus, O Brahmin, for that man who performs the Aśūnyaśayana vow,
there shall never arise a lack of wealth;
nor shall a woman become a widow as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
From the Matsya Purāṇa:
"O best of kings, a couple is never born with deformity or for the sake of sorrow;
nor do their sons, cattle, or jewels ever go to ruin."
For seven thousand and seven hundred kalpas,
he who keeps his bed unforsaken is honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"His vow of the Unempty Bed (Aśūnyaśayana) accomplishes virtue, pleasure, and wealth;
a man becomes one whose sovereignty is unimpeded—of this there is no doubt."
And that woman, O King, who knows the dharma and performs this vow according to the rules,
does not become an object of grief for her circle of kinsmen.
O best of men, by performing this great vow, one does not incur widowhood, misfortune, or abandonment by a husband for three births. Thus, O King, has this excellent second lunar day been described.
Having fasted upon which, O King, a man shall himself attain prosperity and growth.
Thus ends the Aśūnyaśayana-dvitīyā-vrata.
Brahmā said:
Having worshipped Brahmā and a celibate student (brahmacārin) on the second lunar day, [one should perform the rite].
Having fed them all according to the prescribed rite, one shall become a master who has reached the further shore.
The root mantras and the limb mantras are proclaimed by their respective names;
and as before, the Lord of the Lunar Days (Tithīśvara) should be visualized seated upon a lotus petal.
Brahmā is the lord of the lunar days (tithi).
Worship is performed with offerings of fragrance and flowers according to one's capacity;
even if performed with deceit or hypocrisy, it yields fruit.
A fire sacrifice performed with a stream of clarified butter, fuel sticks, curd, milk, food, and honey,
while the mind is tranquil, yields the same fruits as previously described.
This vow is to be explained in the same manner as the Vaiśvānara-pratipad-vrata. Thus ends the Brahma-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Agastya said:
Henceforth, O King of kings, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed Kānti-vrata, to be observed on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
At night, one should diligently perform worship and honor Baladeva and Keśava; one should worship the feet for Baladeva and the head for Keśava.
Having thus worshipped the supreme form of Viṣṇu, the wise man should worship on that day the other form known as Soma, which consists of two kalās.

Having assumed the form of Soma and the form of Viṣṇu, one should worship his two feet with the mantra "to Baladeva. Having thus worshipped these two limbs with "to Keśava" for the head, one should worship the form of Śeṣa. On that day and on the second day, the two *kalās*—that which possesses those two *kalās*, namely the two powers called Baladeva and Keśava, characterized by restraint (*nigraha*) and grace (*anugraha*)—become manifest.
The wise one should offer the *arghya* with the mantra of Parameṣṭhin.
He states that very mantra for Parameṣṭhin, who is Viṣṇu in the form of the Moon.
Salutations to you who are the embodiment of nectar, the bearer of all medicinal herbs,
the sovereign of the world of sacrifice, Soma, the Supreme Self.
O King, having offered the *arghya* to the Moon with this mantra,
that Brahmin should eat barley meal with ghee at night, O King.
He is a true sage, he is a true brahmin; by him, having offered food to the brahmin, he himself should eat—this is the meaning established.
Furthermore, during the four months beginning with Phālguna, one who is pure should [offer] milk-rice mixed with ghee.
One should perform the sesame oblation (tilahoma) at the beginning of the month of Kārttika, and likewise with barley.
During the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, one should perform oblations of ghee;
one should eat sesame and rice at night—this indeed is the sequence of the ritual.
It follows as a matter of course that one should eat barley-food during the four months beginning with Kārttika;
therefore, when the year is complete, having fashioned a silver image of Soma,
covered with white cloth and adorned with white flowers and unguents—
In this very manner, having honored the twice-born, one should then bestow it upon him;
for he shall become radiant in the world of the Aśvins, omniscient, and pleasing to behold.
"By your grace, O Nārāyaṇa of gentle form, salutations be unto you!
Having spoken this mantra, one who is restrained in speech should give [the gift] to a Brahmin.
As soon as it is performed, a man becomes radiant;
this was performed in ancient times by Soma, the son of Atri, O King.
Then, at the conclusion of the vow, Janārdana himself became truly pleased.
Thus concludes the vow of the Second Day of Kānti, together with its concluding rite (udyāpana), as declared in the Varāha Purāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, I shall describe that supreme [vow] which brings about the pacification of all obstacles.
Listen to the supreme procedure for offering the respectful water (arghya) to the newly risen moon.
When the moon is visible in the west at the time of dusk, O Pārtha, having divided the sun’s path into twelve parts, one should likewise offer an oblation (arghya) to the moon.
The meaning is that one should offer the *arghya* oblation when the moon has moved twelve degrees past the first lunar day (*pratipad*), that is, on the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*).
Indeed, when the time of twilight has arrived on the second day of the bright fortnight,
one should establish a new silver moon upon a circle made of cow dung.
One should depict the God together with Rohiṇī using sandalwood paste,
along with flowers, sandalwood, and karkandhu fruits mixed with rice.
O King of kings, a wise person should offer the *arghya* with dūrvā sprouts, excellent jewels, fruits, and white garments, while reciting this mantra.
[380] Karkandhu fruits are jujubes (*badara*).
"You are ever new, being born again and again at the end of each month;
swell as you come together—thus, O King Soma, homage be to you!"
Whoever, being composed, offers this arghya— which bestows the fruit of all desires— to Soma month after month according to this rite;
Having offered the *arghya* together with rice cooked in milk (*śālyanna*), O Brahmin, one obtains all desires and attains a long life.
O son of Kuntī, a man who eats at night with a serene face and eyes becomes endowed with good reputation,
fame, beauty, and nourishment.
Surrounded by sons and grandsons, and abounding in cattle, grain, and wealth, he shall remain in the mortal world for a hundred years; having died, he shall go to the city of the Moon.
There, that best of kings dwells in heaven,
enjoying divine pleasures together with excellent women until the dissolution of all beings.
If you desire all incomparable prosperity, then month after month here, perform my command;
[worship] Soma with sandalwood and other offerings, O delighter of the Lunar dynasty.
Offer the respectful water (arghya) to him who has just been born and has just arisen.
Thus ends the procedure for offering the *arghya* to the newly risen moon, as told in the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"I shall likewise describe this other second [rite], which grants all desires."
Having observed this fast, a person obtains all the desired objects of their longing.
O King, having reached the second day of the bright fortnight of Caitra,
a person should properly perform a ritual bath in river water at the conclusion of the day.
Having fashioned a crescent moon mandala, one should worship it with white pigments,
white flowers, fruits, and abundant quantities of milk-rice (paramānna).
With sugarcane, products of sugarcane, and pure salt,
one should worship the Lord of Gods or the Moon at the end of the day.
Alternatively, having drawn a mandala, one should worship it as situated in the sky;
having performed an oblation with clarified butter, one should eat at night while maintaining silence.

One should perform worship and fire-offerings with the name-mantra; thereafter, one may eat food purified with oil, provided one does not do so like a god [at will]. One should avoid food cooked in oil for a year.
Having performed this vow correctly for a year while remaining pure, a man attains great good fortune and goes to the heavenly world.
O King, foremost of the Yādava lineage, this vow has been declared as purifying, destructive of enemies, bestowing good fortune, and removing disease.
Likewise, a woman should also perform her duty with diligent effort.
Thus ends the vow of Bālendradvitīyā in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"He who desires a beautiful form, good fortune, or excellent women [should perform this]."
O lord of men, on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
one who has restrained his self should dwell for one year subsisting on flowers alone.

The meaning is that, having begun the vow on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should perform the vow for a full year, subsisting only on flowers even on other second days of the bright fortnights. O King, one should eat only those sacrificial flowers that are seasonally available, after having given them to the Brāhmaṇas.

The flowers suitable for oblation are worthy of worship and are not forbidden for consumption. Furthermore, the two Aśvins should be worshipped here with their name-mantras, as they are heard of as the bestowers of the fruit [of the vow].
"He who gives golden flowers along with cows at the conclusion of the vow—the two gods, lords of the three worlds, are well-pleased with him."
Likewise, O Aśvins, you two should grant divine desires and even a radiant celestial chariot,
delighting the world for a very long time with the women of the gods.
And having come here at the end of the kalpa, this twice-born man, honored by the brahmins and learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, shall remain so for seven future births.
A donor, with a self-controlled mind and eloquent speech, free from mental and physical ailments,
surrounded by sons and grandsons, shall rejoice for a long time together with his wife.
One shall possess a share of the kingdom in the most beautiful and righteous land of Madhyadeśa.
This second [constellation] named Puṣya has been described by me to you.
Thus concludes the vow of Puṣyadvitīyā as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārtha, these well-known lunar days beginning with the second exist;
four of them, occurring every four months during the rainy season, are of great merit."
[383] O Pārtha, the lunar days (tithis) have not been mentioned by me anywhere as lords of the cows (gopatis).
I shall now reveal them correctly; listen to them all with a concentrated mind.
The first occurs in the month of Śrāvaṇa, likewise the second in Bhādrapada;
the third is in the month of Āśvayuja, and the fourth shall be in Kārttika.
In Śrāvaṇa it is named Kaluṣā; likewise, in Bhādrapada it is Gor-malā;
in Āśvina it is Pretasaṃcārā; and in Kārttika it is considered Yāmyakā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

Why is she called "the turbid" (kaluṣā)? Why is she considered "the filth of the cow" (gomalā)? Why is she the "haunt of the departed spirits" (pretasaṃcārā)? And why is she proclaimed as "belonging to Yama" (yāmyā)?
Kṛṣṇa said:
Long ago, when the slaying of Vṛtra had occurred and Purandara had regained his kingdom,
the horse sacrifice was undertaken for the purpose of removing the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Out of anger, Indra struck down the murder of a Brahmin with his thunderbolt;
it was cast upon the earth in six forms: into trees, water, and the surface of the ground.
Having distributed that [gift] to a Brahmin and to the Fire in due order,
a woman shall have that sin cast off on the second day of the month of Śrāvaṇa at the rising of the moon.
A woman, a tree, a river, the earth, fire, and likewise a slayer of a Brahmin—these are considered impure; even a sacred bathing place becomes defiled when touched by such things.
In ancient times, the earth was submerged in the blood of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
therefore, it is impure by eight finger-breadths, as is the menstrual flow of women.
All rivers have water as their impurity, and fire has the crest of smoke as its impurity;
since these move within her, she is therefore considered to be impure.

[384] They wander about, abandoning those who have already performed penance, in order to accept those who have performed penance. For this very reason, some penance must be performed for her every year.
Gīr, Girāṃ, Bhāratī, Vāṇī, Varā, Medhā, and Sarasvatī are synonyms. Since Gīr carries impurity (mala), the second [Girā] is considered to be "impure" (malā).
Those who revile the gods, sages, ancestors, and the sacred laws—atheists and rogues—for them that speech is a mass of impurity; therefore, the second speech is called "impure."
During forbidden times for study, they teach and recite the scriptures—
the grammarians, the logicians, and the followers of the Vedas— those whose impurities are born of words.

And those [days] are arranged in the second fortnight; therefore, the meaning is that speech and impurity cease therein, and thus the worship of Sarasvatī should be performed on that day. For the ancestors are called "the departed" (pretas), and their movement occurs on that day.
And in the second [world] among the worlds, there is that path frequented by pretas;
likewise, there are the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, Ājyapa, and Somapa [ancestors].
The ancestors and grandfathers who have passed away are called *pretasaṃcaras* because they move about as spirits;
they are honored by sons, citizens, and grandsons with the *svadhā* mantras.
Satisfied by the offerings of ancestral rites (śrāddha) and sacrifices, they depart from there along the path frequented by the departed spirits (pretasaṃcarā).
Therefore, the meaning is that a śrāddha must be performed even on that day.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, [this applies] to the second day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
Formerly, Yama was always fed at his own home by Yamunā;
on the second lunar day, during the great festival, those dwelling in hell were also gratified.
Though liberated even from evils, they are freed from every bond;
having fallen away from excessive attachment, they all abide in spontaneity.
A great festival took place for them, bringing happiness to the realm of Yama;
therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is called Yamadvitīyā in the world.
O Pārtha, food should not be eaten by the wise from the hand of this woman in her own home;
rather, it should be eaten with affection from the hand of a sister-in-law, for it increases nourishment.
And gifts should be bestowed upon the sisters according to the prescribed rite,
with gold ornaments, garments, worship, hospitality, and food.
All sisters are to be honored; in their absence, those who have entered the path [of religious life]. "Those who have entered the path" means sister-friends.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, [the offering] from the hand of a paternal uncle's sister is for the first [day].
O King, on the second day [of the lunar month], [the bride] should likewise receive [the hand] from the hand of her maternal uncle’s son;
on the third day, from the hands of the daughters of her father’s and mother’s sisters.
Furthermore, one should eat from the hand of one's co-born sister;
"sister related by the paternal uncle" means a sister through connection with the paternal uncle, that is, the daughter of the paternal uncle.
One should eat from the hands of all such sisters; this increases strength.
O Pārtha, I have explained to you in its entirety, along with its secret teachings, that which brings merit, fame, and long life, and which accomplishes dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
On that lunar day on which the divine King Yama was fed by Yamunā out of sisterly affection for her brother,
he who here eats from the palm of his sister’s hand [attains the same merit].
He attains the most excellent jewel, beautiful and fragrant.
Thus ends the Yamadvitīyā-vrata from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen now to me regarding that which is to be performed on the following second lunar day.
It bestows all branches of knowledge, is meritorious, and removes the defects arising from impaired intellect.
Well-bathed, having performed his prayers and completed his morning rituals,
he should remain celibate, with anger subdued, and with speech, body, and mind under control.
One should fashion a square mandala with the remaining rice grains;
in its center, having arranged an eight-petaled lotus with heaps of flowers.
In the pericarp, one should visualize the goddess Śrī, the beloved of Hari, holding a lotus in her hand,
with a lotus-like face and lotus-like eyes, resembling the filaments of a lotus.
Sarasvatī, Rati, Bhūti, Dānti, Kānti,
Maitrī, and Vidya— these are always proclaimed as the eight divine powers (śaktis).
One should install them, as appropriate, upon the eight petals;
they are worshipped with their respective name-mantras joined with their initial syllables.

"By means of the conjunction with the respective initial syllables" means by means of the mantras formed from the initial letters of those respective names; for example, *saṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*. This should be understood to apply likewise to those [deities] to be mentioned hereafter.

One should remember Prajñā, Medhā, Prabhā, and Sattvā in the northern direction, and Chāyā and the others, who possess mixed colors, individually in the intermediate directions in their respective order.
Nandī, Dakṣa, Aruṇa, and Siddha are the guardians of the cardinal directions in order;
Viṣṇu, Śeṣa, Ruru, and Caṇḍa are recorded as the lords of the intermediate corners.
Outside, eight gatekeepers are stationed in pairs in the cardinal directions—
two in each direction:
Vakratuṇḍa, Mahādaṃṣṭra, Nīlajihva, and Bṛhacchiras.
One should visualize Krodhekṣaṇa, whose face and eyes are blazing, also known as Kāla,
with the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures upon lotuses in the cardinal directions.
In each of the directions, there is a pair of treasures.
Vyāsa, Kratu, Manu, and Dakṣa are remembered as the four teachers.
The word "in the directions" (dikṣu) is understood to carry over [from the previous verse].
Atri, Dyumant, Kavi, and Kaṇḍa are situated in the intermediate directions.
Desiring to enter from the cardinal and intermediate directions,
