Vaśiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jīmūta, Parāśara, Śāṇḍilaka, Hara, Kānta, and the one renowned as Mitra were also present.
The wise one should cause such a well-constructed maṇḍala to be made;
he should worship it with sandalwood, agallochum incense, and white flowers.
Having offered milk-rice prepared with milk according to one's means,
along with *śrīlatā* flowers, lotuses, white blossoms, and rice grains.
With fruits, flowers, and leaves of the bilva, with blossoms of the nandyāvarta, with jāti and keśara flowers, and those arising from the mallikā and campaka;

*Śrīlatā* is *padminī*; *padma* is a flower, while *kusuma* is the filament (*kesara*). Their separate mention is for the sake of emphasizing their abundance. *Sita*, *puṇḍarīka*, *nadyāvarta*, *tagara*, *keśara*, *baluka*, *mallikā*, and *muhuraka*—one should worship the beloved of the Lord with these and the seed-syllable of Śrī as appropriate.
Outside, one should worship the eight gatekeepers situated in the directions, and the twelve stationed [within].
He has a curved trunk, great tusks, a blue tongue, and a massive head;
he has a wrathful gaze, a radiant face, blazing eyes, and is also known as Kāla (Time).
Visualizing the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures upon lotuses in the cardinal directions,
one should remember that Vyāsa, Kratu, Muni, and Dakṣa are the four preceptors.
And the Śaktis [should be worshipped] with their respective mantras; this is the rule prescribed for every instance. This ritual should be performed only in the morning, never in the afternoon.
Having thus worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed rite, together with Śakti and the other attendants,
one should perform circumambulations, prostrations, recitations of hymns, and so forth.
One should recite the Śrīsūkta and other Vaiṣṇava hymns.
The Śrīsūkta is well known, beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāṃ hariṇīm" and so forth; the "other hymns" refer to the Puruṣasūktas.
Having thus completed the ritual worship according to the rules, one whose mind is focused on no other [should proceed].
One should present a cow, an inviolable animal, and a water-pot to one's teachers.
"A cow, an inviolable animal" means a bull (*vṛṣa*) and a milch-cow (*dhenu*); the meaning is that one should present both a bull and a cow.
Furthermore, there are vessels filled with parched grain and five vessels filled with sesame seeds.
A woman may offer vessels filled with turmeric powder;
one should give gold to a householder and food to the hungry.
[389] Then, having saluted the preceptor who bestows knowledge, the wise disciple should request him, saying: "Grant knowledge to me who have sought refuge."
Having been thus previously honored in the presence of the deity,
the teacher should impart the vidyā to that disciple who is observing the vow.
Discipline is the cause for attaining knowledge;
it has been correctly explained by me, O Brahmin, by which one reaches the highest state.
"The highest state" means the supreme condition.
Whether one seeks to attain high family prosperity through knowledge, or the supreme state of the Supreme Person— thus,
by the power of this second observance...
Having attained the knowledge of the Self, he goes to the Supreme.
Thus ends the Vidyāvrata as declared in the Garuḍa Purāṇa.
On the second day of the bright fortnight, one should offer a meal of salt to the Moon;
upon completion, the giver of a cow goes to the abode of Śiva by means of a Brāhmaṇa.

The grammatical construction is: "One should give salt-food to a Brāhmaṇa. Here, Soma is understood to be the deity, as indicated by the statement, "And this is remembered as the Soma-vow of the gods. This refers to the Soma-vow mentioned in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "At the end of the Kalpa, this is remembered as the Soma-vow of the King of Kings (Soma)."
Puṣkara said: On the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, having bathed with water from the horns of cows,
and having put on white garments when the sun has risen, one should approach that deity.
Having performed the worship of the young moon with perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
as well as with lamps, incense, prostrations, and an abundance of food.
Having worshipped the Moon with yogurt, fine rice, molasses, and salt,
as well as with offerings to the Brahmins;
On the second lunar day, one should perform worship with the name-mantra while the moon is in the form of a crescent; one should continue this practice as long as the moon has not set.
One should take food consisting mostly of cow's milk products and spend the night lying on the ground.
O best of the twice-born, when the year is thus completed, during the month of Soma—

"In this manner" means that every month on the second day of the bright fortnight, one should perform the worship of the Sun and the Moon according to the prescribed rite. "Saumya" refers to Mārgaśīrṣa. Having performed the worship of the young moon according to the specific traditional injunctions, [one should give] two garments, a jar of liquid, and gold to a twice-born man.
Having given [the gift] with devotion as before, one shall become a fulfiller of the vow.
One should perform worship and offer food. Regarding the commencement of the vow, "cow-products" refers to milk and the like.
By means of this vow, the knower of dharma thus dispels disease;
likewise, O best of men, he attains good fortune and nourishment.
He attains his single desired object,
as well as supreme fame and abundant dharma; through that practice, he attains all desires.
In this way, either a man or even a woman attains it.
Thus ends the Ārogya-dvitīyā-vrata from the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Both Puruṣa and Prakṛti are proclaimed to be the entire universe.
Everything is of the nature of Agni and Soma; thus it has been proclaimed.
Vāsudeva and Lakṣmī are proclaimed to be those very two;
on the second day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one who has fasted and conquered his senses [should worship them].
A man should worship Vahni with the *Puruṣasūkta*.

The phrase "having fasted" (*sopavāsaḥ*) means that having observed the fast on the first lunar day (*pratipad*), he should worship Vahni on the second day; for it is prescribed later that his meal shall consist of milk and ghee.
[He should worship] with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and an abundance of food.
O knower of dharma, one should worship Lakṣmī and the boon-granting Lord Hari in the water,
and likewise worship that best of men with the Śrīsūkta.
Having caused a man to carry Harisoma, a fire, and a water-pitcher, one should worship Agni and Vāsudeva together upon a single [seat].
One should give gold, silver, or copper as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
A wise man should sustain his life with milk mixed with ghee.
"Prāṇayātrā" means the maintenance of life.
Having performed this vow for one year and having fasted properly,
one is liberated from all sins and finds the means to liberation.
[392] He obtains his desired pleasures, as well as meritorious worlds and the entire earth; moreover,
he who is deformed gains beauty, and he gains the most excellent speech.
As well as Yaśas, the foremost, and his principal sons.
Thus ends the vow of the second day of the Prakṛti-Puruṣa, as declared in the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The two Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, are celebrated as the Nāsatyas.
These two alone, O King, are proclaimed in the world as the lords of the sun and the stars.
Since the two Aśvins are celebrated as those who delight in traveling by horse,
one should observe a fast and restrain the senses on the second day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
One who is self-restrained and pure should worship the two Nāsatyas, the physicians of the gods,
by offering perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
Having fashioned their forms, a person should worship the two Nāsatyas;
for the form of the Nāsatyas was described by Viśvakarman:
"The two divine physicians should be depicted with two arms and mounted on horses."
Divine medicinal herbs should be placed in their two right hands.
O twice-born ones, two books should be made and displayed on the left arm;
likewise, one should offer a garland of lamps for them, especially at night.
He should give both gold and silver as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins;
then, having worshipped that pair of Viṣṇu there for a year, he should proceed.
He becomes possessed of radiant splendor and is born indeed with keen vision;
he should sustain his life with curd mixed with clarified butter.
Having performed the Netra-vrata for twelve years, one becomes a renowned lord of the earth;
thereafter, he becomes handsome and a crusher of the hosts of his enemies.
Delighting in the Dharma, he was the foremost among the assembly of kings.
Thus ends the Netra-vrata from the Viṣṇudharmottara.

Thus concludes [this section] in the Caturvargacintāmaṇi composed by Śrī Hemādri— the venerable Hemādri, who is the sovereign of all faculties, an expert in all branches of knowledge, and the illustrious Great God (Mahādeva) among the great kings.
In the section on Vows (Vratakāṇḍa), the second-day vows [394].
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Now, the third set of observances:
having undertaken creation for the benefit of others, one should maintain an equal vision toward all beings everywhere.
The virtuous Hemādri has compiled this collection of desired rites for the third-day vows, as observed in the Ākhyāta Purāṇas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Kṛṣṇa, why have you not proclaimed to me this triad of third days (tṛtīyā)— occurring in Caitra, Bhādrapada, and Māgha— which bestows beauty, good fortune, and happiness?
Am I devoid of devotion, or have I strayed from the path of the Three Vedas? This is well known throughout the world; for what reason has it been concealed?
Kṛṣṇa said: It is my conviction that you are skilled in dharma and artha and are omniscient;
therefore, because this vow is world-renowned, it was not explained to you by me.
If you have the inclination to listen, O joy of the Kurus, then let it be heard:
who else in this world is a listener to me equal to you?
Jayā and Vijayā, the two attendants of Umā, arrived;
questioned by the daughters of sages who desired their cherished fruits, he spoke.
Indeed, for you who always know the mental fluctuations of the Goddess,
by what vow and fast, and on which day, did Pārvatī [perform her penance]?
"O fair-faced one, she attains satisfaction when worshipped with certain mantras.
Having heard those words of theirs, Jayā spoke with respect:
Listen, for I shall describe the vow accompanied by festivals, which is delightful to men and women and bestows the fruit of all desires.
On the third lunar day of the month of Caitra, having first performed the cleansing of the teeth,
one should undertake the observances of fasting with a spirit of devotion.
Even while observing a fast, she may wear collyrium, betel with areca nut, vermilion, and red garments; this is the supreme means for ensuring one is not widowed.
A widow should perform the rite of worshiping the Noble One according to the path of the ascetics, and a maiden at her own will; hear now the procedure for this.
One should have a beautiful cloth-canopy made with silken cloths and fine fabrics,
perfumed with the fragrance of flowers, and adorned with auspicious ornaments.
With coral garlands hanging and strung, with a divine canopy spread within,
with full water-jars set out, and with virtuous brahmins seated upon the pedestals.
One should have a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) made in front, measuring one cubit and provided with a girdle;
for, having bathed there, become pure, and put on two clean garments—
Having worshipped the gods and the ancestors, one should then proceed to the temple of the Goddess;
having honored Gaurī, who is beloved by the Lord of Cows, with her eight names.
With the eight names to be mentioned [hereafter], [one should worship] those beloved by the Lord of Cows (Śiva) and beloved by the Bull-bannered One (Śiva),
having anointed them with saffron and with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood, using flowers produced at that very time which are swarming with bees attracted by their fragrance.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the consecration with excellent incense:
"Pārvatī, Lalitā, Gaurī, Gāyatrī, Śaṅkarī, Śivā."
This group of eight names is always dedicated to Umā Satī,
[offered] with sweetmeat balls (laḍḍūka), sugar-coated sweets (khaṇḍaveṣṭa), guṇaka sweets, and siṃhakesara.
One should provide various kinds of pure foods prepared with ghee, such as those made with soma, alaṃkā, sugarcane juice, curd-rice, and cakes.
One should worship Umā with pleasing food offerings that are dear as life to her vision,
[using] *siṃhakesara* flowers whose forms are curled like the mane of a lion,
as well as coriander, cumin, *bhavya*, saffron, salt, and molasses.
One should place safflower, sugarcane stalks, and turmeric in front.
The excellent and auspicious fruits are the coconut, the orange, the citron, the pomegranate,
the pumpkin, the cucumber, the round fruit, the wood-apple, and likewise the jackfruit.
"Round" means having a circular shape and not over-ripe. "Trapusa" is the cucumber fruit; "dadhittha" is the wood-apple (*kapittha*).
Then, one should place other fruits that have appeared in season before [the image], together with a collection of mechanical devices, mortars, stones, and winnowing baskets.
One should offer to Bhavānī collyrium for the eyes, an applicator stick, a tool for manicuring the nails,
a stainless mirror, and a bell.
Having worshipped with devotion and according to one's capacity the Goddess, the beloved of Śaṅkara, with the sounds of conchs and trumpets and the resonance of auspicious songs;
Then, at the time when the sun has set, the maidens, filled with joy, should perform their bath with fresh water-jars for the increase of their good fortune and prosperity.
The term "maidens" (*kumāryaḥ*) is an elliptical designation for those who observe the vow. At the end of every watch (*yāma*), bathing and the worship of the Goddess should be performed;
it is highly recommended that the fire-oblation (*homa*) be offered with sesame seeds and clarified butter while reciting those very names.
Seated in the lotus posture, the virtuous woman, with that very same wet garment,
should pass that night intent upon a single drop of water from Gaurī’s mouth.
Some sing with great joy, some dance with delight,
and some relate stories centered on virtue, pleasure, and wealth.
And some women with slightly arched brows dance before the Goddess, in harmony with song and rhythm, neither arrogant nor confused.
Hara and Gaurī are pleased by dance; they are pleased by song;
or else all the inhabitants of heaven are gratified by sincere devotion.
Betel, saffron, and flowers should be given to the married women who keep watch; however, for others, it is forbidden.
She should spend that night with her female friends, accompanied by actors, parasites, soldiers, servants, goads, spectacles, festivals, and those skilled in song and dance.
Thus, having bathed at the time of dawn and having worshipped Pārvatī, he should,
according to his means, ascend the scale while adorned with garments and ornaments.
One should weigh oneself with sugar,
or with white salt; or else, according to one's capacity, with saffron, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
And some wise men even desire the gift of mountains.
In this very manner, with the mantras for the sacrificial pit, the pavilion, and the ritual materials,
she weighed herself against salt and molasses right there.
By some supreme power, her good fortune has been rendered incomparable;
having thus prostrated before the Goddess and asked for her forgiveness, one should then enter the house.
Having addressed the brahmin couple, and having honored them with garments and ornaments as well as fed them, he should also give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Whatever is most desired by oneself— be it a bed, a vehicle, clothing, ornaments, or cattle— all that one should offer to them.
Some desire betel-leaf— golden, with jeweled fruit, and sprinkled with powdered pearls—
to be given to their circle of female friends.

In place of the leaf, gold; in place of the leaves, gems; in place of the betel nut, pearls—such betel should be given to the circle of female friends. Having fed the newly married woman with food that is not sour and is predominantly sweet, she herself should eat together with her own kinsmen and relatives.
And whatever beautiful offerings, such as food presented before the Goddess,
one should take all of that to every house, distributing it with an untiring mind.
[399] One who performs the divine *dantavāyanaka* rite shall thereafter have accomplished all that was to be done.
In common parlance, *vāyanaka* is called *vāyana*.
Indeed, this ritual performed in the month of Bhādrapada bestows all forms of happiness.
And according to the rules for the seven grains, one should worship Umā while she is situated in a winnowing basket;
the word "winnowing basket" (sūrpa) is to be understood as standing in the place of the full water-jar (pūrṇakalaśa).
Since cow’s urine is to be consumed, she is therefore designated by the name "Cow’s Urine" (gomūtra).
Listen to me regarding the special observance on the third day of the month of Māgha:
having performed everything previously mentioned, at dawn, upon a bed of barley;
Having established [the deity], one should worship Umā along with her son with *kunda* flowers;
for this reason, the fourth day is called by the name *Kunda*.

Having performed everything previously mentioned on the third day, "at dawn" means that on the fourth day one should worship Umā together with her son and accompanied by Vināyaka. As for the form of Umā, O Great King, it should be auspicious, seated upon a white throne, made of gold, and holding a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
And Vināyaka should be fashioned with an elephant's face and four arms;
these three [observances] on the third lunar day have been described to you as granting all desires.
Just as it was formerly proclaimed by the daughters of the sages through their victory,
so too does some woman perform this auspicious vow.
Endowed with beauty and good fortune, she who dies is honored in heaven;
O Bhārata, no woman in her family shall ever be unfortunate.
[400] Neither a son nor a servant shall be ill-behaved, nor shall there be any obstacle;
neither poverty nor disease shall arise in that household.
There that woman, radiant as polished gold, shall take her delight;
and other women as well shall practice the vow with the approval of the Brahmins.
Having worshipped the reciter with devotion through ornaments, clothing, and other offerings,
they shall become endowed with various forms of happiness, their desires unfrustrated.
They will come to pass, O best of the Kurus, eldest of the lineage; homage be to you!
In Māgha, she has a footstool adorned with highly precious gems;
in Caitra, her limbs are anointed with heaps of various flowers;
and in Nabhasya, she consists of fresh young grass grown by the sun.
Having fully worshipped the beloved of Śambhu, women attain power.
Thus ends the vow for the third lunar day of the months of Caitra, Bhādrapada, and Māgha from the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"What is the use of speaking much here, or with a long string of syllables?"
Listen now to the account of the single, imperishable third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha.
Whatever bathing, recitation, fire-offering, Vedic study, libation to the ancestors,
or gift is performed there, all that shall become inexhaustible in this world.
This is the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga; therefore, it is called Yugādi.
It pacifies all sins and bestows all happiness.
[401] Long ago in Mahodaya, O Pārtha, there was a merchant named Sunardhana;
he was pleasant-spoken, truthful in conduct, and a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins.
Although he was preoccupied with his household affairs, his mind remained fixed solely on the recitation of meritorious stories;
by him, the third lunar day joined with Rohiṇī was heard being proclaimed.
When it is conjoined with Mercury, then it yields very great fruit;
whatever is given on that day indeed becomes inexhaustible.
Having heard this, he offered libations to the ancestors and the gods in the Ganges; then, returning home, he brought water-pots filled with food and water.
In the waters, [he should place] large jars filled with pure water,
as well as barley, wheat, and chickpeas, along with parched grain flour, curd, and boiled rice.
The merchant, being pure and with a purified mind, gave to the Brahmins, according to his ability, products made from sugarcane and milk, along with gold.

He stood for as long as it took to fill jars with water and food— jars filled with water from the midst of the water, not with water drawn out— even though he was being restrained by his wife, whose mind was attached to her household duties; and she, realizing that everything is perishable, remained standing there.
O Pārtha, with his mind attached to the Dharma, after a long time he passed away while recollecting Vāsudeva.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he was born as a Kṣatriya in Kuśāvatī;
and his prosperity, endowed with righteousness, became inexhaustible.
He performed great sacrifices accompanied by excellent gifts for the officiants,
and he constantly gave away cows, gold, and other such gifts day and night.
He enjoyed pleasures according to his desire, gradually satisfying the poor and the blind;
nevertheless, his wealth remained inexhaustible and did not undergo depletion.
Whatever wealth is given on the third lunar day with faith, even in the absence of material resources—this has been fully explained to you; now hear the ritual procedure for this occasion.
Having reached the third lunar day (Tṛtīyā), having bathed and offered libations to the deities,
one should then take a single meal and worship Vāsudeva.
Water-pots with golden handles, along with cooked rice and all kinds of flavorful juices—
all types of grain suitable for the summer season are highly praised as gifts in this regard.
One should indeed give gifts of umbrellas, vehicles, cows, land, gold, and clothing;
whatever else is most dear to oneself, that should be given without hesitation.
All this has been told to you; what else do you wish to hear? There is nothing that remains untold for me; may it be well with you, O sinless one.
On this lunar day, what is offered in sacrifice or given in charity does not reach its destination;
therefore, the sages have declared this third day "Inexhaustible" (Akṣaya).
Whatever is performed by men on this day, dedicated to the gods and the ancestors, [becomes inexhaustible].
And all that, O Bhārata, descendant of Bharata, is indeed inexhaustible.
Thus ends the Akṣayatṛtīyā vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "By what dharma, by what vow, and by what observance for women..."
Great good fortune arises, as well as many auspicious sons.
[403] Wealth, grain, gold, as well as clothing and ornaments,
and constant non-separation from her husband, sons, and friends.
Tell me correctly, O Kṛṣṇa, for your compassion toward me is indeed great.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pārtha, I shall proclaim the most excellent of vows;
by performing which a woman becomes fortunate and gives birth to many children.
Endowed with wealth, grain, gold, and so forth, as well as female and male servants,
she performed the Umā-Maheśvara vow for the sake of the welfare of the world, together with Pārvatī.
O Pārtha, it was declared of old, yet even today it has not become famous on earth;
[it occurs] on the third day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa for those who are composed in mind.
Having observed the fast, O Indra among kings, and being deprived of all enjoyments,
one should wrap Śiva in a white cloth and Ambikā in a red one.
Afterwards, the woman, imbued with a spirit of devotion,
should burn incense and feed the devotees of Śiva and Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the devotees with devotion and without deceit. Having observed the fast as vowed,
and having bathed and worshipped Lalitā, who dwells upon half of Hara’s body, one should proceed.
Having performed singing, instrumental music, and so forth, and having rested for a moment upon the ground.
Then, at the time of dawn, having bathed in natural water and put on white garments, a woman should utter this speech:
Homage, homage to you, O Lord of Gods, who bear Umā as half of your body;
O Mahādeva, homage to you, who dwell in half of Hara’s body.
Having placed Śiva in her heart, the Goddess should mutter [the mantra] until she returns home;
thereafter, she should worship the Lord Īśāna with flowers produced in season.
With the Goddess situated on the left side and Maheśvara on the right, she,
intent on meditation, should burn incense with guggulu in the fire.
Various kinds of food offerings (naivedya) cooked in ghee should be presented according to one's capacity;
one should indeed perform the Vaiśvadeva rite well-prepared with sesame seeds and clarified butter.
Then, having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should eat the sacrificial oblation while restraining speech;
thus, for twelve months, one should worship the two Maheśvaras.
Then, with a joyful inner self, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana);
one should fashion Śiva out of silver and likewise Umā out of gold.
Gaurī, adorned with all ornaments, is mounted upon a bull;
having anointed Śiva with sandalwood paste and Pārvatī with saffron.
Thereafter, one should worship with fragrant and most beautiful flowers;
then, having performed a circumambulation, one should utter this mantra:
May the two deities Umā and Maheśvara, the grandfathers of all the worlds,
be forever well-pleased with me through this vow.
Having spoken thus to the Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and conquered anger,
one should devotedly announce the vow to him, or to a reciter endowed with virtuous qualities.
Having thus performed this vow with her mind dedicated to Maheśa,
the woman goes to the supreme abode where the Goddess, beloved of Śiva, resides.
There she shall dwell for as long as fourteen Indras [reign],
surrounded by Apsarases and likewise by Kinnarīs.
When he attains human status and is born into a pure family,
O King, he enjoys happiness through sons, grandsons, daughters, and so forth.
Upon death, she goes to the city of Śiva and rejoices together with Śivā.
[One should worship] Umā made of gold and Maheśa consisting of a silver mass,
and those two, seated upon a beautiful bull made of silver.
Having performed this worship, enveloped in a pair of red and white garments,
a woman becomes one who is not widowed and is endowed with the happiness of her children.
Thus ends the Umāmāheśvara-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Many [observances] have been proclaimed for the third days of the bright fortnight."
Declare the vow of immediate succession (ānantarya-vrata), which is joined with both [the previous two] as the third.
For the welfare of those who observe vows and disciplines, and especially for women,
there should be offerings of food and the ritual tasting of names, performed in various ways month after month.
Kṛṣṇa said: Listen to the Ānantarya-vrata, which has not been declared even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the other foremost of the gods, and which is unprecedented among all tantras.
O Great King, one should undertake this vow in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa;
one should eat only at night on the second day and observe a fast on the third day.
Having worshipped the goddess Umā in due order with flowers, incense, and other offerings,
one should devoutly present a sugar doll according to one's capacity.
At night, O Brahmin, she should consume curd and sleep alone upon the ground;
at dawn, O King, she should feed a couple according to the prescribed rites.
The attainment of the fruit of the horse sacrifice arises; there is no doubt in this matter.
Likewise, on the third day of the dark fortnight, one who has conquered his senses and observes a fast [attains the same].
One should worship the goddess named Kātyāyanī and offer a coconut;
having consumed milk, one should sleep at night, free from desire and anger.
On the third day of the month of Pauṣa, one who has fasted and subdued his senses should feed a Brahmin couple; he shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
Having worshipped her by the name Gaurī, one should offer *khaṇḍavartī*.
A *khaṇḍavartī* is a food item shaped like a coil made from sugar (*śarkarā*).
Then, having consumed water mixed with *kuśa* grass, one should sleep on the ground with the senses subdued.
Then, at dawn, one should feed a couple endowed with physical beauty.
Having asked his forgiveness and paid him homage, she would obtain the fruit of much gold;
then again, in the month of Māgha, during the dark fortnight, she observed her vows with restraint.

Then, having worshipped the Noble Lady by name, one should offer *svādyaka* (edible offerings such as betel-leaf and the like). Having obtained honey, one should sleep at night, abstaining from all sensual enjoyments.
Having fed a married couple, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In the same manner, during the month of Phālguna, she who is pure in her vows and observes a fast should worship the goddess named Bhavyā and then offer a conch with water;
having consumed sugar, she should sleep at night free from envy.
Having fed a couple at dawn, one obtains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice;
this occurs again on the third day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, O Bhārata.
Having worshipped Viśālākṣī, she should offer *pūrikā* cakes;
having consumed rice-water, the wise woman should sleep at night.
One should feed a married couple in the morning; one shall obtain the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
On the first third-day of Caitra, being pure, having bathed, and with senses subdued, [one should perform this].
Having worshipped Śrī by name, one should offer *vaṭaka* sweets;
then, having consumed a *bilva* leaf, one should sleep, intent on meditation.
Then, at the clear break of dawn, by worshipping that very couple of brahmins and prostrating before them, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Then, on the third day of the dark fortnight of Caitra,
having fasted properly and worshipped the goddess named Kālī, she should consume flour and sleep at night.
Having offered cakes as an oblation, one should then recount the auspicious story of his birth;
by feeding a married couple with devotion, one obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Thus, having fasted during the month of Vaiśākha with her senses subdued,
she should worship the goddess Caṇḍikā and offer honey-based preparations.
Having prepared *madhukapūraṇapūrikās* with honey,
and having consumed *śrīkhaṇḍa* at night, one should sleep on the ground before the Goddess.
Having fed [the deity] and offered gifts, one obtains the fruit of the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow.
Likewise, on the third day of the dark fortnight, fasting and free from envy,
she should worship Kālarātri with delightful flowers and incense.
Having given barley gruel enriched with jaggery and having scattered sesame seeds, one should sleep at night;
in the morning, a couple should be fed, and one shall obtain the fruit of the *atikṛcchra* penance.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having fasted and observed her vows,
she should worship Skandamātā and offer Indrajyoti.
Having meditated upon the Goddess, one should cause [the recipient] to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sleep during the night;
in the morning, having fed the couple, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a daughter in marriage.
When the month of Āṣāḍha has arrived, on the third lunar day, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
one intent on devotion should worship the goddess named Yaśodharā.
One should drink *karambhaka* as an offering at night with water from a cow’s horn;
*karambhaka* is barley meal mixed with curd.
By feeding a couple in the morning, one obtains the fruit of a gift of land.
Likewise, on the third day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the goddess named Kuṣmāṇḍī;
one should offer before her parched grain flour mixed with sugar and clarified butter.
Having sipped water from a water-pot, one should sleep on the ground before the Goddess;
at dawn, having fed a couple, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
Then, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should observe a fast and worship Caṇḍaghaṇḍā;
there, one should offer boiled grain as the food offering and drink water infused with flowers at night.
O King, at dawn, one should devotedly feed a Brahmin couple with *kulmāṣa*— grains of grain that are half-boiled. One obtains the fruit of saving the lives of the ignorant twice-born.
In the same way, on the third day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the goddess named Rudrāṇī and offer divine *siddhapiṇḍas* as a food offering (*naivedya*).
Siddhapiṇḍas are roasted barley flour made into balls.
Having eaten oil-cake, one should sleep at night free from envy;
by honoring a Brahmin couple, one obtains the fruit of both sacrificial rites and charitable works.
Likewise, having fasted on the third lunar day at the beginning of the month of Bhādrapada,
one should worship Kamalāmayī with various kinds of flowers and sacrificial offerings.

Then, having consumed the *karṇāvarta* offering of the Goddess—which is smeared with *palala*—and having sipped fragrant water, she should sleep with a joyful mind. *Karṇāvarta* refers to food of a specific shape; *palala* is ground sesame.
Having fed a couple at dawn, one obtains the fruit of gifting an entire village;
likewise, on the third day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the goddess Durgā.
One should offer to the Goddess a *nandīphala* fruit filled with molasses and clarified butter;
having consumed cow’s urine, one should sleep with a tranquil mind. (Note: *Nandīphala* refers to the fruit of the *nandīvṛkṣa* tree.)
Having fed a couple at dawn, one shall always obtain the fruit of a Satra sacrifice;
and in the month of Āśvayuja, one should worship Nārāyaṇī with devotion by name.
Having observed a fast,
she should offer sweetmeats made of sugar as an oblation (*naivedya*).
Having consumed [the remains], she should apply red sandalwood [paste] and sleep that night before the deity.
Having fed a brahmin couple at dawn, the devoted wife obtains the fruit of providing water-stations on a path devoid of water in the heat of summer.
Likewise, O Kṛṣṇa, on the third lunar day, one should worship Svastitāmrā and offer as an oblation boiled rice with sugar.
Having consumed these kusumbha seeds while remaining self-restrained, one should sleep;
then, having fed a couple in the morning, one attains the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
On the third day of the month of Kārttika, one should worship her by the name Svāhā;
one should prepare milk-rice (pāyasa) with ghee, sugar-candy, and other ingredients as an offering.
Having conquered anger, she should sleep at night after drinking water mixed with saffron;
in the morning, having fed the couple and prostrated before them, she should ask for their forgiveness.
In an extremely difficult year, one shall obtain the fruit of the Navāhnika rite;
likewise, on the third day of the dark fortnight, she who has observed the vow and fasted [attains it].
Having respectfully informed his own guru, who is an expert in the meaning of the treatises on Dharma,
he should then draw a nine-naved mandala that bestows boons.
One should have an image of the god Śiva made of gold together with Umā;
pearls and sesame seeds should be placed by them in the eyes.
One should place coral upon the lips and earrings on the ears;
for the god, one should provide a sacred thread, and for the goddess, a brilliantly shining necklace.
Having anointed the goddess, who wears red garments, and Maheśvara, who wears white clothing,
with sandalwood paste, one should worship them with flowers and incense.
Having worshipped the maṇḍala, the preceptor should then perform the fire sacrifice (homa);
therein, he should devoutly worship the goddess named Aparājitā.
Having consumed honey and water, one should keep a vigil at night,
accompanied by festivals such as the Jaya festival, made enchanting with the sounds of lutes and flutes.
It was exceedingly beautified by the sounds of auspicious songs and spectacles,
and by betel, food, vermilion, flowers, saffron, and lamps.
Having thus celebrated the festival, well-adorned and honored on all sides by her circle of friends, she should pass the night free from envy.
Then, at the clear dawn, having performed the auspicious rites of consecration and having prepared a new mattress provided with a ball and other such items, she remained there.
Having extracted the deity from the maṇḍala, one should place him upon a couch;
it should be adorned with canopies, banners, garlands, and the splendor of a water-pot and a mirror.
Having adorned it with flowers and perfumed it with guggulu incense,
one should devoutly feed couples before it according to one's desire.
One should gratify them with various kinds of food and drink, with cooked meals, and with sweet flavors;
then, having placed prepared betel-leaf and sandalwood paste in their hands.
One should utter this by name before the deity and the preceptor:
"May the beloved of Umā, together with Pārvatī, be pleased with me."
And having purified the remnants, he should then provide [the cow] with food—
a cow that is red in color, of good character, beautiful in form, and yielding excellent milk.
With its two horns adorned with gold, its hooves joined with silver,
provided with a bronze milking vessel, and draped in red cloth;
Abundantly adorned with the beauty of bell-ornaments, anointed with white sandalwood paste,
and worshipped with garlands of flowers, she stands before the God.
Having circumambulated the Guru three times, one should offer everything— along with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, and food consisting of both hard and soft edibles.
Furthermore, having undertaken her vows, she should recite before her guru this hymn to the deity: "Just as Umā and Maheśvara are inseparable and worshipped by the gods,
so may my husband be inseparable from me through abundant prosperity."
Having prostrated with his head upon the ground, he should say to the guru, "Forgive me.
In this way, the supreme Ānantarya-vrata is properly concluded.
Listen to the fruit of merit for that man or woman who should perform [this]:
[he shall be honored] by the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Mahoragas.
Surrounded by the daughters of gods, daityas, and sages,
he sported as he desired in a celestial chariot that moved at will.
Having uplifted the lineage of her husband and her father, she, honored by the immortals and followed by Brahmā and the other gods, goes to the eternal world of Viṣṇu.
Whether it be a man or a woman, they go [to that state]; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
O King, having enjoyed divine pleasures there by the remainder of their merit, they are born on earth as an unconquered sovereign ruler over the whole world.
Or she may be born as the queen of a sovereign king;
just as the goddess Tārā enjoys pleasures together with her husband,
so too does she enjoy them with her own husband, the lord of the three worlds.
Just as Hari enjoys himself at ease with Śacī and Lakṣmī, his consorts,
so too, O lord of men, does he constantly enjoy himself together with her.
O Pāṇḍava, just as Arundhatī dwells in the hearts of sages who reside there, so too does she enjoy good fortune through unceasing continuity.
With whichever husband she performs this supreme vow,
she shall not suffer separation from him for seven lifetimes.
This great vow of immediate retribution has been correctly explained to you;
because you are my devotee and my friend, this supreme secret has been revealed by me.

It should not be given to one who is undisciplined, nor under any circumstances to one who lacks devotion; if it is given to an atheist, a rationalist, or a wicked person, the giver becomes a partaker in the sin.
This third lunar day, which is proclaimed aloud by widows as they hasten away according to a specific rule,
should be observed with due ritual after fasting upon its conjunction at the beginning of the fortnight.
He experiences no difference whatsoever from his sons, friends, and kinsmen.
Thus ends the vow for the third lunar day of Anantarya as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
For what purpose do excellent women worship [the deity] residing in the Madhu tree?
O Blessed One, you tell me that Gaurī is the wife of the Teacher of the World.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Formerly, during the churning of the Ocean of Milk, a Madhu tree emerged;
it was planted here by mortals with honey for the sake of the sages.
Where, honored with flowers and fruits, he serves as an offering of poison for wealth, as a slayer of the multitude of diseases, and as a bestower of good fortune upon women.
Adorned with beautiful clusters of blossoms, she was seen by Lalitā in the forest;
there resided the Great Goddess Pārvatī, the beloved of Śaṅkara.
Vijayā and Jayā, together with Gaṇeśa and the Daughter of the Mountain,
were stationed there and worshipped by the deities with flowers and fruits.
O King, for the sake of fulfilling his heart's desire, he was served with various kinds of foods by Lakṣmī herself,
as well as by Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, and Gaṅgā.
O King, having arrived with Rohiṇī, Rambhā, Arundhatī, and Suśīlā,
these women worshipped Mūlaśaṅkarī.
Being pleased with them, those goddesses, bestowers of boons,
granted their desired fruit to her who had fasted on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
Having bathed and remained in celibacy, on another day thereafter,
she should go to Madhuvana and worship Gaurī with a disciplined mind.
Meditating with this mantra upon the auspicious image of Pārvatī—
her breasts covered by a deer skin and adorned with a crown of matted locks— she remained absorbed in contemplation.
One should worship the Goddess, who is mounted upon a chariot drawn by a cow and intent on meditation upon Rudra,
with perfumes, flowers, lamps, lac, and sandalwood.
With filaments and sweet fluids, joined with gold and rubies,
she is Ambikā, the goddess Ṛṣikā, Mūṣikā, Lalitā, and Umā.
May Gaurī, who delights in the forest of penance, grant me good fortune;
may Kālī, Kāsī, Satī, Devī, Rudrāṇī, Pārvatī, and Śivā likewise grant it.
Bowing with devotion by means of the eight limbs, may she grant me husband and sons;
may they, with ever-pleased countenances, bestow upon me good fortune.
May she grant birth in a family free from widowhood in every lifetime,
remaining immortal within every limb and member of the body at every sacred festival.
"May Gaurī attain good fortune, which possesses pleasant sights, touches, and tastes.
Having uttered this mantra, the woman becomes possessed of wisdom.
And one should honor the auspicious and eminent married Brahmin women with safflower,
cumin, salt, molasses, and ghee.
With various *rāga* pastes, fruits, powders, and delightful, excellent sandalwood;

with various foods, including those cooked with powders; with *rāga* pastes made from flowers and sandalwood—sandalwood scented with *campaka* and other blossoms; with *kāleya*, yellow sandalwood, and white sandalwood;
and with vermilion, well-dyed garments, and various auspicious cloths.
With purifying offerings of yellow-colored cakes made of sesame and rice.
With incense sticks of *aśoka*, with qualities of wicks, with fullness of ghee, and with trees of impurity.
Having worshipped Mahādruma with a special food offering called *aśaukavarti*,
and having performed a circumambulation, one should then give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin.
This vow was proclaimed of old by Kāṃsyāya, O King.
All those who shall practice it will become free from disease;
they will possess beautiful major and minor limbs and will be pleasing to the sight of the world.
Having remained in the mortal world for a hundred years, they shall then go to the auspicious city of Rudra by means of a swan-vehicle resounding with the tinkling of small bells.
Having gone there, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they shall sport for one kalpa;
having returned again to the mortal world, they will become vessels of all happiness.
The noble women should worship the most beautiful Madhuvṛkṣa tree with highly precious offerings, enriched with jewels, saffron, and filaments.
The greedy one longs for the couch, which is celebrated by swarms of bees seeking its sweetness.
Having offered this together with fruit and unbroken rice grains at the Madhūka tree,
a woman here becomes like Gaurī, resembling the God of Love himself.
Thus ends the Madhūka vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, when is the Meghapālī vow ever performed by men?"
What is the meritorious practice to be performed, and what kind of creeper is that said to be?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja,
the Meghapālī [cow] should be given with devotion by women as well as by men.
Those who desire merit should offer [the oblation] with sprouted rice, wheat, and the seven types of grain,
mixed with sesame and rice.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, what kind of creeper is that Meghapālī?
What are its characteristics, and what is its mantra? Tell me this.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: The red vallī creeper with its clusters of blossoms and leaves resembling betel-leaf is found in gardens, but not on paths or in the mountains.
Or, O King, when it is seen arisen in a pure place,
one should worship Meghapāla with fruits, flowers, and likewise with unbroken grains (akṣata).
With dates, coconuts, oranges, pomegranates,
citrons, wood-apples, and the seven kinds of grain that have sprouted;
[417] With *trapusī*, *irvāru*, *cīnaka* balls made from ground sesame,
[a line appears to be missing here],
*trapusa-bālakam*, *irvāru*, *karkaṭī*, and *cīnaka* are well known.
Then, in the first vessel, they [placed] dūrvā grass and curd,
mixed with sesame seeds and rice, along with fragrant sandalwood.
O Bhārata, having performed worship with fragrant substances, jasmine flowers, and even *karkandhu* fruits, one should offer [the gift] with this mantra.
With this, one should reverently recite the mantra declared in the Vedas, "Bhadrā.
And women and Śūdras, O Bhārata, should worship her with a salutation.
Having thus worshipped that Meghapālī,
O tiger among men, a man or a woman attains the supreme goal.

It destroys countless sins, even those born of negligence or from other births— those "born of other births" meaning those not produced by trade, not produced by what is for sale, and not produced by what is unsellable. When worshipped, this Meghapālī grants whatever is desired in the heart.
Having remained there for a hundred years, proud of her good fortune,
that mortal attains the three worlds, and being born again into an excellent family, she achieves the same.
Indeed, that man or woman who, out of fear of hell, offers a gift of fruit to Meghapālī so as to obtain a beautiful body—
whatever deceptive tricks for inducing madness were employed [by her]— [he or she shall surely suffer].
It destroys evils by its own power through the fault of worldly existence.
Thus ends the third vow from the Meghapālīya section as spoken in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I ask about another vow lasting for twelve months."
What indeed is this practice called Lalitārādhana according to the sequence of months?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to that ancient vow as it was [performed] by him,
and to the conversation between Śaṅkara and the Great Goddess, which increases merit.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, which was filled with many flowers and fruits,
the Goddess spoke there to her husband, the Lord of the World.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, for the benefit of the world and for the increase of my own joy,
please explain with great care the supreme vow of the third lunar day."
Indeed, O God, three types of people always worship me with devotion:
those who are unfortunate, those who are powerless, and likewise those who are destitute.
Therefore, O Lord, I ask you in order to alleviate their distress,
so that they may be endowed with happiness, beauty, charm, and excellence.
O best of gods, you have described [the fruits] resulting from sons, good fortune, and floods of wealth;
therefore, please explain to me with diligence that vow which brings happiness to women.
Īśvara said:
On the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, one who is observant of vows,
being composed, should wash his feet, hands, and face.
Having observed the fast and the restraints, beginning with the cleansing of the teeth,
one should go to a river at midday with sesame seeds and auspicious *āmalaka* fruits.
Having bathed and emerged from the water, and having put on two white garments,
one should adorn oneself with fragrant and beautiful flowers, as well as with pleasing substances such as saffron and the like.
O Goddess who are fond of devotion, one should thus worship you with devotion using fragrant substances such as camphor, as well as food offerings such as sugar and other sweets.
Just as a woman named Īśānī, while conversing with delightful songs and instrumental music provided by those endowed with great wealth, caught the water from a water-clock.
One should place a bright copper vessel, filled with water and unbroken grains (akṣata) and accompanied by gold,
before the twice-born, while likewise joining the palms in the añjali gesture.
The twice-born should perform the consecration with that very [substance],
accompanied by mantras, using water purified by *darbha* grass while reciting the supreme meditation on Śiva.
And a woman, meditating upon you and intent on auspicious contemplation,
having abandoned passion and other defilements from afar, shall receive the water with her head bowed.
O Bhadreśvarī, Great Goddess, Lalitā, beloved of Śaṅkara, who has come from Brahmāvarta and is born from the womb of Brahman!
O Mother, you who delight at Gaṅgādvāra and are purified by the waters of the Gaṅgā,
grant me good fortune, health, sons, and likewise all the wealth desired by my mind.
Bestow it upon her; be well-pleased, O Goddess! Salutations, salutations!
This is the mantra for consecration:
Then, having been consecrated with devotion and a joyful heart,
one should give gold to him and have him sip water infused with *kuśa* grass.
Having sipped water and become purified, she should spend the night on a bed of kuśa grass,
meditating upon Īśānī while seated upon a layer of darbha grass.
On the second day, having bathed thereafter and likewise worshipped Pārvatī,
the twice-born should be honored according to one's ability, and a married woman should be fed.
Then, with speech restrained, she should herself eat the remaining food along with her family;
thus, in the first month, she should worship the goddess named Īśānī.
In the second [incarnation] she is named Pārvatī; in the third, the beloved of Śaṅkara;
in the fourth, you yourself; and in the fifth, the mother of Skanda.
The daughter of Dakṣa is remembered as Mainākī in the sixth [chapter],
Lalitā by name in the seventh, and Satī likewise in the ninth.
In the tenth month, the goddess is renowned as the bestower of good fortune;
she is remembered as Umā in the eleventh month and as Gaurī in the twelfth.
Kuśa-grass water, milk, clarified butter, cow urine, cow dung, fruit,
a leaf from a hollow tree, or kadamba, as well as water from a cow’s horn or curd [are the substances for purification].

Having fasted for each month in succession, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as vegetables and the prescribed fast-foods (prāśana), and offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability.
Endowed with faith, she gives to the most excellent of Brahmins,
the reciter, safflower, moist salt, cumin, and molasses.
One should designate the god as being present in the vermilion, the turmeric, and the winnowing basket;
month after month, the mantra shall consist of the syllable "ga" and twelve syllables.
The Goddess [is to be recited] preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and joined with the word "homage" at the end.
"Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Īśānī; oṃ go, obeisance to Pārvatī; oṃ guṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkarapriyā," and so forth.
O Dear One, when these mantras are worshipped, she is pleased by the Brahmins.
Being pleased, I shall grant all desired objects with affection.
When this vow is completed, one should honor a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas,
together with his wife, with perfumes, incense, and other offerings.
"Know the Brāhmaṇa to be Maheśvara and his wife likewise to be Gaurī. Having spoken thus, O Dear One, one should worship the Brāhmaṇas and the couple.
Food accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given, as well as two white garments;
O beloved of mine, red garments should be given to the Brāhmaṇī.
Listen now to the fruit obtained by one who has thus properly observed this vow:
having enjoyed all pleasures, he shall go together with the king.
Having attained the higher and lower worlds for a hundred thousand years,
she rejoices together with her husband, just as Śacī does with Indra.
Having attained human birth once again, she, along with that very husband,
was honored by her mother-in-law in a virtuous family endowed with prosperity, free from all affliction.
And for as long as seven births, she shall not encounter widowhood;
she shall likewise obtain sons, enjoyments, beauty, good fortune, and health.
A devoted wife should conduct herself as one who is dearer than her own life to her husband;
she should listen to the Lalitā-vrata being recited for her devotee.
I have spoken out of affection; she too shall attain good fortune.
That woman among the refined ladies of the mortal world who, having worshipped the worshipful one whose graceful body is worthy of honor,
places upon her head a jar filled with scented water, becomes the most distinguished ornament among them.
Having obtained the Lord of Beings as her husband, she enjoys the earth.
[422] Thus ends the Lalitā-vrata as spoken in the Bhaviṣyottara-purāṇa.
Bhīṣma said:
O Lord, O Great Sage, please describe some vow that bestows the fruits of good fortune and health, destroys adversaries, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Pulastya said: Formerly, when stories concerning the propitiation of Lalitā had begun, the God, the slayer of asuras, spoke thus to Umā.
I shall now proclaim that auspicious [teaching] which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Īśvara said: Listen attentively, O Goddess, for this is likewise a source of infinite merit—
the supreme means of propitiation for both men and women.
In the month of Nabhasya, or Vaiśākha, or again in Mārgaśīrṣa,
on the third day of the bright fortnight, having bathed with white mustard seeds;
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead, mixing together gorocanā, cow’s urine, mustā, cow dung, curd, and sandalwood.
Since it bestows good fortune and health and is always dear to Lalitā,
on the third days of each fortnight, a man or a married woman should wear red garments and white flowers.

In the *Matsyapurāṇa*, the wearing of red garments by the man is prescribed: "On the third day of each fortnight, the man indeed [should wear] two yellow garments" (423). Since the wearing of red garments by the man is thus stated, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between those two for the man.
A widow should indeed wear only a single white garment;
a maiden, however, having put on two fine garments with subtle threads.
Then one should bathe the image of the Goddess with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), then with milk alone,
and likewise with honey, as well as with water scented with flowers.
One should worship with white garments and various kinds of fruits;
one should always perform the worship of Lalitā with coriander, cumin, salt, jaggery, milk, and thickened milk, along with white unbroken rice grains and sesame seeds.
Dhānyaka is coriander; ajā is cumin. Arcā is an image.
One should perform the ritual of gathering [offerings] from the feet upward, fortnight by fortnight, with meditative concentration (samādhi).
"Salutation to Varadā for the feet; salutation to Śivā for the ankles."
Salutation to Aśokā for the shanks; likewise to Bhavānī for the knees;
to Maṅgalakāriṇī for the private parts; and likewise to Vāmadevī for the hips.
Salutations to Padmodarā for the belly; salutations to Kāmaśrī for the chest; salutations to Saubhāgyadāyinī for the hands; and salutations to Śaśimukhapriyā for the arms.
Salutation to Pārvatī, who dwells in the mirror, with a gentle smile;
likewise salutation to Gaurī, and to Sunetrā for her nose and eyes.
To Tuṣṭi, the forehead; likewise to Kātyāyanī, the head.
Homage to Gaurī, homage to Tuṣṭi, homage to Kānti, homage to Śrī.
"Salutations again and again to Rambhā, to Lalitā, and to Vāsudevī"—
this is the mantra for the worship of all limbs.
Having thus worshipped according to the rule, one should draw a lotus in front.
It is endowed with twelve petals and possesses a pericarp made of saffron.
One should place Gaurī in the east, and after that Aparṇā;
likewise, Bhavānī in the south, and after that Rudrāṇī.
One should place the gentle one in the west, then Madanavāsinī;
the fierce Pāṭalā in the northwest, and then Umā in the north.
Having established Lakṣmī, Svāhā, Svadhā, Tuṣṭi, Maṅgalā, Kumudā, Satī,
and Rudrāṇī in the middle, one should place Lalitā upon the pericarp.
In the four corners of the *atardana* [diagram], one should write the eight deities beginning with Gaurī in their respective directions;
on the eight outer petals, one should write Umā and Āmekam (or Emekam) one by one.
The married woman, having caused the sounds of songs and auspicious music to be made, should place [the offerings] with flowers, white unbroken grains (akṣata), and a salutation.
One should worship with red garments, non-red garlands, and unguents;
one should cause excellent vermilion and a garland to be placed upon the head.
Since vermilion, saffron, and bathing are always desired by the Goddess,
one should always worship Gaurī with blue lotuses during the month of Nabhasya.
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should worship the Goddess with bandhujīva flowers; in Kārttika, with śatapatra lotuses; and in Māgha, with great devotion, with kunda flowers.
In the month of Phālguna, one should worship Umā with Sindhuvara or Jāti flowers;
in Kṣetra, with Mālikā vegetables; and in Vaiśākha, with fragrant Pāṭala flowers.

[425] One should worship Umā with *sinduvāra*, *guṇḍīmallikā*, and *mahūvaka* in the month of Jyeṣṭha; with lotuses and *mandāra* flowers in Āṣāḍha; and with *javā* in that same month; then in Śrāvaṇa, one should worship her with *kadamba* and *mālatī* flowers.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, water with *kuśa* grass,
*bilva* leaves, *arka* flowers, barley, and water from a cow’s horn.

Then one should have [the child] consume sesame-water and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in succession. O fair-eyed one, this is declared to be the "first feeding of solid food" (annaprāśana), which should be performed on the third lunar day of every fortnight beginning with the month of Bhādrapada.
One should likewise conceive of the Brāhmaṇa as Śiva and the Brāhmaṇī as Gaurī.
Having fed them, one should honor them with devotion by means of garments, garlands, and ointments;
one should give yellow cloths to the men and saffron-dyed garments to the women.
One should give to a woman parched grain, *ajājī* seeds, salt, sugarcane, and molasses; likewise, one should give a golden lotus to a man.
[One should pray: "O Goddess, just as the Lord of Gods does not depart, abandoning you..."
In that same way, may my husband not go elsewhere after having completely abandoned me.
One should utter: "May Kumudā, Vimalā, Nandā, Bhavānī, Vasudhā,
Śivā, Lalitā, Kamalā, Gaurī, Satī, Rambhā,
and Pārvatī be pleased during the months beginning with Nabhasya."
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed adorned with a golden garland,
along with twenty-four couples, or half that number, according to one's ability.
Or else, one should worship [the deity] at the end of each eight-month period during the Cāturmāsya festivals;
likewise, one should also honor the instructor and then the Guru.
Where the Guru is not honored, all ritual actions there are fruitless;
this third [practice], which was described as being infinite, bestows the fruit of the bliss of a son.
The Goddess is the remover of all sins and the increaser of good fortune and health;
one should never transgress this [rule] through stinginess regarding wealth.
Whether it be a man or a woman, one falls downward through deceit;
likewise, a pregnant woman, a woman who has recently given birth, a maiden, or one who is ill [falls] at night.
When she is pure, she should then have it performed by another while remaining self-restrained;
she who observes this third [day] shall obtain infinite fruit.
She shall be honored in the world of Gaurī for a hundred billion kalpas;
even one who is destitute of wealth should perform fasts for three years.
By means of the ritual procedure for the flower-mantra, she too enjoys that fruit.
Whoever, while dwelling in the world, thus recites or hears this account of the circle of vows of the Daughter of the Mountain,
and even grants his approval, he too shall become divine.
And he is to be worshipped by the Kinnaras and the women of my household.
Thus ends the vow of Ananta-tṛtīyā as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By what means does auspiciousness accrue to women in their homes within the world of mortals?"
[427] Endowed with all necessary utensils, it brings about an increase in happiness and good fortune.
O Kṛṣṇa, tell me of this unsurpassed majesty, which is beloved and free from any rival; be gracious and look upon me with a favorable countenance.
Kṛṣṇa said:
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, variegated with various minerals, Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī: "What virtuous vow have you performed?"
By which you possess such extreme good fortune that you are beloved, O woman of excellent complexion.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, formerly I lived as a maiden in the presence of my father.
There, O Master, I questioned my mother while she sat before me."
"O Mother, tell me of some vow that increases good fortune.
When I had spoken thus, the goddess, my mother, then said to me:
"O blessed lady, perform with diligence the unsurpassed Rambhā-vow,
by which you shall obtain from Śaṅkara the desire cherished in your heart."
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, having bathed and being intent upon your observances,
kindle five fires on your sides— fires blazing with garlands of flames and receiving oblations.
The Gārhapatya, the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Sabhya,
the Āhavanīyaka, and the fifth, the splendor of the Sun— these are the five fires.
Thus, having become the central one among these, remain facing the east,
meditating upon the four-faced one seated upon a lotus.
Bring the Goddess before you— she who has the skin of a deer as her parasol and breasts, who wears matted locks and bark garments, yet is adorned with every ornament.
Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahākāyā, Mahāmanāḥ,
Mahāmāyā, Mahādevī, and Mahāmahiṣanāśinī.
Sarasvatī, the great virtuous one, was proclaimed as the "Vataraṇī" (the Deliverer).
At that time, she became intent on beholding him, permeated by her deep emotion.
Then, the high-souled Brāhmaṇas performed the fire-oblation (homa) in every direction.
Then, worship of the Goddess should be performed with flowers, incense, and so forth,
as well as various kinds of blameless food offerings cooked in ghee.
And one should cause the eight auspicious items of good fortune (saubhāgyāṣṭaka) to be placed before the Goddess:
namely, cumin, cumin seed, safflower, and saffron.
O daughter, the fifth [ingredient] is flat beans; there should be salt, sugar, and molasses.
A flower-garland should be made, scented with perfumes, incense, and other fragrances.
One should remain in the lotus posture until the sun has set;
then, having prostrated before Rudrāṇī, one should utter this mantra:
In the Vedas, in all the scriptures, in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld,
Śiva has been seen and heard of many times, yet never apart from devotion.
You are Śakti; you are Svadhā and Svāhā; you are Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī.
Grant me a husband, grant me a home, grant me sons; homage be to you!
Having thus asked for forgiveness and prostrated again and again before that goddess, he said:
"By your power, grant me a beautiful house, variegated and with many stories."
It was adorned with covered walkways, lotus ponds, and streets; its walls were richly furnished with pillars and arched windows, and its gateways were embellished with jewels.
Adorned with rubies, sapphires, and lapis lazuli,
it should be given according to the rules for a house-donation to a renowned Brāhmaṇa.
Having honored her together with her husband and provided all necessary articles,
bow down and offer that which grants whatever the mind desires.

That food offering (naivedya) placed upon the winnowing basket should be given to the married women; having performed this according to the prescribed rite, one should thereafter ask for forgiveness after honoring the couples with wealth and sweet flavors.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, having been thus instructed, I formerly observed the Rambhā-vrata;
at the conclusion of the vow, I gave an excellent house to Devadatta."
"Lopāmudrā, together with her husband, was honored in this dwelling;
by virtue of that vow, O Lord of Gods, I have obtained you as my husband, O Śaṅkara."
Standing upon half of my body, I am proud of my beauty and power.
Thus have I related to you that which was told to me by my mother:
"O Blue-throated One, salutations to you, O Śaṅkara, remover of my distress!"
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O son of Kuntī, this very rambhā-vrata, which has been practiced by me since long ago, shall now be performed by women and men on earth; it is well known throughout the world.
They shall obtain a wife, sons, a home, enjoyments, and the prosperity of their lineage;
and for women, beautiful splendor and good fortune, as well as a household life that fulfills all desires.
It increases the beauty and charm of the young, the middle-aged, and the elderly.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, by this dharma of the vow, in the next world one travels in a celestial chariot that fulfills all desires and grants every wished-for object.
Having enjoyed great pleasures in the world of Rudra, O delighter of the Pāṇḍavas,
you shall be born in an auspicious region of the mortal world, abounding in wealth and grain.
O Pāṇḍava, in the enchanting land of Āryāvarta between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, and within a lineage of kings devoted to righteousness.
There is no doubt that he will be born endowed with beauty and good fortune;
likewise, a highly fortunate woman obtains the full fruit in this manner.
By the power of this vow, one shall become devoted to the dharma of Śiva;
having enjoyed vast pleasures, one’s mind shall be focused solely on Rudra.
One who dies here, liberated from karma, shall become an attendant of Rudra.
May there be well-being that removes the fear of worldly existence; this was practiced in the world of men by Gaurī while she resided in her own mother’s abode.
That woman who, devoted to her own duty, observes this vow on earth shall obtain a husband equal to Brahmā, Śiva, and Keśava.
Thus ends the *Rambhāvrata*, consisting of the practice of the five fires (*pañcāgni-sādhana*), as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"I shall now describe the *Rambhā-tṛtīyā*, which destroys all sins."
It bestows the fruits of happiness and good fortune, and wards off all diseases.
It removes all suffering, is meritorious, and likewise bestows sons and grandsons;
it crushes the pride of co-wives and brings about beauty and sovereignty—auspicious indeed.
Formerly told by Śaṅkara out of a desire to please Pārvatī, listen to this,
O King, which is the supreme benefit for all beings.
Purified by devotion, the Goddess should observe the rules of the fast for a full year, having observed the fast on the third lunar day.
I shall perform the breaking of the fast every month on the following day;
may that supreme vow reach its completion for me without obstacle.
"I have come to you for refuge; lift me up from my misfortune.
Having thus formed this resolve according to the prescribed rules, O son of Kuntī, she remained firm in her determination.
With devotion, intent on meditation, having performed her ablutions, and with her senses subdued, a woman— whether at a river, a pond, a tank, or in her home— remains self-controlled.
One should worship Pārvatī by name at night after consuming water infused with kuśa grass;
then, at dawn, one should feed the Brahmins, especially those who are devotees of Śiva.
Having given them salt along with gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
the self-restrained and virtuous woman should feed fair-complexioned women according to her ability.
O King,
she who performs the Pārvatī-vrata according to this ritual procedure shall deliver more than a hundred generations of her lineage; of this there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, one is glorified in the realm of Śiva;
on the third lunar day of the month of Pauṣa, one should worship her by the name Girijā.
One should consume cow’s urine at night and feed the twice-born at dawn;
thereafter, one should cause gold and cumin to be given according to one's means.
One shall dwell in the world of Śakra for a kalpa and thereafter go to the city of Śiva;
on the third day of the month of Māgha, one should worship the goddess named Sudevī.
One should consume cow’s urine at night and sleep at night free from envy;
during the day, one should give gold and a vessel of kuśa grass to a twice-born man.
Having dwelt for a long time in the world of Viṣṇu, one attains the abode of Śiva;
during the month of Phālguna, one should consume cow’s milk at night while reciting the name "Gaurī."
At dawn, one should feed the Brahmins and the married woman according to one's ability;
having given them spices along with gold, one should dismiss them.
Having obtained the fruit of the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices, she shall go to heaven;
O King, in the month of Caitra, one intent on devotion should worship Viśālākṣī.
Having consumed curd, she should sleep; in the morning, she should give gold along with saffron.
Endowed with auspiciousness and good fortune, upon death, she shall go to the city of Śiva.
On the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the goddess named Śrīmukhī;
at night, one should consume clarified butter and again give it to a twice-born man.
Having worshipped both gold and sugar, one should ask for forgiveness;
one obtains all desires and, upon death, shall go to the city of Śiva.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the goddess named Nārāyaṇī with flowers and lamps;
one should consume salt at night and then sleep alone for one night.
Having fed the twice-born devotees of Śiva in the morning as much as they desire,
he should feed the women living in his own household with various kinds of food and edibles according to his ability.
One should offer betel and gold, bowing down to bid him farewell;
one should have him consume ghee at night and again give [gifts] to the twice-born.
Having worshipped with gold and sugar, one should ask for forgiveness;
one obtains all desires and, upon death, shall go to the city of Śiva.
O King, on the third day of the bright fortnight in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
having risen early in the morning and performed the cleansing of the teeth, one should [proceed].
At the time of death, one goes happily to that place where the Goddess and Maheśvara reside,
after having consumed the water mixed with sesame seeds known as Mādhavī during the month of Āṣāḍha.
At dawn, one should feed the Brahmins and give them jaggery mixed with gold;
having enjoyed all prosperity and happiness, one shall become an attendant of the Goddess.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, having worshipped Śrī, one should drink water produced from a cow's horn;
at dawn, having fed a Brāhmaṇa, one should give a gift along with gold and sesame seeds.
Having enjoyed pleasures upon the surface of the earth, he attains Goloka;
likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship her by the name Subhadrā.
Having consumed the juice of bilva leaves, she, observing celibacy, should sleep;
at dawn, she should give it to an eminent Brahmin along with gold and fruits.
Having become the sovereign of all worlds and having enjoyed manifold pleasures,
one attains the abode of Brahmā through the power of this vow.
On the third day of the month of Āśvina, having worshipped the beloved of Śiva,
one should consume rice-water in the morning and feed the Brahmins.
And here a sacrificial fee is prescribed: sandalwood together with gold;
having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, one is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
In the month of Kārttika, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) at night after performing a vigil with musical instruments,
and in the morning, one should feed the twice-born.
O best of the Bharatas, one should adorn those of virtuous conduct along with their wives with garlands, garments, and ornaments, and likewise feed the young women.
Upon its completion, one should have a beautiful golden image of Umāmāheśvara made;
the form of Umāmāheśvara is described in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
On her left side, Vāruṇī should be depicted; Śiva should be made four-armed, holding a rosary, a trident, and a mirror in his hands.
He has one face and three eyes, with his body's left half formed by his beloved;
according to the *Vibhavasāra*, the canopy is made of five colors.
And here a bed is prescribed, provided with all necessary furnishings;
one should also give a milch cow, accompanied by her calf and endowed with good character.
One should offer a soft seat, a white parasol, a water-pot,
divine sandals and shoes, and a pair of white garments.
And a yellow sacrificial thread made of silk,
together with a conch shell and a mother-of-pearl, and a brilliantly shining mirror.
Red cloth with shell-patterns should be given as a garment for the woman;
O King, having installed Umā and Maheśvara upon a copper seat.
Meditating upon Maheśvara, she should perform worship with devotion using various divine,
fragrant flowers, leaves, and fruits.
With food offerings cooked in ghee and adorned with rows of lamps,
and with pumpkins, coconuts, pomegranates, and citrons;
With cumin, salts, safflower, and likewise with saffron,
with well-purified vessels of juices, and with various kinds of songs and instrumental music;
One should worship the Lord of the Gods together with His consort and ask for His forgiveness;
then, having invited a twice-born man who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
O fair-faced one, having seated that best of kings together with his wife, who were anointed with divine sandalwood paste, amidst the resonance of Vedic chants;
Having had him clothed and adorned, one should present everything to him;
the fruit that would arise from doing this in such a manner cannot be described by me.
Endowed with all the aforementioned fruits and well-honored by all the gods,
she who is born again and again in a great auspicious age shall obtain all her desires.
At the end of that, O best of kings, O observer of noble vows, a woman or a man who possesses devotion to Śiva undoubtedly attains union with Śiva.
He too attains that fruit, and not otherwise, as spoken by Śiva;
O best of kings, it was formerly practiced by Rambhā for the sake of good fortune.
Therefore, this [vow] with Rambhā as the third is the supreme bestower of good fortune;
he who am I is that very Lord of Beings (Śiva), and she who is Gaurī—of this there is no doubt.
Thinking thus, O fortunate one, go for refuge to Pārvatī;
she is the beloved of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, and she became known on earth by the name Rambhā, created by me as her third [consort].
Having fasted while consuming the prescribed number of tooth-sticks, a woman obtains many desired fruits.
Thus ends the vow of names as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, who is the goddess called Harikālī on earth?"
Why is she worshipped by women when she resides in moist grain?
What does she grant here when worshipped? Tell me everything, O Keśava.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, listen from me to this divine ancient story.
There was a beautiful maiden, a daughter of Dakṣa, named Kālī.
She was dark in complexion, with the luster of a fresh blue lotus,
and she was given to Tryambaka, the trident-bearing Mahādeva.
She was wed according to the prescribed rites amidst the sounding of conchs and trumpets,
accompanied by the gods who had come on a sacrificial procession and by the chanting of the Brahmins.
Once the marriage had been performed, the Three-eyed Lord sported with the maiden in various ways that increased the delight of the mind.
Then, on one occasion in the assembly of the gods, the bull-bannered Lord,
accompanied by Viṣṇu and Sadāyava, was seated in a beautiful audience hall.
There, the Destroyer of Tripura playfully summoned those who were present—
Kālī, dark as a blue lotus, accompanied by the hosts of the Mothers of the Gaṇas.
Come, come, O Mati! You are Kālī, with a luster like that of crushed black collyrium;
because of your extreme beauty, your form is dear to me, even though you are Death itself.
Having spoken thus, that goddess, ashamed and filled with indignation,
her eyes copper-red from sighing and gasping, spoke in a voice faltering with tears.
The young girl wept with a loud sound and, with her lower lip quivering, said:
"O Lord, why is she who is Gaurī called by the name 'Gaurī'?"
"O Lord, since you have given me this comparison— likening me to crushed black collyrium—
in the assembly of gods and siddhas in the presence of Vāsudeva."
"Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, I shall offer this body as a libation into the blazing fire.
Having spoken thus, Harikālī, though being restrained, was filled with rage.
She released her green-hued luster upon the grassy meadow;
in her wrath, she cast her body into the blazing fire.
Furthermore, she became Gaurī in the home of the King of Mountains;
established as half the body of Mahādeva, she is worshipped by the gods.
That splendor born from her own body which was released by the goddess Kālī onto the grassy meadow became once again the goddess Kātyāyanī, endowed with the power of Māha.
O Pāṇḍava, many such services for the gods have been performed by her;
listen to me as I tell you of the boon granted to her by the satisfied hosts of deities.
And those men or women, especially, who shall worship her who resides in Śāhala as Kālī, the bestower of boons—
Freed from all sins, proud of their happiness and good fortune,
they shall become long-lived, endowed with husbands and sons.
Thus, O Great King, that Gaurī, established as Harikālī among the crops,
is to be worshipped with devotion by means of this mantra.
O Harikālī, born from the name of Hari, beloved of Hari,
