who always abides in the form of grain, salutations to you, the remover of the distress of those who bow before you!
Having thus worshipped that goddess and given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the brāhmaṇa,
one should then dismiss her with this mantra at a beautiful body of water.
"You have been worshipped by me with devotion; go, O Goddess, to the abode of the gods, for the destruction of my misfortune and for the sake of returning again."
Thus, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, whoever— whether a man or a woman intent on devotion— should observe the Harikālī vow every year according to the prescribed rite.
The fruit that one obtains by taking [this] cannot be attained by any other means;
such a person shall live long in the world of mortals, perfectly fulfilled in all desires.
Surrounded by sons, grandsons, friends, allies, nephews, and daughters' sons,
he shall live for a hundred years on this earth enjoying pleasures;
then, at the end of his body's life, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Vīrabhadra, Mahākāla, Nadīśvara, and Vināyaka—
all become gracious and favorable in countenance through the practice of this vow.
Having worshipped the Goddess, the daughter of the Himālaya mountain, known as Harikālī, who holds in her winnowing basket the seven kinds of cultivated grain,
with offerings of food, drink, and the sounds of rising songs and musical instruments;
Human beings attain happiness for a very long time.
Kṛṣṇa said: On the third day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should perform [this rite] on a prepared grassy plot,
having arranged gems, grains, and sprouted seeds.
With dates, coconuts, and likewise with sweet fruits;
with citron, safflower, coriander, and likewise with jambīra fruits.
Having gratified [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, fruits, incenses, and food offerings such as sweetmeats,
and having approached [the image] consecrated with a ruby;
O Great King, she should be worshipped with devotion by means of bells, musical instruments, and the like, with auspicious and divine songs, and with sacred narratives, while reciting this mantra.
Obeisance to her who has arisen from the name of Hari, who is beloved by Hara and Kālī, who always abides in the form of grain, and who removes the distress of those who bow before her.
Having thus worshipped that goddess, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin;
having kept a vigil at night, when the sun has slightly risen in the morning—
[439] At night, she should be led to a body of water by married women;
then, at that delightful pool, one should dismiss her with the mantra itself.
Having been honored by me with devotion, O Goddess, go to the abode of the gods for the destruction of my misfortune and for the sake of returning again.
Thus, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, whichever man or woman devoted to piety performs the Harikālī-vrata every year according to the prescribed rule, [attains the fruit].
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing this, that cannot be attained by any other means;
he shall live long in the world of mortals, highly honored with all his desires fulfilled.
Surrounded by sons, grandsons, friends, allies, nephews, and granddaughters' sons,
she shall live for more than a hundred years, endowed with enjoyments upon the earth.
Then, at the end of the body, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
[there dwell] Vīrabhadra, Mahākāla, Nandīśvara, and Vināyaka.
Through the practice of vows, all become gracious and well-disposed.
Having worshipped the Goddess, the daughter of the Himālaya mountain, known as Harikālikā, who holds seven types of sprouted grain in her winnowing basket,
with offerings of food, vigils, and the rising sounds of song and instrumental music;
Human beings attain happiness for a very long time.
Thus ends the Harikālī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Tṛṇavindu said:
"By means of which vow or observance one attains non-separation [from the Lord]..."
By that means, a woman shall always obtain sons and go to that very state.
[440] And how, O Brahmin, is a widow honored by her husband alone in the next world? Tell me, by what means and with what wealth may she always live in happiness?
Anilāda said:
"The conduct of Umā, the *lalitā-vrata* of Bhavānī,
her birth from Himavat in childhood, and her liberation from Dakṣa’s wrath."
Having seen the great mass of supreme fortune belonging to the noble-souled goddess, Vasiṣṭha described that vow to Arundhatī; listen to it.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Arundhatī, listen to this vow which increases good fortune;
it is the Aviyoga-vrata, which secures for women the state of non-widowhood.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having bathed and being fond of white garments,
she should eat milk-rice at night on the second lunar day after seeing the moon.
Having sipped water and become pure, one should prostrate like a staff before Śaṅkara;
having saluted him with joy and recognized him as the Supreme Lord.

Oṃ! A tree made of udumbara wood, eight finger-breadths in length, auspicious, situated in the northern direction, with its tip intact, possessing its bark, free from blemishes, and firm, should be taken.
Restraining her speech and facing the east, she should chew the tooth-stick;
then, on the second day, with her mind fixed on that vow, she should sleep upon the ground.
Then, having risen during the auspicious hour of Brahmā on the third lunar day, she,
having performed her duties and bathed well, was dressed in white garments and adorned with white garlands.
Having fashioned auspicious images of a man and a woman out of rice flour,
and having placed them in a bamboo vessel, she should worship them with devoted intent.
One should observe the fast, completely abstaining from all enjoyments;
having conversed with heretics and others, one should bathe and avoid them.
Then, O fair-hipped one, at night, having performed worship, celebrated a festival,
and raised the sound of musical instruments, one should observe a vigil there.
Having worshipped those two figures made of flour according to the prescribed rite,
one should cause them to be given, along with gold, to an eminent brahmin at the break of dawn.
O illustrious lady, one should perform this according to one's ability, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
for one should first conceive this Umāmāheśvara rite within one's mind.
The Brahmin, moreover, should cast that flour-made couple into deep water;
when this has been done, he should feed couples who have performed auspicious rites.
Having fed Śiva-devoted twice-born men with sweet food according to one’s capacity,
one should perform [this rite] every month, provided with various kinds of food.
Furthermore, when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived at the end of Kārttika,
I shall proclaim your names according to the sequence of each month.
For the purpose of worship and recitation, and for the sake of attaining the desired goal,
one should [worship] Śaṅkara together with Gaurī during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
One should worship Gaurī or Pārvatī during the month of Puṣya;
and one should worship Bhava and Bhavānī during the month of Māgha.
In the month of Phālguna, one should worship Mahādeva together with Umā;
in Caitra, one should worship the three-eyed Lord and Lalitā.
One should conquer Sthāṇu, accompanied by Lolanetrā, in the month of Vaiśākha;
and one should conquer Rudra, together with Rudrāṇī, in the month of Jyeṣṭha.
O lady of pure smiles, one should worship Paśunātha together with Satī in the month of Āṣāḍha,
and the god Śrīkaṇṭha along with the supreme goddess Subhadrā in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Likewise, in Bhādrapada, one should worship Bhīma together with Kālarātri;
and in Āśvayuja, one should worship Śiva with devotion along with Gaṅgā.
In the month of Kārttika, one should worship Īśāna and the goddess Śivā;
for without [worship] by name every month, the perfection of the vow is not attained.
I shall now fully describe those flowers which one should employ in worship each month, for they indeed bring immediate delight.
First, one should employ blue lotuses; in their absence, one should devotedly employ other pure and fragrant flowers found in the forest.
Karavīra, bilva leaves, kiṃśuka, kuñja-mallikā,
pāṭalī, kadamba, tagara, droṇa, and mālatī.
Aśu, kuṅkuma, droṇa, and kuravaka—

these, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, should be offered with devotion according to the aforementioned sequence throughout the twelve months, out of a desire to do what is pleasing to the Lord.
And so, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should be performed every month;
for indeed, no other purifier is remembered as superior to the pañcagavya.
When the vow has been thus performed, O blessed lady, endowed with devotion to Śiva,
at the end of the year [one should offer] a canopy and a banner adorned with a garland of small bells.
Out of devotion to Śiva, one should offer a bell, a lamp, and a pair of garments;
having heated and anointed it, one should fashion a golden lotus.
According to one's means, a gift should be offered for the satisfaction of the God of gods;
one should place silver and a pair of images before the deity.

Having offered various kinds of food offerings accompanied by song and instrumental music, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Śambhu; then, having bathed, one may go to one's own home.
Having bathed, one should give to the preceptor that pair— a square image of Mahādeva and a triangular image of Umā— along with pearls and other ornaments.
Thereafter, one should feed twelve of the best of the twice-born who observe the vow;
and as many couples as there are, one should honor them with devotion according to one's capacity.
Having caused a beautiful and auspicious Umāmāheśvara image to be fashioned out of gold, measuring exactly one karṣa in weight for each part.

The form of Umāmaheśvara is to be understood as described in the Rambhātṛtīyā-vrata. One should place sixty-four pearls, an equal number of corals, and an equal number of topazes upon a copper vessel.
Having wrapped it with cloth, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
all of this, together with the essence, one should present to the preceptor.
Or else, he may give a substitute for those Brahmins who observe vows or for couples;
if unable to do so, he should give a ransom, avoiding any dishonesty regarding his wealth.
Having given gold and garments, one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness;
[one should also give] forty-eight jars, an umbrella, and sandals.
On that day, he gave all the prepared food along with gold, honored with curds, auspicious water,
and other offerings, without restriction, to the poor, the blind, the deaf, and others.
One should prepare food and drink that is well-prepared and pleasing to oneself;
one should not make it deficient or excessive according to the measure of one's own wealth.
If wealth is not available, one should fulfill [the rite] through visualization;
this bestows non-separation, grants beauty, good fortune, and riches,
bestows long life and sons, fulfills all desires, and grants the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the Aviyoga-tṛtīyā-vrata as declared in the Kālikā-purāṇa.
The Fish [Incarnation] said:
"In the same way, I shall describe another [vow] which bestows the fruit of all desires."
That which those learned in the Purāṇas know as the "Bed of Good Fortune" (Saubhāgyaśayana).
Long ago, when the worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, Mahas, and the rest— had been consumed by fire,
the collective auspiciousness of all those worlds then became concentrated in one place.
And having reached that Vaikuṇṭha, it remained upon the chest of Viṣṇu;
then, O King, after a long time, during the process of creation once again—
In this world enveloped by egoism, yet endowed with both Pradhāna and Puruṣa,
a dispute broke out between the Lotus-Seated One and Kṛṣṇa.
Arising in the form of a *liṅga*, blazing with a fierce appearance,
it rested upon the chest of Viṣṇu, whose body was scorched by it.
By virtue of his good fortune, that which flowed from his chest in accordance with justice took the form of a liquid essence;
yet it did not reach the surface of the earth.
Thrown up into the sky by the wise son of Brahmā,
it was drunk by Dakṣa as soon as it reached his mouth, which caused him to possess beauty and charm.
The great power and energy of Dakṣa Parameṣṭhin was produced;
that remainder fell upon the earth and was born as eightfold.

Sugar-cane, the king of trees (*tavarāja*), *niṣpāva* beans, *ajāji* cumin, the product of cow's milk (*gokṣīra-vikāra*), *kuśumbha*, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and salt as the eighth— this is called the "Auspicious Octad" (*saubhāgyāṣṭaka*).
The most excellent sugar was the king of your [sacrificial] offerings.
That which was drunk by the son of Brahmā, the knower of yoga and knowledge,
likewise became his daughter, who is therefore called Satī.
Transcending all worlds, she was graceful; for that reason she is called Lalitā.
O King, the wielder of the Pināka bow married her, who is the most beautiful woman in the three worlds.
What can a man or a woman not attain by worshiping with devotion her who is manifested solely for the sake of auspicious fortune and who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation?
Manu said:
O Janārdana, tell us how the propitiation of that Mother of the World is performed, and how the ritual procedure for the world comes into being; explain that to us.
Matsya said:
Having reached the month of Vaiśākha, on the third lunar day beloved by the people,
during the forenoon of the bright fortnight, one should perform a bath with sesame seeds.
On that day, it is said, that goddess of excellent complexion, being truly the soul of the universe, was wedded with the marriage mantras.
Together with her, one should worship the Lord of Gods on the third lunar day,
using various kinds of fruits, incenses, lamps, and accompanied by food offerings.
Having bathed the image with the five products of the cow as well as with scented water, one should worship Gaurī together with the Moon-crested Lord.

Although the term "image" (*pratimā*) is mentioned without qualification, a pair of images made specifically of gold should be fashioned for Gaurī and Śiva, because it will be stated later: "One should offer a pair of golden images.
"Salutation to Pāṭalā"—with these words, one should worship the feet of the Goddess and of Śiva;
and having proclaimed "To Śiva," one should worship both the ankles with "To Jayā."
One should worship the pair of thighs with "Obeisance to Triguṇa" for Rudra and "Obeisance to Bhavānī";
the two knees with "Obeisance to Śiva" for Rudreśvara and "Obeisance to Jayā."
Having praised Harikeśa, likewise [one should say] "Obeisance to the Giver of Boons";
to Īśā, Śaṅkaṭī; to Rati, Śaṅkara; and to Śaṅkhaka.
And on both sides of the belly, at the two corners, [one should worship] the wielder of the trident with the mantra "Obeisance to the Trident-bearer";
one should also worship the stomach with "Obeisance to you, Maṅgalā."
One should worship Rudra as the Self of All, and the two breasts as Īśānī;
likewise, one should worship Śiva as the Self of the Vedas, and the throat as Bhadrāṇī.
He should worship Viśveśa with "To the destroyer of Tripura," the two hands with "To the infinite one," Hara with "To the three-eyed one," and the two arms with "O beloved of the fire of time."
One should worship the ornament-holder with "To Saubhāgyabhavana" and Śiva as the ornament-holder; and the face of the Trident-bearer with "To Svāhā and Svadhā" and "To Īśvara."
The two lips, which dwell in the honey of the *aśoka* tree, should be worshipped as the granters of desires;
likewise, Hara should be worshipped for Sthāṇu, and the face for Candramukhapriyā.

The meaning is that one should worship Hara with the mantra "Namo ’rdhanārīśaharam asitāṅgīti nāsikam" (Homage to the half-woman Hara; Asitāṅgī to the nose), and with "Ardhanārīśāya namaḥ" (Homage to the half-woman Lord) [one worships him]. Furthermore, one should worship Lokeśa with "Nama ugrāya" (Homage to the Fierce One) and Lalitā to the eyebrows.
To Śarva [he gave] the slayer of Pura, and likewise to Vāsudevī, Alaka.
"Salutation to Śrīkaṇṭhanātha; one should likewise worship the hair [of the deity].
Likewise, by means of the two mantras for the worship of the locks of hair, one should worship the hair of Umā and Īśa—this is the meaning.
To her who possesses a form both fierce and gentle, salutation to the head; salutation to the All-Self."
Having worshipped Śiva according to the rules, one should place the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka) before him.
One should set out these eight items: ghee, parched grain, safflower, milk, cumin, tavarāja, sugar-cane juice, salt, and coriander.

Because this bestows good fortune (*saubhāgyakṛt*), it is therefore called the "Eightfold Good Fortune" (*saubhāgyāṣṭaka*). In this context, ghee and milk are considered as one item; furthermore, cow's milk is included among the eight because it is mentioned previously in the *Matsyapurāṇa* itself as a modification [of the general term]. *Kustumburu* is coriander (*dhānyaka*). *Tavarāja* is a specific kind of sugar.
Having thus presented all of that before the two, Śiva and Śivā:
O subduer of enemies, having consumed the water from a horn in the month of Caitra, one should sleep upon the ground.
Rising again at dawn, having performed his ablutions and prayers, and being pure,
he should worship a Brahmin couple with garlands, garments, and ornaments.
One should present two golden images endowed with the eight marks of good fortune to a Brāhmaṇa, saying: "May Lalitā be pleased by this."
In this manner, one should always consume [the food] on the third lunar day for as long as a year;
listen to me regarding this specific detail concerning the mantra for the gift at the time of consumption.
Cow-horn water is prescribed for Āṣāḍha; cow-dung for Viśākhā;
Mandāra flowers for Jyeṣṭha; and Bilva leaves are remembered for Āṣāḍha (Śuci).
Having consumed curd in the month of Śrāvaṇa, water infused with Kuśa grass in Nabhasya,
milk in the month of Āśvayuja, and ghee mixed with curd (pṛṣadājya) in Kārttika;
Pṛṣadājya is ghee mixed with curd.
In Mārgaśīrṣa one should consume cow urine, in Pauṣa ghee,
in Māgha black sesame seeds, and likewise in Phālguna the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Lalitā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Bhavānī, Kumudā, Śivā, Vāsudevī, as well as Gaurī, Maṅgalā, Kamalā, and Satī.
And at the time of giving, one should proclaim, "May Umā be pleased," [offering] jasmine, *aśoka*, lotus, *kadamba*, blue lotus, and *mālatī*.
Kulattha, karavīra, bāṇa, amlāna-kuṅkuma,
and sinduvāra are prescribed for all months in their respective order.
The *bāṇa* is the blue *kuraṇṭaka*; the *amlāna* is the *mahāsahā* flower; and the *sinduvāra* is the *nirguṇī* flower.
The *japā*, saffron flowers, *mālatī*, and *śatapatrikā* are recommended when available, as is the *karavīra* at all times.
Having thus observed the fast according to the rules for as long as a year,
a man, or a woman, or a maiden, out of devotion, having worshipped Śiva and Śivā according to their capacity,
should at the conclusion of the vow give a bed equipped with all its furnishings.
Having established a golden image of Umā and Maheśvara along with a bull made of cow-gold upon a hawk-shaped pedestal, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Household utensils, such as pillows and the like; a pair of golden cows, since it is impossible to place the primary [image] upon a bed;
and other pairs of garments and so forth according to one's ability—having honored [the deity] with gifts of grain, ornaments, and cows, and with accumulations of wealth.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth and devoid of pride, one should perform the worship;
he who thus correctly observes the Saubhāgya-śayana-vrata, [attains success].
One attains all desires and enjoys the state of infinity;
performing this, one should practice the renunciation of even a single fruit.
O lord of men, there he attains fame every month,
along with good fortune, health, beauty, long life, clothing, and ornaments.
O King, she would not be liberated for three hundred billion years,
unless she performs the Saubhāgyaśayana vow for twelve years.
Having performed [this] seven or eight times in the abode of Śrīkaṇṭha, he shall dwell properly, being honored by the immortals, for as long as thirty thousand kalpas.
Whether it be a woman or even a maiden, O lord of men,
she too, cherished by the grace of the Goddess, attains that same fruit.
Whoever should even merely hear it, or should give it as a gift, or even apply their mind to it,
shall likewise become a Vidyādhara and dwell for a long time in the heavenly world.
[450] Thus concludes the Saubhāgyaśayana-vrata as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Next, I shall describe the Gaurī-vrata, which increases the good fortune of women.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform the Gaurī-vrata.
Having observed the fast with diligence, one should perform this ritual procedure,
wearing red garments and being free from anger and greed.
On a sacrificial ground measuring one cubit, a fragrant mandala should be prepared;
one should draw a circle with saffron and camphor.
Indu is camphor, and śīta is sandalwood.
In the center of that [array], an image made of gold should be worshipped;
in its absence, however, one made of honey, fashioned by someone in ancient times, may be used.
Or it should be made from red sandalwood according to the prescribed measurements;
or else, she [the image] should be worshipped there for a month with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) according to the ritual rules.
She who consists of the five nectars is born from the five nectars;
she should be worshipped with red flowers, combined with jasmine and campaka,
as well as with trumpet-flowers, oleanders, and red lotuses.
It was adorned with *pārijāta* trees, *mallikā* and *kubjaka* flowers, as well as red lotuses,
land-lotuses, *kiṃśuka*, *sumana*, blue lotuses, and *ketaka*.
Thus she should be worshipped with effort using flowers and other offerings;
one should repeatedly anoint her with camphor and saffron.
One should cause various kinds of jewels, crowns, armlets,
earrings, ornaments, girdles, and so forth to be bestowed here.
Edible offerings should be prepared with care, including vessels of clarified butter,
cool thick milk, and smooth, viscous curds.
Then one should cause to be offered karambha, fresh butter (navanīta), as well as śikhariṇī, pānaka, water, and candrapānaka.
Red garments and the various ritual requisites should be offered first;
furthermore, at the conclusion of the worship, the preceptor himself must be honored with great effort.
Then, providing gold, garments, food, and drink without stinginess regarding wealth,
one should keep a vigil at night and likewise feed young maidens.
I shall declare the names of the goddesses month by month in their proper order,
as well as the specific substances for consumption according to the prescribed sequence.
Gaurī, Umā, Lalitā, Subhagā, Bhagamālinī, Manonmanī, Bhavānī, Kāmadā, and Bhogavardhanī.
One should worship Ambikā, Kṛṣṇā, and Rudrāṇī in sequence. These are for the bright fortnight; now hear likewise for the dark fortnight.
Rati, Dhṛti, Buddhi, Mati, and Puṣṭi are proclaimed;
likewise Prajñā, Medhā, Caryā, Śrī, Raktā, and Kīrti.
Where one may personally observe the vow with five white and five black items,
it is established as beneficial due to incapacity and the absence of other materials.
In that regard, the consumption [of the substances] should be performed according to the very path prescribed by the scriptures.

If the specific pair of substances prescribed for each respective month is unavailable, or if one is unable to consume them because they would cause disease and so forth, then one should consume, in successive order across the twelve months, whatever is available and whatever is beneficial. This is the meaning of the phrase "due to inability" and so on. I shall explain [the substances] month by month, in sequence, during the bright fortnight.
Milk, curd, ghee, cow urine, and water infused with kuśa grass.
Water with bilva leaves, as well as other water with sandalwood,
water with jasmine petals, and indeed lotus filaments.
O Six-faced One, it is taught that Nāgakesara, Lavanga, and Candana [are used] during the bright fortnight, beginning from Caitra.
Now listen to that which is being described regarding the consumption [of the sacrificial food] during the dark fortnight:
one should cause [the practitioner] to consume *balākā*, *kolaka*, and *śatāvarī*.
Vana, laghu, sura, dāru, sārivā, śaṅkhapuṣpikā, śirīṣa,
combined with surabhī, as well as red pigment and pearl.
The twelfth fast, consisting of water for the weight of the body, has been described to you;
thus is known the Gaurī-vrata, which bestows good fortune upon women and grants sons.
This excellent vow bestows long life and health upon women both in this world and the next;
having abandoned this, there is no other vow beneficial for women.
Therefore, with every effort, one should observe the vow of Gaurī;
likewise, [one should offer] collyrium, red cloth, betel-leaf, and saffron.
A mirror, a fan, an umbrella, a seat, an excellent vehicle,
and all household utensils made of gold or copper.
And at the conclusion of the vow, one should diligently give garments and ornaments to the preceptor, as well as to women and young girls.
These should be offered with great effort if one desires one's own prosperity;
thus has this Gaurī-vrata been described along with its secret.
[453] Thus ends the Gaurī-vrata as declared in the Kālottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the third day of the bright fortnight, having fasted and subdued his senses,
he should draw three mandalas with colored powder, each one separately.
Likewise, a person should make the mandala white on the right side;
then he should make it red in the center for Ravi, and similarly white for Dhruva.
Among these, the three steps of Viṣṇu should be worshipped by means of a maṇḍala:
the first step upon the earth, and the second in the solar maṇḍala.
But on the third day, being restrained and pure, one should worship the god Dhruva with the *homamantra*.
O twice-born, the worship is performed with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, as described in the description of the mandala.
The sacrificial mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ param" is thus prescribed.

O best of the twice-born, a woman or a Śūdra should likewise offer unbroken rice grains (akṣata), sesame seeds, and clarified butter into the fire with the mantra "To Trivikrama," using the three combined together.
One should give copper, silver, and gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability,
and one should feed the most excellent Brahmins a meal consisting of the three sweets.
On that day, one should sustain one's life with the three products of the cow;

for on the day of the vow, the practitioner is considered to be fasting by virtue of avoiding all other food. Having fasted on the second day, one partakes of the "three products of the cow" on the third day—where "gavya" refers to curd, milk, and ghee.
Having performed this for three years, at the conclusion of the vow, [one should give] a three-year-old cow.
But by giving a cow to a Brahmin, one shall obtain all desires.
O best of men, O slayer of enemies, his movement becomes unimpeded upon the earth, as well as in the intermediate space and in heaven, even though he be but three years old.
Practicing the Trivikrama vow for three thousand years,
she relinquishes all mental, verbal, and physical [impurities].
O illustrious one, having thus purified all evil,
a man is born into a great and wealthy family, endowed with beauty and riches.
Free from disease, having all his goals accomplished, and being a fulfiller of the three aims of life,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for twelve years after performing [this rite].
There too, he beholds the eternal bestower of boons, the most excellent, the ancient Person who has Lakṣmī as his companion— the omnipresent Lord, unfailing and inconceivable.
The eternal cause for the destruction of suffering.
Thus ends the vow of Trivikramatṛtīyā as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now proclaim the second; listen to the Traivikrama vow.
The earth is the first quarter, and the intermediate space is likewise the next.
[455] The procedure for the third and subsequent [offerings] is to be known as that of the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus.
Vahni is remembered as the lord of the earth, and Anala is the lord of what remains beyond.

Likewise, the Lord of the Quarters and the Sun [bestow blessings] upon you; on the third day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, one who has fasted and subdued the senses [attains] the three steps of Viṣṇu.

Having bathed in the water of the Kālī well at dawn, a man should worship the Fire-god while observing a fast on the second lunar day; "having observed the fast" means he has undertaken the vow of fasting. At dawn—that is, in the morning—he should offer perfumes, garlands, salutations, lamps, incense, and food.
Then, having bathed in the river water when the sun had reached the meridian, [he performed his rites].
Having performed the worship of Vāyu and given parched grain flour (saktu) to a twice-born man,
one should bathe in water as cold as snow and worship the Sun in the evening.
Then, being pure and restrained in speech, he should eat sacrificial food at night;
having thus performed this unsurpassed vow for a year, O King.
Having completed [the rite] in the month of Vaiśākha, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins—copper, silver, and gold, O Yādava; these are the three metals.
Having performed this Traivikrama vow for one year with devotion—consisting of these three items: a pair of garments and a turban—a man [attains his goal].
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled,
traveling by means of a celestial chariot the color of the sun and adorned with garlands of tinkling bells.
By playing the lute and the drum with a brother-in-law who is rich in virtue,
one attains the heavenly world as a bird that travels at will.
Having approached the three desires, one obtains the three boons—
food, long life, and sacred learning— when the one whose banner is Garuḍa is pleased.

Having attained the three steps— the most excellent in the sky of those who uphold the Dharma— which are worshipped by the three types of *kokila* birds and which grant all desires to the destroyer of the Danuja race; [456] he is worthy of honor.
A person proceeds to whatever destination they desire.
Thus ends the vow of Trivikrama on the third lunar day as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O highly fortunate one, I shall describe to you the Traivikrama-vrata.
O tiger among kings, listen as I describe that third [state] to you.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, a man who has properly fasted should perform the worship of the Earth with incense, garlands, and ointments.
One should devoutly give lamps, various jewels,
and vessels filled with seeds along with gold as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
In this manner, the worship of the intermediate space is prescribed during the month of Āṣāḍha;
therein, O twice-born one, a sacrificial fee as well as a pair of garments should be given.
Furthermore, worship of the Sun should be performed in the month of Śrāvaṇa, exactly as before;
in that rite, one should cause an umbrella and a pair of sandals to be given as a sacrificial fee.
Thus, in this manner, the first breaking of the fast shall occur after three months;
then after another three months, and again after three months.
Then, O sinless one, another three months [are to be observed] in this manner;
thus, the four sets of fast-breaking meals for the eternal dharma are to be understood.

The worship of the deities is performed according to the very same procedure as the first breaking of the fast; the completion of all the fasts is accomplished through the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other rites.
By performing the first breaking of the fast, one obtains the fruit of the *Vahniṣṭoma* sacrifice;
likewise, O King, by the second breaking of the fast, one obtains the fruit of the *Atirātra*.
On the third breaking of the fast, one obtains the fruit of the Viśvajit and Vājapeya sacrifices;
on the fourth breaking of the fast, it is said that one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya.
Upon a divine celestial chariot, sun-bright in color, garlanded with networks of tinkling bells,
drawn by swans, and resounding with the music of lutes and drums.
Endowed with a multitude of excellent celestial nymphs, traveling at will, and beautiful,
he becomes one who fulfills his desires as he pleases for a long time, without a doubt.
Having attained birth as a human being, one may encounter three stains;
these stains are thoroughly purified by learning,
birth, and likewise by action— of this there is no need for deliberation.
For him who worships the three steps of that incomparable Trivikrama, the Lord of the moving and the unmoving, all his desires are fulfilled.
All will attain prosperity; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the Trivikrama-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, a pure man, fasting, [should observe the vow].
Having performed the worship of the Trimūrti on the third lunar day according to the prescribed rite,
[458] The worship of the three forms (trimūrti) is the worship of the three forms— wind, sun, and moon—
with pure waters mixed with water from wells, rivers, ponds, and so forth, at dawn;
one should worship the wind at daybreak on a clean, auspicious spot that has been anointed.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food, using primarily barley; one should also give clothing to the twice-born.
At midday, one should worship in the fire and give gold to the Brahmins;
at the time of sunset, one should worship the moon in the water.
This means that one should worship [the deity] while meditating upon the moon in the water; and this means that at midday, one should worship the sun while meditating upon it in the fire.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with clarified butter, and silver is prescribed as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, O knower of dharma, that man should eat at night, avoiding oil.
Having performed this vow for a full year without weariness,
one attains the heavenly world for a thousand years.
Having attained human birth, O highly fortunate one, he then becomes a king on the earth after having observed the vow for a full three years.
For five thousand years he is honored in the heavenly world;
then, having attained human birth, he becomes a king on earth.
Having observed this unsurpassed vow for twelve years, a man becomes free from disease, handsome, beloved, and wealthy.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should then feed a thousand brahmins;
one should provide food consisting mostly of the three sweets and give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability.
Thereafter, one attains heaven for ten million years.
Then, having reached the human realm, he becomes a righteous king,
possessing a blazing wheel, wealthy, a lord of Dharma, and beloved by the people.
Thus ends the Rājyavrata as described in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Rambhā said: "O Great Goddess, in the world of the gods there are courtesans endowed with happiness."
Likewise, all women in the world of mortals are devoid of good fortune.
O Supreme Goddess, how do they obtain fortune and enjoyments? O Pārvatī, how may good fortune arise for them in birth after birth?
Thus, out of compassion, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, tell me everything regarding fasting,
vows, and likewise religious observances;
O Supreme Goddess, explain all this to me according to the proper method.
Pārvatī said:
Listen, O blessed lady, to this supreme secret which bestows the fruit of all desires and is the ultimate means for bringing about good fortune for unfortunate women.
Then follows the Koṭīśvarī vow, renowned as Lakṣeśvarī;
it occurs on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada.
In that [rite], the vow should be undertaken for a period of four years;
it must be performed by means of fasting every year, O beautiful one.
O beautiful-eyed one, having prepared one hundred thousand unbroken grains of rice or sesame seeds, O lovely lady, one should then cast them into water.
[460] An image of the goddess Sulocanā should be fashioned from materials mixed with milk;
having made it, one should surround it with a wall of flowers adorned with flower garlands.
Having established the goddess Pārvatī, one should worship her according to the power of one's devotion;
one should worship her with various flowers, saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood.
With perfumes, incenses, and flowers— saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood—
and likewise with perfumes, incenses, food offerings, and various kinds of fruits.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with a fine garment, saying:
"Salutations, salutations to you, O Queen of Gods; O Mistress of Lakṣmī, may salutations be unto you!"
O Koṭīśvarī, homage to you; homage to you, O beloved of Hara!
O Goddess Umā, homage to you; let there be homage to you, O Kātyāyanī!
Homage to Kālī, Mahākālī, Śivadurgā; homage be to you! Homage to all the Rudrāṇīs, O Aparṇā, beloved of Śaṅkara!
O Goddess who works for the welfare of all beings, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra.
The worship mantra:
Homage, O Goddess Lakṣeśvarī, O Koṭīśvarī; homage be to you!
Accept this water offering given by me together with Śaṅkara.
The Arghya-mantra:
"O auspicious lady, this vow was formerly performed by Indrāṇī;
it was performed by Saṃdhyāvalī and Sāvitrī, and it was performed by Arundhatī in the past."
O auspicious lady, Damayantī and Rohiṇī performed this excellent vow;
at the conclusion of the sacrifice, they should feed married women according to their ability, looking upon them with joy.
[She should perform the rite] with married women whose husbands are living,
according to such a procedure, while remaining constant in her vow.
Then, for her, there shall be no poverty, nor separation from what is beloved.
A woman shall have eight sons and a husband who is preeminent in virtues—
one who is handsome, virtuous, beloved, learned, pleasant to behold,
a lord, a king, long-lived, and dear.
One shall become— or attain—
the state of being beloved by all people, as well as a donor and an enjoyer who is virtuous,
righteous, heroic, and as pleasing to behold as the moon.
She is beautiful, fortunate, virtuous, and one who reveals the sovereignty of her husband;
she is of righteous character, well-conducted, and speaks the nectar of her words.
Bestowing compassion upon all, she shall possess incomparable good fortune;
together with her husband, that woman of noble form shall rule a supreme kingdom.
At the time of death, he rejoices together with him in the third heaven for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years.
Having performed this in former times, Indrāṇī obtained Indra as her supreme husband;
Rohiṇī obtained the Moon as her husband by practicing the lunar vow.
"O Goddess Raṇyā, having obtained as your husband the Sun, the Lord of Aditi and protector of the virtuous, this has been told to you, O blessed lady: perform the Koṭīśvara vow;
O Rambhā, carry out this enchanting practice known as Lakṣeśvarī."
Thus ends the Koṭīśvarī Vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
I shall now describe another third-day vow that destroys all sins.
Those who know the ancient traditions understand this [work] to be Rasakalyāṇinī.
Having reached the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,
one should perform a bath in the morning with cow’s milk and sesame seeds.
One should bathe the Goddess with honey and likewise with sugarcane juice,
and again with scented water and indeed with saffron for worship.
Having worshipped the right limbs, one should then worship the left limbs;
one should worship the feet and the ankles of the Goddess with "Salutation to Lalitā."
Salutations to the shanks and knees for peace, and likewise to the thighs for prosperity;
salutations to the waist for Madālasā and to the belly for Maṅgalā.
[One should worship] the breast with "Madanavāsinyai," the neck with "Kumudāyai," the arm and the tip of the arm with "Mādhavyai," and the smile on the face with "Kamalāyai."
The eyebrows and forehead to Rudrāṇī, and likewise the locks of hair to Śaṅkarā;
the crown to Vindhyavāsinī, and again the locks of hair to Kālī.
To Madanā, the forehead; to Mohanā, the eyebrows;
to Candrārdhadhāriṇī, the eyes; and to Tuṣṭi, the face.
Salutation to Utkaṇṭhinī for the throat; salutation to Abhayā for the breast;
to Rambhā for the left arm; and salutation to Viśokā for the hand.
The heart [is offered] to Madanagāminī, the belly likewise to Pāṭalā;
the hips to Suratavāsinī, and the thighs to Campakaśrī.
Salutation to Gaurī for the knees and shanks; salutation to Gāyatrī for the ankles;
salutation to Dharādharā for the feet; and salutation to Viśokā for the head.
Homage to Bhavānī, to Kāminī, to Kāmadevī, to the Fortune of the World; homage again and again to Ānandā, to Sunandā, and to Śubhadrā.
[463] Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should honor a Brahmin couple,
free from envy, by feeding them with sweet food and drink.
Having given a water-pot with a ladle and a pair of white garments,
one should then worship a golden lotus with perfumes and garlands.
May Kumudā be pleased here; she shall observe the vow of salt.
Having offered three water-pots and a golden lotus with the mantra "May Kumudā be pleased," one should undertake the vow: "I shall not eat salt for a month.
According to this procedure, one should always worship the Goddess month after month;
one should avoid salt in the month of Māgha, and likewise, molasses in Phālguna.
O King, likewise, one should avoid meat in the month of Caitra, as well as in Madhu and Mādhava;
one should avoid fermented drinks in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and similarly, cumin in Āṣāḍha.
One should avoid milk in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise curd in Bhādrapada;
similarly, ghee in Āśvayuja, and then salt in Kārttika.
In the month of Kārttika, *ūrṇā*; in the world, *marjikā* is known as *rasālā* and *śikhariṇī*. In Mārgaśīrṣa, however, it is *dhānyaka*, while in Pauṣa, sugar (*śarkarā*) is to be avoided.
At the conclusion of the vow, these [offerings] are completed month by month.
One should give it at the time of twilight, accompanied by a vessel of food.

"At the conclusion of the vow," and so forth. Among these items such as salt, jaggery, and the rest, whichever was renounced in a particular month, at the conclusion of that month's vow, one should give a preparation made with that very salt or other substance, accompanied by a vessel of food consisting of the *laḍḍuka* and other items to be described. [The items are: *laḍḍukas*, white wafers (*śvetavartī*), *saṃyāva*, *pūrikās*, *pārikās*, *ghṛtapūras*, flour-cakes (*piṣṭhāpūpa*), and *maṇḍakas*.
One should offer milk-porridge, leafy vegetables, curd-rice, and *indurtha-śokavartika* upon a water-jar (*karakopari*) in the sequence beginning with the month of Māgha.
Kumudā, Mādhavī, Gaurī, Rambhā, Bhadrā, Jayā,
Śivā, Umā, Rati, Satī, as well as Maṅgalā and Ratilālasā.
In due order, in all cases beginning with Māgha, one should proclaim, "May [the deity] be pleased.
In every instance, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is prescribed.
Remaining constantly observant of the fast, or if unable, it is prescribed that one eat only at night;
furthermore, when the month of Māgha has arrived, [one should place] sugar upon a water-pot.
Having fashioned a golden image of Gaurī, endowed with the five jewels,
and measuring the size of a thumb made of gold, together with a rosary and a water-pot;
[He should be] four-armed, joined with the moon, and covered by a white eye-cloth;
likewise, there should be a pair of white cows, richly adorned with gold and clad in white garments.
One should give food along with clothing, saying, "May Bhavānī be pleased.
He who performs the Rasakalpāṇinī vow according to this rite—
He shall perform [this]; from all sins he is liberated at that very moment, and for thousands of billions of existences he will never again be born into suffering anywhere.
O lady of beautiful countenance, whatever fruit is obtained by a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices, that a woman or a maiden who performs [this rite] shall attain.
Even a wretched widow shall partake in that fruit;
endowed with good fortune and health, she is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
Whoever thus recites this or hears it incidentally,
being liberated from all impurities, goes to the world of Pārvatī;
and whoever gives even a thought to people for the sake of this vow, [attains the same].
He shall be an unfailing leader for people of vast destinies.
Thus ends the Rasakalpāṇinī vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O highly fortunate one, listen to the vow that should be performed on the third lunar day.
By which a twice-born man destroys the sin commenced through infinite births.
One who is afflicted by other calamities such as the torments of malevolent planets should perform this rite of pacification, restraining speech, body, and mind.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or a mandala with unhusked white rice grains;
one should fashion a mandala marked with a wheel and lotus from unhusked white rice grains.
And there one should invoke the Lord, the all-pervading Narasiṃha,
whose gracious, sweet, and noble gaze destroys all suffering.
To Hari, the Supreme Person, who is expert in destroying every fear, who grants fearlessness to those tormented by fear, and who bestows the most excellent boons upon those who give; [I bow].
O lady of beautiful hips, there was a face most gracious toward those who had sought refuge and dispelled their distress, and eyes that were free from passion.
With four infinite arms skillful at crushing the faction of opposing forces,
he was like another lofty mountain of silver encircled by garlands of lightning.
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, and a forest garland,
and embellished by the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, Nandaka sword, and other weapons.
With variegated *jāti* flowers, unbroken white rice grains,
mango blossoms, *mallikā* and other such flowers, and *nandyāvarta* blossoms.
With unbroken grains, bilva leaves, its fruits, and its sprouts;
with sesame seeds mixed with cooked rice, and with the sprouts of the tulasī and śrī-latā creepers.
With blue lotuses, water lilies, and white lotuses together with their filaments,
mixed with powdered saffron, sandalwood, camphor, and agallochum.

With various and unprecedented fragrances, uncrushed and gathered whole grains that are unblemished; with *nandyāvarta*, *tagara*, and unseparated whole grains; with perfected and prepared *śrīlatā*, *padminī*, blue water-lilies (*kuvalaya*), and lotuses (*utpala*); with *kesara*, *vakula*, saffron (*kāśmīra-kesara*), and powdered incense;
with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and food enriched with molasses and the three kinds of honey;
and with melodious songs, beautiful dances, and the display of musical instruments.
Having properly worshipped the Lord of Gods with circumambulations, prostrations, hymns of praise, and other offerings, while imbued with devotion, according to the ritual prescribed by rule.
It was endowed with various medicinal herbs, possessed the waters of various sacred fords,
was filled with various flavors, and was adorned with various flowers.
One should place before [the deity] a full water-pot (pūrṇakumbha) strewn with various seeds, provided with various cloths, and accompanied by various bunches of kusha grass.
With one-pointed mind, he should invoke the deity Sudarśana therein,
having worshipped him properly according to his ability by means of the very path previously described.
Having established four jars according to the sequence starting from the east,
one should likewise meditate upon these [deities] within them, in order, at the corners.
In those eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should place those [implements], beginning with Nandaka:
the Nandaka, the pestle, the lotus, the mace, the sword, the conch, the noose, and the spear; these are likewise to be arranged in that same manner on their exterior as well.
Having performed the installation of the world-protectors (lokapālas), one should worship them everywhere;
likewise, one should likewise adorn the central jar as well as the others.
Having thus completed the worship according to the rules, the wise man,
with one-pointed mind, should recite the Sudarśana mantra ten thousand times.
The wise one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times for each vessel;
then follows the consecration of the sacrificial pit and the establishment of the fire according to the prescribed rule.
Having prepared the consecrated fire, one should offer oblations for the sake of universal pacification,
using pure sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets, as well as clarified butter and milk.
With the leaves and blossoms of the *śrīlatā* creeper, *bilva* leaves and flowers,
sprouts of *dūrvā* grass smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), along with seeds, rice grains, and mustard seeds;

One who desires long life should use *darva* twigs; one who desires prosperity, those produced from the *bilva* tree; and one who desires good fortune, the fortunate one, should use threads made from the leaves of the *śrī-latā*.
One who possesses fortune or desires fortune [should worship] with milk; one desiring health, with cow’s clarified butter and likewise with sesame seeds;
one desiring nourishment, with *apāmārga* plants; and one seeking to ward off untimely death, with *gadrūci* plants.
There is untimely death for one associated with untimely death;
through lotuses, Lakṣmī and nourishment are unimpeded, as are they through water-lilies (kumuda); through jasmine flowers there is the attainment of land, and through nandyāvarta blossoms, the same.
One attains sovereignty through white lotuses with single petals;
and [sovereignty] through silver, bees, and the like, as well as through gold and champaka flowers.
Through seeds, rice, grains, and so forth, the attainment of those respective things will occur;
when any one of these is seen, whatever boon one desires shall be granted.
By means of ten thousand repetitions, one undoubtedly attains that [result];
it is the certainty of the mantra that the libation (tarpaṇa) is said to be double the number of the fire-oblation (homa).
They say that for him, this recitation should be twice that amount; this is the sequence of the ritual procedure.
At the time of commencing the application, one should observe the restrictive rules.
Performing three [observances] day after day, one should conclude them during the night;
the "assignments" (niyoga) are the excavations within the mandala, and the "restrictions" (niyama) are silence and so forth.
One should also conclude the three [observances] pertaining to the night first, day after day.

He should perform the three—fire-oblations, libations, and recitations—day after day, every single day; and the number [of repetitions] should be according to the number of oblations previously resolved upon. Eating sacrificial food, having conquered anger, and restraining his speech, body, and mind, the sage, devoted to virtuous conduct, should bathe daily at the three periods of the day.
He should not speak untruth, he should not be without the sacred fire, he should be a celibate student who has conquered fatigue;
he should be fair-complexioned, free from envy, constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, and pure.
Either fasting or subsisting on vegetables, having considered the relative weight of fruits, he should diligently undertake these observances until their completion.
The observances consist of eating sacrificial food, eating only vegetables, and fasting. Likewise, the increase in the number [of recitations] is caused by the gravity of the desired fruit.
Ten thousand is best, or as many as one's arms can count; the intellect follows that result.
Having thus performed [the rite] correctly, one should bring together the preceptor and the practitioner.
Taking the middle pitcher, one should perform the bathing in the presence of the deity.
[469] To the practitioner and the patron—she whose great flames are well-kindled, illuminating the very quarters of space—save him from calamities; may prosperity be granted! Homage to her.
The high-minded preceptor should also perform his consecration with other [mantras] as appropriate, using their respective mantras in his presence.
Oṃ! You who are consecrated for the shattering of the mountain-like masses of the Daityas;
O Padma, Śaṅkha, and Manonanda, protect this one too, O Nandaka!
Oṃ! O crusher of the adversaries' pride, whose face is agitated by their trembling heads;
O beloved of Kamalākānta, protect this man, O wielder of the mace!
O lotus, as beautiful as the play-lotus of the Supreme Self— who sports in the protection of the world from the fear of its arising— protect this [creature] as well.
May that goddess Kaumodakī mace indeed bestow auspiciousness,
she who serves as a shimmering ornament upon the lotus-hand of Mukunda.
Oṃ! May that excellent bow Śārṅga of Viṣṇu protect him—the bow by which his life was snatched away from all the Rākṣasas and Danujas through its own twanging sound.
The Lord of the Gods, whose voice is skillful at piercing the wombs of the Daitya women,
has a mouth filled with bees and the clearly flowing red ichor of elephants.
O you who feed upon the life-force, fat, and blood of the lords of Daityas and Rakshasas!
May the volleys of arrows from the hand of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow protect this man everywhere.
May Śakti—the goddess of power, whose weapon is the discus—protect him from calamities; she is capable of destroying the strength and vigor of enemies headed by their weapons.
Having bathed in this manner, one should perform the rite of *nīrājana* for the image adorned with new garments, ornaments, and so forth,
and should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin.
Having given a boon to the preceptor and sacrificial fees and so forth to his kinsmen,
he should also give abundantly according to his means to others who may have need of it.
Then, having been brought into the midst of the twice-born, he was bathed by them and presented with an auspicious appearance,
using sesame, sandalwood, parched grain, unbroken rice, white mustard, and sandalwood paste.
The Brahmins should pronounce the *svasti* blessing, and he should also cause benedictions (*āśis*) to be made;
the skillful teacher, using water from a ritual grass-bundle (*kūrca*), should perform the words of auspiciousness.
O God, grant abundant life and abundant prosperity upon this earth,
as well as inexhaustible health and imperishable peace of mind.
May the Lord of Śrī grant auspiciousness, remaining unassailed even by existing diseases of the lineage, intellect, and so forth, and likewise bestowing an abundance of knowledge.
May there be well-being and auspiciousness; may there always be prosperity for you. May the Lord of Śrī protect you from calamities and from fears.
Having thus performed the rite of protection, one should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors;
in the east it should be made with rice, and in the south with *kṛśara* (rice and sesame) food.
In the west, one should offer milk-rice; likewise, in the center, pure food;
in the corners, with the Śaktis, one should offer food mixed with jaggery; and then, outside of that.
The high-minded one should offer an oblation for all purposes with all kinds of substances;
thus has the vow of peace (śāntivrata) on the third lunar day been proclaimed, O high-minded one.
It pacifies all suffering, destroys all diseases,
bestows all happiness upon women, and grants the fruit of one's desire for food.
It pacifies all suffering, brings prosperity, and destroys all sins.
But that mortal who performs this, endowed with faith and devotion,
becomes liberated from all afflictions and attains ultimate peace.
In the case of bad dreams, vomiting, seizures, severe afflictions, and other calamities;
upon the onset of poison and the like, and during the loss of a son or the depletion of wealth.
In the event of the loss of a kingdom, civil unrest, famine, or oppression by enemies;
or when afflicted by the pains of fever, eye disease, severe splenic disorders, leprosy, or fistula-in-ano.
When there is an accumulation of intense suffering due to consumption, epilepsy, and other such ailments,
a person whose essence is wisdom should perform this ritual bath.
A man who is pleasant-faced, reddish in complexion, wise, and esteemed for his learning prospers happily after overcoming thousands of great calamities.
Thus concludes the Śānti-vrata as declared in the Garuḍa Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
"In the same manner, I shall likewise describe another third-day vow (tṛtīyā) that destroys sins."
But in the world, this [state] which produces intense bliss is not known as "sour."
Whenever the third lunar day of the bright fortnight coincides with the asterism Āṣāḍhā,
or with Rohiṇī, or Punarvasu, or Hasta, or Mūla;

The asterism Āṣāḍha is Uttarāṣāḍhā, the asterism of Brahmā is Abhijit, and the asterism of the Waters is Pūrvāṣāḍhā. At that time, one should properly perform a bath with darbha grass and scented water,
wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes.
O King, one should worship Bhavānī with devotion using fragrant white flowers,
together with Bhava, as she sits upon a seat of cloth.
Salutation to Vāsudevī for the feet; then salutation to Śaṅkara for Hara;
salutation to Śokavināśinī for the shanks, and salutation to Ānanda, O Lord.
One should worship the thighs with "To Rambhā" and for Śiva, the wielder of the Pināka bow;
the waist of the Goddess with "To Ānandinī" and for the trident-bearer, the wielder of the Śūla.
Likewise, [he offered] the navel to Mādhavī and to Śambhu for Bhava;
the two breasts to Ānandakāriṇī and to Śaṅkara, the wearer of the moon.

One should worship the throat with "Salutation to Utkaṇṭhinī," Hara with "Salutation to Nīlakaṇṭha," the two hands with "Salutation to Utpaladhāriṇī," and the Lord of Sacrificers with "Salutation to Rudra."
And [he gave] his two arms to Parirambiṇī, and Hara to Nṛtyaśīlā;
O Lord, he gave his face to the Goddess Vināśinī, and again to Vṛṣeśā.
And [he offered] a smile to Smaraśīlā, eyes to Viśvavaktṛ and to her who is intent upon him, and [eyes] to Damanavāsinī, to Viśvadhātrī, and to the Trident-bearer.
The two eyebrows are for Netṛpriyā and for Tāṇḍaveśa, O All-pervading Lord;
the forehead of the Goddess is for Indrāṇī and for Havyavāha, O All-pervading Lord.

A crown for the Goddess Svāhā, and indeed for Śambhu, the bearer of the Gaṅgā; may the two auspicious ones, whose bodies are the universe, who are the foremost of the universe, and whose feet and hands are the universe, [be pleased].
"I bow to Pārvatī and Parameśvara, whose faces are serene.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules, he [should again] stand before the two Śivas.
One may draw lotuses and water-lilies of various colors with colored powder,
as well as a conch, a wheel, a swastika, and likewise a half-coin.
As many particles of dust as fall from that cloud of pollen upon the earth,
for so many thousands of years shall one be honored in the world of Śiva.
With devotion, one should give to a twice-born man four vessels of ghee along with gold, as well as a water-pot filled with water.
One should offer these for four months as an antidote;
thereafter, for the next four months, one should do as before upon the water-pot.
Thereafter, one should give forty vessels of sesame seeds,
along with gold, as before, having placed them upon water-pitchers.
[One should also offer] scented water, flower-water, sandalwood, and saffron-water.
Unripened curd or milk, as well as water from a cow's horn;
Likewise, flour-water, water mixed with the powder of kuṣṭha,
similarly water with uśīra, and likewise water from yava-vallī;
Having consumed sesame-water, one should sleep during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa;
it is taught that this consumption should take place twice in each fortnight throughout the months.
White flowers are recommended in every instance for the worship of Śiva;
at all times of making offerings, one should recite this mantra.
May Gaurī, who is eternally pure and the source of all auspiciousness, be pleased with me forever;
may the exquisitely beautiful Bhavānī grant me good fortune and the attainment of all perfections.
At the end of the year, one should offer salt together with a jar of jaggery,
sandalwood, a cloth for the eyes, and likewise a lotus made of gold.
Likewise, one should offer a golden image of Umāmaheśvara together with sugarcane fruits,
as well as a very white bed spread with coverlets and provided with pillows.
"To a Brahmin who has a wife, [one should say] 'May Gaurī be pleased with me'—
this third [vow], named Ārdrānandakarī, is eternal."
Having fasted upon which [day], a man goes to that supreme abode of Śambhu;
he also attains constant bliss in this world, of this there is no doubt.
Endowed with long life and health, one shall never encounter sorrow;
and whether it be a woman, a maiden, or likewise a widow,
she too attains that fruit through the grace of the wielder of the trident (Śūlapāṇi).
Having thus observed the fast as an antidote according to the ritual procedure for mantra worship,
one attains the world of Rudrāṇī, from which rebirth is difficult to encounter again.
The person who constantly hears this, or causes others to hear it,
attains the world of Rudrāṇī, from which rebirth is difficult to obtain.
The person who would constantly hear this, or even cause it to be heard,
is honored for ten thousand years by the worlds of Śakra together with the gandharvas.
Whether she be a widow or a woman with a living husband, she who observes the third lunar day— which bestows bliss and removes all suffering—
shall experience the greatest joys within her own home and, thereafter, [attain further happiness].
Accompanied by her beloved, Gaurī joyfully proceeds to Gaurīpura.
Thus ends the Ārdrādāna-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. Sumantu said:
A devoted wife, whose life is her husband, is intent upon the service of her husband.
Even though she was thus engaged in perverse conduct, she remained pure in her eating and drinking.
Observing a fast on the third lunar day, she should avoid salt.
Regarding "sopavāsa" (with fasting): having observed the fast on the second day at the commencement of the vow, she should avoid salt on the third day.
Let her indeed undertake this vow with devotion until the end of her life;
Gaurī, being well-pleased, grants her beauty and good fortune as well.
A woman who is charming, salty with beauty, heart-stealing, praiseworthy, and pleasing to the minds of men; a husband who is likewise pleasing to the mind of his wife—such a union is delightful.
O King, by observing the Gaurī-vrata and abstaining from salt, one obtains [these fruits];
moreover, listen to that which was spoken by Umā in the past.
Thus, O Lord, while Dharmarāja was listening,
I created this infinite vow which brings about good fortune for men.
But a mortal woman who shall observe this vow will rejoice together with her husband for as long as my husband Hara remains.
Indeed, that beautiful and virtuous woman who finds a noble husband should,
for the sake of this vow, subsist on food free from pungent flavors.

With her mind fixed on me and her thoughts centered on me, she whose husband is devoted to me and who is my own possession should have a golden image of Gaurī fashioned and adorned with perfumes and ornaments.
One should clothe her in very fine garments and adorn her with flower ornaments;
on the bright lunar day, one should offer salt, nectar, jaggery, and oil to the Goddess.
O descendant of Bharata, [one should offer] pieces of *kadu* (ginger), cumin, conch-shell, and leaves;

the remainder [of the context] implies this is during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). [One should also offer] balls of molasses (*guḍapūpa*), as well as cakes (*apūpa*) and sweets wrapped in sugar-candy (*khaṇḍaveṣṭa*), O King.
These should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with Vedic knowledge and has heard much.
On each bright lunar day, one should always offer a golden image according to one's ability;
however, O King, those who lack wealth may indeed offer one made of honey and milk according to their means.
O Hero, she eats food free from pungent condiments and salt at night, remaining well-restrained in speech;
Gaurī is ever present with her, sleeping upon a bed of grass spread on the ground.
A maiden who desires a husband who is pleasing to her mind obtains such a husband;
indeed, having sported with him for a very long time, she remains with him alone.
Having established a continuity, he goes along with that very [continuity] to enjoy the diverse splendors of the Citraśikhaṇḍins in this world and in the world beyond.
But the queen, O great king, was a widow devoted to her vows;
she remained constantly self-restrained toward her husband and was always intent upon his worship.
Having cast off her body here and bestowed her beloved upon the city of Hara,
she shall draw her husband away from the messengers of Yama and rejoice in heaven.
Having wandered for a hundred times ten million years, she returns once again;
together with her husband, she obtains the desired fruit previously described.
Thus, this lunar day, known as the third, is honored by the world;
it is always especially meritorious, or particularly so in the month of Vaiśākha.
There is no doubt that it is auspicious in the month of Bhādrapada or indeed in Māgha;
or even in either Māgha or Bhādrapada, they declare this to be a source of fortune for women.
O Bhārata, the third day of the month of Māgha is indeed common to all the world; on this day, [offerings] of jaggery and salt [should be made].
O King, giving gifts brings about the highest welfare for both women and men;
the Goddess is pleased by molasses, and Śaṅkara by salt.
On the third day of the month of Bhādrapada, which is celebrated in the world by the gods as the inexhaustible (akṣayā), balls of molasses (guḍapūpa) should be prepared.
The man who gives water-pots filled with streams of water here,
O hero, goes indeed to the worlds of Hetimālin.
The gift of water is indeed praised, as is the gift of sweetmeats, O Bhārata;
and on the third lunar day in the month of Vaiśākha, O Indra among kings, so too is the gift of sandalwood.
The goddess is satisfied with water, while Bhava himself is indeed pleased by sweetmeats;
however, due to the gift of sandalwood here, there is no rebirth in a human womb.
O tiger among the Kurus, that lunar day which occurs in the month of Vaiśākha is known as the inexhaustible third day (Tṛtīyā) in this world; it is celebrated here by the gods.
O hero, the man who gives water-pots provided with water-vessels in this [river], goes indeed to the worlds of Hetimālin.
Thus, O hero, this third lunar day has been described as most excellent;
by fasting upon it, O King, a man shall attain growth of intelligence and prosperity.
Thus ends the vow of the Saltless Third (Alavaṇatṛtīyā-vrata) as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
Gaurī, Kālī, Umā, Bhadrā, Durgā, Kānti, and Sarasvatī—
Maṅgalā, Vaiṣṇavī, Lakṣmī, Śivā, and Nārāyaṇī, in due order.
Beginning from the third day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform worship; thus one shall become a partaker of heaven.
The meaning is that, beginning from the third day of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship every month with each individual name:
either Rudra as Ardhanārīśvara, or Umāśaṅkara.
One who worships a woman according to the prescribed rite shall obtain non-separation [from his beloved].
Or, just as one might always worship the Lord in the form of Viṣṇu,
so too by worshipping her who stands on the left side of the Lord, one shall obtain all desires.

Having fashioned an image of Ardhanārīśvara or Umāmaheśvara out of gold or other materials, one should worship the Goddess situated on the left side with the names Gaurī and so forth. Alternatively, having fashioned the form of Hari-Hara as the Lord joined with Viṣṇu, one should worship each individually with the names Keśava and others located on the left half. Having fasted and worshipped the deities known as Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara with incense, garlands, lamps, and other offerings, and having honored them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) while reciting their respective names, one obtains the desired fruit through the constant remembrance of all these names—more so than all sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, or even the gift of a hundred thousand cows.
Thus ends the vow for the third lunar day as declared in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
Brahmā said:
"On the third lunar day, by worshipping the Lord of Wealth (Vitteśa), one will certainly be born endowed with abundant wealth."
The word "having worshipped" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Furthermore, in transactions such as buying and selling, the profit shall possess divine qualities.
The root mantras and the limb mantras are proclaimed by their respective knowledges;
and the Lord of the Lunar Days (Tithīśvara) should be depicted situated upon a lotus petal in the east.
Worship performed with offerings of incense and flowers according to one's ability—
even if performed with deceit or hypocrisy— bestows its fruit.
An oblation consisting of a stream of clarified butter, fuel-sticks, curd, milk, food, and honey,
when performed with a tranquil mind, yields the fruits previously described.
This vow is to be explained like the Vaiśvānara-pratipad-vrata. Thus ends the Kuberavrata as described in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Agastya said:

After this, O Great King, listen to the vow that brings about good fortune, by which good fortune quickly arises for both women and men. It is on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
Having fasted, eating only at night, being pure and speaking the truth,
one should worship Hari along with Śrī, or Rudra together with Umā.

In this context, the phrase "of the deity" refers to the prescribed characteristics of the image, since it will be stated later that "one should then give it to a Brāhmaṇa. And that [image] should primarily be made of gold.
Furthermore: "To Gabhīrāya" for the feet; "to Subhagāya" for the hips;
"to Devadeva" for the belly; and "to Śrīkaṇṭha" for the chest.
Having thus worshipped Viṣṇu together with Lakṣmī, the wise one should offer to the head with "To Trilocana" and to all sides with "To Rudra."
In the worship of Viṣṇu, however, one should employ Vaiṣṇava mantras;
or, having worshipped Hara together with Gaurī with perfumes, flowers, and so forth in due order,
one should then perform a fire-oblation (homa) before Him with honey and clarified butter.

O Great King, together with sesame seeds and the mantra "Obeisance to the Lord of Good Fortune," one should then [place] that which is free of oil and mixed with alkaline salt upon the surface of the earth.
One should eat food made of wheat; such is the prescribed rule. On the second lunar day of the month beginning with Āṣāḍha, one should feed [the deity] with milk-rice (pāyasa).
After that, however, barley-food [should be given] to one who is a worthy recipient,
who is discerning, free from physical defects, a master of the Vedas, and who conducts himself virtuously.
O King, one should give it to a person endowed with virtuous conduct, even if he is of small mind;
one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa accompanied by swords and vessels.
One vessel contains honey, the second is filled with ghee,
the third with sesame oil, and the fourth is combined with jaggery.

The fifth is with *lavaṇāparṇa*, and the sixth is combined with cow’s milk. O King, by giving these juices, whether a woman or even a man, one shall become fortunate and handsome within seven lifetimes.
Thus ends the vow of Saubhāgyatṛtīyā as declared in the Śrī Varāha Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the most excellent of all vows."
It generates good fortune and bestows the fruits of one's desires.
Brahmā said: Listen, O Brahmin, according to the prescribed rite, to the third [period] consisting of three watches,
which, through the proper performance by women, bestows heaven and good fortune.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should observe a fast;
having gathered the ritual requisites at night in the pavilion for the worship of Gaurī.
O best of sages, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus within the pavilion;
there, with a well-concentrated mind, one should worship Umā and Maheśvara.
One should place Gaurī on the eastern petal, Lalitā on the southeast;
Umā by name on the south, and likewise Svadhā on the southwest.
In the west, however, is Vāmadevī; in the northwest, Mūlagaurikā;
in the north, Śubhagā; and likewise in the northeast, Girijā.
One should worship Umāmaheśvara in the center with perfumes and flowers;
having placed a water-pot there, one should fill it with rice grains.
A *bhṛṅgāra* is a water-pot (*kalaśa*).
Then, in front of that, one should prepare a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit and provided with a girdle (*mekhalā*).
Having placed a bell in the corner, four vessels filled with water should be set out.
Having offered oblations of clarified butter with ghee, one should perform a sesame oblation;
having offered a hundred oblations with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should remain composed in mind.
Or else, O sage, a Brahmin observing the vow should offer oblations with the name "Gaurī";
furthermore, the practitioner of the vow should perform his bath on the northern side of the sacrificial pit.
O Lord, O tiger among the twice-born, one should first perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a jar placed in the south-eastern direction during the first watch of the night.
[482] In this manner, one should perform the ritual bathing and the fire-oblation (homa) every watch of the day;
then, when the clear dawn has appeared, [one should honor] the most excellent of the twice-born together with his wife.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with garments, ornaments, and decorations,
one should offer red cloth to the preceptor’s wife and white garments to the preceptor.
O Sage, having performed the worship of the Goddess in this manner according to the prescribed rite for four years, it becomes the supreme means of generating good fortune.
Then, on that very same day, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana),
[placing] a golden image of Umāmaheśvara upon a clean couch.
Then, O Sage, having properly worshipped with devotion using garments, perfumes, incense, garlands of lamps and the like, as well as various kinds of food offerings.
In the same way, one should worship the preceptor and his wife as an excellent twice-born;
likewise, one should give a cow to the preceptor, accompanied by garments and ornaments.
One who is well-composed should feed four couples here;
having offered a golden image of Umā and Maheśvara with devotion, one should ask for forgiveness.
Whoever performs this correctly according to the prescribed rite shall possess good fortune and health;
in this very life they will attain prosperity, and upon death, they shall go to the city of Śiva.
One who desires the fruit should not perform the third [day] without the prescribed ritual;
his labor is as futile as digging into a mountain.
Whether it be a woman or a man, O tiger among men, O sage, one obtains the fruit as described by the prescribed rite; this which I have spoken, O twice-born ones, is the truth.
[483] Thus ends the vow of the third lunar day of Hari as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He who should avoid salt on the third lunar day beginning with Phālguna..."
At the end of the year, one should give a bed and a house equipped with all necessary furnishings.
At the end of the month, that is, at the end of the year,
having honored a Brahmin couple with the words, "May Bhavānī be pleased," this vow which eternally bestows the world of Gaurī is called the Saubhāgyavrata.
Thus ends the Saubhāgyavrata as declared in the Garuḍa Purāṇa:
Having consumed cow’s urine and barley-gruel on the third lunar day of the month of Kārttika, one should observe the *nakta* fast for one year; at its conclusion, one should become a donor of a cow.
One shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa, and thereafter become a king here on earth;
this is the vow known as Bhadrāvrata, which brings about all auspiciousness.
Thus ends the Bhadrā-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Furthermore, he who should perform an anointing in the temple of Śiva on the third lunar day—
Śivā being Pārvatī.
At the end of the year, cows are to be given, as well as the Bhavānī-vrata.
Thus ends the Bhavānī-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa:
"The man who, on the third lunar day, eats food that has not been cooked over fire..."
Having given a cow, one attains Śiva, from whom a return [to worldly existence] is difficult to find;
this is remembered as the vow of good conduct (*śīlavrata*) that produces great bliss for men.

Thus ends the vow of moral conduct (*śīlavrata*) as declared in the *Padma Purāṇa*. Furthermore, by giving a cow made of molasses (*guḍadhenu*) in the month of Māgha or Caitra, one who observes the *guḍavrata* on the third lunar day is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
One who possesses jaggery is one who avoids jaggery;
this is indeed called the Great Vow (mahāvrata), which produces supreme bliss.
Thus ends the Great Tṛtīyā Vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
On the third day of the bright fortnight, one should draw [the image] upon a pair of auspicious cloths;
thereafter, one should worship Śiva and Umā with yellow pigment (rocanā), black aloeswood (asita), and camphor (karpūra).
O child, with garlands of gold and jewels, one should recite the pair of mantras which were previously described as bestowing the fruit of all desires.
That very same pair of mantras is written here:

*namaḥ samastabhuvanasargasthityantakāraṇa | īśāna dhyānaparama yogigamyāyate śiva ||* Homage to you, O Śiva, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe, the Sovereign, who is most worthy of meditation and accessible only to yogis.
Salutations to Śivā, who took half the body of Viśveśa;
truly, salutations to the Mother of all that moves and is immobile here, the granter of desires.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, the recitation of mantras, worship, and fire-offerings should be performed;
this king of vows is always beneficial for women so that they may never be separated [from their husbands].
One should cause that [image], rich with flowers and jewels and adorned with cloth, to be given;
it bestows great merit, great fortune, and grants all desires.
But, O twice-born one, there shall be no separation from his brothers through that [merit];
nor shall there be disease or calamities as long as the vital energy of his lineage remains.
