For that duration, he shall shine and rejoice for a long time in the world of Umā.
Thus ends the vow of the third lunar day (Aja-tṛtīyā-vrata) as declared in the Śrī Devīpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
In this regard, I shall proclaim an ancient history (itihāsa).
Just as it was with the wife of the King of Kāśī, O best of the twice-born.
In the past, there was a king in Kāśī known as Jayasena;
he had a thousand wives endowed with great beauty.
In that very same way, he obtained another beloved and most beautiful wife,
the daughter of the wise Viśvaka, the sovereign king of Madra.
Having risen from sleep in the morning and gone to the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā,
she fashioned an image of Gaurī made of clay consisting of five lumps.
But when he manifests through radiance, then he makes himself—
earth, fire, wind, and space itself.
"She creates for the sake of creation"—thus she is called Tatpañcapiṇḍikā;
thereafter, she worshipped her with exactly five mantras.
Then, with perfumes, fruits, garlands, incenses, and most beautiful garments,

they are not overcome by obstacles while it is being carried out;
having fallen from the heavenly world, they then go to the supreme goal.
[505] Thus concludes the Kṛcchracaturthī vow with its supplementary rites as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata;
on the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should observe a fast with the senses subdued.
On the fourth day, having performed the auspicious worship of Vāsudeva,
one should give gold as a sacrificial fee to a brahmin who is a celibate student.
Likewise, having worshipped the god Saṅkarṣaṇa, the teacher of the world,
one should give a well-prepared bed to a householder during the month of Vaiśākha.
Having worshipped the god Pradyumna according to the prescribed rites in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one should then offer fruits, roots, and cow's milk to him while he resides in the forest;
and likewise, having worshipped Aniruddha, the teacher of the world, in the month of Āṣāḍha.
One should give a gourd vessel to a twice-born man established in yoga;
this is declared to be the breaking of the fast, and one is glorified in the heavenly world.
When the second breaking of the fast arrives, one is honored in the world of Śakra; then,
when the third breaking of the fast arrives, one comes to the same realm as Keśava.
The repetition of the vow is performed by observing three fasts;
thus has this supreme vow for the stages of life (āśramas), which destroys all impurity, been declared to you by me.
[506] Thus ends the vow for the stages of life (āśramavrata) as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now declare to you another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata;
Hari is said to be fourfold in nature, and there are likewise four sacrificial fires.
A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires and possesses the fourfold fire should observe a fast on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
Having worshipped the fourfold Vāsudeva with unwearied devotion,
one should give sixteen vessels filled with sesame seeds to that best of the twice-born.
Gold for gold, a garment, and even a balance of ghee—
[the deficiency] being one *karṣa* less than the gold.
Having performed this vow thus for a year, unweariedly, [one becomes purified].
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
By means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, he goes to the heavenly world;
that man shall possess radiant splendor, a blazing fire, and be beloved by women.
He conquers his enemies in battle and likewise becomes possessed of wealth.
Those fires which have indeed entered the four [directions] are said to be Vāsudeva in his fourfold form.
Whoever should honor a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires, by him even the God is then honored.
[507] Thus ends the Agni-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
O King, all the hosts of gods were born from a portion of Vāsudeva;
likewise, the Sādhyas and the Suras were born from an even greater portion.
Even there, Hari is remembered as fourfold in his supreme aspect:
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and the heroic Kṛṣṇa.
O Yādava, Hari has been born as the fourfold self of the householder's dharma. Know that those two among the Ādityas who are called Mitra and Varuṇa are none other than Hari and Kṛṣṇa, O Yādava.
Those two who were mentioned among the Ādityas as Śakra and Viṣṇu, the best of gods, are again Nara and Nārāyaṇa among the Siddhas and Sādhyas.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, O lord of men, one should worship the Lord of Gods, who is fourfold in nature, while observing a fast according to one's financial means.
Having observed this vow for a full twelve years,
a person does not fall into an evil state of existence and finds the means to liberation.
Then, having attained sovereignty over the forest, he attains equality with the Supreme Person;
for he is the Lord of all, possessed of incomparable power.
Freed from suffering, he is the protector of the world.
[508] Thus ends the vow of the four forms as spoken in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śuka said:
O Bhārata, when the fourth lunar day coincides with a Tuesday,
one should perform a bath with clay, adorned with rubies.
Reciting the mantra "Agni is the head of heaven," he should stand facing north;
however, the Śūdra remains silent, reciting the mantra pertaining to the earth, while abstaining from all enjoyments.
Then, after the sun has set, having smeared the courtyard with cow dung and decorated it on all sides with flower garlands and unbroken grains of rice;
Having worshipped, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with saffron;
however, in the absence of saffron, red sandalwood is prescribed.
Four water-pots should be prepared, provided with various kinds of food and edibles,
and filled with red śāli rice and rubies.
Having placed those [offerings] in the four corners, as well as various fruits and all such things as perfumes and garlands, one should likewise present them.
Having worshipped a tawny cow with golden horns,
silver hooves, a bronze milking vessel, and a cloth,
as well as a very gentle, red bull capable of bearing the yoke;
The seven grains together with the inferior ones.
The seven grains are barley, wheat, dhānyaka,
kaṅgu, śyāmāka, chickpeas, and cīnaka; likewise, there is a man the size of a thumb.
[509] A golden [image] with four arms and very long staff-like arms, seated upon a golden pedestal,
[was placed] in a vessel over jaggery and mixed with clarified butter.
All this should be given to that twice-born man who knows the tones of the Sāman chants, who has conquered his senses, who is a worthy recipient, and in whom the threefold morality has arisen.
Nor indeed to one who is a householder and possessed of hypocrisy.
O son of the Earth, of great splendor, born from the sweat of the wielder of the Pināka bow; desiring beauty, I have come to you—accept this water offering; salutations be unto you!
Having offered the *arghya* with this mantra using water mixed with red sandalwood,
one should then honor the excellent Brahmin with red garlands, garments, and other offerings.
With that very mantra, one should give land together with a pair of cattle,
and according to one's ability, one should also give a bed furnished with all its accessories.
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear to one in one's home—
each of those should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that very thing to become inexhaustible.

Then, having performed a circumambulation and dismissed the eminent brahmins, that bull among the twice-born should eat at night food mixed with ghee, avoiding pungent and salty items. A man who is able should perform the Aṅgārakāṣṭaka vow in this manner.
"Aṅgārakāṣṭaka" refers to the eight [days] beginning with the fourth day of Aṅgāraka (Mars). Or rather, it consists of four; I shall now tell you what merit belongs to that.
Endowed with beauty and good fortune in birth after birth,
he shall become a devotee of Viṣṇu and Śiva, and a sovereign over the seven continents.
"One is honored in the world of Rudra for thousands of cycles of sleep.
Thus ends the Aṅgāraka-caturthī-vrata as described in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
One should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa on the fourth lunar day (Caturthī) for all undertakings;
he bestows freedom from obstacles and the desired goal in the world of the gods.
There is no doubt that he creates obstacles for the ignorant in their ritual actions;
therefore, at the beginning of all rites, the Lord of the Gaṇas is to be worshipped.
The root mantras and the limb mantras are proclaimed by their respective names;
and as before, the Lord of the Lunar Days (Tithīśvara) should be visualized seated upon a lotus petal.
The Lord of the lunar days (Tithīśvara) here is Gaṇeśa. His specific form and manner [of worship] should be observed in the Kṛcchra-caturthī vow.
Worship is performed with offerings of fragrance, flowers, and food according to one's capacity; even if performed with deceit or through negligence, it still yields fruit.
An oblation performed with a stream of clarified butter, fuel-sticks, curd, milk, rice, and honey,
and offered with a tranquil mind, yields the fruits previously described.
This vow is to be explained like the Vaiśvānara-pratipad-vrata. Thus ends the Gaṇeśa-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Sūta said:
On the fourth day, O best of kings, one should not eat after bathing in a river;
having put on red garments and being anointed with red unguents, one should remain thus.
Then, with a red-colored mind, one should worship Gaṇādhīśa Vināyaka,
beginning with a bath using water mixed with red sandalwood, according to the prescribed ritual.
Having smeared [the image] with red sandalwood paste, one should worship it with red flowers;
then he again offered sandalwood mixed with ghee.
And the food offering should consist of turmeric, jaggery, and sugar-candy soaked in ghee;
having thus worshipped Vināyaka for a year, one should then offer praise.
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, I shall praise you, Vināyaka—
the great Gaṇapati, the heroic, the honored one who increases victory.
He has one tusk, two tusks, and four tusks; he has four arms, holds an axe and a trident in his hands, has blood-red eyes, and bestows boons.
This Āvikeya is of the color of a stake (śaṅku), fierce, the leader of the staff-bearers,
deep red, holding a staff, with a face like fire, and fond of oblations.
I bow to that leader of the Gaṇas, the son of Umā, who is formidable and fierce, and who creates obstacles for men in all their undertakings if he is not worshipped.
Madamatta Virūpākṣa, born from the mouth of Bhava,
resembling ten million suns and possessing a luster like red collyrium.
I pay homage to the wise, perfectly steady, and peaceful Vināyaka.
Homage be to you who have the form of Brahmā; homage to you who have the form of Viṣṇu!
Homage be to you who have the form of an elephant; homage to the Lord of elephants! Homage to you who have the form of Mount Meru and Mandara; homage to the dweller on Kailāsa!
Homage to the destroyer of obstacles! Homage to you, the celibate one!
Homage to you, the god praised by devotees! O Vināyaka, by you was the ancient [path] established for the accomplishment of the purpose of all the gods.
Having assumed the form of an elephant, all the Dānavas were terrified;
thus, the desires of both the sages and the deities were fulfilled.
Therefore, O son of Bhava, you are worshipped by the foremost of the gods;
having propitiated you, the leader of the Gaṇas, the omniscient one who can assume any form at will.

For the sake of accomplishing his purpose, wearing red garments and using red flowers and water infused with red sandalwood, he should perform recitation on the fourth lunar day while engaged in worship.
Whether three times a day or once a day, one who is disciplined and self-controlled [should approach] a king,
a prince, or indeed a royal minister.
Or the Lord of All Obstacles may bring the kingdom, together with its realm, under his control. O Vināyaka, the Lord of Obstacles, grant me constant freedom from obstacles!
"You have been praised by me with devotion and especially worshipped;
one obtains all that fruit by praising the god Vināyaka.
For such a person, no adversity shall arise, nor shall he suffer defeat."
No obstacle shall arise for him; having been born, he shall become one who remembers his past lives.
Whoever recites this hymn shall obtain a boon within six months.
Within one year he attains accomplishment; there is no doubt about this.
Thus ends the Gaṇeśa-caturthī vow as declared in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa. Sumantu said: O King, the auspicious and peaceful Caturthī for women is traditionally remembered as being of three kinds.
In the month of Bhādrapada, the bright fortnight is auspicious and honored by Lokeśa.
O King, bathing, giving gifts, fasting, and likewise recitation performed at that place becomes a hundredfold through the grace of the Elephant.
The gift of molasses, salt, and ghee is remembered as bringing auspiciousness;
likewise, O hero, the feeding of Brahmins with molasses cakes brings merit.
On the fourth day, O tiger among men, one should always honor women—
the mother-in-law, the father-in-law, and one's own mother— with offerings of molasses and salt.
By the favor of Vighneśa, all those women shall indeed become fortunate;
one should especially worship young maidens according to this rite.
Thus ends the Śivā-caturthī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Sumantu said: O Lord of the Earth, likewise, that which is the fourth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha—
She, the giver of all peace, shall indeed always bring about eternal peace.
O Lord, bathing, giving gifts, offerings, and every ritual act performed upon this [elephant] shall always become a thousandfold through the grace of Dantin.
O King, whoever observes a fast on that day and worships Vighnanāyaka,
for him all rites such as the fire-oblation (homa) shall become multiplied a thousandfold.
O descendant of Bharata, by offering salt filled with jaggery and smeared with ghee to Vighneśa after a meal, one obtains a thousandfold reward.
[514] O King, O Hero, O Joy of the Kurus, one should especially honor one's own guru, even women, with jaggery, salt, and ghee at all times.
Thus ends the Śānti-caturthī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa. Sumanas said: Listen to this auspicious rite, which brings happiness, bestows well-being, and grants good fortune.
O tiger among the Kurus, perform the fourth [rite], which is auspicious and bestows beauty and good fortune.
This vow of happiness is of great merit, bestowing beauty and health;
it is extremely subtle, easy to perform, auspicious, meritorious, and brings about bliss.
O Hero, it yields fruit in the hereafter and bestows a divine form;
it consists of grace, amorous play, coquetry, laughter, and auspicious gestures.
O descendant of the Kurus! By means of the vow of happiness, everything auspicious shall come to pass, once the Lord of Gods has been worshipped by the son of the King of Brahmins and Śiva.
When the day of Mars falls on the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight, then that fourth day should be known as "Sukhā" (the pleasant), for it is indeed the "Sukhā Caturthī."
O noble one, in ancient times, while Bhīma and Mā were staying on Mount Hima, having engaged in sexual union,
the sun and the moon fell to the earth.
O Great Hero, just as he was easily nourished by the earth through great effort, so too was he born upon her— red and arisen from the red.
Because he was produced by Umā from her menstrual flow (ārtava), he is indeed called Aṅgāraka;
he is also known as Aṅgada and Aṅgārakānti, for he is always the lord of the limbs (aṅga), O King.
Because he bestows good fortune and other blessings, he is considered Aṅgāraka;
indeed, whoever, endowed with faith, observes the fourth lunar day with devotion by eating only at night—
O King, a man or a woman who observes the fast with undistracted mind should worship Kuja with devotion, using red flowers and ointments.
And the true nature of Aṅgāraka is to be understood from the Aṅgāraka-caturthī-vrata described in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa with devotion and endowed with faith,
he, being pleased, shall bestow good fortune and the perfection of beauty.
O descendant of Bharata, having previously formed a resolution and performed his bath according to the prescribed rules, he should take up earth and worship it with this mantra:
In this world, you were indeed previously worshipped by Kṛṣṇa when he was lifting [the Govardhana mountain];
therefore, burn away my evil deeds that have been accumulated by me since long ago.
Reciting this mantra, the hero should show it to the Sun;
[the water] purified by the rays of the Sun and fit for drops of the Gaṅgā’s water.
Having placed that clay upon his head, he should apply it to all his limbs;
thereafter, he should perform his bath in auspicious water preceded by the recitation of mantras.
O Waters, you are all that have been gathered by the Daityas and Dānavas;
you are the sources of those born from sweat, from eggs, from sprouts, and from wombs.
I have bathed in all the sacred fords and in all the springs;
likewise in the holy sites such as Kāśī and in the lakes such as Mānasa.
Having bathed in various rivers and natural pools,
while meditating and reciting this mantra, one should then perform the ritual ablution.
Then, having bathed and become pure, and having returned home,
one who knows the mantras should touch a sacrificial ladle, an *aśvattha* tree, a *śamī* tree, and a cow, while reciting the mantra.
O Hero, having offered *dūrvā* grass with the mantra ending in "namaḥ," as well as a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree,
and then having beheld the cow, one should circumambulate the Goddess while offering salutations.
Having touched [the image] with his hand, he should then recite this mantra:
"O Goddess, you are Nirṛti, composed of all the gods; you have been worshipped.
Therefore, I touch you and I bow to you; being saluted, become the destroyer of my sins."
Having entered silently, she should worship the household deities;
then, having washed her feet with earth and sipped water for purification, she should enter the fire-chamber.
One should perform the fire-oblation there with these excellent mantra-words:
"To Sarva, to Sarvaputra, and to the son of Pārvatī."
To Kujā, to Lohitāṅga, and to Graheśa Aṅgāraka—
with mantras preceded by the syllable Oṃ and accompanied by the word Svāhā.
O Hero, O King, one hundred and eight times, or even half a measure,
with these mantra-words, out of devotion, whether intentionally or unintentionally.
With fuel-sticks of khadira wood, with barley and sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter,
and with various other kinds of edible foods, one should perform the rite according to one's ability, endowed with devotion.
[517] O Hero, having performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should then install the deity upon the ground—
whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, or of *bhadradāru* wood, O King.
It may also be made of devadāru wood or likewise fashioned from śrīkhaṇḍa (sandalwood).
The *bhadradāru* (deodar) is the *śarala*.
He should be worshipped with saffron filaments in a vessel made of gold or silver,
or otherwise with other auspicious red leaves, flowers, or even fruits.
O Hero, one may perform [the rite] with various red substances, or else do so out of devotion;
for as long as wealth and mind are maintained according to one's ability, O Hero.
The merit of the donor increases a hundred-thousandfold as long as a man worships with devotion and according to his ability a vessel made of copper, bamboo, or even clay, using saffron filaments.

Oṃ, homage to Aṅgāraka; [worship] the feet. Oṃ, homage to Kuñjara; the face. Oṃ, homage to Bhīma; the shoulders. Oṃ, homage to Maṅgala; the arms. Oṃ, homage to Vajra; the thighs. Oṃ, homage to Svedaja; the shanks. Homage to Nikha; [worship] the waist.
With these mantra-words, one should worship the anthropomorphic form in a concave vessel.
O Son of Earth, Great God, born from sweat, wielder of the Pināka bow!
Seeking form, I have taken refuge in you; accept this water offering; homage be to you!
The Arghya mantra:
O you who are born from the limbs of Mahādeva, born from the womb of the Earth;
O Aṅgāraka, Great King, Red-bodied One, homage be to you!
The mantra of petition:
A Brāhmaṇa who worships with fragrant flowers, incense, and other offerings,
[should present] jaggery-rice, ghee, milk, wheat, and *śāli* rice grains.

O King, having regard for his own capacity, one who has restrained his senses should indeed give to the Brāhmaṇas from his wealth; he should not practice stinginess regarding his riches while they are available. And by practicing stinginess regarding his wealth, he shall not partake in the fruit in the world hereafter.
Śatānīka said:
"Combined with Aṅgāraka (Mars), how many fourth lunar days are to be observed as fasts with eating only at night? Are they to be observed for a specific number of times, or indeed only once?"
Sumantu said:
When the fourth lunar day coincides with a Tuesday,
one should fast on that very day and offer worship to Mars (Kuja) according to the prescribed rites.
O Lord, having observed the fast at night on four occasions joined with Mars,
listen to what the procedure is for each of those fourth days.
One instance of the word "fourth" (caturthī) denotes a specific lunar day, while the other refers to the number four.
[The gift should be] ten gold pieces, or half of that, or even half of that again;
it may be placed with devotion in a vessel made of gold, silver, or even copper.
O Hero, the vessels should weigh twenty palas, or twenty and a half palas, or twenty karṣas; one should not have them made less than this.
According to one's means and with devotion, having established [the deity] even in a copper vessel or a hollowed-out wooden vessel,
one should wrap it with a red cloth.
Having fashioned a flower mandala and perfumed it with divine incenses,
one should worship the deity residing therein in due order with the previously mentioned mantras.
With many kinds of food and edibles, other esteemed fruits,
garments, coverings, vessels, beds, sandals, and excellent seats;

O King, one should give that [image] to a Brāhmaṇa along with an umbrella, flowers, and the finest perfumes, according to one's ability and in accordance with one's wealth, together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O mighty-armed one, [he gave] a cow endowed with good character, possessed of excellence, auspiciousness, and eloquence, and joined with Aṅgāraka.
Having given according to this rite, one shall partake of the fruit as described.
Thus, O Purāṇa, has been told to you that most excellent lunar day among all lunar days.
Having fasted there, O Bhārata, a man attains a divine form,
O Hero— one equal to Atri in beauty and possessing the splendor of the sun in brilliance.
Equal to Indra in splendor and always smiling with strength,
the king, having obtained such a boon, goes to the abode of Sīma.
"O King, by the grace of Gaṇeśa, the Lord of Obstacles, [the merit] is reckoned as that of the Gaṇas for those who read, listen, and especially perform [this work].
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed; of this there is no doubt. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the Sukha-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa:
"O Great King, on the fourth lunar day, one who observes the vow while fasting should give sesame-rice as a gift; he himself then eats only rice mixed with sesame."
[520] "He eats during the night while fasting by day"— this is the resolution of the contradiction.
When the accomplishment of the assembly occurs within two years,
Vināyaka, being pleased, grants him his desired fruit.
Thus ends the Gaṇapatī-caturthī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Skanda said:
"O Blessed One, by what vow may incomparable good fortune be attained?"
A person prospers in happiness through sons, grandsons, wealth, and sovereignty.
Tell me that, O Mahādeva, the supreme vow among vows,
by the performance of which, O Lord of Gods, a man attains a kingdom.
Even a woman born from the family of a slave may become like a queen;
a prince may conquer his enemies just as Garuḍa conquers the serpents.
A Brāhmaṇa, having attained the splendor of Brahman, becomes a worshiper of all;
even one who is devoid of caste and stage of life attains perfection.
The Lord said: Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the supreme among vows—
the unprecedented vow of Gaṇapati, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
In former times, this was practiced by the Blessed Lady Pārvatī together with Padmā,
Sarasvatī, Mahendra, Viṣṇu, and Dhanada.
O Six-faced One, in a former age, all these other gods, sages, gandharvas, and kinnaras likewise observed this vow;
it is the fourth lunar day of the month of Nabhas that is declared to be merit-bestowing.
O Six-faced One, on that day, or on the full moon of Kārttika, one should observe this vow:
[one should worship] Gajānana, who has four arms, a single tusk, and is Vipāṭin.

Having fashioned weapons that split asunder and flow with rut-fluid, like those prescribed for the difficult fourth-day vow, he [should worship] Vighneśa with gold, seated upon a golden-yellow throne; likewise,
a golden *dūrvā* grass placed upon its base—
that is, upon the seat of Vighneśa.
Having installed the Destroyer of Obstacles (Vighnahantṛ) in a copper vessel within the *sarvatobhadra* mandala, it should be wrapped with a red cloth.
One should worship with white flowers and five types of leaves:
the bilva leaf, apāmārga, śamī, dūrvā, and haripriyā.

*Tulasī* is the beloved of Hari. These indeed are the five leaves (*pañcapatrikā*). Afterwards, one should prepare an offering (*upahāra*) with other fragrant flowers, fragrant leaves, fruits, and sweetmeats (*modaka*).
And one should worship the Son of the Mountain-Dweller with offerings according to the prescribed rites.
The invocation mantra:
O son of Umā, salutations to you, the eternal one who pervades the universe!
Cut asunder the entire multitude of obstacles; I offer to you water for the feet and the respectful oblation (arghya).
The Arghya-mantra:
To the Lord of the Gaṇas, the God, the Son of Umā, the Creator—I now offer this worship; accept it, O Blessed One, salutations!
The incense mantra:
Homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas, the God who grants boons, the Elephant-faced One;
homage to the Son of Umā, the God, the Preceptor of Kumāra.
To the pot-bellied hero, the dispeller of all obstacles.
The Flower Mantra:
May that Lord who sustains all beings, having manifested as Umā and Maṅgala for the sake of slaying the Dānavas and for the grace of the worlds, protect us.
The incense mantra:
To you, the manifestation of supreme light, the bestower of all accomplishments, I offer this lamp; salutations to the Great God, the Self.
The mantra of the lamp: Like Gaṇapati among the hosts, like the great poet among poets,

he who has heard the secret counsel, the eldest, the one with supreme passion, the most eminent Brahmin among Brahmins— he who hears with his splendors as he bestows the fruits of perfection upon the Siddhas.
The mantra for the offering:
O Lord of the Gaṇas, Chief of the Gaṇas, Son of Gaurī, Elephant-faced One!
By Your grace, may this vow reach completion for me, the seeker.

[523] This is the mantra of petition: Having thus worshipped Vighneśa with extensive offerings according to one's means, one should present the presiding Gaṇa, together with his appurtenances, to the preceptor (ācārya).
"Accept, O Blessed One, O Brahmā, O King of the Gaṇas, this circumambulation!
By his word, may this vow, O observer of good vows, reach completion today."
The mantra for the gift:
"Thus, he who performs the concluding rite after practicing this for five years obtains his desired objects and, at the end of the body, the state of Śaṅkara."
Alternatively, one who possesses pure wisdom and has restrained senses should practice thus for three years starting from the fourth [day]; thereby, he shall attain all accomplishments.
One who performs this supreme vow for Vināyaka must perform the morning bath with white sesame seeds, O Six-faced One, without the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati out of gold or even silver,
the wise man should bathe it with the five products of the cow and worship it thoroughly with dūrvā grass.

O Śikhidhvaja, with devotion, one should perform a bath using the ten mantras accompanied by *dūrvā* grass and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) accompanied by *dūrvā*. The worship is performed with the ten mantras, each mantra being recited ten times.
Thus has been told, O child, this auspicious rite which bestows all accomplishments.
This is the vow of Gaṇapati with dūrvā grass; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus is described the Dūrvā-Gaṇapati-vrata as stated in the Saura Purāṇa:
by worshipping Yama on a Thursday that falls on the fourth lunar day (caturthī) under the asterism Bharaṇī,
a man is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes.
Thus ends the Yamavrata as declared in the Kūrma Purāṇa. Agastya said:
"Now, O sinless King, I shall describe to you the vow that removes obstacles."
By performing this correctly here, no obstacle arises.

On the fourth lunar day in the month of Phālguna, O King of Kings, this vow should be undertaken; eating only at night, the breaking of the fast is prescribed with an offering of sesame seeds and rice.
The breaking of the fast consists of eating only at night. That very food should be offered into the fire, and it should also be given to a Brāhmaṇa,
as well as to the divine, heroic Gajānana.
Salutations to Śiva, whose fangs are formidable;
who arises from the bodily impurity of the Daughter of the Mountain;
who holds Kumāra in his hand; and who moves through the sky.
Having thus worshipped with the *manus* (mantras), one should perform the *homa* according to the rule.

"With the *manus*" means with the mantras. I shall state the multiplicity of what is in fact singular; I shall explain the *homa*: the *homa-mantra*, the *homa-substance*, and that which is to be offered into the fire, and so forth. Here, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used for the past, as it occurs in proximity to the present.
Having likewise observed the four-month vow in this manner during the fifth [month],
one should have an image made of either gold or silver and cause it to be given to a Brahmin.
O King, it should be placed in a copper vessel together with four items such as milk-rice (pāyasa),
and with a fifth item, sesame seeds, which brings peace to the Gaṇas.
One should have [the vessels] made of clay or green stones according to this procedure;
and one should cause a silver [vessel] to be offered according to this procedure, with a fire-oblation (homa) performed according to one's capacity.
Having performed this vow in this manner, one is liberated from all obstacles;
as occurred in ancient times when the horse-sacrifice was being performed by Sagara.
Hara employed this very [weapon] by which he destroyed Tripura;
it was also this very vow that I undertook during the churning of the ocean.
This very same [rite] was performed by other rulers of the earth in the past;
therefore, for the sake of unimpeded success, the supreme pacification of obstacles [should be performed].
By the mere performance of this, one is liberated from all obstacles;
thereafter, one goes to the city of Rudra, according to the word of Varāha.

No obstacles ever arise in the home of one who [worships] that which is proud with a beauty like the crescent of the moon on the seventh day— obstacles that would thwart the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and happiness.
The virtuous one worships Vighneśa at night on the fourth lunar day.
Thus ends the vow to Avighnavināyaka as declared in the Varāha Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
When the month of Māgha has arrived, there is the fourth lunar day known as Kunda.
O best of gods, after he has been nourished, the kingdom will then be his.
One should bring all necessary offerings and every kind of utensil;
as well as food cooked in an earthen pot, fruit, vegetables, salt, molasses, and sugar.
O best of the Raghus, sugar-candy, cumin, coriander, and various grains should be given with devotion to the young girls.
Sugar-candy is a variety of sugar;
likewise, one should cause vessels made of clay, especially those for the sun, to be given with the intent: "May the Goddess be pleased with me always."
By this method, O Śakra, good fortune and the lineage of sons increase;
there is no doubt in this matter, for my word cannot be otherwise.
Thus ends the vow of the Kundacaturthī as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
The sages said:
"O son of Sūta, how may one's undertakings be accomplished without obstacles?"
How could there be a lack of renown for men’s sons, good fortune, and prosperity?
When a couple is at strife, when there is a rift among kinsmen,
and when people in the world remain indifferent— how can one gain their favor?
Likewise, regarding the commencement of learning for men, as well as trade and agriculture,
and how the success of victory over an enemy king may be achieved— [how can these be determined]?
"Which deity, when saluted, brings about the success of worship for men?
Sūta said:
"O Brahmins, formerly, when the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas were arrayed for battle..."
Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira questioned the son of Devakī.
"O Lord, tell me how their victory may indeed be unimpeded;
by bowing to which deity did they obtain the entire earth?"
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Worship Gaṇādhyakṣa, the Lord of Obstacles, who bestows success.
O King, when he is fully worshipped, one shall attain all desires.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord, by what rite is the Lord of the Gaṇas worthy of worship? On which lunar day, when worshipped, does the Lord of the Gaṇas become the bestower of success?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, one should worship the elephant-faced [Ganeśa] on the fourth day of the bright fortnight;
or whenever devotion arises, the Lord of the Gaṇas should be worshipped during that month.
Having bathed with white sesame seeds in the morning, O King, one should worship Gaṇanātha at midday according to one's means, using an image made of gold or silver.
Having performed worship with diligence and having bathed [the deity] individually with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
one should indeed offer perfume with devotion under the name "Gaṇādhyakṣa."

"O Vināyaka," [with these words] one offers flowers and incense; "O son of Umā," [with these words] a lamp; "O beloved of Rudra, O destroyer of obstacles," [with these words] the food offering (naivedya).
One should offer clothing that is red in all its parts and flowers covered with auspicious substances;
then, taking twenty-one blades of dūrvā grass and kuśa grass.
One should worship with effort, individually, by means of these names:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, homage be to you, O son of Umā, destroyer of sins!"
O Vināyaka, son of Īśa, bestower of all accomplishments;
O single-tusked one with the face of an elephant, salutations to you whose vehicle is the mouse!
One should worship with diligence, ending with the words "to the Preceptor of Kumāra.
Having taken two blades of dūrvā grass together with fragrant substances, one should perform the worship.
One should worship with each individual name, and with one [name] from all [of them];

with one *dūrvā* sprout, and with the remaining pair [of names]. "From all" means the worship should be performed with all the names. Likewise, having taken twenty-one sweetmeats (*modaka*) cooked in ghee.
Having established the leader of the host nearby, O joy of the Kurus.
O best of kings, ten [offerings] should be given to a Brahmin, and likewise one should eat ten oneself;
one should give one, along with the sacrificial food (naivedya), to the Lord of the Gaṇas.
One should give food to a Brahmin and eat it without oil;
having performed the occasional rites, one should worship one's chosen deity.
O Dharmarāja, when the worship of the Lord of Obstacles is performed in this manner, victory shall be yours; what I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.
One who desires knowledge shall obtain knowledge, and one who desires wealth shall obtain wealth;
likewise, one who desires victory shall attain victory, and one who seeks sons shall find sons.
A woman desiring a husband, a young wife desiring good fortune,
and a widow— by worshipping [her], shall never again encounter widowhood.
In initiations such as those of the Vaiṣṇavas and others, Gaṇādhipa is to be worshipped first;
for when he is fully worshipped, Viṣṇu, Īśa, Bhānu, and Umā likewise [become pleased].
The gods, headed by Agni (Havyavāha), will undoubtedly be honored,
and the hosts of Mothers, beginning with Caṇḍikā, will become thoroughly gratified.
When Siddhivināyaka has been worshipped with devotion, those brahmins who would constantly hear this or cause it to be heard with a concentrated mind [attain success].
"All undertakings are accomplished through the grace of Siddhidātṛ.
Thus concludes the vow to Siddhivināyaka as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Now follows another ritual procedure for this same day, as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
"In the month of Bhādrapada, the bright fortnight is honored in the world of Śiva. On that day, bathing, giving gifts, fasting, and likewise worship—
whatever is performed, O King, becomes a hundredfold through the grace of Dattin."
The word "fourth" (caturthī) is to be supplied here [from the previous verse]. On this day, one must not look at the moon. For this very reason, it was stated by Mārkaṇḍeya:
"If the moon is seen on the fourth day of the bright fortnight when the sun is in Leo, it causes a false accusation; therefore, one should not look at it then."
Also in the Parāśara-smṛti:
"If the sun is in Virgo on the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight, the moon will be visible;
this would constitute a false accusation [of impurity], therefore one should not look at it then."

In this context, by the terms *siṃhāditya* and *kanyāditya*, the lunar month of Bhādrapada is understood, because if the solar month were taken, it would result in a contradiction with the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). To pacify any fault, one should recite: "The lion killed Prasena. And that verse is found in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"The lion killed Prasena; the lion was slain by Jāmbavanta."
"You shall weep for your delicate child, for this is indeed the Syamantaka.
Then, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, there is the Nāga-vrata as described in the Kūrma Purāṇa,
beginning from the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
Having fasted according to the prescribed rites on the lunar day called Yugā,
one should [worship] the great-souled Śeṣa and the other Nāgas, beginning with Śaṅkhapāla.

"Worship should be performed preceded by offerings of flowers, perfumes, and milk. This [rite] should be performed on the fourth lunar day named after the Yuga (the Kṛtayuga), which extends from morning until midday. Likewise, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Having fasted there on that [fourth] at both morning and midday, a self-restrained man should nourish the lords of the serpents with milk and break his fast on the fifth day."
His poisons perish, for there are no serpents for him.
Thus ends the Nāga-vrata.
Now follows the Vara-caturthī-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa, beginning on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa:
"O best of kings, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa..."
And having begun every month on the fourth lunar day, one should worship Gaṇanāyaka.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should, with a concentrated mind, observe the practice of eating only one meal a day, avoiding pungent and salty foods; thus it continues for a full year.
Then, in the second year, one should perform the rite at night on every fourth lunar day after worshipping Gaṇeśa; likewise, in the third year, one should observe the "unbegged" (ayācita) vow.
In this very manner one should perform the practice; on the fourth day there should be a fast.
Then, when that fourth day is complete, one should perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*).
This vow, known as the Varacaturthī, accomplishes all goals.
Thus ends the vow of Varacaturthī as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Now, on this very same day, is the Gaurīcaturthī vow as declared in the Brahma Purāṇa:
"On Umācaturthī, in the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, together with the hosts of Yoginīs..."
Having first consumed [them] and then emitted them again from his own body by means of his own qualities.
Therefore, she should be worshipped there by men and especially by women,
with great effort and perfect devotion, using jasmine flowers and with concentrated minds.
And with [the two hands] smeared with saffron, with red threads together with bracelets,
as well as with water-offerings (argha), flowers, incense, lamps, and indeed with sacrificial oblations (bali).
Women and widows, as well as auspicious Brahmins, should be honored by the guardians with half-portions of molasses, jackfruit, and lavalī.
"Afterwards, for the increase of good fortune, it should be consumed together with one's kinsmen"—
this refers to *pālaka* ear-rings, meaning specific types of earthen vessels.
Thus ends the Gaurī-caturthī-vrata.
Salt, coriander, cumin, black pepper,
asafoetida, ginger, turmeric, and likewise all the other condiments.
On the fourth day, O Bhārata, having eaten only one meal and having given food once to a householder, he likewise places stones upon seven houses.
[532] *Śilā* means realgar (*manaḥśilā*). This is the vow known as the *Śilā-vrata*, which bestows the world of Lakṣmī.
Thus ends the *Śilā-vrata* as described in the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
On the fourth lunar day, one should eat only at night and, at the end of the year, donate a golden elephant—
*vāraṇaḥ* meaning an elephant.
This vow, named Vaināyaka, bestows the pacification of all obstacles.
Thus ends the Vaināyaka-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
O sinless one, I shall describe to you the vow known as Vināyaka-caturthī.
It brings merit, fame, and long life, and bestows the fruits of one's desires.
It is capable of pacifying obstacles, bestows all accomplishments,
is eternally dear to Gaṇapati, and is worshipped by the sages as well.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, this great vow should be undertaken;
O best of Brahmins, it is prescribed that one should eat only at night, and the breaking of the fast consists of rice mixed with sesame seeds.
That very offering should always be cast into the fire or given to a Brāhmaṇa;
or, being self-restrained, the practitioner should offer the naivedya to Vighnarāja in a river or a stream.
One should worship Gaṇapati at night with perfumes and flowers in the proper sequence;
he should be worshipped as established within a water-pot, having been installed with saffron-water.
[533] Then, one should worship them with those names beginning with Sumārga:
Vināyaka, Ekadanta, Kṛṣṇapiṅga, and Gajānana.
Lambodara, Bālacandra, Heramba, Vikaṭa,
Vakratuṇḍa, Ākhuratha, Vighnarāja, and Gaṇādhipa.
Having thus performed the recitation, the fire-oblation, and the worship according to the name of the month,
the devotee should afterwards make a petition with this mantra:
Salutation indeed to the hero who has two mothers and holds an axe in his hand;
salutation to the Lord of Obstacles who has a single tusk, and salutation to the one with a protruding belly.
Salutations to you, the elephant-faced one, the omniscient one, who possesses eight forms;
grant me always freedom from obstacles in the attainment of my desired goals.
Having fed the Brahmins according to his ability and without envy,
he himself should then eat at night, restrained in speech and not disparaging the food.
The Veda enjoins that everyone must eat both morning and evening;
therefore, eating only once [a day] is superior to that, and fasting is even more so.
Alms-gathering is superior to fasting; not asking for alms is superior to alms-gathering;
eating at night is superior to not asking for alms; therefore, eating at night constitutes true austerity.
The gods eat in the forenoon, humans likewise at midday,
the ancestors in the afternoon, and the pretas and rākṣasas at twilight.
And whoever, having passed these times, should eat at night,
he shall obtain that merit which belongs to all those [deities] when they have been fully gratified.
One who eats only at night should practice eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), bathing, moderation in diet, sleeping on the ground, and sleeping on a low bed for the sake of spiritual merit.
Thus, at the end of the year, when the vow is complete, O Gajānana,
here too on the Kṛcchra-Caturthī day, an image of the form described above should be fashioned out of gold or silver and diligently consecrated.
With twelve vessels made of copper, or else of clay or bamboo.
In the morning, one should cause a Brahmin to receive gifts filled with sesame seeds and modakas;
and according to the prescribed rite, one should devoutly give a bull together with a cow.
One should then feed the Brahmins, free from stinginess regarding wealth, providing them with food endowed with the eight qualities and accompanied by the seven types of grain.
Having observed this vow in this manner, one is liberated from all obstacles;
one always attains knowledge, prosperity, fame, and happiness in their entirety.
One without a son obtains a son; the poor man obtains supreme wealth;
one desiring a daughter obtains a daughter, and in the hereafter, an auspicious destiny.
In this regard, an ancient account is heard concerning the means consisting of flowers, incense, and so forth,
as well as jasmine, red saṃbhoga, jāti, and tagara.
O Nārada, these flowers— the *puṣpikā*, the *ketakī*, and the golden forest-flowers (*vānasuvarṇa*)— should be offered every month.
In the absence of fruits as well, the citron (bījapūra) is recommended;
but in the absence of the aforementioned flowers, the hundred-petaled lotus (śatapatra) is distinguished as superior.
The coconut, the citron, the orange, the pomegranate,
as well as the wood-apple and likewise the mango.

At the time of offering the guest-water (argha), one should employ, in this sequence, the fruit of the milk-tree (kṣīrī), the āmalaka, the pumpkin (kuṣmāṇḍa), the cucumber (trapuṣa), and likewise the bhūmīphala.
O single-tusked one, O great-tusked one, son of Gaurī, Lord of the Gaṇas!
Accept this *argha* for the sake of the worship of the vow on the fourth day; salutations be unto you.
The *argha* mantra:
Having taken a hundred-petaled lotus, as well as a *kuṇḍa*, *maruka*, *kaṅkaṇa*, *vīraka*, a large *vinda*, and *vakula* and *aśoka* flowers, one should then perform worship.
He increases his wealth, he prospers in this world through dharma, he accomplishes his desires, and he grinds away his evil—
he who worships the lotus-feet praised by all the worlds.
The primordial deity, the son of Gaurī, whose belly is filled with nectar.

And no obstacles ever arise in the home of one who recites the seventh [chapter], which possesses the beauty of its difficult-to-perceive syllables and bestows the accomplishment of dharma, wealth, desire, and happiness.
On the fourth lunar day, that virtuous person worships Vighnesha.
Whether she be a widow, a married woman, or a maiden, whatever woman observes the fourth lunar day— which bestows bliss and removes all sins—
she shall experience hundreds of joys in her own home and thereafter...
He joyfully proceeds to the abode of Heramba and the Mothers.
And thus, whoever performs this fourth day of Vaināyaka, which bestows boons, shall possess various sons, happiness, beauty, and fame—
[the merit] of Śambhu, whose crest is marked by the crescent moon.
He attains that state which is the very nature of supreme and absolute bliss.
May mortals, having once approached and worshipped the Elder Gaṇapati at Jayantī, be cleansed of their faults;
those blessed ones shall go here to the presence of the Primordial Elephant-Faced One.
Being delighted by the eyes of the women of the city of the gods.
Thus ends the vow of the Night-time Caturthī (Nakta-caturthī-vrata) as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.

Thus concludes [the section] in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Hemādri— the sovereign over all faculties, a master of all branches of knowledge, and the great king of kings— under the auspices of the illustrious Mahādeva.
In the section on Vows (Vratakhaṇḍa), the Vows of the Fourth Day.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Now, the vows of the fifth [lunar day]:
The mind, out of an excess of joy, assumes the graceful form of a most nectar-sweet bee settled upon the pair of lotus-feet of Lakṣmī’s Beloved.
By that Hemādri, whose expansive intellect shines forth,
these vows— which yield abundant fruit— are here set forth for the fifth lunar days.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord, tell me how that prosperity which is difficult even for the gods to attain may be obtained—
whether by gift, by austerity, or even by a vow.
"O best of the Yadus, tell me this, for my mind is inclined toward your omniscience: [is liberation attained] through recitations, burnt offerings, prostrations, or various other purificatory rites?"
Kṛṣṇa said:
Formerly, an auspicious woman, renowned as the daughter of Bhṛgu, was born to the Lord of Śrī;
she was given by the sage to Vāsudeva for my own prosperity.
Vāsudeva, too, having obtained her— she whose breasts were full and elevated,
whose eyes were as broad as lotus petals, and whose face resembled the full moon— [remained with her].
O King, he took delight with me, who illuminated the expanse of the quarters like the radiance of the sun,
who possessed the splendor of rounded hips and the gait of an elephant in rut,
while lost in thoughts of amorous playfulness.
And she, Mānayaśodharā, having obtained as her husband Viṣṇu, the conqueror of the world and the lord of the glorious worlds, considered herself to have achieved her life's purpose.
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! O Blessed One, the entire world is sustained by you;
look upon me with protection, as the earth is nourished by a timely rain on the fifth day.
Having established security, abundance of food, freedom from distress, and health, water arises from the essence; from that, one should offer oblation into the fire.
O Pārtha, the four castes, even when mixed, are protected by kings,
as was seen by the foremost Daityas such as Virocana and others.
Then, having resorted to Agni— who is to be worshipped through asceticism— with self-restraints,
[he performed] sacrifices consisting of the Soma-offerings, the Havis-offerings, the Pāka-offerings, and so forth.
Having honored them with proper conduct, those gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas— who were foremost in the five dharmas and who practiced various forms of mendicancy— [remained there].
The world was pervaded by valor and gradual progression;
and the gods were ever intoxicated by the power arising from the play of Fortune.
Virtue, happiness, truth, and prosperity immediately reside in the home of the righteous;
yet the fickle Goddess of Fortune abandons those who are devoid of truth and purity.
Driven by their devotion to the false gods, those whose bodies were permeated by the influence of Lakṣmī went to the city of Vākula with haughty minds.
Arrogant with pride, they have begun to conduct themselves according to the logic of the Dāmanas, claiming:
"We are the gods, we are the sacrifices, we are the brahmins, we are the world."
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śakra, and the rest of us, all the inhabitants of heaven—having recognized those foremost of Dānavas as being utterly deluded by egoism; [539]
With her mind bewildered, the daughter of Bhṛgu searched for the son of Pṛthā in the waters of the ocean;
she found him who had reached the midst of the Milky Ocean, his wealth and resources exhausted.
The three worlds became devoid of pride and bereft of splendor;
then, perceiving himself to be shorn of his glory, the slayer of Śambara [reflected].
He asked the brahmin Aṅgiras: "Tell me of some vow by which prosperity may be attained, and once obtained, it shall never waver again."
O Sage, even though she is motionless, she is to be enjoyed by friends and well-wishers;
she should not be considered a woman, for she is a maiden who is protected within the home.
"That which for the sake of others cannot even be equaled by well-wishers, friends, or servants"—
having heard these words of Śakra, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati reflected and recounted the auspicious Śrīpañcamī vow.
That supreme vow among vows, which was never before spoken to anyone, I have now related in its entirety, together with its secret mysteries.
Having heard that, the best of men,
along with the Daityas, Dānavas, and Gandharvas, whose sins had been destroyed by sacrifices, began to perform that auspicious rite.
Together with Siddhas of celebrated conduct, with the all-powerful Viṣṇu, with Brāhmaṇas who know the reality of Brahman, with capable kings,
and with some who were of a sattvic nature and others even of a rājasic nature.
O Lord, some have likewise performed this vow characterized by darkness (tamas),
yet with supreme steadfastness in that vow which consists mostly of austerity.
In battle between the gods and the dānavas, there was unfailing success.
Having churned the ocean, the lord of rivers, with the strength of our arms,
we indeed recovered the nectar, leaving behind the denizens of heaven who were striving for it.
Having made this agreement, they churned the abode of Varuṇa,
using Mount Mandara as the churning staff and Vāsuki as the rope.
While the waters were being churned, the cool-rayed, radiant moon was born from the water;
immediately thereafter, Lakṣmī emerged from the midst of the ocean of milk.
Beheld by her, all the foremost among the Daityas and Dānavas looked toward that auspicious chest of Viṣṇu; having seen them,
she [the goddess] was born from the ocean because of that vow performed by Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rite.
Remaining within his body, she became one whose eyes were wandering in confusion;
for this was brought about by Śakra himself through the nature of the Rājasa state.
By that [merit], he attained the sovereignty of heaven with great supernatural power;
yet it was practiced by the Daityas and Dānavas whose minds were shrouded in darkness.
By that, their sovereignty was indeed destroyed as soon as it was attained;
thus he became forever possessed of both divine and human splendor.
O best among the worlds, by the power of this vow, you are preeminent in the world.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, how is this vow performed by men, and when? O Pārtha, at what time is it commenced? Tell me everything, O Janārdana.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, listen now to the Śrīpañcamī vow, which was formerly practiced by Indra when he was deprived of his fortune; it indeed bestows the abundance of prosperity.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the festival of the serpents,
one should observe the vow of fasting and meditate upon Padmā in one's heart.
O protector of the earth, one should have the goddess Lakṣmī fashioned according to one's means from gold, silver, copper, clay, or wood, or depicted upon a painted canvas.
Seated in the lotus posture, holding a lotus in her hand, she is Padmā, whose eyes are like lotus petals;
she is being bathed by the lords of the elephants of the quarters with excellent golden jars.

The creation of the form of Lakṣmī should be understood as described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. It is as follows: "O illustrious one, Śrī should be depicted as arisen, auspicious, with a conch and a lotus in her hands; she is comfortably seated upon a lotus, possessing a lotus in her hand, and beautiful."
She has two arms, her every limb is beautiful, and she is adorned with all ornaments;
furthermore, two auspicious Vidyādharas should be made holding roots upon her head.
Then, when three watches of the night have passed, [one should perform the rite] with earth from a river or otherwise.
One should perform the bath without agitation, according to one's capacity and with proper ritual service.
Having gratified the gods and the ancestors, one should then proceed to the temple of the deity;
there, one should worship the Goddess with flowers appropriate for that season.
Salutations to Capalā for the feet, and to Cañcalā for the knees;
salutations to Kamalavāsinī for the hips, and repeated salutations to Khyāti for the navel.
The two breasts [are offered] to Manmathavāsinī; the two arms to Lalitā;
the neck to Utkaṇṭhitā; and the lotus-face to Mādhavī.
Having worshipped the head with "Obeisance to Śrī," one should respectfully offer the food offering (naivedya),
as well as fruits according to availability and a collection of sprouted grains.
Then the *svavāsinī* should be honored with saffron and flowers;
one should feed her sweet food, prostrate before her, and then bid her farewell.
Then, one prastha of rice accompanied by a vessel of ghee should be given to a Brāhmaṇa with the words: "May that Śrī be pleased with me."
Having completed this entirely, one should then eat while restraining one's speech;
O Bhārata, this should be performed month after month according to this rule.
Śrī, Lakṣmī, Kamalā, Saṃpad, Padmā, and likewise Nārāyaṇī;
Padmadhṛti, Sthiti, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Siddhi, and Kṣamā follow in sequence.
Month after month, O Indra among kings, one should proclaim, "May [the deity] be pleased.
Then, when the twelfth month has arrived, on the fifth day—
Having adorned her with garments and perfumed her with flowers, incense, and the like,
one should place Lakṣmī upon the bed, accompanied by all ritual requisites.
Endowed with the eight auspicious symbols, her breasts covered by a silk veil,
accompanied by the seven grains, and provided with the essences and minerals.
Having duly worshipped the Goddess, who is adorned with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, a vessel, and a seat, [he should give her] to a Brahmin who has a family.
To Vyāsa, the knower of the Vedas, or to whomever he himself may please,
one should give a cow along with its calf and all its appurtenances, and ask for forgiveness.
O Goddess, who emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk and whose abode is the chest of Viṣṇu; O granter of all desires, grant me success—salutations be unto you!
Then, having honored the women living with her with fine garments and auspicious ornaments,
and having fed them, she herself should afterwards eat together with her kinsmen.
O Pārtha, for one who thus performs the Śrīpañcamī vow with devotion,
prosperity shines in their home for twenty-one generations.
But a woman who performs it, having obtained permission from her own husband,
becomes fortunate, beautiful, and the mother of many sons.
He who, having worshipped the daughter of Bhṛgu, performs with devotion this beloved Pañcamī vow of Murāri,
shall enjoy on earth the glory of sovereignty fit for noble people.
Having eaten, he goes to the abode of Madhusūdana.
Thus ends the Śrīpañcamī-vrata as declared in the Śrībhaviṣya-purāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Bhārata, I shall proclaim to you the greatness of the Pañcamī.
She who is renowned as Jaya, the bestower of victory upon those who observe vows.
Because wise practitioners of vows utter the words "victory" and "defeat" on this day,
it should be known as Jayapañcamī, in which the vow is fully perfected.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Pāpanāśinī.
It is the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
Keśava, the Blessed One, Śambhu, as well as the Gaṅgā and other rivers,
the holy sites beginning with Prabhāsa, and the lakes of Jambūdvīpa [are all present].
Let those observing the vow bathe at Prayāga, Puṣkara, the Gaṅgā, and the field of Gayā,
as well as these and other sacred fords.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform a ritual bath on the day of Jayā and other such occasions;
one should bathe many twice-born men with oil and fragrant unguents.
Having gone to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) or a spring (prasravaṇa), one should personally bathe Hari;
the meaning is that he is accompanied by Jayā.
[He is to be visualized] with the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, and Jayā standing on his left side.
White in complexion, seated upon a swan, and with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should worship with various flowers, incense, food offerings, and so forth;
and with these mantras, one should worship that deity and Jayā as well.
To Padmanābha for the two feet, and to Mādhava for the two knees;
to Nārasiṃha for the two thighs, and to Manmatha for the middle.
"To Dāmodara," [he says] for the belly; "to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa," for the eye;
"to Śrīkaṇṭha," for the throat; or "to the bearer of all weapons," for the arms.
"Salutation to the lotus-faced one for the face; salutation to the Soul of All for the head. By this very rite, one should worship the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship that Goddess who is seated upon a bamboo vessel and positioned beneath a jasmine creeper.
Salutation to Puṣṭi at the pair of feet, and salutation to Śrī at the two knees;
salutation to Nadā in the region of the hips, and to Vijayā at the chest.
Having worshipped Śiras on the forehead for the sake of bestowing all goals, and likewise Vijayā on all the limbs according to this rite, one should worship Vijayā and Hari.
Oṃ! Victory to Jayā, victory to the one whose form is victory, victory to the one who has the form of Govinda; victory to Dāmodara—victory! Homage be to you.
The Arghya Mantra:
Having worshipped all the bamboo vessels filled with the seven grains and bound with red thread, one should present them along with fruits.
Just as the Lord whose abode is honey is pleased upon seeing a bamboo fruit,
so too shall all my misfortune vanish through the gift of this bamboo vessel.
The mantra for the gift of a bamboo vessel:
Having given the vessels according to this very rite to a *gosura*—
that is, to a *brāhmaṇa* who is a *gosura*.
Therefore, one should perform the binding of the protective amulet (rakṣābandha) for friends, kinsmen, and relatives;
within the protection, there should be unhusked grains, mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, and yellow pigment (rocanā).
Oṃ! With that [cord] by which the mighty King Bali, the lord of the Dānavas, was bound—by that I bind you swiftly, O Rakṣasī! Do not move! Do not move!
The mantra for binding the protective thread:
"That man who, endowed with devotion, performs the binding of the protective thread,
shall suffer no affliction from the planets, nor shall there be any fear of death."
One is not overcome by spirits, vetālas, rākṣasas, or piśācas;
indeed, he who enters into battle after performing this binding protection shall remain unvanquished.
He conquers all enemies and is not conquered by anyone;
therefore, one should have the protective binding performed with every effort.
But for one who, endowed with devotion, performs a bath on a day such as Jayā,
how could there be any sins for him, just as they are washed away by the flood of the month of Māgha?
A wise person should cause such a rite to be performed as the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice;
indeed, a handful of water is cast by the observer of the vow upon its head.
One is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this matter.
A sonless man obtains sons, and a barren woman conceives a child.
The sick person shall be liberated from diseases and goes to the abode of Hari.
Thus ends the Jayā-pañcamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Bharadvāja said:
"O Brahmin, tell me the procedure for this supreme vow of the fifth day."
This is that very majesty which rains down all desires.
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O Blessed One, I shall describe the supreme ritual of the fifth [tithi],
by the mere hearing of which a person is liberated from sin.
When the fifth day of the bright fortnight is conjoined with the Śravaṇa nakṣatra,
and on that day there is the conjunction of the moon with the Uttaraphālgunī nakṣatra and a Monday;
A man who has previously fasted should undertake the vow on that [day];
on the fourth lunar day, he should eat only one meal, remain celibate, and keep his senses subdued.
A man should be full of devotion, firm in his resolve, and observant of his vows;
then, having risen at dawn and bathed with a restrained mind, he should proceed.
With his wife, who has maintained her resolve, he should perform the worship of the *bilva* tree;
then, at the root of the *bilva*, he should prepare an altar provided with flowers and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
One should place eight jars in the eight directions within that [area],
and in its center, one should place great jars made of the root of the *bilva* tree,
or of gold, silver, copper, or clay, well-endowed with auspicious qualities.
One should cover it with a pair of garments and provide it with the nine jewels; likewise, one should prepare water-pots filled with water from sacred fords.
Dūrvā grass, viṣṇuparṇī, śrīlatā, white lotus, śāla leaf, apāmārga, tulasī, and also jasmine.
Viṣṇuparṇī is praśniparṇī; śrīlatā is padminī. Śālapatra is the leaf of the śāla tree.
Now, the fruits of the bilva, āmra, tāla, tinduka, dhātrī, and rambhā:
among these, tinduka is the fruit of the ṭiburuṇī.
Jambū, panasa, jātī, buddhi, śakti, sarasvatī,
śraddhā, lakṣmī, dhṛti, tuṣṭi, and puṣṭi— these are the eight powers (śaktis).
Elā, sarṣapa, kakkola, tila, karpūra, and padmaka.
Padmaka is a specific type of tree. One of great intelligence should cast all these substances— lodhra combined with māṃsī— into the jars, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
But in the middle [pit], one should place everything that was previously mentioned, such as the ladle and so forth;
then, there [one should worship] the Goddess Śrī, accompanied by her eight powers.
Having invoked [the deity] with the Śrī-bīja, one should perform the worship and other rites therein;
thus, they know that for all [deities], the invocation is performed with the seed-syllable (bīja) of their respective Śaktis.
The seed-syllable (bīja) consisting of the first letter of one's own name, joined with the anusvāra,
one should properly perform worship there at each respective place according to the prescribed rite.
With *śrīlatā*, *jāti*, and *bakula* flowers, with *nandyāvarta* blossoms—
where *nandyāvarta* refers to *tagara*—
and with *elāpatra*, white *bhoja*, and *mallikā* flowers;
A wise person should worship the goddess Śrī with the Śrīsūkta, reciting it verse by verse.

One should worship the Goddess Śrī with the *Śrīsūkta*, beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāṃ hariṇīm," and with offerings of molasses, cooked rice, milk-rice, cakes, mung-bean porridge, curd, śāli rice, milk, and sweet foods.
The worship of the powers such as intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth is performed with name-mantras.
Having done this according to the proper application, one should then choose a boon:
"O Goddess, whose eyes are like lotus petals, salutations to you, O beloved of Śrīdhara!"
O lady of excellent vows, choose me, Siddhārtha, as your husband by means of this vow;
for those who abide in the hearts of beings awaken them to awakening through their own awakened intellect.
O lady of noble vows, make me successful through this vow;
O Goddess, you are Śakti, the eternal Satī, who incessantly envelops all creatures.
O lady of excellent vows, make me successful through this vow;
O Sarasvatī, you who dwell in the lotus, reside within my heart, which is like a vessel of nectar.
O lady of excellent vows, O Śraddhā, sovereign of the faithful, make me worthy of purity through this vow, bringing all beings under your control.
O lady of excellent vows, make me worthy of purity through this vow;
you, O virtuous one, are perceived as the radiant Lakṣmī, bestowing auspiciousness upon the world.
O lady of virtuous vows, make me worthy of purification by means of this vow;
let the nurse hold me in her arms on this auspicious day in the palace.
"O lady of excellent vows, O stainless lotus-born goddess, you who grant satisfaction, make me worthy of purity through this vow; may the virtuous woman be pleased."
O lady of excellent vows, make me worthy of purity through this vow;
you shall kindle the world, which is the abode of auspiciousness, once it has been well-polished.
"O lady of excellent vows, make me worthy through this vow.
Thus, all my desires, guided by you, have been fulfilled.
"By the grace of Indirā and through this vow, I have become happy;
therefore, having thus completed the worship of Śrī with a concentrated mind,"
One should place the joined vessel near the middle one;
therein, one should invoke the Lord Śrīdhara, the Master of Śrī.
Having prepared the pitcher according to the prescribed rite, covered with a pair of garments and endowed with all kinds of jewels, one should perform worship there.
Then, having first established the vessel and invoked the deity, one should worship;
having completed the worship according to the rules, one should then hear the boon.
O Blessed One, Lord of Śrī, Consort of Śrī, Abode of Śrī, who pervades the universe!
By your grace, may my great desires be fulfilled.
In this regard, the wise man should honor Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
having formed a group of nine couples there, he should worship those Vaiṣṇavas with the mantra.
To them he should give ornaments and abundant wealth as is appropriate;
having dismissed those best of the twice-born while they pronounce various blessings upon his prosperity,
he should then cast offerings to the world-protectors in the various directions.
The fast should be observed either together with the bride or with the groom;
one must not engage in conversation with heretics or the like under any circumstances.
If there were such a thing as falling, one would go to hell headfirst;
one would not be intent on vain chatter, nor engage in vain undertakings, nor possess a vain intellect.
One should not sleep during the day or night, nor should one eat in any way whatsoever;
one should never engage in play, derision, or false speech.
One should utter "Salutation eternally to Śrīdhara; salutation to Śrī.
Having passed the day in this very manner, one should then, with a concentrated mind, [proceed] on the sixth lunar day.
Having worshipped the goddess Śrī and likewise the god as before,
he should afterwards feed the Brahmins, together with their wives, according to the prescribed rules.
Then, having given away wealth and other gifts, or having bathed with water from a ritual jar,
he should, remaining silent, eat the remainder of the sacrificial oblation together with his wife.
Likewise, one should give gifts to the poor and excellent food to women;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the teacher and also offer the svadhā oblation to the ancestors.
Upon seeing a bilva tree, one should bow down and proceed while remaining bowed before it.
One should not strike him, nor touch his feet;
one should not step over his shadow, nor eat his fruits and such.
It is always highly recommended to hold a bilva vessel upon the head;
likewise, a hundred-petaled lotus, a single-petaled lotus, the flowers of the śrī-latā creeper, dūrvā grass, kūrca-grass flowers, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and rice grains.
One who desires prosperity, being undisturbed, should always wear it upon the head;
[it bestows] longevity, knowledge, fortune, contentment, health, and supreme luster.
By means of this vow, a human being attains good fortune and the perfection of security;
the king who performs the vow obtains a kingdom and unsurpassed prosperity.
In that region, a Śūdra shall obtain wealth and attain happiness;
and a maiden shall obtain a gentle husband who captivates her heart.
A barren woman shall undoubtedly obtain a desired son quickly;
a woman shall attain supreme auspiciousness through the perfection of this vow;
and a pregnant woman who desires many children shall obtain offspring.
One should worship the Goddess Śrī and the Lord of Gods with milk-rice (pāyasa).
For one desiring prosperity, the worship should be performed according to the previously mentioned procedure;
for one desiring good fortune, the worship should be performed with food prepared in ghee.
Kṣatriyas and kings should perform [their duties] using sacrificial offerings such as fruits and roots.
A student of the sciences, desiring long life, should perform worship according to the prescribed rite with divine oblations, sweet offerings, and milk.
In this very manner, one should perform [the rite] until the end of the rainy season on the fifth day;
or else, it is intended that the ritual should be performed by reciting [the mantra] only once.
Now, this vow is considered to be performed until the attainment of the fruit;
for on this earth, a man enjoys every fruit solely by the power of destiny.
Through connection with that, at that very moment, the fruit may be attained both immediately and over a long period;
moreover, even for the unfortunate and the wicked, prosperity may arise.

By this vow indeed, all sentient beings will certainly [attain their goals] through the rite thus described; and the observer of the vow, clad in the garment of the vow, [should act] according to the prescribed rule.
"This great vow, which brings about all accomplishments for men, has thus been declared.
Thus ends the Śrī Pañcamī Vrata as spoken in the Śrī Garuḍa Purāṇa.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hereafter I shall describe the fivefold form as well as its worship:
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
These indeed are declared to be the five forms of the God of gods;
having reached the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, the wise man [should perform the rite].
Fasting, one should worship the fivefold Lord Hari;
five mandalas should be prepared with five distinct colors.
O Lord of the Earth, the mandala of Pārthiva should be made white in color;
likewise, that of Vāruṇa is white, while that of Āgneya is held to be red.
That which belongs to Vāyu is yellow, and that whose deity is Ākāśa is black;
one should worship them individually with flowers that possess corresponding colors and fragrances.
And according to one's means, O subduer of enemies, with incense, lamps, and food as they may be obtained, as well as with barley, mung beans, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and ghee.
One should offer oblations with five mantras, each separately for all [the elements].
Having offered, one should then offer for all of them together with the formula: *oṃ pṛthivy-aptējovāyvākāśebhyaḥ svāhā*.
Or else, O King, one may offer with mantras containing their specific characteristics or by their names.
Having offered oblations preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability.
Having performed this for a year, then at the completion of the full year,
one should give garments to the Brahmins that are as bright as the finest cloth.
He who performs this fivefold vow of the great elements (mahābhūta-vrata) shall,
in due order, obtain the five sacrifices that have been proclaimed.
For many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world;
having attained human birth, he becomes free from disease, endowed with strength, and a slayer of hosts of enemies.
Endowed with learning, beauty, and wealth,
he was beloved by the people and dear to women.
Thus ends the vow of the five great elements as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Śrī Bhīṣma said:
"O Madhusūdana, by what vow does one's speech become sweet?"
In the same way, [he attains] the good fortune of the people and proficiency in all branches of knowledge.
O best of beings, tell me also how there may be non-separation between husband and wife as well as with kinsmen, and how men may attain a long life.
Pulastya said:
You have asked well, O King; listen to the Sārasvata vow, by the mere recitation of which Sarasvatī is pleased in this world.
Whatever devotee a man may be, he who would perform this unsurpassed vow should first worship the Brahmins at the beginning of that day and then commence it.
Alternatively, on a Sunday, by means of the strength of the planets and lunar mansions,
one should feed the brāhmaṇas milk-rice (pāyasa) and perform the recitation for the brāhmaṇas.
One should give white garments along with gold according to one's ability,
and should worship Gāyatrī with devotion using white garlands and unguents.
With these mantra-words, one should thereafter perform everything with palms joined in reverence,
so that, O Goddess, the Blessed Brahmā, the Grandfather of the Worlds, [may not surpass me].
O bestower of boons, may you remain even after abandoning me;
likewise, may all the Vedas, the Shastras, and whatever there is of dance, song, and so forth [remain].
O Mother, may I not be deprived of them; likewise, may these perfections be mine:
Lakṣmī, Medhā, Dharā, Puṣṭi, Gaurī, Tuṣṭi, Prabhā, and Mati.
"O Sarasvatī, protect me with these eight forms.
Having thus worshipped Gāyatrī, who holds a lute and a rosary of beads, [one should proceed].
During the bright fortnight, the knower of dharma should eat with unbroken grains and devotion, accompanied by a water-pot and a book, while observing a vow of silence both morning and evening.
On the fifth lunar day and on the day of the moon's change, having honored married women,
one should offer on that day a prastha of rice together with a vessel of ghee.
One should offer milk and gold, saying, "May Gāyatrī be pleased.
And likewise, observing silence during the two twilights, one should begin this practice.
One should not eat between meals for thirteen months;
when the vow is completed, one should give a vessel filled with auspicious rice.
O King, one should give a full set of two garments and a very beautiful cow with its calf to a Brahmin who is a knower of the Vedas and a reciter.
To the Goddess, he should offer a canopy and a bell together with white chowries,
sandalwood, a pair of garments, curd, food, and likewise a mountain peak.

The *śikhara* is the cream (*santānikā*) of curd, milk, and ghee; according to the traditional authority of Āyurveda, a *śikhara* is the film that forms on top of a liquid that has stood for a long time.
Likewise, one should also worship the teacher who provides instruction with devotion.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, and adorned with garments, garlands, and ointments—
he who performs the Sārasvata vow according to this rite [attains success].
Through the grace of Sarasvatī, one becomes learned, endowed with wealth, and possesses a melodious voice; indeed, one becomes a poet like Vyāsa or Sakavi.
Any woman who performs this rite shall likewise partake in its fruit;
she shall dwell in the world of Brahmā for as long as three hundred yugas.
Whoever hears or likewise causes others to hear this Sārasvata vow,
he too, with his impurities removed, attains the city of the Vidyādharas.
Those who duly worship Sarasvatī, the mother of the world, by means of this most excellent Sarasvatī-vow,
become pure-hearted through knowledge and possess melodious voices.
Those endowed with beauty possess many virtues and are skillful.

In this vow, the commencement should take place during the bright fortnight on the lunar day of one’s chosen deity, or on a Sunday, or on an auspicious day.
