Thereafter, one should observe silence during the two twilights and at every meal. On the fifth day of the bright fortnight, there is worship of Sarasvatī and worship of married women.
Thus ends the Sārasvata vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Agastya said:
O King, listen with a one-pointed mind as I shall proclaim the vow of peace (śāntivrata),
by the performance of which there shall always be peace for the householder.
O King, beginning on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
one should eat food devoid of sour things for one full year.

At night, one should worship the god Hari seated upon Śeṣa. The image of the deity is four-armed and reclining upon Śeṣa; one foot rests in the lap of Lakṣmī, while the other remains positioned upon Śeṣa. One hand is placed upon his knee, another is at the region of the navel, another supports his head, and yet another holds a cluster of *santāna* flowers. There is a lotus at the navel, and weapons are placed at the sides.
[One should worship] the feet with "To Ananta," and the hips with "To Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
The belly belongs to Takṣaka, while the chest belongs to Karkoṭaka.
Having worshipped the throat with Padma, the pair of arms with Mahāpadma,
the face with Śaṅkhapāla, and the head with Kulika;
One should likewise worship Viṣṇu with all his limbs individually;
the phrase "and also separately" means that one should worship the eight serpents, beginning with Ananta, individually as well.
Restraining one's speech, one should perform a ceremonial bath with milk, dedicating it to Hari.
One should bathe even the Nāgas with the thought that they are Hari;
O best of kings, one should offer milk along with sesame seeds into the fire.
Thus, at the end of the year, one should perform the satiation of the Brāhmaṇas.
Having fashioned a golden elephant, one should support it with one's own ear;
likewise, a milch cow together with her calf, accompanied by a pair of garments and a brass vessel.
And one should offer gold to a Brāhmaṇa according to one's ability;
O lord of men, for him who performs this vow with devotion in this manner,
there shall be constant peace and likewise freedom from fear of the Nāgas.

Those who, on the bright fifth days of the lunar fortnight, worship the Lord of Sacrifice— who rests upon the coils of the serpent Śeṣa, who is the source of the waters, and whose banner bears the king of birds— and who consume food that is neither sour nor sweet, [attain their goal].
For them, there shall be no fear whatsoever arising from the *nāgas*.
Thus ends the *śāntivrata* as declared in the *Varāhapurāṇa*. Sumantu said:
O King, the fifth lunar day is beloved by the nāgas and increases their joy;
indeed, on the fifth day, there is a great festival for the nāgas.
Vāsuki and Takṣaka, Kāliya and Maṇibhadraka,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Airāvata, and Karkoṭaka and Dhanañjaya.
These men, who always bestow fearlessness upon living beings as givers of life,
bathe the nāgas with milk here on the fifth lunar day.
They grant them safety as a gift of life within their own families.
When the serpents were being scorched by their mother day and night, they were extinguished by the milk of cows; thus, the milk of those [cows] is indeed difficult to obtain.
Śatānīka said:
O great sage, how were the serpents terrified by Mātṛkā? For what purpose and on what account did the destruction of that terrible curse occur?
Sumantu said:
"Uccaiḥśravas, the king of horses, was born from the nectar and possessed white wings;
seeing him white, Kadrū, the sister of the mother of the Nāgas, [was filled with envy]."
The word "said" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Behold this white jewel among horses; behold it, for it was born from the nectar of immortality. For those children of your lineage are likewise endowed with all-white splendor."
"This one, possessing the excellence of a form that is entirely white, is neither black nor red;
how is it that you, O Vinatā, have called him whose nature is black 'your own'?"
Kadru said: "O Vinata, if you, who possess two eyes, can see that one-eyed creature endowed with black skin, then make a wager."
Vinatā said: "O Kṛṣṇā, since you did not show me the hair revealed by Keśin, you shall become my slave;
however, Kadrū shall become my slave."
Thus, having made that wager, when they had departed filled with wrath,
and after Pradeva had been cursed first, Kadrū reflected deviously.
Having summoned his sons, he said: "Becoming small, stay upon the excellent horse; [be there] to increase the victory of Vinatā, my eldest sister, who is free from debt."
Though you have accused me, seizing upon the mother of the Nagas with the intellects of those seeking victory,
I, standing firm in my own dharma, shall not carry out that great command.
Having heard these words of her sons, Kadrū, overwhelmed with anger, cursed all her sons, saying: "The fire of Vachakīśa shall consume you."
When a great deal of time had passed, O Janamejaya, the Pāṇḍava performed a snake sacrifice, which is indeed difficult for others on earth to accomplish.
"In that sacrifice, the purifier (Agni) will surely burn [us], there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, Kadru became silent, overcome with anger.
Then the Grandfather, the progenitor of the world of Brahmā, said to them all:
"The sacrificial session shall conclude on the fifth day of the bright fortnight."
"In that regard, Nanda shall be yours; by him you will become joyful.
Having spoken thus to all the serpents, the Grandfather of the God of Gods returned once more to the third heaven, while the nāgas remained established in their own abode.
Therefore, O Great King, this fifth [gift] is beloved by the virtuous;
it was indeed given of old by Brahmā as a source of joy for the Nāgas.
Furthermore, I shall declare to you the observance regarding the fifth [lunar day],
by performing which a man never fears the race of nāgas anywhere.
O King, [one should offer] serpents made of gold, silver, or even clay— namely the serpents Vāsuki,
Takṣaka, and so forth, as mentioned in the first verse—
along with *karavīra* flowers, *śatapatra* flowers, and *jātī* petals, O observer of excellent vows.
Likewise, having honored the most excellent serpents with fragrant incense,
one should afterwards feed the Brahmins with ghee, milk-rice, and sweetmeats.
Having first provided food for the Brahmins according to their desire, one should dismiss them, saying:
"May the Nāgas, whoever they may be upon the surface of the earth, be pleased."
Those who are on the Himālaya and on the Vindhya, those situated in the intermediate space and in heaven,
those in rivers, oceans, lakes, and ponds—
Or those who dwell in step-wells and ponds—to all of them indeed be homage! Having thus paid obeisance to the Nāgas and honored the Brahmins, one should dismiss them.
Then, O lord of men, he himself should eat together with his servants;
first, he should eat sweet food, and thereafter as he pleases.
Learn from me the fruit that belongs to one who is thus endowed with self-restraint:
upon death, he goes to Nāgapura, being honored by hosts of apsarases.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, he rejoices for the duration of a solar cycle;
or, returning here to this world, he shall become a king, a sovereign over a mandala.
But he is born enriched with all kinds of jewels, as well as vehicles and other such things;
he shall become a king for five births in each successive Dvāpara age.
Free from mental and physical ailments, and accompanied by sons and grandsons, [one prospers];
therefore, they should be honored and revered with offerings of ghee, milk-rice, and guggulu resin.
Thus ends the Ānandapañcamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Sumantu said:
O King, a man bitten by a snake, having met his death, goes to the lower realms.
By moving downward, it becomes a serpent; it will be without poison—of this there is no doubt.
Śatānīka said: "Tell me what must be done when one's father, brother, daughter, mother, son, or wife has been bitten by a snake."
O best of Brahmins, tell me, O tiger among the twice-born, what gift, vow, or fast must be observed for his silence, so that I may indeed perform it.
Sumantu said: O descendant of Bharata, listen to the procedure for increasing the strength of the Nāgas, which involves properly fasting on the fifth lunar day; I shall explain it to you one by one.
One's own single year;
O King, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
that too is declared most meritorious and should be observed by one desiring a favorable rebirth.
On the fourth [lunar day], a single meal is prescribed, and on that same day, eating at night is proclaimed. Having fasted on that fifth day by abstaining from food during the daytime,
one should fashion a serpent made of silver or, alternatively, made of gold.
Then, if one lacks the means, one may use an image made of wood or clay;
otherwise, it should be made of gold, equal to the moon, or of silver. On the fifth lunar day, one should likewise worship with devotion the Naga Pañcapaṇa.
O King, having bathed [the deity] with milk and other liquids, along with *karavīra*, *padma*, and fragrant *jātī* flowers, as well as perfumes, incense, and food offerings;
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins with ghee, milk-rice, and sweetmeats;
[and likewise worship] Ananta, Vāsuki, Śaṅkha, Padma, and Kambala.
Likewise, O King, [he saw] the Naga Karkoṭaka, the Naga Aśvatara, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Śaṅkhapāla, Kāliya, and Takṣaka.
One should worship the great nāga Piṅgala month by month in due order;
having honored him with diligence, one should observe the practice of eating only at night on the fifth lunar day.
Having performed this twelve times in the month of Bhādrapada, O King, one should,
at the end of the year, provide a great feast according to one's ability.
Out of devotion, for the sake of the Brahmins, ascetics, and the Nāgas,
one should fashion a golden Nāga adorned with jewels, according to the Itihāsas and Vedas.
One should indeed give a cow together with her calf and provided with all necessary utensils;
at the time of giving, one should recite this while remembering the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa.
To the all-pervading, the sustainer of all realms, the infinite and unconquered one:
whatever members of my family have been bitten by serpents and have fallen into a downward state, [may they be liberated].
"O Govinda, by this gift of a vow, may they become partakers of liberation.
Having thus spoken, [he should offer] unbroken rice grains mixed with sesame seeds and sandalwood paste.
One should again pour water into the water in the presence of Vāsudeva;
by this rite, all those who perform the worship shall become immortal.
O best of kings, O delighter of your lineage, having rescued all those born of your family, even those who have gone astray shall attain the heavenly realm.
Attended by hosts of celestial nymphs, he goes to the presence of Viṣṇu;
he who is free from stinginess regarding wealth shall obtain all this fruit.
Those who, on the fifth lunar days of the bright fortnight, worship the serpents at night with offerings of flowers along with food,
shall indeed find protection from snakes in their homes.
Endowed with meaning, their limbs were illuminated by the rays of jewels.
[563] Thus ends the vow for the fifth day (Pañcamī-vrata) for the extraction of one bitten by a snake, as told in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Sumantu said:
In the same way, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the fifth day,
a person endowed with faith who paints serpents using colors such as black and others—
One should worship with perfumes, incense, clarified butter, guggulu, and milk-rice;
then the serpents, Takṣaka and the others, will attain satisfaction.
For one who has not been born into a family of Nāgas for seven generations, there shall be no fear from them nor any harm from them;
therefore, a wise person should, with every effort, refrain from worshipping the Nāgas.
Likewise, O joy of the Kurus, on the fifth day of the month of Āśvayuja,
one should fashion serpents out of kuśa grass and worship them together with Indrāṇī.
The Nāgas, such as Ananta and others mentioned in the previous vows;
Śacī, two-armed, with a garland of offspring in her hand and seated upon an elephant—
having bathed them with clarified butter, water, and milk, O Lord of the People.
He who, being pure and endowed with devotion, duly honors the Nāgas on that day with wheat, milk-boiled rice, and various kinds of foods;
One should worship them, O tiger among the Kurus; for him, O King, Śeṣa and the other nāgas become pleased in this world, and he attains peace, O Lord.
Having attained the world of perfect peace, he rejoices for eternal years,
where this mantra is always recited for the purpose of neutralizing poison.
Oṃ kurukulle hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Those who, at night on the white fifth days of the lunar fortnight,
offer worship with flowers to the serpents who are hostile to devotion;
For in their homes, the nāgas indeed grant fearlessness;
all of them become radiant with the light from the jewels upon their hoods.
Thus ends the Śānti-pañcamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Īśvara said:
"The man who worships the Divine on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna..."
Restraining his senses and moderate in food, he should perform worship according to the rite of the five offerings.
The hooded snakes do not bite him for fifteen years;
the poison does not affect his own family nor even the family of his mother.
"Therefore, one should worship him with effort, especially on the fifth lunar day.
Thus ends the Anantapañcamī vow as spoken in the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Īśvara said:
O fair-faced one, beginning from the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
the poison-destroying [lines] should be drawn on both sides with cow dung.
Having fashioned the Kaustubha gem and the serpents, one should worship Nidrā;
O fair-faced one, having bathed [the deity] with ghee, water, and milk.
O Goddess, having worshipped with wheat, milk, and various parched grains (lāja),
one should worship according to the rules with curdled milk and sprouts of dūrvā grass in due order.
[565] And with offerings of perfumes and flowers, one should satisfy the Brāhmaṇas;
or else, endowed with faith, on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Furthermore, a wise man who has not yet painted [them] should likewise paint elephants— colored with black and other pigments— which are like preceptors, upon a street or within his own home.
One should worship them with perfumes, incense, milk, and milk-rice;
then Padmaka, Takṣaka, and the others will attain satisfaction.
For seven generations of his lineage, there shall be no fear from snakes;
the mantra liberates even one who has consumed snake venom.
When one merely recites this, poison never takes effect. Oṃ kukulaṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Thus, O Goddess, has been described the unsurpassed *nāga-vrata*.
Having heard and having recited which, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the *Pañcamī-vrata*, which removes the poison of serpents, as declared in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*.
Īśvara said:
"The fifth day (*pañcamī*) that occurs in the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*) of the month of Bhādrapada..."
She is declared to be most meritorious and renowned for the desire to attain the heavenly realm.
And for twelve years, O fair-faced one, on the fifth day one should eat but a single meal; on the fourth day, however, it is proclaimed that one should observe the *nakta* fast.
On that fifth day, O beloved, one should fashion a serpent made of abundant silver, or else of gold,
or even of metal, or perhaps of clay.
On the fifth day, one should worship with one's capacity the serpent known as Pañcaphaṇa with karavīra flowers,
śatapatra flowers, and beautiful jātī blossoms.
One should worship the supreme nāga with perfumes, flowers, and incense;
thereafter, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with ghee, milk-rice, and sweetmeats.
A man [should worship] the serpent named Ananta, Karkoṭaka, Aśvatara,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Śaṅkhapāla, Kālika, and likewise Takṣaka.
And the great naga Piṅgala is proclaimed [as the deity] month after month;
at the conclusion of the vow, the breaking of the fast should be performed with milk and the feeding of Brahmins.
One should give a Naga fashioned from gold and silver, as well as a cow;
likewise, garments should be given to a Brahmin of immeasurable splendor.
One should always worship all the serpents with devotion,
especially on every fifth lunar day, with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Thus ends the Nāgapañcamī Vrata in the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sumantu said: That lunar day, the fifth (Pañcamī), is auspicious, bestowing prosperity, and removing all sins.
But whoever should completely avoid ritual actions in this [state], [he attains liberation].
"One should bathe the nāgas with milk, and they will become friends.
Thus ends the Nāgamaitrīvrata in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa.
Sumantu said:
O King, likewise, on the fifth day of the month of Bhādrapada,
a man endowed with faith who should paint [the deity] using pigments such as black and other colors—
One should worship with perfumes, incense, clarified butter, fruits, and milk-rice;
having worshipped the best of the twice-born with milk-rice enriched with ghee.
One should personally consume that [offering] with speech restrained and free from envy;
then the serpents, Takṣaka and the others, will attain satisfaction.
For seven generations of his lineage, there shall be no fear from snakes.

Thus ends the Ālekhyapañcamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa. Furthermore, by performing the milk-vow (payovrata) on the fifth lunar day and giving a golden serpent to a twice-born man, no fear arising from serpents shall befall him.
This is declared to be the supreme serpent-vow, which brings about universal friendliness.
Thus ends the Sarpapañcamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Having fashioned an elephant out of sesame flour, adorned with gold,
equipped with a girth and a goad, and likewise provided with a rider;
In the same way, the phrase "tadvat" (likewise) refers to the nature of the mantra-elephant described in the continuous vow (*nirantaravrata*):
it is accompanied by a garland of stars (*nakṣatramālā*), holds a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) and a throne (*pīṭha*),
has its eyes fixed upon the tips of its tusks, and is clothed in a pair of red garments.
Having honored a Brahmin couple with garlands and ornaments, one should offer them modakas made from the tips of the teeth [of the deceased] in a copper vessel or a small bowl.
One should give an ear-ornament and a garment free from stains;
for this, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is declared to be the delight of the trees of the forest.
It delivers even those who are suffering through wildernesses and mountain fastnesses, both in this world and in the next; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
O King, those who perform this vow called Paurandara on an auspicious day shall dwell for a very long time in the world of Indra.
On a meritorious day, specifically on the fifth lunar day (pañcamī), according to the context; thus is described the Paurandara-vrata as stated in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"Having worshipped Lakṣmī on the fifth day, the king should observe a fast."
At the conclusion of the year, one should give a golden lotus together with a cow.
He indeed attains the station of Viṣṇu, and Lakṣmī [is his] in birth after birth;
this is the vow known as Lakṣmī-vrata, which destroys suffering and grief.
Thus ends the Lakṣmī-vrata as declared in the Yamapurāṇa.
Sitāśva said:
"O Lord of the gods, I have heard many vratas."
Now, please explain to me the vow that destroys all sins.
Brahmā said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the most excellent of vows,
renowned as Ṛṣipañcamī, which is supreme and the remover of all sins.
O Indra among kings, by practicing that which dispels the hells,
they cite this ancient history as an illustration.
O best of the twice-born, there lived here in Videha a man named Utanka;
his wife was Suśīlā, who was devoted solely to her husband.
Her two children were indeed her finest ornaments;
her son had studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences, including the Pada and Krama recitations.
And within that same family, he even married a daughter;
however, as soon as she was wed, she unexpectedly met with widowhood.
Indeed, she remained there protecting her daughter in her father’s house;
tormented by her daughter's sorrow, he [the father] established his son in the household.
Having reached a forest on the bank of the Gaṅgā together with his wife,
that best of the twice-born taught the Vedas to his disciples there.
The daughter, highly esteemed by her father, was devoted to serving him;
having performed that service, she once became exhausted.
It is said that at midnight, while she was fast asleep, she turned into a mass of worms;
and seeing her in such a state, naked and without a bed, [he departed].
Filled with compassion for her mother, the disciples reported:
"We do not know anything at all regarding that virtuous queen who was in such a state."
"O Mother, a heap of worms has now appeared;
it looks like a thunderbolt's fall," said the disciples upon hearing this.
With a bewildered mind, she quickly approached his side;
seeing him in such a state, she lamented, deeply afflicted by grief,
beat her breast, and fell into a profound swoon.
Having regained consciousness in an instant, he raised her up, wiped her,
and taking her in his arms, led her into the presence of her father.
"O Master, tell me, virtuous lady, by what evil deed has she become infested with worms while fast asleep in the middle of the night?"
Having heard these words, the sage, devoted to meditation,
understood and revealed her deeds in a previous birth.
The seer said: "In a previous birth, seven lifetimes ago, she was indeed a Brahmin woman;
then, being childless, she was born as Drupadī while still in her menses."
O sinless one, through the power of that evil deed, her body becomes like that of a worm,
and she remains possessed by a state of menstruation.
On the first day she is like a Cāṇḍālī woman; on the second, a village pig;
on the third, she is said to be a washerwoman; on the fourth day, she becomes pure.
Likewise, having seen her who had gone to her companions’ company treated with contempt,
she was born into a stainless family of the twice-born through the power of her observed vow.
"Due to the insult to this vow, there is now the fear of becoming a mass of worms;
all this reason has been told to you for the sake of the maiden."
Suśīla said:
"By the mere sight of whom the birth of those like me— possessing the splendor of Brahman— is rendered pure within the lineage of the twice-born."
Those who do not perform sacrifices are born as masses of worms in a state of conflict;
O Lord, tell me of that most wonderful vow.
The sage said:
O Suśīlā, listen attentively to that supreme vow among all vows,
by the performance of which one is instantly liberated from this sin.
The destruction of the accumulation of suffering arises here; of this there is no doubt. Auspicious things increase, and prosperities become free from calamity.
When the fifth lunar day of the bright fortnight occurs in the month of Nabhasya,
one should perform a ritual bath in a river or similar body of water and observe the prescribed restraints.
Having performed his daily rites and other duties, he should go to Dvāravatī and bathe the sages with devotion according to the rules, using the auspicious essences of the five nectars.

One should worship Dvāravatī— the sacrificial hall of the Agnihotra— because it is endowed with many smoke-vent openings; having anointed it with fragrant sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, one should honor it with various flowers, perfumes, incense, and lamps.
Having covered [the image] with auspicious garments and sacred threads according to the prescribed rite,
one should then offer the *arghya* accompanied by food offerings and auspicious fruits.
The Arghya-mantra:
Kaśyapa, Atri, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Gautama, Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha— these seven are remembered as the sages (ṛṣis).
This narrative should be heard; one should prepare a meal of vegetables, remain in celibacy, and be devoted to the meditation of the sages.
One should properly observe this vow according to this procedure;
whatever merit arises from it, choose that with a concentrated mind.
Whatever merit is found in all vows, whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords,
and whatever is gained from all gifts bestowed— that is obtained by the completion of this vow.
The woman who observes this vow becomes a partaker of happiness;
endowed with beauty and charm, she is blessed with sons, grandsons, and other progeny.
In this world one shall always be fortunate, and in the next world there will be an inexhaustible state;
by the power of this vow, one remembers one's former birth.
Thus ends the Ṛṣipañcamī vow as declared in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"By worshipping the Nāgas on the fifth lunar day, one is not overcome by poisons."
And he obtains a wife who bears a son, and he shall attain supreme prosperity.
The root mantras are proclaimed by their own names, as are the limb mantras;
and Tithīśvara is to be fashioned as before, situated upon a lotus petal.
The lord of the lunar day (tithīśvara) here is Nāga;
offerings of perfumes and flowers are prescribed according to one's ability.
Even worship performed with deceit, however, yields fruit.
An oblation performed with a stream of clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, curd, milk, rice, and honey,
when offered with a peaceful mind, bestows the fruits previously described.
This vow is to be explained like the Vaiśvānara-pratipad-vrata;
thus ends the Nāga-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
The king of horses, born from the nectar, possessing the speed of the wind and the swiftness of thought—
Uccaiḥśravas, who is worthy of worship, [was born] on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
In that very place, the Gandharvas, the kinsmen of horses, were to be worshipped;
some bore feathered arrows, while others were adorned with feathers.
Bhīma, Citraratha— who was renowned as the scorner of all—
and likewise the illustrious Sāliśiras and the highly famous Pradyumna.
And Nārada, Kalinda, the Gandharva Hāhā,
Huhu, Suvāhu, Tumburu, and likewise the lord Citraratha.
And the famous Citrāṅgada, the heroic Citrasena,
Siddhapūrṇa, and the highly illustrious Badarīparṇāśa.
Brahmacārī, Ratiguṇa, Suparṇa, Atibala,
as well as Viśvāvasu, Surendra, and the Gandharva Atiparākrama.
Thus, these should be worshipped with auspicious songs of various kinds,
with offerings of water for the cows, with ants, with supreme food, and with unbroken grains.
With curd, molasses, milk, and abundant rice flour,
as well as with incense, garlands, lamps, and the recitation of benedictions by the twice-born.
For when the kinsmen of horses are thus properly honored,
they bestow strength, long life, and invincibility in battles.
"Health and supreme nourishment are likewise ordained.
Thus ends the Śālihotra Horse Pañcamī Vow.
Having bathed in water infused with all medicinal herbs, one should worship the Lotus-born [Brahmā] on the fifth lunar day.
And he who gives all household utensils while in the householder stage of life;
The mortar, the pestle, the winnowing basket, the grinding stone, and the cooking pot as the fifth; the water-jar full of water, and whatever else follows these.
Having placed these in the house of householders, O Supreme Person.
A woman who attends to the household utensils never comes to grief;
this is known as the "vow of the home," which bestows all happiness.
Thus ends the Gṛhapañcamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. By performing worship on the fifth lunar day, a man becomes like the moon;
he attains abundant longevity, prosperity, and preeminent fame.
Thus ends the Saubhāgyavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
On the fifth lunar day, a person should likewise worship the goddess Pṛthivī;
he attains that very [result] through effort—of this there is no doubt to be made.
Thus ends the Pṛthivī-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharma. Having performed the worship of those ten Viśvedevas who were previously mentioned by me, one shall attain heaven on the fifth lunar day.
From the Vāyu Purāṇa: Kratu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, the two Virocanas,
Purūravas, and Bhādravās are proclaimed as the Viśvedevas.

Thus ends the vow for the attainment of beauty as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Furthermore, he who performs worship with Varuṇa-mantras at Puṣkara shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires.
With *vāruṇa* flowers and *puṣya* flowers—one should likewise perform worship with the *puṣkara* flower as the best. Thus is the Śrīprāpti-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Having worshipped according to one's means on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, [one should proceed].
One would obtain this very fruit, as declared for the year, all at once.
Thus ends the Śrīvrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
[one should worship] Umā, Medhā, Bhadrakālī, as well as Kātyāyanī, Dhṛti, Svāhā, Svadhā, Ṛddhi, Anasūyā, and likewise Kṣamā.
Surabhī, Devasenā, Velā, Jyotsnā, and Śacī; Gaurī, the wife of Varuṇa, and likewise Dhūmrāṇī.
By worshipping the mother of one's chosen deity as well as the consort of that deity, one attains their desires and is freed from sorrow; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the vow for the fulfillment of desires as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. O King, by worshipping Airāvaṇa, Vāyu-tuṇḍa, and Uccaiḥśravas at that time, one attains victory.

Thus ends the Vijaya-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Thus concludes [this section] in the Caturvargacintāmaṇi composed by Śrī Hemādri, the sovereign lord of all sciences and master of all faculties, the great god of the great king of kings.
In the section on vows (vratakhaṇḍa), the fifth-day vows (pañcamī-vratāni).
Now, the sixth-day vows (ṣaṣṭhī-vratāni).
The Goddess of Speech (Bhāratī) constantly occupies his lion-throne,
the Lord who reclines upon the ocean of milk dwells within the lotus of his blossoming mind,
and the wish-fulfilling tree (Kalpadruma) rests upon the praiseworthy palm of his right hand.
Hemādri defines that desired group of sixth-day vows.
Vikrānta said:
"Tell me that rule by which men obtain perfection of form, health, and abundant residence in heaven."
Agastya said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one! Since I have been questioned by you, O sinless one, I shall explain all of that; from this, spiritual welfare will arise."
Listen, O King, I shall declare that which bestows liberation upon all men,
and which was formerly kept secret, O King, by the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra.
And this was previously related by Śaṅkara to the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) concerning all the Asuras and likewise the Rākṣasas.
This, which destroys great sins, was proclaimed by the six-faced one;
having performed it, even a killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a drinker of liquor, or one who has violated the teacher’s bed [is purified].
O best of men, even one who has set fire to a house, a poisoner, or one devoted to every kind of evil,
is liberated from all sins upon hearing this vow.
It is all-meritorious, purifying for men, and a destroyer of wonders;
it is for the benefit of the worlds, O best of kings, as it is for you.
Listen, O King, to the supreme majesty of this most meritorious vow.
The sixth lunar day in the dark fortnight of the month of Proṣṭhapada, when conjoined with Mars,
the Vyatīpāta yoga, and the Rohiṇī nakṣatra— that sixth day is known as Kapilā.

Proṣṭhapada is Bhādrapada; and in this context, it should be understood as ending with the new moon (darśānta), because the conjunction with Rohiṇī is possible only then. The second [lunar day] is of great merit and difficult to encounter for one observing the vow anywhere;
the sixth [lunar day] at the end of the year, moreover, is joined with that same [conjunction].
O King of kings, the auspicious rising [of the festival] is remembered as occurring in the bright fortnight between Caitra and Vaiśākha;
indeed, it is considered supreme at Dvāravatī even during Vaiśākha.
If the thousand-rayed sun is in the hand [of the moon], then the vow should be undertaken by the wise;
for whatever is offered in sacrifice, given, or bestowed on this day [is of great merit].
It is impossible to state the total measure of that merit;
rather, it occurs at the time when the sixth lunar day is joined with these specific qualities.
On the fifth day, the wise practitioner should take a single meal;
on the sixth day, having risen at dawn, he should first perform the cleansing of his teeth.
Having formed an añjali filled with water, one should recite this mantra:
"O Lord of Gods, today I am fasting, devoted to you and having you as my supreme refuge."
"I shall worship you with devotion; be my refuge, O Bhāskara!
Having thus made this resolve and offered the *arghya*, he then became pure in that place.
Having bathed with diligence in a river, at a sacred ford, or in a lake, or in a pond,
a large pool, or even at home, one who is self-restrained—
One should grind together devadāru, uśīra, kuṅkuma, elā, manaḥśilā,
patraka, padmaka, and yaṣṭīmadhu with cow’s milk.
Having stirred it with milk and the medicinal paste, one should perform the bath accompanied by the mantra:
"Oṃ, you are the waters, O Lord of Gods, and indeed the lord of the luminaries."
O God, destroy my evil born of the actions of speech, mind, and body;
having performed the bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should cleanse [the deity] with the five-fold offerings (pañcabhaṅga).
With five types of twigs and five kinds of sprouts, one should diligently fetch pure earth for the purpose of bathing, [reciting]:
"O Earth, you are purified by Brahmā; you have been consecrated by Kāśyapa."
"Make me pure forever; deliver me from all evil.
With this mantra, a wise man should worship Varuṇa.
O Varuṇa, with noose in hand, Lord of all waters, O Master!
Today I pray to you; O Lord of the gods, make me pure.
You are Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Ravi, Sūrya, and Dvādaśātmaka;
you are the maker of light, the dispeller of darkness, the God, the Lord of All, and Hari.
On ground smeared with cow dung,
a wise man should draw the Sarvatobhadra mandala using saffron.
Therein, in the center, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a beautiful pericarp. One should place Sūrya on the eastern petal; one should place Tapana on the southeast petal;
Suvarṇaretas on the southern petal; and one should place Ravi on the southwest petal.
One should place Āditya on the western petal, Divākara on the northwestern petal,
Prabhākara on the northern petal, and Sūra on the northeastern petal.
One should place the god bearing intense rays and Brahmā;
one should place the god whose form is the support, Varuṇa, in the center.
He saw the thousand-rayed sun, endowed with both subtle and gross qualities,
omnipresent and omniform, as the very sun situated in the center.
The Sun-god, mounted upon his chariot drawn by seven horses, holding a lotus in his hand,
with a rosary and a bow in his hands, and adorned with earrings and a crown.
One should have a golden [image] made there, endowed with various kinds of jewels;
according to one's capacity, it should weigh more than a *pala*, or even half of that, or even a *karṣa*.
One should have a golden Māruta [image] made, as well as a silver chariot;
having adorned it with seven horses, one should place the chariot standing before him.
Having assumed such a form— reddish like the son of Vinatā, holding a horse, and possessing long thighs— one should dissolve [the object] upon a lotus.
Upon that, one should place the deity, adorned with red garments,
embellished with red sandalwood paste, garlands, and so forth, and exceedingly beautiful.
Having placed the charioteer in front, the pure person should worship Aruṇa with fragrant red flowers and other offerings according to their capacity.
Oṃ! May Aruṇa—the son of Vinatā, the divine witness of actions, the dispeller of darkness, who possesses seven horses and seven reins—be gracious unto me.
Having worshipped the charioteer with this mantra immediately thereafter,
one should arrange for the recitation by the deity of the five items beginning with *prabhūta*.
Having worshipped [the deity] who is abundant, stainless, essential, worthy of attainment, and supremely auspicious,
one should then worship the Sun with blazing powers (śaktis).
Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Bhadrā, Vinatā, Vimalā, Anaghā,
Amoghā, Vaidyutā, and the ninth is Sarvatomukhī.
Whether impure or pure, even if one has reached every possible state,
whoever remembers the god Bhāskara becomes pure both externally and internally.
Having placed Bhāskara on the crest-lock and Sūrya on the forehead,
one should place Bhānu between the eyes and Ravi there in the mouth.
One should place the radiant Bhānumat on the throat, and Padmagarbha, the god who destroys darkness, in the two hands; one should likewise place [the deity] upon the two breasts.
One should place Jātadeva in the navel and Bhānu on the hips;
Ugrasūrya in the region of the genitals and Tejorūpa on the two shanks.

Having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) as described, one should place the entire form— endowed with both subtle and gross qualities— upon the two feet, take up the vessel, and worship it accordingly.
It was adorned with *karavīra* and *arka* flowers, red sandalwood, and *campaka* blossoms,
as well as fragrant flowers, incense, and saffron.
Mārtaṇḍa, Bhānu, Āditya, Bhāskara, Tapana,
Ravi, Haṃsa, and Divākara— from the feet up to the crown.
One should worship these limbs: the feet, the calves, the two knees, the thighs, the hips, the navel, the chest, and the head.
One should bring the vessel for the *arghya* offering, whether it be made of silver or even copper;
one should fill that divine vessel with water for the sake of the *arghya*.
There, with a concentrated mind, one should worship those deities starting from the east;
then, one should worship the deities of the directions with perfumes, flowers, and ointments.
Having taken water in a vessel along with flowers, fruit, and sandalwood,
and having knelt upon the ground, one should offer the *arghya* to the Sun.
O you who contain the Vedas within, salutations to you; O you who contain the Vedas within, let there be homage to you.
To you whose form is unmanifest, accept this water offering; let there be homage to you.
O eternal four-faced one, O Lord of Dharma, whose form is Brahman;
to you who are established in the creation and maintenance [of the world], accept this arghya—salutations be unto you!
The God who assumes the form of Viṣṇu, clad in yellow garments and possessing four arms, the source of all worlds—accept this water offering; homage be to you!
To you, the god who has the form of Rudra, the Blessed One bearing the trident, who indeed could burn the three worlds—accept this water offering; homage be to you!
You are Brahmā, you are Viṣṇu, you are Rudra, and you are Prajāpati;
you alone are the self of all beings—accept this water offering, homage be to you!
He is the self of time, the self of all beings, the self of the Vedas, facing in every direction;
he is the destroyer of birth, death, old age, sorrow, and the fear of saṃsāra.
The glorious Lord Divākara is the destroyer of the calamity of poverty;
Bhānu is golden-crystal, Svarṇaretas, and Devākara.
O you whose horses are tawny and who wear a garland of rays, accept this water of honor; salutations be unto you!
You are celebrated through your fourfold forms and your eightfold manifestations.
Established in four forms and measured by eight, you are the source of the threefold melody of the Sāman at the sacrifice; accept this water of honor, homage be to you!
Then, with perfumes, flowers, as well as incense, lamps,
and food offerings, according to one's ability, one should pray to the Sun deity.
I praise Agni; homage to you! Homage to you, Jātavedas!
Homage indeed to Īśa, and homage indeed to Agni—homage, homage!
O Goddess, grant us peace; salutations to you, the source of the world's birth, salutations again and again!
O you whose form is the Self, salutations to you; O you whose body is the universe, salutations again and again!
You are Brahmā, you are indeed Viṣṇu, you are Dhātṛ, and you are Hutāśana;
O Lord of the Gods, I desire liberation and I pray for it.
O Lord of the Gods, I pray to you, the God who is the soul of all, whose eyes are said to be everywhere, whose feet and faces are everywhere, and who is omnipresent.
Having recited this mantra, one should pay homage to the Sun;
with the mantra "saṃ varcasā," one should wash the face with water from both hands.
One should gaze at the sun with the verse beginning "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad";
one should mutter these two hymns, "ud u tyaṃ" and "citram," in the presence of the gods.
And in the very first corner, one should likewise cause the fruit-offering to be made with fruits,
flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and various kinds of edible foods.
And there, in an auspicious place, one should prepare a bed for the Lord;
[one should offer] the six grains, the six flavors, the deity, and the silver Great Lord.
The wise man should likewise have a figure of a person made with a sword in hand;
covered with a pair of garments, he should place it upon the salt.
With this very mantra, one should then perform the bath, the offering of water (argha), and worship:
"Homage to you, who have the form of wrath, with sword in hand, intent on striking."
Seeing you desiring to slay him, all the deities offered oblations;
the summit of Mount Meru was pervaded by you, possessing the brilliant splendor of the fierce sun.
Therefore, I shall worship you; accept this water offering (*arghya*); homage be to you! Then, having passed the night with the sounds of singing and instrumental music, [he continued].
Then, when the sun has risen, one should perform the fire-oblation according to one's ability;
there, one should worship the deities and the preceptor according to the rules and according to one's capacity.
A twice-born man should offer oblations of fuel-sticks of the *arka* tree, as well as sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter,
and likewise cooked sacrificial rice (*caru*) and clarified butter.

One should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra "Ā kṛṣṇena," followed by oblations with the Vyāhṛtis, and then the Sviṣṭakṛt offering immediately thereafter. One should worship the goddess Kapilā, who destroys sins, together with her calf.
[One should give] a cow adorned with a pair of garments and a bell, decorated with golden horns,
having a golden mouth, silver hooves, and provided with a bronze milking vessel.
With this mantra, one should give her to a Brāhmaṇa according to one's capacity: "O Kapilā, you are worthy of worship by all the gods; you are Rohiṇī."
Since she consists of all objects of desire from every side, therefore grant me peace—
that Lakṣmī who belongs to all the gods and who resides among the gods.
May that Goddess, in the form of a cow, grant me peace—
she who dwells within the bodies of the Rudras and she who is beloved by Śaṅkara.
May that Goddess, in the form of a cow, dispel my sin—
she who is Lakṣmī upon the chest of Viṣṇu and Svāhā of the Fire-god.
That power which is the energy of the moon, sun, and fire, appearing in the form of a cow, is for the sake of prosperity;
she is the Lakṣmī of the four-faced Brahmā and the Lakṣmī of Kubera.
May that cow, who is the Lakṣmī of the world-protectors, be a granter of boons to me.
You are *svadhā* for the foremost of the ancestors and *svāhā* for the consumers of the sacrifice;
you who are called *vaṣaṭ* in the world, O Cow, may you grant me satisfaction.
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me;
may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
The mantra for the worship of cows:
"Whoever, having touched and paid homage to cows, performs a circumambulation,
by him the earth with its seven continents has been circumambulated."
Homage to you, O Goddess Kapilā, who destroys all sins;
O Mother of Cows, you ought to protect me, who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
The mantra for the gift of gold: "O you who are the embryo within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha, the golden seed of the sun;
since you bestow the fruit of infinite merit, grant me peace."
The mantra for the gift of ornaments:
"Since a pair of red garments is dear to the Sun,
may Sūrya grant me peace through the offering of them."
The mantra for the gift of clothing:
One should cause a pair of garments and gold to be put on.
One should cause the recipient to wear the gold ornament and the garment upon their respective parts of the body.
Endowed with these attributes, one should give a cow to a twice-born man;
one should diligently offer the Sun-god along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) while reciting this mantra.
Bhāskara was born from Vidhi, Bhāskara himself resides within all substances, and he is the giver of Bhāskara; therefore, Bhāskara indeed belongs to me.
The mantra for giving:
"I accept the sun; the sun indeed gives.
The sun is the savior for both; therefore, the sun is truly mine."
The mantra for the acceptance [of the gift]:
"Afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice and molasses;
and one should especially give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability."
Even anyone who possesses little wealth should perform this rite according to their own capacity; they too shall obtain that same fruit.
Then, out of devotion to the teacher, one should offer everything with all one's vital energy:
cows, land, gold, garments, rice, salt, and sesame seeds.
Having given all this, he should then pray to the Kapila cow:
"O Kapila, you are of meritorious deeds; O sinless one, you whose actions are virtuous!"
Lift me up who am wretched, and grant me freedom from fear as I speak.
Even for one who does not give, nor for a non-giver,
you are always served by the sounds of celestial musical instruments;
likewise by the Vidyādharas, Siddhas, hosts of Bhūtas and Nāgas, and the Grahas.
There, the gods, established in the number of the hairs of a tawny cow,
remain stationed in the sky and constantly release a rain of flowers.
O Goddess Suprabhā, produced from the fire-pit by Brahmā;
salutations to you, O auspicious Kapilā, who are honored by all the gods.
Victory to you, O eternally great being, the auspiciousness of all sacred fords and the like!
Lead the donor, together with his own kin, swiftly indeed to the world of Brahmā.
Having circumambulated the giver of the components of the vow and bowed to the preeminent brahmins,
they should pronounce blessings for the arrival of sons, grandsons, and wealth.
Possessing health, beauty, and good fortune, and being freed from all suffering,
he shall reach Goloka at the end and, with a long life, partake in bliss.
When he falls from heaven, he becomes a righteous king;
having enjoyed a kingdom free of thorns, he rules over the earth consisting of seven continents.
Oh, how meritorious is this vow, which destroys all suffering!
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme fruit of giving.
In a vessel made of great knowledge, for one of virtuous conduct,
this vow— the best of all vows, foremost and of great fruit— becomes inexhaustible.
"It will surely deliver the donor to the imperishable and undecaying state.
Thus all the hosts of gods and the multitudes of beings were filled with joy.
Standing in the sky, they dance at the arrival of this auspicious day,
for the sake of the seer who is a worthy recipient, learned in the Vedas, and a householder.
Thus, he who gives a tawny cow according to the rite prescribed by rule goes to the supreme abode, from which he does not fall again.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*, however, there is this specific instruction:
"On a pure ground smeared [with cow dung] and adorned with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*),
one should place a flawless jar filled with sandalwood water."
Endowed with the five jewels, accompanied by *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
together with a pair of red cloths as a canopy, and joined with a copper vessel;
One should have a chariot made with a single wheel, beautifully decorated and with golden rims;
one should likewise have an image of the Sun fashioned, complete with golden ornaments.
Having placed [the vessel] upon a water-pot (kumbha), one should likewise worship it with perfumes and flowers;
one should worship the god Āditya with his own names as they have been declared.
O Āditya, Bhāskara, Ravi, Bhānu, Sūrya, Divākara, Prabhākara—homage to you; deliver me from the cycle of existence.
Since you bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, therefore grant me peace.
The prayer mantra:
Homage, homage to you, O granter of boons, Lord of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus!
Homage to you whose form is the universe, whose abode is the universe; let there be homage to you!
Having thus worshipped the Sun, the God of gods, according to the prescribed rite,
one should worship a tawny cow with garments, garlands, and unguents.
The mantra for the gift:
May the divine-formed Sun, the eye of the world, the twelve-fold soul,
the Lord accompanied by Kapilā, grant me liberation.
Therefore, O Kapilā, you who are meritorious and the purifier of all the world,
having been given away along with Sūrya, become the bestower of liberation upon me.
Thus ends the Kapilā-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Īśvara said:
Beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, that which is now stated for the purpose of the vow [is as follows].
Having observed the fast on the sixth lunar day according to the prescribed rite, one should especially worship the six-faced deity.
At that time, one should especially fashion a beautiful image made of clay,
having six faces and twelve arms, resembling a child and possessing a golden luster.
The gentle god, whose vehicle is a peacock and who is filled with loveliness,
is adorned with a spear, a bell, a banner, weapons, a noose, and a cock;
he holds a staff, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā, as well as a sword, a quiver, and a bow.
Having worshipped with supreme devotion by means of offerings of white flowers.
One should cause the offering of food, perfumes, garments, and indeed hymns to be presented;
likewise, having taken the juice of the *brāhmī* plant, along with the ghee and fruit of a tawny cow.
Having addressed it with the Sārasvata mantra one thousand and eight times.

One should worship the preceptor with devotion using garments, gold, food, and vehicles, employing the *sārasvata-mantra*, that is, the mantra of Sarasvatī. Subsequently, at the conclusion of the vow, it is beneficial to consume the juice of *brāhmī* mixed with ghee.
It should be performed month by month until the end of one year;
one should practice this for one full year with purity and celibacy.
He too would become a great poet on earth like Vācaspati;
he grasps the scriptures at once and stands at the head of all disputants.
Rākṣasas and Vināyakas never harm him; nor do the most terrible Skanda-grahas, nor the evil Apasmāra-grahas.
By the power of this Great Army Vow (Mahāsenavrata), they do not cause harm;
this supreme and most excellent vow, which increases prosperity, should be performed.
To the six-faced son of Pārvatī, Guha, Skanda, Kumāra,
Kārttikeya, as well as the youth and the destroyer of Krauñca.
One should worship Tārakārātisaṃjña, as well as another, Kṛttikāsuta, Vaiśākha, and Viśākha, month by month.
The Sun, joined with the digit of the Sun and adorned on the crown by the Moon—
these are the mantras to be understood in sequence for the twelve [deities], O Śikhidhvaja.
Thus ends the Kumāra-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Kālottara.
Skanda said:
[Regarding] King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, who had attained his kingdom...
Once, Durvāsas, the best of sages, arrived to see him.
The son of Dharma, possessed of great splendor, with palms joined in reverence, asked him:
"O best of sages, I wish to hear about that vow and to perform it."
Durvāsas said: Listen, O illustrious king, to the supreme vow among all vows, which,
when merely performed here, fulfills all desires.
O best of kings, even one whose vows are unbroken should effect the destruction of all evil,
if by fate such a day should be obtained while living.
The sixth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada,
conjoined with the Vaidhṛti yoga and the Viśākhā nakṣatra on a Tuesday, is renowned here as Campā.
A sixty-year-old cow is difficult to find among gods, asuras, and humans;
in the Kṛta age it is fifty years old, and in the Dvāpara age, likewise.
In the Kali age, it is difficult to find even a thirty-year-old [cow],
whereas formerly, in the Kṛta age, such a one was used by Viśvakarman.
From that fruit, he attained the status of a Prajāpati and universal sovereignty,
as did Pṛthu, Kārtavīrya, Bhūta, and Nārāyaṇa.
By means of this [rite], together with Umā, through their mutual desire for one another,
he who performs it according to the rules enjoys infinite fruit.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O sage, I wish to hear that procedure in detail as you speak it:
what are the mantras, what are the observances, and what would her characteristics be?
Durvāsas said:
When the sixth lunar day (Ṣaṣṭhī) in the month of Nabhasya is joined with the Vaidhṛti yoga and the conjunction of the Moon and Mars in a double-deity asterism (Dvidaivatyarkṣa), it is called Campā.
Viśākhā is a lunar mansion presided over by two deities.
On the fifth day, one who observes the vow should perform the restriction (*niyama*) of fasting;
the meaning is that one should observe the single-meal (*ekabhakta*), which is a subsidiary rule (*aṅga*) of the fast.
One should perform the Campā-ṣaṣṭhī vow according to the words spoken by the preceptor;
then, at the clear dawn, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Having properly undertaken his vow, a man makes this resolve:
"O Lord of Gods, today I am fasting; I am your devotee, devoted solely to you, having determined my capacity to complete the vow endowed with all its constituent parts."
I shall worship you with devotion; be my refuge, O Bhāskara!
The mantra of resolve:
Then, the knower of mantras should perform his bath in pure water such as that of a river,
having applied earth with mantras and using white sesame seeds.
O Son of Savitṛ, you are indeed supreme; my sin, which has been cast away by your splendor within the water, may it vanish in a thousand ways.
[592] The prayer-mantra:
"O Lord of Devas, you are the waters and indeed the lord of the luminaries;
O God, destroy my sin committed through speech, mind, and action."
The mantra for bathing:
Then one should offer libations to the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors.
Thereafter, returning home in silence, one should avoid conversation with heretics.
One should have a bright, square, and very beautiful sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) prepared;
one should place there a flawless jar endowed with the five jewels.
Covered with a pair of red garments and smeared with red sandalwood paste,
one should place upon it a vessel made of either gold or copper.
One should draw a twelve-spoked lotus with a pericarp using saffron;
upon it, one should place a golden image of the Sun, together with his chariot and Aruṇa.
According to one's capacity or the extent of one's wealth, and avoiding any stinginess regarding money,
one should worship him with perfumes and flowers, preceded by the prescribed ritual and mantras.
One who is self-controlled should perform the bathing of the Arka tree with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta);
thereafter, one should perform the supreme worship with scented water.
With various kinds of divine perfumes— camphor, agallochum, and saffron—
and with many fragrant fruits produced therefrom.
One should have a pavilion constructed there, adorned with garlands of flowers;
one should make it as beautiful as possible on all sides, both below and above.
Then one should worship the god Bhāskara upon a lotus:

"Obeisance to Āditya! Obeisance to Tapana! Obeisance to Puṣan! Obeisance to Bhānumat! Obeisance to Bhānu! Obeisance to Aryaman! Obeisance to Viśvavaktṛ! Obeisance to Aṃśumat! Obeisance to Sahasrāṃśu! Obeisance to Khanāyaka! Obeisance to Mukara! Obeisance to Sūrya! Obeisance to Khaga!
With the first mantra among these, the worship is performed in the center; with the other twelve, the worship is performed in order starting from the eastern petal.
The mantra for the worship of Āditya:
"O Divākara, by the worship of you, may all the evil deeds committed by me throughout a thousand previous births go to destruction."
The prayer-mantra:
May the divine son of Vinatā, the witness of all actions, the dispeller of darkness,
who possesses seven horses and seven reins— may Aruṇa be gracious unto me.
The mantra for the chariot worship:
Then one should worship the Lord Acyuta seated upon that chariot,
in due order, with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the eight-syllable mantra.
The eight-syllable *ghṛṇi* mantra is to be understood through the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*).
It is the self of time, the self of all beings, the self of the Vedas, and faces in every direction;
it is the destroyer of the fear of birth, death, old age, disease, and worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).
The *arghya* mantra for at sunrise:
Then one should worship a white, milch cow together with her calf,
adorned with garments, neck-ornaments, and decorated with bells and horns.
O Goddess, created by Brahmā, destroyer of all sins,
you ought to protect me, O Mother of the Cow, who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
May the cows— the mothers of the world, beautiful in form and manifold in appearance—
approach me, just as rivers flow toward the ocean.
That goddess Lakṣmī who belongs to all the gods and who resides among the gods— may she, in the form of a cow, dispel my sin.
The splendor that belongs to the world-protectors, the splendor that belongs to Yama,
and the power of the moon, the sun, and Indra— may that cow be the bestower of boons upon me.
The mantra for the worship of the Cow:
Then one should perform an oblation of sesame seeds one hundred and eight times with the Sāvitrī mantra;
thereafter, one should consecrate that cow [with the thought], "May the Sun be pleased with me."
Then one should give to the preceptor the image of the Sun with his chariot and Aruṇa,
together with a water-pot, jewels, garments, and all necessary ritual implements.
I give to you this chariot, Bhānu, equipped with all its accessories;
may the Sun-god fulfill my heart’s desire for a dwelling.
The mantra for giving:
"O Sun, O Ravi, O Infinite One, O You whose face is turned everywhere,
you ought to grant the attainment of the heart's desire for both [parties]."
The mantra for receiving [the gift]:
"I give to the Brāhmaṇa this auspicious divine cow, who consists of all objects of value, who embodies all sacrifices, and who comprises all forms of giving."
The mantra for the gift of a cow:
I accept the auspicious goddess Surabhi, who consists of all sacrifices. O Giver of Boons, purify both; become the savior of both.
The mantra for the acceptance [of the gift]:
Then one should feed twelve Brahmins according to one's ability;
one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and, having prostrated before them, dismiss them.
O best of the twice-born, may that cow—which constitutes his unimpaired vow—be greeted with blessings;
may she be delighted by those blameless benedictions.
Then, having performed the sacrifice, he himself should eat the remains of the food intended for the twice-born.
Surrounded by his sons, his wife, and many other people,
he who thus treats Campā in this manner enjoys the ultimate fruit.
The rule for lords has been declared, as well as the domain of those lords;
indeed, this vow should be performed by all who fear suffering, according to their own capacity.
He who is capable of following the primary rule but conducts himself according to a secondary rule, his effort therein shall be fruitless; for he is not a master when resorting to a secondary rule.
On the fifth day, the observer of the vow should perform the restrictive observance according to the teacher's instruction;
on the sixth day, he should perform his bath after having offered libations to the ancestors and the deities.
Having returned to his own home, the practitioner, observing silence, should meditate upon the Sun in his mind;
he should then place an unblemished jar and likewise a clay vessel upon it.
Upon that, one should place a golden sun made from a single *pala* of gold, fashioned with devotion, according to one's financial means, and likewise reddish in hue.
Having personally received the command from his guru, he should himself worship that Lord of the World with the six-syllable mantra, using fragrant substances and flowers.
"Oṃ, salutation to Sūrya"— this is the mantra.
Having worshipped the deity according to the rules with fruits, flowers, and other offerings,
one should present everything to Sūrya, saying, "May Sūrya be pleased with me."
Then, at the clear dawn, the observer of the vow, having gone to the teacher’s house,
should present the sun along with all the ritual implements to the preceptor.
Grain, flowers, fruits, clothing, jewels, cattle, and so forth—
whatever one gives at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse with ten million times ten thousand cows;
O Indra among kings, all other gifts of sacred fords, as well as sixteen other kinds of gifts, do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of Campā.
O Pārtha, Campā is comparable [to other cities], yet Campaikā alone excels it;
she is like Āditya, Tapana, Pūṣan, Bhānumat, Bhānu, and Aryaman.
Viśvavaktra, Aṃśumān, Deva, Sahasrāṃśu, Khanāyaka,
Sūra, Sūrya, and Khaga— the Worshipful One— are to be worshipped in sequence on the petals starting from the east.

"O Deva" is an epithet for Aṃśumat. "Āditya" is to be worshipped in the center, while Tapanas and the others are to be worshipped on the eastern petals and so forth; this is the meaning. The rule regarding the vow beginning with "on the fifth day" and so forth pertains specifically to those who lack wealth. Thus concludes the Campā-Ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O best of the Bharatas, the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa should be known as meritorious, sin-destroying, auspicious, cooling, and dear to Guha.
Having slain Tāraka on the sixth lunar day, Guha shone like the King of the Stars;
therefore, that lunar day became beloved by Kārttikeya.
Acts such as bathing and giving charity performed there are said to be inexhaustible for those who behold the son of Gaṅgā (Bhīṣma) situated in the southern direction on this day.
They are liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, having fasted on this [day], one should [offer] a Kumāra made of gold.
O Great King, having caused [the image] to be made of silver, or of clay, or of wood,
by means of Arthasāra, he was free from desire and resentment.
Then, having bathed in the afternoon and properly performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
the wise man should remain seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), meditating on Gāṅgeya according to his ability.
Then the learned Brāhmaṇa, taking a new water-pot,
should face southward and pour a stream of water upon his own head.
Born from the circle of the staff, purified by the prosperity of worldly existence—
this stream of the Gaṅgā, O Kumāra, has been poured upon your head.
Having meditated thus and having worshipped the orb of the sun in the sky,
one should thereafter worship the son of Kṛttikā with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
O divine general Skanda, Kārttikeya, Bhavodbhava,
Kumāra, Guha, Gāṅgeya, wielder of the spear— homage be to you!
Having worshipped with these names and words, one should present the food offering;
indeed, the fruits such as the jackfruit and others that grow in the southern direction [should be offered].
One should worship sandalwood produced from the Malaya mountains and camphor, which is dear to the Lord;
one should also always honor the goat and the cock standing at his side, who are ever beloved.
Having worshipped the peacock with all its parts, as well as the golden one visibly present,
and the cart of Kṛttikā at his side— the beloved of Skanda— [one should proceed].
Then, with those very names, an oblation should be performed using sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter;
having thus completed it according to the rule, O Yudhiṣṭhira, [one should offer] one pala.
Having caused [the recipient] to consume [the offering], one should sleep at night on a bed of darbha grass placed upon the ground;
likewise, [one may offer] coconut, citron, orange, and jackfruit.
O King, the jambīra, pomegranate, grape, bilva, and āmalaka,
as well as the fruit of the plantain and cucumber, are beneficial for the heart in that order.
Having consumed [the medicine] month by month, one should abstain for one month;
in the event of unavailability, one should proceed with twelve fruits produced in that region and season, in due order.
O King, it becomes complete for one who eats only at night, and not otherwise;
[the deity appears] visibly as a goat or a cock fashioned of gold.
In the morning, one should say to the reciter, "May Senānī be pleased.
Guha, the six-faced son of the Lord of the Army, is the enemy of Krauñca.
Gāṅgeya, Kārttikeya, Svāmī, Bāla, Grahāgraṇī, Chāgapriya, Śaktidhara, and Kumāra— these are remembered as the twelve.
One should recite "May [the deity] be pleased" for all [deities] in their respective order throughout the months;
having first fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should afterwards eat while remaining silent.
Thus, at the end of the year, in the month of Kārttika, O Bhārata,
one should worship Kārttikeya with garments and ornaments.
He who is unable [to perform it] every month should perform this once a year,
preceded by worship and fire-offerings (homa), according to the annual ritual procedure.
One should give everything, especially to the best of the twice-born who is the reciter;
when this book is completed, O Pārtha, one shall have crossed over the ocean of existence.
Whether it be a man or even a woman, whoever performs this with devotion,
having attained auspicious desires in this world, goes to the same realm as Indra.
The mighty-armed Kārttikeya is indeed always worthy of worship;
it is declared that no one other than Kārttikeya is to be honored by kings.
He who, while going forth to battle, worships the Son of Kṛttikā,
shall conquer hosts of enemies, just as Indra conquered the Dānavas in combat.
Therefore, having fashioned a beautiful image of Kārttikeya,
the wise man, having observed it properly as if he were situated in the southern direction, should proceed.
Having installed a golden image or similar representation in one's home according to one's capacity, one should worship it;
by worshipping it with devotion, one shall attain all desires.
But he who always observes the night-fast on the sixth lunar day, dedicating it to that All-pervading Lord,
shall be liberated from all sins and become dear to the Son of Gaṅgā.
Endowed with faith, one should go three times toward the southern direction to behold the Lord of the Gods of gods himself, the son of Paśupati.
Having immediately abandoned evil-mindedness, he becomes one whose self is perfectly tranquil;
liberated from suffering and misfortune, he dwells in happiness for a long life.
Having died, he goes to the city of Śiva and rejoices for a long time like Skanda;
thereafter, he is born into a family of the foremost of the twice-born who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
In that prosperous city, where the inhabitants were devoted to righteousness, performed sacrifices, and practiced charity,
he was endowed with all virtues and had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
O best of the Bharatas, one who is compassionate toward all beings, whose mind is solely fixed on Skanda, and who is steadfastly devoted to the meaning of the Purāṇas,
is born free from the bonds of karma and attains the supreme state.
Thus I have declared the entire, supreme majesty of Skanda;
whoever shall read or hear this with devotion, even they are liberated from sins.
He who worships the primordial god born from the lotus, the beloved son of Śambhu and the daughter of the Mountain King,
shall experience unrestrained joys in heaven once again.
He becomes a general who protects the kingdom from its enemies.
Thus ends the Kārttikeya-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, please now describe the ritual procedure for the Ṣaṣṭhī [fast].
It pacifies all diseases and bestows the fruits of all desires.
"I have heard that the Sun, when worshipped, grants all desires;
therefore, O Keśava, tell me how one may propitiate the Maker of Day."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O best of men, I shall now describe the Viśoka-ṣaṣṭhī;
by fasting upon it, a person shall never again encounter sorrow in this world.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should perform a bath with black sesame seeds;
having first cleansed the teeth, one should take a meal of kṛśara.
With rice-porridge made of sesame and rice,
one should observe the vow of fasting and remain celibate during the night.
Then, having risen in the morning, purified by bathing and ascetic observances, one should remain pure.
Having fashioned a golden lotus, one should worship it with the thought,
"This is the Sun," using red oleander flowers and a pair of red garments.
Just as the world becomes free from sorrow when you have risen,
so may I be free from sorrow in every birth through devotion to you.
Having thus performed the worship, one should honor the twice-born according to one's ability on the sixth lunar day;
then, having consumed cow urine, one should sleep and thereafter rise purified.
Having honored the Brahmins with gifts, including vessels filled with molasses,
and having covered them with cloth, he should present all of this to his preceptor.
Having eaten food without oil or salt on the seventh lunar day while observing silence,
one who desires prosperity should thereafter listen to the Purāṇas.
By this procedure, he should perform everything for both fortnights until the seventh day of the bright half of the month of Māgha.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-pot accompanied by a golden lotus,
as well as a bed with its furnishings and a tawny cow that yields milk.
But he who, free from stinginess regarding his wealth, performs this rite according to the prescribed rule—
this being known as the Viśoka-Ṣaṣṭhī— attains the supreme goal.
One who has arrived here in this world does not become a partaker of grief for as long as twelve births; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Whatever desire one prays for, that one obtains in abundance;
but he who acts without desire attains the supreme state.
Whoever should recite or even hear this "Sixth [Verse] that Destroys Sorrow," they too,
being freed from evil through devotion to the Sun, shall become happy.
Those men who, having observed a fast, worship Bhāskara, who fills the quarters with the mass of his rays,
shall be free from suffering and grief, together with their kinsmen and friends.
Having wandered upon the earth, they attain the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the Viśoka-ṣaṣṭhī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"I shall likewise describe another auspicious vow, the Phala-ṣaṣṭhī."
Having fasted upon which, a person becomes liberated from sins and becomes a partaker of its fruit.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
remaining firm in his observances and free from envy, he should clean his teeth and sleep during the night.
Then, at the clear dawn, having had a golden lotus and a single fruit made according to his means, he should do so free from deceit.
Then, having bathed at the confluence at midday and performed his daily rites,
he returned home and worshipped the God, the Teacher of the World.
Having prepared a lotus in a vessel made of udumbara wood or clay, along with fruit and sugar, according to his ability, O best of kings.
One should worship with flowers, incense, and so forth, as well as with various food offerings and fruits;
and having arranged a vigil accompanied by song, dance, and festivities, one should perform the rite.
Having bathed in the morning and become pure, having fulfilled his duties and being free from illness,
he should diligently honor the guru with garments, garlands, and ornaments.
Having offered all that to the Sun with the words, "May Bhānu be pleased," he should feed the Brahmins with devotion and then eat himself while maintaining silence.
O tiger among the Kurus, on the seventh day one may worship one's own chosen deity;
however, that fruit must be avoided until the fifth day of the dark fortnight.
Having again performed the previously mentioned oblation combined with the five fruits,
one should fast on the sixth lunar day and offer [the gift] on the seventh according to the prescribed rule.
Furthermore, another fruit must be abandoned until the fifth bright lunar day;
in this manner, O King, one who is restrained by his vows [observes] two sixth days for one year.
Having fasted and given [the gift] in due order, one should recite the mantra of the Sun;
according to one's ability, [one should give] a copper-colored cow along with its accessories and milk.
The garments or ornaments of the couple should be of those same colors.
Bhānu, Arka, Ravi, Brahmā, Sūrya, Śakra, Hari, and Śiva [are his names].
"May the glorious Tvaṣṭṛ, the manifester, and Varuṇa be pleased"—
thus one should recite each name individually on the seventh lunar day of every month.
O Ravi, just as the desires of your devotees are never fruitless,
so may I attain infinite fruits in every birth.
Whoever performs this Phalaṣaṣṭī, which bestows infinite fruit,
is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of the Sun.
And having come here, this king, together with his sons and grandsons, shall find all his undertakings successful; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever should behold it being made, or likewise follow after it,
or hear it, or read it, he too shall become a partaker of auspiciousness;
[he shall obtain] a golden fruit, a complete jar, and a canopy.

Having fasted according to the rules for sixty [days], a mortal should bow to the Sun— the one whose feet are rubbed by the crest-jewels of gods and demons— and give [an offering] to an eminent brahmin; thus he attains the perfection of his desired fruit.
Thus ends the Phala-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Śrī-Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"O King, O Mṛpa, one who eats fruit on the sixth lunar day, especially during the month of Kārttika,
shall regain his own kingdom without delay, even if he has been deprived of his realm."
O Great King, the sixth lunar day always grants all desires;
it should be observed with diligent effort at all times by one who seeks victory.
The beloved of Kārttikeya is the single great lunar day, the sixth;
for it was on this day that the high-souled one attained the lordship over the divine army.
Since Skanda was formerly endowed with glory on this [sixth] day, therefore one should never eat on the sixth lunar day; one would thus always obtain the fruit of Bhārgavī.
O observer of noble vows, having offered the *arghya* to Kārttikeya and standing facing the south, one should offer curd, ghee, water, and flowers with this mantra: "Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu."
O Skanda, son of the Seven Sages, commander of the army, possessed of great strength; born of Rudra, Umā, and Agni, six-faced, the offspring of Gaṅgā—homage be to you!
May the divine General be pleased; fulfill the desires of your friends by giving choice food and whatever else you possess to the Brahmin.
Afterwards, he eats at night, using the ground as his vessel;
such is the fruit declared by Skanda for one established in the sixth-day vow.
Listen to that in its entirety as it is being told by me, O Great King:
he who, on the sixth lunar day, shall subsist on fruit and eat only at night.
Whether during the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, one who is self-controlled and observant of celibacy attains success,
fortitude, nourishment, sovereignty, long life, and freedom from disease.
Skanda will undoubtedly bestow both benefits for the next world and for this one;
indeed, if one is unable to observe a fast, the practitioner of the vow may subsist on food at night.
One should not eat oil on the sixth lunar day, nor during the daytime, O joy of the Kurus;
for that man who observes the *nakta* fast on the sixth day, O best of the Bharatas, [attains great merit].
Completely liberated from all sins, one shall always go to the son of Gaṅgā;
here, Gāṅgeya is Svāmikārttikeya.
And there is a certain residence in heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Having come here at the proper time, he shall partake of the fruits as described;
he will become a king of kings, worthy of being venerated even by the gods.
Thus ends the Skanda-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
By worshipping Kārttikeya, one is born as the best among the twice-born.
He will be wise, endowed with beauty, long-lived, and a increaser of his fame.
The root mantras are proclaimed by their own names, as are the limb mantras.
Here, Kārttikeya is the Lord of the Lunar Days (tithīśvara);
the Lord of the Lunar Days should be depicted as before, seated upon a lotus petal.
Worship performed with offerings of incense and flowers according to one's ability—
even if done with deceit or hypocrisy— bestows its fruit.
An oblation performed with a tranquil mind, consisting of streams of clarified butter, fuel, curd, milk, rice, and honey, bestows the fruits previously mentioned.
This vow is to be explained like the Vaiśvānara-pratipad-vrata. Thus ends the Kārttikeya-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pārtha, I shall proclaim the meritorious sixth [lunar day] known as Mandāra, which destroys all sins and bestows all desires.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, a man who has controlled his senses, having eaten light food and used a tooth-stick, should sleep upon the ground.
But a man who is deprived of all enjoyments should observe a fast on the sixth lunar day;
having obtained permission from an excellent brahmin, he should pray to Mandāra at night.
*Mandāra* is *rājārka*.
Then, having risen at dawn and performed his ablutions, he again honored the twice-born and prepared the *mandāra* flower, anointed with saffron.
Likewise, one should fashion a very beautiful golden figure of a man holding a lotus in his hand;
having made an eight-petaled lotus out of black sesame seeds in a copper vessel.
One should worship with mandāraka flowers saying "To Bhāskara" in the eastern petal, and likewise with a salutation saying "To Sūrya" in the southeastern petal.
Likewise, in the south [offer] to Arka and to Yajñeśa;
in the southwest (nairṛta), [offer] with "To Vasudhāman"; and in the northwest (vāyavya), to Caṇḍabhānu.
Having worshipped [the deity] in the north with "O Kṛṣṇa," and thereafter with "For the sake of bliss," one should worship Hari as the Puruṣa in the pericarp with one's whole being.
Having wrapped it in white cloths and honored it with offerings of food, garlands, fruits,
