and so forth, one should present all of that to the preceptor.
Restrained in speech and facing the east, he should eat [the food] without oil or salt;
by this procedure, he should perform everything month after month on the seventh lunar day.
One should perform this for a year, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
and at the conclusion of the vow, one should place [the image] upon a water-pot.
One desiring prosperity should give [this] joined with the sun to the best of the twice-born.
"Joined with the sun" means joined with a golden sun.
Homage to the Lord of Mandāra and to the abode of Mandāra.
O Sun, deliver us from this ocean of saṃsāra.
One should perform that rite for the sixth lunar day known as Mandārā according to this procedure;
free from sin, happy, and blessed, one is honored in heaven after death.
Holding this lamp that dispels the darkness of the veil of delusion,
a person walking in the pit of saṃsāra shall not stumble.
Whoever reads or even hears this celebrated Mandāra-ṣaṣṭhī, which bestows the fruits of all desired objects, is liberated from all sins.
Having fasted on the sixth lunar day and worshipped the Sun upon the pericarp of a sesame lotus with *karavīra* tree flowers during the day,
those men who perform this never fail to attain their goal.
Those who give cows, land, gold, and sesame seeds obtain the fruit [of their merit].
Thus ends the Mandāra-ṣaṣṭhī vow as declared in the Śrī-Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
[Tell me of that which] causes the destruction of disease, the loss of beauty, and misfortune.
O Keśava, tell me of that vow which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
Kṛṣṇa said: That which the God, the Destroyer of Tripura, formerly spoke to Umā regarding the worship of the Sun amidst excellent narratives.
I shall now proclaim this supreme method of propitiation for both men and women, which grants the accomplishment of virtue, pleasure, and wealth.
Listen with focused attention to this which destroys all sins:
in the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should subsist on a single meal a day.
Having first cleaned his teeth, a man should observe a fast on the sixth lunar day;
he should bathe with a paste of white mustard seeds for the purification of the body.
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead using yellow pigment (rocanā), black cow urine, musta grass, sandalwood, cow dung, curd, and black agallochum (kālāguru).
Since it bestows good fortune and health through stone, red petals, and so forth,
[one should offer] a garland, saffron, betel, vermilion, and two red garments.
Indeed, having observed a fast, a woman should perform this rite which increases auspiciousness;
a widow, however, should do so in solitude, while a maiden should wear white garments. Then, in her own home, she should worship the Sun with cool water.
Then, having bathed in the afternoon, remaining very silent and firm in his vows,
he should install the image of the Sun with water mixed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should anoint [the deity] with red sandalwood paste and saffron,
and worship with red agasti flowers and karavīra blossoms.
One should offer incense of guggulu as well as kunduruka,
having adorned [the image] with red cloths embellished with black aloe-wood.
There, a copper vessel filled with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and water,
mixed with *karavīra*, blue lotuses, red flowers, and auspicious *koraṇḍaka* blossoms [should be placed].
With red agasti, javā flowers, mālatī, kunda, and mudgara blossoms.
Then, with *mucukunda* flowers, other fragrant *śatapatra* lotuses,
yellow orpiment, tips of *kuśa* grass, white mustard seeds, sesame, and lotuses— along with curd, saffron, and filaments— as they were available, [he performed the worship].
O King, having raised his hands high, he should offer this *arghya* with these words:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, thousand-rayed maker of day!"
May this worship be complete; accept this water offering, homage be to you!
[I offer] milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter, accompanied by various kinds of foods.
Then, having offered the food oblation (naivedya), one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Sun;
having worshipped him with the mantra "dhātāram" and prostrated again and again.
Having fashioned a floral mandala and likewise keeping a vigil at night,
the listening to or the recitation of this Purāṇa is recommended.
This should be heard from a Brāhmaṇa or, in some cases, from another reciter;
one should spend the entire night with songs, dances, and instrumental music.
Thus, in the month of Āśvayuja, one should worship Aryaman;
in Kārttika, Mitra is to be worshipped; and in Mārgaśīrṣa, Varuṇa.
In the month of Puṣya, he is to be well-worshipped as Aṃśumān; in Māgha, he is to be worshipped as Bhaga;
in the month of Phālguna, as Indra; and in Caitra, as Vivasvat.
Pūṣan is to be worshipped in Vaiśākha; in Jyeṣṭha, one should worship Parjanya. Tvaṣṭṛ is to be worshipped in Āṣāḍha, and one should worship Viṣṇu in Śrāvaṇa.
Then, at dawn on the bright seventh lunar day, one should perform a ritual bath;
one should worship the deity upon the ground with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings.
Then, having prostrated before the Lord of Gods, one should perform worship upon all the limbs:
the two feet are to be worshipped as Dhātṛ, and then the throat as Vivasvat with the salutation "Namaḥ".
One should worship the nose with "Obeisance to Pūṣan," the two eyes with "To Parjanya," the forehead with "Obeisance to Tvaṣṭṛ," and the head with "To Viṣṇu."
Thereafter, one should honor the teacher who instructs in the path of the vow, with land, gold, and garments; one should avoid stinginess regarding wealth.
When the reciter is honored, the Sun-god is always pleased;
thus one should worship him every month for the duration of a year.
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins milk-rice with clarified butter, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one’s ability; let the Sun-god also be invoked.
Then one should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) oneself together with one's kinsmen.
Now I shall describe the concluding rite (udyāpana); let the sequence for this be heard.
Having fashioned a beautiful pavilion with auspicious cloth curtains,
one should make it fragrant with saffron and adorned with divine ornaments.
Having fashioned a celestial palace with foliage hanging from its edges,
one should place in its center a red pitcher endowed with the five jewels.
Having placed [the vessel] upon a jar together with a copper plate,
one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp using black sesame seeds.
Having fashioned a golden image of the Sun, holding a lotus in his hand and standing upon a chariot,
one should place it upon the pericarp of the lotus after bathing it with clarified butter and other substances.
Then, having bathed, anointed himself, and put on two clean garments,
and having worshipped the gods and the ancestors, he should proceed to the temple of the gods.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with the twelve names,
and having worshipped [them], one should subsequently offer oblations (naivedya).
One should satisfy them with milk-rice mixed with ghee, sweetmeat balls, sugar-candies,
*somālaka* fruits, *kokarasa* fruits, and other auspicious offerings that are pleasing to the sense of smell and quick to reach it.
With *śrīphala* fruits, *mātuluṅga*, coconuts, pomegranates, *kūṣmāṇḍa*,
round *karkaṭa*, oranges, jackfruit, and so forth.
One should offer all fruits that are in season and worship with the sounding of conchs and trumpets, and with songs and dances.
Then, at the time of dawn, having bathed the Sun with new jars, one who is observant of the vow [attains his favor], since he is the bestower of good fortune and health.
An oblation with sesame seeds and clarified butter using those very names is highly recommended;
thereafter, one should perform the Sūrya-sacrifice in front of the Sun.
One should smear a level ground with red sandalwood paste,
measuring one cubit, two cubits, or even four cubits.
One should draw the solar disc with realgar and vermilion,
using fragrant red flowers, incense, saffron, and other such substances.
Having performed worship, one should offer the ritual food (naivedya) consisting of ghee and milk-rice according to the rules;
one should place before [the deity] a water-pot accompanied by gold and a cloth.
One should give betel, saffron, and flowers to the female ascetics;
then, with garments, friends, and kinsmen, one should ask her for forgiveness.
Thus, at the conclusion of the sixth [day], on the morning of the seventh, the observer of the vow,
having bathed with the materials previously prescribed, should have the twice-born perform the fire-oblation (homa).

With the mantra beginning with "ākṛṣṇena," one should offer one hundred and eight oblations using fuel-sticks such as those of the *arka* tree, along with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and molasses.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brāhmaṇas;
having fed the twice-born, one should honor them with various garments.
In this matter, they praise twelve auspicious cows accompanied by garments;
one who is self-controlled should give them to Brahmins along with an umbrella, a pair of shoes, and a yoke.
When one is unable [to give all], then one should give a single milch cow;
thereafter, having honored a Brahmin endowed with virtuous conduct with perfumes and other offerings.
O Pāṇḍava, one should give that image to him while reciting the mantra with the Khāna rite.
Oṃ, homage to the Sun, who brings about the destruction of all darkness!
By your gift, O Ravi, may all my heart’s desires be fulfilled—
may I obtain a cow accompanied by a chariot and garments, as well as land suitable for crops.
One should give [the gift] together with gold, saying, "May the Sun be pleased";
and one should place an umbrella and a pair of sandals in front of the maṇḍala.
Having placed Aruṇa in front of that [altar], one should place the seven horses before him;
in the space between them, however, one should place Revanta, and behind him, the two Aśvins.
One should know Śani to be in its south, as well as the deities of the directions and time (or the guardians of the directions) in their proper order;
and gifts such as beds and houses should be bestowed there.
For those desiring eternal satisfaction for the ancestors and the gods through ancestral rites (*śrāddha*),
this lunar day (*tithi*) thus bestows all desires upon men, O wise one.
Excellently bestowing happiness, gentle, and granting the world of the Sun,
even one of meager wealth should observe the fast on every sixth lunar day.
On the seventh lunar day, one should feed a Brahmin for eight years;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should present a cow to a Brahmin of radiant conduct.
O King, by performing [the rite] without interruption, he too shall obtain that fruit;
constant and eternal devotion to the Sun will arise within him.
O Pārtha, he who thus performs this unsurpassed vow [shall travel] in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and shine like ten million suns.
[The lakes] were filled with throngs of Apsarases, frequented by gods and Gandharvas,
abounding in swans and cranes, and resounded with the noise of musical instruments and singing.
Accompanied by all his friends, including Godhūma, Māna, and Camara, who were endowed with various flavors, as well as by many Kinnaras who shone like suns.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot together with hosts of Vidyādharas,
he goes to the supreme abode where the radiant Sun resides.
As long as the moon, sun, and stars endure, and for as long as the seventy kusha eons last, so long shall one be honored in the world of the sun for a thousand yugas.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures together with three persons,
and having remained for a long time in happiness in the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others;

Endowed with sons and grandsons, devoted to the performance of sacrifices, charity, and sacred rites,
he was wise, righteous, heroic, and proficient in all the scriptures.
Devoted to Brahman, a true poet, a speaker of truth, one who has conquered his senses,
eloquent, a worthy refuge, benevolent of mind, and intent on compassion for the miserable and the helpless.
O Pārtha, whether it be a man who, having conquered his enemies in battle, enjoys the earth he has won,
or a woman who does so, she too partakes in that fruit.
The queen of a universal monarch shall have her sovereignty destroyed;
likewise, the co-wife shall be crushed, while she [the former] shall possess good fortune, health, and sons.
Whether one be a slave or anyone else, whoever should observe this vow shall rejoice for a very long time and dwell happily in their home.
His prosperity, victory, and indeed the three aims of life increase;
upon death, he attains heaven, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot.
He shall dwell in the worlds of the sun, endowed with all desires,
served by celestial women and attended by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
Amidst the sounds of instrumental music and song throughout many series of Manvantaras,
one who has attained the yoga of knowledge shall enter the solar disc.
O Lord of Men, if one wishes to worship the Sun-god on this sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Nabhasya after fasting,
one should honor the most excellent of the twice-born with gifts of cows, land, gold, and garments.
Having bestowed joy, he proceeds to the abode of the Sun.
Thus ends the Sūrya-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata with its concluding rite (sodyāpana) in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Agastya said:
O Great King, now hear from me as I speak of the Kāma-vrata.
By which even those desires that are merely conceived by the mind are fully accomplished.
He who observes this vow for one year, eating only fruit on the sixth lunar day,
and eating only at night on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha;
On the sixth day, however, the wise man should consume one fruit of the earth;
thereafter, he should carefully eat pure boiled rice while maintaining silence.
O Indra among kings, having remained for that one day on the seventh lunar day, one should break the fast on the eighth with Brahmins, O King, or else with fruit alone.
One should perform the fire-ritual and worship Keśava in the form of Guha according to the prescribed rule, and observe the vow for one year.
"Keśava in the form of Guha" means that one should worship Viṣṇu in the form of Kārttikeya.
This interpretation is justified because the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas establish that all deities are but single forms of Viṣṇu.
Kārttikeya is six-faced, Guha, Senānī, and the son of Pāvaka.
The youth Skanda and Viṣṇu are thus to be worshipped by their names;
at the conclusion of this vow, one should provide a feast for the Brahmins.
One should present a six-faced [image] made entirely of gold to a Brāhmaṇa, saying:
"O Six-faced God, may all my desires be fulfilled."
By your grace, may this be accepted with devotion according to the rite for a long time;
having given this to a Brāhmaṇa along with a pair [of garments] while reciting this mantra.
Accompanied by a pair of garments;
thereafter, all desires indeed flourish in this very life:
one without a son obtains sons, and one without wealth obtains wealth.
One whose kingdom has been lost shall regain it; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Thus ends the Kāma-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as described in the Varāha Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"Where there is a vessel completely filled and provided with honey..."
One should give one Magadhan prastha of black sesame seeds.
One should prepare three *prasthas* of rice separately.

The vessel is a bowl to be filled with four *prasthas*; "threefold" means three *prasthas*. "Separately" means that one should keep the vessels for the ghee, honey, sesame, and rice distinct. The measure of a *prastha* according to the Magadha standard is stated in the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*).
Then one should worship the Sun with perfumes, flowers, and incense, especially with various musical instruments accompanied by diverse instrumental music.

There, in that celestial abode, is where the sky is established.
The construction of the celestial vault (*vyomanirmāṇa*) according to the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
At the base it should be square; there, [the dome] is circular with great arms (projections). Beyond that, another square is auspiciously situated upon the first.
The fourth part, the sky-element, is said to consist of the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha);
furthermore, Vaiśvānara is proclaimed to be the central portion in the pillar.
Furthermore, one should place another lotus there like a noble throne;
in its center, within the pericarp, is the Sun.
"One should place the lords of the directions and time upon its eight petals in every direction.

Having reached the world of the Sun, he rejoices for eternal years;
when his merit is exhausted, he returns here and is born into a prosperous family.
Intelligent, fortunate, illustrious, meritorious, and virtuous in giving, he attains the world of the Sun once again; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Vyoma-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, one who is well-restrained [should observe this vow].
A woman, having bathed at dawn and being fond of white garlands and garments, [should proceed].
Having adorned herself with fine garments and ornaments and taken sand in a new bamboo vessel, she should go home with her face turned downwards.
Having observed a fast with diligence, she should worship the Goddess there,
having prepared a beautiful pair of garments adorned with flower garlands.
Having established that goddess there, one should worship Hari with flowers.
Regarding the phrase "that goddess," it means that one should bring sand from within the water and, having fashioned it into five lumps in a bamboo vessel, worship the goddess made of sand.
Then, one should meditate upon the goddess Lalitā, who dwells in the penance grove.
The lotus, the oleander, the Nepalese jasmine, and likewise the Arabian jasmine;
Having taken a special Nepalese flower— the remainder of the sentence being that one should worship with it—
one should take blue lotuses, ketakī flowers, and excellent tagara;
each of these should be taken eight hundred times, or indeed twenty-eight.
Taking unbroken flower buds, one should worship the Goddess with them;
having become a practitioner of the vow, one should pray to Girijā, the beloved of Giriśa,
at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, or the Nīla mountain.
Having bathed at the Kanakhala tirtha, he slew the husband of Padmavati.
O Goddess Lalitā, most beautiful one, bestower of happiness and good fortune, grant me infinite prosperity; may it be the supreme destroyer of all evil.
Having thus worshipped according to the ritual procedure with this mantra and most beautiful campaka flowers, one should place the food offering (naivedya) before [the deity].
With cucumbers, water-melons, pumpkins, and coconuts,
along with pomegranates, citron fruits, tūṇḍīras, bitter gourds, and varvaṭas;
Having created a splendor before him with fruits produced at that very time—
*trapuṣa*, *vālukam*, *ekavālu*, *karkaṭī*, and *tuṇḍīra*, which is a species of tree—
he surrounded him on all sides with rows of lamps made from sprouts grown from nothing else.
Together with incenses possessing their respective qualities, with *somālaka* and *karaṅkaka* resins,
with perfumes and flowers, with ear-ornaments, with *modakas* and *upamodakas*,
and with various kinds of food offerings according to the extent of one's wealth.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rites, one should observe a vigil at night with songs,
instrumental music, actors, dances, and various kinds of performances.
Accompanied by her female friends, that virtuous woman should spend the night lying down;
however, she should not close her eyes for the four watches of the night.
An unfortunate woman, one who has met with misfortune, or a barren woman shall become blessed through the closing of her eyes;
having thus performed the vigil on the seventh lunar day, she should lead [the image] to a river.
Then, having honored it with perfumes and incense preceded by song and instrumental music,
O best of men, one should present that food offering and other gifts to the foremost of the twice-born.
Having bathed and returned home, he should duly offer oblations into the sacred fire and worship the gods, the ancestors, human beings, and married women.
And fifteen Brahmin maidens should be honored with various kinds of food and drink, after giving abundant gifts.
Having said, "May Lalitā be well-pleased with me," one should dismiss her;
whoever should perform this vow shall attain the perfection of good fortune.
And it is known as Lalitā-ṣaṣṭhī, which destroys all sins.
Whether it be a man or a woman, hear now the fruit of his merit,
O best of kings— that which cannot be obtained through other vows or gifts.
Indeed, this is attained through austerities or even through religious observances;
and having experienced incomparable prosperity and good fortune right here in this world, it is so obtained.
O Pārtha, having placed her foot upon the heads of her co-wives, that illustrious woman died and reached the city of Śiva, where she was honored by gods, asuras, and pannagas.
He attains a vision of the Goddess and rejoices with her;
then, having returned here due to the remainder of his merit, he possesses a meritorious disposition for good fortune.
In the Satya and Tretā Yugas, a woman was as dear to her beloved as Sītā;
O Pārtha, whoever should hear this or recite it in the assembly of the virtuous,
he too, liberated from sin, is glorified in the world of Śakra.
On the sixth day, she who, having taken sand from within the water in an excellent bamboo vessel, worships it in due order,
and keeps a vigil at night with modest dress and conduct;
He would act [thus], and he shines like the moon in the three worlds.
Thus ends the Lalitā-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, O King, having fasted on the sixth lunar day according to the prescribed rites, [one should proceed].
Having fashioned a mandala of a wheel and lotus, one should place Sudarśana in the pericarp.
One should worship the weapons of the world-protectors upon the petals;
the wheel-oil and the lotus joined to the hub of the wheel.
Having established one's own weapons in front, the worshipper should perform the rite.
Also with red sandalwood, white mustard seeds, and the sprouts of red lotuses.
One should worship with red garments, fragrant substances, and ornaments such as jewelry;
one should also present an offering of molasses-rice accompanied by cakes and fruits.
O Sudarśana, Great Discus, whose flames pervade the quarters of space,
you who crush the circle of the Daitya-enemies, destroy my adversaries!
May you, O World-Protectors, bestow upon us at all times fearlessness, victory in battle, and auspiciousness, even from all their weapons.
Just as Viṣṇu is the foremost among men and Lakṣmī is the foremost among women,
so may this discus, the destroyer of enemies, fully grant me victory.
May all my weapons, resembling the form of a wheel, remain ever undisturbed and present before me at all times.
O Sudarśana, protect my army, which is joined by a multitude of rutting elephants, chariots, and horses, and consists of a flood of joyful and well-nourished foot soldiers.
Having thus prayed with devotion, he should receive his own weapon;
thereafter, the wise man should cause a circular mandala to be drawn in front of him.
Combined with rice, filled with sesame seeds,
free from blemishes, covered with cloth, and endowed with all medicinal herbs.
One should place four water-pots in the four directions,
and in the center as well, one filled with all medicinal herbs and endowed with the five jewels.
Having placed a water-pot covered with a pair of garments there,
one whose mind is focused on no other should invoke the deity Sudarśana into it.
One should place the conch, Nandaka, Śārṅga, and the mace Kaumodakī in the jars starting from the east, and worship them in their respective locations.
One should offer milk-rice, rice with meat, rice with mung beans, and that which is produced from curd; all these are considered appropriate for the Madhu sacrifice according to the circumstances.
Alternatively, the five weapons should indeed be worshipped in five jars:
the discus, the conch, the lotus, the Śārṅga bow, and the sword Nandaka along with the mace.
"But outside, one should place the weapons of the World-Protectors in pairs.
Regarding "in pairs," this means two for each jar.
At the front of that, [one should place] a great staff covered with yellow silk.
Having established the form of Tārkṣya and having fixed the banner at the front,
one should thereafter worship Tārkṣya with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings.
One should offer there an abundance of cakes, fruits, roots, and food;
one should also perform circumambulations, prostrations, recitations of hymns, and other such acts.
Just as the wind melts away a dense mass of clouds,
so may the King of Birds scatter those who bear me enmity.
Having thus prayed and completed the worship according to the rules,
the practitioner should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors with kṛśara-rice.
With kṛśara-rice and rice mixed with sesame seeds;
having brought a golden lion-throne before him—
that "lion-throne" being a lion-seat.
Having placed the king upon it, adorned with all ornaments, [he departed].
Having brought a golden vessel, one should invoke the deity Sudarśana therein with his specific mantra and worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having prepared a wick combined with *siddhārtha* seeds and wrapped in red cloth—
where *siddhārtha* refers to mustard seeds—
one should light it, place it there, and perform worship according to the prescribed ritual.
Then, having circumambulated [the deity] three times, the woman should cast [the weapon] toward the east;
having performed the circumambulation and the lustration ceremony (nīrājana),
there is the bestowal of weapons with the mantra of Hetirāja.
Having invoked Sudarśana, the king of weapons,
with its respective mantra, one should offer the vehicle and other items;
this very same procedure is prescribed for the ornaments and so forth in that context.
At the commencement of war, during great portents, when oppressed by an enemy army,
during the distress of losing a kingdom, or when afflicted by grief, disease, and the like;
In the event of separation from a beloved wife, the loss of a son, or the decline of one's strength,
one should perform a ritual bath with a concentrated mind on the sixth day of the bright fortnight.
This rite is to be performed when an omen has been observed, or on the king's birth-star;
and at the commencement of battle, the monarch should worship the banner of Tārkṣya.
Having placed it at the forefront of the battle, one should hoist the three excellent banners;
from the initial movement of the banner, the determination of success or failure is made.
One should declare victory from the Śakracala mountain, defeat in the south,
the destruction of enemy armies in the west, and flight in the north.
In the southeast, the lord perishes; in the southwest, there is the destruction of strength;
in the northwest, the death of horses; and in the northeast, the depletion of wealth.

[624] If the banner is severed in another intermediate direction, there will be gain; such is the examination. If the binding is severed, it portends remembrance [of past lives]; if the staff is broken, it portends [the arrival of] another.
A wise man, skilled in battle, should know that which has been done to reside within his own body; having first examined everything, he should then act.
In other matters as well, the determination of existence is exactly like this:
first the recitation of auspicious words by the brahmins, and afterwards the feeding of the brahmins.
Then, on the following day, one should perform the worship with that very name;
one should take food together with one's kinsmen, using the remnants of the Brahmins' meal.
With the remnants of the Brahmins— that is, with what remains after the feeding of the Brahmins—

one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher and a liberal fee to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth as long as the vow is being completed.
One should not speak untruth; one should offer the gift of celibacy.
This is declared to be a blessing that destroys all diseases.
This vow pacifies all suffering and brings victory to everyone;
it bestows nourishment upon both those who hear it and those who perform it.
This shall be the supreme authority for kings and bestows abundant welfare;
thus has been fully described the Ṣaṣṭhī-vrata, which grants the fruit of all desires.
Thus ends the Sudarśana-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the glorious Garuḍa Purāṇa.
Āditya said:
Having diligently observed the night-meal (nakta) according to the rules on the sixth day of the dark fortnight, [one should proceed].
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, at the beginning, one should worship [the deity] as Aṃśumān.
Having consumed cow urine according to the prescribed rule, a person should sleep at night without food;
such a man obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Likewise, they desire the thousand-rayed, radiant Sun even at Puṇya;
there, a man who has undertaken the vow shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In the month of Māgha, on the sixth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform the rite called Divākara;
by consuming cow’s urine at midnight, one shall obtain the fruit of a cow-sacrifice.
In the month of Phālguna, one should worship with sesame seeds and consume sesame;
one shall obtain a fruit equal to that of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And in the month of Caitra, on the sixth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the deity named Haṃsa;
by consuming white flowers, a man shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
In the month of Vaiśākha, on the sixth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the deity named Sūrya;
having drunk the meritorious water of kuśa grass, he should have conquered anger and subdued his senses.
One shall obtain the fruit of the Vainateya sacrifice and that of the Mahāmedha sacrifice;
having worshipped the Lord of the Day (the Sun) in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should drink water from the horns of cows,
and thus enjoys the entire fruit of the gift of ten million cows.
Having worshipped the one named Arka in the month of Āṣāḍha and having consumed cow-dung,
one attains residence in the same world as Arka for two hundred years.
Having worshipped the one named Āryaman in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should drink milk;
for more than ten thousand years, he rejoices in the abode of the Sun.
On the sixth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the deity named Bhāskara;
by consuming a single sprout of dūrvā grass, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
In the month of Āśvina, one should worship the seven-horsed [Sun] of the God of gods;
having consumed curd according to the rules, one shall obtain the fruit of the lotus.
On the sixth day of the month of Kārttika, one should worship the deity named Śakra;
eating only a fruit with cow’s urine as the meal, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
"Gomūtraphala" refers to a fruit (phala) that has been soaked in cow's urine (gomūtra).
At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to the worship of the Sun,
offering milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with honey and well-saturated with clarified butter (ājya).
According to one’s means, one should offer gold and garments to them with devotion;
moreover, one should offer a black, milch cow to Sūrya.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of that man who, with devotion, performs the Kṛṣṇa-ṣaṣṭhī vow in this manner continuously for one year.
Freed from all sins and endowed with all desires,
that man rejoices in the world of the Sun for eternal years.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇa-ṣaṣṭhī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"The sixth lunar day (ṣaṣṭhī) is a day fit for sacrifice and is common even to the deities;
[it is observed] by eating once a day, by eating only at night, and likewise by eating only what is unasked."
By means of fasting and giving gifts, avoiding oil and alkaline substances,
one honors this Blessed Lord, the Sun-god of supreme splendor.
I shall tell you that secret by which it may be seen quickly;
it is a divine vow to be kept in secrecy, which bestows fruit in this world.
By performing this vow, he shall not be poor in his family;
one should observe the sixth lunar day (ṣaṣṭhī-tithi) and provide a meal for a Brāhmaṇa.
Having prepared śāli rice with milk and added sugar,
one should cause it to be offered for one year, combined with abundant ghee.
Poverty does not come upon those men who have been born in his family, those who will be born in it, or those who exist in it here.
Thus ends the Adāridrya-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa:
By means of hymns, recitations, offerings, and worship of Vivasvat,
and by fasting on the sixth lunar day, one is indeed liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the Ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Brahma Purāṇa: He who, having observed a fast on the fifth day, worships the Sun on the sixth,
observing the rules of his vow and endowed with devotion to the Sun;
Or on the seventh day, O highly fortunate one, he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.

Thus ends the Ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Brahma-purāṇa. Furthermore, those men who diligently observe the vow on the sixth lunar day (Ṣaṣṭhī) of the bright fortnight falling on a Tuesday, as well as those women who do so individually, [attain their respective goals].
O best of gods, nothing will be difficult for them to obtain;
for, O Skanda, the fruit of their merit shall result from the union of the two.
O best of gods, by performing worship during the three conjunctions throughout the months, inexhaustible merit arises; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus ends the Ṣaṣṭhī-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "He who,
beginning from the month of Vaiśākha, fasts on the fifth day and worships Bhavānī on the sixth day with diligence for one year,"
One desiring a son shall obtain sons; one desiring wealth shall become wealthy;
and even one desiring heaven shall attain heaven—my son, when satisfied, grants this.
And those men who shall praise the Lord with my hymn will obtain their cherished desires in both worlds, even beyond the darkness.
The Lord who destroyed Krauñca is designated as fourfold in nature: Kumāra, Skanda, Viśākha, and Guha.
By worshipping him on the sixth lunar day, a man obtains his desired sons;
there is no doubt that a man attains welfare for the children in his home.
Thus ends the vow for obtaining a son as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
by performing the worship of the sages on the sixth lunar day, one shall obtain happiness.
Thus ends the Sukhavratam as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "O King, O sinless one, by moving about the side of Skanda, the side of Rudra,
and the side of Yama, one shall obtain liberation from disease."
[629] Thus ends the vow for liberation from disease as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Likewise, having worshipped Kālapāśa and Jvaravyādhiśa, one should perform the rite.
One attains liberation from disease, as well as from wind, fire, and forest conflagrations.

Thus ends the *Rogahara-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata*, as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. Thus [ends the section] composed by Śrī Hemādri, the sovereign lord of all sciences, the supreme ruler of the great kings of the Mālava dynasty.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, within the section on vows (*vratakhaṇḍa*), the vows of the sixth lunar day (*ṣaṣṭhīvratāni*).
[630] Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Now, the vows of the seventh lunar day: Even Kali, along with the first youth of the current age, no longer maintains rivalry against established customs.
Having received this with a loud and resonant voice,
this very Hemādri now narrates the vows of the seventh lunar day.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, I have previously heard from Śāṇḍilya this supreme vow,
the most secret of secrets, meritorious and known as the practice of austerity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord, how should the vow known as the practice of austerity be performed?
Tell me in detail, along with its secret teachings and the accompanying mantras.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen attentively, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
to the vow of austerity which should be observed during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa by one who desires prosperity.
Established in that state, the excellent Brahmin, a master of the Rigveda and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas,
knowing the Brahman, should offer the arghya oblation upon the surface of the earth on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kṛṣṇa.

O son of Kuntī, having recited three sections of the Ṛgveda, one should then recite the "Beloved of the Sun" (sūryavallabha) in the order of its quarters, as well as the "Kanikṛt" and that which is heard from Aditi.

The offering of the *arghya* consists of presenting it according to the sequence of the feet. O eldest son of Pāṇḍu, the wise twice-born man should perform this with the previously mentioned Vedic mantras while subsisting on a single meal, eating only at night, or eating only what is unasked for.
Śūdras who are devoted to the Sun should offer the *arghya* without mantras;
however, they should place the name at the beginning, followed by a mantra ending in the dative case.
O King, it is recited in all the scriptures that the supreme mantra for Śūdras is as follows:
having placed [the mantra] in a copper vessel together with fresh flowers and unbroken grains of rice...
Mixed with red sandalwood and adorned with *dūrvā* sprouts,
there should be red *karavīra* flowers as well as red lotuses.
Mixed with *koraṇṭaka* flowers, along with *javā* and *aśoka*,
as well as *kiṃśuka*, *agastya* blossoms, *karavīra*, and *mālatī*.
One should place mucakunda, kunda, śatapatra, and mallikā flowers— these, as they may be available— into a copper vessel.
Gorocanā, tips of kuśa grass, śrīkhaṇḍa, and saffron;
likewise, sesame seeds, rice, white mustard, curd, saffron, and stamens.
Saffron filaments and safflower—
O King, having raised both arms high, one should offer this excellent *arghya* with these;
then, having formed the *vyomamudrā* and paid obeisance, one should conclude the rite.

[632] Regarding the *vyomamudrā*, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "When the two hands are joined together with the fingers resting upon the wrists, and there is an internal space between them, they call that the *vyomamudrā*. Thus it is said.
In this case, because no image is mentioned, the offering of *arghya* is to be made directly to the solar disc itself.
O King, in this manner, following the sequence of the months for as long as a year,
when the vow is completed, one should, endowed with faith, give gifts to the Brahmins.
O Pārtha, twelve refined vessels filled with milk-rice (pāyasa) and a golden lotus according to one's capacity are prescribed as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the Brahmins.
O Dānava, one should give a pair of saffron-colored garments to the God;
he who thus properly performs that which is known as the practice of austerity—
Whether a man or a woman, one who is well-disposed through devotion to the Sun goes to that abode where the divine Divākara dwells.
Being worshipped by hosts of Apsarases like another Vṛndāraka (the gods),
he attained a preeminent birth, free from suffering and misfortune.
By the grace of Āditya, devotion toward him shall become unwavering.
[The vessel] should be filled with pairs of Udumbara fruits,
accompanied by Darbha grass, and filled with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata).
O King, he who, having prepared the *arghya* according to the rules, should offer it,
goes to the world of the one of stainless radiance.
Thus ends the vow for the performance of penance as spoken in the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"In ancient times, the lord of sages named Lomaśa went to Mathurā."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, he was thus honored by Vasudeva and Devakī.
Having sat down and related various meritorious and delightful stories,
the king then proceeded to relate this narrative.
"O daughter, those sons born to you again and again were killed by Kaṃsa;
O Devakī, you have become distressed by the grief for your sons, having lost your children."
Just as Candramukhī, the beloved of Nahuṣa,
became distressed, yet later, having observed her vow, she herself became one whose calf was unharmed.
You yourself, O Devakī, shall become exactly so; of this there is no doubt.
Devakī said:
O Brahmin, who was that moon-faced woman who became the beloved of Nahuṣa? What meritorious vow did she perform, which likewise increased her progeny?
O Lord, it shatters the pride of co-wives and bestows good fortune and health.
Śomaśa said:
O King, in ancient times in Ayodhyā there was a famous king named Nahuṣa. He had a beloved queen, endowed with beauty, whose face was like the moon.
Likewise, in that very city, there was a brahmin named Viṣṇugupta;
he had a wife named Guṇavatī, who was likewise fair-faced.
Between them there was a firm and enviable mutual affection. Then those two friends indeed went to the bank of the Śarayū for the purpose of bathing.
When he arrived, the women of that city, both those who had come with him and others,
bathed and prepared a mandala, within which they manifested his visible form.
Having caused an image of Śiva, the peaceful Śaṅkara, together with Umā, to be fashioned,
he should worship it with devotion according to the prescribed rite using perfumes, flowers, and consecrated rice.
Having prostrated, those excellent women, wishing to depart, questioned her;
they said, "Śaṅkara has been worshipped by us together with Pārvatī."
Having tied this thread made of [sacred] fibers, one's own self is offered to Śiva;
this should be worn for as long as life endures.
Having heard those words of theirs, O Devakī, these two friends also made an agreement there and tied a beautiful cord with their arms.
Then, surrounded by their own female companions, they went to their respective homes;
after a long time, that auspicious vow of hers was forgotten.
And that cord was forgotten by Candramukhī while she was intoxicated;
likewise, O auspicious lady, everything was forgotten by Bhadramukhī.
O lady of auspicious countenance, after some days and nights had passed since her death, she became a female monkey; due to the violation of her vow, that virtuous woman was born as a hen.
When he reached his death in due time for the sake of their friendship,
he was born in Gokula, a place crowded with cattle and lacking a presiding deity or a mother.
Born as a Brāhmaṇī, she likewise became a Kṣatriyī;
she then became the queen and beloved wife of the lord of the earth.
She who was formerly known as the famous Candramukhī became the renowned Īśvarī;
she who was Bhadramukhī by name became the one named Bhūṣaṇā.
That Agnimitrā was given by her father to him through his family priest;
she became exceedingly beloved, for she was Bhūṣaṇā, who was fond of ornaments.
Adorned with the finest ornaments and herself decorated with beauty,
that delightful woman had sons endowed with every virtue.
Endowed with beauty like their mother and virtuous in character like their father,
those two friends were likewise born with the recollection of their former lives.
Furthermore, their joy remained uninterrupted just as it had been before;
then, after a long time had passed, that beloved of Satya departed.
In her middle age, that queen gave birth to a single son who was afflicted by disease, mute, devoid of wisdom, and of discordant voice.
Even so, O illustrious lady, he died at the age of nine;
thereupon, she was deprived of her ornaments, and as the mistress of the house, she was distressed by the loss of her son.
Surrounded by her friends and sons out of affection and great love,
Bhadrā was adorned not by ornaments, but by her very own form.
Seeing that she was a worthy wife, the mistress blazed with rage;
then, filled with intense jealousy, the brahmin woman sent her back to her home.
That queen reflected upon the slaughter of her son;
having resolved it in her cruel mind, she began to torment her other sons.
Seeing that those sons of yours, though slain and struck down, live again free from ailment, he called Satī Bhūṣaṇā and said: "This is most wonderful."
Having seated her upon an excellent throne with great honor,
that queen, who had lost her children, asked her while overcome with wonder.
Speak the truth, O highly fortunate lady: what meritorious deed have you performed?
Was it a gift, a vow, austerity, service, or fasting?
By whom your sons were slain now live again, free from ailment;
for thus, O fair-faced one, she who has many sons is as if truly alive.
Wearing ornaments that are never removed and ever dwelling in the heart of your husband,
O Queen, you shine exceedingly, like lightning at the end of the summer heat.
Bhūṣaṇa said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall tell you of the deeds performed in another birth;
why have you forgotten everything that was done in Ayodhyā?"
O fair-faced one, due to a deficiency in our vows caused by negligence,
you were born as a female monkey and I likewise as a hen.
Nevertheless, neither you nor anyone else has caused any deficiency in your vows;
for my part, having taken refuge in Śaṅkara with my whole being and heart, [I have acted accordingly].
"O blessed lady, it is by that mental disposition through which [the act] was performed while in the animal realm;
this indeed is the cause, and I do nothing else."
Lomaśa said:
Having heard this and having grasped the deeds performed in her previous birth,
the Goddess together with her once again performed [the rites] perfectly.
By the power of this vow, having experienced incomparable happiness through the birth of sons, grandsons, and others, she passed away and went to the city of Śiva.
Therefore, O auspicious lady, you too should observe this vow;
once this divine vow has been undertaken, you will have a living son.
Devakī said: "O Brahmin, this vow of yours will not indeed properly bestow happiness; it does not cause the increase of progeny, nor does it grant a dwelling in the world of Śiva."
Lomaśa said:
In the month of Bhādrapada, on the seventh lunar day,
having bathed in a body of water and having drawn an image of Śiva and likewise Ambikā within a mandala, one should worship them.
Having worshipped with devotion, one should make a vow while binding a thread upon the hand:
"For as long as I live, my very self has been offered by me to Śiva."
Having thus made this agreement, it was reported to Śiva;
having thus made this agreement, from that time forth [the practice of] the cord [began].
A twice-born man should wear a ring made of gold, silver, or even thread on his hand;
he may eat cakes or rolls while seated on a horse-leaf mat.
O auspicious one, out of fear of breaking the vow, you yourself must consume those [substances];
when the vow is completed, a gold or silver ring and a garment should be given according to your means.
Having placed it upon a copper vessel, one should present it to the Brahmins;
and a ring should especially be given to the preceptor.
Having thus completed that vow which increases one's progeny with flowers, saffron, vermilion, betel, collyrium, and sacred threads;
Being completely liberated from all evil and having experienced delightful happiness,
and having increased their lineage, they are glorified in the world of Śiva.
All this has been told to you, along with the vow associated with the narrative.
O Devakī, perform it with diligence; you shall become one whose sons live.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Having spoken thus, that best of sages vanished on the spot;
and he performed with every effort that which had been instructed by the wise one.
By the power of this vow, Devakī gave birth to me;
therefore, O Pārtha, it should be performed by men, and especially by women.
This auspicious vow removes sin and always bestows a continuous stream of happiness;
whoever hears this with devotion or communicates it to others [shall likewise attain such merit].
Even he who performs this vow together with its narrative is liberated from sins.
Any woman who, desiring happy liberation, shall practice this Sāntānika vow while fixing Śiva in her heart;
Having abandoned incomparable suffering and swiftly cleansed of all impurity,
that woman, by virtue of her vow, becomes one whose offspring are beautiful beings.
Thus ends the Amuktābharaṇa-saptamī vow from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Bhīṣma said:
O Blessed One, [please describe] that which enables one to cross over the difficult ocean of saṃsāra.
Please describe some vow that bestows heaven, health, and happiness.
Pulastya said: O Pārtha, I shall proclaim the Saura-dharma [the duty toward the Sun] regarding the Kalyāṇa-saptamī;
I shall explain its ritual procedure correctly and in due order.
But when the day of the Sun occurs on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, that is called Kalyāṇinī and is also designated as Vijayā.
In the morning, one should perform a bath for her with cow’s milk;
wearing white garments, one should fashion a lotus out of unbroken grains of rice.
Facing east, one should place the eight-petaled lotus in the center, along with its circle and pericarp;
then, one should install the Lord upon all the petals, starting from the east in due order.
To the east, one should worship with "Salutation to Tapanīya," and then to Mārtaṇḍa;
to the south, "Salutation to Divākara," and to Vidhātṛ in the southwest (Nairṛta).
In the west, one should fashion [the mantra] "to Varuṇa" and "to Bhāskara";
in the northwest, "to Saumya," and on the eighth petal, "to Vikartana."
In the beginning, at the end, and in the middle, let there be salutation to the Supreme Self;
having worshipped with these mantras, which are illuminated by concluding salutations.
One should worship with devotion upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) using white garments, fruits, edibles, incense, garlands, and ointments, as well as molasses and salt.
Then, O best of the twice-born, one should dismiss [the deities] with the *vyāhṛti* mantras;
according to one's ability, one should offer libations with devotion using molasses, milk, ghee, and other such substances.
A person, having made such a vow, should present a vessel of sesame seeds and gold to the preceptor, rising early in the morning.
Having performed his ablutions and recitations, he should eat ghee and milk-rice together with Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and free from the "cat-vow" (hypocrisy).
One should present a vessel of ghee together with gold and a water-pot;
"May the Blessed One be pleased here"—thus the Sun declared the fruit [of this offering].
By this procedure, one should perform everything month after month;
having thus completed all of this at the end of the year, O King.
One should perform the rite according to one’s ability while recollecting the Sun-god in the heart;
then, in the thirteenth month, one should give thirteen cows.
One who is destitute of wealth and unable to perform [other] rites should give even a single milch cow, adorned with clothing and ornaments and possessing horns tipped in gold.
One should not practice stinginess with wealth, for through greed one falls downward;
he who performs the Kalyāṇasaptamī according to this rule [attains the highest state].
Having heard this, or even by reciting it, one is liberated from all sins;
the performer, having resided in the city of Śiva for one kalpa, returns here.
O King of kings, one becomes a king just as Rāghava did in the Tretā age.
One should worship [the deity] within the pericarp of a five-, eight-, or ten-petaled lotus with flowers, incense, ointments, and other offerings.
On the sixth day, on the following day, she will surely become here a vessel of auspiciousness, a sun-like dispeller of the suffering of people.
Thus ends the Kalyāṇasaptamī vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the Kamalasaptamī vow.
By the mere recitation of which the Sun-god is pleased in this world.
Having bathed on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha,
one should place a golden image of the Sun upon a lotus within a vessel of sesame seeds, using white mustard seeds.
Then one should worship with garments, sacred threads, ornaments, perfumes, and flowers:
"Homage to you who hold a lotus in your hand; homage to you, the sustainer of the universe.
O Maker of Day, homage to you; O Maker of Light, let there be homage to you."
Then, at the proper time, having honored a Brahmin with garments, garlands, and other ornaments, one should give him a water-pot.
One should offer a sun-god image together with a lotus, having adorned it according to the prescribed rite;
one should observe a fast, remaining steadfast in the highest discipline.
When the night has turned to dawn on the eighth day, one should feed the twice-born according to one's ability;
afterwards, one should eat oneself, avoiding meat.
According to this procedure, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight month after month,
one should perform everything with devotion, free from stinginess regarding wealth.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a golden lotus,
and one should also give a cow adorned with all ornaments according to one's ability.
Whoever should perform the Kamala-saptamī according to this rite— providing fans, seats, lamps, and whatever else has been prepared in the house— [attains the fruit].
Freed from mental and physical ailments, a vessel of happiness and good fortune,
he shall enjoy pleasures for a long time in the mortal world and, upon death, go to the city of the Sun.
Having remained there for many eons, that lord of men returns here and is born into a family of kings, enriched with every prosperity.
There too, devoted to the Sun, having propitiated the Maker of Light through vows and having attained birth after birth with such devotion to the Sun;
O Indra among kings, after seven births, one then attains the supreme state—
that goal for which the siddha sages and the gods, led by Indra, have achieved perfection.
O best of the Bharatas, those who are weary of worldly existence attain unimpaired effort;
thus was this vow of Mahendra proclaimed by the Self-born One.
O King, this narrative, having been told by Nārada himself to me after he had achieved victory, is most secret.
Whoever sees this, hears it for even a moment, reads it with devotion, or applies their mind to it,
shall likewise attain unshakable prosperity in this world.
He goes to the world of the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas.
[642] Thus ends the vow of Kamalasaptamī as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
I shall now describe Śarkarāsaptamī, which destroys all impurities;
through it, longevity, health, and sovereignty arise in infinite measure.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava, endowed with faith,
one should bathe in the morning and, wearing white garlands and unguents, perform the rite with white sesame seeds.
Having drawn a lotus with its pericarp upon the sacrificial ground using saffron,
one should place incense and flowers upon it while reciting "Obeisance to Savitr."
One should place a flawless water-pot together with a vessel of sugar,
having wrapped it in a white cloth and adorned it with white garlands and ointments.
One should worship him with gold according to one's ability while reciting this mantra:
"For he is composed of all the Viśvedevas, as it is declared by the Vedic seers."
O Eternal One, you alone are the very essence of immortality; therefore, protect me.
Then, having drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should sleep on the ground at its side.
One should remain standing while reciting the Saura-sūkta and listening to the Purāṇas;
then, when day and night have passed, on the eighth lunar day, having performed the daily obligatory rites.
One should present all of that to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas,
and one should feed as many Brāhmaṇas as possible with milk-rice mixed with sugar and ghee.
He himself should eat without oil or salt, or he may eat in the presence of the recipient;
by this procedure, he should perform everything month after month.
At the end of the year, being composed in mind, one should again give to a Brāhmaṇa a bed covered with cloth and a silk garment, accompanied by sugar and gold.
It should be provided with all necessary utensils, as well as a single milch cow.
And one should give a house according to one's ability, furnished with all its household utensils;
or, having prepared it with a thousand *niṣkas*, one should give it, or even with a hundred.
One should offer a lotus according to one's own capacity— whether with ten, three, or even a single *niṣka*— while remaining free from stinginess regarding wealth.
The *padma* is a golden lotus.
From the mouth of the Sun as he drinks nectar, drops of nectar fell;
from those were produced what are known as rice, mung beans, and sugarcane.
And sugar is superior even to that, being like the nectar of sugarcane juice;
it is beloved by the Sun, and therefore sacred sugar is used for offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
This Śarkarāsaptamī bestows the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
it pacifies all miseries and increases one's progeny of sons.
Whoever performs this with supreme devotion shall indeed attain the state of the righteous;
he shall dwell in heaven for one kalpa and thereafter go to the highest station.
He who hears this sinless [teaching], or remembers it, or recites it, goes to the world of the Lord of the Gods;
and he who imparts it to people bestows intelligence upon them.
He is to be worshipped by the women of the immortals and by the kinnaras.
Thus ends the Śarkarāsaptamī vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What is the fruit of a body that is transient, even if it be well-nourished?"
O delight of the Yadus, you have spoken thus because you have been deprived of the Māgha bath.
[644] Tell me, what should be done by that embodied being who fears worldly existence, if his body is capable of the morning bath during the month of Māgha?
O best of the Yadus, women are not capable of enduring physical hardship,
both because of the delicacy of their bodies and likewise because of their inherent weakness.
And how might they be beautiful, fortunate, and blessed with good offspring?
For all this is the fruit of one's own merit alone.
"O Teacher of the World, tell us how women may obtain very great merit with little effort during the month of Māgha; for that bath indeed [should be described]."
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O best of the Pāṇḍavas, listen to this secret spoken by the sages,
the Acalāsaptamī vow, which has never been told by me to anyone."
O best of the Kuru lineage, there was a courtesan named Indumatī, endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtue, who was the delight of Magadha.
She had a slender waist, beautiful hips, and full, elevated breasts;
her limbs were perfectly proportioned, and her face resembled the full moon.
Her beauty and delicacy are sung of by Kāma;
by the mere sight of her, even Kāma himself becomes overcome with desire.
Her form, like that of the moon, brings delight to the eyes;
she is as captivating to all the world as the science of subjugation.
One day in the morning, O King, as she stood facing him,
the instability of worldly existence was reflected upon within her heart.
While this world is sinking into the ocean of the poison of worldly existence,
filled with the crocodiles of old age, death, and fever, no one awakens.
[645] With his body as a vessel that has no bottom, fashioned by the artisan Time,
and enveloped by the dense mass of his own karma, he is cooked by the fire of time.
Those days of men which pass devoid of dharma, action, and purpose never return here again, unlike those men who are devotees of Hara.
On whichever day worship, ritual bathing, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors are not performed, that day of men is in vain.
For when a man is attached to his sons, wife, and home,
death seizes him and departs, just as a she-wolf carries off a lamb.
Having reflected thus, the courtesan Indumatī,
who moved with the gait of an elephant, then went to the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
Having bowed with humility to the seated sage Vasiṣṭha and joining their palms in reverence, they spoke these words.
Indumatī said:
"O Lord, neither have I given gifts, nor offered oblations, nor observed fasts or vows;
nor have I worshipped Śambhu or the wielder of the Śārṅga bow with devotion."
Now, tell me some vow that I may perform while practicing asceticism,
by which I may cross over this ocean of existence from the flood of the mud of the waters of suffering.
Having heard these exceedingly piteous words of hers many times over,
Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, spoke out of compassion.
O fair-faced one, perform the bath on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, which bestows the fruit of all desires and generates beauty and good fortune.
Having taken a single meal on the sixth day, you should keep the water motionless on the seventh;
at the end of the night, you should move it after placing a lamp upon your head.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, that which is both immovable and moved—the water—should be remembered as the cleansing of all impurities; therefore, one should bathe in it.
O descendant of Bharata, having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, on that very day she performed the ceremonial bath for Indumatī and gave gifts properly according to the prescribed rites.
By the power of this bath, having enjoyed pleasures according to her desire,
she attained the leadership of a host of apsarases in the world of Indra.
O lord of the people, the ritual bath of Acalāsaptamī has been described to you;
it pacifies all sins and increases happiness and good fortune.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The greatness of the seventh-day bath has been heard by me in its entirety;
now I wish to hear the procedure accompanied by the mantras."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having worshipped the Sun on the sixth lunar day while subsisting on a single meal,
one should go in the morning on the seventh day to a very deep body of water.
Whether it be a river, a lake, a pond, or even a natural pool dug by the gods—
possessing water easy to enter and undisturbed by wicked creatures.
As long as one is not moved by beasts of prey, water, birds, aquatic creatures, fish, or turtles, for that long one should perform the bath.
With devotion, an oil lamp dyed with vermilion should be offered in a vessel made of gold, silver, or even copper.
[647] Having become composed in mind and having placed a lamp upon the head,
one should meditate on the Sun within the heart and recite this mantra:
Salutations to you who possess the form of Rudra; salutations to the Lord of the tastes.
Salutations be to Varuṇa; salutations be to you, O dweller of the waters.
Having bathed and offered libations to the deities, one should carry a lamp across the water;
then, with sandalwood paste, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus together with its pericarp.
In the center, one should worship Śiva together with his consort, conjoined with the Praṇava;
on the eastern petal, Ravi is to be worshipped, and likewise Bhānu on the southeast petal.
A wise person should worship Vivasvat in the south, Bhāskara in the southwest;
Savitṛ is to be worshipped in the west, and Arka is to be worshipped on the northwest petal.
To the Moon, to the Thousand-rayed Sun, and to Śiva, the Soul of All;
these [deities] are to be worshipped with mantras preceded by the Praṇava (Om) and joined at the end with the word "namas" (salutation).
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having separately honored him with flowers and fragrant incense, one should dismiss him with the words: "Clothed in garments, you may go to your own place."
When the thousand-rayed sun has departed, having returned to its own abode,
a capable person should, according to their means, [offer] in a copper vessel or even one made of clay.
One should place sesame paste along with ghee and jaggery;
having fashioned a golden lamp, one who is unable to do so may use one made from sesame paste.

A lamp-vessel filled with oil, having covered it with a red cloth, one should then worship it with flowers and incense. Then, one should cause those Brahmins to recite [the mantra] and give the *tālaka* (the vessel) with the mantra.
By the grace of the Sun and by the fruit of my morning ablution,
I have indeed bestowed this lock [of hair] upon you, which removes evil fortune and bad dreams.
A *tālaka* is a palm-leaf ornament, a specific type of ear-jewel.
Having worshipped the instructor, one should also worship the Brahmins and others.
Then, for the entire day, one should remain intent on meditation upon the Sun.
Listening to those very stories or others connected with the Dharma, as well as engaging in conversation,
sight, touch, and so forth with heretics and the like;
The wise man should avoid [unwholesome food] and consume it sparingly; then, together with his kinsmen, he should eat at night after having fed the poor according to his ability.
This has been told to you, O Pārtha, which brings about beauty and good fortune—
the bath on Acalāsaptamī, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
Whoever thus recites this, or whoever hears it incidentally— this is the "Seventh-Day Bath" that destroys the impurities of the Kali age—
and whoever bestows even the understanding of it upon people with diligence.
Having gone to that beautiful palace, he is attended by female monkeys.
Thus ends the Acalāsaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
I shall now describe another auspicious vow, the Śobhanāśubhasaptamī.
Having fasted upon which, a person is liberated from disease, sorrow, and suffering.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, having performed his ablutions and recitations and being pure,
he should cause the best of the twice-born to recite [the texts] and begin on the seventh day of the bright fortnight.
One should worship Kapilā with devotion using perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
I bow to her who was born from the Sun and who is the abode of the entire world.
I [invoke] you, whose body is entirely auspicious, for the sake of all accomplishments;
having then brought a prastha of sesame seeds placed in a new copper vessel.
Likewise, [one should offer] a golden bull, accompanied by garments, garlands, and molasses,
along with various kinds of fruits, edible foods, and all necessary ritual implements.
At the time of twilight, one should give [the offering] with the words, "May Aryaman be pleased";
then, having consumed the five products of the cow, one should sleep on the ground, free from envy.
Then, having bathed well at dawn, a man should devoutly gratify the twice-born with this ritual procedure,
giving [the gift] month after month.
One should offer two garments, a golden bull, and likewise the worship of the Vedic meters and horses;
and at the end of the year, a bed provided with a multitude of sugarcane stalks.
It should be provided with a bed, a pillow, a vessel, and a seat;
and a prastha of sesame seeds in a copper vessel, together with golden bulls.
"One should give everything to a knower of the Vedas, saying, 'May the Soul of the Universe be pleased.
O King, he who performs the Śubhasaptamī according to this rule [attains the fruit]."
For him, there shall be prosperity, victory, and happiness in birth after birth;
he shall be honored by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas in the abode of Hara.
Having become the lord of the Gaṇas, he shall dwell [there] until the end of the four ages;
then, returning here once more, he will become a sovereign emperor.
This auspicious seventh [chapter], known as Śubhā, was brought from the world of the gods by Nārada for the sake of the deities; it has an extent of one hundred crores [of verses].
For the destruction of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, it was proclaimed by the compassionate Nārada and has now been related by me to you.
Whoever should recite this, or hear it with devotion, or even see it being given,
even they shall have their bodies here freed from all evil.
One attains the leadership of the Vidyādharas.
Whoever observes this vow for as long as it lasts, engaged in the sevenfold application of the seventh [day],
shall in due course become the sovereign of the seven worlds.
Having become [that], one goes from state to state unto the station of Murāri.
Thus ends the auspicious Śubhasaptamī vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe that which destroys all sins.
It is meritorious, bestowing all desires, and is known by the name Mandārasaptamī.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, a man who eats light food and has used a tooth-stick should then observe a fast on the sixth day.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should consume the mandāra flower at night;
then, rising at dawn, one should perform ablutions and again [feed] the twice-born.
Having fashioned eight *mandāra* flowers, one should feed [the deity] according to one's ability;
*mandāra* here refers to the *rājārka*.
Likewise, one should place before [the deity] a very beautiful golden [image] holding a lotus in its hand.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus out of black sesame seeds in a copper vessel,
one should place a golden mandāraka flower in its center and perform worship.
And likewise, with a salutation, one should worship [the sun] on the eastern petal with "To Sūrya"; in the northeast, one should worship the one named Mitra with a salutation;
similarly, to the south, "To Arka," and then to the southwest, "To Aryaman."
In the west, one should worship with "vedadhāmne," and in the northwest with "caṇḍabhānave";
in the north, one should worship "pūrṇe," and thereafter with "ānandāya."
Having placed the Puruṣa upon the pericarp with the mantra "sarvātman," and having enveloped him in white garments, [he should honor him] with edible foods, garlands, fruits, and so forth.
Having thus worshipped all this, he should give it again to one who knows the Vedas;
then the householder, restrained in speech and facing the east, should eat food free from oil and salt.
By this procedure, one should perform [the rite] on every seventh lunar day, or month by month,
for as long as a year, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
At the conclusion of this very vow, having placed [the image] upon a water-pot,
one who desires prosperity should give it away along with cows according to one's means.
Homage to Mandāranātha and to him who reclines upon the Mandāra tree!
May you indeed deliver us from this ocean of saṃsāra.
Whoever performs the Mandāra-saptamī according to this rite shall become exceedingly happy in the world and rejoice in heaven for an eon.
Holding this lamp that dispels the terrifying darkness of the flood of evils,
a man walking through the night of saṃsāra shall not stumble.
The one called Mandārasaptamī bestows the fruits of all desired objects;
whoever recites or even hears it is likewise liberated from sins.
[652] Thus ends the Mandārasaptamī vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, how is that seventh day (Saptamī), which you have described to me as bestowing the fruit of universal sovereignty, to be observed by human beings?
Kṛṣṇa said:
In the land of Kamboja, there was a king named Yaśodharman;
in his old age, he had a son who was afflicted by every kind of disease.
Humble, he asked those bulls among the twice-born about the ripening of that karma;
and they said: "O King, this man was a miserly Vaiśya in his previous birth."
O King, on the seventh day of the chariot festival, he saw a vow being performed;
by the power of witnessing that vow, he was conceived within your womb.
"Because he was not a giver when he had wealth, for that reason he has become afflicted by disease.
Then the king asked: "What should be done for me in this matter?"
O King, let that very thing which brought you the gain of reaching this abode upon its being seen be performed; it is known by the name Ratha-saptami.
This vow removes sin, by which the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) is attained.
The king said:
"O Brahmin, tell me the complete vow, along with its ritual procedures and mantras,
which bestows all prosperity upon both the wealthy and the poor."
The twice-born said:
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, a householder should invite [the deity];
the bath should be performed with white sesame seeds, especially if a river is not available anywhere.
O King, having duly worshipped the gods and others according to the duties of one's caste in pure water, one should then proceed to the abode of the Sun.
Having properly paid homage to the Sun with auspicious flowers, incense, and unbroken grains of rice,
one should afterwards return home and perform the five great sacrifices.
Having first fed his guests, servants, children, the elderly, and dependents,
he himself should eat while the day still remains, remaining silent and avoiding oil.
Having summoned at night a Brahmin who is knowledgeable in the ritual rules and has mastered the Vedas,
and having honored him, one should undertake the vow while fixing the Sun in one's mind.
"Having become fasting on the seventh day and having abandoned all enjoyments, I shall eat on the eighth day, O Eye of the World; grant that it be free from obstacles for me therein."
Having recited this, O best of kings, one should pour water into water;
then, having dismissed that brahmin, one should sleep on the ground with senses subdued.
Then, having risen at dawn, the man, having performed his necessary duties and being purified,
had a divine chariot prepared, adorned with a network of tinkling bells.
Equipped with all necessary implements, adorned on all its parts with jewels,
made of gold and silver, and provided with a horse and a charioteer.
Then, at the time of midday, the observer of the vow, having performed his ablutions and other rites,
should look ahead without glancing to the sides, avoiding conversation with heretics.
Reciting the Saura-sūkta, the wise man should return to his own abode,
having completed his daily obligatory rites and performed the recitation for the Brahmins.
One should place that supreme chariot in the middle of the cloth mandala,
having worshipped it on all sides with fragrant saffron.
One should surround it on all sides with garlands of flower-lamps,
and having perfumed the top of the chariot with incense mixed with agallochum.
One should have the Sun-god, possessing all perfect characteristics, bathed in a golden chariot according to one's wealth, while remaining free from stinginess regarding one's means.
Through deceit he incurs impairment; from impairment his hood becomes defective.
Therefore, having worshipped the God together with his chariot and his charioteer, [he should proceed].
With flowers, incense, and likewise perfumes; with garments, ornaments, and decorations;
with various kinds of fruits, edibles, and food offerings cooked in ghee.
One should worship the Sun with devotion using these three mantras in sequence:
"O Bhānu, Divākara, Āditya, Mārtaṇḍa, Lord of the Worlds!"
O ocean of waters, protector of the world, creator of beings, sun;
O inconceivable dispeller of the distress of those who bow to you, O all-knowing jewel, O pervasive Lord!
O Viṣṇu, O Haṃsa, O Lord beyond all beings, O Creator of the beginning, middle, and end;
O Lord of the Universe, [forgive me] for that which is devoid of devotion, devoid of ritual action, and devoid of mantra.
"By your grace, may my worship here be complete. Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should pray for whatever is in the heart.
The Sun grants what is requested when he is propitiated with devotion by men;
even one devoid of wealth may accomplish all this through the prescribed ritual.
A chariot with its driver and horses, painted on a wall with colors,
as well as a golden sun fashioned according to one's ability.
Having performed worship in great detail according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should observe a night vigil with the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
With various sprinklings and meritorious recitations of sacred narratives and the like,
one who has taken refuge in the sanctuary of Bhāgīrathī should witness the chariot procession.
With eyes closed, the wise man should pass that night;
then, having bathed at the clear dawn and fulfilled his duties, he should [honour] the twice-born.
One should satisfy them with various desires, gifts, garments, and ornaments;
those who know the Veda understand this to be equal to the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
Therefore, wise men should give gifts according to their ability;
indeed, a chariot equipped with all its accessories should be given to the preceptor.
O King, what can one who has thus observed the vow not attain within the three worlds, having offered red garments, a pair of cloths, and a red cow?
Therefore, O best of kings, perform the Ratha-saptamī vow with every effort,
so that your son may become healthy and his own island of refuge.
By the power of this vow and through the grace of the Sun,
he shall become possessed of great splendor, great strength, and great prowess.
Having renounced vast enjoyments and having made his kingdom free of thorns,
that mighty-armed one gave [gifts] on the Rathasaptamī day, even though he was deceased.
Having produced sons and grandsons, he will go to the world of the Sun;
remaining there for one kalpa, he will become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Kṛṣṇa said:
Having thus related everything, that best of brahmins returned the way he had come;
the king, for his part, did everything as instructed.
Everything that was commanded by the lord of the twice-born came to pass;
thus, O prince, he attained the status of a universal monarch.
O scorcher of foes, it is heard in the Purāṇas that he who hears this with devotion, or whoever recites it, is indeed Māndhātā.
The Sun is pleased with him alone who always hears [this teaching] and attains fearlessness;
[he gives him] such a supreme chariot, yoked with chariot-horses,
golden, and joined with the one of a hundredfold golden radiance.
And he who gives [gifts] on the seventh days of the bright fortnight of Māgha enjoys the earth, moving indeed upon the wheel of non-attachment.
Thus ends the Ratha-saptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
O Mahādeva, in the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, one who has conquered the senses—
Having fasted on the sixth lunar day, with offerings of perfumes and flowers, |||
Having worshipped the Maker of Day, one should sleep at night before him;
then, having awakened on the seventh day, one should worship the Sun with devotion.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth,
[offering] pieces of sweetmeat, *modakas*, and likewise cakes made of sugarcane and molasses.
When the first year is complete, on the seventh lunar day,
