the wise man should perform the festival procession of the God of gods, carrying it out according to the previously mentioned procedure.
"By the previously mentioned procedure" means by the procedure for the chariot procession established in the section on various lunar days (tithis).
One should perform the vow of a quarter-kṛcchra; having mounted the chariot, one should behold the Sun, the Lord of the World, with devotion, and he goes to the supreme goal.
On the third day, eating only one meal is prescribed; on the fourth day, eating only at night is taught.
Then, having fasted on the fifth and the sixth days,
one who has performed the accumulation [of merit] should break the fast on the seventh day after beholding the God seated upon his chariot.
Having worshipped the three-eyed God according to the prescribed rites with devotion,
one should fashion a golden chariot placed upon a copper vessel.
One should place the honored, new "void" (*vyoma*) made of jewels in the middle of the chariot;
the construction of this void is to be understood as already explained in the *Vyoma-ṣaṣṭhī-vrata*.
One should place a ruby in the center and place a pearl in the east.
An indranīla gem in the south, and a makaradhvaja in the west.
O Destroyer of Andhaka, the wise one should place coral in the north and Rudra; he should place the All-Knowing One there, white, yellow, white, and red as well.
One should place these nine cloths in all directions upon the chariot-structure,
which is adorned with bells and ornaments, and [place] banners there as well.
Having well-adorned the chariot, which is equipped with a canopy, with garlands of flowers,
and having worshipped it according to the prescribed rules, one should offer it to the Sun-god.
Then, having fed a Brahmin, one should present it to the teacher;
whoever studies the Saptamī-kalpa along with its narrative, which belongs to Śaṅkara.
That twice-born one is to be known as the preceptor for the castes in their respective order;
for the followers of Sūrya, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, he is the Lord of Pārvatī.
But if gold is not available, one should prescribe a silver chariot;
if that is unavailable, one should have a copper chariot or a celestial chariot made;
and in the absence of copper, a chariot made of flour is prescribed.
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa the Great God (Mahādeva), accompanied by gold, seated upon a copper vessel, and provided with a pair of saffron robes.
O Mahādeva of great splendor, as previously stated, [this should be given] to the reciter, adorned with the five jewels, clothed in white garments, and possessing auspicious limbs.
But according to one's own capacity, O Virūpākṣa, one should avoid stinginess regarding wealth;
this Rathāṅgā-saptamī, O Hara, is meritorious and removes sins.
This great *Rudra* hymn has been proclaimed and recounted to you by me;
[through it, one performs] bathing, giving, fire-offerings, and the worship of the Lord of the Planets.
O Bhūdhara, a hundred-thousandfold merit exists for prosperity;
thus, this most meritorious seventh day has arrived in the month of Māgha.
Having fasted with devotion on this day, a man becomes an attendant of the Sun;
a Brāhmaṇa attains divinity, and a Kṣatriya shall attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
A Vaiśya indeed attains the status of a Kṣatriya, and likewise, a Kṣatriya attains the status of a Vaiśya; moreover, a maiden may obtain as a husband one who is endowed with learning and humility.
A childless woman shall obtain a son and good fortune, O lord of men;
and even a widow, by fasting upon this [day], attains the highest world.
O beloved of Pārvatī,
for as many as seven births, neither woman nor man shall encounter widowhood; rather, having many sons and great wealth, they shall attain the state of being dear to their husband.
[659] Thus ends the Rathāṅgasaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa.
Vāsudeva said:
O best of the Kurus, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha,
eating a single meal is prescribed, and on the sixth day, eating only at night is declared.
O you of noble vows, some desire the fast on the seventh day;
others here desire that the propitiation be performed on the sixth, and indeed on the seventh.
Having observed a fast on the sixth lunar day, a wise man should worship the Sun with gathered karavīra flowers mixed with red sandalwood.
O mighty-armed one of noble vows, one should worship the God of gods, the Sun, the Lord of planets and Śaṅkara, with fragrant guggulu resin.
"Śaṅkara" means "the maker of happiness.
Thus, one should worship the Sun for four months beginning with Māgha,
and for the sake of one's own purification, consume cow dung as well.
And here, for the sake of self-purification, one should perform a bath with cow dung;
one should also feed Brāhmaṇas of divine enjoyment according to one's ability.
Those originating in the divine abodes of heaven are celestial (*divya*), while others are terrestrial (*bhauma*). Even during the months beginning with Jyeṣṭha, white sandalwood is prescribed;
indeed, white substances are meritorious and endowed with auspicious fragrance.
Black agallochum is likewise prescribed as incense, and milk-rice (pāyasa) is known as the food offering;
with that very [offering], O high-minded one, one should feed the virtuous Brahmins.

O observer of noble vows, one should cause [the devotee] to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and perform a bath with that very substance. O tiger among the Kurus, it is prescribed that in the months beginning with Kārttika, worship should be performed with Agasti flowers, and Aparājita should be used as incense.
Having bathed, one should offer the sacrificial food (naivedya) and feed Brahmins according to one's ability.
One should consume water infused with *kuśa* grass and perform ablutions for the sake of accomplishment,
at the conclusion of the third meal during the month of Māgha, O high-minded one.
In that place, food and charity are declared to be twofold;
and the wise should perform the worship of the God of gods according to their ability.
Furthermore, O observer of noble vows, the gift of a chariot and the procession of the chariot should indeed be performed when one possesses the means,
for the sake of attaining a chariot.
"The gift of a chariot here, as described, should be given when one has the means.
Thus, my son, has this auspicious Rathāṅgasaptamī been explained."
The seventh [tithi] is thus celebrated as great, bringing immense merit and great prosperity;
by fasting upon it, one attains wealth, sons, fame, and knowledge.
Thus ends the Mahāsaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā..."
Mahājayā, Nandā, Bhadrā, and Vāmā are proclaimed [as the goddesses].
When the constellation consisting of five stars occurs on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, then that seventh day is to be known as Jayā.
The "five stars" (pañcatāraka) are Rohiṇī, Aśleṣā, Maghā, and Hastā. Whatever is given, offered as oblation, recited, used for libation, or as worship of the gods during that [lunar mansion],
all is said to be multiplied a hundredfold, as is the worship of the Sun.
When the swan has ascended the hand, that which is the supreme seventh day of the bright fortnight—
the swan being the sun—
one should perform the rite for the Sun according to this procedure for one year.
One should devoutly have an image made of gold, two-armed and holding a lotus;
O Lord of the Cowherds, three fasts were previously observed on that day.
The wise have declared that the breaking of the fast occurs after the first four months; O observer of noble vows, it is said that *karavīra* flowers are to be used here.
Sandalwood and likewise red sandalwood are prescribed for incense, as is guggulu;
and *kāsāra* and *sitāsāra* are indeed to be offered as food (*naivedya*) to the Sun.

Kāsāra, prepared by frying wheat flour with sugarcane juice and ghee, is well known in the world as *sitātāra*, being abundant in sugar. Having worshipped Mārtaṇḍa, the lord of the gods, according to this rite,
one should devoutly honor the Brāhmaṇas with various kinds of food and edibles in accordance with the rules.
One should feed the Brahmins *kāsāra* (sweet rice pudding); this breaking of the fast will be fruit-bearing.
One should likewise eat it oneself, remaining restrained and observing silence.

On the fifth day, eating only once a day is prescribed; on the sixth, eating only at night is proclaimed. Having observed a fast on the seventh, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the eighth.
In this [rite], one should bathe with *siddhārthaka* seeds and consume milk-rice (*pāyasa*);
may the Sun be pleased here, and likewise, the tooth-stick should be made from the *arka* tree.
Listen now to the second rite for breaking the fast as I describe it:
here one should take jasmine flowers, as well as *śrīkhaṇḍa* and sandalwood.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as an oblation to the Sun, employ the Vijaya incense,
feed the Brāhmaṇas, and, O Lord, one should eat oneself as well.
In this rite, one should recite the name of the deity, "May Ravi be pleased with me";
one should then consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and use a tooth-stick made of khadira wood.
The procedure for the second breaking of the fast has now been declared by me;
learn from me also the rule for the third breaking of the fast.
In this rite, the wise man should worship the Sun with Agastya flowers;
for his own anointing, sandalwood and saffron are prescribed.
Sihlaka is prescribed as incense; it is supremely pleasing to the Sun.
The food offering (naivedya) should consist of śāli rice accompanied by rasāla.
Rasāla is Śikhaṇḍinī. Furthermore, one should give gifts to the Brāhmaṇas, feed them, and likewise feed oneself;
one should consume water infused with Kuśa grass and use Badarī wood for cleaning the teeth.
One should recite the name of the god Vikartana so that he may be pleased;
at the end of the year, the worship of the God of gods must be performed according to the prescribed rite.
And with offerings of perfumes and flowers, as well as various sprinklings,
with gifts of cows and land, and with the gratification of the Brahmins.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods who stands before him,
he should cause the recitation of the most meritorious book of Dharma to be performed.
Having diligently honored the reciter with garments, perfumes, and likewise incense,
one should stand before the deity and then utter the mantra.
O God of gods, Lord of the world, destroyer of all diseases,
lord of the planets, scorcher of the worlds, maker of light, dispeller of darkness!
This seventh [day] of the god of gods, named Jayā, has been performed by me through your grace; it is auspicious, blessed, and a remover of sins.
O Hero, O Lord, for one who performs the Saptamī vow according to this rite,
all [the merit of] his bathing and other rituals shall become a hundredfold.
O Hero, by performing this seventh [rite], a man shall obtain fame;
it is taught that he gains wealth, grain, gold, sons, long life, and strength.
Having attained this, O tiger among men, he goes to the heavenly world;
then, returning again to earth, he becomes a righteous king.
Thus, O Hero, this seventh [chapter] named Jayā has been told;
when performed, heard, or remembered, it bestows the world of Haṃsa.
Thus ends the Jayāsaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
If the seventh day of the bright fortnight should fall on a Sunday, [it is known as Jayāsaptamī].
The seventh is named Vijayā; what is given on that day yields great fruit.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, and likewise fasting—
all these on Vijaya-saptamī destroy even the greatest sins.
On the fifth day there should be a single meal; on the sixth, they prescribe eating only at night;
on the seventh, however, there should be a fast; and on the eighth, the breaking of the fast occurs.
Devoted to fasting on the sixth lunar day, one should worship the Sun seated upon a lotus;
likewise, being devoted to fasting on the seventh day of victory (Vijayā-saptamī) and intending to observe the fast,
one should worship with devotion and full faith using offerings of perfumes and flowers.
Having prepared the ground for worship, one should lie down to sleep before the deity.
While reciting the Gāyatrī, or the Saura-sūkta,
or the three-syllabled Mahāśveta mantra, or even the six-syllabled one,
he should then wake up on the seventh lunar day and perform his ablutions before the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Having worshipped the Lord of Planets and performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite,
one should afterwards feed the Brahmins with devotion and the Lord of the Gaṇas.

Having given rice of the *śāli* variety, cakes, and sweets filled with sugar according to his ability, he should then dismiss the Brahmins after giving them a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his means.
Thus, O God, has this meritorious Vijayasaptamī been described;
by fasting upon it, a man shall go to the supreme station of Vairocana.
Red oleanders, saffron for anointment,
and the Vijaya incense— these indeed bring satisfaction to the Sun on this day.
This [place] is meritorious, a remover of sins, and a destroyer of great transgressions;
O Lord of the Gaṇas, whatever is given or offered here becomes inexhaustible.
Thus ends the vow of Vijayā-saptamī as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"The seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is known as Trilocanā."
She is called by the name Jayantī; she is meritorious and likewise a destroyer of sins.
O beloved of Pārvatī, hear now the procedure by which one should observe the fast;
for the learned have declared that there are four ways of breaking the fast.
On the fifth day, one should eat a single meal; on the sixth, a night-meal is prescribed;
on the seventh, a fast is observed; and on the eighth, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place.
O observer of noble vows, in the months of Māgha, Phālguna, and likewise Caitra,
arka flowers are auspicious, as is saffron for anointment.
The food offering consists of sweetmeats, rice, incense, and so forth;
the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is declared to be the supreme means of purification.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, one should feed the Brahmins with modakas according to one's ability;
O Lord of Beings, one should indeed offer śāli-rice with devotion to the twice-born.
Whoever thus worships Bhāskara, who is honored by the world,
shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every fast-breaking meal performed in this manner.
Having worshipped on the second fast-breaking day, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
this applies to the months of Vaiśākha, Jyaiṣṭha, and Āṣāḍha, O observer of good vows.
In the offering mantra for the Sun, one should indeed employ hundred-petaled lotuses;
white sandalwood is for Mars, and guggulu is said to be the incense.
The food offering consists of molasses-cakes and the consumption of cow dung;
the meal for the Brahmins is likewise declared to consist of molasses-cakes.
This second narrative is a means of fulfillment that destroys evil;
now hear the third, O Lord of Gods, for the purpose of worshipping the Sun.
O Lord of Gods, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, as well as in Bhādrapada, O All-pervading One,
and also in the month of Āśvina, red sandalwood is desired.
Here, *mālatī* flowers and the *vijaya* incense are desired;
for the food offering, there should be *ghṛtapūpa* cakes when feeding the twice-born.
The consumption of water infused with *kuśa* grass is the supreme means for purifying the body;
this third breaking of the fast is also declared to be the destroyer of sin.
O King, for the sake of your welfare, I shall now describe the fourth *pāraṇa*, which yields the fruit of both the *rājasūya* and *aśvamedha* sacrifices and is dear to the Sun-god.
O hero, O tiger among men, listen now to the flowers in their entirety for the months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Pauṣa.
Red karavīra flowers, as well as red sandalwood,
incense called amṛta, and likewise milk-rice as an offering.
Likewise, the *vajra* from the *arjunīya* tree is considered the supreme elixir;
as are *aguru*, *candana*, *mustā*, *sihlaka*, and *vṛṣaṇa*.
One should prepare an incense born of nectar consisting of equal parts of *arjunīya*,
cow’s urine, *vajra*, and clarified butter;
here, the names of the great-souled Bhāskara have been declared.
"Citrabhānu, Bhānu, Āditya, and likewise Bhāskara—may they be pleased. Thus one should direct [the invocation] at all fast-breaking ceremonies (pāraṇas).
O Mahādeva, whoever performs the worship of the Fire-god according to this rite on this lunar day attains the supreme state.
Having performed this on the seventh day, O Bhīma, one shall obtain all desires;
he who seeks sons obtains sons, and he who seeks wealth obtains wealth.
One who is diseased is freed from disease and attains abundant auspiciousness;
O Bhīma, when a full year has passed, worship should be performed for the Sun.
With offerings of perfumes and flowers, with the gratification of Brahmins,
with various kinds of sprinklings, and with the worship of the reciter.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should worship the Brāhmaṇa;
having worshipped the reciting twice-born, one should utter this statement:
"O King, in matters of dharma, in matters of wealth, and in all matters of desire, victory is always mine."
Then he should dismiss the Brahmins and the reciter, that best of the twice-born;
by acting thus thereafter, he shall always attain victory.
With his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of the Sun,
having ascended a supreme celestial chariot born of the splendor of poetry.
In brilliance he resembles the sun, and in splendor he is the best of birds;
the sun is the "bird-born" (kavija) and the fire is the "wise one" (kavi), and gold is born from that [fire]. The "pataga" is the sun.
Thus is the Jayantī vow described in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Brahmā said: O Lord of Gaṇas, that seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada is renowned as Aparājitā, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
One should prescribe a single meal for the four [days], a night-meal on the fifth,
a fast on the sixth, and the breaking of the fast on the seventh.
In this regard, four items for breaking the fast have been declared by the wise:
*karavīra* flowers and red sandalwood paste.
The incense offering is with guggulu resin, and the food offering consists of molasses cakes;
this is the prescribed ritual for the months beginning with Nabhasya (Bhādrapada).
Likewise, flowers of the *aśoka* tree and saffron are for the unguent;
for incense, *sihlaka* is prescribed, or else that which originates from the *bilva* tree.
In the months beginning with Phālguna, the food offering (naivedya) consists of śāli rice,
rasālā, red lotuses, and likewise aloe-wood and sandalwood, O Lord of Beings.
Anantadhūpa is prescribed as the incense, and molasses cakes as the food offering;
likewise, sandalwood with *granthiparṇa*, agallochum, and *sihlaka*.
"O Bhūteśa, one should burn mustā, indu, and sugar for three days;
this, O best of gods, is called the Ananta incense."
*Granthi* is *granthiparṇī*, and *indu* is camphor.
For this procedure has been thus declared by the wise for the months beginning with Jyeṣṭha.
Listen, O observer of good vows, to the names of the deity and the substances to be consumed.
"Bhaga, Aṃśumat, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Tripurāntaka—may they all be pleased at every conclusion of the fasts. Thus one should proclaim.
Cow’s urine, the five products of the cow, ghee, and warm milk—
if a man performs this seventh [day] according to this procedure, [he attains the fruit].
He too shall always be invincible by his enemies in battle;
he shall slay his foes and conquer them, and he shall attain the three aims of life—of this there is no doubt.
Then, having attained the three goals of life, one shall reach the city of Bhānu by means of offerings of perfumes and flowers, and by listening to the Purāṇas.
O Lord, by the gift of horses and by the gratification of Brahmins,
and by honoring the reciter who is always dear to the Sun-god.
Having truly conquered his enemies, he goes to the same world as the *haṃsas*,
by means of that vehicle born of Śukra’s seed, which has the son of the River (Bhīṣma) as its banner.
For one who resembles the lord of rivers shall become the lord of rivers;
gold born from semen is gold, and gold born from the waters is also indeed gold; the lord of rivers is Varuṇa.
Thus ends the Aparājitā-saptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
When the sun enters its transit (saṃkrānti) on the seventh day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa),...
Then indeed that seventh lunar day, beloved of the Sun, becomes Mahājayā.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, and the worship of ancestors and gods—
all these are declared by the highly effulgent Tapana to be multiplied ten millionfold.
But that man who, with devotion, bathes the Sun in this [tirtha] with clarified butter,
shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and thereafter go to the abode of the Sun.
The devoted man who bathes the Sun with milk,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of the Sun.
O Sañjaya, having remained there for a long time, he becomes a king;
this seventh [vow], O Destroyer of Tripura, has been described as leading to great victory.
Having fasted with devotion, a person shall obtain an unshakable state in heaven;
from there he goes to the supreme abode, reaching which he no longer grieves.
Thus ends the Mahājayā-saptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"That which occurs on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa..."
O Hero, she is called Nandā, the auspicious one who brings joy to all.
On the fifth day, however, a single meal is prescribed; on the sixth, a night-meal is proclaimed;
and on the seventh, the wise declare that one should observe a fast.
One should present here jasmine flowers, fragrant sandalwood,
and incense blended with camphor and agallochum.
One should offer curd-rice with sugar as an oblation dear to the Sun;
one should give that very same food to the Brahmins and likewise eat it oneself.
This is the procedure for the first breaking of the fast for the sake of worshiping the Sun;
O Lord, there are palāśa flowers as well as sacrificial sandalwood.
Camphor, *sihlaka*, costus, *uśīra*, sandalwood, as well as *granthi*, *vṛṣaṇa*, *bhīma*, saffron, *gṛñjana*,
and likewise myrobalan (*harītakī*), O Bhīma— this is called the "sacrificial mark" (*yajñāṅka*).
*Gṛñjana* is a variety of onion.
Incense, awakening [substances], and the prescribed food offering (*naivedya*) consisting of sugar-candies and other sweets;
black agallochum, *sihlaka*, *cāṇakya*, and likewise *vṛṣaṇa*.
O Lord of the Sky, one should feed the Brahmins with sandalwood, tagara, musta, prabodha, and sugar, as well as cāṇakya and radish preparations, along with sweets such as *khaṇḍa*.
Having consumed a bilva leaf, one should then eat while remaining silent;
this is proclaimed as the rule for the second elephant.
One should bring blue lotus flowers, incense of guggulu, and an offering of food; those with faces like the dust [of the earth] perform this for the pleasure of the Sun.
With faces covered in dust and mouths filled with grit and powder, they are to be fed.
O Hero, the application of sandalwood ointment and the consumption of mustā grass are declared;
thus, O Hero, the supreme rite for the third [offering] has been described.
Listen to the names of the God which always purify men;
a wise person should recite them, saying, "May Viṣṇu, Bhaga, and Dhātṛ be pleased."
The excellent man who always performs the Nandā rite according to this procedure shall attain his desires in this world and obtain the Creator himself.
One desiring a son shall obtain a son; one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
a seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge, and likewise, one seeking fame shall obtain fame.
Having thus obtained all his desires, he rejoices for eternal years;
then, having gone to the abode of the Sun, he delights in the realm that increases joy.
Thus, O twice-born one, I have described to you this goddess known as Nandā, the mother of Nanda;
by fasting upon her and likewise hearing [her story], one truly rejoices as if having attained the Sun himself.
Thus ends the Nandā-saptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, when the lunar mansion of the Sun (Pūrvaphalgunī) occurs, [one should observe this vow].
When that which is to be attained has been acquired in its entirety, then she shall attain auspiciousness.
The constellation of Savitṛ is Hasta.
On the fourth day one should eat a single meal, and on the fifth one should prescribe eating only at night;
on the sixth it is said that one should not ask for food, and after that comes the fast.
[672] O Hero, the Lord of the Gods has declared that libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed with ghee by the wise,
as well as with milk and likewise with sugarcane juice.
Having bathed the Lord of Gods, one should anoint him with sandalwood paste;
one should offer guggulu resin to him and likewise present a canopy before him.
Made from wheat flour, pure and resembling the moon,
it is golden, adorned with jaggery, and beautified with red flowers.
Wherever the horn of Īśāna is located here, one should indeed place a pearl;
at its tip, one should place a ruby or a red gem.
A wise person should place emerald in the southwest, ruby in the northwest,
or a lotus in the north, according to his own capacity.
One should avoid heretics, those engaged in improper occupations, and those who act like cats;
on the seventh lunar day, one should feed the king and avoid sleeping during the day.
Whoever performs the Bhadrasaptamī according to this rite, Bhadrā bestows auspiciousness upon him on the seventh day; may his vow be successful.
All his kinsmen always go to that auspicious [state];
since he is incapable [of performing it], by what rite is its fruit bestowed?
The delightful divine emblem known as Vyomabhadra is said to be made of rice flour,
four-cornered, and beautiful.
It is combined with clarified butter that is fit for consumption, flavored with pieces of sugar-candy,
and especially enriched with the powder of the four aromatics (caturjātaka) and raisins.
"With the powder of the four *jātaka*s" means with the powder of cardamom, cloves, cinnamon leaves, and *nāgakeśara*.
And with coconut fruits of auspicious fragrance, O Lord of the Gaṇas,
the wise one should place an indranīla gem in the center of the *bhadra* according to his capacity.
One should place the puṣparāga, marakata, padmarāga, and likewise atoyama and māṇikya, in sequence, in the corners.
O Lord, it should be one *prastha* in measure, or perhaps half a *prastha*;
having prepared it according to this rite, one should place it before the Deity.
One should give it either to the reciter or personally to the one who feeds him;
whoever, having performed this rite according to the prescribed rule, bestows auspiciousness, [attains success].
Having attained auspicious things, he shall indeed go to the abode of the Lord of Rays;
from there, mounted upon a celestial vehicle, he shall go to the world of Brahmā—of this there is no doubt.
In brilliance he was like the sun, and in beauty he was equal to Atri;
[Atri] is the moon.
In splendor he was equal to the Lord of Rays (the Sun), and in majesty to Śaṅkara.
Therefore, having returned once more to earth, he shall become a lord of cattle; of this there is no doubt.
"O hero, through the grace of Gopati, one is born possessed of good fortune;
thus, O hero, this seventh [observance] named Bhadrā has been described."
O hero, O Lord of the Gaṇas, by fasting upon which a man may attain the world of Brahmā— those who hear it here, those who recite it, and those who perform it [attain that same goal].
"Having reached the moon, they all go to that eternal Brahman.
Thus ends the Bhadrāsaptamī vow as declared in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*.
Sumantu said: "A woman who is devoted to the Sun will certainly become a man;
and as for how even a woman may obtain an excellent husband, listen now."
O Hero, the Nikṣubhārkavrata always increases the affection of the Sun; it prevents separation and accomplishes virtue, desire, and wealth.
Then, on the seventh or the sixth day when the sun has entered [a new sign],
one who observes a fast should perform an oblation with clarified butter at every offering.
Having fashioned an auspicious golden image of the deity Nikṣubhārka, or alternatively a silver image, one should install it and worship it with clarified butter and other offerings.

Nikṣubhā is the wife of the Sun; the Sun is accompanied by her. With oblation after oblation—that is, with cow's clarified butter—the fashioning of their forms is according to the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "The Sun, however, should be made together with Nikṣubhā, adorned with a garment and armor."
His rays should be fashioned on the left and right hands.
In his other two hands, the lotus-seated one [holds] two lotuses;
and upon the single-wheeled chariot with six spokes, he stands through devotion to Niṣkubha.
The god who has Aruṇa as his charioteer should be depicted seated, possessing four arms, endowed with great splendor, and adorned with girdles.
Having adorned them with perfumes and garlands, with pairs of beautiful garments,
with all kinds of mantra-consecrated foods, and with celestial chariots, banners, and yak-tail whisks;
O King, one should feed those devoted to the Sun as well as the officiating priests;
and with devotion, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), saying, "May the Sun be pleased."
Having placed it in a copper or bell-metal vessel and covered it with a white cloth,
one should prepare the image in the center of the sanctuary.
Having placed that vessel upon his head, adorned with a canopy and decorated with banners, umbrellas, and the like, he should proceed to the temple of the Sun.
One should announce this vow to Nikṣubhārka, the Lord of Days;
one should place the vessel, adorned with flowers, upon his seat.
Having circumambulated the Sun and prostrated before him, one should seek his favor;
having attained this meritorious vow, hear what fruit one shall obtain.
In worlds belonging to the Sun, he rejoices at will together with the sons of the Sun, riding great vehicles resembling mountains and shining like the twelve Ādityas.
For thousands of millions of years and hundreds of millions of years,
he rejoices with the highly fortunate ones and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, by virtue of that specific merit, endowed with all desirable things,
he reaches the world of Brahmā and attains supreme bliss.
Falling from the world of Brahmā, the illustrious one, honored by the virtuous and saluted by gods and asuras, attains the status of Prajāpati.
Having enjoyed pleasures here for a long time, he is glorified in the world of Soma;
and from Soma, having reached the lunar world once more, he becomes equal to Indra.
And having reached the world of the Gandharvas from the world of Indra, he rejoices;
together with the lord of the Gandharva kings, he shall dwell happily in enjoyments.
Adorned with the wondrous power of great jewels,
even having reached the world of the yakṣas, he rejoices according to his desire.
Fallen from the world of the yakṣas, he sports upon the summit of Mount Meru;
having successively reached the abodes of the world-protectors, he rejoices.
Wherever one may dwell throughout the entire circle of the earth, even unto the ends of the world and the light of the world,
there one shall always be happy and obtain all that without exception.
Having obtained a kingdom, he rejoices in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
through Āditya, he attains enjoyment and good fortune—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Nikṣubhārkasaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa. Sumantu said: "She who, being self-restrained and observing the vow, [fasts] on the sixth and the seventh [lunar days]..."
Having thus spent one year with the desire to conquer the great worlds.
At the end of the rainy season, having fashioned an image of the renowned Nikṣubhārka,
one should understand that the creation of the form of Nikṣubhārka is as prescribed by the fixed vows.
Having performed the ritual procedures beginning with the bath, [one should worship] the one renowned as Nikṣubhārka.
One obtains the desires mentioned before; one obtains the qualities mentioned before.
By means of vehicles made of Jāmbūnada gold, he rejoices for a long time in heaven;
having gone to the beautiful city of the Sun, he obtains the entire fruit.
Having enjoyed all desired pleasures in all the worlds, beginning with that of the Sun,
she shall eventually return to this world and obtain a king as her husband.
[677] Thus ends the first [chapter]. That noble woman who likewise observes a fast on the single seventh day of the dark fortnight shall go to the supreme abode of the Sun of immeasurable splendor.
At the end of the rainy season, having fashioned a beautiful image made of rice flour,
one should worship it with yellow unguents, garlands, and yellow garments.
Having performed everything as previously described, the protector of the earth, possessing the luster of gold and minerals, should offer it all to the Sun.
He is glorified in the world of the Sun for thousands of millions of years;
having enjoyed all desired pleasures in the worlds of the Sun and others, he dwells there.
Having arrived in this world in due course, she finds a lord as her husband—
one of noble birth, endowed with beauty, and proficient in all the scriptures.
Thus is the second [vow]. She who remains without food, restrained by this vow for a year, should,
at the end of the year, fashion an elephant out of flour and offer it.
Having fashioned a silver lotus with a pericarp made of gold,
and having placed it there with devotion, one should perform everything else as previously described.
Whatever evil may have been committed through desire, such as the killing of an embryo and so forth, all that is destroyed by the gift of an elephant; there is no doubt in this matter.
Accompanied by Nārāyaṇa, the man is honored in the world of the Sun for a full hundred million years in a celestial palace of great lotuses.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures in the seven worlds beginning with Saura,
she returns in due course to this world and finds a lord among men as her husband.
One who is of noble birth, endowed with beauty, proficient in all the scriptures,
possessed of all auspicious marks, and provided with wealth and grain.
Possessing great enthusiasm, great heroism, great steadfastness, and great strength.
Thus ends the third [chapter]. Now, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, she who is firm in her vow remains for one year fasting and deprived of all enjoyments.
At the end of the year, one should offer a *nikṣubhārka* made from all kinds of fragrant substances,
enriched with gold, gems, and pearls, after having fed an excellent Brahmin.
Together with his wife, he [shall go] by means of most wonderful Great Vehicle chariots, adorned with divine gandharvas, to that wise reciter who is learned in the Itihāsas.
O lord of men, he shall sport for a hundred yugas in the world of the Sun,
resembling the Sun in radiance and like Hari in splendor.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures in the world of men according to his wish,
he returns in due course to this world and becomes a righteous king.
O King, he who thus performs this meritorious vow, which removes the fear of sin,
goes to the supreme state by means of this Nikṣubhārka rite.
O mighty-armed hero, endowed with supreme faith for one year,
at the end of the year, one should feed the reciter together with his wife.
Having fed the couple who recite the Mahābhārata,
one should honor them with perfumes, garlands, garments, and likewise with ornaments.
Having prepared a copper vessel adorned with vajras and filled with gems,
one should offer a golden *nikṣubhā* and an *arka* according to one's capacity.
It should be known that *nikṣubhā* means "the one who causes to revolve," while *arka* is proclaimed to be the "designator."
Thus ends the section on the four Nikṣubhā-Arka rites as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Saptāśvatilaka said:
"O Vainateya, listen to the procedure for the Saptamī vow."
For this is the supreme secret, the ultimate means of propitiating the Sun.
The first [rite] should be performed with white mustard seeds, the second with arka-pods,
the third with black pepper, and the fourth with nimba-leaves on the seventh day.
The fifth [day] joined with the sixth should be performed, as should the sixth and the seventh of the fruit;
the seventh is the impelling [day], O Hero, and is proclaimed as the seventh.
"Endowed with six" means endowed with the six modes beginning with *siddhārthaka*.
Thus, these seven sevens should be performed by one desiring prosperity;
accordingly, I shall describe their non-confusion in due order.
The seventh day of the bright fortnight should be observed either in the month of Māgha or Mārgaśīrṣa;
there shall be no violation of the rules caused by [the passage of] a fortnight or a month.
The meaning is that, due to distress, it should be performed in another month or fortnight. However, one should indeed perform the cleaning of the teeth when half a *prahara* remains;
"when half a *prahara* remains" means during the remaining half-*prahara* of the previous day.
In that very regard, I shall tell you the fruit of tooth-sticks.
From *madhuka* there shall be the attainment of a son; from *rājavṛkṣa* one obtains victory;
and upon the occurrence of the *āḍharūpaka* [dream], one attains greatness everywhere.
By using the *aśoka* one becomes free from sorrow; by using the *aśvattha* and *vadara* one gains fame;
and by resorting to the *śirīṣa*, one attains abundant prosperity.
For one who frequents the priyaṅgu tree, supreme good fortune shall arise;
through constant attendance upon the plakṣa tree, the accomplishment of all desired aims shall occur.
In Badarī and in Bṛhatī, one is quickly liberated from disease;
Bṛhatī is the *ḍoraka* (a type of creeper).
Sovereignty is attained in Viṣṇu, and an accumulation of wealth in Khadira.
There is the destruction of enemies under the Kadamba tree, and the gain of wealth under the Atimuktaka.

With *atimukta* one gains a beautiful body; with *kārāṅgudī*, one becomes a king’s favorite; with *cūta*, one attains sovereignty; with *panasa*, good fortune; with *paṅkaja*, long life; and with *avimukta*, the attainment of wealth.
One who has not been released from his vows should not eat; nor should he use a tooth-stick that is diseased,
half-dry, withered, or devoid of fire.
One should eat only a span’s worth of food, avoiding both what is too long and what is too short;
sitting comfortably, facing either north or east, one should remain restrained in speech.
Having placed it in his heart as he desires and having consecrated it with this mantra, the wise man should use the tooth-stick.
Having granted a boon, O tree, I recognize you as the fulfiller of desires;
O tooth-stick, grant me constant success—homage be to you!
Having likewise recited [the mantra] three times, one should chew the tooth-stick;
afterwards, having rinsed that wood, one should cast it away in a clean place.
If it falls facing upwards, success is achieved; likewise if it remains facing forward.
However, if it falls otherwise, one should bring it back and release it again.
If it falls again in such a way that it resembles a tooth-stick, one should know that there is no success; therefore, that seventh [line] is not to be accepted.
But the student (brahmacārī) should sleep that night while attending to auspicious rites,
wearing an unblemished garment, pure, and endowed with proper conduct.
When that night had passed, having risen in the morning, O bird,
the wise man should wash his face and perform the cleansing of his teeth before eating.
Having sat down and become pure, having bowed his head to the Sun,
and having performed the recitation as desired, he should then offer oblations into the fire.
Then, at the time of afternoon, having bathed in the waters of Śṛṅgodbhavā and performed the ritual sipping of water according to the rules, he remained silent, dressed in white garments, and pure.
Having worshipped the god Divākara according to the prescribed rite with devotion,
one should sleep before the deity, intent on the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
Henceforth, I shall declare which specific fruits a man of fixed vows may predict from the dreams he sees on the seventh lunar day.
Having duly completed all the rites, such as recitation and fire-oblations,
one should lie down on the ground and meditate upon the God of gods.
If a man sleeping here should see the rising sun,
or the banner of Indra, or the moon, all his prosperities shall be fulfilled.
A bull, an elephant, a calf, a lute, healthy people,
erotic sentiment, and a spotless mirror bring a festival of happiness when obtained by the hand.
The flow and sprinkling of blood brings about supreme sovereignty;
likewise, climbing seven trees shall swiftly bestow lordship.

Milking a buffalo signifies the attainment of supernatural powers; milking a cow indicates the acquisition of elephants and horses; obtaining the kingdom of the Gandharvas is the gain of the sun’s radiance.
O bird, one might leap upon and devour a lion, a cow, or even serpents;
one might consume one's own limbs, bones, fire, or drink liquor.
That man who eats milk-rice (pāyasa) from a vessel made of gold or silver,
or indeed from a lotus-leaf vessel, shall attain supreme sovereignty.
In both gambling and debate, victory indeed brings success;
likewise, the glowing of the limbs and piercing of the head lead to prosperity.
They praise the wearing of white garlands and garments, as well as the constant acquisition of cattle and birds, and likewise the smearing with excrement.
There will be safety by means of a horse-vehicle, and the arrival of subjects by means of a chariot;
and from eating various heads, one places prosperity within one's hand.
He has committed incest with those who should not be approached; he has acquired the highest study of the Vedas;
he treats gods, the best of the twice-born, heroes, gurus, elders, and ascetics [with contempt].
O Lord of Birds, they know that what people say regarding a man in a dream is indeed true; their vision is auspicious and their blessing is effective.
A kingdom might exist even at the cost of cutting off one's own head; there might be abundant wealth upon weeping; a kingdom might be attained through the acquisition of food while bound in fetters.
He who ascends a mountain, a horse, a lion, a bull, or even an elephant,
as well as a celestial chariot, attains great sovereignty.
Seizing the planets, the stars,
and the earth itself, the king on this world becomes one who uproots all beings.
O Lord of Birds, he who encircles those whose jewels have crossed the threshold,
or who travels by crossing even the ocean to its further shore;
For him, O hero, there shall be the complete fruit resembling a lotus;
even for one who leaps over a mountain, there shall likewise be success and victory.
O bird, if one should eat raw meat, excrement, or various kinds of fruit,
there will be a swift arrival of wealth, or perhaps [the encounter] is with a worm.
The acquisition and even the sight of ugly women,
as well as union with auspicious things, health, wealth,
sovereignty, or the attainment of a kingdom— these are said to be indicated when one dreams of such things.
In this matter, O bird, there should be no doubt regarding those various things seen;
however, having seen an auspicious dream, one should not go back to bed again.
And in the morning, O Lord of Birds, one should recount the dream exactly as it was seen to a wise person,
to Bhojakas, to Brahmins, to friends, or to the deities.
Then, at the time of midday, having bathed and with a disciplined mind,
he likewise worshipped the god Divākara according to the prescribed rites.
Having performed the correct recitation, remaining silent, and having offered oblations into the fire,
he should then depart from the temple and feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Jewels, garments, fragrant substances,
fragrant garlands, sacrificial food, mantras, and a milch cow— these one should offer to the reciter.
Gifts should be given as long as one's desire remains,
even if there should be no acquisition for the reciters.
Those Brahmins who deserve [offerings] by virtue of their superior intellect,
whose sins have been destroyed by the knowledge of the mantras, or those who are devoted to the study of the Sāmas.
Or those who know the Yajus and are conversant with the rules of the Ṛks.
Having performed this seven times sevenfold, a man endowed with devotion—
How could one who is faithful and free from malice not obtain the fruit that results from performing ten horse-sacrifices?
Having performed [these rites] on seven seventh-days, a human being attains that fruit.
O Hero, there is nothing difficult to obtain in this world that cannot be gained through the seventh-day observances;
nor, O Lord of the People, is there any disease in this world that does not cease because of these.
Those families which are fierce and those which are ill-situated here—
all of them are pacified, just as serpents are by Garuḍa.
Having thus duly performed the seventh [day] and seven others with specific vows and observances here, a man of virtuous character,
endowed with the fruits of learning and wealth, shall be possessed of happiness and merit.
He goes to that eternal realm which is in the direction of the sun of piercing rays.
This is the procedure for the seven Saptamīs, beginning with the cleaning of the teeth and ending with the feeding of Brahmins.
Thus ends the vow of the Siddhārthaka-Saptamī and others as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:

Having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rule with flowers, incense, and other offerings, the wise one should thereafter devoutly present an offering of food (naivedya) according to his capacity.
Among flowers, the Jāti is the most excellent; among incenses, the Vijaya is supreme;
among perfumes, saffron is the best; and among unguents, red sandalwood is preeminent.
In the offering of lamps, ghee is best; for the food offering, sweetmeats (modaka) are supreme.
By these, the Lord of Gods is pleased and he also grants his presence.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rites and having also performed a circumambulation,
he bowed his head to the Sun, the god of gods.
Then, seated comfortably and facing the sun, one should look [at it];
having thus prepared the white mustard seeds, holding them in the hand together with water.
The grammatical construction is:
"A man, having placed his desire— that which he wishes for— in his heart as he pleases,
should look upon the Siddhārthaka [flower], satisfying the Brahmin by touching him once with his teeth."
The word "at night" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
O one of excellent vows, having taken two [drops] on the second and seventh [days],
exactly three indeed must be drunk on the third and seventh [days].
On the fourth day one should drink four [mouthfuls], on the fifth five, and on the sixth six; such is the Vedic revelation.
On the seventh day, a person should drink seven [draughts] combined with water;
the word "water" (vāri) here denotes a liquid, since the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) will be mentioned later.
This mantra, beginning with "āditya," is to be understood as the consecration formula for this purpose.
For it is always heard everywhere in the world that the name "Siddhārthaka" brings success;
therefore, O Sun, act so that my purpose may likewise be accomplished for those who seek it.
Then, having touched the sacrificial oblation, one should perform the recitation as is appropriate;
and one should offer oblations into the fire according to the rite prescribed by rule.
In this very manner, the seven subsequent seventh-day rites should always be performed.

In this manner, six sets of seven [days], beginning with the *arkasaṃpuṭa* and increasing by one each time, should be performed individually. Their respective mantras are to be understood as those stated for the *arkasaptamīs* that will be described later. Starting from water up to the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), there is one [day] with water, and two [days] combined with clarified butter.
The third is combined with honey, and the fourth with curd;
five are joined with milk, and six are mixed with cow dung.
O twice-born one, one should drink the five products of the cow seven times along with white mustard seeds;
whoever performs the Sarṣapa-saptamī according to this rite [shall attain success].
Having been a man in this world who possessed many sons, much wealth, and was always successful in his aims, he goes to the Fire-god after death.
Thus end the Sarsapa-saptami vows as declared in the glorious Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Sumantu said: That which was previously narrated by Āditya himself to the bird (Garuḍa)...
The seven Saptamīs of the mighty-armed Aruṇa are highly honored.
The first [is made] with *arka* capsules, the second likewise with black peppers;
the third with neem leaves, and the fourth with the seven fruits.
The fifth is Anodanā, the sixth is Vijayā, and the seventh is to be known as Kāmikī; learn from me the procedure according to rule.
Having undertaken the vow with one's wife during the bright fortnight, on a Sunday, when the northern solstice has begun, under a lunar mansion bearing a masculine name.
In all circumstances he should be a celibate student, endowed with purity, having his senses subdued,
devoted to the worship of the Sun, self-controlled, and likewise intent upon recitation and fire-offerings.
On the fifth day, one with a restrained mind should take only a single meal;
on the sixth day, one should not engage in sexual intercourse and should avoid honey and meat.

The phrase "performing at night" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. One should lead one [type of] woman with *arka* capsules, another with black peppers, and yet another with neem leaves; the one called "the fruit" [is attained] by eating fruit.
Without rice, without food, fasting according to the prescribed rule,
subsisting on air for a day and night, one should perform the Vijaya-saptamī rite.
Likewise, the wise man should perform these six [rites] seven times each month according to the prescribed rule; thereafter, he should perform the Kāmakī rite.
Then, having taken their names, [he should place them] separately in individual vessels.
One should place all those vessels into a new jar that has its body smeared with white sandalwood paste and is adorned with garlands of flowers.
Abounding in wealth, grain, and gold, resembling pure kunda flowers and the moon,
and rich with leaves of the *aśvattha* and *aśoka* trees, they were accompanied by curd-rice.
Therefore, whether it be a fool or any other man who does not understand that purpose,
he should extract [the essence] alone and perform it without hesitation.
O scorcher of foes, that which is performed every month according to that very same rite until it has been completed seven times should be known as the *kāmikī*.
Thus, O King, these seven sets of seven have been proclaimed by Vivasvat himself; the man who performs them with devotion goes to the abode of the Sun.
His limbs were smeared with white sandalwood paste and adorned with garlands of flowers;
he was richly endowed with the seven types of grain and gold, and resembled the pure kunda flower or the moon.
With offerings consisting of leaves rich with *aśvattha* and *aśoka*, accompanied by curd-rice and enclosed within *arka* leaves,
one obtains stainless wealth extending to seven generations.
Indeed, for one who constantly desires a beloved son, there shall be union with Marīci;
all body hairs fall away by means of nimba leaves—of this there is no doubt.
[689] And with abundant fruits, sons, grandsons, and even daughters' sons; and through the absence of hunger, wealth, grain, gold, and silver likewise.

Likewise, O King, by fasting, a monarch constantly attains fame, gold, health, and progeny, and he conquers his enemies in victory. When worshipped according to the prescribed rites, she who grants desires fulfills all wishes.
One desiring a son shall obtain a son; one desiring wealth shall obtain inexhaustible wealth;
one desiring knowledge shall obtain knowledge; and one seeking a kingdom shall attain a kingdom.
This bestower of desires grants all desires, O delighter of the lineage.
Whether it be a man or a woman, whoever performs the aforementioned Saptamī vow with self-restraint attains the supreme goal.
If a breach of the vow should occur through delusion, negligence, or greed,
then one should not eat for three nights, or else undergo the shaving of the hair.
Having performed this expiation, one becomes a practitioner of the vow once again,
until seven seventh-days have been reached, joined with the number seven.
"Joined with seven" means multiplied by seven, that is, forty-nine. Having worshipped the Sun on the seventh lunar day with garlands, incense, and so forth,
and having devoutly fed the twice-born, a man shall attain imperishable heaven.
He who bestows gold upon the mouths of Brahmins on the seventh lunar day obtains that as inexhaustible and goes to the world of the Sun.
[690] Thus ends the Saptasaptasaptamī-kalpa as declared in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa.
Sumantu said:
Now follows the group of seven Saptamīs beginning with Arkasaṃpuṭakā. [The text] beginning with "Samudreśavana" [is broken]; she explains [it] once again as one [unit].
Thus, the ritual procedure for the Saptamī has been told to you in brief.
I shall speak to you of it in detail; listen with a focused mind most attentively.
Having fasted properly on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
one should bathe and worship the Sun with flowers, perfumes, and ointments.
O mighty-armed one, adorning the divine Sun-god with arka flowers, fragrant guggulu resin, white sandalwood, and incense.
Having worshipped the Sun during the day with an offering of jaggery-rice and three palas [of the same], one should sleep at night in front of him.
The wise man should mutter the supreme mantra on the ground until sleep comes,
while meditating upon the Great-Souled One, the God of gods, the Sun.
With a concentrated mind, one should always perform recitation, worship, and likewise fire-offerings and worship using the six-syllable mantra,
accompanied by the sound of a hundred [recitations].
Having first performed the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred thousand times,
one should thereafter perform all other rites, such as further recitations, with an undisturbed mind.
O Hero, for the sake of one's own welfare, and for the accomplishment of the goals of wealth and sons:
*Oṃ*, let us know the Maker of Light; let us meditate upon the Thousand-rayed One;
may that Sūrya inspire us.
[691] Thus ends the section on the Sāvitrī.
This recitation has been declared by the Sun himself to be supreme;
by reciting it even once, a human being becomes purified—of this there is no doubt.
Then, on the morning of the seventh day, having bathed with a restrained mind,
O King, one should worship Bhāskara with devotion according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Or else, O King, a man should devoutly feed Brahmins with divine enjoyments according to the rules for the pleasure of the Sun-god.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; rather, one should feed those worthy of a meal.
One should likewise feed those devoted to the Sun, and one should not feed anyone other than those devoted to the Sun.
The Brahmin who observes the seventh [lunar day] and partakes of the meal at the proper time is skilled in the Saura Tantras; he is indeed a devotee of the Sun.
O King, these twice-born ones are, in brief, those who may be fed by the Sun;
they have been declared thus, O best of the Kuru lineage. Now hear from me concerning those who are not to be fed.
He who takes pleasure in another's wife brings about the disease of leprosy;
likewise, those devoted to other deities and those who act as astrologers [bring similar consequences].
He who delights in slandering others, as well as a temple-attendant (*devalaka*),
these indeed have been declared by the Lord himself to be persons whose food is not to be eaten by Brahmins.
O King, because she was said to "fit" (ghaṭeta) within the assembly of Brahmins who possess the threefold knowledge (trayī-vidyā),
she is therefore remembered as Sānughaṭā.
O hero, that twice-born man in the assembly of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, who possesses that vessel, is called a "vessel-holder" (ghṛī).
For those who listen with devotion to the recitation of the book according to the prescribed rule,
that which is composed as an Itihāsa by Bhānu is called a *samasyā*.
O tiger among the Kurus, this was proclaimed by the one who travels through the sky himself:
"He who would be the author of that [work] is considered its composer."
O tiger among kings, that brahmin was hostile toward the Sun;
he lived off the gains of others and likewise subsisted on the poetic fragments of Vyāsa.
O Bhārata, these ancient Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas,
which were spoken here by the god Bhānu himself as the "Jaya," [should be recited].
O King, that Brahmin who lives by reciting these [texts] should be known as one who lives by victory (jayopajīvī), and likewise as a mere reciter (vācaka).
Wherein the Seven Horses (Saptāśva), out of devotion for the pleasure of the Sun-god,
[are praised], as well as the Āruṇeya and other scriptures, and likewise the Saptāśvatilaka.
But he who knows the solar [mantras], that brahmin is a knower of the Saura-tantra;
likewise, he subsists by the victory of Vyāsa and lives by means of poetic riddles.
O King, he who constantly worships the Sun should indeed worship Bhāskara;
he goes to the supreme abode where the wise behold Him.
O King, he who is like a patron and like the god Divākara is declared by Bhāskara to be one who should be diligently honored with a meal.
O joy of the Kurus, that brahmin who censures food and likewise does not honor it should be known as a devotee of another deity.
O King, if a barber who is shaven-headed, deformed, pale-complexioned, and carrying a conch and a lotus should enter the house of any man, [that man’s lineage shall perish].
The gods, the ancestors, and the sun-god come to the house of that brahmin,
O king of kings, who indeed performs his work through his livelihood.

O scorcher of foes, the worship of the gods should likewise be performed only in the temples of the deities; furthermore, the consumption [of offerings] and the presentation of food offerings (naivedya) must be accompanied by their presiding authority.
He should be known as a world of gods, yet among Brahmins he is the lowest of Brahmins;
there is no entitlement for earthly Brahmins to perform worship of the gods.

O tiger among the Bharatas, one should especially avoid [the consumption of meat] in all temples by way of one's livelihood or through exercising authority, with the sole exception of the temple of Śiva.
O King, O Lord, it is traditionally held that the authority over the worship of the gods or the performance of fire-rituals belongs to the Brahmins; of this there is no doubt among the worlds.
By worshipping the gods, they indeed attain the supreme goal;
for they partake of the food offering (naivedya), thereby as it were feeding the Sun himself.
They indeed worship the gods, and by that they have attained divinity;
having worshipped the gods, O Lord, they partake of the food offering.
They go to the supreme abode where the Sun-god dwells;
O King, there are indeed two Brahmins who are the twice-born attendants of the Sun.
The reciter and the one who serves the meal—these two alone have attained the highest state.
Having gone to his house himself, he should touch the [reciter's] feet with both hands out of devotion.
And likewise, O Brahmin, you are one who observes vows; therefore, O Lord, show me your favor.
The Sun-god is pleased with you, O Brahmin; please eat your meal in my house.
O high-minded one, when you, the sun, are satisfied, by that the gods are satisfied;
and at that moment, the Brahmin should also say this.
"I shall do so for the sake of my own welfare or yours, O Lord," having thus addressed him, one should then go to one's own home, O joy of the Kurus.
Likewise, O King, at the time of afternoon, having offered oblations to the god Divākara and to the sacrificial fire with devotion, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Likewise, rice of the *śāli* variety, mung beans, fragrant ghee,
cakes filled with jaggery, milk, curd, and jaggery itself.
O best of the Bharatas, the Sun attains satisfaction from these seven kinds of food for seven years; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Likewise, śiyukunda that is very sour, as well as rājamāṣa beans,
kulotthaka, lentils, sesame seeds, and even aṇakya.
One who desires his own welfare should not offer these to the Sun:
that which is foul-smelling, that which is harshly spoken, and that which is excessively sour.
One should certainly not offer rice mixed with other grains to the Sun;
having thus fed all the twice-born, one should consume the entire *saṃpuṭa*.
Having bowed his head to the god while holding water,
O King, he departed from the city and proceeded toward the northeast direction.
O mighty-armed one, having seen the supreme Arka plant born in a pure place— neither too high nor too low— and having worshipped it with *kakola* incense;

"By *khakholka*" means by the *khakholka* mantra. It is as follows: "Homage to *khakholka*. Having taken two leaves—one situated on the branch facing northeast, belonging to that tree which stands upon the earth, located at the tip of the branch, attached to very fine young shoots, yet distinct from one another—one should return home. Because of the use of the dual number, the abode of two leaves is understood.
Having bathed and worshipped the Sun with *arka* flowers while reciting "O *khakholka*," and having fed the Brahmins, he should say: "May the Sun be pleased with me."
Having consumed the *arkapuṭa* with the mantra, O Hero, one should then eat while remaining silent,
touching the vessel with the teeth in front of the Deity.
Oṃ! The sun is auspiciously enclosed; may it be ever-blessed for you, and may I always praise it as most auspicious for me.
Grant me indeed prosperity, and through this consumption [of the offering], become the bestower of wealth.
O King, O lord of the earth, reciting this mantra while facing the sun,
one should remain standing with palms joined and body bowed, accompanied by water, O monarch.
O King, he who eats after having first tasted [the offering] goes to the supreme state;
by this method, the Saptamī vow should always be performed with devotion.
O mighty-armed one, for as long as a year, a king who with faith performs this seventh-day rite for the pleasure of the Sun shall bring joy to the Sun.
His wealth shall become inexhaustible, immovable, and attained through human effort;
having achieved this perfection, Kauthumi, a singer of the Sāman hymns, came [to this state] in ancient times.
And having been freed from leprosy by chanting the Sāman,
the high-minded Bṛhadvalka, Janaka, Yājñavalkya, and Kṛṣṇaja likewise attained liberation.

Śāmba was born from Kṛṣ� having worshipped the Sun, O King, she attained the state of one whose soul is identical with the Sun. This most blessed and meritorious seventh lunar day (Saptamī) is the destroyer of sins.
O King, for those who read, listen, and especially perform it,
this should always be carried out according to the rules for the sake of their welfare, O monarch.
O mighty-armed one, Arkapriyā is the destroyer of great sins.
Thus ends the Arkasaṃpuṭasaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Sumantu said:
O King, having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, Bhānu, the bestower of desires—
And having fed the Brahmins especially according to one's ability.
On the seventh day, the lord of men should also consume black pepper;
having taken one hundred whole, unblemished, and very firm grains of pepper.
O King, one should cause him to consume the pepper without touching it, while reciting this mantra:
"Oṃ khakholkāya svāhā! May the beloved one be pleased; may there be union with the beloved, svāhā!
Having thus offered this prayer, one should eat the *marīca* while remaining silent.
One attains union with the beloved at that very moment; it is not otherwise.
Thus, O Hero, this seventh auspicious day bestows the company of loved ones; he who performs a festival on this day shall never suffer separation.
O best of men, Prajāpati spoke thus to his sons and others:
"Therefore, O mighty-armed one, perform this rite which bestows what is dear."
O hero, in ancient times, having observed the fast on the seventh day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa according to the prescribed rites, Indra,
the lord of thousands, attained union with them.
O lord of men, Rāma also, together with Damayantī and even with Sītā, having fasted on this [day] along with the fire of Rāma’s lineage, [attains success].
[697] Thus ends the Marīcasaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa.
Sumantu said:
O Hero, O King, listen with one-pointed mind to the third and the seventh [vows];
that which is known as the Nimbapatra is remembered as the destroyer of sin, the eradicator of evil.
Likewise, he should perform another method of worship by which he worships Ravi,
the God of gods, who holds a mace in his hand and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Likewise, I shall declare the procedure for worship; learn from me the extraction of the mantra, which is meritorious, the remover of all sins, and the destroyer of all diseases.

Oṃ, homage to Khaṅkolya. This is the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). *Vidi viva* is for the head (*śiras*). *Śrī jvala ṭhaṭha* is for the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Oṃ, homage to the one with a thousand abodes (*sahasradhāman*) is for the armor (*kavaca*). Oṃ, homage to the Lord of All Splendor (*sarvatejo’dhipati*) is for the weapon (*astra*), blazing with a thousand rays; *vava vajraghanaṃ*. Oṃ, homage to her who exists in the past, exists in the future, and will exist in the future (*bhūtabhavya-bhūtabhāvinī*); *vava bhūtavandhaḥ*. Oṃ, blaze, O eye, blaze, blaze forth, *ṭhaṭha*; this is the form of fire (*agniprakāra*). Oṃ, let us know the Sun (*āditya*), let us meditate upon the one whose nature is the universe (*viśvabhāva*); may that Sūrya inspire us. This is the Gāyatrī for the rite of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*). Oṃ, homage to the Soul of Dharma (*dharmātman*), in the east. Homage to Yama, in the south. Oṃ, homage to the Lord of the Staff of Time (*kāladaṇḍanāyaka*), in the west. Oṃ, homage to Raivata, in the north.

Homage to Śyāmapiṅgala in the northeast. Oṃ, homage to Dīkṣita in the southeast. Oṃ, homage to Vajrapāṇi in the southwest. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, homage to Āditya in the northwest. Oṃ, homage to Candra, the lord of the moon, in the east. Oṃ, homage to Aṅgāraka, the son of the Earth, in the southeast.

Oṃ, homage to Budha, the son of Soma; [place this] in the south. Oṃ, homage to Vāgīśvara, the lord of all sciences; [place this] in the southwest (nairṛtyā). Oṃ, homage to Śukra, the great seer, the son of Bhṛgu; [place this] in the west. Oṃ, homage to Śanaiścara, the son of Ravi; [place this] in the northwest (vāyavyā). Oṃ, homage to Rāhu; [place this] in the north. Homage to Ketu; [place this] in the northeast (īśānyā). O Blessed One, garlanded with immeasurable rays, Lord of the entire world, you who ride upon seven horses, possess four arms, and bestow the supreme siddhis—O you whose speech is like sparks of fire, come, come! Accept this water-offering (argha) which has reached my head. O you whose form is the foremost of splendors, infinite flame! Ṭhaṭhaḥ!
The mantra for the invocation with the *arghya* offering:
*Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, Āditya, who possesses a thousand rays; go happily so that you may return again.* The mantra for the dismissal (*visarjana*).
Listen; I shall explain here the entire procedure in due order, as well as the ritual for the *dīrghā*, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
O King, best of the Bharatas, the preceptor, having sprinkled the ground before the deity with water purified by mantras according to the prescribed rule, [proceeded].

For the sake of purification, one who knows the mantras, being well-composed, should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) after having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra upon the heart and other limbs of the body.
One should perform the *satarjanī* mudrā and purify the end of the night;
one should also perform the purification of the underworld and the earth, as well as the enclosure of fire.
One should perform the purification of the space while recollecting the weapon-mantra;
[the guardians are] Yama, Soma, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Īśāna, and Agni.
This is proclaimed as the Rudra-Nairṛta-Vāyavya wing;
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp in a clean place.
Then, having performed the invocation, one should invoke the Sun by means of the mudrā;
there, one should establish the Khaṭvīṅka, his own form who brings about the worlds.
One should establish, and indeed cause to be established, the one whose body is mantra by means of mantras;
O King, one should place him in the heart of the God of Gods.
Having placed the head in the northeast, one should install Śiva in the southwest;
one should place the lotus in the east, with the mind fixed in one-pointed concentration.
One should place Soma, the bestower of prosperity and highly honored, in the northeast;
likewise, the armor in the northwest, and the weapon in the west.
In the southeast [is] the son of Soma; in the south, Bṛhaspati;
in the southwest, the preceptor of the Dānavas; and in the west, Śanaiścara.
Likewise, one should place Rāhu in the northwest and Ketu in the north;
these beings, born from the splendor of the gods, are located in the second enclosure.
One should establish the twelve Ādityas, the descendants of Kaśyapa, who possess great power:
Bhaga, Sūrya, Aryaman, Mitra, and Varuṇa; and likewise—
Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, and the mighty Vivasvat,
Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, as well as Candra, and Viṣṇu is said to be the twelfth.

Salutation to Indra in the east, to Yama in the south, to Varuṇa in the west, to Kubera in the north, to Īśvara in the northeast, to Agni in the southeast, to Nirṛti in the southwest, and to Vāyu in the northwest.
Also: Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Revanta, and Vināyaka.
Likewise, the goddess Mahāśvetā and Queen Suvarcalā,
as well as the two other renowned ones, Daṇḍanāyaka and Piṅgala.
These two should be placed in front of the Sun by one who knows:
the goddesses Siddhi, Buddhi, Smṛti, and likewise Utpalamālinī.
But those worthy of worship by the world should be placed on the right side, all around:
Prajñā, Tantrī, Kṣudhā, Brāhmī, Hārītā, and Tuṣṭi.
And [the goddesses] on the side of the shadow are to be known; these are the powers of the gods.
One should offer a lamp, food, ornaments, clothing, and flowers with the mantra.
These should be constantly offered according to this rite to the form of the God together with his attendants; by doing so, one always goes to the Sun.
Having attained supreme desires, he shall thereafter become equal to the sun;
O King, whoever worships the Sun-god according to this rite [shall achieve this].
Through the grace of Ravi, O King, one shall go to the supreme, imperishable state;
likewise, one obtains sons and invincibility against enemies.
Having worshipped the Sun according to this rite on the sixth lunar day,
[one who is] victorious over anger and has conquered the senses...
[701] Then, O King, on the seventh day one should eat a nimba leaf with this mantra:
"O nimba sprout, may it be well with you; may there always be great prosperity for you."
"Bestow blessings upon me as well; through consuming [this], you shall become a destroyer of disease.
Thus is the mantra uttered.
Having consumed it in this manner, O King, one should sleep on the ground before the deity.
On the eighth day, one should worship the Sun once again according to one's capacity;
thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins, having given them sacrificial fees according to one's means.
One should eat afterwards while restraining speech, avoiding sweet and sour foods;
thus is this Nimbasaptamī to be observed for the duration of a year.
By performing even the seventh [observance], one is liberated from all diseases;
being freed from all diseases, one goes to the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the Nimbasaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Sumantu said: Now, O Lord of the Earth, in the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight—
Having observed a fast on the seventh day, one should worship the Sun according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship the Sun here according to the Māheśvara rite;
then again, having worshipped the Maker of Day on the morning of the eighth day.
One should give fruits to the Brahmins, saying, "May Mārtaṇḍa be pleased," [offering] dates,
coconuts, and citrons.
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, he himself should subsist on fruit;
first, however, having respectfully consumed a single very small piece of fruit.
O best of the Bharatas, one should then consume the remaining portions with the mantra;
O best of the lineage, by partaking of the fruit, one shall indeed attain the status of Indra.
"May all my desires be fulfilled in every respect. Having said this, O joy of the Kurus, one should eat those fruits.
O best of the Kurus, he should eat nothing else at all until his throat;
thus, O joy of the Kurus, one should subsist on fruit alone on the eighth day.
Thus, O mighty-armed one, the Phala-saptamī should be observed for the duration of a year;
when performed, it bestows sons and grandsons.
Thus ends the vow of Phala-saptamī as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Sumantu said:
Having fasted properly on the sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha, [one should proceed].
One should worship the Sun with devotion by means of flowers, incense, ointments, and other offerings.
The procedure by which one should worship that deity is now being told to you;
O King, it is the ritual according to which Vaiśravaṇa should be worshipped.

Oṃ *prajvalane* svāhā! Oṃ *agniprakāraḥ*! Oṃ, homage to the one blazing with a thousand rays, svāhā! Oṃ *yaṃ vaḥ*! Oṃ, homage to the Earth, who nourishes all medicinal herbs, svāhā! "O Earth, homage to you"—this is the mantra for the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of making oneself or the deity complete). In the body of the deity, or within one's own self: Oṃ, homage to the Self of Dharma (*dharmātmane*), in the east. Oṃ, homage to Dharma, in the south. Oṃ, homage to Revanta, in the west. Oṃ, homage to the one whose form is a constant flame, in the north. Oṃ, homage to the one dark-brown, tawny, and red, in the northeast (*aiśānī*). Homage to the blue-and-red one, in the southeast (*āgneyī*). Homage to Īśāneśvara, in the southwest (*nairṛtī*). Homage to Vajrapāṇi, in the northwest (*vāyavī*). Oṃ, homage to the one whose body is like Hara, possessed of great strength and prowess, the sovereign lord of all splendor, svāhā!
Salutation to the bearer of the supreme power.

First, the eastern door-keeper: *Oṃ, homage to the one whose body is Hara and who bears the form of a thunderbolt.* Second, the door-keeper from the south: *Oṃ, homage to the green one.* Third, from the west: *Oṃ, homage to the horse-faced one.* Fourth, from the east: *Oṃ, homage to the horse-faced one.* Thus, the four door-keepers. *Oṃ, svāhā to the one with the splendor of a jasmine flower, the moon, and a hero.* First horse: *Oṃ, homage to the one with red eyes, red color, and radiance.* Second horse: *Oṃ, homage to the one with the color of milk and radiant energy.* Third horse: *Oṃ, homage to the one with the color of crushed collyrium.* Fourth horse: *Oṃ, homage to the one of intense brilliance.* Fifth horse: *Oṃ, homage to the one with the color of the sky and to the one wearing a blazing garland.* Seventh: *Oṃ, homage to the one who is like a mountain-cart, to the armored one, to the son of Kaśyapa, to Prajāpati.* *Oṃ, homage to the infinite god.* *Oṃ, homage to the one with extraordinary valor and brilliance.*
The invocation mantra:
Oṃ, Bhāskara, God above all gods, go, go to your own abode as you please, for the sake of returning again.
The mantra for dismissal (*visarjana*).

With the *Gāyatrī*, there is the offering of the welcome, the respectful water (*arghya*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), the bath, the hospitality, as well as the presentation of perfumes, flowers, incense, offerings (*bali*), oblations (*homa*), and other gifts.
[704] There is also the *mukulī* lotus-mudrā, and likewise the *niṣkarā* and another.
The one called Nāga, Vyomamudrā, and Ugrā are remembered as the supreme [mudrās];
these seven are indeed the supreme mudrās, as are the Koṭimudrās.

Oṃ, salutation to Khakholka; this is the heart. Oṃ, salutation to Tripiṣṭapa; this is the head. Oṃ, salutation to Tejas; this is the crest-lock (śikhā). Salutation to Āditya, the Lord of Splendor; this is the armor (kavaca). Salutation to Āditya, blazing with a thousand rays; this is the weapon (astra). Salutation to the Lord of Splendor; this is the face. Oṃ, salutation to the one who rides the ram and the bull; this is the secret organ (guhya). Oṃ, salutation to the Thousand-Rayed One; this is the feet. Oṃ, salutation to the Lord of Radiance; this is the back. Oṃ, may we know Bhāskara; may we meditate upon the one with a thousand spokes of light; may that Sun impel us.
Sumantu said: Having worshipped according to this rite, one should fast on the sixth lunar day while remaining pure;
then, on the seventh day, one should again worship the bed of the Sun in front of it.
One should feed the Brahmins with either curd or milk-rice;
having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should approach them with faith.
Having drunk the milk of a cow, O joy of the Kurus, you must remain standing;
you are fragrant—may it be well with you, may prosperity be yours for the sake of happiness.
"Likewise, O auspicious one, may you indeed be a bringer of prosperity to me through this food.
With this recited mantra, there is the drinking of milk.
Whatever is to be chewed with the teeth is traditionally known as *odana*.
Food to be chewed, food to be sucked, and likewise food to be licked—these three types of boiled rice are proclaimed.
"Water is said to be non-rice; therefore, one should avoid it.

[705] Regarding the phrase "one should avoid that," the word "that" refers back to rice (*odana*). Therefore, one should avoid only rice, and not even a drinkable liquid, because the latter is not rice. This is the mantra for consuming the food.
Thus, O bull of the Bharatas, this is the seventh [observance] called Anodanā;
by fasting with devotion upon it, a man shall obtain wealth and grain.
Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of the Sun.
