Thus ends the Anodanā-saptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Sumantu said:
"O descendant of Kuru, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,"
O King, fasting, one should worship the Sun with devotion according to the prescribed rite.

Standing before the deity with a mind that is pure, one-pointed, and focused, O King, one should recite the mantra to be chanted, having conquered anger and subdued the senses, as previously described.
O Vāyu, most powerful one, may there be welfare for you; may there always be welfare for you.
Grant me also welfare, and through this consumption, become a slayer of enemies.
"By means of this recited mantra, one whose breath is restrained and who abstains from food [attains success].
Śatānīka said:
"By reciting which mantra would the Blessed One grant his vision?"
Or perhaps by means of a hymn? Tell me that, O you of noble vows.
Sumantu said: When I, full of devotion, had praised him with a thousand names,
then the divine Sun-god appeared before my very eyes.
Śatānīka said:
"O twice-born one, I wish to hear the thousand names of Savitṛ, by means of which you obtained a direct vision of the god Divākara himself. [706] 5.
Sumantu said: This hymn is the most auspicious of all auspicious things, the destroyer of all sins, highly meritorious, and the dispeller of all calamities. (6)
There is no fear whatsoever that is not pacified by this;
O King, a person is freed from fever when this hymn is recited. (7)
Furthermore, other diseases are pacified for one who recites or hears [this],
and likewise all desires are fulfilled exactly as wished.
The man who, having heard this from the beginning, enters into battle,
shall conquer his enemies in combat and return home unhurt.
It brings the birth of sons to the barren, the destruction of fear to the frightened,
it acts as a catalyst for the living, and it is the supreme medicine for the poor and for those afflicted with leprosy.
O King, whoever recites this shall indeed attain the highest welfare; it wards off all seizing spirits and demons that afflict children. 11.
With all his intentions fulfilled, he enjoys ultimate happiness;
[he is sought] by those seeking dharma for the sake of dharma, and by those seeking happiness for the sake of happiness.
This should be studied by men desiring sovereignty for the sake of attaining a kingdom;
it brings knowledge to Brahmins and victory to Kṣatriyas. (13)
This [work], which brings cattle and increases the merit of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, undoubtedly comes to those who read or hear it. (14)
Listen to that, O best of kings; with a disciplined mind I shall speak it to you—the thousand names renowned as belonging to Bhāskara, the God of Gods. [707] 15.
Oṃ! He is the knower of all, the conqueror of all, the creator, the soul of all, and the one whose face is turned in every direction;
he is the Lord of all, the source of all, self-restrained, and one who has mastered his senses. 16.
He who has time as his support, the maker of time, the destroyer of desire, the annihilator of longing;
the great yogi, the one of great intellect, the great-souled one, and the one of immense strength. || 17 ||
The Lord, the All-pervading, the Master of beings, the Self of beings, the Sovereign of the world;
Śiva, whose self is the past, the future, and the present, and who brings about the end of all beings.
The one worthy of refuge, the delight of Kamalā, the son, the increaser of joy, the chooser, the giver of boons, the yogi, the well-restrained, and the illuminator. || 19 ||
He who has attained the supreme vehicle, the highest life-force, whose soul is joyful, self-restrained, and dear;
he who has a thousand feet, who is perfectly virtuous, and adorned with divine earrings.
Wearing no bodily defects, firm-souled, the progenitor whose vehicle is the wind,
he is one of concentrated mind, the supporter, the ordainer, and the performer of auspicious rites.
Kapardin, the creator of the cosmic age, Rudra, the one of excellent wisdom, the lover of dharma;
he who is both united and detached in nature, the perfected soul, the foremost among the accomplished. || 22 ||
He is of inconceivable form, the most excellent body, the great yogi, the Great Lord; he is the beloved, the enemy of Kama, the Sun, self-restrained, and undisturbed.
He is Desire, the compassionate creator, the awakener of Kamalākara;
he is the seven-horsed sun, the inconceivable self, the supreme among the most merciful.
The one who revives, the lord of life, the one whose essence is recitation, the living soul, the lord of the world;
the unconquerable, the abode of the universe, the sharer of portions, the bull-bannered one. || 25 ||
Vṛṣākapi, the creator of the cosmic cycles, the sun that brings about the end of the cycles,
he whose chariot has a single wheel, the silent one, the possessor of a divine chariot, and the foremost among charioteers.
[708] Free from anger, garlanded with rays, a mass of splendor, the consumer of oblations;
the maker of day, the creator of the day, the god, the god of gods, the lord of the sky. || 27 ||
Lord of the Day, the Invoker, the Priest, the one who carries the oblation to heaven, the Maker of Day;
the Sacrifice, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Nourisher, the one whose seed is gold, the supreme and the inferior. || 28 ||
The knower of the high and the low, the deliverer, the garlanded with rays, the captivator of the mind;
the wise one, the lord of wisdom, the Sun, the progenitor, Viṣṇu, the radiant one. (29)
Sadāgati, Gandhavaha, Vihita, Vidhi, Āśuga;
Pataṅga, Sthāṇu, Vihaga, Vihaṅga, Vihata, Vara. || 30 ||
Haryaśva, Haritāśva, Haridaśva, the beloved of the world, Antaka, Sarvadamana, Bhāvitātman, and the best of physicians. || 31 ||
The maker of light, the Lord of the world, honored by the vision of the world;
he is Time, the fire at the end of the aeon, the burner, the one who causes intense heat. || 32 ||
Virocana, Virūpākṣa, Sahasrākṣa, Purandara, Sahasraraśmi, Mihira, adorned with various garments and ornaments. (33)
Khaga, Pratardana, Dhanya, Hayaga, Vāgviśārada, Śrīmān, Aśiśira, Vāgmī, Śrīpati, and Śrīniketana. || 34 ||
Śrīkhaṇṭha, Śrīdhara, the illustrious Śrīmān, the abode of Śrī, the bestower of wealth;
he who moves at will, the great illusionist, the Great Lord whose intentions are known. (35)
He is the performer of sacred rites, one whose mind is suited to the right path, and who is compassionate toward his devotees;
he is fame itself, the eternal maker of renown, and he is always adorned with earrings, clad in armor, and mounted on a chariot.
Hiraṇyaretas, Saptāśva, Prayatātman, Parantapa, Buddhimān, Aparashreṣṭha, Rociṣṇu, and Pākaśāsana. (37)
Samudrodha, Nado, Dhātā, Māndhātā, Kaśmalāpaha;
Tamoghna, Dhvāntahā, Vahni, Hotā, Antakaraṇa, Guha. [709] 38.

He is the possessor of cattle, the one of restrained bliss, the Lord of beings, the celestial garment of the prosperous, the eternally risen, the one whose chariot is eternal, the Lord of gods, and the one worshipped by the gods. || 39 ||
The unconquered, the victorious, the conqueror, the moving, and the nature of the stationary; the bliss of life, the ever-moving, the knower, and the one who bestows the ether. || 40 ||
He is Parjanya, Agni, Tithi, Stheya, Sthavira, Aṇu, and Nirañjana;
he is Pradyotana, mounted upon his chariot, the illuminator of all the worlds. || 41 ||
He is the eternal, the sacrificial post, the one of great heroism, the swan who delivers one from the cycle of existence;
he is the creator of the universe, the cause of action, the sun, and the lord of the Maruts. || 42 ||
Marutvān, Dahana, Tvaṣṭṛ, Bhaga, Bhāgya, Aryaman, Kapi, Varuṇa, Aja, Jagannātha, Kṛtakṛtya, and Sulocana. || 43 ||
Vivasvān, Bhānumān, Kārya, Kāraṇa, Tejasāṃnidhi, Asaṅgāmī, Tigmārcis, Varmaṃsu, and Dīptadīdhiti. || 44 ||
The thousand-rayed one, the ruddy one, the thousand-eyed maker of day;
he who possesses rays, who possesses beams, who possesses splendor, and whose radiance is stainless. (45)
Bhāskara, who knows the tasks of the gods, the omniscient one, the one with piercing rays; the eldest of the gods, the lord of the gods, the one of vast knowledge, the master of speech. || 46 ||
A treasury of splendor, possessed of great brilliance, of vast renown, the teacher Bṛhaspati;
free from delusion, powerful, wise, liberated, and the increaser of fame. || 47 ||
The great physician, Gaṇapati, Gaṇeśa, the leader of the hosts;
the intense one, the scorching one, the burner, the inflamer, the scorcher of the universe. 48.
Kārtasvara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmānanda, Abhinandita, Padmanābha, Amṛtahara, Sthitimān, Ketumān, and Nabha. || 49 ||

[710] Without beginning or end, undecaying, the universe, the friend of the universe, compassionate, the sovereign, clad in armor for the next world, eloquent, the wearer of the *kaśukī* garment, the creator of all beings. || 50 ||

He is the one whose mind is signless, the most excellent, the refuge, facing all directions; he is the diver, the dust-colored, the intolerant, the one endowed with all, and the one equal to the sacrificial rite.
He whose banner is the Dharma, who delights in the Dharma, the destroyer, self-restraint, and the restrainer;
he who removes the suffering of those who bow before him, the immeasurable one, whose purpose is accomplished, the Lord of Recitation.
Pervading the sky, he is the Truth, the immeasurable Self, and most enchanting;
he is the captivating one, the sun, the horse, the wind, the season, and possesses the splendor of the fire of time.
Easy to serve, possessed of great splendor, and the cause of the mantras of the worlds;
Mahendra is praised, he who is the object of hymns, the reason for praise, and the maker of light. 54.
The venerable Sahasrakara is free from disease, the bestower of happiness, and blissful;
he is the destroyer of illness, the gracious-faced one, the embodiment of well-being, and the sky-like garment of auspiciousness. (55)
Ārogyakaraṇa, Siddhi, Vṛddhi, Ṛddhi, Ahaspati, Hiraṇyaretas, Ārogya, Viśva, Buddha, Budha, and Mahat. (56)
He is the one who bows down to those who bow, the possessor of fortitude, the performer of both dharma and adharma,
the bestower of delight, beloved by all, the endurer of everything, and the warder-off of all enemies.
Aṃśu, Vidyotana, Dyota, Sahasrakiraṇa, Kṛtī, Keyūrī, Bhūṣaṇa, Hrāsī, Bhāsita, Bhāsana, and Anala. || 58 ||
The protector who removes the suffering of those seeking refuge, the priest, the firefly, and the best of birds;
he is considered the illuminator of all, yet the one whose light is not blinding, and the taker of all splendor. 400, 59.
He is auspicious, the doer of good, the perfect one, the maker of perfection, and the seer; he is the creator of welfare, the embodiment of the cosmic order, and the vessel of all that is auspicious.
He performs acts of pacification, is serene in soul, perfectly tranquil, and most dear to the supreme;
he is of noble deeds, well-guided, of radiant splendor, and has eyes like a bull.
He is the possessor of splendor, the lord of splendors, the sovereign of the three worlds, and one who brings others under his control;
he is radiant, possessed of great fame, the preserver of the social orders, the overseer of the castes, and a lover of offerings.
He is glorious, the abode of the Vedas, radiant, the primordial nature, and the foundation;
he moves through space, possesses swift motion, is fleet-footed, endowed with speed, and is the bird of the sky.
The Lord of Cows, the Lord of the lunar mansions, the sole possessor of cattle, the Destroyer; the progenitor, Parjanya, Jīva, the Lamp that illuminates everything. || 64 ||
The witness of karma, eternally established in yoga, the wind-god, the destroyer of Tripura;
the slayer of Rākṣasas, the pacifier of obstacles, the wearer of the diadem, and the lover of tranquility. 65.
He is garlanded with rays, possessed of excellent intellect, accomplished, eternal, and distinguished;
he is the embodiment of refined conduct, auspicious conduct, and is entirely devoted to the practice of virtuous behavior.
Mandāra, Mātura, Daṇḍa, Kṣudhāpa, Pākṣika, Guru, Avaśiṣṭa, Viśiṣṭātman, Vidheya, and Jñānaśobhana. || 67 ||
He is dear to Mahāśvetā, unknowable, the singer of the Sāman, and the bestower of liberation;
his self is proclaimed by all the Vedas, he is the abode of all the Vedas, and he is without decay.
He is the embodiment of the Vedas, the knower of the four Vedas, the upholder of the Vedas, and one who has mastered them;
he is active in ritual, unattached, victorious, most excellent, and the bestower of boons. (69)
One who observes vows, one who maintains his vows, the kinsman of the world, the adorned;
the unadorned, the imperishable, the wise, the learned, the one whose intentions are known.
(70) The source of forms, the ornament, the one to be adorned, the one who prospers, the one honored by the worlds. (500)
Cakrapāṇi, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the lord of the gods, who is affectionate toward the world. || 71 ||

The lord of kings, the mighty-armed, the primordial nature and its transformation, the enjoyer; the dispeller of darkness, the most excellent, the one who turns the ages and the creator of the beginning of the ages. 72.
He is immeasurable, the eternal source, free from ego, and the Lord;
he is of auspicious radiance, auspicious, beauty itself, the performer of auspicious deeds, and the bestower of auspiciousness.
He is truth itself, possessed of high praise, the maker of the sound "na," the bestower of growth, and fire;
he is the sustainer of strength, the giver of strength, a kinsman, greatness itself, and the foremost among the powerful.
He is the bodiless one, the king of serpents, Indra, the lotus-born, and the lord of the Gaṇas;
he is the year, the season, the leader, and the one who sets in motion the mouth of time. || 75 ||
The lotus-eyed one, the lotus-born, the powerful lord of the immortals, the one of beautiful form, the wise one, the moon, Govinda, the first-born of the universe. || 76 ||

Clad in yellow garments, clad in black, naked as the directions, Hari who transcends the senses; he who surpasses Indra, whose self is of manifold forms, Skanda, the conqueror of the cities of enemies.
He is the powerful one, the wielder of the trident, the child, the cause of liberation, and not born from a womb;
he is all-encompassing, the conqueror of the mirror-less [ignorance], the destroyer of suffering, and the annihilator of inauspiciousness. || 78 ||
The performer of auspiciousness, the deliverer, the swift, the remover of distress;
the great mantra of distinct syllables, the branchless one, and the lover of sacrifice. || 79 ||
Viśvakarman, Mahāśakti, Jyotīśa, Vihaga, Vicakṣaṇa, Dakṣa, Indra, Pratyūha, and Priyadarśana. || 80 ||
Unwearied, the abode of the Vedas, knower of the Vedas, one who understands the inner disposition;
the maker of light, conqueror of enemies, accompanied by his attendants, the charioteer of Aruṇa;
Kubera, he of the excellent chariot, Skanda, the honored and esteemed preceptor. || 81 || 600 ||
The king of planets, the lord of planets, the circle of planets and constellations. || 82 ||
Bhāskara, Satatānanda, Nandana, Naravāhana; Maṅgalākṣa, Maṅgalavān, Maṅgalya, and Maṅgalāvaha. || 83 ||
He is auspiciousness itself, possessed of beautiful conduct, the observer of vows who bestows all things upon all;
he is four-faced, garlanded with lotuses, pure in soul, and the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him.
Possessing nothing, true to his promise, devoid of qualities yet endowed with virtues, pure, complete, lotus-eyed, disciplined, and having transcended all ulterior motives.

He is the thousand-rayed one, the lord of sacrifices, the possessor of all wealth, the benevolent-minded, the eloquent, the one with excellent vehicles, the wearer of garlands, the one who has taken his meal, and the beloved of Hari. (86)
Brahmā, Pracetās, Kathita, Pratītātman, Sthitātmaka, Śatabindu, Śatamakhā, Garīyān, and Analaprabha. || 87 ||

The steadfast one, the most exalted, the wealthy, the supreme person, the king of sciences, the sovereign lord, the serpent, the possessor of knowledge, the bestower of prosperity, he who abides. || 88 ||
He whose form is indescribable, the glorious one, free from sin, the source of many blessings;
he who is well-established, possesses a divine chariot, is golden-hued, and is the abode that supports liberation. (89)
Free from duality, the destroyer of dualities, the creation, the one who enters creation, the illuminator;
compassionate, the subtle supporter, the protector, he who is fond of security, insecurity, and stability. || 90 ||

The upholder of the earth, the lord of the world, the manifest one, the pure-souled, the three-eyed, the Great Boar, the doer of what is dear, the creator, the enjoyer, and the bestower of fear. || 91 ||
He is the bearer of the four Vedas, inconceivable, sleepless, and possessing various seats;
he is the universal monarch, the bestower of steadfastness, the perfect one, and the Great Lord. || 92 ||
Vicitraratha, Ekākī, Svapna, Supti, Parāvara; he who causes all to abide in curdled milk (curds), he who is established in stability, and he who is fond of stability. || 93 ||
He is partless, possessing beautiful nails, wealthy, and dear to Indra;
he is rich in cattle, the lord of the dwelling, the possessor of the earth, and the bestower of riches.
The powerful and wise Oṃkāra is the Reality established in the three;
he is the source of volition, the maker of the day, the Blessed One who brings about the cause.
He is the blue-throated one, the lord of wealth, the beloved speaker of the four Vedas;
he is the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, the vow, the priest, the exclamation Svāhā, and the offered oblation.
The destroyer of men, the joy of men, the man, Nārāyaṇa, the wise one;
the dispeller of doubt, the wind, the waters, and he who is saluted by the gods. 97.
The embodied one is the stainless drop, free from sorrow, the flow of the stainless;
he is the illuminated among the luminous, the lightning, the double lightning, and the powerful rain-cloud.

The king, who milks the heat (of his enemies), whose path is black (with smoke), who is honored by the assembly, who is honored by Sāvitrī, who is released, who is free from anger, and who is sovereign, has been dismissed. 99.

He who possesses seven flames, seven horses, and is honored by the seven worlds; he who is perfect, the seeker of goals, the Lord of the World, the benevolent-minded one, and the lover of beauty. || 100 ||

He is the soul of all, the staff of all, the possessor of seven horses, and the beloved of the seventh day; he is the great intellect, the source of wisdom, the pure, the wise, and the slayer of Madhu. || 1 ||
Aṅgiras, the knower of destinies and times, the comet-like one, the one with a beautiful banner;
he is happy, the bestower of happiness, bliss itself, the sage most beloved by Kārtika. || 2 ||
The scorcher, the inflamer, the heat-giver, the storehouse of ascetic power;
the lord of rays, the thousand-rayed one, the doer of what is dear, the bringer of joy. || 3 ||
Delight, the beginning of the expanse of space, heaven, the sky-born, the lord of the worlds, the father of the world, the one with a pleased mind, the all-in-all, Guha, and Anala. || 4 ||
All-pervading, the joy of the world, the leader of the world, the slayer of the enemies of the gods;
the auspicious one, the maker of auspiciousness, the eldest, the highest of the high, the supreme. (5)
The supreme one, Merumeya, then Dhāraṇa, the supporter of the earth;
the bearer of the stream, the King of Dharma, the promoter of dharma and non-dharma. || 6 ||
Rathādhyakṣa, Paśupati, Tvaramāna, Mano’nala, Uttara, Anuttara, Tāpī, Tārāpati, and Apāmpati. (7)
He is the proclaimer of merit, meritorious, the cause, and the refuge of the three worlds;
he is Svarbhānu, free from misfortune, and the performer of distinguished and supreme deeds.
The destroyer of disease, the secure one, the divine, the all-conquering man, the sole lord,
the master of the chariot, the father of Śanaiścara, and the white one.
Vaivasvata, Guru, Mṛtyu, Dharmanitya, Mahāvrata, Pralambahāra, Sañcāra, and Pradyotodyotitānala. || 10 ||
The mantra consisting of one hundred syllables, the embodiment of mantra, possessed of great power, the contented soul, the most beloved, Śambhu, the Lord of the lords of the Maruts. || 11 ||
He is the destroyer of the course of saṃsāra, the one who ferries across the ocean of saṃsāra;
he has seven tongues, possesses a thousand rays, has a blue interior, and is unconquered.

The banner of Dharma, the immeasurable self, the bestower of the fruits of dharma and adharma; the witness of even the slightest act, the teacher of the world, the lord of the world, whose vehicle is his own will. || 13 ||
The sacrificial post of Dharma, the tree of Dharma, bow in hand, wielder of the bow;
bearer of the Pināka, possessed of great energy, master of manifold illusions, and great consumer. || 14 ||
The hero, the best among the powerful, the preeminent among all bearers of weapons, attainable through knowledge, difficult to propitiate, red-limbed, and the crusher of enemies. 15.
Khakhalka, Dharmada, Nitya, Dharmakṛt, Trivikrama, Bhagavān, Svāmī, Revanta, Akṣara, and Nīlalohita. || 16 ||
The solitary one, the one without a clan, the triple Veda, Vyāsa, the progenitor, the victor in assemblies,
the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, fire, the terrible one, and the one whose weapons and arms are all things.
Arhan, Parameṣṭhin, Nākapālin, Diviṣṭhita, Vadānya, Vāsuki, Vaidya, Ātreya, and Aśvapadākrama. || 18 ||
Dvāpara is the supreme giver, supremely endowed with the splendor of Brahman;
he is the inhabitant of the North, the mirror-like one, holding a lotus in his hand and bearing the moon.
Cool, with a serene countenance and a face resembling the interior of a lotus,
possessing a body like the sun at evening or midday, he is indefinable and a great chariot-warrior.
The great chariot-warrior, the great Lord Śeṣa, who is free from all passion and darkness, stood firm like one holding a royal parasol, composed and reflective.
Non-violent, pure-minded, peerless, and the crusher of enemies;
the giver of all, the giver of wealth, liberation itself, the one who wanders, and the bestower of much. || 22 ||
The Lord is the remover of the affliction caused by Varuṇa; he is all-pervading, immutable, possessed of a captivating form, radiant, beautiful, and a source of excellent splendor. || 23 ||
He is of beautiful luster, the form of beautiful luster, the one with beautiful eyes, and the lord of the Nikṣubhas;
he is dear to kings, the maker of sound, the lord of the planets, and the dispeller of darkness.
The god who is the enemy of Saihikeya, the giver of boons, the leader of the excellent ones,
four-armed, the great yogin, the lord of yogins, and likewise the master of horses.
All this that you asked of me has been told to you—
what the son of Parāśara told me regarding the thousand rays of the Sun.
The recitation of the names of the Sun brings merit, fame, and long life; it destroys evil dreams and brings about liberation from bondage. (27)
But that man who, being self-restrained, should constantly hear or recite this, for him inexhaustible heaven and food shall be secured. (28)
There shall be no fear of kings, robbers, or thieves, nor any fear from diseases;
he shall be ever victorious in prosperity and attain the highest good. [717] 29.
He shall be renowned, fortunate, learned, pleasant-faced, and lovely to behold;
he shall live for a hundred years, free from all afflictions. || 30 ||
Whoever, being pure and observant of rules, recites this thousand names of Aṃśumat at dawn with a well-concentrated mind,
the diseases sent by the gods will avoid him from afar.
Terrified, like all the lords of the great serpents before Suparṇa. || 31 ||
In this manner, O King, one should recite at night until overcome by sleep;
then, O Hero, one should again recite with devotion while facing the east or another direction.
Having worshipped according to the rules and honored the best of the twice-born,
he should afterwards eat meatless food, restrained in speech and well-composed.
Having given sacrificial fees to the Brahmins according to his capacity, O lord of men,
he should thus observe the Vijayā-saptamī for as long as a year.
He shall conquer all enemies and go to the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the vow of Vijaya-saptamī as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
At what time is the Saptamī known as Jayadā prescribed?
O son of Devakī, tell me: what is the fruit of any kind of religious observance?
Kṛṣṇa said:
When the seventh lunar day (saptamī) of the bright fortnight coincides with a Sunday, that saptamī is named Vijayā; whatever is given on that day yields great fruit.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and likewise fasting—
performed at any time on Jayasaptamī, these destroy even the greatest sins.
He who performs circumambulation of the Sun with fruits and flowers undoubtedly obtains a son endowed with all excellent qualities.
The first [offering] is with *nālikera* fruits, the second with *bījapūraka* fruits,
the third with red *nāraṅga* oranges, and the fourth with plantain fruits.
The fifth [offering] is with straight *kuṣmāṇḍa* fruits; the sixth with ripe *tenduka* fruits;
the seventh is known to be with eggplants (*vṛntāka*), using one hundred and eight [of them].
With pearls, rubies, sesame seeds, and likewise with *karkaṭaka* gems,
with *gomeda*, diamonds, and lapis lazuli, by a number of one hundred and eight.
With fruits of *iṅguda*, *badara*, *bilva*, *karamarda*, and *varbhaṭa*, as well as *āmrātaka*, *jambīra*, *jambū*, and *karkaṭikā*.
On the Vijaya-saptamī, one should perform circumambulations of the Sun with flowers, incense, fruits, leaves, and sweetmeats cooked in ghee.
One should offer a circumambulation of the Sun with other seasonal fruits that are unbroken and free from nodes; one should prescribe a fruit [as a reward] for each fruit offered.
One should not enter, nor converse, nor touch anything at all;
for when the sun is meditated upon with one-pointed mind, it bestows exceedingly.
A stream of wealth (vasordhārā) should be offered to the Sun with cow’s ghee;
one should fasten a moon-shaped parasol and a banner adorned with small bells.
One should wrap it with saffron, flowers, and cloths;
having offered pure food offerings, one should then ask the deity for forgiveness.
O Bhānu, Bhāskara, Mārtaṇḍa, Caṇḍaraśmi, Divākara!
Grant me long life, health, sovereignty, and sons; homage be to you!

O King, the Vijaya-saptamī should not be observed by one who is engaged in restrictive vows [alone], but rather through fasting, eating only at night, or eating a single meal consisting of begged food.
The sick man is liberated from disease, the poor man shall attain prosperity,
the childless man obtains sons, and the seeker of knowledge is honored in the assembly.
O Pārtha, when the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) falls on a Sunday during the bright fortnight,
one should pass seven such Saptamīs by eating only mung beans at night.
Having bathed on the ground upon palāśa leaves and having offered oblations according to the prescribed rule,
one should, upon the completion of the vow, give gold mixed with mung beans as a gift.
O King, for a man who observes the seven seventh-day vows conjoined with the Sun, [the offerings] are either mudga beans for Sūrya or mushrooms for Kava.
One should accomplish all rites by means of the six-syllable mantra;
the fire-oblations, worship, and the consumption [of the remnants] should be performed with one hundred and eight repetitions.
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with ghee and sesame seeds; the ritual consumption [of water] should be done with sandalwood water;
and worship should be performed with excellent *karavīra* flowers available at that time.
When the vow was thus completed,
O Pārtha, he then presented a golden vessel containing an image of the Sun-god fashioned from gold according to his means.

The manifestation in the form of the Sun should be understood as that described in the *Nikṣubhārkasaptamī-vrata*. One should give a cow dressed in ochre-colored cloth along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a virtuous Brahmin who is a reciter, using this mantra:
O Bhāskara, homage to you; O Yaśaskara, let there be salutation to you!
O Śreyaskara, be gracious; O Lord, grant me my desire.
Gifts of land, houses, and beds should be given here with faith,
O Pārtha, by one who desires eternal joy.
The expedition of kings who desire victory is praiseworthy;
indeed, those men who have set out will then certainly become victorious.
For this reason, O Pārtha, it is renowned in the world as Vijayāsaptamī;
thus, this lunar day immediately bestows the fruit of all desires.
Bestowing fruits both in this world and the next, and granting the realm of the Sun,
through its performance a wise man becomes long-lived, free from disease, and happy.
Having come here, one becomes a king surrounded by elephants, horses, and chariots;
and whatever woman performs [this rite], she too partakes in that fruit.
That seventh lunar day (saptamī), which bestows eternal victory upon the surface of the earth and is the most excellent among all dates according to the eminent sages,
belongs to those who contemplate the worship of the lotus feet of the Sun.
Vijayā always bestows victory upon men.
Thus concludes the vow of Vijayā-saptamī as declared in the Śrī-Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall describe to you another, supreme ritual manual for Saptamī.
Beginning from the month of Māgha, O Yudhiṣṭhira, during the bright fortnight.
Having made a firm resolve on the seventh lunar day, the observer of the vow should remain so for one year; having worshipped Varuṇa in the month of Māgha, he should likewise worship the Sun.
O best of kings, according to the procedure for the Brahmakūrca rite and according to one's capacity,
one should feed Brahmins on the eighth lunar day with rice mixed with sesame flour and molasses.
The entire fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is obtained by worshipping the Sun as Tapana in the month of Phālguna.
One obtains the rare fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice by worshipping Vedāṃśu on the seventh day of the month of Caitra.
On the seventh day of Vaiśākha, a man who worships the deity Dhātṛ undoubtedly attains merit equal to that of the Uñchādhvara sacrifice.
A person duly obtains the merit of the Paśubandha sacrifice by worshipping Indra on the seventh day of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
The attainment of the fruit of the horse sacrifice arises; there is no doubt about this. Likewise, by worshipping the Sun on the seventh day of the month of Āṣāḍha, [the same result is obtained].
One obtains the abundant fruit of a sacrifice involving much gold by worshipping the Ātapa deities on the seventh day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
O Pārtha, a man who, being pure, worships Ravi on the seventh lunar day of the month of Bhādrapada with devotion, obtains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
One shall obtain the fruit of the Tulāpuruṣa gift by means of jaggery;
on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja, one should worship the Sun.
One obtains the fruit of the gift of a thousand cows through devotion;
on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one should worship the deity named Saptāśva.
The meritorious soul who worships [the Sun] in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa according to the prescribed rite shall obtain the fruit of a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
A man indeed obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice by worshipping the Sun according to the prescribed rites during the month of Puṣya.
One shall obtain the fruit of the private recitation of all four Vedas,
as well as he who performs the worship of the Name and other rites on the seventh day of the dark fortnight.
One should diligently observe this for one year while fasting;
O Pārtha, when the vow is completed, one should commence the Sūrya-sacrifice.
On a pure ground in a level location, smeared with red sandalwood paste,
[the site] should be one cubit, two cubits, or even four cubits in size.
One should draw the solar disc with vermilion of intense redness,
and [worship it] with red flowers, lotuses, and incenses such as kunduruka and others.
Having performed worship, one should offer various food offerings cooked in ghee;
one should place water-filled jars before [the deity], accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
O best of kings, twelve [offerings] of red color, well-anointed, should be made here;
then the fire-rite must be performed by one who has properly offered oblations into the sacrificial fire.
With the mantra beginning with "ākṛṣṇena," one should offer eight hundred oblations using fuel-sticks from the Arka tree, along with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and molasses.
Then a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brahmins individually;
red garments should also be given to those twice-born ones who are devoted to recitation.
In this rite, they praise twelve cows adorned with garments;
one should cause a parasol, a pair of sandals, and likewise [other gifts] to be given to each one.
One devoid of wealth is unable to give the gift of twelve cows;
for even a single cow that is well-behaved, red in color, and yielding milk [is sufficient].
It should be given to the instructor without any stinginess regarding wealth;
then, having dismissed those Brahmins, he himself should eat while remaining restrained in speech.
O Pārtha, he who performs this Saptamī vow with devotion becomes free from disease, handsome, eloquent, and long-lived.
Furthermore, by one who is liberated from long-term diseases or seized by leprosy and the like,
this vow which removes affliction should be performed with diligent effort.
In this world, there is no medicine other than the Sun that so effectively destroys disease;
he who finds his sole refuge in the Sun is devoted to the welfare of all beings.
From seeing or touching him, the destruction of disease occurs;
otherwise, how could there be no possibility of disease for those devoted to the Sun?
O best of the Bharatas, he who observes the vow of the birth [of the Lord] every month on the seventh lunar day beholds the Supreme Lord before his very eyes.
Observing a fast and devoted to the Sun, intent on the welfare of all beings,
a man should, on the eighth lunar day, eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) in the company of Brahmins.
He whose eleventh year is his seventh in divine form,
having pierced the orb of the sun, goes to the eternal Brahman.
This vow, O Great King, destroys all that is inauspicious;
it pacifies all suffering and bestows health upon the body.
And at the end, the sage Nārada declared this to be the bestower of the world of the Sun.
Those who observe the fast on the seventh day of both the bright and dark fortnights,
and worship Amitadīdhiti with his name-syllables—
they are always happy and free from all diseases.
Having become attendants of the sun, they dwell there for a very long time.
Thus ends the vow of the Twelve Seventh Days as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Sumantu said: He who, subsisting on cow dung, should cast [it] for twelve seventh days of the bright fortnight, [attains the fruit].
O Indra among kings, he may subsist on the food of beggars or even eat withered leaves.
Subsisting on milk, or eating only one meal a day, or again subsisting on alms-food,
or even subsisting on water, one should worship the Sun.
With various offerings of flowers— lotuses, fragrant lilies, and water-lilies—
and with diverse kinds of perfumes, incense, guggulu, and sandalwood.
O best of men, having honored him with sugar-water and other offerings, as well as various ornaments, gold, food, and so forth, a man [attains great merit].
O hero, that fruit which is obtained through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees is attained here solely on the seventh lunar day of the Sun.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, he is honored in the world of the Sun;
thereafter, O King, he is born into a great family of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Thus, with devotion and a concentrated mind, one should worship Vivasvat every month according to the prescribed rite,
and with devotion, one should recite these names.
In the month of Māgha he is Viṣṇu, and in Mādhava he is Aryaman;
in Śukra he is Vivasvat, and in the month of Śuci he is Divākara.
Parjanya is to be praised in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise Taraṇi in Nabhasya;
and in the month of Āśvayuja, the Sun-god Mitra is to be celebrated.
In the month of Kārttika, the Sun is to be known as Mārtaṇḍa, possessing a golden luster;
in Mārgaśīrṣa, the Sun is proclaimed as the destroyer of all sins.
In the month of Puṣya, he is to be known as Pūṣan, possessing a golden luster;
in Māgha, he is to be known as Bhaga; and indeed, in Phālguna, he is Tvaṣṭṛ.
In this manner, one should recite the names in succession for the pleasure of the Sun;
as for the ritual procedure for offering incense, it should be performed according to the rules on the seventh lunar day.
The man who performs [this] with devotion attains the supreme goal;
in splendor he resembles Hari, and in radiance he is like the sun.
All this has been told to you; listen to that which destroys sin.
One should never speak of it to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who lacks devotion.
O Hero, one should not give to a doer of evil, nor to one who has not undergone ascetic heat;
one should not give to a man of dark deeds, nor to an atheist, nor to one of cruel actions.
[726] Thus ends the vow of the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) involving cow dung and other substances, as declared in the glorious Bhaviṣyapurāṇa.
Sumantu said:
O Hero, that seventh day which is observed after drinking water and so forth should always be known as the "Water-Seventh" (Udakasaptamī), which bestows happiness.
Thus ends the Udakasaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Whatever Saptamī has been mentioned, after that I shall describe another auspicious one:
a man should consume whatever he has purchased for three cowries.
With this price, the embodied soul should consume whatever is obtained;
whether it be inedible or edible, no deliberation should be made in this matter.
By this procedure, the seventh lunar day known as Varākā should be observed.
Thus ends the Varāṭikāsaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the Saptamī known by the name Rahasyā.
For she is the purifier of purifiers and the destroyer of great sins.
A person who performs this [rite] on the seventh day delivers seven descendants, seven ancestors, and seven preceding generations from existence; of this there is no doubt.
One cuts through diseases, overcomes difficult-to-conquer enemies,
and attains a rare honor, even by performing the Saptamī vow just once.
One seeking a daughter obtains a daughter; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
one seeking sons obtains sons; and one seeking dharma shall attain dharma.
Observing all the commitments (*samaya*), the wise one should perform these;
listen, O Lord of Beings, as I speak for the sake of your welfare.
A person devoted to Āditya should worship Gaṇanāyaka on the seventh lunar day; he should indeed practice universal friendliness toward all beings or meditate upon the Sun-god.
On the seventh lunar day, one should not touch oil, nor wear blue garments;
one should neither bathe with *vāmālaka* nor engage in any quarrel.
Likewise, a wise person should neither give nor drink impure food or liquor;
he should not harbor malice toward anyone, nor should he practice harshness.
One should not address a Caṇḍāla or a woman in her courses with harsh words;
nor should one touch a place where a corpse has been, nor look upon a dead body.
One should not dance with excessive passion, nor should one play musical instruments;
one should not sleep with a woman for one's own sake, nor should one indulge in gambling.

One should not weep with the shedding of tears, nor should one eat the "five-fingered" (pañcaśākika). The "five-fingered" refers to the five types of finger-like parts: tubers, roots, fruits, leaves, and flowers. One should not pull lice from the head, nor should one engage in idle chatter.
One should avoid speaking of what is undesirable to another, for it causes excessive sorrow.
One should not snap one's fingers, nor laugh, nor sing, nor even a song;
one should not strike any living being, nor should one engage in overeating.
One should indeed avoid sleeping during the day, as well as hypocrisy and deceit;
one should also diligently avoid wandering about on the public road.
[728] Now, O Destroyer of Tripura, hear another rite concerning this:
the Saptamī known as Sarvadā (Always) should be observed beginning from the month of Caitra.
In the month of Madhu (Caitra), the Sun-god is to be worshipped as Dhātṛ;
in Vaiśākha, as Aryaman; and in Jyeṣṭha, he is proclaimed as Mitra.
In Āṣāḍha, Varuṇa is to be known; Indra is said to be in Nabhas;
Vivasvat is in Nabhasya, and Parjanya is remembered in Āśvayuj.
Pūṣan is [the deity] in the month of Kārttika, while in Mārgaśīrṣa he is called Bhaga;
Vivasvat is [the deity] in Pauṣa, and Tvaṣṭṛ is said to be [the deity] in Māgha.
Viṣṇu, the Sun-god, is to be worshipped and honored in the month of Phālguna;
on every seventh lunar day, the wise man should feed those who prepare his meals.
Food mixed with ghee should be given, having fed [the recipient] according to the prescribed rite;
furthermore, a gold māṣaka should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the one who performs the feeding.
Food with ghee and indeed red garments should be given;
O best of the twice-born, if no cooks are available, the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given instead.
In the same way, endowed with supreme faith, one should always especially honor those worthy of being fed— the Brāhmaṇas who have cultivated themselves for an aeon.
Thus, O Leader of the Gaṇas, these seven have been recounted to you;
when heard, they remove sin and bestow the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the vow of the seventh lunar day (Saptamī-vrata) as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Pitāmaha said:
"O Ghanāghana, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna..."
A man or a woman who has observed the fast, having worshipped that Dispeller of Darkness, [attains the fruit].
Chanting the name of the Sun with devotion, filled with pure intent, and having conquered his senses,
he should glorify the Sun alone both when rising and when sitting down.
Then, when another day arrives— the eighth— being self-restrained, having bathed and properly worshipped the Sun, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.
Having performed the fire-oblation dedicated to Ravi and completed the ritual acts,
he should prostrate before the god Ravi and utter these words:
May that Lord of Gods, Vibhāvasu, who in former times was propitiated by the gods so that Sāvitrī obtained her desire, grant all my desires.
Having worshipped him thoroughly, Diti obtained all her desires exactly as she wished;
may the Lord of Heaven, being pleased with me, grant all my desires.
Having lost his kingdom, that lord of gods worshipped the Sun and regained his realm for the sake of his desire; may he grant my desires.
Having thus worshipped and especially performed the ritual offering here,
one should then properly eat sacrificial food (haviṣya), O you whose banner bears the bird.
In Phālguna, Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha— the last of these being the supreme—
by means of these four months, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) may be accomplished.
One should likewise worship the Sun with *karavīra* flowers for four months,
burning black agallochum as incense and consuming water produced from a cow's horn.
One should also offer food offerings and sugar-candies to the Brahmins;
now, listen to another matter regarding the rites to be performed beginning with the month of Āṣāḍha.
Jāti flowers are praised; guggulu is said to be the incense.
One should eat water from a *kutapa* cloth; milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is considered the appropriate food offering (*naivedya*).
One should eat that very [remnant] oneself and perform the remaining rites as before.
Kutapodaka is water with *kuśa* grass;
in the months beginning with Kārttika, cow’s urine is for the purification of the body.
The great incense is thus specified, as well as the red lotuses for worship.
The *Mahāṅgadhūpa* is described in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* as follows:
"O Kṛṣṇa, camphor, saffron, nut-grass, agallochum, and likewise storax;
a fan, sugar, and likewise black storax—these constitute the *mahāṅga*."
This incense known as Mahāṅga is always dear to the God.
One should eat water from a *kutapa* vessel; milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is considered an appropriate food offering (*naivedya*). One should indeed present *kāsāra* as an offering to the Sun-god.
Furthermore, every month, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin according to one's capacity.
The gratification of the Sun by one’s own will constitutes the breaking of the fast once the time for the fast has passed;
according to one's capacity and as is appropriate, one should avoid deceit regarding wealth.
The Sun, who possesses seven horses, is considered to be worshipped for the sake of one's pleasure through sincerity alone;
at the conclusion of the fast, the Sun should be worshipped and bathed according to one's ability.
When propitiated, the Sun shall grant all desired objects without obstruction;
this meritorious seventh lunar day (Saptamī) removes sins and fulfills every wish.
The one whose banner is Garuḍa grants all desires as they are wished for:
the sonless obtains a son, and the destitute shall obtain wealth.
One overcome by disease shall obtain health; a maiden shall find a virtuous husband;
and one who has been away on a journey shall obtain reunion—by fasting on this day, one shall attain all these.
He obtains all desires and rejoices even in the world of the gods; "gone to the world of the gods" (gogata) means gone to heaven.
Having returned again to earth, O Kṛṣṇa, he becomes a king equal in wealth to those who possess nothing.
Equal toward wealth and non-wealth, such a man would be equal to Śakra on the surface of the earth; of this there is no doubt, by the grace of the Lord of Cows (Kṛṣṇa).
Thus ends the vow of Kāmadā-saptamī as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa. Sumantu said:
Now, O high-minded one, in the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight—
The first [lunar day] there is to be observed as a fast; hear now what the procedure for it should be.
On the fourth day, he should not ask for anything; on the fifth, he should eat only once;
on the sixth, devoted to fasting, he should have conquered anger and subdued his senses.
Having worshipped the Sun with offerings of fragrance and flowers,
O Putraka, you should sleep at night on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the deity.
Meditating in his mind upon the God who destroys the suffering of all beings,
who pacifies all defects, and who annihilates all sins.
Having awakened on the seventh day, one should perform a feeding of Brahmins after worshipping the Sun with flowers, incense, and unguents.
Indeed, they declare that the offerings for the deity there consist of fruits:
dates, coconuts, and likewise mangoes.
The wise have declared that mātulaṅga fruits should be offered here;
having thus fed the brahmins, one should then feed them oneself.
[732] Likewise, O observer of excellent vows, listen to another [method] for when these are unavailable:
one should have an image of Gaṇanāyaka fashioned from the flour of rice and wheat.
One should cook these cakes made with molasses in their center and clarified butter in their interior,
mixed with nutmeg and cumin, and offer them to the Sun.
One should offer to the Sun seeds of cumin mixed with cardamom, cinnamon leaves, and nagakesara, combined with sugar and edible foods.
Then, having performed the fire-ritual and fed the Brahmins,
this unsurpassed vow should be observed in this manner for twelve months.
O King, one who gives fruit should subsist on fruit alone for month after month;
he should perform this vow with devotion, providing a meal for a Brahmin.
Listen also, O observer of excellent vows, to the procedure for the ritual bath and the sipping of water:
cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water with *kuśa* grass.
O observer of noble vows, sesame seeds, a paste made from mustard seeds, white clay,
a paste of dūrvā grass, ghee, water used for washing a cow’s horn,
and the exudation from a jasmine bush are recommended for the act of bathing.

Ghee mixed with the paste of *dūrvā* grass; the washing of a cow’s horn—that by which a cow’s horn is cleansed; and the exudation from a *jātī* bush, along with the roots, branches, and sprouts of the *jātī*—these, when consumed, are indeed destroyers of all sins.
The wise know that these should be used in the month of Bhādrapada, beginning from the first day, in their respective order.
Having thus reached the end of the rainy season and having fed the best of the twice-born,
O Mahādeva, one should then present divine and terrestrial offerings to them.
Those belonging to a temple are divine; others are terrestrial.
Furthermore, fruits made of gold according to one's capacity, or a cow with its calf, or land endowed with crops—these are the offerings.
Or else a palace, or a ground-floor mansion, provided with all kinds of grain.
One should give a house with an earth-built palace equal to the royal palace of Rājagṛha; one should give red garments, a copper vessel, and coral.
Listen now to what is required for one who possesses wealth, and for me, the poor man.
Having fed the twice-born with fruits, flowers, and likewise sesame flour, one should present them with silver fruits.
One should present to the preceptor a pair of garments dyed with mineral pigments,
along with gold for Mahādeva and accompanied by the five precious gems.
In this manner, dear one, the breaking of the fast is properly completed at the end of the year;
thus indeed is this most meritorious seventh lunar day, which destroys all sins.
Having fasted upon which all men go to the state of the Sun,
being constantly honored by the gods and by the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The man who always worships the Sun with this [hymn] goes to the Maker of Day,
liberated from poverty, suffering, and sin.
A Brāhmaṇa attains liberation; a Kṣatriya goes to the state of the Moon;
a Vaiśya reaches the world of Kubera; and a Śūdra shall obtain the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
A sonless man obtains a son, and an unfortunate woman becomes fortunate;
even a widow, being devoted, shall worship the Sun with this [hymn].
O giver of honor, a woman shall not suffer widowhood in another birth;
for this Phala-saptamī should be known as equal to the Cintāmaṇi jewel.
It is remembered as bestowing all desires upon those who recite it or hear it with devotion.
Thus ends the Phala-saptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Agastya said:
When the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, during the bright fortnight, O Lord of the Gods...
By fasting on the seventh lunar day, this vow bestows the attainment of a son.
Having made firm resolve on the sixth day, one should worship Hari on the seventh;

the worship of Hari, that is Viṣṇu, is performed with name-mantras. With flowers, there is an ablution of those forms by the gods, beginning with Brahmā. By the gods, the deity who has gone to Yama is surrounded by his Mothers.
Then, at the clear dawn of the eighth day, being self-restrained,
he should worship Govinda, Hari, according to the prescribed rule and ritual.
According to the previously mentioned procedure and the Vaiṣṇava path, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and worship specifically with the Gopāla mantra, "O Govinda.
In front of Him, one should perform the oblation with black sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas with devotion and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to one's means.
Then, one should first eat a single *bilva* fruit oneself;
the mantra for consuming the *bilva* during the *phala-saptamī* observances has been stated [previously].
Afterwards, one may eat as desired, including oily foods and the six flavors.
A man who observes the fast according to this very procedure every month on the eighth day of the dark fortnight will obtain a son, even if he is currently childless; of this there is no doubt.
And at the end of the year, a pair of black cows should be given to a twice-born man.
This, which I have proclaimed to you, is known as the Putravratam.
Having performed this, a person is liberated from all sins indeed.
Thus ends the Putrasaptamī vow as declared in the Vārāha Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
Listen now to the Sarvāpti Saptamī in the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Having fasted upon which, O Supporter of the Earth, one attains all desires.
Avoiding conversation with heretics and the like, devoted solely to the Sun,
he should worship the Lord who dwells in the rays with a focused mind and a humble posture.
The breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) beginning with the month of Māgha and ending with the month of Śuci is prescribed for six months.
"Ending with Śuci" means ending with Āṣāḍhī.
The first is named Mārtaṇḍa, and the second is proclaimed as Arka.
The third is Citrabhānu, and after that Vibhāvasu;
the fifth should be known as Bhaga, and the sixth is proclaimed as Haṃsa.
In the first six types of compounding, sesame seeds are used for bathing and sipping;
in the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed.
Having performed the worship of the deity according to the prescribed rite every month, bathing and consuming [the sacred water] is praised as the destroyer of sins.
One who possesses faith should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin according to one's own ability;
and at the conclusion of the breaking of the fast, one should perform the propitiation of the deity with devotion.
One should worship the Sun, the lord of the day, according to the rules and with devotion according to one's ability;
indeed, one should eat at night, avoiding oil and alkaline substances, in honor of Viṣṇu.
Having fasted thus on the sixth day of the dark fortnight, or else on the seventh day,
the knower of dharma, intent upon pleasing the Swan, should remain awake throughout that night.
One obtains all desires, whatever one wishes for with the mind;
she is renowned in the worlds by herself as "The Seventh," the Attainment of All.
For this [practice], once undertaken by those intent on their duties, has been performed as desired;
it fulfills all the wishes of those who take refuge in it day after day.
Thus ends the *Sarvāpti-saptamī-vrata* as declared in the *Śrī-Bhaviṣyat-Purāṇa*.
Brahmā said:
"On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, whatever man performs this sacrifice..."
One should repeatedly recite with devotion the name of the deity, "O Balin."
Having thus performed one hundred and eight worship-rites to the deities,
one who is pure should recite [the mantra] while bathed at the time of departure, as well as upon rising, stumbling, or sneezing.
One should not converse with heretics, those who have fallen from their caste, or likewise those who dwell among the lowest castes;
rather, one should worship the sun endowed with faith.
And one intent on meditation should mentally recite this to the Sun:
"O Haṃsa, O Haṃsa, O Compassionate One, be the refuge for those who have no refuge!"
"O Sun, be the savior of those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra!
Having thus propitiated him and observed a fast with a restrained mind, [he remained there].
Or else, on another day, having consumed the *ārjunīyaka* once in the forenoon—
the *ārjunīyaka* being cow dung once—
having bathed and performed worship, one should again proclaim the name "Haṃsa."
And one should likewise pour three streams of water upon the two deities.
In the same way, one should perform worship during the months of Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha;
having established an excellent destiny in the world of mortals, that man indeed attains it.
And having departed, O Kṛṣṇa, he shall go by means of an auspicious, divine swan;
indeed, through the grace of Dharmadhvaja, he shall become equal to Saṃkrandana.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, as well as in Śrāvaṇa, likewise in Bhādrapada,
and in the month of Āśvayuja, a person [should act] according to this procedure.
Having fasted and performed worship, one should likewise recite "Mārtaṇḍa";
by consuming cow's urine, one goes to the city of the Sun and is glorified.
For one who has propitiated the Lord of the worlds and disciplined the self,
there is likewise remembrance of the Sun at the time of death, as it is heard in the scriptures.
O Kṛṣṇa, this procedure for the consumption of milk has been declared by me;
one should perform it according to the rule for four months, beginning with the month of Kārttika.
Having performed it according to that very same rite, one should proclaim, "O Bhāskara!
At the time of death, he who has devotion to Bhāskara goes to the world of Bhānu.
Every month, one should give gifts to the twice-born according to one's inclination;
however, when the Cāturmāsya period is complete, one should perform the recitation of sacred texts.
Whether it be a discourse on the Mother, a hymn of praise to the Sun,
or even the hearing of the Dharma, these are always desired by one who bears the banner of righteousness.
The Sun is the banner of Dharma;
having worshipped the reciter, one should therefore perform the rite with faith,
as well as the ancestral offering (śrāddha) with cooked food and oblation by means of a twice-born man.
And likewise, one should recite the name of the Sun, for his seed is indeed divine and desired;
thus, at the end, one should proclaim the names of the gods, which is the most excellent course.
O Godharādhara, it has been told to you how a human being always attains the three kinds of results throughout the three worlds through this fast-breaking ceremony (pāraṇa).
By that [first], a human being attains sovereignty as well as enjoyments;
likewise, by the second, a person may obtain enjoyments from an enemy of his lineage.
Indra is the enemy of the *gotra*.
By the third breaking of the fast, one shall likewise attain the world of the Sun. Thus has this supreme means for attaining the [higher] states been fully explained.
O tiger among gods, regarding the procedure for the vow of the seventh lunar day (saptamīvrata) that has been described:
whoever performs this seventh-day rite with faith shall transcend the three states of existence.
Likewise, through devotion, a woman indeed attains a threefold destiny;
this meritorious rite, which removes sin, is declared to be "Trigati."
Through this scripture, it always grants the course of the sun for the sake of propitiation;
it removes all sins and fears for those who read and listen to it.
Likewise, among meritorious deeds, those that bestow the preeminence of the three goals of life (trivarga) are always the foremost.

Dharmas are those which grant the excellence of the three goals. In this context, regarding the vow of the *helin*s, there are specific names—Haṃsa, Mārtaṇḍa, and Bhāskara—common to the three sets of four-month observances (*cāturmāsya*).
Thus ends the description of the Trigati-saptamī-vrata as declared in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
The Sun said:
"He who, having fasted on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,
worships me with devotion— over him I shall exercise my sovereign power."
Having observed the fast on the sixth day, O best of heroes, he who would worship me with devotion and respect on both seventh days of every month, one by one, [attains the fruit].
One year is my own;
I grant him sons born from his very body,
as well as wealth, fame, progeny, and constant, supreme health.
O Brahmin, he who in the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, though having conquered his senses,
speaks ill of heretics, outcasts, and low-castes while his senses remain unsubdued;
Having observed the fast according to the rules on the sixth lunar day, and having worshipped me with devotion using white garlands and unguents, the wise man should sleep upon the ground at night.
Rising again on the seventh day and having performed the rites of bathing and so forth,
one should worship me, O Brahmin, and then perform the *vīra-homa*.
Having worshipped with devotion the lotus-eyed Hari with an oblation,
[he performed] the Vīra-homa and Agni-homa, which have the forms of Hari and Viṣṇu;
likewise, he honored the twice-born with curd-rice, milk, and milk-porridge.
Having properly fasted on the sixth day of that very dark fortnight, [he should proceed].
"Of that very [month]" refers to the month of Māgha.
One should worship with red lotuses, rich in fragrance, and with red flowers.
Thus, the man who always worships me with devotion according to the prescribed rule—
"O Lord of the Gods, both of them obtain the fruit of having a son.
Thus ends the Putrasaptamī vow as described in the Āditya Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
When the asterism Karo occurs on the seventh day of the bright fortnight,
then that most meritorious seventh day is declared to be the destroyer of sins.
*Kara* means *hasta*. Indeed, this conjunction occurs during the dark fortnight (*bahula*) of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods, Citrabhānu, the Teacher of the World, on that [day], one is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; there is no doubt in this matter.
And he who observes the fast on that day with a restrained mind,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Whatever gift is given with the sun in view,
or whatever oblation is performed there, all that shall become inexhaustible.
Having recited even a single verse from the Ṛgveda with a mind full of faith,
one certainly obtains the fruit that belongs to the entire Ṛgveda.
The Sāman yields the fruit of the Sāmaveda, the Yajus that of the Yajurveda,
and the Atharvan yields the entire fruit of the Atharvaveda to one who recites it.
Because the Sun destroys all sins here without exception on this seventh day of the dark fortnight under the asterism Kar, it is therefore called Pāpanāśinī (the Destroyer of Sins).
Having worshipped the Sun in this [place], he goes to the city of Saumanasa,
having ascended an excellent celestial chariot produced from camphor.
O Kṛṣṇa, you are like the city of Saumanasa, the world of the gods, camphor, and Durvarṇa;
you resemble the sun in splendor,
the moon in radiance, Atri’s son in beauty, and Hari always in valor.
There he rejoices for a very long time together with hosts of gods.
Thus ends the Pāpanāśinī Vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"O Acyuta, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada..."
Having bowed his head to the god, he should worship him for seven days.
O Hero, with offerings of flowers, incense, and so forth, and with the satiation of the *kutapas*—
that is, the Brāhmaṇas and others—
he, self-restrained, should avoid conversation with heretics and the like.
Having given a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin, he should eat at night while restraining his speech.
Whether standing, speaking, or setting out, and in cases such as hunger or stumbling,
one should practice the recollection of the names of the Sun and likewise their vocal recitation.
Having fasted for twelve months in succession according to this very procedure,
and having fully worshipped the Teacher of the World on the completion of the breaking of the fast;
Through merit and through hearing this, one shall lead others to prosperity and attain nourishment;
thus, the pure person who performs the worship of Āditya in this manner.
Or a woman, having ascended to heaven, enjoys the fruit of infinite merit.
Thus ends the Anantaphala-saptamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
Having purified oneself, one should worship [the deity] with flowers, incense, and other offerings during the bright fortnight.
On the seventh day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the foremost of gods, whose vehicle is the horse.
Having attained here the vast, divine, and inexhaustible state that follows from dharma,
one goes in the next world to the auspicious celestial realm of the Lord of Birds.
Immediately after the religious duties, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) said here that the Sun-god,
being self-restrained and refraining from conversation with heretics and the like,
should give a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin and eat at night while remaining silent.
One should cause the anointing of the God of gods to be performed every year.

It should be understood that [the thread] is without defects, of a single color, fashioned from beautiful cotton thread, shaped like the sloughed skin of a snake, well-sewn within, measuring one hundred and twenty-two finger-breadths for the medium size, and one hundred and eight finger-breadths for the short size. All of this has been explained in detail in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*, in the *Sāmbopākhyāna*.
Regarding this, it is said: "On the seventh day, the foremost of gods [is worshipped]; likewise, the auspicious, white, and new [thread is used].
They know that the purificatory threads (*pavitra*) here are indeed as [efficacious] as those in other celestial realms."
Likewise, in this month of the Lord,
a man who, being free from physical defects, ascends [the mountain] with devotion toward the Sun among the gods born in the sky, O Acyuta, is celebrated as such.
Having performed the ritual according to the rules so that no limb is deficient, one should feed the Brahmins with devotion.
Amidst the sounds of conchs and trumpets and abundant Vedic chants,
he ascends a divine vehicle and comes to the world of Heli.
Having fasted for twelve months in succession according to this very procedure, and when the final breaking of the fast is complete, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.
Thus, that pure person who performs the worship of Āditya shall go to the highest world, having dedicated it to the Maker of Day.
Whatever fire-offerings and worship are performed there, all that shall become inexhaustible.
Thus ends the Avyaṅgasaptamī vow as declared in the Śrī Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Pulastya said: I shall now describe another [vow], known by the name Phalasaptamī.
Having fasted upon which, a man becomes liberated from sins and a partaker of heaven.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the fifth day, one who is firm in his vows,
having fasted on the sixth day, should have a golden lotus fashioned.
One who knows the Dharma, having fashioned a golden image of a single fruit, should give it together with sugar to a Brahmin who has a family.
At the time of twilight, one should give [an offering] with the thought, "May the Sun be pleased with me";
and having honored the Brahmins with devotion on the seventh lunar day, one should partake of a meal of milk.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should practice the renunciation of fruits until the seventh day of the dark fortnight arrives;
having fasted on that day, one should perform the ritual according to this very sequence.
In the same manner, one should give a golden vessel accompanied by a golden lotus,
joined with a bowl of sugar, and adorned with cloth and garlands.
Having fasted on both seventh lunar days for a year according to this very procedure, one should offer gifts in sequence and recite the mantra of the Sun.
May Bhānu, Arka, Ravi, Brahmā, Sūrya, Śakra, Hari, Śiva,
the illustrious Vibhāvasu, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Varuṇa be pleased.
And on the seventh day of every month, one should recite each name;
practicing this, one should perform a single renunciation of fruit at the beginning of each fortnight.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should honor a Brahmin couple with garments and ornaments;
one should give a jar of sugar accompanied by a golden flower.
O Ravi, just as the desires of your devotees are never fruitless,
so may I obtain infinite fruits in birth after birth.
Whoever performs this Phala-saptamī, which bestows infinite fruit,
becomes purified of all sins and is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Whatever sin, such as the drinking of liquor and so forth, was committed in the ten previous lives—
all that comes to destruction for one who observes the Phala-saptamī vow.
One who constantly observes this seventh [vow] shall be free from disease and shall deliver twenty-one generations of men— both those born and those yet to be born.
Thus ends the Phala-saptamī vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Viṣṇu said:
Birth in a noble family, health, and wealth are indeed difficult to obtain in this world.
O Lord of the World, tell me that by which the third [state] is attained.
Brahmā said:
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
when there is conjunction with the asterism Hasta, one should [worship] the origin of the world.
Having worshipped the Sun according to the prescribed rite, one should observe a fast with offerings of garlands, perfumes, incense, and fresh food.
The vow consisting of the worship of a corresponding cow for each cow received, joined with gifts and other practices, lasts for one year;
*yavya* means a month.
And one should give gifts to the foremost of the twice-born;
listen now, O hero, as that is being told.
A vajra, rice, barley, gold, barley-food, water, a water-jar,
a food-vessel, an umbrella, milk-food, and that which is rich in molasses and treacle.
In that same manner, one should give clothing in due order.
On that lunar day prescribed by rule, having worshipped the Teacher of the World with offerings of cow-products and barley,
he should present a vessel of food covered by a vessel full of food, a water-pot filled with water, and food consisting of rice mixed with molasses and treacle.
One should eat grains for the sake of purification;
learn now those things which are to be consumed here.
Cow’s urine, water, ghee, raw vegetables, dūrvā grass, curd, rice, barley,
sesame seeds, and lotuses— [these should be used] with water heated by the rays of the sun.
And milk should also be administered in a monthly sequence.
He obtains birth in a preeminent family, filled with wealth and grain, adorned with lotuses, and where all suffering has been destroyed; and he possesses unimpaired sense faculties.
One becomes free from disease, wise, and happy.
"Surrounded by lotuses, surrounded by Lakṣmī"—
thus ends the Nayanaprada-saptamī vow as described in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
O bull among sages, I shall likewise describe the Viśoka-saptamī,
by fasting on which a man never experiences sorrow here in this world.
Having bathed with black sesame seeds on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha,
and having first cleansed his teeth, he should take his meal of kṛśara.
Having observed the vow of fasting, he should remain celibate during the night;
then, having risen at dawn, he should perform his ablutions and recitations, being pure.
Having fashioned a golden lotus, one should worship it with the thought,
"This is the Sun," using *karavīra* flowers and a pair of red garments.
Just as the world is always free from sorrow through you, O Āditya,
so may I likewise be free from sorrow in every birth through devotion to you.
Having thus performed worship on the sixth lunar day, one should devoutly honor the twice-born;
then, having slept and consumed cow’s urine, one should rise and perform the daily obligatory rites.
Having diligently honored a Brahmin, one should present to that Brahmin a very fine vessel filled with jaggery and accompanied by a garment.
On the seventh day, one desiring prosperity should eat food without oil or salt while observing silence;
thereafter, the listening to the Purāṇas should be performed.
By this procedure, one should perform everything for both fortnights until the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-pot accompanied by a golden lotus;
one should also give a bed with its furnishings and a tawny cow that yields milk.
Whoever performs the Viśoka-saptamī according to this rite, free from stinginess regarding wealth, attains the supreme goal.
For as many as a hundred and fifty million lifetimes,
he shall not encounter sorrow, being free from disease and poverty.
Whatever desire one may long for, that one obtains in abundance;
but he who acts without desire goes to the supreme Brahman.
Thus ends the Viśoka-saptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Agastya said:
Now, O Great King, there is another vow known as Ārogya (Health).
I shall relate that supreme merit which destroys all sins.
Having fasted on the seventh day of that very month of Māgha,
one should worship the god Bhāskara, the eternal one whose form is the universe.
"O Āditya, Bhāskara, Ravi, Bhānu, Sūrya, Divākara, Prabhākara— thus is the Lord, the omnipresent Sovereign of all, to be worshipped."
Having taken food on the sixth day, one should observe a fast on the seventh;
one should eat again on the eighth—this indeed is the rule and the sequence.
Whoever worships the Sun according to this rite for a full year,
for that person health, wealth, and grain shall arise in this very birth.
"And a happy state in the hereafter, reaching which one does not return"—
thus is described the Ārogya-saptamī-vrata as stated in the Varāha Purāṇa.
Sumantu said: "Indeed, I shall fully declare to you the unsurpassed solar vow (sūryavrata),
which is the supreme means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa."
And he who, on the seventh day of the month of Pauṣa, observes the practice of eating only at night,
with his senses subdued and speaking the truth, bathes with cow urine and cow milk.

O Śāṇḍileya of noble vows, he who diligently observes a fast on the seventh lunar day of both fortnights and worships the Sun and [the deity] Śāṇḍileya at the three junctions of the day, [attains great merit].
The fire belongs to Śāṇḍilī;
he should always sleep on the ground, renouncing all enjoyments.
When a month has passed, O subduer of enemies, [he should worship] on the seventh day with clarified butter and other offerings.
Having performed his bath and a great worship with the Sūrya-mantra, O Bhārata,
he should offer as an oblation one prastha of cooked rice prepared with milk.
Having fed eight twice-born Sāmavedic singers who are devoted to the Sun,
O great king, one should also give a tawny cow to the Maker of Light.
I shall describe the fruit of the merit for one who thus performs this unsurpassed Sūryavrata, which is endowed with the fulfillment of all desires.
By means of celestial palaces resembling ten million suns, fulfilling all desires,
filled with hosts of apsaras, and endowed with great majesty.
Adorned by hosts of Gandharvas with the sounds of music, dance, and song,
he was fanned with yak-tail whisks and praised by gods and asuras.
Endowed with wealth and sovereignty, he goes from the thousand-rayed sun to that supreme abode where the radiant Ravi dwells.
A youth who recites the number of hairs on that cow is honored in the world of Śūrya for as many thousands of yugas as there are hairs on the body of that Kapilā cow born in her lineage.
Having enjoyed desired pleasures together with those born of twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Having attained the yoga of knowledge, one shall go to the abode of the Sun;
so too shall he who, when the month of Māgha has arrived, observes the practice of eating only at night.
Eating oil-cake mixed with ghee while having his senses fully controlled,
he should observe a fast on the seventh day of both fortnights.
O lord of men, on the eighth day one should perform the consecration with clarified butter for the Sun;
and one should give a young cow, dark-blue in color, to the Lord of Day.
O king of kings, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Phālguna goes to the beautiful city of the Sun and enjoys pleasures according to his desire.
Having conquered anger and mastered his senses, he should subsist on śyāmāka grain and milked nīvāra rice,
and remain devoted to fasting on either the sixth or the seventh lunar day.
On the eighth day, however, there is a great ablution with the five products of the cow, clarified butter, and so forth,
as well as with earth from the top of an anthill and the like, and cow’s urine, cow dung, and so forth.
Having bathed [the image] with the barks of milk-exuding trees, one should worship it;
then, one should offer a reddish cow to the Lord who wears a garland of rays.
A cow is called *saurabheyī*. Having gone to the beautiful city of the Sun, she rejoices for eternal years.
Furthermore, when the month of Caitra has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night (the *naktabhojana* vow) [attains this merit].
O King, eating śāli rice mixed with milk and with his senses restrained,
he should offer a young Vaiṣṇavī pāṭalā flower to the Sun.
The cow itself belongs to Viṣṇu;
by means of vehicles made of topaz and followed by various swans,
she goes to the beautiful city of the Sun, which is difficult for those of unrefined souls to attain.
O King of kings, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Vaiśākha,
consuming curd-rice while having conquered anger and subdued his senses;
Sleeping in a cow-pen, sleeping on the ground, wearing a single garment at night,
and he should observe all the general rules as they have been prescribed.
The general rule includes not conversing with heretics and the like.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, however, one should perform a bath with ghee and other substances;
and, O King, one should give a single young cow, adorned, to the Sun.
Adorned with great vehicles that possess the luster of conch shells, white lotuses, and the moon,
and yoked with white Garuḍas, he shall go to the abode of the Sun.
Surrounded by women of surpassing beauty who possess the fragrance of blue lotuses, he rejoices for an inexhaustible time.
O mighty-armed hero, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Jyeṣṭha,
consuming milk-rice with ghee and honey, [attains great merit].
He should sit in the *vīrāsana* posture at night and follow the cows throughout the day.
Remaining seated in the *vīrāsana*,
he should always act for the benefit of the cows and refrain from harming them.

On the seventh lunar day of both fortnights, one should perform the ritual procedures such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*). The phrase "of both" refers to both fortnights. Furthermore, one should give a smoke-colored cow, adorned with ornaments, to the Sun.
He rejoices for inexhaustible time in incomparable Great Vehicles that resemble blue lotuses and are adorned with great lions.
He who, being self-restrained, observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Āṣāḍha,
should eat milk mixed with sixty-day rice only once [a day].
O Great King, one should give a cow of auspicious appearance to the Sun;
and one should perform the general ritual procedure, O sinless one, as previously described by me.
In vehicles resembling pure crystal and drawn by peacocks,
endowed with the powers of *aṇimā* and the other superhuman faculties, he shall roam in the sky like the sun.
When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, he who is devoted to the welfare of all beings should observe the practice of eating only at night, consuming food consisting of rice mixed with milk.
