One should give a yellow-colored cow to the Great-Souled Bhāskara;
one should perform the entire procedure exactly as it has been proclaimed.
Traveling by means of various magnificent Mahāyāna vehicles drawn by swans and cranes,
the glorious one goes to the City of the Sun and obtains the previously mentioned fruit.

O Hero, O Soul of the Universe, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Bhādrapada, taking refuge at the foot of a tree and consuming only the remnants of the sacrificial offering—
Out of compassion for all beings, O Hero, one should sleep at night in a sheltered place and should give a young cow to the high-souled Bhāskara.
With celestial palaces that resemble the moon in appearance, adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli, furnished with ruddy geese, and granting all desires;
Having gone to the beautiful city of the Sun, he, who is worshipped by gods and asuras,
rejoices in great vehicles until the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa.
The illustrious one who, having conquered anger and subdued his senses, observes the practice of eating only at night and consuming only ghee during the month of Āśvayuja, [attains great merit].
One should give a cow, radiant with the color of a lotus, to the Sun of immeasurable splendor—
a young, milch cow, fully equipped with ornaments for her back.
With celestial chariots that fulfill all desires, which resemble clear pearls, are adorned with sapphires, and are accompanied by jīvañjīvaka birds;
O King, resembling the sun in brilliance, he shall go to the world of the sun;
resembling the moon in beauty, he shall go to the world of the moon; and resembling Śukra in luster, he shall go to the world of Śukra.
O Indra among kings, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Kārttika,
subsisting on milk-rice, speaking the truth, and having his senses subdued;
One should give a cow to Divākara that possesses a radiance equal to the blazing sun;
one should also perform the previously mentioned rite, O King, and thus one shall become equal to the Sun.
In great vehicles resembling mountains, which are like the flames of a forest fire and are set in motion by great lions, the happy one rejoices like the sun.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming barley-food mixed with milk while his senses are restrained;
O tiger among the Kurus, one should likewise give a black cow adorned with various ornaments to the Sun, or else one should perform the prescribed ritual.
Endowed with supreme splendor, he goes to the delightful city of the Sun by means of vehicles resembling white lotuses and yoked with chariots of white horses.
Non-violence, truthful speech, non-stealing, patience, and uprightness;
performing the fire-sacrifice at the three periods of the day, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at night.
O descendant of Kuru, by fasting on both fortnights on the seventh lunar day,
one who performs this supreme vow while relying upon these qualities [attains the following].
The seventh [verse] is declared to possess both [qualities]: it removes all diseases and fears, pacifies all sins, and bestows the fruits of all desires.
One who desires the vast abode of the Sun of immeasurable splendor should always observe the Sūrya-vrata according to these and other such rules.
Thus ends the vow of the "Double Seventh" (Ubhayasaptamī) as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall tell you yet another gift that destroys all sins.
It is called the Ādityamaṇḍaka, which bestows the desired fruit.
One should prepare a well-cooked ball of jaggery, filled with cow's ghee, which has the luster of the sun's orb, using either bright barley flour or wheat flour.
Having worshipped the Sun with devotion, one should prepare an auspicious mandala before him,
made specifically from red sandalwood or, preferably, from saffron.
Having placed a *maṇḍaka* there and worshipped it with red flowers,
one should offer it along with gold and cloth, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
O Pāṇḍava, it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa with this mantra:
"Born from the splendor of the Sun, fashioned by the hand of the King."
"O Brahmin, for my own welfare, please accept this excellent cake.
The Brahmin, too, should recite the mantra and receive that which is dear to Bhāskara.
Offered by one devoted to the Sun himself, out of a spirit of devotion to Him,
it grants all desires, bestows wealth, accords with righteousness, and likewise grants sons and happiness.
"May he accept this *maṇḍaka* given for the pleasure of Āditya;
by performing this with devotion, a person is liberated from all sins."
One whose self is enriched with wealth and grain, who is the soul of all beings, who is affectionate toward devotees,
and who is devoted to the worship of Āditya, is thereafter glorified in heaven.
And having come here, O Indra among kings, through the exhaustion of his own merit,
he shall become a sovereign of a mandala, with all his desires and purposes fulfilled.
O King, on the day of Rathasaptamī, that which is equal to a great gift should be bestowed;
it should be given every year by one who desires the ultimate fruit.
By giving even a single [gift], sins are destroyed throughout childhood, youth, and old age; by giving many, one becomes a partaker of merit.
He who, being of undaunted spirit, having prepared an unbroken *ādityamaṇḍaka* made from wheat flour or barley flour,
should duly present it to a twice-born man;
Surely he is the one who adorns the circle of the immeasurable.
Thus ends the Ādityamaṇḍalaka-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"O sinless Kṛṣṇa, I shall now describe to you another [vow], the Mārtaṇḍasaptamī."
Having fasted on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa, [one should worship].
Having duly worshipped Mārtaṇḍa while muttering "Mārtaṇḍa," one should worship Kutapa with devotion, endowed with supreme faith.
The *kutapa* is the sun;
being composed through fasting and offerings such as incense and oblations to Pūṣan,
one should again recite the name "Mārtaṇḍa" with the mind fixed upon him.
O you whose banner is Garuda, one should give a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin according to one's ability;
whether sleeping or waking, or even when stumbling, one should utter the name "Mārtaṇḍa."
One should avoid conversation with heretics who persist in improper conduct;
likewise, one may consume cow urine, cow dung, curd, or even milk.
One should consume that which has arisen from the *godeha* for the sake of self-purification;
on the second day, O dear one, there is again the worship of the Sun in that very same place.
Having come together under that very name and having given a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin,
he should then eat that which has been prepared from the body of a cow.
In this very manner, having fasted throughout all the months, being self-restrained and pure,
the wise man should, according to his ability, give daily provisions for cows every month.
Furthermore, when the year has concluded, having given daily fodder as before to another cow,
hear what fruit one enjoys.
The fruit that a man enjoys by giving five cows with golden horns and a bull as the sixth to the twice-born every month— [that fruit he obtains].
By fasting according to this vow, one fully attains all that;
and one reaches that world where Mārtaṇḍa dwells.
O Kṛṣṇa, there is no doubt that such a person becomes equal to Śāṇḍilya in splendor.
"Equal to Śāṇḍileya, equal to Agni"—
thus is described the Mārtaṇḍasaptamī vow as stated in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Lord,
tell me of that one Saptamī which destroys sins, by fasting upon which a man attains the desires dear to his heart.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On a day of the Sun during the bright fortnight, when the sun’s northern course has begun,
and under a lunar mansion bearing a masculine name, one should undertake the Saptamī vow.
Savrīhaka rice, sesame, barley, along with mung beans and black gram,
wheat, meat, honey, sexual intercourse, bronze vessels,
ointments, collyrium, and powders from stone slabs— these are [the items to be avoided].
One observing the vow of the sixth lunar day should avoid these two days for the sake of the successful accomplishment of one's desired goal.
Having gratified the gods, the ancestors, and the hosts of sages with handfuls of water, and having worshipped the lamp held in the hand of the maiden of the sky,
he offered into the fire sesame seeds and barley grains repeatedly smeared with clarified butter.
One should sleep on the ground, placing the sun and the universe within one's heart.
Having avoided those substances which have been prohibited here for thirteen days, and having consumed pure chickpeas on the sixtieth day, [one should do so] for one year.
O Bhārata, a person attains whatever is desired by the mind.
The mention of chickpeas (*caṇaka*) is for the purpose of indicating the exclusion of all internal [leguminous grains]; otherwise, the exclusion of rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth would be redundant.
Thus ends the vow of the seventh lunar day (*saptamī-vrata*), consisting of the avoidance of thirteen items, as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.
Vasudeva said: Thereafter, with a concentrated mind, I shall describe the occasional sacrifices (naimittika-yajñas) here,
specifically on the seventh lunar day, during eclipses, and at the transits of the sun.

With this verse beginning "I shall now describe the occasional rites," the author makes a general promise to perform sacrifices during eclipses and transits; he first describes the *satrasaptamī* sacrifice with the words beginning "On the seventh day of the bright fortnight.

"On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, having eaten sacrificial food (*havis*) once during the day, and having properly performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) at twilight and prostrated before Varuṇa..."
Varuṇa is here, and Sūrya;
having restrained his senses and meditated upon Him, the wise man should sleep,
lying upon a bed of *darbha* grass at night, having bathed in the morning and being well-composed.
At the beginning and likewise at the end of everything, one should worship Varuṇa as before;
the Bahvṛca, however, should offer oblations into the fire after having duly conceived it as the Sun-fire.
I shall describe, in brief, the rite of making the sun into fire and the libation:
having inscribed the syllable Oṃ with the Astra-mantra and sprinkled it upon the fire with the Sāvitrī-mantra.
With the *astra-mantra* and with the *Sāvitrī*, the Gāyatrī of the Sun. All of this should be understood as having been stated by Nikṣubhā specifically on the seventh [day].
Having scattered and spread darbha grass upon the ground in the desired place, one should touch the vessels in the manner of a wheel, with their tips pointing eastward and northward.
Having prepared a purifier (pavitra) made of two kuśa blades, with tips intact and measuring a span (prādeśa),
one should sprinkle the vessels with it, purify them, and then dissolve [the impurities].
Having performed the rite of encircling with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) over the vessel situated on the northern part using a firebrand with flames,
one should then perform the purification by sprinkling (utpavana) three times.

Having wiped the sacrificial ladles and other implements with those same *darbha* grasses that have been sprinkled with water, one should offer oblations into the fire that has likewise been sprinkled; there, one should worship the Sun as before.
O tiger among the Yadus, one is purified by holding the vessel on the ground with the hand spread out, using the left hand; however, one is not purified if it is held in mid-air.
In the intermediate space, beginning with the *trika*,
the wise one should take [the substance] with his right hand upon pure ground and offer it into the fire;
all the rites previously enjoined should be performed with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
With the heart-mantra,
having offered oblations and satisfied [the deity] with this, one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, one should worship Varuṇa with reverence for Varuṇa.

One should give pieces of sugar-candy to the Brahmins according to one's ability, and one should also give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's means; thus the fruit born of sacrifice is obtained.
And thus, in the month of Phālguna one should worship Sūrya; in Caitra, the garlanded Vāṃśumālin;
in the month of Vaiśākha, Dhātṛ; and in Jyeṣṭha, one should sacrifice to Indra-Ravi.
One should worship Bhaga in the month of Āṣāḍha, likewise Bhādrapada in Śrāvaṇa;
Parjanya in Āśvina, and Tvaṣṭṛ in Kārttika.
If one worships Mitra in Mārgaśīrṣa and Viṣṇu in Pauṣa, one obtains,
day after day, the fruit that is said to result from performing sacrifices throughout an entire year.
One endowed with devotion and faith shall swiftly attain all that;
thus, when a full year has passed, one should indeed construct a golden chariot.
It was yoked to seven horses, adorned with various jewels,
resembling the sun in its brilliance, and beautiful, fashioned from pure gold in its center.
Having adorned it with jewels and placed it upon a golden lotus,
he set that excellent chariot in place and stationed a charioteer at its front.
Having honored the preceptor— who knows all ritual manuals and is surrounded by twelve Brahmins who are, in sequence, the presiding deities of the months— at the front of the chariot;

The solar deities presiding over the months are those mentioned for each respective month; therefore, the meaning is that one should worship the preceptor surrounded by twelve Brahmins who have been purified by devotion to them.

One should indeed honor the preceptor, who turns like the sun, with wealth, jewels, and other gifts. Having thus fully honored the Brahmins who are the lords of the months, one should then present the offerings.
One should offer a chariot, a wheel, a morsel of food, a garment, or auspicious land to the preceptor,
and one should present [these] to the twelve lords of the months.
Thus, having offered ornaments such as gold and gems according to one's devotion and capacity,
and having prostrated before him, one should announce that the vow is complete.
"Thereafter, there is no fault here in performing the vow," [he said] repeatedly,
"so be it," by the lords of brahmins together with the teachers.
Having had the *Bahvṛcas* offer benedictions, he should say, "May [the deity] be pleased. "O Āditya, by whatever desire you have been propitiated through these vows..."
May it grant you that desire; may your vow be fulfilled, especially toward the virtuous Brahmins and those who are destitute.
Having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability to the poor, the blind, and the wretched,
and having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should thus complete this vow.
Having performed this for seven years, the king becomes righteous;
and he shall become a man who is a donor and exceedingly dear to the Sun.
For more than a hundred years, he happily enjoys a realm three hundred leagues in circumference, free from rivals and thorns.
Even one devoid of wealth, having performed the vow and fast as prescribed, should give a copper chariot with devotion and offer everything as stated.
He enjoys a vast circle of the earth eighty yojanas in extent;
even so, one who is destitute of wealth might give a chariot made of flour.
Happy, he enjoys [the earth] for more than a hundred years up to sixty yojanas;
and at the end of the kalpa, he attains the world of the Sun and shall obtain the Veda once again.
Thus ends the vow of the Vijayā-yajña-saptamī as declared in the Śrī Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Sumantu said: Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, and restraint of the senses—
Worship of the Sun, carrying fire, contentment, and the avoidance of theft.
O child, this is the general rule that always applies to all vows:
he who, having undertaken the ritual procedure of the seventh day, does so out of ignorance is considered *tāmasa*.
He who would abandon [the vow] out of desire or even fear should be known as fallen by the wise;
however, that man who observes the fast on the seventh lunar day and eats only at night [attains merit].
Having observed a fast on the fifth day, eating but a single meal on the sixth,
he should offer well-prepared vegetables along with excellently prepared hard and soft foods.
Restraining his speech, a man should eat at night as an offering to the gods and the Brahmins;
for as long as he lives, whoever shall observe this vow,
his prosperity, victory, and indeed the three goals of life will increase.
Upon death, he attains heaven, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot.
And he rejoices in the world of the sun for many *manvantaras*;
then, having returned here at the end of time, he punishes his enemies on all sides.
Surrounded by sons and grandsons, being a donor and firm in his vows,
O King, he enjoys the highest realms, unconquered by enemies in battle.
O tiger among kings, having fasted on the seventh lunar day while subsisting on vegetables and traveling by vehicle,
that sacred ford known as Gaya was indeed reached.
Because the Kurus there subsisted on vegetables for a long time,
Vivasvat designated that field as Dharmakṣetra, Kurukṣetra.
The seventh, ninth, sixth, third, and likewise the fifth lunar days—these are indeed the "slaves to desire"; on other days, they are not [the slaves] of women.
The seventh day of the month of Māgha, likewise the ninth of Aśvayuja,
the sixth of Bhādrapada, and the third of Vaiśākha are indeed auspicious.
The fifth day of the month of Bhādrapada is to be known as the meritorious Nāgapañcamī;
thus, these specific lunar days (tithis) within their respective months are auspicious.
Having prepared well-prepared vegetables along with various kinds of food and snacks,
and having given them to a Brahmin according to his ability, the observer of the vow eats afterwards at night.
O descendant of Kuru, this vow should be undertaken during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika;
the first breaking of the fast is traditionally prescribed after four months.
And here, worship of Vibhāvasu should be performed with Agasti flowers; "Vibhāvasu" refers to the Sun. Saffron is the unguent, and Aparājita is used as incense.
One should perform the bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and likewise consume that same substance;
here, milk-rice (pāyasa) is to be offered as the food oblation, and worship should be performed for the Fire-god (Vibhāvasu).
At that very time, vegetables should be given to the Brahmins, and then one should eat them oneself,
accompanied by auspicious greens and provided with various kinds of food and drink.

"Śubha" refers to vegetables that are not prohibited. O King, on the second breaking of the fast, one should offer to the Lord flowers that possess auspicious fragrances, as well as white sandalwood."
There should also be agallochum incense and an offering of molasses cakes;
here, the bath is with water infused with *kuśa* grass, and the ritual consumption is with cow dung.
In the third [offering], there are *karavīra* flowers as well as red sandalwood;
and among incenses, *guggulu* is always dear to the God.
O Great-minded One, the food offering should consist of śāli rice mixed with curd;
for the Brahmins, that same offering should be provided along with various kinds of foods to be chewed and licked.
O Lord, having given it prepared with black pot-herbs (*kālaśāka*), the wise know that a bath with a paste of white mustard (*gaurasarṣapa*) is prescribed here for the discerning one.
The consumption of that very [consecrated food] is auspicious, bestowing fortune and removing all sins;
at the conclusion of the third fast, a meal should be provided for the Brahmins.
The recitation of the Purāṇa and its listening are likewise praised;
one should do so having bathed before the deity and in the presence of the Brāhmaṇas.
One should have it heard from a Brahmin reciter, and not from one born of another caste;
one should cause all the Brahmins to hear it and honor them with devotion according to one's ability.
O King, one should present two stainless garments to the reciter;
when the reciter is honored, the god Bhāskara is always pleased.
Karavīra flowers as desired, likewise red sandalwood,
guggulu resin as desired for him, and a vessel as desired.
O descendant of Kuru, for that [devotee] of Savitṛ, clarified butter is as desired, the reciter is always as desired, and the breaking of the fast is indeed as desired.
Thus, this seventh lunar day is always meritorious and beloved by the Lord of Cows (the Sun);
having fasted upon it here, a person shall never be joined with misfortune.
The specific details regarding the milk [observance] on the first lunar day (pratipad) should be understood. This is the Śāka-saptamī vow.

Beginning on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one who performs it every month until the seventh day of the bright fortnight for a period of four months must break the fast on each of those respective seventh days. Thus, the breaking of the fast occurs three times in a single year; in this same manner, such a vow should be performed throughout one's life in subsequent years as well. This is the Śāka-saptamī vow as described in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Nārada said:

What rite is to be performed for a miraculous chest disease, and by what means is Alakṣmī destroyed? Furthermore, what procedure is prescribed for the ritual bathing of women whose children have died, and so forth?
Śaṅkara said: O ascetic, sins committed in the past bear fruit there in the form of disease and misfortune, as well as through the slaughter of one's beloved.
To counteract that, I shall now describe the rite called the "Seventh-Day Bath," which brings about auspiciousness and destroys the affliction of disease.
Just as death is seen among children who are still drinking milk,
so too is it seen among those other than the elderly, even among those in the prime of youth.
I shall explain that which is peaceful through the consecration for those who have given birth to stillborn children;
this very [rite] is the destroyer of mental confusion during extraordinary calamities.
O mighty-armed one, O rich in asceticism, this will happen when the Kalpa begins,
and when Vivasvat’s son Manu, the unsurpassed, appears there as well.
And when the twenty-fifth age, known as Kṛta, occurs there, he will flourish in the lineage of the Haihayas.
But there shall be a heroic husband, the powerful Kārttikeya;
as the seventh, he will protect the entire surface of the earth.
O Nārada, for seven times seven thousand years,
as soon as he was born, a hundred sons were then produced from her.
But by the curse of Cyavana,
he shall meet his destruction when a thousand-armed son is born to him.
O Nārada, the divine Kṛtavīrya propitiated the thousand-rayed Sun-god through fasts, vows, and Vedic hymns.
He will obtain the bathing with [the waters of] the Asvattha tree for the sake of his son's life.
This was indeed seen by Kṛtavīrya, as well as this [mantra] consisting of several suns;
it pacifies all evils and always destroys impurity.
Enough with this great distress, O lord of men; your son shall live for a long time—what need is there even to mention the destruction of his sins?
I shall describe the seventh-month bathing ceremony for the benefit of all the world,
O Nārada, for a woman who has lost her children at birth and is now in her seventh month of pregnancy.
Alternatively, all this is commended on the seventh day of the bright fortnight,
having obtained the favorable strength of the planets and stars and having performed the recitation by Brahmins.
Enough with this great distress, O lord of men;
your son’s birth star is such that a wise man should avoid that lunar day.
In the same way, having performed [the rites] for the elderly and the sick, and likewise for others,
one should remain standing on ground smeared with cow dung.
One should offer four oblations of red śāli rice mixed with milk to Sūrya and Rudra, and especially to the Mothers.
O Nārada, one should first recite the hymn dedicated to Sūrya and offer oblations of clarified butter; likewise, one should offer them to Rudra with the Rudrasūkta.
In this rite, fuel-sticks of *arka* and *palāśa* should likewise be offered;
furthermore, a fire-oblation (*homa*) of one hundred and eight barley grains and black sesame seeds must be performed.
Then, having offered eight hundred oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis*, the wise one should likewise perform the ritual bath with those very same mantras.
Having had four beautiful jars placed in the corners by a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, who holds Darbha grass in his hand and acts according to the prescribed rite;
Furthermore, one should place five and five [offerings] in the center, adorned with curd and unbroken rice grains;
and one should set down a flawless jar consecrated with the solar mantra.
One should fill [the vessels] with water from sacred fords, combined with gold and jewels,
all of them containing all medicinal herbs and infused with the water of the five products of the cow.
Adorned with fruits of the five jewels and wrapped in cloths,
[they should be placed] at a place where an elephant, a horse, a road, an anthill, a confluence of rivers, a cow-pen, or a herd of cattle meet.
Having gathered together and brought clay, one should place it into all [the jars] alike; that is, having gathered and unified it,
[one should place it] into the middle [jar] among the four jars containing water.
There, the brahmin, reciting solar mantras,
took hold [of the child] along with seven women whose limbs were free from defect.
Having been honored according to one's ability with garlands, garments, ornaments, and so forth,
women who have given birth to stillborn children should perform the consecration while wearing their clothes.
"This boy has been declared long-lived, and likewise this Jīvaputrā;
so too are the sun and the moon together with the planets, lunar mansions, and stars."
May Śakra together with the world-protectors, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— may these and all other gods always protect the young boy.
Neither Saturn nor Rāhu, nor any of the minor planets (vālagraha) anywhere,
shall cause affliction to the child, his mother, or his father.
Then, wearing white garments, a young woman together with her husband,
and the preceptor for women together with his wife, should worship Tryambaka.
Then, having fashioned an image of Dharmarāja out of gold and placed it upon a copper vessel, one should present it to the preceptor.

Dharmarāja, however, should be depicted seated upon a buffalo; in his right hand he holds a staff topped with a skull, above which is a sword, and in his left a shield. Furthermore, eight other figures of smoky-grey color should be drawn together on his left side. In his right hand, the noose of Yama should be drawn.
Citragupta should be made holding a leaf and a pen.
[He is to be honored] with garments, gold, jewels, and the like, and with food offerings such as milk-rice mixed with ghee.
There, one should honor the Brahmins, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
and having eaten together with the Guru, the succession of mantras should be recited.
May this man be long-lived, eloquent, and happy for a hundred years;
whatever evil he has committed, may it be cast into the mouth of the submarine fire.
May Brahmā, Rudra, Vasu, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Śakra, and Hutāśana protect [us] from all evils; may they all be bestowers of boons in every way.
One should honor the Sun while he speaks these and other such words;
and having prostrated before a tawny cow according to one's ability, one should dismiss him.
Having prostrated before the Guru together with his sons, as well as before Ravi and Śaṅkara,
he should eat the remnants of the oblation, saying, "May there be salutation to Āditya."
This very same [rite] is seen to be effective during times of extraordinary velocity and in the case of bad dreams;
one should always perform it while avoiding the day of birth and the natal asterism of the performer.
Performing this on the seventh day of the bright fortnight for the sake of peace, one does not come to grief;
this hymn of praise to the Sun on the seventh day bestows merit and long life.
Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born, he vanished on the spot;
by this very procedure, the king became long-lived.
Even though it has been cultivated for a year, this earth shall be rich with crops;
all this has been told to you regarding the supreme ritual bath on the seventh lunar day.
It pacifies all evils and is supremely beneficial for the ignorant;
one should seek health from the Sun and wealth from the Fire-god.
One should seek knowledge from Śaṅkara and the goal of liberation from Janārdana;
this shall be the destroyer of great sins, supremely beneficial, and a promoter of strength.
And he who hears this with a one-pointed mind—
The sages declare that for him, too, there is success.
Thus ends the ritual bathing on the seventh lunar day as described in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*.
Sanatkumāra said:
Desiring the highest auspiciousness, Vinatā, having fasted on the seventh lunar day, should worship Hari, the abode of all auspiciousness and the divine Lord.
Having prepared a square mandala provided with unbroken grains (akṣata),
one should invoke therein the Lord Śrīśa together with Indirā.
With lotuses, jasmine flowers, *nandyāvarta* blossoms, single-leaved leaves, *bilva* petals, *dūrvā* grass, rice grains, and filaments.
One should worship with sweet fruits, roots, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
The four vessels—made of clay, silver, copper, and gold—[should be used].
Desiring a vessel free from flaws, one should have it made with a capacity of one *droṇa*;
there, the wise man should also place four earthen jars.
Accompanied by a measure of four prasthas, together with cloth,
salt, sesame seeds, turmeric powder, and coriander;
Then, having placed earth [in it], one should likewise cause it to be deposited in the *śānti* jar,
which is filled with clarified butter, honey, curd, and milk.
The one of great intelligence should place the water-pots and the vessels in front;
he should worship eight women who have sons and for whom their husbands are their deities.
Endowed with all auspiciousness and adorned with all ornaments,
the wise man should give to them as appropriate for the sake of auspiciousness.
Then one should worship them and cause sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to be given to them;
thereafter, in their presence, one should pray to the Lord of Śrī.
Grant supreme auspiciousness; salutations to you, O abode of blessings!
O you whose eyes are beloved by the Consort of Indirā, O you who are dear to the eyes of the Consort of Śrī!
O Lord of Śrī, whose two four-armed hands are fond of the embrace of the creeper-like Śrī;
O You with long, auspicious eyes, grant me supreme auspiciousness!
Then, having had the auspicious rites performed for her by those women and young ladies,
and having obtained their permission, she completed the worship of Hari and dismissed them.
O Dhanañjaya, the preceptor should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas;
having first made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), this is the rule for it, whether performed by the son or even by the father.
Either the preceptor or the king should perform this rite of worship in his own city;
it should be carried out with the eight-syllable mantra.
Then, on the eighth day, one should perform the worship of the deity as before;
together with eight women, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) while reciting the mantra.
The husband who desires happiness must observe the fast;
on the eighth day he should break the fast and provide a meal for the Brahmins.
The preceptor should receive the sacrificial fee and likewise complete the vow;
from this, there arises health, longevity, nourishment, and the bringing of happiness.
It is the source of auspiciousness for women and likewise bestows sons and grandsons;
a woman desiring a son shall obtain a son, and one desiring long life shall obtain it as well.
Desiring the highest auspiciousness, one shall obtain it through this vow;
even a man finds fame, renown, strength, and long life.
May there be long life for kings, extensive knowledge for the foremost of the twice-born,
abundant prosperity for the Vaiśyas, and happiness for the Śūdras.
This vow must always be performed by one who desires victory for oneself;
for those seeking to engage in battles, this vow must be performed first.
Even a maiden, performing this supreme vow, shall obtain a husband;
thus indeed has this most excellent Saptamī-vrata been proclaimed,
which bestows all merit upon men and grants all nourishment on earth.
Thus ends the auspicious vow (maṅgalya-vrata) as declared in the Garuḍa Purāṇa. Now follows the Sūrya-vrata.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, having fasted properly on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra,
one should perform the worship of the God of gods on the seventh day.
O King, having performed his external bath and smeared himself with cow dung,
a man should then properly smear the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) with white clay.
There, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus together with its colors;
one should place the god of gods, Vibhāvasu, there in the pericarp.
O King, one should place the two deities who follow the ritual substances on the eastern petal;
and on the southeastern petal, one should place the two Gandharvas who bring about the seasons.
And one should place two auspicious Aṅgārakas on the southern petal;
likewise, O Great King, one should place two Patrinairṛtakas on the southwestern (nairṛtya) petal.
O best of kings, the two highly fortunate sons of Kadrū are in the west, moving according to the seasons;
likewise, there are two Yātudhānas in the northwest.
And one should place two sages on the northern petal;
O best of the twice-born, one should place a single planet on the northeastern petal.

And these gods and others have been shown according to the sequence of the seasons beginning with spring. O Brahmin, you ought to tell me which specific deities and others follow the Lord Ravi in whichever particular season.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O king of kings, during the spring, the two deities Dhātṛ and Aryaman, along with the two Gandharvas Tumburu and Nārada, sang in the celestial realm.
Oṃ! Tumburu and Nārada, the two Gandharvas, sang in the sky.
And Kṛtavelā and the Apsaras Puñjikasthalā,
as well as Hotṛ and Prahotṛ, the two preeminent leaders of the Rakṣas-grāmaṇīs.
The serpent Vāsuki and likewise the two best of sages follow after Śita,
as do the two spring deities, the Grīṣmikas.
The sages Atri and Vasiṣṭha, as well as Dakṣa and Takṣaka,
Menakā and Sahajanyā, and the two Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū.
Ratha and Cala are the two village chiefs, as are both Rathakṛṣṇa and Pauruṣādau; Vadha and Yātudhāna are likewise remembered as those two.
Kuja likewise follows [the sun] during the summer heat, as does the planet [Saturn].
Now learn from me, O God, those who follow the divine Sun during the rainy season.
Indra, Vivasvat, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu;
likewise Elāpatra the serpent, and Śaṅkhapāla the nāga.
Śuci, Sena, Ugrasena, Vrata,
and Aruṇi together with the Apsarases Pramlocantī and Nimlocantī— these are they here.
O lord of men, the Yātudhāna, as well as the two serpents and the tiger, pass him by during the rainy season; however, the planet presided over by the priest of the gods (Jupiter) approaches him.
Henceforth, O lord of men, learn from me concerning the autumn season:
Parjanya, Pūṣan, Bharadvāja, and Gautama.
And the Gandharva Citrasena, together with Sukavi,
Viśvāsin, and Ghṛtācī— thus there were two divine Apsarases.
The elephants were Airāvata, the renowned Dhanañjaya, Senajit, and Suṣeṇa;
and there were two Rākṣasas of earth-shaking prowess.
Those two likewise departed, as did the two mighty Yātudhānas;
and the planet Śanaiścara follows the sun.
After this, O King, I shall declare to you [the progeny] of Hemanta;
these two, Aṃśa and Bhaga, together with Kaśyapa and Kratu.
And the serpent Mahāpadma, the snake Karkoṭaka,
the Gandharva Citrasena, and the very powerful Ūrṇāyu.
The Apsarases and the Gandharvas led by Pūrvavit and subject to Urvaśī;
and Tārkṣya and Ariṣṭanemi, two Rākṣasas of terrible prowess.
Likewise, O King, two exceedingly powerful Yātudhānas thundering at the forefront,
and the planet Budha, follow after the Sun.
Henceforth, O knower of dharma, listen as I speak concerning the winter season:
Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, Jamadagni, and likewise Viśvāmitra.
Likewise, the two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara, the offspring of Kadrū;
and the Apsaras Tilottamā, as well as the enchanting goddess Rambhā.
Grāmaṇīrati, Satyajit of great fame,
Brahmopeta, Vairakta, and likewise Yajñopeta.
The Gandharva Dhṛtarāṣṭra and another named Sūryavarcas,
as well as Candramas, the king of the planets, follow after the sun.
These luminous beings nourish the sun, that supreme source of splendor;
for in this way, O King, they perform their pursuit during the cold season.
These groups of seven and twelve are not to be inferred from these positions;
likewise, the group of six follows the sun alone.
They placed the Sun, the supreme light among lights, upon [the chariot] with their own splendor;
likewise, the seers perform this for you with these various words.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases worship him with beautiful songs and the like,
while the Vidyā-grāmaṇīs pay him special honor here.
The serpents depart for the realm of Vaiśvānara, and the Yātudhānas follow after them;
likewise, the attendant grahas lead [the others] away according to the prescribed rule.
For these very gods, austerity is performed according to their respective images,
in accordance with what is appropriate, in accordance with dharma, in accordance with truth, and in accordance with their strength.
Just as this sun exists according to the capacity of beings, so too does its power bring about their success;
by its brilliance, it destroys the inauspicious karma of living beings.
In summer, winter, and the rainy season, being released from heat,
cold, and rain, as well as from night and day,
he moves about here under the influence of the seasons to perform his service.
They gratify the gods, the ancestors, and human beings.
O subduer of enemies, their worship should be performed individually with perfumes, garlands, and ointments, as well as with incense, lamps, and food offerings.
Having thus performed the worship of all [the deities] immediately thereafter,
one should perform a fire offering (homa) with ghee for the Sun, consisting of one hundred and eight oblations.
And one should likewise give eight to each of the others, O best of men.
For the others—the deities placed upon the lotuses—the remainder is that there are eight oblations for each.
Likewise, one should feed one Brahmin for each of all [the deities] by name;
and, O best of the Yadus, one should give them sacrificial fees according to one's ability.
O best of men, having thus observed this vow for one year,
at the conclusion of the vow, he should give a milch cow to a Brahmin learned in the Purāṇas.
And then, O best of the Yadus, one should duly give excellent gold;
for this vow, which grants all desires, was proclaimed by the Self-born One himself.
By performing this vow, one shall attain the world of the Sun;
furthermore, if one performs this great vow for twelve years, [the result is even greater].
O King, having pierced the solar disc, one attains union with Viṣṇu;
this vow destroys sin,
brings prosperity and fame, and annihilates enemies.
O King, in this world and likewise in the next, it is thus the cause of heaven as well as of liberation.
Thus ends the Sūryavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
[775] Now follows the Marudvrata.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having fasted properly on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra,
one should perform the worship of the seasons on the seventh day, in their respective places.
There, O King, one should have a seven-circled *śreṇī* constructed;
the *śreṇī* should be made level with the ground and provided with seven circles.
The meaning is that, having established seven rows, one should then form seven mandalas within each row.
A mandala should be made with perfumes, each marked individually with its own name:
Ekajyotis, Dvirjyotis, Trijyotis, and Mahābala.
O King, best of monarchs, one should likewise place [the syllables] in the first row according to the sequence of one, two, three, four, and five, as has been described.
"In sequence" means that one should assign the seven names beginning with Ekajyotis and ending with Saptajyotis. They are:
Īdṛk, Sadṛk, Vacas, Anyādṛk, Pratisadṛk, as well as Mitas, Saṃmitas, Amitas, and Mahābala.
Then, on the second row, one should place them in due order:
Kṛtajit, Satyajit, and likewise Sukhena Senajit.
One should likewise place these gods in the third row: Śrutamitra, Anumitra, and Purujit.
Ṛta, Ṛtavāda, Vidagdha, Āraṇa, Dhruva,
Satya, and Dhātṛ— one should place these on the earthly [altar] in the fourth row.
[776] And such was Sadṛkṣa, and so too was Etādṛg; Amitāśana, Krīḍita, Saptavṛkṣa, and the highly renowned Sarabha.
O lord of men, one should place seven deities in the fifth row:
Dhartṛ, Duryodhani, Bhīma, Aniyukta, Kṣaya, Saha, and [the seventh].
And on the sixth row, one should install the seven deities in their proper order:
Dhṛti, Vapuḥ, Anādhṛṣya, Vāsaḥ, Kāma, Jaya, and Virāj.
And likewise, O King, one should arrange seven [stones] on each of the seven rows;
O King, the first row shall be joined with the seventh.
The second is like the luster of a lotus petal; the third is like blood;
the fourth should be yellow in color; and the fifth resembles white.
The sixth is like the sky [in color], and the seventh is black in hue;
O twice-born one, garlands and unguents should be offered to them, corresponding to their respective colors.
There, forty-nine lamps should be offered;
one should present the food offerings and other oblations individually for each of the deities.
One should offer clarified butter into the fire with the individual names [of the deities],
and one should feed the Brahmins there, together with the gods and the Siddhas.
Having performed this vow for one year, O best of men,
he should give gold, an unwashed garment, and a milch cow.
One should offer the vows to a Brahmin who is a knower of the Purāṇas.
But there was a brahmin there, O Indra among kings, who was fully conversant with the ritual injunctions regarding the vow.
O best of men, one who desires to ascend [to heaven] should perform this vow;
likewise, one who desires a son, one who desires wealth, or even one who desires prosperity.
Likewise, O King, one who desires victory,
or one who desires prosperity, or again one who desires knowledge, should perform this very vow.
For this indeed bestows all desires, whether for one who desires knowledge or otherwise;
for this bestows all desires, it is purifying and a destroyer of sins.
This auspicious vow, which bestows heaven, is declared to be the most excellent among vows;
by performing this vow, one enjoys heaven for a long time.
Having attained human birth, he would likewise fall from heaven before long.
Endowed with wealth, beauty, and strength,
he was beloved by the people and dear to women;
his body free from disease, he had destroyed the faction of his enemies.
Likewise, he is eloquent and possesses the wealth of the scriptures in this world.
Thus ends the Marud-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Now follows the Turaga-saptamī-vrata.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O lord of men, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra,
one should prepare a mandala with clay upon a surface smeared with cow dung.
There, an eight-petaled lotus should be made with beautiful colors;
having observed a fast, a person should worship the Sun-god in its center.
And likewise Aruṇa, Punnāga, and another, Nikumbha.
[He saw] Yama, Kāla, and likewise Manu the Second;
as well as Śanaiścara, the Queen Chāyā, and Revanta.
O Rāma, one should worship the seven meters, the rain, the sky, and Piṅgala upon the filaments; and the aforementioned deities upon the petals.

The deities beginning with Dhātṛ and Aryaman, as prescribed for the Sūryasaptamī vow, have been mentioned. O King, the worship of the directions and time should be performed outside the lotus diagram with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food offerings.
When the vow is completed, a ruru deer should be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having obtained the fruit of the horse sacrifice according to its power,
and having attained the worlds of Purandara,
O King, they fasted for a very long time.
The splendor of the sun approaches here.
Thus ends the Turaga-saptamī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Now follows the Sita-saptamī vow.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having fasted on the seventh lunar day, one should worship the Sun with lotuses;
having fasted on the seventh lunar day, one should worship the Sun with lotuses.
Whether in an image or on a sacred spot, one should worship according to the rules with white flowers,
white sandalwood paste, and offerings of *vaṭaka* cakes and *pūraṇa*.
At the conclusion of the vow, one who desires the destruction of enemies should give two very white garments to an eminent brahmin;
likewise, O King, so too should one who desires good fortune.
Likewise, at the end, he attains the worlds of the Sun.
Thus ends the vow of Sitāsaptamī as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Now follows the vow of Ubhayasaptamī.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
By this very procedure, whatever man performs the two seventh days every month for as long as a year may last, [he shall attain the fruit].
Thus he obtains the merit of the horse sacrifice and goes to the world of the Sun;
O King, he uplifts his lineage and enjoys all desires.
Thus ends the vow of the two seventh lunar days as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follows the Sūryavrata.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having shaved his head, he who worships the Sun—
Tapanas becomes pleased with him, and he obtains the merit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice.
By worshiping with devotion using cakes mixed with jaggery, as well as those cooked with salt,
along with offerings of gold, one obtains the fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice.
He who eats only at night on the day of the sun and worships the Sun attains his desired wishes and goes to the world of the Sun.
Just as all desires become fulfilled for those who worship the Sun, so too,
O hero among men, does supreme health come to pass.
The worlds of the deceased are likewise those of Savitṛ.
Thus ends the Sūryavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follows the Muktidvāravrata.
Yājñavalkya said:
That vow of mine which is called the "Gate of Liberation," described as destroying evil deeds and slaying the multitude of diseases—
that rite known as Akṣīṇa shall grant liberation.
Tell that to me, O Lord of the Gods, through your grace.
That which has been proclaimed throughout the seven continents as the remover of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin,
which brings about the destruction of all karma, and which is the sole dharma for the fulfillment of all desires— [that he knows].
It is declared to be the gateway to liberation, as well as the bestower of satisfaction upon the gods.
The Blessed One said:
Even by means of hundreds of thousands, tens of millions, and billions of sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha),
that fruit which is obtained by men through the vow of Muktidvāra is attained.
Even one who has not practiced the path of yoga, though acting according to his own whims,
is liberated by this vow if he is then disciplined and remains immortal.

[781] O Sage, because of the fear for their bodies, men— even those who contemplate the supreme truth— do not [remain] free from disease when cows, Brahmins, or their own masters are being killed in the great ocean.
They also obtain the fruit by means of this vow and so forth.
O Sage, since you did not hear his ritual procedure correctly when it was previously kept secret by me, I shall now speak of it.
Likewise toward a son, a friend, and a wife.
Having reached the seventh [tithi], one should perform the brushing of teeth with the hand,
uttering "Homage to Arka," and then, being devoted, use an arka twig.
Alternatively, under the Puṣya asterism, one should likewise perform an immersion in water after having offered a purifying oblation to the gods with the mantra consisting of *arka* fuel-sticks.
One should draw a red sandalwood lotus in the courtyard using cow-dung water;
it should have sixteen petals, along with a central seed-vessel and pericarp.

Having sprinkled the courtyard with cow-dung water, one should draw a lotus with red sandalwood paste, complete with a central seed-vessel (*garbha*), petals, and pericarp (*karṇikā*). Within the center of the pericarp and the petals, one should worship the deities to be described:
Tapan, Āditya, Pūṣan, Aryaman, Sūrya, Mitra, Jaleśvara, Bhānu, Cāra, Viṣṇu, Samārtaṇḍa, and Savitṛ.
And one should place the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun) in due order upon the petals of the directions, beginning with the east.
[782] Āro is Maṅgala. Bhānu, Haṃsa, Aryaman, Vradhna, Vikartana, Divākara, Saptāśva, Saptakiraṇa, and Samastagrahanāyaka— these are the names of the Sun.
One should first place Prabhākara, Suviṣada, Pataṅga, Lokasākṣin,
Vivasvat, and Mihira upon the eastern petal of the womb [mandala].
To the destroyer of darkness, the twelvefold one, the maker of light, the eye of the world, the architect of the universe, the undecaying, the supreme Self, the most excellent.

One should worship the uncreated Creator in the pericarp; thus, sixteen [names] are to be written in the pericarp and at the points where it joins the petals. Furthermore, the Supreme Lord is likewise to be understood as the forty-eight names to be inscribed.
"Oṃ, salutation to Him, the Savitṛ"—thus, in due order, is the invocation with the word "salutation."
Then one should prepare a seat and offer water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya);
one should also present red scents, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), red flowers, and incense.
One should offer salutations;
[one should offer] lamps with the five fragrant ingredients and red garments.
Alternatively, [these should be offered] in a vessel made of silver or copper, as prescribed, containing a lotus.
Adorned with red perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, and jeweled earrings,
it is six finger-breadths in height, thick, and hung with a broad garland.
The wise man, free from stinginess regarding his wealth, should place a golden lotus upon the pericarp of a red sandalwood lotus.
The word "should do" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Then, O twice-born one, having cast red perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and red flowers into a vessel made of gold or copper, which is said to be adorned with lotuses;
Taking water together with the fruits of the five jewels in his joined palms,
he placed his hands at his forehead and knelt upon the ground.
Beholding the sun, one should offer the *arghya* with the mantra:
"Oṃ, salutation to you, the cause of all causes, the soul of the universe, who is devoid of birth and end."
I bow to those who are caressed by the crests of the gods and asuras, and kissed by the crest-jewels upon the heads of the lords of the gods.
O You of infinite power, [I seek] the attainment of all goals from You, who are the abode of the Lord of the essence of waters, whose feet are the refuge for the sporting swans.
Be gracious, O Lord of All; [thou art] the entire, immutable [reality].
O Lord of the supreme lords,
bestow upon me my desired goal; O giver of liberation,
having recited [the mantra] and worshipped, one should then offer [the oblation] to the Sun.
On the solar day (tithi) corresponding to the sun's sign and its asterism (nakṣatra),
having given a red cow along with clarified butter and other offerings, and well-equipped with excellent utensils, one should observe a fast on that very day.
One should meditate; however, if on the second day there is a conjunction with the waning of the lunar day (tithi) and the asterism (nakṣatra), then the fast should be observed.
One should offer [the ritual] on the first day, and on the second day...
Then, a devotee of the Sun-god, seeking the merit of a vow, [approached].

When, even though the second [tithi] has been established, it enters into conjunction with the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*), then there is no fasting nor the offering of *arghya* on the previous day; rather, the meaning is that one should perform the vow on the second day and offer the *arghya*. The "Lord of Day" is the Sun; the tithi that extends over the sunrise is to be accepted for the family's fasts.
Lord Nimbārka is the bestower of the fruits of the desired objects for these [practitioners].
Thus, from the statement in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"At the end of the meal, one should eat the best food after having consumed saffron with water on the ground;
when this vow has been performed, one attains the paths to liberation which are very difficult to obtain."
Month after month, one should perform worship, giving, and so forth, excluding the two breasts;
setting aside all other forms of giving, hear now the specific rule.
One should avoid the *karkandhu* and the *dhānya*, wherein both flower and fruit are present;
thus, one should worship the twelve suns with each individual juice.
Elā, guggulu, nāgakeśara, murā, and the other twelve [ingredients],
saffron, camphor, aguru, devadāru, sarala, nutmeg, and granthika.
Take musk, sandalwood, leaves, keśara, water-lilies, kambola,
kastūrī, seru, haṃsarasa, vālaka, lotuses, a small amount of maṭora, and vacā.
Whatever among these is exhausted, he should himself replenish it and employ it again:
ketaka, vakula, mallikā, atimukta, jasmine, padma, kumuda, and yūthikā.
One should avoid the *pāṭala*, *kuruvaka*, *atimuktaka*, *kubjaka*, *tagara*, *karṇikāra*, *muni*,
the red-flowered *śatapatra*, *kadamba*, *sinduvāra*, *mucukunda*, *javā*, *campaka*, *kukhīra*, and *aśoka* flowers; and among these, one should likewise avoid jaggery as previously specified.
*Kukhura* is *raktakuruṇṭa*; *atimuktaka* is *mādhavī*; *karṇikā* is *karṇikāra*; the sage (*muni*) is *agastya*.
*Kharjūra*, *nāraṅga*, *madhūka*, *jambu*, *kavīra*, *evā*, *arka*, *kapittha*, and *bilva*.
There were *drākṣā* and *mṛdvīkā* grapes, pomegranates and *tinduka* fruits, as well as the beautiful fruits of *bhallātaka* and *rāmaphala*.
Eggplant, *kāliṅgaka*, coconut, pumpkin, wood-apple,
*bimbaka*, jujube, *kośātaka*, citron, and *tutthya*.
They occur in pairs according to their respective times.
Rice, mung beans, sesame, mottled beans, mustard, paddy, millet, chickpeas, and likewise wild rice;
Rājamāṣa,
caraka, atasī, puṣṭikāma, sūramarkaṭa, along with vṛntāka, tripuṭa, and black— these are [to be avoided].
Flour made from *śyāmāka* and *nīvāra* grains.
One should discard [the grain] in proportion to its abundance among the crops, having obtained the price for every pair of pairs; likewise,
one should avoid *cukra* along with milk, sugarcane juice, and extracts.
Likewise, molasses and clarified butter on the ninth day, and sugar.
One should rotate [the vessel] joined with the Vaitara mantra,
and then place curd according to the sequence beginning with the Upāya mantra.
One should consume these— sweet, salty, bitter, astringent, pungent, and sour— two by two, according to their seasonal appearance, for two months each.
Having likewise completed the thirteenth year and the corresponding vow in every respect at that time,
if one does not offer a Kapila cow according to the prescribed rite,
one nevertheless attains the grace of the Sun.
One who possesses desire attains all great fruits, such as sovereignty over the gods, great kingship, and abundant enjoyments; one who is free from desire attains imperishable liberation.
Just as their emergence is reckoned in their own numbering, so too are the particles of dust upon the earth,
the grains of sand in the ocean, and the falling of torrents of rain.
In the same way, there is no limit to the number of fruits for you, who are the gateway to liberation.
Thus concludes the vow of Muktidvārasaptamī as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa. Now follows the Bhānu-vrata.
Pulastya said:
On the seventh lunar day, one should eat only at night and, at the end of the year, give a cow along with gold;
one thus attains the world of the Sun—this is known as the Bhānu-vrata.
Thus ends the Bhānuvratam as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
[787] Brahmā said:
On the seventh lunar day, having worshipped Citrabhānu, the Sun, the lord of the constellations,
with red perfumes and flowers, one shall obtain great health.
The root mantras are proclaimed by their own names, as are the limb mantras;
and like a lotus, the lotus-petal [arrangement] is performed according to one's capacity.
Even if performed with deceit or hypocrisy, worship nevertheless yields fruit when offered with streams of clarified butter,
fuel-sticks, curd, milk, rice, and mung beans.
The oblation performed with a peaceful mind yields the results previously described. This is indeed called the Vaiśvānara vow;
thus ends the Citrabhānu vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Now follows the vow dedicated to the Sun:

he who observes a fast on the seventh lunar day should, at the conclusion of the year, give a golden lotus and cows according to his capacity, accompanied by a water-pot, at the end of the fire-oblation.
This is known as the Saura-vrata, which bestows the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the Saura-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Now follows the Dhānya-saptamī-vrata:
having worshipped the Sun and seven kinds of grain on the white (śukla) seventh lunar day.
One who eats only at night gives what is fit for a householder, together with salt.
The household implements belong to the house.
It carries across seven other members of the lineage as well as oneself.
This is called the *dhānyavrata* (grain-vow), a vow that bestows the happiness of grain.
Thus concludes the Dhānyasaptamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Now follows the Bhāskara-vrata:
"The man who, having observed a fast on the sixth day, [performs it] on the seventh..."
He who performs the Śrāddha according to the rules, saying "May the Sun be pleased," shall be liberated from all diseases and attain the heavenly world.
Thus ends the Bhāskaravrata as declared in the Kālikāpurāṇa. Now follows the Tapovrata:
On the seventh lunar day of the month of Māgha, one should remain clothed in half of a night-garment and become a giver of cows.
One attains the heavenly world; this is what is called the path of austerity in this context.
Thus ends the vow of austerity (tapovrata) as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Now follows the Arkasaptamī vow:
one should drink water mixed with the pulp of the Arka plant.
In succession, one adds one to each of the fourteen [categories] once again.
Having completed the observance over two years, it shall be fulfilled;
for this Arkasaptamī is the granter of all desires and is well-pleased.
Thus ends the Arkasaptamī vow as declared in the Brahmā Purāṇa.
Now follows the Putrīyasaptamī vow.
Puṣkara said:
O best of the twice-born, O Rāma, in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the bright fortnight,
one who is self-restrained and pure should observe the Putrīyā Saptamī.
Or else, listen to what was done by that ritual of one desiring a son.
One who desires a son should perform the *putrīyā* rite, which bestows sons. Having eaten sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and bathed his head, he should worship the Sun-god;
then, sleeping on the ground, on the second day he [should bathe] with the urine of a bull.
Having bathed and likewise anointed himself, he should draw a mandala in an auspicious place;
there, he should arrange an eight-petaled lotus with beautiful colors.
In the very center of its pericarp,
one should worship the Sun-god with red sandalwood paste, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Having thus performed the worship of Bhāskara, the bestower of all desires, with foods to be chewed, foods to be swallowed, as well as drinks, incenses, and lamps;
Having abandoned all desires, one should eat only at night;
having become one for whom the teeth serve as a mortar, one should perform this vow for a year.
At the conclusion of the vow, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brahmins according to one's capacity;
likewise, a feast for the twice-born should be prepared, consisting primarily of the three sweets.
And at the end of the night, he should likewise sleep on the ground once again.
O Rāma, this supreme vow for obtaining a son, which destroys all impurities, has been declared by me to you as a means of propitiating the best of gods.
And likewise, this has been stated as the destroyer of all diseases.
Thus ends the Putrīyasaptamī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follows the Kāmavrata:
having likewise worshipped the wife of Sūrya, Suvarcasā, on the seventh lunar day, [one should proceed].
One obtains all desired objects; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus ends the Kāmavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Now follows the Śailavrata:
by worshipping the desired mountain at that time, one shall become happy.
The worship, however, is performed with the mantra.
Thus ends the Śailavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follows the Saridvrata.
"By always worshipping the beloved river, one becomes a partaker of merit.
Thus ends the Saridvrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Now follows the Vahni-vrata: "By performing the worship of Vahni (Fire), one attains the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Thus ends the Vahni-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Now, the Vāyu-vrata:
"By performing the complete worship of Vāyu, one attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the Vāyu-vrata as described in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Now follows the vow of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣivrata).
Having worshipped the seven sages, it is likewise remembered as being established in the Soma sacrifice;
thus one attains those seven [heavens] and finds the state beyond the sages (atimārṣya).
Thus ends the Saptarṣi-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follows the Muni-vrata:
on the seventh lunar day, O tiger among sages, one should worship the desired sages.
One obtains the fruit of sacred study and enjoys the fruit of that abode.
Thus ends the vow of the sages as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. Now follows the *Abhīṣṭasaptamī* vow:
having worshipped the oceans, the man should then light nine lamps.
And from the netherworlds, O highly fortunate one, he attains his desired earth.
Thus ends the Abhīṣṭasaptamī-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa.
[792] Now follows the Saptamīloka-vrata.
O King, by honoring these seven worlds, one shall become happy;
likewise, one shall attain great wisdom and an incomparable state.
Thus ends the Saptamīloka-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follows the Nadī-vrata:
"The Maṅgās are of seven kinds, and likewise the goddess Sarasvatī."
A person who worships [it] certainly attains the seven knowledges.
Thus ends the Nadīvrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follows the Sugativrata:
having performed the worship of Surendra, one shall indeed attain the supreme state.
Thus ends the Sugati-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Now follows the Jayanta-vrata:
one should worship Jayanta, the son of Śakra, and shall become happy.
Thus ends the Jayantavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Now follows the Vidhānadvādaśasaptamīvrata. Listen, O Nārada, to the determination regarding these aforementioned Saptamīs.
He who would attain peace through remembrance [of him] is freed from all sins.
[793] They know that bowing to Śātanā brings about the destruction of all evils;
therefore, one should approach the Sustainer there according to the rules for fasting.
On the seventh day of the month of Caitra, one obtains the fruit of an Atirātra sacrifice;
and he who worships Parjanya on the seventh day of the month of Vaiśākha [obtains the same].
One indeed obtains the fruit of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice there by beholding Vibhā, the radiance of the sun; for the word *bhā* signifies both pervasion and light.
Vibhā is indeed the Nirukta, and Vibhāvasu himself [is the deity].
He who worships Varuṇa on the seventh day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, [attains his goal].
A human being obtains the fruit of ten stages of mastery when the gods,
for the sake of nectar, went forth with shouts of victory.
They worship the goddess Jayā, and that is remembered as her nectar;
in the month of Āṣāḍha, a person should worship the Sun on the seventh lunar day.
One obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage;
for on the seventh day, the Asuras and Danavas were thus conquered by the gods.
Because the three worlds were won after the gods, including Indra, propitiated him during the fear of Tāraka in battle, it is therefore called Vijaya-saptamī.
On that day, the person who worships me with devotion,
having bathed and properly sipped water, wearing white garments and with palms joined in reverence;
Always wearing the sacrificial thread, a celibate student, with senses subdued, free from anger, not fickle, steady-minded, and composed in concentration.
Devoted to me and with senses fully controlled, he should likewise perform meditation and worship along with Samba;
furthermore, he must not touch a woman in her menses nor one who has recently given birth.
One should not address a group of women, nor should one ever engage in sexual union with them;
likewise, one should not step over urine, excrement, or spittle.
Then, having sprinkled [the site] according to the rule with water purified by mantras,
the sacrificer, seeking a boon, should smear it with clay.
With flowers offered at the appropriate times, and with incense dear to the Sun,
as well as with lamps, parched grain, barley, mung beans, sesame seeds, and white mustard.
The wise one should indeed worship with sandalwood and other heart-pleasing fragrances and with mandalas;
in the first location of the pedestal, the world of earth (bhūrloka) is proclaimed.
In the second [sphere] is Bhuvarloka; Sva is established in the third;
Saharloka is in the fourth, while Janaloka is in the fifth.
The world of heat (tapoloka) is indeed in the sixth, while the world of truth (satyaloka) is in the seventh;
he who, endowed with faith and devotion, should worship this mandala, [attains these realms].
The gods who pervade the seven worlds would be honored by him who worships the circle of friends with both play and laughter.
He too rejoices, free from all feverish distress, together with the dwellers of heaven—
those who possess virtuous conduct, discipline, and compassion, and who are endowed with self-restraint and purity.
O Brahmin, on this earth, there is no food whatsoever that is not fit to be eaten by those who are endowed with auspicious conduct and who contemplate the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras.
With sacrifices, offerings, and well-prepared vessels of oblations,
as well as with milk-rice, rice-and-pulse mixtures, various kinds of foods, and meats.
With excellent fruits and roots, as well as vegetables dear to the sages,
[the vessels] were likewise filled with curd, filled with milk, and filled with molasses.
A vessel filled with parched grain should be offered, and the mantra should be recited again and again;
at the time of conjunction (saṅgava), one should worship with devotion astrologers who are endowed with virtuous conduct.
When they are satisfied, the God is pleased and grants all desires;
hear now from me as I proclaim the fruit of that merit.
They flourish with sons and grandsons, and with wealth, grain, cattle, and sheep;
horses, gold, garments, and male and female servants are obtained.
Those women who worship the Sun with devotion on the seventh lunar day shall become radiant,
illustrious, and adorned with every ornament.
For they shall become beloved of their husbands and their own kinsmen,
and they shall rejoice happily together with their husbands in the world of the Sun.
Returning again to the human state, they are born indeed into great families possessing vast wealth, and they become my devotees.
By giving cows, gold, garments, jewels, pearls, and then wealth, one who bestows these on the Śukla Vijaya-saptamī shall indeed be gratified.
And one should worship with various kinds of offerings out of devotion,
such as full vessels of wine and the like, as well as side dishes and honeyed sweets.
Rice of the śāli variety, as well as meat, various kinds of vegetables,
fruits according to the season, curd, milk, ghee, and honey.
Whatever gift is given on the seventh day becomes inexhaustible;
because of that, one attains victory over the three worlds, and thus it is called Vijayasaptamī.
On the seventh day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, a person should worship the Sun;
liberated from all sins, he shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
On the seventh day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, a person should worship Tvaṣṭṛ;
he obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and attains great prosperity.
The sage then declared that austerity to be named Santapana;
furthermore, through its connection with Marīci, it is called Marīcasaptamī.
I shall now proclaim its fruit, which is both auspicious and meritorious;
beginning from the very first Brahmā, it was formerly [attained] by the gods together with Indra.
The Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and birds, the great Ṛṣis and serpents, the mountains, the Vidyādharas, and the hosts of Pitṛs, together with the throngs of Apsarases.
Those of great splendor await the rising of the Blessed One just as they do that of the sun, and as sandalwood trees await their own kindling by heaps of wood.
And the blessed Lord Fire, the sun with its seven horses,
mounted upon a smokeless chariot-body, having Aruṇa as his charioteer.
The light of the lamp rises up, illuminating the sky with its rays;
it is honored by the asuras accompanied by shouts of victory.
Likewise, the forest that lies within is known as Ādityavana;
it is a hundred yojanas in width and ten times that in length.
There those many trees have broad branches in the form of sense objects;
from them arises the wind, which is entirely dependent upon sense objects.
One should always apply to living beings diseases of various kinds,
so that those beings of middling nature [may worship] the Sun with ninety-six [offerings].
I take refuge in the God of gods for the sake of pacifying the afflictions of the earth;
he destroys the disease arising from the bodies of sentient beings.
It cures leprosy, ringworm, pustules, itching, vitiligo, elephantiasis,
as well as dropsy, abdominal tumors, diarrhea, and internal abscesses.
Heart disease, jaundice, abdominal distension along with throat obstruction,
headache, pain in the flanks, eye pain, and choleraic vomiting.
The one called ādhmāna, the one consisting of vāta, the one with sāman, the one called vāta itself,
the one from wasting (kṣaya), the second type of kāsa, and the one arising from the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika).
Constant loss of strength, disease, and what is undigestible for the stomach—
these and many other diseases that cause the gradual destruction [of the body].
And while intending the destruction of beings, he bestows long life;
for in the mere twinkling of an eye, the Sun has passed beyond.
Having ascended the mountain of sunrise and illuminating all directions,
the Blessed Sun remains for a moment with his rays tipped with poison.
As soon as that [moon] has risen, being pure and with a restrained mind,
one should undertake the twelve-month vow on the seventh day of the bright fortnight.
Having bathed and become pure, one who is self-restrained and compassionate toward all beings should face the east and, having offered an oblation of flowers to the great-souled Mihira,
should then offer incense while circumambulating.
Having prostrated before the deity with his knees, he should place black pepper in his mouth;
having sipped water, the man should then observe a fast for either the full day or the night.
Then, having risen at dawn, pure, bathed, and wearing clean garments,
he should become self-restrained, facing the east, and placing the sun within his heart.
One should worship with perfumes, garlands, and fragrant incense;
according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should offer these to Bhāskara.
With offerings, as well as with foods and well-prepared vessels for the bali-oblation,
one should give according to the mantra and recite it again and again.
The mantra is: *Oṃ namo sūryāya*.
Thus, Vardhamāna [attains] the rays for twelve months.
Listen as I proclaim the fruit of merit for that person who shall observe the seventh day of the bright fortnight.
Having become well-clothed, handsome, fragrant, well-adorned, elegantly dressed,
and beautiful in form, that man possessed a radiance like the sun.
In this world, having attained long life and abundant enjoyments,
surrounded by sons and grandsons, and provided with male and female servants;
From here and there, one shall obtain great happiness in the heavenly world;
and returning from there once more, one is born into a great family.
For twelve months, a man who is consecrated shall become wealthy, possessed of many sons, and endowed with enjoyments.
The seventh-day rite is called Marīca-saptamī after the name of Marīci;
he who worships Indra on the seventh day of the month of Bhādrapada [attains merit].
Having fasted there according to the prescribed rules, one obtains the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice;
[this was taught] by the great seers, such as Bhṛgu and others, who were seekers of dharma and rich in asceticism.
But Āditya, who had been honored with vegetables, roots, milk, and fruits,
revealed himself visibly as the thousand-eyed Lord of Rays;
pleased, he invited the one whose wealth is asceticism to choose a boon, saying, "I am gratified."
The sages said:
"If the Sun-god is pleased, let this alone be our boon:
that our ascetic merit shall not diminish through envy, pride, or anger."
Having said to them, "Let it be so," he vanished right there;
for the thousand-rayed one of great splendor was pleased with us because of the fruits.
Endowed with great fruit, this is named Phala-saptamī;
listen as I describe the procedure for this very Phala-saptamī.
According to the previously described procedure, having bathed, being pure, wearing white garments, and remaining self-restrained while facing the east, he should [worship] the rising sun.
Adorned with a white garland and having applied ointment to the ground,
and having sprinkled it with fragrant flower garlands and gazed upon the sun;
Having prostrated himself on his knees and praised the Sun with words,
he offered flowers of fragrant scent as a sacrificial gift.
Having offered aloe-wood incense and having gathered a heap of fruits before him as they are available, one should present them to the Sun.
Of mangoes, hog-plums, and rose-apples; of wood-apples, *tinduka* trees, and *parūṣaka* and *kovidāra* trees; and likewise of date-palms.
Fruits indeed should be given; one should avoid what is cut or withered.
The observer of the vow, being self-controlled, should eat with particular care and purity.
Thus, through these twelve common characteristics, a man becomes like a fruit-bearing creeper;

Endowed with wealth and grain, surrounded by sons and grandsons,
and having enjoyed human pleasures in this world, he is glorified in the realm of the Sun.
But returning from there once more, he attains greatness;
he is born into a great family possessing many yogis and abundant wealth.
The Brāhmaṇa shall become one with all the gods; the Kṣatriya shall be victorious;
the Vaiśya also obtains enjoyments; and the Śūdra shall attain happiness.
If a man wishes to practice agriculture, he should do so after worshipping Phalasaptamī;

Whatever grain one sows in the field, that shall yield abundant fruit;

A person sells his wares without any difficulty and lives happily;
for in this world, his profit becomes highly fruitful, as its result is great.
If a person should ever employ wealth for the sake of profit, he shall obtain great profit; he shall receive back exactly what he has invested.
By means of women, one obtains fruit—namely sons as well as daughters.
Thus has been described to you the gratifying Phala-saptamī, which bestows rewards.
Then, in the month of Āśvayuja,
they worship Vivasvat with various kinds of food and drink, as well as fruits, roots, and juices.
A wise person should cause a cart to be given furnished with all these [ingredients];
therefore it is called a "cart" (śakaṭa), for this is the root-meaning that is intended.
Therefore, because food is offered to the Arhat, that [act] is indeed beyond reproach;

All seeds and medicinal herbs, as well as all the waters that flow from the netherworld (pātāla),
Pṛthī indeed bestows there at the appropriate time, in accordance with the king's will.
For the nourishment of medicinal herbs and for the increase of strength in men, there is also that which is without cooked rice;

For one year, with diligent effort, a man should worship the Sun during both fortnights according to the procedure previously described.
Now hear from me the fruit of merit resulting from their observance of the fast;
listen as I speak, for that too must be avoided.
One should avoid sexual intercourse, honey, meat, and the products of the cow; likewise, one should avoid falsehood, giving testimony for a family, and the property of others.
One should avoid birth-impurity, death-impurity, and a woman in her courses;
he who protects these during the two months [of impurity] is like a father protecting his own children.
Having protected it with effort both in this world and the next,
those who perform the Saptamī vow according to this ritual method [attain the fruit].
A man obtains all his desires and attains a worthy wife;

And having returned from there again, he is born into a great family,
which is delighted by lutes and harps resplendent with jewels and lapis lazuli.
Being sung to by apsarases, he shall indeed attain eternal happiness;
endowed with divine marks, he is honored in the world of the Sun.
When that austerity is exhausted, the man, having attained the earth,

Resembling the sun to the worlds and as dear as the young moon,
he practices again and again through that very yoga of cultivation.
Whoever should worship me on the day of Mitra with the splendor of Mitra,
having become pure and fasting, being entirely devoted to my adoration.
One should honor the Brāhmaṇas and the Bhojakas according to one's ability;

A human being obtains his desired objects especially when the sun is in the threefold sphere of the image and the sky.

But those worlds which are the fourteenth, situated in the very center of the cosmic egg,
cease their coming and going by relying on the causal relationship of action.

Śakra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera preceded by Agni—

Having worshipped Pūṣan on the seventh lunar day of the month of Pauṣa with his senses restrained, one attains the memory of past births; there is no doubt that he performs the Naramedha sacrifice.
In the month of Pauṣa, those ancestors, both divine and human, attained excellent nourishment;
