She has been declared as "Īpsitā" (the Desired One) by Viṣṇu himself for the sake of the worlds.
A man who worships Bhaga on the seventh lunar day of the twelfth month always obtains the fruit of giving much gold.

It is better for me that these [mantras], whose resolutions are established by the world and perfected by the Siddhas, are merely remembered;

On the twelve seventh lunar days, the Sun is to be worshipped; one attains health in his likeness. Worship, indeed, is performed with mantras. Thus, one should constantly worship the Sun throughout the twelve months;
by that, one performs eight thousand sacrifices accompanied by all the ritual fees.
He would be as one who has bathed at all sacred fords and bestowed all gifts;
indeed, he should fast every fortnight on the seventh lunar day while performing worship of the Sun.
He becomes beloved among women and they indeed become submissive to him;

One attains the gateway to liberation and moves through the sky like the sun,
according to the secret method revealed by the great seer Nārada.
Thus end the various *dvādaśasaptamī* vows as declared in the *Ādityapurāṇa*.
[805] Now follows the *puraścaraṇasaptamī* vow.
The sages said:
O son of Sūta, tell us about the seventh [topic], known as *puraścaraṇa*.
By what procedure should it be performed, and at what time should it be undertaken?
Sūta said:
I shall proclaim to you that which was formerly told by Mārkaṇḍeya to King Rohitāśva when he questioned him with devotion.
The great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, a brahmin who remembers seven kalpas,
was questioned by Rohitāśva and by Harita, the son of Candra.
Rohitāśva said:
"O virtuous sage, tell me some means for the destruction of that sin which a man commits, whether through ignorance or even knowingly."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "In this world, a threefold sin arises for men: that which is mental, that which is vocal, and the third, that which is physical."
Once remorse has been felt, whatever mental sin arises from what has been said perishes at that very moment.
By the word of the gurus, all of that indeed perishes;
such is the rite for the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa)—this truth has been spoken by me.
He should offer that food-offering (naivedya) to the foremost of Brahmins as prescribed;
by performing the penance exactly as stated, he shall thereafter attain purification.
Alternatively, if the king, having discovered the truth, inflicts punishment upon him,
he thereby attains purification, even if he were indeed guilty.
He who, out of shame before the foremost of Brahmins, does not speak at all,
nor whom the king does not recognize, shall die while still within his own body.
And Vaivasvata Yama himself is the one who executes its judgment;
therefore, a wise person, having committed a sin, should strive with effort to avoid further sin.
O Lord of Sages, an expiation must be performed for all prescribed sins exactly as declared by Brahmā.
Please explain some vow, or a gift, or even a fire-oblation,
by the performance of which one becomes free from sin through the practice of *puraścaraṇa*.
Indeed, that man who performs subtle vows in every respect is somehow capable of performing expiations for all [transgressions].
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O King, there is a meritorious vow known as *puraścaraṇa*,
and [another] known as *puraścaraṇa-saptamī*, which is dear to the Sun.
Just as, O King, a scribe born of Yama, being present there with his whole soul,
erases a hundred records of sin by means of various [virtuous deeds].
Therefore, O Great King, act according to my words as they truly are,
so that you may be liberated from all evil arising from the body.

Salutation to Pataṅga for the feet; to Mārtaṇḍa for the knees;

And [he offered] his arm to Padmahasta, his heart to Tīkṣṇadīdhiti,

Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed ritual, one should place camphor as the form [of the deity],

taking water mixed with red sandalwood in a conch shell.

whatever misdeed has been committed, whether through ignorance or even with knowledge—
"O God, once the expiation has been performed, please accept my offering of honor (arghya).

Having given him food and a sacrificial fee according to one's ability,

Having joined his palms in reverence and gazing up at the sun,
and having bowed to the sun, he should recite this mantra:
"O Lord, this vow has been undertaken by me in your presence;
O Bhāskara, may it reach its fulfillment without obstacle through your grace."
Then, O prince, when the month of Phalguna has arrived,
one should worship the God with Kunda flowers according to that very same procedure.
One should offer incense of guggulu and an offering of cooked rice;
cow dung is prescribed as the substance for consumption for the purification of all sins.
In the month of Caitra, the astrologers have declared that one should consume incense derived from dates and drink water infused with kuśa grass to attain purification of the body.
In Vaiśākha, one should worship with *kiṃśuka* flowers and perform the rites according to the rules;
the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of ghee, meat from the village, and cakes.
Then, O King, the consumption of curd must be performed as a purification of the body;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, worship with the *pāṭalā* flower should be offered to the Sun.
Incense made of guggulu is said to be supremely pleasing to the Sun;
for the food offering, parched grain is prescribed, and clarified butter is remembered as the substance for consumption.
Ghee causes the destruction of sins for the sake of purification from the tawny one (Kapilā).
O King, in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the Sun with *munipuṣpa* flowers.
O King, one should offer incense and agallochum with supreme faith;
the food offering is said to be *ghārikā*, and the consumption is with honey.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the sharp-rayed Sun with the Kadamba flower;
for the food offering, one should present sweetmeats (modaka), and as incense, one should bring Tagara.
Having obtained water from a cow's horn, one is liberated from all sins;
on the full moon day of Bhādrapada, one should first offer milk as a food offering.
Incense produced from nakhi, and milk as the food offering;
in the month of Āśvina, worship with lotuses and fried cakes with ghee as the naivedya.
Incense is declared to be saffron, and camphor is prescribed for consumption;
the worship of the Sun-god with Tulasī is proclaimed as the duty in the month of Kārttika.
O King, the food offering consists of delicious sweets, and the incense is saffron-based;
the consecrated water known as *calicaṅga* purifies all sins.
In the month of Saumya (Mārgaśīrṣa), one should perform worship with Bhṛṅgarāja;
the food offering should be Karṇikā flowers, and the incense should be made from jaggery.
The consumption of *kakkola* fruit is for the propitiation of Bhāskara;
worship of the Sun with heaps of *śatapatra* flowers is prescribed for the month of Pauṣa.
One should perform all those things previously mentioned for consumption, including the innate incense and the food offering together with the *kulīya* cakes.
At the conclusion, O best of kings, one should give to a brahmin— born of a household of those who share in the six [occupations]— for the purification of all sins.
Then, O best of kings, one should provide desired food according to one's own capacity;
he who thus observes this Saptamī born of the Sun—
[810] "One who is completely liberated from all evil attains a state of stainless purity.
The Brāhmaṇas said:
"Thus was it indeed told of old to the wise Rohitāśva."
Since Mārkaṇḍeya performed it, O illustrious one, you too should perform it.
Thus ends the *Puraścaraṇa-saptamī-vrata*, as declared in the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Thus [ends the section] composed by Śrī Hemādri, the sovereign of all sciences and master of all faculties, under the auspices of the illustrious Mahādeva, the supreme king of kings.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, within the section on vows (*vratakhaṇḍa*), the observances of the seventh lunar day (*saptamīvratāni*).
[811] Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Now, regarding the vows of the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī-vrata),
which serve as a garland for the pavilion of the three worlds and are like a creeper of fame for the minds of people:
Gold and other such things completely destroy all affliction; thus has the vow for the eighth lunar days been described.
In that regard, the Jayantī vow is described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Pulastya said:
"O best of the twice-born, when Rohiṇī occurs on the eighth day of the dark fortnight..."
That lunar day is called Jayantī; it is the remover of all sins.
Whatever sin was committed in childhood, in youth, in middle age, or likewise in old age, that fasted lunar day destroys the evil accumulated over many births.
In the Vahnipurāṇa,
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O King, when in the Kali age there occurs the Rohiṇī [nakṣatra] on the eighth day of the dark fortnight..."
She is declared by name to be Jayantī; she should be observed as a fast with great effort.
O King, Govinda, being well-disposed on that lunar day, washes away the threefold karma of men committed throughout seven births in this world.
And there, O protector of the earth, fasting is prescribed according to the rules as the destroyer of great sins; of this there is no doubt in the world.
O King, in the Tretā, the Dvāpara, and even in the ancient Kṛta Yuga,
this [day] was observed as a fast by the learned when it was conjoined with Rohiṇī.
The sages who discourse on Brahman broke their fast upon separation;
for when a vow based on conjunction is undertaken, it is broken even if only one person is separated from the group.
In that very place one should perform the breaking of the fast; thus do those who know the Vedas understand.
Therefore listen, O protector of the earth: when the Tāmasa Kali age has arrived, there will be a supreme vow concerning the birth of Vāsudeva.

The fifth case ending is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*) with respect to birth. He will become [the son] born of Devakī; however, Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, was already propitiated by Devakī in the past.
O best of kings, at the conjunction of Rohiṇī, at midnight—
Govinda was born in the form of a child with four arms.
Having seen the Lord of the worlds and having bowed to him whose banner is Garuḍa,
Devakī, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words.
Devakī said:
"O lotus-eyed one, out of affection I cannot endure separation;
therefore, O Madhusūdana, having beheld such a form as this, I am filled with apprehension."
Vāsudeva said:
"O beautiful lady, you shall see me without doubt this very day;
O Devakī, I shall come into your sight in the form of a child."
If Rohiṇī occurs at midnight on the eighth lunar day conjoined with the seventh,
that seventh day shall be meritorious as long as the moon and sun endure.
Those fortunate men who shall worship you, O Goddess, with flowers and other offerings on this day, [shall see] me established upon your lap.
Those who offer arghya at midnight when the moon is conjoined with Rohiṇī,
and the wise man who has fashioned an image of Indra made of silver together with Rohiṇī— [they shall obtain great merit].
O best of men, one should place the arghya offering there in a vessel made of gold or silver, measuring twelve finger-breadths in width.
One obtains all desires both in this world and in the next,
by taking water in a conch shell together with flowers, fruits, and gold.
Having placed one knee upon the ground and offered the *arghya* oblation to the Moon,
which brings benefit to the worlds,
a person immediately attains his own sinless state even through mere recitation.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should [worship] a couple fashioned from darbha grass.
Having established Anagha and Anaghī, together with many sons,
in an auspicious place smeared with cow dung;
Having bathed, one should worship with fragrant flowers and unguents,
while reciting the mantras spoken in the Ṛgveda and mentally contemplating the Daṇḍaka hymn.
His wife, born from his bones, [gave birth to] the sinless Vāsudeva and the group of sons beginning with Pradyumna, as described in the Harivaṃśa.
"Oṃ ato devā avantu... and other such mantras are prescribed for the twice-born; "ato devā avantu... and so forth are well-known from the *Bahvṛca* [Ṛgveda].

With fruits and tubers produced in their season, and with new, auspicious water-jars.
A golden pitcher and a water-jar;

"I shall not kill this living being; this is the truth, the great truth proclaimed by the Great One.

O Pārtha, he who performs this worship of Anagha year after year,

Having attained great fame in this world, one who dies goes to the abode of Hari;

Then, by means of the conjunction with the eighth lunar day, one shall attain perfection.

Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, listen to the supreme Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow, which removes all sins.
The propagation of the Dharma in the world is the supreme means for pleasing Rudra.
Then, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the full moon day, the observer of the vow should first perform the cleansing of the teeth and undertake the discipline of fasting or eating only at night.
The classification is established by way of the distinction between those that are capable and those that are incapable:
the *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *jambū*, and *kadambaka*;
as well as those born from *drākṣā*, *kaustubha*, *kāmrātaka*, *karīra*, *arjuna*, and *jāti*.
One should perform the cleansing of the teeth every month in due order,
using *karavīra*, *kumbhapuṣpa*, *maruka*, and likewise *kuṃśuka*.
Sandalwood, bilva leaves, pāṭalā, bhoja-mallikā, jasmine,
and śatapatra flowers, or golden flowers, [should be offered] in sequence.
Milk-rice porridge, rice-and-meat dishes, sweetmeats, and dumplings; stuffed cakes, fried pastries, flour-cakes, and *adhibhakta*, as well as *pūrikā*.
Jaggery-rice, sugar, and likewise clarified butter—
these are the food offerings for Śiva before the Guru for one year on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
A celibate student who has conquered anger and is devoted to the recitation of auspicious mantras,
having performed his morning ablutions and other rites during this division of the day;
Having gone to the abode of Śiva, O Pārtha, before the Guru and Śiva,
one should remain a celibate student, with anger conquered, and devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Having performed the rites of bathing and so forth here during the division of the day,
O Pārtha, go to the temple of Śiva preceded by the offering of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Then, having performed the ceremonial bath of the Liṅga with excellent water and having anointed it with sandalwood paste, one should worship it with the finest flowers.
And with devotion, incense mixed with *vāguru* should be offered to the God of gods by the best of the twice-born, using the *Śivasūkta* and the *Śivasūktas*.
Likewise, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship [the deity] as Śaṅkara;
having first consumed cow dung, one should sleep at night with the senses subdued.
O King, by performing a fire-offering (homa) with black sesame seeds before Śiva every month,
a person obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Thus, having worshipped the Great Lord named Śambhu under the Puṣya asterism,
and having consumed clarified butter on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having consumed cow urine, he should sleep on the ground with his senses subdued;
in the month of Māgha, he should worship the Lord of the Gods named Maheśvara.
Having consumed cow’s milk at night, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice;
and in the month of Phālguna, having worshipped Mahādeva, one should consume sesame seeds.
By worshipping Sthāṇu with devotion in the month of Caitra and consuming barley, one obtains the complete fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
By worshipping Śiva in Vaiśākha and consuming water infused with kuśa grass, one undoubtedly attains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
A man shall obtain from devotion the fruit that is gained from the Phalamedha sacrifice;
having worshipped Paśupati in the month of Jyeṣṭha, he should drink water from the horns of cows.
One obtains the unsurpassed fruit of giving a thousand cows;
in the month of Āṣāḍha, one devoted to worship should honor the deity named Ugra.
One who, having conquered the senses, eats cow dung at night after worshipping the deity named Sarvanāman in the month of Śrāvaṇa, shall obtain the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice.
One should cause [the disciple] to eat the tip of an *arka* leaf; therein one should worship the Lord of All.
One undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a sacrifice involving much gold.
On the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the deity named Tryambaka;
by consuming a bilva leaf at night, one obtains the fruit of gifting an entire village.
In the month of Āśvina, one devoted to worship should honor the deity named Bhava;
by consuming rice-water, one obtains the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Having worshipped the one named Rudra in the month of Kārttika, one should drink water;
thus one obtains the fruit of teaching all four Vedas.
One observing the vow should consume liquid substances once, like the *āpośāna* rite,
having taken them with the thumb and the ring finger, so that the water falls [from the fingers].
Having thus worshipped with flowers and other offerings as prescribed, the devotee should pray to the Lord with this mantra:
O Soul of the Universe, O Great God, that which was ordained by you for this vow—
the cleansing of the teeth, the food offering, the consumption of flowers, and so forth— [is to be performed].
Whether through delusion or greed, that which was not performed according to the mantras has been fully accomplished by your grace, O Śambhu, O Great Sage.
Month after month, one should thus worship Maheśvara in the form of the Liṅga,
or Rudra in the form of an image, accompanied by Soma and seated upon a water-pot.
[Soma] together with Umā. Regarding the creation of the form, however, [it is stated] in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:

O descendant of Yadu, mirrors and blue lotuses should be placed in the two left [hands];
Śumbhu should be single-mindedly devoted, a giver, and one whose body is as dear as that of his beloved.
The three-eyed Mahādeva, adorned with all ornaments—
the practitioner of the vow should worship Śaṅkara according to the rules, preceded by the mantra.
On all the eighth days of the dark fortnight, one should always feed Śiva-devoted ascetics and Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability, and one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
At the conclusion of the vow, having fashioned a golden image of Śaṅkara—
meaning Śaṅkara accompanied by Umā—

One should perform a great festival with perfumes, flowers, fruits, incense, and various auspicious food offerings, as well as through worship, hymns of praise, and sacred narratives.
Likewise, one should offer to the Lord a bed provided with all its accessories,
as well as a canopy, a fan, a water-pot, a bell, a pair of sandals, and so forth.
Then, at the time of dawn, having bathed and worshipped the wielder of the trident (Śiva),
and having performed the necessary rites for the Brahmin, one should offer that to Śivā.
Then, having duly said, "May Śiva be ever pleased with me," [he should give] a cow adorned with clothes and ornaments, together with black sesame seeds.
Then, however, one should feed the Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva with devotion,
using milk-rice mixed with clarified butter, and one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

With a mind solely intent on the meditation of Śiva, one should, according to one's ability, give gold, garments, and even the weapons of Śiva, having consecrated them with the *śikhā* [mantra], for the pleasure of Śiva.
Black water-pots filled with water and accompanied by sesame seeds and edible offerings should be provided;
twelve portions of food, along with a pair of an umbrella and sandals, should be given.
A black, milch cow, together with its utensils, should be given to the reciter;
he should proclaim, "May Rudra be pleased with me."
For Rudra, one should provide black water-pots, sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas), and a canopy;
here, one should likewise arrange a black banner equipped with small bells.
O Pārtha, he who thus performs this unsurpassed vow is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
This vow, which yields great fruit, was practiced by Indra and the other thirty-three gods;
they all attained divinity through the power of this very vow.

Virtue, long life, sovereignty over the hosts, the state of being a grasper of virtues, and likewise the non-grasping of faults— O Pāṇḍava, what more need be said here? Śaṅkara is pleased by this vow of the eighth day of the dark fortnight when it is performed with devotion.
Not so by austerities, nor by gifts, nor by vows, nor by ablutions at sacred fords;
thus has this Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow been fully described to you, O Pārtha.
Having heard which, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
O King, one whose soul is purified by Śiva, having fasted on this Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow with recitations of the names [of the deity] as they arise during the ritual consumptions,
gives away black water-pots and a black cow.
He who proceeds to that supreme state of the moon-crested Lord.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Listen, O Dālbhya, to another optional vow that bestows progeny upon men.
When this is practiced, there shall be no interruption in the offering of the ancestral rice-balls (piṇḍa).
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Caitra, he who, having bathed with a restrained mind,
worships Kṛṣṇa and performs a ritual offering to Devakī;
Remaining without food, one should chant the name of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the universe;
likewise, while seated, having bathed, or when experiencing hunger, stumbling, and so forth, one should continue chanting.
During the worship of Kṛṣṇa as well, one should recite [the name] seven times;
one should not speak with heretics, those who follow improper occupations, nor with atheists.
At dawn, having bathed with water, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a brāhmaṇa;
and having performed worship, one should eat [the remains] of Kṛṣṇa himself, the Lord of the Universe.
Having fasted for three months during the months of Vaiśākha and Jyeṣṭha,
one should bathe Hari, the Lord of the God of Gods, with clarified butter at the conclusion of the vow.
Having likewise spent three months in the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada,
and similarly in the month of Āśvayuja;
Having fasted, a man should worship the God with sacrificial oblations when the time for breaking the fast has arrived;
likewise, he should do so after fasting during the months of Pauṣa, Māgha, and Phālguna.
When the fourth fast has been completed, one should bathe the Lord Hari with ghee;
this applies likewise to the man or woman who has observed the fast in such a manner.
The continuity [of this merit] is never interrupted at any time for that man or woman who [observes] this eighth day of the dark fortnight.
Having observed the fast with joy, he attains liberation within the three worlds;
and through the abundance of sons and grandsons, he is glorified in heaven after death.
[821] Thus, O Dālbhya, has this Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow been described by me.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Viṣṇu said:
"When the sun has entered Virgo, that which is the eighth day of the dark fortnight..."
And she is the remover of sin, meritorious, and the increaser of Śiva’s bliss.
O Three-eyed One, bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and the worship of ancestors and gods— indeed, every such act performed on that day brings delight to all.
O Sage, a *śrāddha* and a *homa* performed on that day are especially meritorious;
therefore, one should perform the *śrāddha* with great effort and diligence on that occasion.
The wise know that on the fifth day there should be a single meal, and on the sixth, eating only at night;
on the seventh day there should be a fast, and on the eighth day one should worship Śiva.
Having worshipped Śiva with devotion, one should perform the śrāddha for one's father;
having performed the śrāddha according to the rules, one should eat that which was offered to the ancestors.
Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony there after having worshipped the Three-eyed One (Śiva),
for him your ancestors remain satisfied for fifteen years.
Having thus performed this vow for one's own sake alone with such devotion for one's own year,
one should worship the supreme deity, the destroyer of Tripura, by means of his names.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship Śambhu; likewise, others [should worship] Śaṅkara.
In the month of Kārttika, one should worship Śiva, and similarly, everything [is dedicated] in Mārgaśīrṣa.
Likewise, the fierce Īśana is proclaimed for the month of Pauṣa; Mādhava is proclaimed for Māgha;
the one named Ina for Phālguna; and one should proclaim Rudra for Caitra.

likewise, Mahādeva in Āṣāḍha, and Tryambaka in Śrāvaṇa, O twice-born one.
Learn from me these names of the months and the corresponding food-offerings:
cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass.
For the purification of the body, one should consume cow-gallstone, the five products of the cow, earth from Mount Mandara, as well as sesame, food, and milk.

Kuśa grass and flowers, as well as the agasti flower;
sihla, vijaya incense, buffalo fat, and guggulu.
O best of Brahmins, he who thus worships the god Śaṅkara, the destroyer of Tripura,
goes alone to the supreme state.
One should honor the Brahmins, and especially the reciter,
as well as the devotees of Mahādeva with devotion— the twice-born followers of the Pāśupata path.
Thus, he who performs the śrāddha on the eighth lunar day and during the aṣṭakās,
having worshipped Sureśāna along with Śiva, wise brahmins, and sages;
His ancestors remain satisfied,
O tiger among sages, for fifteen divine years— seven, seven, and seven.
Whatever supreme vow one may thus observe with devotion on the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī day,
whatever desire that person may long for, they shall attain it.
One desiring a son shall obtain a son; one desiring wealth shall obtain riches;
a seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge; and one desiring a daughter shall obtain an excellent daughter.
Thus ends the Śivakṛṣṇāṣṭamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Now follows the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī-vrata.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of the Gods, tell me in due order how that entire ritual for the eighth day of the dark fortnight is performed; it must be carried out accordingly.
Īśvara said: Now, when the winter season has arrived, specifically in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
having observed the *nakta* fast and become pure, one should consume cow’s urine at night.
"Having performed the rite at night, it is called the *nakta-kalpa*. Or one may bring food from wherever it is available; as one eats the food, so one should eat.
By that which is consumed or eaten during the night, it is designated as *nakta*."

"By that [fasting] at night, and by having consumed [the food]," means that in some cases it is by having consumed it, and in other cases it is without having consumed it. "Having worshipped Śaṅkara with devotion according to the rite of the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice shall become eightfold."
And one should remember the name of Śaṅkara in the evening, at night, and during the day;
having consumed cow's ghee in the month of Pauṣa, a person should observe the practice of eating only at night.
One who, purified and intent on offering hymns of praise, worships Śambhu with devotion, obtains the merit of eight Vājapeya sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
In the month of Māgha, one should prescribe the practice called Māheśvara, consisting of consuming only milk;
having worshipped Śaṅkara with devotion, one should sleep at night without food.
By chanting the name of Maheśa, one obtains the merit of eight horse-sacrifices;
in the month of Phālguna, however, one should glorify Mahādeva on the dark lunar day.
Having consumed sesame seeds and remained without food, one should recite [the mantra] at night with a concentrated mind;
then, while reciting the name of the God and likewise remembering Śaṅkara.
The fruit of reciting these names in the former instance is said to be eightfold that of the Rājasūya sacrifice; therein, he is called Mahādeva.
In the month of Caitra, having worshipped and honored Sthāṇu while consuming honey,
one should eat according to the prescribed rule at night and sleep during the night without food.
By conquering the great mantra of Sthāṇu, it becomes equivalent to eight horse-sacrifices;
one should indeed worship the god Śiva with water from kuśa grass during the month of Vaiśākha.
Having recited the auspicious mantra there, one obtains the fruit of a human sacrifice;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should drink water from the horns of cows at the shrine named Paśupati.
O Brahmin, by reciting [this] to Paśupati, one obtains the merit of ten million cows;
furthermore, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should proclaim the name "Ugra."
One should consume cow dung there; one shall obtain the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice.
He who recites the Ugra mantra, which bestows all accomplishments, [attains success].
At night, one who is well-purified in mind should consume the *arghya* while recollecting the mantra;
this is declared in the Śrāvaṇa [month] as "Sarva," and its fruit is the destruction of all desires.
One who, well-purified in mind, recites the Tryambaka mantra while remembering the Sun,
is honored in the world of Rudra for more than a hundred crores of years.
He who indeed recites the *ambaka* mantra on the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada and consumes a *bilva* leaf shall obtain the fruit of initiation into the Vedas (*śrutidīkṣā*).
There, with a single-minded and well-cultivated focus, one should recollect the Mother;
O Hero, in the month of Āśvayuja, there is the consumption of rice-water.
One should thus remember the Lord by name and obtain eight lotuses;
furthermore, having consumed curd in the month of Kārttika, one who is well-purified attains Rudra.
He who remembers Rudra, the destroyer of all sins,
at night shall obtain the eightfold fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Devoid of mantra, devoid of ritual action, and devoid of devotion, it does not succeed;
for without mantra, O Goddess, even with effort, it becomes futile.
One should recite this mantra with all effort for that entire duration;
O Goddess, when the vow is completed at the end of the year, there is great fruit,
by whose very grace one attains the state free from all affliction.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "of which mantra. "O Lord of the Gods, by your grace, one should offer the vow to Śambhu during the Hemanta, the Śiśira, and likewise the beautiful Śarad seasons."
"O God, this most honored vow has indeed been completed;
having thus informed you, O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, be present here."
"O Lord of the Gods, by your grace I shall recite [the mantra] according to my ability;
at the end of the year, an offering is prescribed even with bulbs, roots, and fruits."
And one should worship with supreme devotion the Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva and firm in their vows according to one's ability; let this favor be granted to me.
"I shall perform the meritorious *tarpaṇa* (satiating rite) for the vow, as enjoined by Śiva.
(*Tarpaṇa* means fulfillment.
Having thus worshipped, he should afterwards offer various kinds of foods, both solid and soft, in great abundance.
A beautiful, milk-yielding black cow should be given away,
adorned with golden horns, silver hooves, and ornaments of bells.
Clad in a pair of garments, adorned with flowers and garlands, and auspicious—
O beautiful goddess, a cow should be given to the preceptor for the sake of spiritual welfare.
One should know the teacher to be Śiva, and Śiva to be in the form of the teacher;
there is no difference between the two, the teacher and Śiva.
For this reason, O Goddess, men should then worship the Guru,
who constantly delivers them from the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
Neither mother, nor father, nor kinsmen are equal to him;
whatever gift is given to the Guru, Sadāśiva always accepts it.
Therefore, the guru should always be worshipped with every effort;
thus has been told everything regarding this supreme rite on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
The man who performs this rite for a full year,
being fully endowed with all his desires, proceeds to the supreme state.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow as declared in the Devīpurāṇa. Now follows the Lakṣaṇārdrā vow.
Skanda said:
O God, Lord of Gods, I have heard from you the vows that bestow beauty and fortune in this world, and grant both heaven and liberation.
O Lord, please describe that vow by which, through the giving of even a small amount of wealth, one comes to possess dharma, artha, kāma, and beautiful form endowed with excellent qualities.
Īśvara said:
"O child, there is a certain vow based on the conjunction of a lunar day and a lunar mansion;
O King of kings, it occurs when the Ārdrā asterism arises in the month of Nabhasya."
This Umāmāheśvara vow should be observed on earth;
it bestows health, sovereignty, good fortune, and the perfection of physical beauty.
Having had a golden pair fashioned for them according to one's ability,
one should worship Gaurī and Giriśa with devotion at night, having made a formal vow (saṃkalpa).
The form of Umā and Maheśvara should be understood as prescribed for the first Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī.
Having bathed [the image] in turn with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and water,
one should worship it with perfumes and honor it with heaps of flowers.
Having wrapped it with a pair of cloths that are either red, yellow, white, or mixed with red, one should worship it with these mantras.
Salutations to you, Śaṅkara; salutations to the stainless Śiva;
salutations indeed to the self-existent, the infinite, Bhava, and the future one.
Salutations again and again to the All, to the one of universal form, to the Omniscient;
salutations to Īśāna, to Saṃbhava, and to Virūpākṣa Śambhu.
O Great Goddess, renowned as Vasudhā, Lalitā, Śivā, Śāntā,
Raudrī, Mahāvaktṛī, Durgā, and Gaurī— homage be to you!
O you with beautiful lotus feet and eyes like lotus petals, O fair-faced one who faces in all directions;
O Sovereign, O Indrāṇī, O Rudrāṇī, O Rambhā—Goddess, salutations, salutations!
Salutations again and again to Śarva, who possesses all forms and is omniscient;
[I offer] leaves, flowers, water, leaves, fruits, and lotuses with sandalwood paste.
Having completed [the offering] to Ambikā and Īśa, one should utter this mantra:
"Obeisance to Gaurī, the mother of Skanda; obeisance, obeisance to her who is the form of Viṣṇu."
Homage to the Lord of Beings, homage to the Lord of Form!
"Accept this water offering, O Virūpākṣa, entreated by me for the sake of beauty;
together with your wife, O Mahādeva, O God of gods, homage be to you!"
Having offered the *arghya*, one should then offer incense mixed with *aguru*,
as well as a lamp, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel, and various kinds of fruits.
Then, with thirty-two incense sticks firmly prepared for the Sun,
and with an equal number of auspicious wheat-flour cakes made from rice flour;
Having filled it with those [five] characteristics, having made it well-lit and wrapped with thread,
and having provided it with dried food mixed with the five flavors.

One should offer to Umā and Maheśvara, accompanied by the *nāndī* rite, edible foods made of wheat or wheat flour, marked with auspicious signs and the impressions of fish and other symbols; as for the liquids, these are curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugar; and as for the dry food, it is the *modaka* sweetmeat.
First, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin and that golden pair [of figures].
To one who is devoted, who asks for it, who possesses true knowledge, who maintains a family,
who is solely intent upon self-knowledge, and who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
It should not be given to an atheist, nor to one who observes no vows, nor to one whose senses are unsubdued, even if he is characterized by noble lineage, good conduct, and virtuous behavior.
Having given [the gift] to one devoted to Īśvara and having prostrated, he should dismiss him;
then, after eating food with his circle of friends, he should consume as many auspicious marks as there were [gifts].
Then, for half a night, meditating upon Soma, Śiva, and the Queen of the Gods,
he performs thirty-two such [observances]. He who thus observes this vow on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhasya—
This is renowned as the meaning of the characteristics; hear now its fruit.
With his soul purified of all sins and endowed with all sovereign powers, he enjoys all objects of enjoyment together with Maheśa; thereafter, at the reversal of time, [he attains liberation].
He becomes a righteous king, endowed with strength and valor;
he shall possess beauty, good fortune, charm, wealth, long life, and fame.
Having reached the end of his time there, he is then honored in the heavenly world for the duration of a thousand cycles of four yugas, by the grace of Umā and Rudra.
When the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhasya coincides with the lunar mansion Ārdrā,
then one should fashion a golden couple in the forms of Śiva and Girijā, according to their characteristic features.
He who gives a full meal consisting of flour-cakes along with savory juices to his preceptor,
having partaken of that festive feast joined with yoga, shall go to the eternal realm of Sambhu together with the entire universe.
The Ārdrā-vrata as described in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Now, the Soma-vrata. Anilāda said:
Now I shall further proclaim another vow that brings supreme welfare;
listen attentively to its meritorious illustration according to the prescribed rule.

On the day of the moon's conjunction (Monday) and on the eighth day of both fortnights, one should worship Soma according to the prescribed rite with abundant food and a lunar disc upon the emblem of the Moon-crested Lord.

Regarding the two fortnights (*pakṣa*), in both cases the restriction is that the conjunction of the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) and Monday is intended; *prājyānnam* means food consisting largely of clarified butter (*ājya*). One should meditate on Hara in the right half and the all-pervading Hari in the left upper half. By the three qualifiers—“Soma,” “accompanied by the moon,” and “Hari in the left half”—the nature of the left half as being the form of Candra-Hari is stated. Having bathed the *liṅga* as before with substances beginning with clarified butter and ending with sugarcane products—that is, with those known as the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) beginning with clarified butter.
One should smear the right half with sandalwood mixed with moon-essence (camphor), and the left half with saffron and agallochum; likewise, one should prepare a thick *arghya* offering.
With [incense] joined with camphor and joined with *indu*, and with thick *uśīra*;
one should likewise worship the portion of Hara with gold and the moon. One should especially worship the portion of Hari with a pearl and sapphire.
With a moonstone joined by the moon,
and subsequently encircling it with auspicious flowers, one should have a flower-pavilion constructed;
then one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) again with twenty-five sets of five [offerings].

With both hands joined at the heart, one should bow down again and again with a mental disposition directed toward both the Goddess and the God, according to the ritual procedure for the lustration (*nīrājana*) consisting of meditation upon Hari and Hara. One should also present the food offering (*naivedya*) with auspicious edible foods prepared with clarified butter.
Having honored the Brahmins who observe their vows as well as the Fire-god,
Vibhāvasu is Agni.
Having fed couples together, one should honor them according to one's ability.
O observer of noble vows, having worshipped one's parents on the eighth day according to this rite, [one attains the fruit].
Those two parents are indeed the Goddess and the God.
Now listen to what must be performed at the end of that year:
having worshipped the two pairs of white and yellow [squares] according to the previously stated rule.
One should likewise provide a canopy, as well as banners and small bells;
or else, by means of the movement of incense, two very beautiful lamp-trees.
The movement of incense refers to the burning of incense; the two lamp-trees are supports for lamps shaped like trees.
Having arranged these and other such items as before, one should perform the feast.
Indeed, he who shall do this for five years will undoubtedly [attain success].
Having reached both worlds, he shall go to the state that is free from suffering;
those who live without wavering in their resolve should practice with self-restraint.
One should perceive that the river itself is manifest here in human form;
one should not touch food given by a wicked person, nor indeed shall one become miserable.
He is never at any time afflicted by fevers, seizing spirits, or similar ailments.
In that vow, worship and fire-offerings (homa) are performed with name-mantras.
Thus ends the Somavrata as described in the Kālikāpurāṇa.
Now follows the Śaṅkarārkavrata.
Anilāda said:
Then, by this path, having reached that very auspicious eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) through conjunction with the Sun or according to the previously mentioned procedure, a man—
However, the wise man should worship the Sun residing in the right eye;
he should join it with a ruby and gold—listen now to this application.
Having applied saffron and red sandalwood below the forehead,
one should draw a circle in the center and worship Hara there as before.

The meaning is that, having applied a coating in the shape of a half-moon and a circle in its center, one should place a gold-mounted ruby in the middle of the circle and fashion the eye in the form of the sun.
In the absence of rubies and the like, one should employ gold everywhere;
for that [gold] is the supreme seed of Rudra and is always pure.
A white garland, excellent bark garments, and an offering of food drenched in ghee [should be presented];
the remainder of the ritual details is to be performed according to the previously established injunctions.
But having stayed here on the seventh lunar day, one who has conquered the senses should worship Śaṅkara conjoined with the Sun, and then consume cow's ghee as his fast-breaking meal.
Having fasted and observed the fast,
one should perform this according to the previously mentioned rule for the ritual of the five trees;
by doing so, having enjoyed pleasures in the worlds of the Sun and other deities, one shall go to the Supreme.
Having crossed over this, one becomes powerful, undepressed, and dear to one's own kin;
moreover, in this world, one shall become wealthy and possessed of followers.
Thus ends the Śaṅkarārkavrata as declared in the Kālikāpurāṇa.
[833] Now follows the Somāṣṭamīvrata.
Nandi said:
Now I shall further describe another supreme vow that brings about the highest welfare— the venerable Śivaloka-vrata, which bestows all prosperity upon men.
On the eighth day of both fortnights,
one should duly worship Soma, who bears the crescent moon upon his crest, at night according to the prescribed rite.
[He should worship] Soma together with Umā. As for the form [of the deity], it has already been explained in the context of the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
Having bathed in a pool of pure water—or at home or in a temple—with a paste of sesame and mustard seeds, one whose mind is solely intent upon Śiva [should proceed].
Having caused the Lord of Gods to consume the *brahmakūrca*,
the practitioner of the vow should then worship the God and the Goddess with the *brahmakūrca*— which is the five products of the cow— and with the mantras of their names beginning with "Vāma."
One should smear the right half with sandalwood mixed with *indu*—
*indu* being camphor—
and the left half with saffron and *turuṣka*, while reciting the mantra.
Turuṣka is silhaka.
One should place a blue gem upon the head of the Goddess and a pearl above Śiva;
thereafter, one should worship them with flowers that are neither too red nor inferior.
One should again perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with twenty-five lamps;
one should also offer auspicious, pure, white fruits prepared with ghee.
Having thus worshipped Śiva-Soma and offered praise, one should afterwards conclude the rite;
likewise, even another person who is devoted may do so for the initiated disciple using the name-mantra.
Then, composed and well-purified, one should offer sesame seeds cooked in the *brahmakūrca* mixture into a prosperous fire according to the rules, while reciting the *Sadyojāta* mantra.
Having indeed reached the eighth [day], at dawn— not even at that very moment—
he should feed Brāhmaṇas of strict vows together with their wives, using that *brahmakūrca* [mixture].
Having likewise given gold and silver according to one's ability, one should dismiss [the deity], saying:
"May Śiva and the goddess Umā be forever pleased with me at all times."
O sage, having thus propitiated Śiva, the Lord of Gaurī, ten times over,
listen now to all that must be performed at the conclusion of the vow.
Having reached the great festival at the proper season, one should worship the Supreme Lord with white flowers, as well as with incense, food offerings, and auspicious fruits.
One should worship the canopy, the beautiful parasol, and the functional bell— this section on the worship of Śambhu— with offerings according to one's capacity.
Then, with devotion, one should honor the Guru along with his wife with garments and ornaments made of gold and silver; one should also respect a devotee of Śiva.
[One should likewise give] a cow with silver hooves, golden horns, accompanied by a cloth, and a bronze milking vessel.
One should give a cow with its calf and a bull possessing auspicious marks;
and the observer of the vow should honor the virtuous with food, clothing, and nourishment.
Afterwards, the self-restrained householder should eat the remnants of the sacrifice;
O Pārtha, he who thus performs the Somāṣṭamī vow with devotion—
Freed from all sins, he shall attain the world of Śiva.
Whatever fruit a man obtains through gifts at Kurukṣetra and other sacred sites,
that same fruit a man who knows this obtains by worshipping her according to the prescribed rite.
Thus ends the Somāṣṭamī vow as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Now follows the Arkāṣṭamī vow.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall tell you another vow as well, which bestows the fruits of desire,
grants all merit in the world, and destroys even the greatest sins.
O King, when the eighth day of the bright fortnight coincides with a Sunday,
that day should be observed as a fast with great effort according to that very same ritual procedure.
One should worship Maheśvara, the Lord of the gods of gods, together with the Goddess;
for this very distinction regarding Śiva resides here in his vision.
One should worship Bhānu with devotion using auspicious perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata); likewise, one should worship Śiva with white flowers and Ambikā with red flowers.
With divine red and white jewels, one who possesses devotion should worship the Lord;
one should anoint the Goddess with saffron and Maheśvara with sandalwood.
In the absence of all precious gems, one should cause gold to be given there,
while reciting the Rudra-bīja and the Sūkta which is always dear to Rudra.
A pair of white and red garments and an offering of food cooked in ghee [should be presented];
the remainder of the extensive ritual procedure is to be performed according to the previously established rules.
However, having fasted here, one should perform the breaking of the fast by consuming cow-water (*gojala*).

"Cow-water" means cow-urine; "by the previous procedure" means by the procedure prescribed for this vow in the *Bhaviṣyottara*. Together with sacrificial food (*havis*), one should eat along with kinsmen and those who travel in chariots.
Whoever performs this Sūryāṣṭamī vow according to the previously mentioned procedure, [attains the fruit].
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of the Sun.

"By the previously mentioned procedure" means by the procedure for this vow as stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara*. Although the procedure for the Somāṣṭamī mentioned in the *Bhaviṣyottara* should not be adopted here due to its lack of continuity [with the present context], it has nevertheless been written because of its similarity to the present case. Since there is no difference in adopting the procedure for the Somāṣṭamī vow mentioned in the *Skandapurāṇa*, there is no cause for objection. [He should be honored] with sacrificial food (*havis*) along with his kinsmen and those who seek his favor.
Whoever performs this Sūryāṣṭamī vow according to the previously mentioned procedure,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Or, having come here, he shall indeed become a king, a lord of the earth,
illuminated by the sun, the sole vessel for health and all happiness.
One who bestows grace upon the distressed shines with majesty like the sun;
O scion of the Kuru lineage, if the eighth lunar day should ever coincide with the moon or the sun, one should fast on that day.
Worshiping Hara, whose crest is marked by the crescent moon, together with me,
a person attains through devotion the supreme state of Murāri.
Thus ends the Arkāṣṭamī-vrata as declared in the Śrī-Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Now follows the Puṣpāṣṭamī-vrata.
Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the auspicious and greatly meritorious fruit of the monthly worship:
he who observes a fast on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa—
One should bathe [the deity] with ghee and milk, worship with *karavīra* flowers,
perform the fire-ritual according to the rules, and then provide a meal for the Brahmins.
Having fashioned the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) according to the *Kanyākarṇitasūtra*,
and having prepared it with various fragrances, such as saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood;
He who, having observed a fast on the seventh day, devoutly offers a meal to Brahmins on the eighth day,
shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, he will indeed become a king on the surface of the earth; there is no doubt about this, occurring on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada.
Having bathed me with devotion using either milk or ghee,
O Goddess, one should perform worship according to the prescribed rite using Apāmārga.
"Mounted upon a swan-vehicle, he shall go to my world.
On the eighth day of the month of Āśvayuja, one should worship with all kinds of flowers.
Mounted upon a beautiful, golden carriage adorned with garlands of banners,
he proceeds to my abode, joined by the most excellent rays of light.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, whatever man bathes [the deity] with honey and milk and worships with Jātī flowers, [attains the fruit].
Having ascended a golden vehicle adorned with a network of tinkling bells,
O Goddess, he goes to the supreme realm, beloved by the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
And in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, whatever man bathes [the image] with the five products of the cow and worships it with devotion using red flowers.
Having observed a fast on the seventh day, a man should, on the eighth day, bathe [the deity] with curd and milk and anoint him with saffron according to the prescribed rite.
Having transcended the three worlds, he goes to where I am;
that man who, on the eighth day of the month of Pauṣa, worships me with devotion.
Having bathed Unmattaka with flowers and ghee,
he ascended a divine vehicle known by the name Puṣpaka.
Having reached my abode, he rejoices for eternal years—
whosoever worships with bilva leaves on the eighth day of the month of Māgha.
Having bathed me with devotion using divine sugarcane juice,
[one obtains] a vehicle equal in brilliance to the blazing sun and equal in luster to the god of fire.
That man who, with fragrant water, [performs the rite] in the month of Phālguna, ascends [to my realm] and rejoices eternally in my world; of this there is no doubt. [839]
By worshipping with *droṇa* flowers, one shall obtain the abode of Indra;
likewise, O Goddess, that man who [worships] in the month of Caitra with water and flowers.
Having bathed [the deity], O beautiful one, one should worship with devotion using *arka* flowers;
he obtains the great fruit of a sacrifice involving much gold.
Furthermore, whatever man, in the month of Vaiśākha, on the eighth lunar day,
bathes [the deity] according to the prescribed rite with water scented with camphor and agallochum;
He who worships with auspicious fragrance shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
likewise, he who bathes me with curd on the eighth day of the month of Jyeshtha.
If a man worships with animal flowers on the eighth day of the month of Āṣāḍha with fresh waters from various sacred fords, he shall go to the supreme goal.
Having bathed [the deity], one should worship with devotion using *dhustūra* leaves;
such a person is honored in heaven by Gandharvas, Uragas, and Yakṣas.
And she sports with me for as long as there are fourteen Indras,
O Goddess, who should thus observe the eighth-day vow for a year.
There is no returning for him; I speak this truth:
[he attains] Nīlakaṇṭha, Śambhu, and all Bhīma Maheśvara.
Virūpākṣa, Mahādeva, Ugra, Tryambaka,
Īśvara, and Śiva— O Goddess, these are worshipped in all the worlds;
one should recite these names of the months during those respective months.
Thus ends the Puṣpāṣṭamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
[840] Now follows the Tindukāṣṭakāṣṭamī vow.
O best of the twice-born, that man who worships the three-eyed Lord of Gods on the eighth day of the waxing moon in the month of Jyeṣṭha shall go to the world of Īśa.
Likewise, during the months of Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and the following one,
he should worship for those four months with clusters of blue lotuses and kadamba flowers.
One should worship Śambhu, the destroyer of Tripura, the three-eyed one, and the slayer of Andhaka,
with a multitude of fragrances and with guggulu resin.
O Brahmin, one should cause him to eat the *ṭemburuka* fruit, which purifies the body;
*ṭemburuka* is the *tinduka* fruit.
One should repeatedly invoke the name of the God as "Bhāskara."
O Brahmin, [this applies] in the month of Āśvayuja and likewise in Kārttika, O twice-born one.
Likewise, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and in the month of Pauṣa,
one should worship the Lord Hara with devotion according to the prescribed rite, using flowers from the *unmatta* plant.
One should worship Hari, the Lord of Gods, with *unmatta* flowers, *dhustūra* blossoms, and incense of camphor and *aguru*. Then,
one should duly consume barley while reciting the name "Virūpākṣa."

In the months of Māgha and Phālguna, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the Three-eyed Lord with devotion using hundred-petaled lotuses during the months of Caitra and Vaiśākha.
With great incense and with incense prepared according to the rules,
one should worship the god Hara, the destroyer of Tripura, in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
With *kakkola*, *aguru*, camphor, *darpa*, saffron, and sandalwood,
as well as the four-fold mixture (*caturjāta*), there is indeed the great *yakṣakardama*.
Thus addressed, one should worship him with offerings of food and pieces of sugar-candy,
saying, "O Maheśvara! O best of Brahmins, he who thus worships the god Maheśvara on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
going alone and solitary, attains the supreme goal.
O best of the twice-born, hear that which was desired by the God of gods:
for the flower, the *unmaka* is always used; for the incense, black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇāguru*).
Sandalwood is the best among all fragrances; milk-rice is always the offering.
The worshiper is a Pāśupata, entirely renouncing all worldly enjoyments.

O King, having thus worshipped Hari according to the rite prescribed by Rudra, his beloved priest, who was knowledgeable in the ritual manuals and skilled in recitation, performed the honors for the Brahmins.
One should perform worship at the *liṅga* using names such as Śaṅkara and others. At the end of the year, one should offer a meritorious oblation (*bali*) as well as the recitation of sacred texts.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for him who performs these with devotion.
He attains the heavenly world, radiant with a splendor like that of semen.
Thus ends the Tinduka-ashṭakā-aṣṭamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Now follows the Dāmpatya-aṣṭamī vow:
"O best of Brahmins, O sage, in the month of Kārttika, a man desiring a son [should observe it]."
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, O twice-born one, he should worship according to the prescribed rite.
[842] Having fashioned an image of the omnipresent Lord together with Umā out of darbha grass,
he should worship Him with offerings of perfumes, flowers, garments, and ornaments.
To the best of the twice-born [he gave] straight darbha grass, resembling blue beryl, with their roots, devoid of flowers, measuring a span in length, and provided with tips.
O best of Brahmins, having taken [the materials], one should fashion the god Nīlakaṇṭha, the lord of Umā, and that goddess Satī, Umā, according to the prescribed rule.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and various kinds of fruits and edibles,
as well as with various spectacles and musical instruments played by the mouth, O observer of noble vows.
O best of Brahmins, he who performs this Umāmāheśvara vow with devotion,
even if alone, attains the supreme goal.

One's own year consists of four breaking-fast days; thus it is proclaimed by the wise as one’s own single [cycle]. However, the first [cycle] consists of three months, with the breaking-fast days beginning from Kārttika.
In the months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, and likewise the following month,
[one should worship] with the flowers, fruits, and various kinds of edible offerings of the Unmattaka plant.
One should smear the Lord with white sandalwood paste from the *dhūstūra* tree grown in a cemetery;
one should offer guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter as an oblation, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as the supreme food offering.
One should perform the bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then partake of it;
the name "Mahādeva" is indeed recited, and likewise "Gaurīdevī."
O best of the twice-born, in the months of Māgha, Phālguna, and likewise Caitra,
one should repeatedly worship the God with *mālatī* flowers and other blossoms;
[one should address Him] by the name "Virūpākṣa" and the Goddess by the name "Umā."
One should worship the Lord, the All-pervading One, according to the rules with agallochum incense;
likewise, one should devoutly and according to the rules anoint those two with saffron.
One should offer boiled rice with curd as a food offering (naivedya) to the Trident-bearer;
likewise, one should consume water infused with kuśa grass for the purification of one's own body.
Likewise, O Sage, one should worship Dhara with karavīra flowers and red lotuses during the months of Vaiśākha, Jyaiṣṭha, and Āṣāḍha.
With *prājāpatya* incense and with *rasālā* and *modaka* sweets—
*rasālā* being *śikhariṇī*—
Śiva and Śivā, O Brahmin, are indeed proclaimed by those names.
For both bathing and the ritual consumption, ghee and black sesame seeds are recommended by the wise.
Agallochum, storax, and incense are known as the "Prājāpatya" offering;
during the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, [one should worship] with clusters of jasmine and kadamba flowers.
One should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite, as well as Hara, the destroyer of Tripura;
O Sage, one should worship the Lord of Gods with the four-fold elixir (catuḥsama) according to the ritual injunctions.

Whoever should worship the god Hara with these four offerings— incense mixed with agallochum, *kṛśara* rice, fried cakes, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), along with the "four-fold" blend of cinnamon, cardamom, small cardamom, and saffron— and complete the fast on the fourth day; [he shall attain his goal].
One who desires attains the fourfold group of aims without a doubt;
furthermore, one who is free from desire shall obtain the fourth alone.
The fourth is liberation.
Just as a man desiring liberation attains that desire for liberation,
so one who desires a son obtains a son, and one who desires wealth obtains wealth.
A seeker of knowledge certainly obtains knowledge from Śaṅkara;
having performed this for one year, he should propitiate Hari at the end of the year.
O Brahmin, for the pleasure of Śaṅkara, one should feed the Brahmins with various spectacles and with offerings of food, and likewise feed a married couple, O Vipra.
O Sage, the wise one should conceive of the reciter, a learned Brahmin together with his wife,
as Śambhu, and his wife as Lalitā.
O best of the twice-born, having gratified the couple many times with various kinds of foods and edibles, one should give safflower and red garments to them.
Furthermore, O Sage, one should give as a sacrificial fee to the reciter two golden images:
Mahādeva and his wife Lalitā.
Whoever, endowed with faith, should thus worship the god Hara,
he shall mount a supreme, divine vehicle made of gold.
Resplendent with brilliance like Śukra and radiant with luster like Hari,
he shall go to the supreme, immovable abode of the Trident-bearer;
returning from there, he shall become a king on earth, a lord of the world.
Thus ends the Dāmpatyāṣṭamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Now follows the Pitṛīya-vrata.
Pulastya said:
When the month of Proṣṭhapada has passed, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
a man or a woman desiring a son should observe a fast on that eighth day.
[845] Having bathed in a lake, or in water, or in a pond, she who knows the Dharma—
listen now to how she should perform the worship of Vāsudeva.
Having bathed Govinda, the teacher of the world, with a prastha of ghee,
one should thereafter bathe him with honey and then with curd.
After performing the ritual bath with milk, one should subsequently dry [the image] with all medicinal herbs mixed with water, as well as with all seeds and fruits.
Having bathed her, O Rāma, she was anointed with sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, camphor,
and likewise with auspicious nutmegs.
Then, having worshipped the Teacher of the World with flowers blooming in that season,
having offered incense of agallochum, and having presented the desired food offering;
Having especially consumed cow's milk along with *punnāga* fruit,
and having subsequently offered oblations with the *Puruṣasūkta*, one will certainly [attain] stability.
Whether it be a Śūdra or even a woman, having offered oblations into the fire of the Teacher of the World by name,
and having presented vessels of barley, fruits, and likewise gold;

For the sake of a son, one should perform the *prāśana* rite with auspicious fruits bearing male names; for the sake of a daughter, with those bearing female names. Then, having eaten as desired, [the ritual is concluded].
One obtains sons and daughters, as well as all desired objects;
one should offer the sacrificial oblation (haviṣya) to the God of gods and to the protectors of the earth.
Having performed this for a year, one attains the desired vow.

Although this supreme vow, which is ever-conducive to righteousness, has been declared by me to you as leading to the acquisition of a son, nevertheless, by means of this very vow, all desires [shall be fulfilled].
In this world, people obtain [their results] through what they have done.
Thus ends the Putrīya-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
[846] Now follows the Santānāṣṭamī-vrata.
Pulastya said:

Listen, O Dālbhya, to this supreme and desirable vow which bestows progeny upon men; by fasting according to it, the continuity of one's lineage and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to one’s sons is never interrupted.
He who, having bathed on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Caitra with a restrained mind,
worships Kṛṣṇa and performs the worship of Devakī;
After fasting from food, a man, having observed the fast for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the universe,
should recite the mantra at night with a disciplined mind.
During the worship of Kṛṣṇa as well, one should recite [the names] seven times,
while avoiding heretics, those who perform forbidden acts, hypocrites, crows, and atheists.
Then, having bathed at dawn and given a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin,
he should eat after performing worship to Kṛṣṇa alone, the Lord of the Universe.
Having fasted for three months during the months of Vaiśākha and Jyeṣṭha,
one should indeed break the fast and bathe Hari, the God of gods, with ghee.
In the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and likewise Bhādrapada,
having fasted, the second breaking of the fast should indeed be performed as before.
O best of the twice-born, the third breaking of the fast occurs likewise in the months of Āśvina, Kārttika, and Mārgaśīrṣa;
and the fourth occurs in Pauṣa, Māgha, and Phālguna.
At the completion of each fast, one should bathe Lord Hari with ghee;
likewise, at the conclusion of every fast, one should give ghee to the Brahmins.
Having performed the vow, he goes to the celestial realm (nāka);
having returned to the human state, he attains liberation (nirvṛti),
and he likewise achieves the increase of his progeny.
As far as the earth, girdled by the ocean, extends.
Thus ends the Santānāṣṭamī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Now follows the Maheśvarāṣṭamī vow.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O lord of men, beginning thus from the bright fortnight on the eighth day of the month of Saumya,
one should worship the three-eyed God of gods while observing a fast.
On the gentle eighth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
whether at a *liṅga*, or in an image, or in a lotus, or on a pedestal,
[one should perform worship] after bathing with various kinds of offerings, such as an ablution with ghee and milk.
By means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and an abundance of food,
as well as by song, dance, instrumental music, and the propitiation of the sacrificial fire.
O best of men, having duly honored the brahmins with offerings and,
at the conclusion of the vow, having given a milch cow;

He obtains the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world; that is to say, he attains the result of that specific sacrifice named Pauḍarīka. Having performed this for two eighth-month periods as well as for a year, a man [attains these results].
Having duly obtained the fruit of the horse sacrifice and enjoyed pleasures in the world of the gods,
he then attained the worlds of Maheśvara.
He attains union with Him before long.
Thus ends the Maheśvarāṣṭamī-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follows the Vasu-vrata.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Dhruva, Adhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa,
and Prabhāsa— these are remembered as the eight Vasus.
O lord of men, he who, having fasted, worships on the eighth day this Vāsudeva, who consists of eight aspects, through his primordial power, shall [attain success].
O Yādava, O lord of men, beginning from the month of Caitra and from the bright fortnight,
one should recite [the mantra] in the mandala or before the images.
O King of kings, [one attains merit] through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food,
as well as by bathing externally and by sleeping on the ground.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should always give a cow to a Brahmin according to one's capacity;
having performed this vow and bathed, a man attains all his desires.
He attains the Puṇḍarīka [world], uplifts his own lineage,
and having reached the world of the Vasus, he rejoices like Śiva himself.
Possessed of great splendor, devoted to truth, free from disease, and having conquered his senses;
devoted to truth and humble,
he shall likewise be endowed with wealth and grain.
And likewise, he shall be beloved by women.
Thus ends the Vasu-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Now follows the Kālāṣṭamī-vrata.
Pulastya said:
Likewise, when the auspicious eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhasya is joined with the lunar mansion Mṛgaśiras,
it is known as Kālāṣṭamī.
On that lunar day, Śaṅkara sleeps in all the Ekaliṅgas;
it is traditionally taught that when spring is present there, worship yields inexhaustible merit.
The Ekaliṅgas, accompanied by Vṛṣabha and Gaṇapati, are well known as facing westward.
There, the wise man should bathe with cow urine and water;
having bathed, he should worship the Three-eyed Lord with Dhustūra flowers.
Incense is made from the resin of saffron flowers, and the food offering consists of honey and clarified butter.

The *keśara* is the *bakula* tree. Having uttered, "May Virūpākṣa be pleased with me," one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the food offering (*naivedya*) along with gold to a Brahmin, O best of the twice-born.
In the same way, in the month of Āśvayuja, having fasted and subdued his senses,
one should perform a bath with cow dung on the ninth day and offer worship with lotuses.
Similarly, because it is stated that one should observe a fast in the month of Āśvayuja, it should be understood that a fast is also to be observed in the preceding month.
One should fumigate with the resin of the Sarja tree and offer honey and sweetmeats as a food offering;
having observed the fast on the eighth day, one should perform the ritual bath on the ninth day.
"May Virūpākṣa be pleased with me; the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed with sesame seeds.
In the month of Kārttika, one should bathe with milk and perform worship with Karavīra flowers."
Incense should be offered with the resinous exudations of the *śrīvāsa* tree, and the food offering (*naivedya*) with honeyed milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Along with the food offering, silver should be given as a gift to the elder brother.
Śrīvāsa is the Sarala tree; [it is offered] to an elder Brāhmaṇa.
Immediately thereafter, one should say: "May the Lord Sthāṇu be pleased.
Having observed a fast on the eighth day, one should perform the ritual bath on the ninth day.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the ritual bath is prescribed; therein, worship originating from the Rudra-mantras is enjoined. This worship, or *arcā*, consists of flowers from the *śamī* tree.
The incense is the resin of the *śrīvṛkṣa* (bilva) tree, and the food offering (*naivedya*) consists of honey and sweetmeats (*modaka*).
The *śrīvṛkṣa* is the *bilva* tree;
the food offering (*naivedya*) is red rice, and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed.
Furthermore, the wise should utter: "Salutation! May all be pleased."

In the month of Pauṣa, there should be a ritual bath, worship with sacrificial oblation (havis), and the breaking of the fast with sacrificial oblation— by "sacrificial oblation" is meant clarified butter (ghṛta).
This incense is the exudation of the Madhuka tree, and the food offering is honey-cakes (madhuśaṣkulī).
The ocean is declared to be the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the gratification of the Teacher of the World;
one should say, "Obeisance to you, O Lord of Gods," and proclaim, "O Three-eyed One."
In the month of Māgha, one should perform a bath with *kuśa* water or worship with *mṛgamada*;
*mṛgamada* is the musk of the female deer.
The incense should be the resin of the *kadamba* tree, and the food offering (*naivedya*) should be rice mixed with sesame seeds.
One should present an offering of milk in a vessel along with gold, saying:
"May Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā, be pleased with me."
In this manner, one [vow] is prescribed, with the breaking of the fast occurring after six months;
at the conclusion of the breaking of the fast, one should perform the ceremonial bathing of the three cows in due order.
Having anointed the deity with gorocanā, sandalwood, and saffron, one should worship him and say:
"Protect me, for I am wretched; O Lord, I am yours."
I bow perpetually to the Lord Śaśāṅkanātha.
Then, O best of gods, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Phālguna, a fast accompanied by self-restraint should be observed.
On the second day, one should then perform a bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
one should worship with kunda flowers and incense with sandalwood.
O Sage, one should offer as an oblation rice with jaggery and ghee in a copper vessel,
and provide a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) along with the oblation to the twice-born.
One should give gifts to the Brāhmaṇas after worshipping Rudra by name;
in the month of Caitra, one should perform a ritual bath with Udumbara fruits and worship with Mandāra flowers.
The wise one should offer incense of guggulu known as mahiṣa, smeared with clarified butter;
likewise, he should present clarified butter mixed with water as an offering that brings satisfaction.
O Nārada, one should cause a sacrificial fee and an offering of food to be presented to the beloved of Umā, reciting: "O Lord of Nandin, homage be unto you! [852]
Endowed with faith, one should perform a pleasing offering for the Lord of the Gods;
in the month of Vaiśākha, bathing with fragrant water mixed with saffron is prescribed.
O Lord, the worship of Śaṅkara is said to be performed with *bhūtamañjarī* flowers;
the incense is made with flowers called *sūryākhya*, and the food offering consists of fruit and ghee.
The flower of the *arka* plant is called "Sūrya";
it should be addressed by the wise as "Īśa" and "Kālaghna.
One should present water-pots together with food offerings to the Brahmins.
One should also give a pair of sandals and an umbrella as an offering according to one's ability, saying:
"Homage to you, O destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, the annihilator of Puṣpadanta!"
One should recite this with devotion for the pleasure of the Lord of the World;
the ritual bath in Āṣāḍha is prescribed, as well as worship with bilva fruits.
For the purpose of incense, there are flowers of the dūstūra and likewise storax;
the food offering consists of cakes with ghee, and the sacrificial fee is likewise with ghee.
Then one should utter this: "Salutations to you, O destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Having performed a bath with musk in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Hari.
One should offer incense made from the leaves and fruits of the śrīvṛkṣa tree as well as aguru;
one should present an offering of food with ghee and sweetmeats (modaka) filled with curd.
Curd-rice, rice mixed with sesame, fried grain cakes, and *śaṣkulī* pastries;
as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), a white bull and a beautiful tawny cow.
One should give gold and red garments to a Brāhmaṇa;
moreover, the name of Śambhu should be pronounced by the wise as "Gaṅgādhara."
With these six months thus described, the breaking of the fast is most excellent;
in this manner, having fully worshipped the Bull-bannered Lord for a complete year.
A man who is devoted to Maheśvara attains inexhaustible worlds.
This meritorious vow, which brings about the exhaustion of all [karmic bonds] and is auspicious, was spoken by Rudra himself, O divine sage; it is so and not otherwise.
Thus ends the Kālāṣṭamī vow as declared in the Vāmana Purāṇa.
Now follows the Rukmiṇyaṣṭamī vow.
Skanda said:
O Blessed One, O Lord, you have told me everything that I desired;
now I wish to hear about someone born upon this earth.
Since such a thing as separation from one's son might happen at any time,
by whom has prosperity been proclaimed as something that always belongs to those dwelling in the home?
Śaṅkara said:
Listen, my son, I shall proclaim the most excellent of vows;
by the mere performance of which, whether a woman or even a man, [attains the highest goal].
Nowhere shall there be separation from her sons, nor anywhere shall she ever be separated from her husband;
nor shall there arise any deficiency in household utensils or wealth.
O Six-faced One, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
there is that [day] known as Rukmiṇyaṣṭamī, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
In that year, having become pure in the morning and observing the prescribed restraints, a woman should,
during the first year, plaster her house with clay so that it has only a single entrance.
Having respectfully placed all the household utensils within it,
as well as rice in the form of stūpas, and likewise clarified butter and other flavorful liquids;
Dolls should be fashioned there from cloth, wood, or even teeth, as well as those painted with various colors; hear their names from me.
Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī, Baladeva and Arundhatī,
Pradyumna and his wife, as well as Aniruddha and Uṣā.
One should visualize Devakī, Vasudeva, and all the others there;
then one should worship them all in succession with the eight kinds of incense, unbroken rice grains, and other offerings.
When the rising of the moon has occurred, one should offer the *arghya* to that moon:
"O you who resemble a conch or a jasmine flower, the lamp of the courtyard of the sky!"
"Accept this *arghya* offered by me; salutations to you, O Śaṅkara.
This is the mantra for the *arghya* offering to the Moon.
Having offered the *arghya*, one should then eat together with friends, kinsmen, and relatives.
Then, at the time of dawn, one should with a joyful mind give that auspicious house, filled with all kinds of objects, to the maiden.
Then, in the second year, one should indeed construct a face-temple;
having filled it as before, one should present it to the maiden.
Then, in the third year, having constructed a facing temple and having completed it in its entirety as before, one should present it to the maiden.
Then, having established the fourfold bliss in the fourth year,
one should establish that which possesses five gates in the fifth year and that which is joined with six faces in the sixth year.
Having prepared it, one should diligently offer it to the maiden with four faces in the fifth year,
with five openings in the sixth year, and joined with six faces in the seventh.
Having prepared it, one should diligently offer it to the maiden for seven years;
then, in the seventh year, one should perform the auspicious concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having constructed a great house with seven doors, whitewashed with lime,
he provided it with a bed, a cotton mattress, a vehicle, an umbrella, and sandals.
A mirror, a fly-whisk, as well as a pestle and a mortar,
and large vessels and bowls made of bell-metal and copper.
Having gathered all the household utensils within the house from every side,
as well as Kṛṣṇa, Rukmiṇī, and the charming Pradyumna—
Having fashioned [images] out of gold according to one's ability and draped them in yellow garments,
one should worship them by means of fasting and keeping a vigil throughout the night.
Then, at the time of dawn, having arrived at that house,
he honored the twice-born man along with his wife with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
Therefore, one should give this house and also a well-behaved cow.
