O son, when the vow has been performed in this manner, a man shall not encounter miseries,
nor shall a woman afflicted by grief for her son, O Six-faced One.
Thus ends the Rukmiṇī-aṣṭamī vow as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Now follows the Durgā-vow.
Brahmā said:
I shall proclaim the vow of the Goddess, which accomplishes all desires.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should subsist on air alone.
Having bathed, having assumed the *sārdhapuṭa* posture, having conquered anger, and being endowed with the prescribed rites,
he should bathe the Goddess first with water, and again with milk and water.
Then one should cause guggulu incense along with turuṣka to be offered;
*turuṣka* is *sihlaka*.
Then follows a bath with scented water and another bath with plain water.
Having anointed [the deity] with sandalwood paste, one should worship with bilva leaves;
one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) to the Goddess as an oblation and feed [the recipient] with that same food.
According to one's ability, one should give maidens and twice-born men as gifts, and offer them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), while uttering:
"May Kātyāyanī be pleased with me at all times."
O Bhārgava, having performed that fast for oneself,
one obtains the supreme fruit of the horse sacrifice and goes to the world of the Goddess.
Having thus come to this stage, a king is born upon the earth;
through that, he attains the supreme yoga which brings about the attainment of auspiciousness.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, one should likewise have the tips of the horns of a cow smeared with clay and used as a support for one's own body.
[857] But on the eighth day of the bright fortnight— the word "on the eighth" is to be supplied here— one who has bathed with *vāmālaka* flowers, being pure and free from attachment,
should worship the Goddess with *yūthikā* flowers and bathe her with milk.
One should smear [the image] with saffron mixed with sandalwood water;
then one should offer cakes as a food offering (naivedya), as well as earrings,
aloe-wood incense as an offering, and lamps with sesame oil.
Therefore, he should cause those maidens to wed twice-born men who abide in virtuous conduct.
With that food offering of cakes and the like,
one should not look upon heretics nor those excluded from the scriptures.
Gifts should be given according to one's ability, and an auspicious benediction should be pronounced.
Having performed the breaking of his fast, he obtains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice;
he goes to the world of Viṣṇu and is likewise reborn as a brahmin.
Rich in wealth, born into a great lineage, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
possessing sons, wealth, and enjoyments, one shall attain happiness and become auspicious.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvina, one should perform a bath with clay;
thereafter, O child, one should bathe the Goddess with curd and sugarcane juice.
Having taken *rocanā* and *candana*, one should burn them as incense along with *bālaka*;
likewise, one should worship [the deity] with lotus petals mixed with sugar and *sanakha*.
For the food offering, one should present red fish meat as well as that from the porcupine,
along with wheat-based delicacies cooked in ghee.
Having fed the maidens and also the twice-born, he should ask for their forgiveness;
according to his ability, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given, as well as that meal for himself.
A human being obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
such a person becomes healthy, happy, and blessed in this very world.
By reciting the names of Durgā, one is glorified in her world;
O descendant of Bhṛgu, in the month of Kārttika, one should bathe with earth from the roots of Darbha grass.
Having bathed the Goddess with scented water and worshipped her with uśīra, one should anoint her;
incense made of the five flavors should be offered, and lamps should be lit with sesame oil.

The food offering (*naivedya*) consists of the five flavors, along with *volarāla*, *kanduru*, *śrīveṣṭa*, and *guggulu*; likewise, barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), and a meal for virgins, Brahmins, and oneself. Having had the benediction (*svastivācana*) recited, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is given, [with the thought]: "May Śiva be pleased."
By this method, my child, one obtains the fruit of the gift of knowledge;
as a knower of the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, at the end of that life, one attains the state of Śiva.
Likewise, O Bhārgava, having bathed on the eighth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa with clay from the mountain, one should then bathe the Goddess with water from a sacred ford.
One should apply an ointment made of vālaka, kuṣṭha, jātī,
and gajāhvaya (where gajāhvaya refers to nāgakesara);
one should offer black agallochum as incense and kindle lamps with clarified butter.
The offering should consist of curd-rice, and the maidens should be fed with that very same food.
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's ability, and that constitutes the breaking of the fast for oneself;
saying "May Umā be pleased with me," one shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In this very life one becomes wealthy and enjoys pleasures, and at the end of the body, one reaches the abode of Brahmā;
having bathed with the tips of *dūrvā* grass on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, one should wear white garments.
Having conquered anger, one should bathe the Goddess with camphor water and anoint her with saffron, spikenard, valerian, and sandalwood.
The wise one should burn incense and worship with *kuruṇṭaka* flowers;
he should offer *kṛsara* mixed with jaggery as a sacrificial gift, and indeed, maidens should be fed by him.
Having performed his own breaking of the fast, he should indeed honor the twice-born according to his ability, [saying]:
"May the goddess Nārāyaṇī, who is ever pleased, be gracious to me."
O Lord of the Kings of Planets, by performing this act, one obtains the fruit of gifting land;
becoming fortunate and endowed with wealth, one shall attain auspiciousness in the hereafter.
O Bhārgava, having bathed with the earth from the horns of cows in the month of Māgha,
one should likewise bathe the Goddess with water, milk, and ghee.
One should bathe [the deity] again with waters, smear [him] with saffron,
offer incense made from *devadāru* wood, and worship with *kunda* flowers.
With that [offering], one should indeed feed maidens and Brahmins with an oblation filled with ghee;
she herself should also partake of it, and let the sacrificial fee be given with the thought, "May Jayā be pleased."
One obtains the merit that is the fruit of all sacrifices; there is no doubt about this.
Having bathed with mustard seeds and water infused with fruits in the month of Phālguna while reciting the names of the Goddess, [one attains this result].
Likewise, O Guha, there is worship with sugar-cane juice and even more with that water, as well as with the application of yellow pigment (rocanā) and with the hundred-petaled lotus (śatapatrikā).
The lamp should be fed with ghee, and the incense should be sandalwood, not sugar; for the food offering, one should use *aśokavartī* lamps, and the meal should consist of young girls.
And one should perform that for oneself, and have the benediction (svasti) recited;
for Vijayā, Sukhadā, Nityā, Sumukhā, and Cetanā always bestow victory and happiness.
O Śukra, by this method, one endowed with faith shall obtain a fruit equal to that of the Rājasūya sacrifice; thereafter, the entire world will consist of the Goddess.
On the eighth day of the month of Caitra, one should bathe with earth and water at the Mātṛsnāna;
having bathed the Goddess with waters from sacred fords, one should smear her with an ointment of *madana*.

One should worship with incense made of gold and *sauśīra*, and with *atimuktā* flowers; the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of rice cooked with milk (*śālija-bhakta*), sugar, and young girls as well.
And that food, indeed, should be for one's own self; one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability for the sake of fulfilling all desires and for happiness, which is truly unconquered.
By clothing a maiden of a noble family, one obtains the fruit of giving gold;
indeed, by bathing with mango fruits on the eighth day of Vaiśākha while remaining pure, one gains great merit.
Having bathed themselves as deities with water from the Māṃsī and Ālaka plants,
they applied an ointment of musk and camphor and offered incense made of the five fragrant substances.
One should perform the worship of the Goddess with Ketakī and Campaka flowers;
the food offering should consist of sugar and milk, and a meal should be provided to virgins and Brahmins.
Having performed that self-sacrifice, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability;
and one should have [the recipient] recite the names Aparājitā, Bhavānī, and Śivā.
"May he be pleased with me at all times and grant my desire;
by this, O Bhārgava, one obtains the merit of bathing in all sacred fords."
At the end, he shall go to the world of the Sun and will always be born equal to him;
on the eighth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, a wise man should bathe with sesame seeds.
Having renounced all attachments, one should bathe the Goddess with water infused with *jātī* fruit and anoint her with fragrant sandalwood paste;
thereafter, O best of planets, one should worship her with *vijaya* flowers.
Vijaya is the *kumbhaka* [breath-retention]. In the food offering (*naivedya*), roasted flour (*śaktavaḥ*) should be given; sugar should also be given for the maidens.
A sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given according to one's means, and one should cause [the priest] to recite the hymn to Carcikā.
O Śukra, one obtains a fruit equal to that of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice;
likewise, on the eighth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should bathe [the deity] with water from a night-stream.
Then, [he should worship] the Goddess with water, kuṣṭha, madhuka, and varadā.
With turbid waters, with madhuka (liquorice),
having bathed and anointed oneself with camphor, sandalwood, and the water of *rocanā*;
the incense consists of sandalwood, camphor, *vāhlīka*, and white *sihlaka*.
White sugar; O Brahmin,
one should cause the girl to eat various foods, rice mixed with sugar, cakes, auspicious drinks,
and likewise provide a meal for oneself.
One should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability and recite the mantra "mahiṣaghnī";
a garland of lamps made with ghee alone bestows all desires.
One should offer white food as an oblation and feed maidens and Brahmins;
one shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices, the gift of land, and all sacred fords.
O Śukra, this excellent vow— the great Durgā-vrata— was observed by me, by Rudra, and by Viṣṇu,
desiring the welfare of the world.
And how, in the past, it was performed by Bhānu in the battle for the destruction of the planets,
as well as by the gods, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, kinnaras, and humans.
O tiger among planets, it was indeed performed by the Apsarases and women for the increase of good fortune; and whoever should perform it according to the prescribed rite, [attains that same result].
By hearing this, a mortal obtains all the pleasures desired by the senses;
he gains his wishes, and even a barren woman gives birth to a son.
Thus ends the Durgā-vrata as declared in the Devī-purāṇa.
Now follows the Aśokāṣṭamī-vrata.
Kṛṣṇa said:
From the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"Those who drink eight buds of the *aśoka* tree under the asterism Punarvasu on the eighth day of the month of Caitra shall never experience sorrow."
Also in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, on a Wednesday with the asterism Punarvasu,
having worshipped Rudra according to the rules with *aśoka* flowers..."
One should eat eight buds of the *aśoka* tree while reciting the mantra;
thus, a mortal shall never experience grief and shall even become endowed with beauty.
In this context, the conjunction of Mercury with the asterism Punarvasu is intended for the sake of excellence.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"The drinking of Aśoka buds and the worship of the Aśoka tree..."
"By performing [this rite] on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one attains liberation.
The mantra for consuming [the offering] is stated in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"O you who are beloved by Aśoka and Hara, born in the month of Madhu..."
"Afflicted by grief, I drink [your sap]; make me forever free from sorrow (aśoka)," so it is said.
However, that which is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* is:
"I bow to you, O Aśoka, who are graced by the month of Madhu."
"Afflicted by grief, I shall eat the flower buds; always make me free from sorrow (*aśoka*).
Thus ends the *Aśokāṣṭamī-vrata*. Now follows the *Soma-vrata*.
Kṛṣṇa said:
When Rohiṇī coincides with the eighth lunar day of the moon, one should then perform the Candra-vrata;
having worshipped Śiva according to the rules with baths consisting of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other offerings.
Anointing with moon-cream or sandalwood paste is beneficial;
likewise, one should worship the Supreme Lord with white garments and flowers.
The food offering should be a jar of milk mixed with white sugar;
the ritual consumption should be with sandalwood paste, and staying awake throughout the night is beneficial.
Those who desire long life should always perform what is beneficial for achieving fame and prosperity;
thus, by the gift of a wife, that which is called the Candra-vrata is accomplished.
Thus concludes the Somavrata as declared for another time.
[864] Now follows the Rājarājeśvaravrata.
When the yoga consisting of Budha and Svāti occurs on the eighth lunar day,
one who has fasted according to the prescribed rule should perform the great ritual bath first.
One should worship Virūpākṣa with body-unguents and the four perfumes,
as well as two large wicks for a long-lasting lamp, numbering one hundred and eight.
One should worship with light saffron incense and white flowers,
and one should offer various kinds of sweetmeats as the food offering.
In the presence of Śiva, one should offer to the preceptor a neck-ornament, a crown, and so forth,
as well as a girdle, earrings, a bracelet, and two rings.
One should worship with supreme devotion the vehicle— either an elephant or, in its absence, an excellent horse— as well as food mixed with sugar and clarified butter.
One shall attain the status of a Rājarājeśvara equal in number to the hairs on one's body;
therefore, this vow is proclaimed as the Rājarājeśvara.
Thus ends the Rājarājeśvara-vrata as taught in the Kālottara.
Now, the Mahāvrata:
when the conjunction of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa occurs on the eighth lunar day.
Then, O child, on the fourteenth day, one should likewise observe the vow.
Having observed the fast according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the great ablution (mahāsnāna) with agallochum, sandalwood, gorocanā, and saffron.
One should offer incense made of auspicious black agallochum along with four great lamps;
the food offering should consist primarily of ghee and be accompanied by barley gruel (yāvaka).
One should offer enjoyments there before Śiva according to the prescribed rite,
having first honored the preceptor with garments, gold, food, and ornaments.
One should place fresh saffron and flowers before Śiva;
likewise, one should offer each of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas in the same manner.
This which is called the Great Vow has been proclaimed by me to you;
it shall shine throughout the entire earth, with its seven continents and oceans.
One should perform a vigil at night with great magnificence,
[honoring] the fathers, the grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers.
Whatever fruit there is for sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons in the worlds of Śiva—
that should be performed by lords of the earth through this rite known as the Mahāvrata.
Thus ends the Mahāvrata as taught in the Kālottara. Now follows the Viśvarūpavrata:
when the conjunction of Revatī and Śani occurs on the eighth day of the bright fortnight.
Or rather, O Mahāsena, listen now to what happened when she was born.
The great ablution (mahāsnāna) should be performed immediately after the daily duties;
with the moon, one should indeed perform the worship of Akṣarāja with jewels.
Cool lotuses should be offered, as well as many ornaments;
likewise, one should offer incense of camphor, and for the food offering, milk-rice with ghee.
One should offer a young, gentle white horse to Śiva;
one should cause eight horses and an elephant to be given to the preceptor.
One who desires a kingdom obtains a kingdom— consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas— for each horse and likewise for each elephant, until the dissolution of all that is summoned.
One desiring sons obtains sons with prowess equal to the wind;
one desiring enjoyments obtains eternal enjoyments through the reality of knowledge (vidyātattva).
Whatever desires one may long for, those very desires one shall obtain;
because it bestows all forms, this vow is thus proclaimed.
Then follows the consumption of water infused with *kuśa* grass and the keeping of a vigil at night.
Thus ends the Viśvarūpa-vrata as declared in the Kālottara.
Now follows the Budhāṣṭamī-vrata.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, O Pāṇḍava, listen as I describe the Budhāṣṭamī vow,
by the performance of which a man never beholds hell at any time.
In former times, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, there was indeed a king named Ilā;
he was accompanied by many servants and surrounded by his friends and ministers.
Unhindered by Mahādeva, he went to the slopes of the Himavat;
it is certain that whoever enters this earth becomes a woman.
Following a herd of deer, that king entered the Umā forest alone with his horse; in an instant, he attained womanhood.
With her full and elevated breasts, she wandered in the empty forest, [thinking]:
"Who are you? To whom do you belong? From where have you come? Is there any purpose for me here?"
Budha beheld that slender woman, endowed with the qualities of beauty and nobility;
on the eighth lunar day falling on a Wednesday, the planet Budha was pleased with her.
He gave her the householder’s life, and she was brought with great satisfaction;
she then gave birth to a son who became famous as Purūravas.
The first king of all monarchs was the founder of the Lunar dynasty;
from that time forward, this eighth lunar day joined with Mercury has been worthy of worship.
It pacifies all sins and destroys all calamities;
O beloved of ignorance, I shall now speak sufficiently of the story of King Karma.
There was a heroic king of the Videhas who, having been struck down by his enemies in battle at Mithilā, left behind a wife who was destitute.
Named Urmilā, she wandered the earth accompanied by her son; upon reaching the region of Avanti, she came to the residence of a Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having performed constant grinding and pounding for the sake of filling her belly,
she gave a small amount of wheat to the two boys.
Due to their wretchedness, their maternal affection, and being tormented by hunger,
that virtuous and auspicious woman met her death in the course of time after many days.
His son, having gone to the place called Videha, sat upon his father’s throne and,
through the power of his goodness, enjoyed the kingdom without agitation.
Having searched for her, that King of Dharma married the maiden born of the Mithi lineage;
she became a devoted wife to her husband and a great heroine.
The fair-limbed woman named Śyāmalā is renowned and heard of in the sacred scriptures;
the King of Dharma himself spoke to that beloved lady of beautiful hips.
O Śyāmalā, you must carry out all the affairs within my household;
bestow gifts upon and employ your own kinsmen and servants as you desire.
But these seven cages, O daughter of Videha, are not to be looked upon by you, for they are extremely restrictive and at times even terrible.
Having said, "Let it be so," she performed her own duty;
at one time, however, the daughter of the Videha king became greatly distressed.
Having opened [the door], he first saw his own mother;
she was being cooked and was crying out, surrounded by the terrifying servants of Yama.
Having been bound, she was tossed about repeatedly in boiling oil with ease;
beholding that very sight, the high-minded woman was filled with shame.
In the second cage, he likewise saw his mother being ground with lime by Śilāpālī, the daughter of Aṣṭaketu.
In the third cage, he likewise saw his own mother being split at the head with saws that were sharp as claws and fitted with bells.
In the fourth cage, in that place, she was crying out again and again while being devoured by terrifying beasts of prey with the faces of donkeys.
On the fifth [stage], she is cast down to the ground; her throat is crushed by the foot, and she is torn asunder by piercing glances and heavy blows.
In the sixth [case], one should visualize her standing in the middle of a vast charnel ground, struck on the head by a mallet,
being incessantly and very firmly crushed as if into pieces.
In the seventh cage, amidst the stench of putridity and the sound of piteous cries,
he saw his mother, a Tathāgata, emaciated by suffering.
Dark-complexioned and with a withered face, the beautiful woman said nothing;
then Śyāmalā, filled with rage, spoke to her husband who had returned from Yama.
"O King, what has been taken from you? Tell me of my own terrible deed, because of which you are being struck with various blows in many ways."
Yama said: "O dear one, O auspicious lady, having seen these seven Piñjarakas, you did not open [the door] for me; you were previously forbidden by me."
"O auspicious lady, it is said that your mother took the wheat out of affection for her son; do you not know that because of this, she has been reduced to a state of distress?"
A gift of a Brahmin’s property, when given out of affection, consumes the family up to the seventh generation;
yet that very same property, when taken through theft, causes suffering as long as the moon and stars exist.
These very beings, who were once wheat grains, have now become most dreadful worms;
they are the same ones that were previously killed by me in a Brahmin’s house for your sake.
Śyāmalā said: "I know all that was done to me by my mother in the past;
nevertheless, having approached you and having found you as a virtuous son-in-law,"
"One is released from being a mass of worms; now act accordingly.
Having heard that, he remained for a long time with his heart possessed by anxiety.
"The Budhāṣṭamī, when perfectly complete, bestows the fruits as described;
this [day] seems to grant that very fruit—perform it quickly," she said to her.
The King of Dharma [spoke] to his beloved, the mistress of his life and wealth, who was seated with him;
and that auspicious Brahmin woman [recalled] her vow from seven past births.
And you, being distressed, were attended by your friends during the Budhāṣṭamī, which, when fully observed, bestows the fruits as described.
Having made a truthful vow before me,
grant that fruit so that your mother may be liberated from the perilous hell of her sins.
Having heard that, Śyāmalā quickly bathed and performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite for her mother; pleased by this, the mother attained liberation.
Urmilā, endowed with beauty, auspicious and possessing a divine body,
ascended an excellent celestial chariot, adorned with divine garlands and garments.
Even today, she is seen by people in the sky near her husband,
beside Budha, in the vicinity of King Mithi, while dwelling in heaven.
It shines forth, O Great King, by the power of the eighth day of the waxing moon.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
If this eighth lunar day on a Wednesday is indeed the most excellent of all,
then tell me its specific ritual procedure and its particular ordinance.
Tell me the procedure for that very [practice], O Lord, if you are pleased with me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen attentively, O Pāṇḍava, to the auspicious rite for the day of Budhāṣṭamī;
whenever the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight falls on a Wednesday, O ascetic.
At that very time, men who eat but a single meal should bathe in a river during the forenoon and, having taken up a new instrument, should seize it.
Having filled it with water, adorned it with gold, and provided it with various foods, one should offer it after performing the rites;
then, having gone home, one should proceed according to the prescribed sequence.
On the eighth day, according to the eightfold ritual, one should offer various foods separately:
on the first [day] with sweetmeats and snacks, and likewise on the second with fried grains.
The third [day] should be celebrated with offerings of ghee-filled cakes, O King, the fourth with *vaṭaka* sweets,
the fifth with white *kāsāra* puddings, and the sixth with auspicious *sīhālaka* preparations.
One should pass the seventh day with bright aśoka-wicks;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the eighth day with sugar-candy-filled confections.
In this manner, friends, kinsmen, and relatives should gradually perform the rites;
staying together in one place, they should eat their meal with feelings of affection.
O Pārtha, one should not abandon food abruptly;
for one should eat only so long as this narrative is being told.

Then, having become composed and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in the presence of the wise man, one should cause it to be given to a Brahmin who is a knower of the Vedas and a reciter.
It was auspicious, made of gold, accompanied by unbroken grains and gold,
honored and anointed with fragrant scents, flowers, and sweet-smelling incense.
One should fashion an image of Budha, the son of Soma, covered in yellow garments and having his characteristic form,
made from one māṣaka of gold or half of that, or even half of the latter.
The form of Budha is described in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Wearing yellow garlands and garments, possessing a luster like that of the Karṇikāra flower,
holding a sword, a shield, and a mace in his hands, seated upon a lion, and granting boons— such is Budha."
But one who is engaged in ritual enjoyment, O son of Kuntī, should offer [the oblation] while reciting the deity’s names:

Oṃ, obeisance to Budha. Oṃ, obeisance to the son of Soma. Oṃ, obeisance to the destroyer of evil intellect. Oṃ, obeisance to the bestower of good intellect. Oṃ, obeisance to the one born of Tārā. Oṃ, obeisance to the one clad in yellow garments.
Oṃ, homage to the gentle planet! Oṃ, homage to the bestower of all happiness!
These are the mantras for worship.
Oṃ, this Mercury accepts [the offering], yet he himself remains established in the substance.
It is given by one in the form of a wise man; may the best of the wise be pleased with me.
The mantra for the gift:
Oṃ! May the wise one, the son of the Moon, destroy the misfortune of us two who possess dull intellects;
may he grant us constant happiness and mental well-being.
Having uttered this, taken [the water], and given it consecrated by mantra,
O Indra among kings, one shall become a rememberer of past births on earth for seven lifetimes.
Endowed with wealth and grain, flourishing with sons and grandsons,
and possessing long life, he shall enjoy abundant and manifold pleasures upon the surface of the earth.
Then, by meditating upon Nārāyaṇa while facing death at Sutīrtha, one attains him;
having died there, O King, he reaches heaven, the city of Purandara.
There he remains until the time of creation, until the dissolution of all beings;
thus, O Pārtha, has this secret Budhāṣṭamī been fully described.
Having heard this, even a slayer of a Brahmin or a killer of a cow is liberated from all sins;
and whoever, having reached the eighth lunar day conjoined with Mercury, worships the Son of the Moon (Mercury) with devotion while he rests upon the palm of the hand.
Accompanied by cooked food and drink, and possessing gold and garments,
he never at any time beholds the face of Yama.
Thus ends the Budhāṣṭamī vow from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Now follows the Dūrvāṣṭamī vow.
Viṣṇu said:
O Brahmin, that man who, having fasted on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, worships Śaṅkara with devotion and endowed with faith;
O Sage, he who worships Gaṇeśa with dūrvā grass attains that supreme abode where the three-eyed God resides; this is indeed beneficial for him.
Gaṇeśa is Maheśvara. By worshipping Gaṇeśa with all kinds of divine fruits, perfumes, flowers, and ointments, as well as with dūrvā grass and deer-meat, one is liberated from all sins.
In a pure place, upon freshly sprouted dūrvā grass, the best of Brahmins, having bathed the liṅga,
should then worship it with perfumes, flowers, and incense.
O twice-born one, one should worship Śaṅkara with devotion according to the rules, using dates, coconuts, and citrons, as well as dūrvā grass.
O best of the twice-born, a man endowed with faith should worship the Three-eyed Lord with curds and unbroken grains (akṣata), and with dūrvā grass and śamī wood.
He shall indeed be born of meritorious deeds and be honored by all the gods;
a seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge, and one who desires a son shall obtain a son.
One who seeks dharma attains dharma; one who seeks a maiden obtains her;
whatever a person may desire in his mind, that he shall obtain.
The person who thus worships Bhūteśa with dūrvā grass and fruits is liberated from the multitudes of sins for seven births; there is no doubt about this.
Having observed a fast on the seventh day, one should worship Śiva on the eighth day,
O best of Brahmins, with dūrvā grass, curd, unbroken rice, and auspicious fruits.
O Dūrvā grass, you are born from the nectar of immortality; you are praised by gods and asuras.
Grant me good fortune and progeny, and become the accomplisher of all my tasks.
Just as you have spread across the surface of the earth with branches and sub-branches,
so too grant me a lineage that is free from old age and death.
The mantra for the worship of dūrvā grass:
Being restrained and pure, one should worship Īśāna with mantras containing his specific marks.
Then, O twice-born one, one should honor the brahmins with various kinds of fruits.
O Brahmin, one may eat food that is not cooked by fire, as well as curd and fruit; however, one should not eat food that is unseasoned with salt, nor that which is mixed with honey.
One who subsists on fruit should give fruits to Brahmins;
by bowing with one's head to *dūrvā* grass, one attains auspiciousness upon auspiciousness.
O Brahmin, he who thus performs the worship of Mahādeva with devotion attains the status of a Gaṇa and is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus, this eighth day, known as the Goddess, is meritorious and removes sin for all four castes, and especially for women.
Thus ends the Dūrvāṣṭamī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Now, regarding the Dūrvāṣṭamī vow:
when the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada has arrived...
The spreading stalks of dūrvā grass were pleasant to the touch and directed toward the northern quarter.
Having brought [the deity] into the house, one should worship with perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
likewise, one should offer fruits and roots, and dismiss [the deity] with lamps and incense.
O Brahmin, having somehow offered everything that has been cooked by fire,
one should likewise eat that which is devoid of being cooked by fire.
By worshipping one's beloved during youth according to the prescribed rite while he stands upon a blade of *dūrvā* grass,
one attains a stable youth wherever one is born.
Thus ends the Dūrvāṣṭamī vow as declared in the Āditya Purāṇa.
Now follows the Aśokāṣṭamī vow.
Bhānu said:
And on all eighth lunar days, the Aśokikā [deity] should also be worshipped with perfumes,
garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and an abundance of food offerings.
Whoever eats on that day during the night when the moon is absent becomes free from sorrow,
wherever she may be born.
And on all eighth days, O Sage, unless it be the bright fortnight;
specifically, O twice-born ones, that which is the eighth day of the dark fortnight following the passing of the month of Proṣṭhapada.
"In that [observance], one must certainly perform the worship of the Goddess according to the prescribed rule.
Thus is described the Aśokāṣṭamī vow as stated in the Ādityapurāṇa. Now follows the Mātṛvratam.
The eighth lunar day is the most excellent of days for the Mothers, as ordained by Brahmā;
on this day, a man should always seek their forgiveness with devotion while remaining without food.
Being well-pleased with him, they grant him security and health.
Thus ends the Mātṛvrata as declared in the Vārāha Purāṇa.
Now follows the Narasiṃhavrata.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, O Brahmin, listen to this Aṣṭamī-vrata being proclaimed;
it is the supreme destroyer of worldly existence for men and the remover of all afflictions.
If a king or a prince desires the destruction of his enemies,
he should, having bathed well on the eighth lunar day, offer an oblation of barley.
One should fashion an eight-petaled lotus either with rice grains or with flowers;
then, one should meditate upon the Lord in the form of Narasiṃha within its pericarp.
He was of fierce form, with great tusks, and thundering with a deep roar; he possessed the splendor of a noble boar with massive, high, silver-white bristles,
and he destroyed his enemies with the movement of his terrifying, curved, and knitted brows.
His lotus-eyes, which are blazing and throbbing, reside within his mouth;
the tips of his fangs emit flames that spread throughout the quarters of space.
His ears were stained with blood from the wounds he inflicted upon the chests of his enemies, split open by his claws;
his lotus-like hands and knees were smeared with the blood of the Daityas as they were crushed against the surface of their broad chests.
One should worship with red flowers, molasses-rice, and fruits and roots;
and in its light, [one should place] a large, flawless jar weighing one *bhāra*.
It is filled with pure water from a sacred ford, mixed with fragrance,
covered with a pair of cloths, and provided with a bundle of *kuśa* grass.
The wise one should place [the image] upon a heap of grain or white rice, provided with all medicinal herbs and endowed with all kinds of jewels.
Or, one should place eight jars in the directions, adorned with auspicious cloths and other ornaments, according to the sequence starting from the east, and place one jar in front.
Having placed two jars each at the gateway,
and having installed the door-keepers outside the jars in their proper order;
Recalling the *rathāṅga*, the *pāñcajanya*, the *śārṅga*, and the *nandaka*,
[he placed them] in the jars in due order, extending as far as the western direction.
Remembering Śara, Muśala, and Candra at the corners,
and then remembering Gadā, Tārkṣya, and Vedātman immediately thereafter.
In each of those places, one should worship by name with a well-concentrated mind;
one should honor them with red unguents, flowers, fruits, and roots.
And in each of those places, one should recite that mantra eight thousand times,
or one thousand and eight times, or even a hundred times according to one's own capacity.
One should mutter the supreme Nṛsiṃha Ekākṣara mantra, or the Anuṣṭubh;
at the conclusion of the recitation, one should prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in front, as prescribed by the scriptures.
It should be two cubits in length and width, provided with a yoni and a navel,
and having either four or three girdles.
The wise know that the vaginal opening resembles the flower of the *unmatta* plant;
having visualized it thus, one should then kindle the sacrificial fire.
In the center of that, one should meditate upon the unsurpassed deity Narasiṃha,
and one should likewise meditate upon the Sudarśana and other weapons in their respective places.
Having first established the fire with the syllable *praṇava* alone, the knower of mantras,
after purifying the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), should perform the invocation of the fire.
Afterward, having strewn grass around the fire with its tips pointing eastward— or even with *kuśa* grass—
one should then cleanse the vessels and sprinkle them in due order.
Having purified even the consecrated water, one should perform its sprinkling;
having purified the materials for the oblation, one should place them to the left (apasavya) of the sacrificial pit.
Having performed the consecration of the clarified butter and having covered the vessels and other implements,
he should properly set down the vessels as well as the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga).
After the invocation of the deity, there is the subsequent offering of the oblation;
one desiring long life should use *dūrvā* grass, while one desiring prosperity should use *bilva* leaves.
One desiring health should perform [the rite] with apāmārga plants, sesame seeds, or ghee;
one seeking victory over death should do so with fresh lotuses smeared with honey.
One seeking wealth should offer flowers from the *campaka* tree, while one desiring the death of an enemy should use those from the *jāti* tree, or even *lākṣā* and *vibhītaka*.
One seeking subjugation (vaśya) should accomplish the rite with mustard seeds sprinkled with salt and black pepper,
or with husks, or with neem leaves, or even with oil.
Likewise, for causing madness, insanity, delusion, or even paralysis,
one may use its seeds, its fruits, or fires kindled with its wood.
If one desires prosperity through white lotuses that are unblemished,
or even by means of the flowers and undamaged leaves of the *śrī-latā* creeper;
With its seeds and sprouts, as well as with rice grains smeared with the three sweets,
combined with sandalwood powder, blue lotuses, and white water lilies;
Likewise, with sandalwood wood or even with cow's milk, one attains supreme nourishment; and with *sahadevī* grown on a single leaf, one attains freedom from disease.
Through grains one attains long life, and through unbroken rice and plantain fruits, health;
whatever the practitioner desires, he shall accomplish by means of that very thing.
This is the common procedure; I shall state it again:
one should perform ten thousand oblations with the appropriate substances according to the rule.
As long as you are superior to that which is to be proven, so long will there be the observation of enumeration.
O Śrīnivāsa, salutations be unto you; O Śrīvṛkṣa, beloved of Śiva!
Having granted me the attainment of my desired object, be the remover of obstacles.
Then, having worshipped the Śrīvṛkṣa seven times and prostrated before it, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with devotion, saying: "May the Goddess Śrī be pleased with me."
Then, observing silence, he should eat auspicious curd,
grain, and fruit— uncooked over fire— in an earthen vessel, avoiding oil and alkaline substances.
O Pārtha, any man or woman who performs the worship of the Śrīvṛkṣa in this manner is liberated from suffering and grief; of this there is no doubt.
For seven successive births, endowed with happiness and good fortune,
the illustrious, fruitful, and truthful woman is honored in the world of mortals.
Those who, on the ninth day, worship Puruṣottama at dawn with a śrīvṛkṣa tree bearing unbroken fruits, granting boons, and with food offerings, desired fruits, garments, and sprouted grains;
Those moons among the lords of men attain prosperity.
Then, having placed the object of the rite (sādhya) before the deity and remaining seated,
one should perform the consecration with water from the jars using the mantra itself.
Having given a sacrificial fee to the preceptor, one should perform a feeding of Brahmins during the commencement of battle,
in times of public agitation, on a royal expedition, or when oppressed by enemies.
In times of fear or the affliction of disease, he should observe the eighth-day vow;
likewise, one seeking knowledge should seek incomparable learning, and one desiring prosperity should seek great fortune.
Whatever one desires, that it nourishes for him; this is the supreme vow.
Thus concludes the Narasiṃha-vrata as declared in the Garuḍa Purāṇa.
[881] Now follows the Haravratam.
Brahmā said:
Worshipped on the eighth lunar day, Lord Hara, whose ear-ornament is the cow's ear,
bestows vast knowledge, as well as splendor, noble birth, and strength.
Śiva is he whose ornaments are cow-ears and whose adornment is serpent-eyes;
he is the destroyer of death, the giver of knowledge, and the remover of sin when fully worshipped.
The root mantra and the limb-mantras are proclaimed by their own respective names.
As before, Ātithīśvara should be fashioned seated upon a lotus petal;
he is to be worshipped with offerings of perfumes and flowers according to one's ability.
Even if performed with deceit or hypocrisy, worship nevertheless yields fruit when offered with streams of clarified butter,
sacrificial fuel-sticks, curd, milk, rice, and honey.

The oblation performed with a tranquil mind yields the previously mentioned fruit. This vow is to be explained as the Vaiśvānara-pratipad-vrata. Thus concludes the Haravrata as described in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Now follows the Sugati-vrata:
One should eat only at night on the eighth lunar days (aṣṭamī) for a year, and at the end of the year, one should gift a cow;
such a person goes to the station of Indra—this is called the Sugati-vrata.
Here, Purandara is the presiding deity.
Thus concludes the Sugati-vrata as described in the Padma Purāṇa.
Now follows the Vṛṣabha-vrata: He who, having observed a fast on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, beholds a bull covered with a pair of white garments and adorned with ornaments.
Having resided for a long time in the world of Śiva, one shall thereafter become a king here on earth;
this Vṛṣavrata, proclaimed here, is the destroyer of all sins.

"Sopavāsa" means having observed a fast on the preceding day. Here, Śiva is the presiding deity. Thus ends the Vṛṣabha-vrata as described in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa. Thus ends the Vṛṣabha-vrata as described in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Now follows the Gurvaṣṭamī vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, tell me of some vow that destroys all sins."
It destroys the state of being a preta and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, in the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, there is the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī);
when it is joined with a Thursday, that lunar day increases merit.
Complete, destroying all sins and annihilating the state of existence as a preta,
one should properly undertake the vow, beginning with the cleansing of the teeth.
O Indra among kings, on that day, the god Bṛhaspati [is worshipped] by one who eats but a single meal,
having performed his bath in a river, a pond, or at home, with self-restraint.
O best of men, one should have a Jīva fashioned from gold or silver;
in its absence, one may have it made even from Śrīkhaṇḍa (sandalwood) according to one's means.
One should eat śāli rice or even sixty-day rice;
having placed the śāli rice in vessels, it should be made perfectly full.
A tawny cow should be given as a gift for the sake of completing the vow;
the Brāhmaṇa should place a jar filled with water and containing ritual substances.
Homage to you, best among the wise; homage to you, expert in ethics!
O thirty-fold god, Lord of the gods, King of the gods, let there be homage to you!
Having worshipped the Lord of the Thirty-three at the outset, he who is praised by Giriśa said:
"O God Bṛhaspati, accept this water offering; salutations to you!"
The Arghya Mantra:
O you who are honored by the heroes, Bṛhaspati, grant me intelligence, grant me prosperity, grant me the goal,
and make my ritual procedure fully complete.
This is the mantra of prayer.
In this very context, I shall relate an ancient history that bestows liberation upon the deceased and is meritorious; listen to it, O high-minded one.
Listen, O mighty-armed King, throughout the entire circle of the earth,
there was a king named Suratha, born of the Lunar dynasty.
Once, having gone to the wilderness, he entered a dense forest;
there was a single silk-cotton tree in a waterless place, scorched by the sun.
In that lifeless, waterless, and terrible place, which struck fear into all living beings,
the king beheld wicked beings resembling Rudra and Antaka.
They were clad only in skin and bone, with hair standing erect and inspiring terror;
they had fearsome fangs and blood-red eyes, having undertaken vows that were the fruit of their former sins.
To them, O Pārtha, King Suratha, freed from his distress, said:
"Who are you in this desolate forest? And why, O you of terrifying countenances, are you here?"
Then those foremost of spirits, being well-pleased, said to Suratha:
"O King, through the ripening of our karma, we have come to this state of being spirits."
Then the king said to the pretas, "Tell me by what action do you remain in this desolate forest, terrifying as ghosts?"
Then, one among them spoke to the king in due order:
"I have committed adultery with another's wife and I have spoken falsehood."
"By the ripening of that karma, I have come to this state of a preta.
Then the second one said, "O King, hear what was done by us."
"I created an obstacle for the cows while they were drinking water," the third then said, "O King, I have committed slander."
"By the ripening of that karma, I have indeed entered the state of a preta.
When this was said, King Suratha, the monarch, spoke.
How is your food, how your drink, and how your rest? Is it well with you?
The preta said:
"Wherever there is food-leavings remaining on the ground, mucus discharged from the nose,
or the dust emitted from the womb— that too is food for women."
"Otherwise, O King, there would be no food; for that reason we feel ashamed.
You should not ask this, O mighty-armed one: 'We do not obtain water.'"
Suratha said:
"O Lord, what is the use of sacrifices, what use of austerities and gifts, or what use of bathing at sacred fords,
if liberation from you could not be attained without this one vow?"
The king said:

"Tell me quickly, what is the vow? What is the procedure? And who is the deity? On which day of the week, on which date, and in which month [should it be performed], so that your liberation may occur?"
The preta said:
O King, when the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada falls on a Thursday, that great vow (mahāvratam) is fully accomplished.
The eighth lunar day of the month of Guru is of great merit and destroys all sins;
on this Budhāṣṭamī, a human being obtains the fruit of [performing the rite] a thousand times.
"I am lost for direction in the forest; O departed ones, show me the way! They then showed the king the path leading to a good destination.
And the king, having returned to his own city and performed the supreme vow,
bestowed the merit of the three recitations upon the hungry ghosts according to the Nara rite.
Then, liberated from their state as pretas and ascending a magnificent celestial chariot,
they joyfully beheld Suratha, the best of kings, who was like two suns.
O Pārtha, for him who thus performs the auspicious vow of Bṛhaspati,
there shall never be any departed spirits (pretas) in his lineage.
Freed from all evil, he goes to the state that is free from suffering.
This secret vow of the Guru-aṣṭamī has been told to you, O Pārtha.
"Whoever hears this is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the Gurvaṣṭamī-vrata as declared in the Śrī Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Thus [ends the work of] the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādeva, the sovereign lord of all faculties...
The Vows of the Eighth Day (Aṣṭamī-vratāni), within the Section on Vows (Vrata-khaṇḍa) of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri, who is proficient in all branches of knowledge.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter:
On the Ninth-Day Vows (Navamī-vrata),
which the assembly of the virtuous highly extols as a supreme refuge once they have attained them.

Victorious is his charming fame, which has purified the three worlds; now, by means of this work composed by Hemādri, the vow for every new-moon day (*navamī-tithi-vrata*)— which removes the sorrow of all people and has been handed down through tradition— is being described.
Now, the Śrīvṛkṣa-navamī vow.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Long ago, when the jewels had emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk...
Having gone to the grove of bilva trees, Kamalālayā rested there.
Saying "This is mine," the gods and dānavas fought one another;
all the asuras were utterly defeated in battle by the wielder of the discus with his discus.
The Daityas were sent to the netherworld (pātāla), while he himself shone with splendor;
because he was the abode of Śrī and Kāma, he is therefore remembered as the Śrīvṛkṣa (the tree of fortune).
Therefore, O best of the Kurus, O sinless one, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship with devotion at the very first break of dawn.
One should worship the Śrīvṛkṣa with various jewels, fruits that have not fallen from fire,
sesame flour, rice, wheat, incense, perfumes, and ointments.
O King of kings, one should worship with devotion, endowed with this mantra, the Goddess Śrī who has been brought to the sky by the rays of the slightly risen sun.
O Śrīnivāsa, salutations be unto you; O Śrīvṛkṣa, beloved of Śiva! Having brought about the highest satisfaction for me as well, be the remover of obstacles.
Then, having worshipped the Śrīvṛkṣa seven times and prostrated before it, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with devotion, saying: "May the Goddess Śrī be pleased with me."
Then, observing silence, he should eat auspicious curd,
grain, and fruit— uncooked by fire— in an earthen vessel, avoiding oil and alkaline substances.
O Pārtha, any man or woman who performs the worship of the Śrīvṛkṣa in this manner is liberated from suffering and grief; of this there is no doubt.
For up to seven future births, endowed with happiness and good fortune,
she is honored in the world of mortals as illustrious and radiant.

On the ninth day, having worshipped the Śrīvṛkṣa— which bears unbroken fruit and grants boons— with offerings of food, flowers, fruits, jewels, and sprouted grains at the time of dawn, one becomes Puruṣottama.
They attain prosperity, O moon among the lords of men.
Thus concludes the Śrīvṛkṣanavamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. Now follows the Dhvajanavamī-vrata.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, listen as I describe the ninth [vow], called Ulkā,
which was proclaimed by Kāśyapa and which destroys the suffering of Tāraka.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, which is well-known by that name,
having bathed in the river and worshipped her— the Blessed One— many great asuras,
recollecting their former boon, were slain in battle.
Assuming various forms again and again, the Goddess descended for the sake of establishing the Dharma against the foremost Daityas who were slayers of their husbands.
Now there was a great son of Mahisha named Raktasura;
he performed austerities for sixty thousand years.
To him, the four-faced one granted sovereignty over the entire circle of the three worlds;
then, having obtained that boon, he did not speak to the sons of Danu.
Having gone to Amarāvatī, he began a battle with Śakra;
seeing that army of Dānavas prepared for combat and bearing uplifted banners, he [attacked].
The Dānava fought together with the gods led by Śukra;
there a river flowed, its waves consisting of floods of blood.
The supreme mace, with its teeth like tortoises, spoke of the Vasu-wealth;
carrying it upon their bilious bodies were the warriors of the gods and asuras.
Then Raktāsura, out of rage, fought with the gods;
those gods were being struck down by Raktākṣa in that great battle.
Having abandoned heaven along with its embrace, its weapons, and its offerings,
they fell and reached the city of Kaṭachatrā, where the beloved of Bhava resides.
Durgā, together with Cāmuṇḍā, is accompanied by the nine Durgās;
first of all is Mahālakṣmī, as well as Nandā and Kṣemaṃkarī.
Śivadūtī, Mahātuṇḍā, Bhrāmarī, Candramaṅgalā, Revatī, and Harisiddhi— these nine are proclaimed.
He who offered them praise was considered by the gods to be one to whom they were bowed down in reverence.
With her lotus feet kissed by the crowns of the gods,
Durgā— both with parts and without parts— is joyful as she chants the name of the Lord of the Universe, the mother who generates happiness for the entire world.
Victorious is Hārakundarī, whose hand holds a sword smeared with blood and fat from the nails and teeth [of her victims],
and who is followed by ghouls adorned with human skulls.

Victorious is that splendor upon the Siddha-banyan tree, the naked one (Digambara), which possesses the beauty of moonstones bound within his fierce and formidable matted locks, blazing with clusters of flaming crests. 3.

Victorious is Goddess Nandā, who bears a water-pot in her hand, whose speech is like a lotus fastened upon her head, and whose beauty is produced by her lotus-like hands—she who removes all suffering. 4.

Victorious is she who dwells in the state of the fierce (raudra-bhāva), whose body is without cause, who is the bringer of well-being, who is clothed in the directions, whose face is deformed, and whose splendor fills the quarters with the loud sound of her howling.

Victorious is Śivadūtī, who from her very first devotion to Śiva possesses great fangs and whose mouth resounds with the roar of the *huṃ* sound, filling the interior of the crying universe with its clamor.
Victorious is she whose face and all the quarters of space are startled by her unbearable, terrifying, and loud laughter;
she who is adorned with the coils of the lord of serpents as an ear-ornament and who wields the tip of a boar’s tusk.
Victorious is the Goddess Bhrāmarī, whose limbs are made to dance by the sound of kettledrums, clay drums, mṛdaṅgas, and kullarikās,
and whose feet are sought after by the bees.

Peaceful, with a most serene countenance, perfected in the practice of the lion’s gaze and meditative absorption, the goddess—four-armed, bearing the crescent moon and the lunar disc—is victorious. (9)
Victorious is the many-formed Revatī Bhadrā, who holds a trident in her hand, and by the blows of her wings and beak, she has pulverized the multitudes of various enemies. 10.
Wandering through the world of the wicked in the abodes of the cremation grounds together with the Yoginīs, she who is named Harasiddhi is victorious;
may that Harasiddhi, saluted by the Siddhas, be triumphant. (11)
[891] Thus Durgā, whose limits are subtle and incomparable, having surpassed even the king of the gods, spoke this along with the deities: "May you be freed from all these fears.
Having bowed down again and again, they approached her who rides upon a lion;
and she, hearing of the fear of those terrified by worldly existence, [spoke] to them out of that [compassion].
Having emerged from that lion along with the Durgās from the city,
she fought together with the Dānavas in a great battle that was like a tempestuous storm.
The maiden has twenty arms and resembles a thick flash of lightning;
even those fierce Asuras of terrible form have not reached that place.
All these are the most excellent among the swift heroes, who have likewise performed well-heated austerities;
for they have escaped from the great planetary influences in this determination of illusion.
For [the demons] from Brahmā down to the lowest have been made known;
how then could Naraka, whose hair is like that of Manu, be surpassed by Indramāri?
Kuṣṭha, Puloman, Śarabha, Sambara, Dundubhi, Khara, Ilvala,
Namuci, Bhauma, Vātāgrya, Dhenuka, and Kali.
Enveloped by Māyā, Bala was a kinsman of Madhu, Kaiṭabha, and Kāla;
in secret, Pauṇḍraka and other lords of the Daityas were those who were proclaimed as the foremost.
All the people, equipped with wealth and cattle, raised their own banners aloft;
both their forms and their colors were described, and their banners were distinct from one another.
O Indra among kings, they appeared like blazing fires—
golden, with golden crests and adorned with golden garlands.
Banners endowed with auspicious marks were raised by various youths;
they were blue, yellow, white, red, and black in appearance—possessing five colors.
There, the foot-cloths should be made clean and variegated with fashioned bubbles;
the banners, shimmering with beauty, should be fashioned so as to be magnificent.
Then those foremost of Dānavas raised a tumultuous roar;
they beat the paṇavas, kettledrums, murajas, and gomukhas.
He caused the ānakadundubhis, conchs, drums, and kettledrums to resound;
thus did Bhavānī and the Daityas and Dānavas engage in battle.
They struck one another with arrows, spears, iron clubs, javelins, and lances;
with barbed darts like grains of millet, with spears, śataghnīs, mallets, and hammers.
Being struck, he blazed up even more intensely with rage in the battle;
the Goddess, mounted upon a lion, swiftly rushed into the midst of the fray.
There were various kinds of banners, both clear and shimmering,
amidst the Daityas' forceful assault in that leaderless battle.
Pleased, the swift-moving goddess gave signs to the gods;
they were all accepted by those who said, "The Goddess shall recite [the mantra]."
But Avidyā, being greatly pleased, instantly brought about their destruction;
she, the Night of Doom for the Dānavas, fell like a shower of meteors.
The daughter of the Fire-god seized the lives of the Daityas;
then, seizing Raktāsura by the throat, she cast him down upon the earth.
The goddess fiercely struck with her sharp trident in the sky;
the Daityas, their hearts shattered, were turned into pieces of flesh.
Nevertheless, though addressed by the goddess, he fell and died;
the god, having repeatedly conquered those asuras, [proclaimed] "Victory! in the city of his enemy.
They saw great banners hanging at the edge of the Kaṇa tree;
on the ninth day, they made the procession joyous, marked by those banners.
O Pāṇḍava, kings who have attained victory by the hundreds of thousands will play musical instruments here,
and devoted men and women alike shall approach you.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord, tell me what kind of ritual procedure is for that ninth day,
along with its secret and its mantra, by which Caṇḍikā is pleased."
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Lord, tell me what kind of ritual procedure is for that ninth day,
along with its secret and its mantra, by which Caṇḍikā is pleased."
Kṛṣṇa said:
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, which is known as Śambarī,
one should bathe and worship the sister of Hari with auspicious flowers.
The youthful goddess, the Blessed One, who rides upon a lion-chariot,
having fashioned various kinds of banners, should worship him in front.
With *mālatī* flowers, lamps, perfumes, incense, and ointments;
with offerings (*bali*), sacrificial animals, and fuel consisting of wine, meat, and fat.
Having fashioned a golden image of the Goddess, mounted upon a lion and possessing four arms, [one should worship her] with curd, sandalwood powder, and fruits that have not been cooked by fire.
O son of Kuntī, one should [worship] her who holds a sword and a spear, who bears a trident, and who is endowed with three eyes,
by means of this mantra— whether he be a Brāhmaṇa or otherwise.
To the auspicious and blessed Kṛṣṇā, who is beneficial to the entire world,
the one who brings entry and the one who brings about the dissolution, who is garlanded with planets and constellations.
I have taken refuge in the auspicious Night; O Blessed One, protect me always from all spirits and piśācas, and from all living beings and reptiles.
Protect my mind from both gods and humans,
and from yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, nāgas, and even from scorpions.
"Protect [me] from all sides against thieves, wicked beings, and violent ones"—
having uttered this, he offered a single preeminent bell from a garland upon a banner.
Then the king should likewise cause them to be placed in the apartments of the queens;
he should feed the maidens, prostrate before them, and ask for their forgiveness.
Having completed the recitation, attained its conclusion, and asked for forgiveness,
one should perform the rite by means of a fast or else by eating only a single meal.
By a man with firm devotion, devotion there is most excellent;
thus, those men who shall worship the Blessed One with banners.
For them, she is the protector on difficult paths, in the perils of thieves, serpents, and fire, in battle,
in the royal court, in the home, in the midst of combat, and upon water or land.
Bhavānī, the source of all auspiciousness, constantly provides protection;
on this ninth day, O son of Pāṇḍu, victory was achieved.
Among these, the ninth [chapter] of the Bhagavatī is always dear to her;
it is blessed, meritorious, a remover of sins, and a destroyer of all calamities.
This should be practiced with effort by those desiring all their wished-for goals.
This worship of the Goddess is beneficial; for that man who, on the ninth day, should offer a golden garland and an excellent white banner,
having attained the desires hidden within his mind, he shall leave them behind.
O Supreme Goddess, he goes to the root of the feet of the body.
Thus ends the Dhvajā-navamī-vrata from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Now follows the Ulkā-navamī-vrata.
Uṣṇa said:
O King, listen as I relate the ninth [tithi] called Ulkā,
which was described by Kāśyapa as the destroyer of Tāraka’s affliction.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, which is renowned among the wise,
one should bathe in a river and duly worship the ancestors and the gods according to the prescribed rites.
Thereafter, one should worship the goddess Cāmuṇḍā,
the beloved of Bhairava, with flowers, incense, various offerings, meat, fish, wine, and spirituous liquors.
Having performed worship, a person should offer praise with this mantra,
placing his joined palms upon his head while kneeling upon the ground.
O slayer of Mahiṣa, O Great Illusionist, O Cāmuṇḍā, wearer of a garland of severed heads!
Having placed this substance [upon the altar], grant me victory, O Goddess; homage be to you!
O Maheśvarī, protect me always from ghosts, spirits, and piśācas, from rākṣasas, from gods, and from humans, and from all fears.
O auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, O Śivā, accomplisher of all goals;
O Brahmāṇī and Kaumārī, you who possess universal forms, be gracious to me!
Thereafter, on the ninth day, one should feed young maidens dressed in blue garments;
having adorned them with undergarments and ornaments, one should ask for their forgiveness.
"Or, according to their wealth and conduct, she may be honored with seven or five [offerings];
for the Goddess is pleased by faith—this is the instruction of the Vīras."
Having sprinkled water and made a mandala with cow dung, one who is pure is traditionally instructed to offer a seat and sit down, and place the vessel before him.
Then one should serve all that well-prepared food, including milk-rice with ghee; they themselves should also eat it in the vicinity of the vessel.
Having gathered grass and likewise having gathered [fuel] from the village,
one should then set it ablaze as food, as long as the fire continues to burn.
When the meal is finished, having sipped water and with a clear mind,
one should meditate upon Cāmuṇḍā in the heart and then become intent on household duties.
By this procedure, one should perform everything month after month;
then, at the end of the year, having fed young maidens.
Having honored him with garments and ornaments and having prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness;
one should give gold according to one's ability, as well as a beautiful cow to a Brahmin.
O Pārtha, for that man who performs the Navamī vow in this manner,
there shall be no enemies, no affliction, no king, and no thief.
O Guha, spirits, ghosts, and piśācas cause fear when weapons are raised; yet for him who has been slain, no such fear exists.
The well-spoken Caṇḍikā, when practiced, protects and bestows victory upon all;
whether a man or a woman, one should observe this vow.
Like a meteor, you always burn away the rivals within their hearts.
That fang of Prakaṭī, which is like a dry, hollow reed, is Kāmākinī; it possesses equal strength with the garland of skulls on the forehead,
and the fierce man [attains success] during the Ulkā-vratas on the ninth lunar days.
Having honored whom does his heart not feel apprehension?
Thus ends the Ulkā-navamī-vrata in the Śrī-Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. Now follows the Ulkā-navamī-vrata.
The sages said:
O Lord of the Gods, hear now about that vow called Ulkā-navamī, which bestows all fruits and by which Pārvatī quickly becomes pleased.
On that ninth day, he slew all the great asuras, such as Mahiṣa and others, who were his enemies in battle; therefore, that ninth day is dear to him.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja, one who is self-restrained,
having bathed, should worship the ancestors, the gods, and human beings in their proper order.
Thereafter, one should recite the mantra of the Great Goddess, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura,
with flowers, incense, food offerings, milk, curd, fruits, and so forth.
Having thus worshipped the Goddess with devotion,
the observer of the vow should then pray to the enemy of Vṛtra (Indra) with supreme faith using this mantra.
O slayer of Mahiṣa, O great illusionist, O Cāmuṇḍā, wearer of a garland of severed heads!
O Goddess, grant me divine health and victory; homage be to you!
O Maheśvarī, protect me always from ghosts, spirits, and piśācas, from rākṣasas, from gods, and from humans, and from all fears.
O auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, O Śivā, accomplisher of all goals;
O Brāhmī and Kaumārī, you who possess universal forms, be gracious to me.
Having caused the maidens to play and having fed them, one should ask for their forgiveness;
and one should give seven, eight, or even one [coin], according to the wealth of the child.
Through faith, the goddess, the blessed Śivā, attains joy;
therefore, one should diligently honor that which arises from the companionship of the scriptures.
For that goddess dwells perpetually within the scriptures;
having sprinkled the ground and prepared a very extensive mandala with cow dung, [one should proceed].
Having given [these], one should sit down together and place the vessel before oneself;
one should cause all that, including the perfected mantras and so forth, to enter into it.
And first, having gathered everything together, one should offer it to the crows,
taking a handful of grass, measuring a span in length and well-restrained.
Having washed what is held in another's hand, one should eat oneself while maintaining silence;
when the fire has been extinguished, having sipped water for purification, one should remain pure with the mind focused on that [act].
Having meditated upon Cāmuṇḍā in one's heart, one should be intent on household duties;
by this procedure, one should perform [this rite] every month throughout the year.
Then, at the end of the year, having fed the young girls and honored them with garments and ornaments, one should bow down and dismiss them.
And he who performs this vow— whether it be a man or a woman— should give beautiful cows with golden horns to a Brahmin.
Like a meteor, she shines upon the earth with splendor among her co-wives;
O Suratha, this is now known as the illustrious Mahānavamī.
It bestows all accomplishments, is meritorious, and destroys all calamities;
for one who possesses it, there shall be no fear arising from within, nor from divine powers, nor from other beings.
For Caṇḍikā always protects one in all calamities, O Śakra;
she is the bringer of peace and prosperity, auspicious, and the bestower of sons, health, wealth, and gain.

This vow, which is dear to Caṇḍī and frequented by sages and Siddhas, should always be performed by men who seek the fruits of the four aims of life; O Suratha, whoever performs this vow even under a pretext in this manner—
Having ascended a celestial chariot crowded with the foremost ladies of the Rudras, he goes to the world of Śiva by means of his auspicious countenance.
Thus ends the Ulkā-navamī-vrata as declared in the Saura Purāṇa. Now follows the Pradīpta-navamī-vrata:
one should prepare a blade of grass measuring one cubit (hasta), positioned between the thumb and the forefinger.
One should take food as long as the lamp has not yet been lit.
The remainder [of the phrase] is "on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina.
Having fully worshipped the Goddess, one who is purified by the sixteen-syllable mantra:
*Oṃ mahābhagavatyai mahiṣāsuramardinyai*.
With the sixteen-syllable mantra "Nāmnā huṃ paṭ," one who worships for a year according to the rules with golden flowers, perfumes, and various jewels shall obtain all desires as prescribed.
The ninth, O child, is known as Pradīptā; it has gold, cows, and water as its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
It is primordial, all-pervading, pure, and unconquered in battles.
Just as the god Maheśvara becomes [the lord] of the host of enemies,
so too does one [attain this] by preparing pills of guggulu according to this very procedure.

Having worshipped Śiva with mantras, one should offer the blazing [substance] into the fire according to the rite; the syntactical connection is that, having worshipped Śiva by means of the previously mentioned procedure, one should offer pills of guggulu into the fire. "With mantras" means with the Durgā-mantras. "In the blazing rite" means when the moon has risen full, at the end of the evening twilight (pradoṣa).
In this case, the reward is either the previously mentioned sacrificial fee or the fruit declared for the horse sacrifice.
Thus ends the Pradīpta-navamī-vrata as declared in the Devī-purāṇa.
Now, the Navarātri-vrata. The gods said:
As long as there is earth, wind, space, water, fire, the moon, and the planets,
so long indeed shall the worship of Caṇḍikā endure forever on earth.
Especially during the rainy season, on the eighth days of the month of Āśvina,
and on the ninth day, this "Great Sound" (Mahāśabda) shall attain renown throughout the world.

Brahmā said: O Indra, king of the gods, this which bestows the fruit of dwelling in heaven has been proclaimed to you as the distinction between superior and inferior [paths] by means of the yoga of ritual action.
O Śakra, having thus slain the one of great power who was a thorn to the gods in former times,
the goddesses and the gratified Vidyās granted him boons.
Śakra said: "O Father, since the terrible Āśvina [battle] was fought on the ninth day every year, I wish to hear about the fasting, recitation of mantras, and other rites associated with it."
When the Daitya named Ghora had been struck down— that is, killed—
Brahmā said:
"Listen, O Śakra, I shall explain to you exactly as you yourself have asked."
It bestows great accomplishment, brings fortune, and destroys all enemies.
For the sake of benefiting the entire world, especially during excessive rains,
it is for the purpose of performing duties by Brāhmaṇas and others, and for the protection of the earth by Kṣatriyas.
O child, it should be performed by Vaiśyas for the sake of cattle-wealth, by Śūdras who desire the happiness of sons,
by women for the sake of good fortune, and by wealthy men who long for further riches.
O Indra, lord of the gods, this great vow of immense merit, which was practiced by Śaṅkara and others,
should be performed by those endowed with devotion to the Goddess.
O Śakra, when Jupiter is in the sign of Virgo, one should begin from the first day of the bright fortnight;
observing the Nandikā vow— that is, the first lunar day— one should subsist on barley, or indeed on kāśa grass, or alternatively, subsist on food only at night.
Bathing at dawn, having conquered the pairs of opposites, worshipping Śiva three times a day,
and devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, he should always feed virgins.
On the eighth day, O best of gods, one should have nine auspicious houses made of wood constructed, or indeed just one, according to the threefold division.
On that [altar], the Goddess should be fashioned out of gold or even silver;
one should worship her with a sword and a trident possessing the characteristics of the time of battle.
Provided with all offerings such as garments, jewels, fruits, and so forth,
one should cause the worship of the chariot, the palanquin, and other items, as well as the offering of oblations to the deities.

The *balidevakī* is that which pertains to the deities who receive offerings (*baligrāhin*), such as the Vināyakas and others. With flowers—namely, the *candra*, *bilva*, mango, *jātī*, *punnāga*, *campaka*, *droṇa*, and *kuruvaka*—one should arrange a diverse worship on the eighth day and observe a fast.
Facing Durgā, one should recite the mantra with a single-pointed mind and well-purified disposition.
O best of kings, when half of the night remains, for the sake of victory,
one should [offer] a well-worshipped buffalo that is five years old and endowed with auspicious marks.
Having recited "Kālakālī" according to the prescribed rule, one should strike with a sword;
then, taking the blood and flesh arising from that [victim], one should employ them in worship and other rites.
One should offer [the substance] consecrated with the Mahākauśika mantra to Nairṛta;
in front of him, the king should bathe, having fashioned an effigy of his enemy from well-ground flour.
Having struck [the image] with a sword, one should offer it to Skanda and Viśākha;
thereafter, one should place the Goddess in a well-prepared earthen vessel along with milk, clarified butter, water, and other substances.
Having worshipped with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood, one should offer incense,
as well as gold, flowers, jewels, and other items, along with new, unwashed garments.
A very abundant food offering should be presented to the Goddess by those who are well-disposed;
one should also honor the devotees of the Goddess, such as young girls, women, and others.
One should gratify the twice-born and the blind heretics with gifts of food;
likewise those men who are devoted to Nanda and those who observe the great vows.
One should perform the chariot procession, known as the Bali, filled with the sound of victory-trumpets;
by this, the Goddess is pleased, as well as by the striking of the breast.
O best of gods, by worshipping with devotion on Mahānavamī, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; this worship grants all desires.
[903] O child, among all the castes, those who are proclaimed as your devotees obtain fame,
sovereignty, sons, long life, and the abundance of wealth by performing this.
Thus is the Navarātrivrata as declared in the Devīpurāṇa. Now follows the procedure for the Mahānavamī festival;
the worship of the Kumārīs is also described in its entirety in the Skandapurāṇa.
One should worship each maiden individually, and likewise increase by one;
one may also worship twice that number, thrice that number, or even a group of nine.
By nine [repetitions] one perceives the earth; by double that, sovereignty;
by increasing by one each time, one obtains security; and by each single [additional repetition], one obtains what is dear.
One should avoid a maiden who is only one year old for the purpose of worship;
for him, there is no satisfaction derived from perfumes, flowers, fruits, and the like.
Starting from a two-year-old girl up to the age of ten,
one should worship her in all undertakings according to the prescribed method as stated in the tradition.
A two-year-old girl is a Kumārikā, a three-year-old is a Trimūrtinī;
a four-year-old is a Kayāṇī, and a five-year-old is a Rohiṇī.
Kālī is six years old, Caṇḍikā is seven years old,
Śāmbavī is eight years old, and Durgā is remembered as nine years old.
Those celebrated by the names Subhadrā and Daśavarṣā are [suitable];
however, those girls who are older than that are excluded from all ritual activities.
For the destruction of suffering and poverty, for the destruction of enemies,
and for the sake of increasing longevity and strength, a man should worship young maidens.
One desiring long life should worship the Threefold Form for the attainment of the fruits of the three aims of human existence,
and for the removal of untimely death, the affliction of disease, and all sufferings.
For the increase of happiness, grain, wealth, health, sons, and grandsons,
the wise man should daily worship Kalyāṇī for the sake of the constant growth of auspiciousness.
A man who desires health and happiness, as well as victory,
and one who constantly desires fame, should worship Rohiṇī.
A man seeking knowledge, seeking victory, especially seeking a kingdom,
and seeking the destruction of his enemies, should worship Kālikā.
One desiring victory in battle should worship Caṇḍikā;
likewise for the destruction of suffering and poverty, and for the enchantment of kings.
For the destruction of great sins, one should worship Śāmbhavī;
she is [employed] in the rite of fierce accomplishment against the enemies of the Kulāṭas.
A wise person should worship Durgā with diligence for the destruction of misfortune and for the attainment of desired fruits, such as good fortune, wealth, grain, and other blessings.
A mortal should worship Subhadrā for the increase of male and female servants;
the method for the worship of the maiden (kumārī) is also stated in that very same place:
"Especially at the time of dawn, having performed an oil massage in particular..."
Then, O Bhārgava, one should invoke the maiden with this mantra.
The invocation mantra:
"I invoke the maiden who is the Goddess Lakṣmī composed of the syllables of the mantra, who assumes the forms of the Mothers, and who is manifest as the essence of the nine Durgās."

I worship the Goddess Tripurā, the support of the three cities, the embodiment of the three aims of life, whose form is knowledge, who is adored by the three worlds, and who is the triple manifestation.
I worship the auspicious Śivā, who consists of the creative powers yet transcends them, whose heart is compassion,
the eternal mother of all well-being, and the source of all auspiciousness.

I worship Lakṣmī, who is the support of the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, whose essence consists of the letters beginning with 'ma', who possesses infinite power, and who is Rohiṇī.
I worship Kālī, who moves at will, auspicious and beloved, whose form consists of arrows and discs, the granter of desires, noble and compassionate.
I always worship the goddess Caṇḍikā, who possesses fierce valor, who is fierce in her power of illusion, and who is the destroyer of the fierce Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
I worship Lakṣmī, the consort of Śambhu, who bestows eternal bliss, who is peaceful, who is saluted by all the gods, and whose very self is all beings.
I always worship with devotion Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of worldly existence, who is difficult to reach and difficult to overcome in action, and who destroys the afflictions of distress.
I worship the goddess Subhadrā, my mother, who is beautiful, whose complexion resembles gold, and who bestows happiness and good fortune.
In this manner, one should diligently perform the worship of the maidens with water-pots,
garments, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other such offerings.
