One should feed them with various kinds of foods and edibles, such as milk-rice and the like;
likewise, those with deficient or extra limbs, those afflicted by leprosy and other diseases, and those of low birth.
Her limbs are covered with bursting tumors from within; she is marked by wounds of blood and pus;
she is blind from birth, squinting, one-eyed, misshapen, and has sparse body hair.
One should reject a maiden who is diseased or born from the womb of a female slave;
however, one should accept her if she is healthy, well-proportioned in limb, beautiful, and free from sores.
One should properly honor a maiden born of the same lineage;
for all undertakings, one should honor a Brāhmaṇa woman, and for the sake of victory, one born of a royal lineage.
"And on the [day of] Dāruṇa, a man should worship one of another species according to the prescribed rite.
Here, the worship of a horse is mentioned in the Devīpurāṇa:
"On an auspicious day, in conjunction with the first lunar day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja..."
Formerly, the one named Uccaiḥśravas first brought forth prosperity.
Therefore, on the following day, he should be honored there by men with devotion;
indeed, the horses should also be worshipped until the ninth day.
Then, day after day, rites for peace and prosperity should be performed for them;
likewise, one should [use] grain, bhallātaka, kuṣṭha, vacā, and siddhārthaka.
One should tie a knot for them with a five-colored thread,
using mantras dedicated to Vāyu, Varuṇa, Sūrya, Śakti, and Viṣṇu.
Day after day, one should perform oblations with offerings to the Viśvedevas and to Agni;
meanwhile, the horses must be guarded by men with weapons in their hands.
"Because of poverty, there shall never be any outsiders there at all.
Regarding this Navarātra, on the sixth day, the consecration of the *bilva* branch and other items should be performed; likewise, it is stated in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"Aiṃ! For the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa and for the grace of Rāma..."
In the past, Brahmā awakened you, O Goddess, at an improper time.
I too have taken refuge [in you]; therefore, on the sixth day, in the evening, I awaken you:
O Śrīphala born on the peak of Śrīśaila, O abode of Śrī!
"You must be led by me; go, for you are to be worshipped in the form of Durgā.
On the seventh day, at dawn, having cut that branch from the tree, one should bring it into the house."
And likewise in that very same [text]:
"Even in the absence of the root, one should insert it into the seventh alone;
likewise, a twig from both of the nine bilva fruits. Thus it is said.
A special worship on the eighth day is prescribed in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"On this eighth day, the most terrible Bhadrakālī, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
manifested together with ten million Yoginīs."
Therefore, on that day,
she should be honored by men who have observed a fast with garments, incense, lamps, garlands, and ointments.
With various kinds of food offerings and vegetables, with oblations and the gratification of Brahmins,
and with bilva leaves, śrīphala fruits, sandalwood, and ghee.

"But on the ninth day, Brāhmaṇas should be honored by all who have performed their ablutions. Thus it is said. If one is unable to perform the worship of Durgā and other rites daily throughout the nine days beginning with the first lunar day (pratipad), it should be performed during the three days beginning with the seventh. Regarding this, Dhaumya says: "The Navarātra rite should be performed in the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina."
Following the sequence beginning with the first lunar day (pratipad) and so forth, until it becomes the ninth day.
"Or it should be performed for three nights, beginning from the seventh day in due order. Thus spoke Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
"The Mahānavamī is meritorious; it is the most excellent among lunar days (tithis)."
This should be practiced by all the gods, and especially by the protectors of subjects.
O Pārtha, for the gratification of Bhavānī, for the happiness of the year,
and for the pleasure of the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, as well as for the festival.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
From what time has this [day] known as the "Great Ninth" (Navamī-mahā) proceeded?
Was it also from the beginning a dear lunar day (tithi) to the Blessed One, Kṛṣṇa?
Does this maintenance of the world proceed from that which was born from the womb of Yaśodā,
or did it already exist previously during the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages?
And as for whatever other living beings are being killed or caused to be killed—
what is the destiny of those slain creatures in the world beyond?
For those who kill themselves, those who cause others to kill, and likewise those who approve of such acts—
O Keśava, you ought to sever all this doubt of mine.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Pārtha, that which is the supreme power, infinite, worshipped by the worlds, the all-pervading self, pure, accessible through devotion, and captivating to the mind— [that is she].
She who is half of the eighth day, the goddess Kālikā, the well-slept Sarvamaṅgalā,
Māyā, Kātyāyanī, Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā, and the beloved of Śaṅkara.
That Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, whom those devoted to yoga meditate upon,
is Śivā Bhavānī, who is worshipped through various forms and various names.
On the ninth day, O Great King, it is worshipped by gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas, by gandharvas, uragas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and men.
This has been proclaimed by other rulers of the earth since the beginning of creation;
it was worshipped in ancient times by the gods, and even earlier by those auspicious ones who preceded them.
The eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja, conjoined with the asterism Mūla, is known as Mahānavamī; it is exceedingly rare even throughout the three worlds.
When the sun has entered Virgo, that eighth day of the bright fortnight which is conjoined with the lunar mansion Mūla is known as Mahānavamī.
By worshipping the Mother who bestows birth and liberation on the eighth and ninth days of the month of Āśvina, a man becomes free from sorrow.
Threatening with *huṃ* sounds, she is supreme in severing the flood of obstacles.
Worshipped on the ninth day, the Goddess bestows incomparable fruit;
she is meritorious, she is pure, and she is the giver of the happiness of the true Dharma.
In that [place], Cāmuṇḍā, who wears a garland of severed heads, is to be worshipped perpetually;
for those living beings, such as buffaloes and others, are indeed employed for her sake.
All of them go to the heavenly realm; no sin is found in those who kill [the victim].
Such merit is not attained through the offering of sacrifices, nor by means of incense and ointments.
Just as Vindhyavāsinī is satisfied with rams and buffaloes,
so too are various living beings slaughtered there for the sake of Durgā.
O Kaunteya, those illustrious ones who have given up their lives in the courtyard of Bhavānī go to heaven,
O Yudhiṣṭhira.
O descendant of Kuru, those men shall have a certain residence in heaven during all the Manvantaras and Kalpas, and they shall be beloved by the Apsarases.
Among all of them, O Yudhiṣṭhira, this ninth [tithi], honored by the gods,
is renowned as being without beginning or end in every year.
Again and again, in her incarnations, Bhavānī is worshipped by the gods;
having descended, she has repeatedly appeared upon earth as the destroyer of the Daityas.
In heaven, the netherworld, and among mortals, she provides protection to her guests;
this very Great Goddess, born from the womb of Yaśodā, [acts thus] in due time.
Having placed my foot upon the head of the demon Kaṃsa, I ascended to heaven;
from that time forth, I have been known as Yaśodānandinī, the slayer of Daityas.
Having established [the deity] on the Vindhya mountain, she was worshipped once more;
though already famous from before, she was worshipped again by her sister for the sake of [her] greatness.
For the benefit of sentient beings on earth and for the pacification of all calamities,
one who has thus observed the fast of the nine nights at Nindhyavāsinī—
With single meals, people— possessed of spiritual power— worship the Goddess in every place,
in every city, in every house, in every village, and in every forest.
Then the wise one should worship with the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and kings— who are bathed, delighted, and joyful— using their respective mantras individually.
O tiger among the Kurus, listen to this procedure for those who are devoted Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Mlecchas, and other human beings, as well as for women.
A king desiring victory should perform the ritual of the "Lohābhisārika" (the iron-encircled rite) in due order, beginning from the first lunar day until the eighth.
In a region sloping toward the northeast,
one should have a divine pavilion constructed, auspiciously adorned with banners, measuring nine or seven cubits.
One should cause a very beautiful pit (kuṇḍa) of one cubit in measure to be made in the southeast,
provided with three girdles and a womb-shape resembling a leaf of the holy fig tree.
Having brought all the royal insignia, as well as whatever weapons and missiles there may be, one should consecrate them all within the pavilion.
Then, having bathed with the Brahmins, pure and wearing white garments,
he should offer clarified butter into the fire with mantras preceded by the syllable Om and containing the names of those [deities].
Formerly there was a Dānava named Loha who possessed great strength;
he was cut into many pieces in battle by the enraged gods.
Whatever iron is seen on earth that originates from his limbs—
for that reason this ritual known as *lohābhisārika* was ordained by the seers.
The king should offer the remnants of the oblation to the horses as their food;
milk-rice mixed with clarified butter should be offered into the fire with the mantras of weapons and missiles.
There, he performed a sacrifice of clarified butter alone with royal insignia and auspicious mantras, while elephants and horses were adorned and tethered to their posts.
Constantly parading through the city with the sounds of Nandi’s drum preceding him,
the king bathed every day and worshipped the ancestors and the gods.
One should honor the royal insignia with fruits, garlands, and ointments;
the remnants of what has been taken should be given to a Brahmin who has performed the initiation ceremony.
From the bringing of that [offering], victory for the king is proclaimed.
[912] I shall now proclaim to you the mantras for worship as they were spoken in the Purāṇas.
When worshipped, they bestow renown, long life, fame, and strength;
just as the moon covers this earth for the sake of auspiciousness.
Thus, clothe the king for the sake of increasing his victory and well-being.
The Parasol Mantra:
You are born of the Gandharva lineage; do not become a defiler of your family, by the word of truth of the Brahmins, and of Soma and Varuṇa.
And by the power of Kūtāśa,
as well as by the splendor of the sun and the ascetic heat of the sages, cause the horse to grow.
By the power of Rudra’s celibacy and the strength of Pavana,
remember the prince and the Kaustubha jewel.

The destination that a killer of a father, a killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a mother, a killer of an embryo, a speaker of falsehood, and a Kṣatriya who faces the east shall go— [that destination he shall attain].
As far as the sun, the moon, and the wind perceive your evil deed, go quickly to that destination; then your sin shall be realized.
O horse, if you desire a change of fortune on this path of battle,
then, having conquered your enemies in combat, may you be happy together with your master.
The mantras for the horses:
"O banner of Śakra, of great heroism, dark-hued one, I worship you! O winged one, son of Vinatā, likewise, O banner of Nārāyaṇa!"
O son of Kāśyapa, O brother of Aruṇa, O abode of Viṣṇu’s vehicle,
O immeasurable one, O invincible one in battle, O destroyer of the enemies of the gods!
Since Garuḍa, with the speed of the wind, is present within you,
protect our weapons, shields, and arrows, and consume our enemies.
The mantra of the Banner:
Kumuda, Airāvaṇa, Padma, Puṣpadanta, Vāmana, Supratīka, Añjana, and Nīla— these eight are of divine origin.
Their sons and grandsons formerly took refuge in eight forests:
Bhadra, Manda, Mṛga, and Rājasaṃkīrṇa.
O great elephant, remember your origin; you were born in forest after forest.
May the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts protect you.
Protect your husband, O lord of elephants; be maintained like a master.
Attain victory in battle; may it be well with you on your journey—depart!
May you have fortune from Soma, strength from Viṣṇu, splendor from the Sun, speed from the Wind,
steadfastness from Meru, victory from Rudra, and valor from the god Purandara.
May the Nāgas protect you in battle, as well as the quarters of the sky together with their deities;
may the Aśvins, along with the Gandharvas, protect you always from every side.
The Elephant Mantra: The Fire-god, the Vasus, the Rudras, Vāyu, Soma, the great sages,
the nāgas, kinnaras, gandharvas, yakṣas, hosts of bhūtas, and grahas.
The Pramathas along with the Ādityas, Bhūteśa together with the Mothers,
Skanda the general of Śakra’s army, and Varuṇa are here as attendants at his side.
May they consume all enemies; may the king attain victory over whatever ornaments have been deployed by his foes from every side.
Let [the weapons] fall upon the enemies, destroyed by your splendor,
just as they did at the slaying of Kālanemi, so too at the destruction of Tripura.
Just as you shone in battle after battle against Hiraṇyakaśipu, and likewise in the war between the gods and the asuras, so too do you shine today; therefore, remember us as well.
Having seen this blue and white [image], may the enemies of the king perish quickly,
defeated in battle by various terrible diseases and by weapons.
May Pūtanā, Revatī, Gaurī, and she who is known as Kālarātri, be instantly restored to health, cleansed by this destruction of you.
The mantra of the banner:
Asir, Viśasana, Khaḍgī, Vikarmā, Durāsada,
Śrīgarbha, Vijaya, and likewise Dharmādhāra.
Thus these eight names of yours were spoken by the Creator himself;
your constellation is Kṛttikā, and your preceptor is the god Maheśvara.
O Janārdana, the divine Creator is your gold and your body; he is your father and your grandfather. Therefore, protect me always.
The Sword Mantra:
Oṃ! O bestower of protection, you who are made entirely of iron, [be present] upon my heart and shield;
protect me, for I am worthy of protection—I must not be slain! Homage be to you!
The Armor Mantra:
O Dundubhi, you who cause the hearts of those who have sought refuge to tremble with rage,
become likewise the increaser of victory for the armies of the lords of the earth.
Just as peacocks rejoice at the sound of living beings.
"May it be so; let your voice bring us joy through its delight, just as the sound of a rain-cloud produces terror in women."
Likewise, may there be terror for our enemy in battle through the sound of musical instruments.
The mantra for the drum:
O great sovereign of all weapons, destroyer of all enemies of the gods!
You are the auspicious ground for the armies and likewise the increaser of victory.
O bow, protect me always together with your most excellent arrows.
The mantra for the bow:
"You are meritorious, the most auspicious among auspicious things such as the sounds of conchs;
since you are eternally held by Viṣṇu, be the bestower of peace."
The Conch Mantra:
O you who resemble the rays of the moon, white as snow and sea-foam;
O you who are delighted by the waving of chowries, beloved of the gods!
The Chamara-mantra: You were fashioned first among all weapons by the wielder of the Pināka bow;
having been extracted from his trident weapon, you were made into a beautiful object for grasping in the fist.
You are dear to Caṇḍikā, the destroyer of all the wicked;
you have been spread abroad and established by the gods.
You are the embodiment of all sentient beings, the destroyer of the impure asuras;
O Churikā, protect me always, grant me peace—homage be to you!
The Mantra of the Knife (Churikā): It was fashioned by Brahmā for the expulsion of the wicked, for the gathering together of the virtuous, and for the successful establishment of worldly affairs.
Bestow glory, bestow happiness, and be the victor of the king!
Strike down all enemies immediately; O Hemadaṇḍa, let there be homage to you!
The Kanakadaṇḍa mantra:
It is named Vijaya-yajada, the slayer of enemies and the doer of what is dear;
it is the destroyer of suffering, the giver of dharma, peaceful, and the annihilator of all misfortunes.
"These eight very powerful lions have been declared to be in your presence;
therefore, O Brahmin, you are sung of by the sages in the Vedas as the 'Lion-throned' (Siṃhāsana)."
Śiva himself is present in you; Śakra, the lord of the gods, is in you;
the god Hari is stationed in you, and for your sake he performs penance.
Homage to you, O auspicious one who is auspicious in every respect; be a source of good fortune for the lord of the earth.
O Lion Throne, conqueror of the three worlds and of all things, homage be to you!
The Mantra of the Lion Throne:
Having performed the ritual of the Iron Process (lohābhisāra) preceded by this mantra,
[one should worship] with fruits, food offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, and ointments.
Having observed the religious observances on the eighth day, one should perform the ritual bath in the forenoon;
[one should worship] Durgā, whether she be represented by a golden image, a silver one, or one made of clay.
Having fashioned it according to one's means from stone, wood, earth, or copper,
it should be placed upon a beautiful spot in the battle-ground, decorated with various carvings of wood.
One should visualize the Goddess situated in the midst of a variegated house, with a designated place laid out before her,
and [anoint her] with sandalwood, saffron, campaka, and the four ingredients ground together with rock.
The goddess, whose limbs were honored with many flowers—
water lilies along with lotuses— and with excellent lamps, incense, and fine food offerings.
With offerings of meat and strengthening oblations, with auspicious sounds rising up,
with victory umbrellas, with chariots, and with crowds of people bearing whisks and white weapons;
With joyful hearts, excellent garments and all else are offered to the Blessed Lady:
O Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Durgā,
Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī, Svāhā, Svadhā— homage be to you!
O Goddess of the Gods, I offer you this sacred bilva leaf, which arises from nectar, is the śrīvṛkṣa tree, and is always dear to Mahādeva.
On that day, one should worship Durgā with *droṇa* flowers;
she is beloved by the Queen of the Gods, and likewise, one who has undertaken the vow stands before her.
Then, having paid homage to Śaṅkha, the king should crush his enemies;
he should desire victory, sovereignty, and abundance for himself.
Bowing again and again, he remembered in his heart the auspicious one—
the slayer of Mahiṣa, the mighty-armed Kumārī, who has the lion as her vehicle.
She was threatening the demons, auspicious, with a sword raised in her hand;
Durgā, wearing a bell, a rosary, and a garland, stood poised at the onset of battle.
Then, with cries of "Victory! Victory!", you should address her thus:
"O auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, O Śivā, who accomplishes all purposes!"
O refuge, O Tryambakā, O Gaurī, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you!
You who are anointed with saffron and smeared with sandalwood paste.
"O Durgā, who possesses the great garland of bilva leaves, I have come to you for refuge.
Having spoken thus, O Kauravya, one should then perform a vigil at night on the eighth lunar day.
One should cause a great festival to be held with actors, dancers, and songs;
having thus spent the night joyfully, at dawn when the sun rises, [one should proceed].
One should cause buffaloes and rams to be slaughtered before him with their necks bowed,
either a hundred, fifty, or even half of that, according to one's desire.
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with jars filled with fermented liquor and spirits;
likewise, one should give that same offering to the Kapālikas and even to wicked people.
Having distributed everything among his friends, relations, and kinsmen, O son of Kuntī, he then,
at the time of afternoon on the ninth day, mounted his chariot.
The king himself, accompanied by his own army, should cause Bhavānī to be paraded through the kingdom,
escorted by highly skilled men who are well-honored and mounted on chariots.
Gradually, by means of the blazing lamps from the lamp-trees of Ambikā,
the warriors drew their swords, while the archers leaped with great agility.
With conchs and drums sounding and many bards dancing,
some hero who had fasted was led away by another man bearing a sword.
One should offer a bali-oblation of meat, along with blood, water, and food, combined with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), using this mantra: [to the beings].
One should cast the bali offering three times each with the trident toward the cardinal and intermediate directions, saying:
"O gods, Ādityas, and Vasus, please accept this bali!"
The Maruts, the Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, the Grahas, the Asuras, the Yātudhānas, the Piśācas, the Mātṛs, and the Uragas.
Dākinīs, yakṣas, vetālas, yoginīs, and likewise pūtanas;
jṛmbhakas, siddhas, gandharvas, mālā-vidyādharas, and mountain-dwellers.
The guardians of the quarters and the guardians of the worlds, those who are the Vighnas and Vināyakas,
and the great sages beginning with Brahmā, who bring peace to the worlds.
May there be no obstacle, nor may there be sin for me; may there be no adversaries. May both the gentle and the fierce spirits and ghosts be bringers of happiness.

In this manner, O Pārtha, one should cause Goddess Durgā, seated upon her chariot, to be paraded through the kingdom; or else, by means of a human vehicle, one should then bring the rite to its conclusion.
Now, when obstacles have arisen, one should perform the pacification of spirits (*bhūtaśānti*),
so that no further obstacles arise and the journey reaches completion.
In this manner, kings and other men as well,
with joyful minds, perform the pilgrimage on the Mahānavamī day of the goddess Nandā’s daughter.
All of them, liberated from sin, go to the city of the Lord;
for them there are no enemies, nor fire, nor thieves, nor obstacles.
O Indra among kings, those with whom Maheśvarī is pleased create no obstacles;
free from disease and devoid of ailment, they enjoy pleasures in happiness.
Men become devotees of the Blessed Lady—what more need be said?
Thus has this great festival of the goddess Durgā been fully described to you.
This destroys all inauspiciousness for those who read or even hear it: [She who],
seated upon the broad back of the demon Mahiṣāsura, pierced by the tip of her trident, possesses arms like staffs with beautiful golden armlets.
Having worshipped Durgā, who is followed by the moon-faced goddess, on the ninth day, mortals cross over the dense thickets of difficulties.

Thus concludes the procedure for the Mahānavamī festival as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*. Now follows the procedure for the Mahānavamī festival according to the *Atharvaṇa Gopatha Brāhmaṇa* [i.e., *Atharvaveda Pariśiṣṭa* 17.2.1–17; the readings from the *AVPar* are provided in brackets].

Then, on the ninth day, in the afternoon, having bathed the mounts and dressed in new garments, the Brahmin should prepare a sacrificial altar (*vedi*) measuring twelve *kuśas*. Having performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) prescribed as "atha tantraṃ," he should sprinkle the ornaments and mounts three times. Reciting the hymn beginning with "paridhīyān niśālām," he should return and perform the consecration. Whatever has been done here by this horse, including its strength and thorns, having performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), he should deposit [the offerings] with the mantras of safety and invincibility (*abhaya* and *aparājita*).

Having offered oblations with his own merits, with *svastyayana* hymns, and with the *Apratiratha* hymn, and having established the fire with the words, "O Agni, drive away the *rakṣases*," he should cover [the site] with garments. Having filled jars made of *udumbara* wood with juices and set them out every day, he should deposit them. Likewise, having mixed other water-vessels and eight vessels of grain, he should worship the deities there in the eight directions: Agni, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Soma, and the two Aśvins. Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* offering in milk, while holding on to the sacrificer, he should offer oblations with these five verses: *agne...*, *samās tvāgne...*, *tvaṃ no agne...*, *mām agne varco...*, *ud uttamam...*, *varuṇasya pāśam...*, *asmad avādhāḥ...* (*asmat...*), *sadasas patim...*, *adbhutam...* (*adbhutaḥ...*), and *aśvinā vācam...* He should offer first on the full moon day; it is said that he should strike the drum. There, he should recite the following consecration formula: *upa śvāsaya...* (Sāmaveda 2.520).

All musical instruments and mounts should be employed; they cause great joy, and one should establish them on the fifth day. On that side, one should offer incense of *guggulu* and *kuṣṭha*, reciting: "O God, let the consumption (yakṣmā) depart; O God, let it come! One should bestow prosperity with the mantra: "The fragrance which is yours, the triple life-span. Having tied an amulet (*pratisara*) with the mantra: "You are the purifier, you are the defiler," one should fasten it with the mantra: "Not afflicted, before the book. Having gone outside and proceeded to the north, having emerged by the outer path, one should perform this for a friend, or for one who has faith. One should diligently perform the rite for the protection of those struck by fear on the ninth day, avoiding the two sides [of the lunar fortnight].
Thus ends the ritual for Mahānavamī in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa; thus ends the ritual for the Mahānavamī festival. Now follows the vow of Ubhaya-navamī.
Śrī Sumantu said:
He who diligently observes a fast at night on the ninth lunar day for one year shall obtain the highest enjoyments in this world and go to heaven in the next.
When the month of Pauṣa has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night—
having conquered his senses, speaking the truth, and being free from desire and anger— [attains the fruit].
One should diligently observe the fast on the ninth day of both fortnights;
one should worship the Noble Lady at the three times of day with offerings of perfumes and flowers.
Having performed the fire-ritual according to the rules, one should prepare a bed upon the ground;
at the end of the month, having performed a ceremonial bath for Bhavānī with ghee and other offerings.
Having performed meditation and a great worship, one should offer it to Caṇḍikā;
one should present as an offering a prastha of rice cooked in milk.
One should feed eight young maidens as well as Vaiṣṇava brahmins; having fashioned an image of the Goddess made of flour, one should worship her by the name Āryā.

Having performed the ritual bath with jasmine flowers, guggulu resin, bilva leaves, and sesame seeds, one should worship the four-armed goddess who holds a trident, and likewise consume the sesame seeds.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who thus worships the Noble One:
seated upon a supreme celestial palace that shines like ten million suns, he shall dwell there.
Fanned by yak-tail whisks and praised by gods and asuras,
he shall go to the beautiful city of Durgā, where Caṇḍikā herself resides.
He sports with the gods and gandharvas until the dissolution of the world,
having enjoyed all desired pleasures together with those born of twenty-one generations of his lineage.
O hero, having returned to earth, he becomes a king upon the surface of the world—
he who, when the month of Māgha has arrived, observes the practice of eating only at night.
Eating rice mixed with ghee while his senses are restrained,
he should be intent on fasting on the eighth day of both fortnights.
O King, one should worship Durgā according to the prescribed rite by the name Gaurī;
having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he is honored in the world of the Sun.
When the month of Phālguna has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming barley-meal while keeping himself far away from women;
O King, having observed a fast on the eighth day of both fortnights,

one should keep the fast in mind and worship Durgā according to the prescribed rite; having resolved upon fasting on the ninth day, one should worship Tryambakā with devotion on the eighth day by preparing [an image] from wheat flour while eating only at night.
O Hero, one should worship the goddess named Durgā, who has eight arms and three eyes,
with all offerings of perfumes, flowers, and oblations that are red.
One should offer black aloe-wood as incense and buffalo meat;
for the ritual bath or the consumption of water, grains or white mustard seeds are prescribed, or barley is traditionally taught.
Whoever should thus worship the auspicious Tryambaka in the month of Māgha,
one should worship him with yellow flowers mixed with sandalwood and agallochum.
Curd-rice is the food offering, and this excellent incense is storax;
for the bath and the ritual consumption, grain and cow’s urine serve to purify the body.
And on the ninth day, having performed a bath for the Great Goddess with ghee and other substances,
one should devoutly feed young maidens and Brahmins according to one's capacity.
O best of kings, he who thus worships the goddess Durgā with devotion goes to the supreme abode where that Caṇḍikā resides.
When the month of Caitra has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming rice flour mixed with milk produced from *śāli* rice;
One should worship the Blessed Lady with devotion, having fashioned her image out of sandalwood,
measuring fifteen armspans, and offering perfumes, flowers, and other oblations.
One should indeed offer incense made of saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood, along with agallochum and camphor, to the Blessed Lady under the name Jvālāmukhī.
O King, one should devotedly offer the animal-headed food-oblation according to the prescribed rite;
having thus gratified the Goddess of Gods, one should then feed the young maiden.
Then, having restrained his speech, he should feed the Brahmins according to his ability;
[he should offer] a golden altar-stool adorned with clusters of rubies and precious gems.
Mounted upon a supreme celestial chariot, he is honored in the world of Brahmā,
O King of kings, during both fortnights of the month of Vaiśākha.
Devoted to fasting, he worshipped Caṇḍikā with devotion;
on the eighth day he ate only at night, and on the ninth day he observed a fast—this should be understood as the procedure for the subsequent months as well.
O Lord, having fashioned an image of the Goddess made of leaves, he addressed her by the name "Bhagavatī."
One should worship the mistress of Śiva, who has eight arms in form, is white in color, and whose face resembles the full moon, with offerings of mallets.
O King, [one should offer] incense made of various heavy camphor and vijaya,
as well as an offering of jaggery cakes or else guggulu resin.
Having thus worshipped them according to the rules, he should then feed the young maidens;
[he who does so becomes] radiant like a flower, resplendent, and as steadfast as Mount Meru.
Having ascended a supreme celestial chariot, he is honored in the world of the gods,
O best of kings, who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Eating excellent, boiled, and pure śāli rice with milk,
one devoted to fasting should worship the tree with devotion on the ninth day.
One should worship with saffron, agallochum, camphor, or incense made from agallochum,
as well as with various foods, foremost among which are *aśokavarti* lamps.
O Indra among kings, O lord of men, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Āṣāḍha,
consuming such things as sugar-candy and milk-rice (pāyasa), [attains great merit].
Devoted to fasting with devotion on the ninth day of both fortnights,
one should worship Durgā with faith under the name Aindrī.
Having fashioned with devotion a golden bird, white in form, possessing the beautiful gait of Airāvaṇa and adorned with various eyes.
With various kinds of special flowers, as well as diverse kinds of edible foods,
with the fragrances of yakṣakardama, and with incenses of agaru and sandalwood;
Having thus worshipped Indrāṇī, one should then feed a young girl, as well as women and Brahmins according to one's devotion; thereafter, one should eat while remaining silent.
Having bathed with the five products of the cow and having consumed the five products of the cow,
O lord of men, he himself meditated upon the Aindrī [mantra] while remaining on the bare ground.
O Hero, whoever should thus worship Durgā with devotion and endowed with faith, being intent on fasting on the ninth day of both fortnights;
O King, one should worship the Brāhmaṇa with devotion and the goddess Caṇḍikā with faith;
indeed, one should always worship her by the name "Kaumārī."
Having devoutly fashioned an image made of silver that truly destroys the bonds of worldly existence,
one should worship it with *karavīra* flowers and with fragrances such as agallochum and sandalwood.
O Hero, the man who, in the month of Bhādrapada, observes the practice of eating only at night, consuming milk-rice and black pot-herbs with faith;
Constantly devoted to fasting on the ninth day of both fortnights,
one should worship with devotion the goddess Vaiṣṇavī, who bears the conch, the discus, and the sword.
O mighty-armed one, one should worship with jasmine flowers mixed with fragrant sandalwood paste,
and one should offer incense made of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and sihlaka.
One should offer an oblation of food accompanied by milk-rice according to one's ability;
she is then gratified by meat, and thereafter the young maidens should be honored.
Having consumed cow-dung according to the prescribed rule, O lord of men, he should then eat while remaining silent,
having gratified the twice-born and women to the best of his ability.
O King, whoever constantly worships the Vaiṣṇavī with devotion in this manner,
ascends an excellent celestial chariot and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O King, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Āśvayuja,
consuming rice with molasses, being self-controlled and having his senses restrained;
Devoted to fasting on the ninth day of both fortnights,
one should worship Māheśvarī, having fashioned a beautiful image of her out of silver.
And likewise, O hero, one should worship the bull with white flowers and ointments,
with incense made of *mahāṅga*, and with food offerings such as sugar-candies and other delicacies.
According to the prescribed rite, one should gratify the Goddess with the flesh, blood, and milk-rice of goats, buffaloes, and rams, exactly as they were slaughtered.
O King, one should devoutly feed a maiden, as well as Brāhmaṇas and women,
with various kinds of foods and meats according to the prescribed ritual.
Having obtained the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, he shall go to heaven,
equal in splendor to the lord of the twice-born and in beauty to the flower-armed god of love.
O King of kings, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Kārttika rejoices for eternal years, mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot.
Eating milk-rice, speaking the truth, and having his senses conquered;
or eating barley-food mixed with milk, with his senses restrained.
One should worship with faith the goddess Vārāhī, who holds a discus,
and should smear her with saffron and the filaments of a hundred-petaled lotus.
One should offer black agallochum and storax as incense to the Goddess;
on the ninth day of both fortnights, one should present as an offering sweetmeat balls made with sugar-candy.
Having thus worshipped Vārāhī, one should then feed a young maiden and likewise Brahmins according to one's capacity; thereafter, one should eat while maintaining silence.
O Hero, having caused [the devotee] to eat sesame seeds, having given gifts, and having offered oblations according to one's ability,
and thus having worshipped Vārāhī, one shall attain heaven.
O King, having sported together with Viṣṇu and with the sporting gods and asuras,
that king shall return to earth and become a sovereign ruler of the whole world.
O King, he who observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
constantly consuming *śaṣkulī* cakes, being self-controlled and having his senses subdued;
One should worship Cāmuṇḍā, the destroyer of the head, according to the rules and with devotion,
using blue lotuses, lotuses, bilva leaves, and kadamba flowers.
Likewise, O King, with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and guggulu, as well as with many kinds of foods to chew and eat, and repeatedly with wine and meat; [928]
Likewise, O hero, O King, with blood and various heads—
of elephants, sheep, buffaloes, and from the piercing of your own body.
On the ninth day of both fortnights, according to the rules and with devotion,
one should feed young maidens, as well as Brahmins and women.
Having bathed with the five products of the cow and having properly consumed [the mixture] according to the rule,
one should then eat, O King of Kings, using the earth as a vessel.
The man who thus constantly worships Cāmuṇḍā with devotion goes to the supreme abode, where that supreme power (kalā) resides.
Having ascended a beautiful golden vehicle adorned with garlands of banners,
one rejoices together with the deities for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
Returning again to the earth, O hero, he becomes a king upon the ground,
resembling Bhṛgu in splendor and like the sun in brilliance.
O hero, you are equal to the moon in splendor, equal to Indra in battle,
equal to Yama in brilliance, and equal to Bṛhaspati and Śukra in intellect.
Thus ends the description of the Ubhaya-navamī vow as told in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa. Now follows the Nāma-navamī vow. Sumantu said:
O Hero, having specifically observed the *nakta* fast on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja, one should worship the goddess Durgā.
Likewise with bilva leaves and water, and with droṇa flowers in every way;
then with burnt guggulu resin and various kinds of solid and soft foods.
Practicing devotion to the Goddess, one should likewise perform her propitiation with excellent food, jewels, and sacrificed goats and buffaloes.
On the ninth day, one should feed the daughters of Brahmins and the wives of Brahmins according to one's ability.
Then, having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should eat at night while remaining silent;
he who thus worships Durgā here, endowed with devotion.
Having obtained the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, he shall go to heaven;
for indeed, O best of beings, everything should be performed in Kārttika just as it was in Āśvina.
O King, having observed a fast on the eighth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
the wise man who worships the Blessed Lady with devotion on the ninth day, according to his capacity—
O lord of men, [one should worship] her by name as "Bhagavatī" with jasmine flowers,
with incense of camphor and agarwood, and with honey and milk-rice.
Having fed the maidens, women, and Brahmins according to his ability,
he should consume cow dung according to the prescribed rule and then eat while remaining silent.
O King, the man who thus worships the Blessed Goddess with devotion,
having obtained the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice, shall thereafter go to the city of Śiva.
O mighty-armed one, on the ninth day as well, a man who has mastered his senses should likewise worship the auspicious Tryambakā by name with flowers, my dear.
Having offered flowers of the *karavīra*, saffron, and filaments,
as well as *sihlaka* incense and an offering of meat-filled pastries (*māṃsapūrika*).
One should honor Brahmin maidens and Brahmin women according to one's ability;
having consumed cow urine according to the prescribed rite, one should then eat while maintaining silence.
The mortal who worships in this manner shall obtain the merit of a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices;
therefore, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, the wise man should worship Caṇḍikā.
O King, [one should worship] the one named Sarvamaṅgalā with jasmine flowers,
and with incense called Prabodha or else with guggulu resin.
O Bhārata, having worshipped Sarvamaṅgalā according to the prescribed rites, a man should indeed offer as an oblation cakes, fish, and meat.
Afterwards, one should feed young maidens, saying, "May Sarvamaṅgalā be pleased.
Having obtained a hundred *godhūma* grains, one is glorified in Goloka.
In the month of Phālguna, O King of Kings, one should always worship the Goddess with the name Caṇḍikā;
one should worship the Blessed Lady with kunda flowers.
O Hero, one should worship him with incense of agaru or even with sihlaka;
one should offer sweetmeats as the food offering, as well as honey, meat, and milk.
Purified by consuming cow’s milk, he should eat while maintaining silence;
having fed those previously mentioned according to his ability and according to the prescribed rule.
Having thus worshipped Caṇḍikā, who is adorned with severed heads, according to the prescribed rite,
the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice shall become a hundredfold.
O mighty-armed one, in the month of Caitra, the noble Blessed Lady is remembered;
one should worship her with devotion according to the rules, using flowers of the mudgaraka tree.
One should worship with incense mixed with agallochum and also with sihlaka;
one should honor [the deity] with incense, a profusion of flowers, and kāsāra.
O King of kings, in the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the Goddess by her name;
one should consume flower-water and then eat while remaining silent.
One should devoutly feed young maidens while offering this [mantra] with *pālāśa* flowers;
likewise, one should offer agallochum as incense and offerings of cakes made with ghee.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, O best of kings, one should worship Ambikā Umā;
having consumed water with kuśa grass and flowers, one should then eat while remaining restrained in speech.
O King, one should worship young maidens, women, and Brahmins according to the prescribed rites with devotion,
using jasmine flowers and pure incense.
One should offer cooked rice from the belly of a Śālī fish as an oblation for Śrī;
having thus worshipped the goddess Śrī, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should worship Umā;
she is known by the name Karṇamoḍhī and is celebrated as Lambakarṇī.
O King, one should worship according to the rules with *śamī* leaves and *kadamba* flowers,
and with incense mixed with camphor and *agaru* for those who bear skulls.
Having worshipped the Blessed Lady, one should then feed a young maiden,
as well as women and Brahmins according to one's ability, O lord of men.
Then, having consumed a leaf of the śamī tree, one should eat while remaining silent;
by thus worshipping Mahākālī, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
O Indra among kings, on the ninth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
a wise person should constantly worship Caṇḍamardinī by the name Nārāyaṇī.
O King, with red sesame seeds, bakula flowers, and kadamba flowers,
one should offer incense of guggulu mixed with ghee, as well as an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) with ghee.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules, one should then feed the young maidens,
as well as women and Brahmins, according to one's capacity and according to the prescribed rites, O King.
O King, having fed [the Brahmins] and consumed clarified butter on the ninth day according to the prescribed rite,
one who thus worships the Goddess shall go to the supreme state.
O King, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should always worship Candrikā according to the prescribed rites by the name Mahānandā.
With white, red, and yellow flowers, O Bhārata, and with all kinds of blossoms,
especially with incense of camphor, agallochum, and guggulu resin.
Having thus worshipped the Great Goddess according to the rules with various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten, such as sweetmeats (modaka) and fried cakes (lopikā), O lord of men.
*Lopikā* is a ball made of wheat flour.
One should devoutly feed young girls, women, and likewise Brahmins;
having fed them, one should then consume a *bilva* fruit for the purification of the body.
Having made the ground his vessel, he should then eat while restraining his speech;
having thus worshipped three times, he is indeed glorified in the world of Brahmā.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to the worship of Durgā,
offering them milk-rice mixed with honey and purified with clarified butter.
Having worshipped the virgins, O tiger among the Kurus, one should here give a tawny cow that is endowed with good character and yields abundant milk, along with its six limbs.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of that man who, with devotion, observes the ninth lunar day known by this name continuously for one year, performing the six-limbed rite.
Completely liberated from all sins and endowed with all sovereign powers,
he shall dwell eternally in the city of Durgā, or else he shall never return to this world again.
Whoever thus performs this meritorious ninth day known by its name,
having attained all desires, shall indeed be glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth obtains wealth;
one desiring a daughter obtains a daughter; and one desiring fame obtains fame.
Thus ends the Nāmanavamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Now follows the Rūpanavamī-vrata. Sumantu said:
O lord of men, having fashioned a trident made of flour in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should prepare a lotus made of silver with a pericarp made of gold.
O Hero, having offered with faith and worshipped the Blessed Lady,
whatever sin may have been committed— even out of desire— such as the killing of a fetus and so forth, [is purified].
The Goddess certainly destroys all that by the offering of a trident;
[the donor], mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, is honored by gods and gandharvas.
For more than a hundred million eons, he is honored in the world of the gods;
he attains the favor of Caṇḍikā and whatever abundant prosperity he may desire.
O mighty-armed one, in the month of Pauṣa, having fashioned a beautiful four-tusked elephant out of gold with devotion, and having placed it upon a golden vessel;
One should duly offer [an ornament] adorned with various gems to Indrāṇī;
thus one worships Indrāṇī with devotion according to the prescribed rite.
Mounted upon Airāvata, he is honored in the world of Soma for more than a hundred crores of years, worshipped by gods and gandharvas.
Having fashioned an excellent ram made entirely of gold during the month of Māgha,
one should present it to Svāhā in a vessel made of gold.
Having offered [an oblation] endowed with the fragrance of cooked rice and adorned with various flowers,
a person who acts with devotion is glorified in the world of Agni.
Having ascended a divine, auspicious celestial chariot adorned with rows of banners,
the king returns once more to earth and becomes a sovereign ruler of a realm.
O King, having fashioned a peacock out of flour in the month of Phālguna,
and having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, one should present it to a young maiden.
Having offered [the sacrifice] according to the rules with devotion,
he ascended an excellent celestial chariot and sported with the gods, the gandharvas, and the high-souled Guha.
O mighty-armed one, in the month of Caitra, having fashioned an image of Garuḍa out of flour and worshipped it according to the prescribed rites, one should offer it to the Vaiṣṇava assembly.
O hero of mighty arms, by offering that which is adorned with various garlands and fragrant wreaths,
one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having mounted a magnificent vehicle with various provisions of food and water,
he travels for more than a hundred million years, blazing with intense splendor.
O Hero, having fashioned a world-worshipped Varāha made of jewels,
one should worship it according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, garlands, and offerings.
With variegated flowers, fragrant guggulu resin,
and offerings of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), one shall obtain the fruit [of the rite] by addressing [the deity] as "Cāmuṇḍā."
And he goes to the supreme world where that Caṇḍikā resides;
all terrifying enemies, such as thieves and the like, flee from him.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, having fashioned a tortoise made of flour and adorned with jewels,
one should further embellish it with the pollen of flowers and with sandalwood paste.
Having offered [this] with devotion to Vāruṇī, one is glorified in the world of Rudra;
one shall ascend an excellent celestial chariot resembling a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon.
Having sported for more than a full hundred million years, O lord of men,
that great king shall return and become a sovereign of a mandala.
Having fashioned a deer made of flour, adorned with jewels, with golden horns and silver hooves in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should offer it to the deities of the wind.
Having worshipped according to the proper rites with flowers, incense, and ointments,
and with an offering of food, O mighty-armed one, he is glorified in the world of Vāyu.
O King, having fashioned a very beautiful Nārāyaṇa vehicle out of flour,
endowed with many ornaments, O Lord of the Earth, in the month of Śrāvaṇa;
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with divine offerings of flowers, garlands, and fragrant blossoms, as well as with rows of banners.
Having offered [this] here to Kauveryā, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
one goes to the supreme abode and is glorified in the world of Durgā.
O Lord, having fashioned in the month of Bhādrapada a buffalo made entirely of gold,
possessing a divine form and adorned with perfumes and garlands;
One should offer it with devotion to Yama; one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
One should offer even a single [offering] with devotion; one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
And likewise, in the month of Āśvayuja, one should offer to the Blessed Lady according to the prescribed rite many kinds of very succulent wheat-based foods and edibles.
O twice-born one, having fashioned a vehicle made of flowers and adorned with various garments,
one who mounts that variegated vehicle is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Having sported with his retinue for more than a full hundred million years,
he gradually returns to this world and becomes a wise man upon the earth.
Endowed with the seven constituents, along with all seeds, juices, and so forth;
abundant in the Bāhula [month], O Hero, it is adorned with canopies and parasols.
In the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Kārttika, being pure and having worshipped with many perfumes and garlands,
one should duly fashion a lunar disc out of gold according to one's ability.
One should offer gold enriched with jewels and pearls under the asterism Rohiṇī;
listen to the meritorious fruit for him who performs this with devotion.
Whatever merit was described by the sages of old in the Vedāntas, one shall obtain that merit multiplied ten millionfold; there is no doubt in this matter.
He goes to the supreme abode where Caṇḍikā, the bestower of boons, resides,
being praised by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, the Gaṇas, and others.
For more than a hundred billion eons, he sports together with the deities,
having enjoyed desired pleasures in the worlds such as the realm of the moon.
Having come here to the surface of the earth due to the exhaustion of his merit, he becomes a king,
always handsome and fortunate, by virtue of the boon granted by Candrikā.
Having dedicated [this act] for ten million eons, men, women,
and eunuchs who give a house to the two Blessed Ladies shall obtain all their desires.
Thus he should perform it at night or even as a single meal;
O King, one who observes the fast on the ninth day according to the prescribed rule— [937] —should do so.
But by restraining the forms previously mentioned, O lord of men,
one obtains the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred royal consecrations.
Having obtained the fruit, O mighty-armed one, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā for thousands of millions of kalpas, being honored by gods and asuras.
Having returned here upon the exhaustion of his merit,
the lord of the earth once again becomes an invincible king, a sovereign of the seven continents.
Thus ends the Rāupanavamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Now follows the Varavrata.
Sumantu said:
O King, on the ninth day, one should subsist on flour for nine years;
the Goddess, who bestows the fruits of all desires, will be pleased with him.
One who observes the vow for as long as life lasts by not eating food cooked with fire shall receive the granting of boons both in this world and the next; she bestows upon him infinite fruit.
Thus ends the Varavrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa. Now follows the Durgā-navamī-vrata.
Sumantu said:

O hero, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja, and likewise in Kārttika and the month following Kārttika, one should remain self-restrained and with senses fully controlled.
[938] And under the Puṣya asterism, one should worship Durgā according to the prescribed rite with jasmine flowers;
one should offer guggulu as incense and molasses cakes as the food offering.
O King, one who is self-restrained should mutter the name *Durgā* one hundred and eight times during the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Caitra, and the month following Caitra.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the months of Caitra, Uttaraphalgunī, or Vaiśākha, being devoted to fasting,
one should worship with jasmine, oleander, and bilva leaves.
With incense made of agallochum, camphor, sihlaka, and vṛṣaṇa.
Sihlaka is the Turuṣka [incense]; the testicles are musk. One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and meat as the food offering (naivedya) to Maṅgalā.
O Bhārata, her name should be chanted thus: "Sarvamaṅgala."
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, as well as Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and the latter half of Śrāvaṇa—
or in Bhādrapada— one should worship Caṇḍikā, the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, during the month of Bhādrapada.
With bilva leaves, muhūraka flowers, and likewise with śātapatika flowers.
With the incense of awakening alone, one should place the food offering of sweetmeats;
that man who thus worships Ambikā, even if he is all alone.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight, fasting and with senses subdued,
[one obtains the merit] of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred royal consecrations.
O Indra among kings, he obtains the fruit [of his merit] and goes to the world of the Sun,
having ascended a divine celestial chariot adorned with golden bells.
Having thus sported on the surface of the earth, O Great King,
Durgā becomes [the deity] in the first meal-break, and Sarvamaṅgalā in the second.
And on the third day, O wise King, the Goddess Caṇḍikā is proclaimed;
first, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed for both bathing and consumption.

O mighty-armed King, [one should worship] with bilva leaves for the second month, and with honey and ghee for the third; thus month by month, O ruler of men, [one should honor] the maidens and the brahmins.
O King, one should feed [the guests] according to one's own capacity with various kinds of foods and edibles;
O ruler of men, at the conclusion of the fast, a great feast should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
Then, O Hero, one should worship Caṇḍikā with offerings of perfumes and flowers,
as well as with various spectacles and the gratification of the Brāhmaṇas.
In this manner, O lord of men, a man devoted to Durgā should worship one image for himself and another with great vows on the occasion known as Mahānavamī.
Seated upon a supreme celestial chariot, he goes to the highest abode,
where the Blessed Lady herself is to be worshipped and honored with sesame seeds and fragrant juices.
Thus concludes the Durgā-navamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa. Now follows the Gopāla-navamī-vrata.
Hereafter, O Kṛṣṇa, you shall hear of the supreme Navamī-vrata.
It is the supreme auspiciousness, the ultimate protection, and the destroyer of all sins.
Likewise, on the ninth day of the month, one should perform a ritual bath in a river flowing to the ocean,
on its pure sandy bank, which has been sprinkled and beautifully adorned.
Viṣṇu, the son of Vasudeva, who is served by the hosts of cowherd girls,
whose chest is adorned with a forest garland, and who is clothed in wild silk garments.
He was surrounded by cowherd boys with dark, curly hair, who were of similar appearance, peerless, and playing together with one another.
Having meditated upon the supreme god Viṣṇu, the Lord of the lords of all worlds,
one should worship him with many wild flowers and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Desiring a fortunate husband, a maiden should observe the vow according to the rules, using fruits, roots, perfumes, and other pure substances.
O Govinda, beloved by the minds of the cowherd women, whose banner bears Garuḍa;
grant me a boon—a husband who is fortunate, well-attired, and dear to me.
Then, one should give to noble women a vessel filled with ghee, filled with turmeric powder, and filled with seeds.
One should also give a boon to the preceptor and likewise offer libations to the Brahmins;
thus is the excellent ninth-day vow named Abhyañjana.
Thus has been described this auspicious rite for women, which bestows all happiness;
a brother or a father seeking a daughter should likewise perform this vow.
For women, this is indeed the vow: the Lord of Śrī is to be worshipped;
the Blessed One, the Lord of the universe, rains down all desires.
Whatever anyone desires, that very success comes to him;
the Blessed One, when worshipped, grants it in abundance—how much more so for women?
For the Blessed One is complete in whatever he intends through his gentle deeds;
being pleased, he bestows the fruit upon them directly.
Thus ends the Gopālanavamī vow as declared in the Garuḍa Purāṇa. Now begins the Rāmanavamī vow.
Agastya said:
O best of beings, Sutīkṣṇa, listen as I shall tell you the secret— the essence of all practices and the most supreme among all gifts.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, during the day under the asterisms Puṣya and Punarvasu,
at the rising of Jupiter and Venus, while the five planets were situated in their exaltations.
When the sun had entered Aries and the Cancer ascendant had arrived,
the Supreme Person manifested from Kauśalyā for the sake of all the world.
On that day, one should always observe the vow of fasting;
there, devoted to Raghunātha, one should keep a vigil on this earth.
On the tenth day at dawn, having performed the timely rites beginning with the twilight prayers,
he should worship Rāma according to the rules, with devotion and in accordance with his means.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
as well as with cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and the like, and likewise with garments and ornaments.
One should diligently please the devotees of Rāma with supreme joy;
thus, he who performs the Śrī Rāmanavamī vow with devotion [attains the fruit].
Even many sins accumulated over numerous lifetimes are reduced to ashes and they surely proceed to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
This dharma is the sole means for the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation for everyone;
even one who is impure or most sinful, having performed this supreme vow, [attains the goal].
He who eats on the ninth day of the month of Āśvina dedicated to Rāma is the lowest of men; he shall be as worthy of worship by all beings as Rāma himself.
Without having performed the Rāmanavamī vow, the best of all vows, one is cooked in terrible Kumbhīpāka hells; of this there is no doubt.
One may perform other vows, but one shall not partake in their fruits;
yet even many great sins committed in secret, once made public,
are utterly destroyed by the Śrī Rāmanavamī vow.
O Sage, by observing even a single Śrī Rāmanavamī with devotion,
a person becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose and is liberated from all sins.
O best of sages, a man who gives an image of Śrī Rāma on the Rāmanavamī day according to the prescribed rite is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Sumantu said: O Sage, tell me in detail how the ritual for the gift of an image of Śrī Rāma is performed, and [explain] it to me, who am devoted to Rāma.
Agastya said:
I shall indeed describe that most excellent gift of a Śrī image,
as well as its ritual procedure with diligence, since you are the best among the Vaiṣṇavas.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnights of the months, one who has conquered his senses should perform the morning bath according to the rules, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Whether at a river, a pond, a well, a lake, or even a spring,
one should perform the twilight prayers and other rites while remembering Rāghava in one's heart.
Having reached his home, O best of Brahmins, he should perform the *aupāsana* and other rites;
he should give gifts to a householder Brahmin who is always devoted to the Vedas and the Shastras.
Devoted to the worship of Śrī Rāma, virtuous, free from hypocrisy,
knowledgeable in the rituals of the Rāma-mantras, and having the mantra of Rāma as his sole means of practice.
Having summoned him and honored him with devotion, he should choose [him] while praying thus:
"O best of the twice-born, I shall perform the gift of an image of Śrī Rāma."
"O Ācārya, through devotion you have become dear to me; you yourself are indeed Śrī Rāma.
Having spoken thus and honored that brāhmaṇa, he then bathed him.
Having anointed his body with oil and wearing white garments, he should wear white perfumes and garlands while meditating on Rāghava in his heart.
Having been thus honored and adorned, and having performed his midday rites,
he should devotedly feed the preceptor at great length with pure, wholesome foods.
One who observes the vow of eating but one meal a day, having conquered the senses, should likewise eat himself while recollecting Rāma in his heart, together with his preceptor.
In the evening, one should spend the remainder of the day listening to the divine story of Rāma;
then, while recollecting Rāma, one should perform the evening twilight rituals and other duties.
Accompanied by his teacher, sleeping on the ground at night with his senses subdued,
he should dwell himself in solitude, his mind dedicated to Śrī Rāma.
Then, having risen at dawn and bathed, he should perform the twilight devotions according to the rules and swiftly complete all his morning duties.
Then, having become composed in mind, the sinless one, accompanied by learned men,
constructed a brilliant pavilion for the giving of gifts in the northern part of his own house.
It has four gates, is richly adorned with banners, provided with a canopy and archways,
is made of mind, exceedingly lofty, and beautifully decorated with flowers and other offerings.
The eastern gate is beautifully adorned with Śaṅkha, Cakra, and Hanumān;
the southern gate is beautifully adorned with Garuḍa, Śārṅga, and Bāṇa.
It was adorned with maces, swords, and armlets on the western side,
and beautifully decorated with lotuses, swastikas, and sapphires on the northern side.
In the center, it should be four cubits wide, elongated, and provided with a pedestal;
it should also be well-endowed with purificatory rites, dance, song, and musical instruments.
There, with a joyful mind, he should have the learned recite the *puṇyāha* formula;
then, O Sage, remembering Rāma alone, he should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
And on this Rāmanavamī, one intent on the worship of Rāma,
having fasted during the eight watches of the night, should worship according to the prescribed rites.
O Rāma, out of devotion to you, I shall diligently offer this golden image for the pleasure of Śrī Rāma; it is performed through devotion to Rāma.
O Rāma, may you, being pleased, swiftly take away my many sins—
those accumulated over numerous lifetimes, those long practiced, and those that are great.
Then, he fashioned a divine golden image of Rāma, weighing one pala,
with two arms and Jānakī seated upon his left lap.
O great sage, [he saw] the Goddess standing there embracing him with her lower left hand, while holding the *jñānamudrā* in her right hand.
Having first bathed the royal scepter made of two palas of gold upon the lion-throne with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship it according to the prescribed ritual.
Restrained and unwearied, having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the root mantra according to the rule during the day, he should thereafter keep a vigil at night.
Having composed the divine story of Rāma, accompanied by devotees of Rāma,
he [performed] in many ways with dances, songs, and hymns of praise to Rāma.
Having likewise taught the Rāmāṣṭaka, [one should worship] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata),
and so forth, as well as camphor, agallochum, musk, kahlāra lilies, and many other such substances in abundance.
The wise man should pass day and night worshipping according to the rules with devotion;
then, having risen in the morning, he should perform the rites of bathing, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and so forth.
O Sage, having completed [the ritual] according to the rules, one should worship Rāma according to the rules;
then, the knower of mantras should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the root mantra.

Then, being composed in mind, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations according to the prescribed rite in either the previously mentioned lotus-shaped fire-pit or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) using the common fire (laukikāgni).
O Sage, remembering Rāma with undivided mind, one should offer milk-rice mixed with clarified butter;
then, having performed [the rite] with devotion, one should worship the preceptor.
With two earrings set with jewels, with various finger-rings,
with perfumes, flowers, consecrated rice, and various most enchanting garments.
Then, remembering Rāma, one should give [the gift] and utter this mantra:
"This golden image of Rāma, fully adorned..."
"O Rāma, today I give you this pair of variegated garments;
may Rāghava be pleased for the delight of Śrī Rāma."
Having thus given according to the prescribed rite, one should certainly bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and likewise give cows, gold, and other gifts to others as is appropriate, according to one's capacity.
He should respectfully give a pair of garments and grain according to his means;
he should eat together with the Brahmins and give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this matter.
O observer of noble vows, one obtains the fruit of gifts such as the Tulāpuruṣa sacrifice.
He is certainly liberated from the sins accumulated over many births;
what more need be said here? Liberation stands within his very hand.
O observer of noble vows, whatever fruit is obtained by performing gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* in their entirety at the highly meritorious Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse,
that same fruit a mortal obtains through this gift.
Thus ends the Rāmanavamī vow in the Agastyasaṃhitā. Now follows the Rathanaṣamī vow. Sumantu said:
Having performed [the preliminary rites] in the month of Āśvayuja, during the dark fortnight, O lord of men,
one should observe a fast on the ninth day and worship the goddess Durgā.
Having honored the chariot with offerings of flowers and incense, and by gratifying the Brahmins, he adorned it with various articles.
It was adorned with garlands of banners, umbrellas, chowries, and mirrors;
joined with lions and various flower-garlands, it was enchanting to the mind.
Having fashioned a golden image of Durgā, adorned with the seat of Mahiṣa—
the form of Durgā being from the Viṣṇudharmottara—
[it should be] standing in the *ālīḍha* posture and likewise four-armed, O King.
The goddess holds a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle in her hands, and likewise bears a trident and a sword.
"And her fourth hand should likewise be made to hold meat.
Having thus placed [the image] in the middle of the chariot, one should worship it with the proper characteristics.
O King, having paraded that chariot along the royal highway on the ninth day amidst the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, he should lead it to the Durgā-tapana.
There, preceded by a vigil, it was adorned with lamps and the like,
O Hero, with various offerings being cast down and children dancing.
There, while worshipping Caṇḍikā, one should observe a vigil;
then, at dawn, having performed the ceremonial bath, one should provide a meal for her devotees.
One should present a chariot endowed with splendor to the Blessed Lady;
having eaten together with one's kinsmen and offered salutations, one should proceed to the temple of the Noble One.
The wise man obtains that fruit which is the best of all vows, the destroyer of all sins,
the merit found in all sacrifices, and the result of visiting all sacred fords—
simply by observing the Navamī vow.
For more than a hundred crores of kalpas he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu;
returning again to earth, he shall become a sovereign emperor.
O lord of men, he who offers to the Blessed Lady a beautiful bed made of deodar wood, furnished with red articles, [attains great merit].
O King, having duly worshipped Caṇḍikā with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
[he should give] as many pieces of fine silk and woolen cloth as there may be in number.
He who offers a bull marked with a trident to the Blessed Lady shall be honored in the world of Durgā for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on its body.
He who [offers] the two-faced Gaṅgā, beautifully adorned for the Blessed One, shall go to the abode of Mahādeva, extending through his lineage unto the seventh generation.
One shall obtain that fruit which is gained by giving the earth with its seven continents;
for as long as the two feet and half the head of the calf have emerged,
for that long the cow is to be known as the earth, and the giver of her is a giver of the earth.
Thus ends the Rathanavamī-vrata in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa. Now follows the Ānanda-navamī-vrata.
Sumantu said:
O Lord of the Earth, Ānandā, Nandinī, Nandā, Mahānandā, as well as the first,
the meritorious ninth, and the great fifth are thus remembered.
O Lord of the Earth, that ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna is called Anandā; it is highly meritorious, auspicious, and the destroyer of all sins.
Having taken a single meal on the fifth day, O King, and likewise eating only at night on the sixth,
one should eat what is unasked for on the seventh, and observe a fast on the following day.
O King, he who thus worships with devotion on the ninth day according to the rules—
having fasted— should worship the Goddess, offer incense and likewise aloe-wood,
and honor her with garlands of mallets as well as other flowers.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as a food offering (naivedya), as well as curd-milk pudding with rice (rasālāmodana);
for, O King, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are highly recommended for both bathing and consumption.
The name of the Goddess, which removes the fear known as Āruṇī, should be recited;
thus has this first fast-breaking rite (pāraṇa), which destroys sins, been proclaimed.
Listen to the second breaking of the fast, which occurs after four months;
it is the *ādīya* śrāddha.
On the ninth day, one should feed Brahmin maidens and the wives of Brahmins.
Month after month, O mighty-armed one, according to your capacity and according to the prescribed rule.
O Lord, the Blessed Lady is to be worshipped in the month of Āṣāḍha, likewise in Śrāvaṇa, in Bhādrapada,
and similarly in the month of Āśvayuja.
O King, having taken a single meal on the fifth day, one should likewise take a meal at night on the sixth;
on the seventh day, however, one should eat only what is unasked for, and on the following day, one should observe a fast.
Fasting on the ninth day, one should worship Śivā according to the prescribed rites;
having obtained the fruit of a horse sacrifice, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
One should likewise smear the Goddess with garlands of jasmine flowers, red sandalwood, musk, unbroken grains, and fragrant scents.
One should offer as incense the highly honored guggulu known as māhiṣya,
and as food offerings, jaggery-cakes and sugar-sweets according to one's ability.
Bathing with bilva leaves and water, as well as the consumption [of the same], is prescribed;
the name known as Durgā should be chanted, which removes the fear of all sins.
Having thus worshipped the Noble One and likewise having worshipped the Guru,
one should feed maidens, Brahmins, and women according to one's ability.
Thus, whoever worships with devotion according to their own means shall indeed ascend the lion-throne and proceed to the world of Brahmā.
[950] On that third fast-breaking day, which destroys all sins,
one should always meditate upon Śiva, the eternally peaceful embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
The month beginning with Kārttika is of great merit and increases the pleasure of Durgā;
it is especially [conducive] for various kinds of flowers, particularly those born in water.
One should worship the Goddess Tryambakā, the Mother of the World, with garlands;
one should also anoint her with fragrant substances such as saffron, agallochum, and camphor.
One should worship with meat-filled delicacies and śrīveṣṭa;
incense made of bilva and agaru, as well as guggulu mixed with ghee, is recommended.
Bathing with sesame seeds, performing oblations with sesame seeds, and the consumption of sesame seeds are excellent;
likewise, one should chant the name of the Goddess, which brings about the destruction of all sins.
At the conclusion, men should recite the incomparable mantra named Aparājita;
thus is that ninth day observed by means of a quarter-kṛcchra penance.
Month after month, O mighty-armed one, for as long as a year,
he indeed obtains excellent sons, wealth, grain, strength, and fame.
Then, having attained vast fame, incomparable health, and prosperity,
he goes to the city of Indra, seated upon a lion throne.
Resplendent with the brilliance of a lotus and endowed with a luster like a lotus,
he who constantly listens from the beginning to this *Anandakalpa* attains the foremost desires and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the Anandānavamī vow.
[951] Now follows the Mātṛvratam.
The king attains victory and enjoys his kingdom free from thorns;
so too do the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and others of low birth.
They attain victory everywhere and are freed from all fears;
therefore, the Mothers should be worshipped with effort according to one's ability.
In front of him, one should honor the devotees of Śiva, especially the preceptor of the vow;
by performing it according to this injunction, one shall attain victory everywhere.
And likewise Brāhmaṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Śivā, Kṣemā, Jayā, and Mahī.
Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍā, Yogeśī, Gaurī, and likewise Ambikā;
Āgneyī, Vāruṇī, Vāyavyā, and the one known as Vyomā.
One should worship Lampā, Gajavaktrā, Gāruḍī, Jayā,
Vijayā, Jayantī, and likewise the other, Aparājitā.
One should likewise worship Siddhārthā, Śuklā, and Utpalā;
and likewise Garuḍā, Rātri, and again Surātri.
She who has the face of a swan and the face of a horse, likewise she with the faces of a lion and a tiger;
she who roars with the face of a jackal, and she who is a female cat, a female bear, and a female monkey.
One should worship Uṣṭravaktrā, Śyāmamukhī, Gomukhī, Sumukhī,
as well as Vairavī and Kṛṣṇarevatī.
And Śuklarevatī by name, as well as Śakunirevatī,
Laṅkeśvarī, Bhadrakarṇā, Śrīśīghrā, and Siddhi herself.
Ghaṇṭākarṇī as well as Nidrā are proclaimed to be the Mothers;
he who always worships them on the ninth day of the month of Āśvayuja, [attains success].
But for one who daily, at the conclusion of worship, always performs this with devotion, there is no doubt that his power remains unimpaired.
The afflictions of the planets do not trouble him, especially the malevolent rites of others;
nor do bad dreams, diseases, malevolent spirits, or obstructive Vināyakas.
His own planets, Pūtanās, Caṇḍas, Ḍākinīs, and likewise Mārikās— all such evils and the sins of famine— are destroyed by the mere remembrance of him.
A woman whose children have died, or one who has borne only female offspring, shall indeed give birth to noble progeny.
Thus ends the vow dedicated to the Mothers.
Now follows the Navamī-vow as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara-purāṇa*:
"O King of kings, on the ninth day of both fortnights in the month of Vaiśākha..."
"Devoted to fasting and worshiping Caṇḍikā with devotion,
he ascends an excellent celestial chariot and is glorified in the world of the gods.
Thus ends the vow of the ninth day of Vaiśākha.
Now follows the Nandā-navamī vow.
Sumantu said: "The ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada—"
Mātṛnandā is proclaimed to be of great merit and the destroyer of sins.
The dark fortnight is the longer one, while the other is the bright.
O joy of the Kurus, he who worships Durgā on that [bright day] according to the prescribed rite shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having eaten only one meal on the seventh day and having fasted on the eighth,
one should worship Śiva according to the prescribed rite with *jātī* flowers and *kadamba* blossoms.
The goddess is surrounded by *dūrvā* grass arranged according to the prescriptions of the scriptures,
as well as by dates, coconuts, cucumbers, and *mālaka* fruits.
O observer of noble vows, one should worship with the seven types of grain and oil-cake;
one should fumigate with curd mixed with clarified butter, incense, and sprouts of dūrvā grass.
Then, O King, one should keep a vigil at night before Nandā,
with various spectacles, the chanting of the Vedas, and flowers and fruits.
O Lord, one should recite the mantra named Nandā one hundred and eight times. O Lord, the mantra named Nandā is:
*oṃ nandāyai namaḥ svāhā huṃ phaṭ*.
Then, at dawn on the ninth day, having performed worship to Caṇḍikā and having gratified the preceptor according to one's ability, one should thereafter feed young maidens.
And thus, O Lord,
one should worship the blessed Nandā for four months: in the month of Āśvayuja, in Kārttika, in the month following Kārttika [Mārgaśīrṣa], and in Mārgaśīrṣa.
O lord of men, it is prescribed that water with *kuśa* grass be used for bathing and for sipping;
thus, O hero, I have described to you this first auspicious breaking of the fast.
In the second [month], listen to me regarding the breaking of the fast, the ritual bath, and the consumption [of food] in the month of Pauṣa;
one should worship Caṇḍikā here by the name Kanakanandinī.
