[She was] adorned with various garlands and flowers, anointed with saffron and agallochum,
and likewise provided with various kinds of food and eatables and with aguru incense.
Having bathed with the five products of the cow, fasting and with his senses subdued,
he worships the great altar and sleeps upon the ground at night.
Again, on the ninth day, having duly worshipped Kanakanandinī and offered oblations to the son of Śāṇḍilī, one should then feed young maidens.
One should worship Agni, the son of Śāṇḍilī,
and the Imperishable One (Acyuta) according to the prescribed rite during the months beginning with Vaiśākha,
O Bhārata, with garlands of *muhurā* and *aśoka* flowers.
One should anoint [the image] with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood;
and [worship it] with incense mixed with agallochum, and with milk-rice.
One should recite the auspicious name called Acyuta, which removes all sins;
furthermore, one should perform a bath with water mixed with yellow orpiment and consume cow dung.
Having observed a fast on the eighth day and worshipped Acyuta,
one should, according to one's ability, feed young maidens, Brahmins, and women on the ninth day.
O Lord, he who duly performs this Nandā-navamī in this manner obtains the fruit of each individual thing he has mentally desired, exactly as prescribed.
Thus ends the Nandā-navamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Now, on this very same day, follows the worship of Durgā as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
The ninth lunar day in the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada is known as Mātṛnandā; it is highly meritorious and proclaimed to be the destroyer of sins.
O descendant of Kuru, whoever worships Durgā there according to the prescribed rite attains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Now, on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, there is the awakening of Durgā as described in the Devipurāṇa:
"Having worshipped both [the eighth and ninth days] during the dark fortnight in the month of Kanyā,
one should awaken the Goddess on the ninth day with the sounds of songs and musical instruments."

In the month of Bhādrapada, during the *kanyā* [solar] transit, on the day ending with the new moon (*darśānta*), is the worship of Durgā as declared in various Purāṇas. Now follows the Mahānavamī vow.
Sumantu said: That ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, honored by the world, is called Mahānandā; it always bestows supreme bliss upon men.
Bathing, giving gifts, performing fire-offerings, and fasting—
whatever is performed by men on this [day] is declared to be entirely inexhaustible.
O Hero, one should worship the Blessed Nandā with garlands of white flowers,
as well as with saffron and agallochum incense.
O Hero, having bathed with various kinds of *modakas* as well as diverse fruits and sesame paste,
one should offer oblations of sesame seeds according to the prescribed rite.
For four months, one should worship the auspicious Goddess Nandā;
with devotion, one should feed young maidens, women, and likewise Brahmins.

O Hero, on the day of breaking the fast during the month of Jyeṣṭha and the following months, one should worship Durgā according to the prescribed rite with clusters of jasmine and kadamba flowers, addressing her by the name Vindhyanivāsinī.
One should cause [the disciple] to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); bathing with that very substance bestows merit.
Likewise, one should offer milk-rice with honey and ghee, as well as excellent rice mixed with curd.
O observer of noble vows, one should indeed worship her with a smiling countenance during the months beginning with Kārttika,
using garlands of kunda flowers and karavīra blossoms.
One should worship with perfumes made of musk, with incense of agallochum,
with offerings of ghee-filled sweets, sugar-coated confections, and bilva fruits.
O Lord of Men, having purified his body by bathing with the water used for washing a cow's horn,
he should worship the goddess Śvetamukhī with devotion according to the prescribed rites, O All-pervading One.
Whoever, having fasted, should thus worship Caṇḍikā for a year,
having attained all the foremost desires, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having played there together with Brahmā for half a night and being honored there,
one who worships the Goddess according to the rules with devotion shall become prosperous in wealth and grain, possessed of sons, and famous upon the earth.
Thus ends the Mahānavamī-vrata in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa. Now begins the Durgā-navamī-vrata.
Brahmā said:
By worshipping Durgā on the ninth day, one overcomes difficulties through her;
in battle and in worldly affairs, one shall always obtain victory.
The root mantras are proclaimed by their own names, as are the limb mantras;
and the lords of the lunar days (tithīśvaras) should be depicted as before, situated upon lotus petals.
In this [rite], Durgā is the presiding deity of the lunar day; her form is worshipped during the Rathanaṣamī vow with offerings of perfumes and flowers according to one's capacity.
Even if performed with deceit or fraud, the worship bestows its fruit.
An oblation performed with streams of clarified butter, fuel-sticks, curd, milk, rice, and honey,
or indeed with milk alone, yields the fruits previously described.
Thus ends the Durgā-navamī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Now follows the Śaurya-vrata.
Agastya said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the unsurpassed vow of heroism,
by which even a coward instantly attains valor.
In the month of Āśvayuja, on the pure ninth day, one should fast;
having made a formal vow on the seventh, one should remain without solid food on the eighth.
On the ninth day, O King, one should first devoutly consume flour;
one should feed the Brahmins with devotion and likewise worship the Goddess.
To the goddess Durgā, the highly fortunate one, the great illusion, and the one of great splendor.
Having thus observed the fast according to the rules for as long as a year, O King,
at the conclusion of the vow, the wise man should feed young boys according to his capacity.

Having bathed with gold-colored garments and other such items, and having worshipped according to one's ability, one should afterwards ask for forgiveness, saying: "May the Goddess forgive me; may she be pleased with me."
By doing thus, one whose kingdom has been lost shall regain his kingdom, without a doubt;
the ignorant shall obtain knowledge, and the timid shall find valor.
Thus ends the Śūryavrata as declared in the Vārāha Purāṇa.
Now, the Vīravrata:
having performed a single meal on the ninth day, one should [offer] maidens according to one's capacity.
Having fed them, one should give an even amount, as well as a golden pitcher and two garments.
For one year, or even until the ninth [day], he should feed [the Brahmins];
likewise, gold should be given as a gift, and upon death, he shall go to the city of Śiva.
In every birth, he shall be handsome and unconquered by his enemies.
This is called the Vīra-vrata, which bestows happiness upon women.
Thus ends the Vīra-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. Now follows the Āgneya-vrata.
Kṛṣṇa said:
On the ninth day, one should worship the Goddess dwelling on the Vindhya with devotion,
using flowers, incense, lamps, and various kinds of food offerings.
Having worshipped it, one should then know the cage well-joined with the *suka* [mantra];
that man who gives a golden one to a Brahmin becomes eloquent.
"By eating once a day [during the day] and at night, one bestows the world of Agni.
Thus is the Āgneyavrata described in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. Now follows the Varṣavrata.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Śṛṅgavān, Meru, Mālyavat,
and Gandhamādana— one should worship these, O bull among the sons of Pṛthā.
O King, O knower of dharma, beginning from the ninth day of Caitra, one should worship the mountains while fasting, O ruler of the earth, with offerings of perfumes, garlands, and food.
At the conclusion of his vow, a man should offer a silver model of Jambudvīpa weighing one *tulā*; he shall obtain all his desires.
A hundred tulās is the *pralaśata*.

One obtains the merit of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world (*svargaloka*). From that point on, having attained human status, one shall become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) king.
"Having ruled the earth for a long time and a portion [of its duration], one attains the heavenly world (*uloka*), and from there, the higher worlds (*adhiloka*).
This is the vow for the rainy season as stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Now follows the vow of Bhadrakālī.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the ninth day, one who has observed a fast should worship Bhadrakālī.
O Great King, starting from the month of Kārttika, one should proceed in due order during the bright fortnight.

At the end of the year, having performed worship with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and excellent food, one should, at the conclusion of the vow, present [the image] to a Brāhmaṇa.
By giving a pair of garments, a man shall obtain his desired wish;
one afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and one who is bound is released from bondage.
And one who is occupied with royal affairs is released from great fear;
therefore, there is no fear from non-humans, nor in any way from humans.
By performing worship according to the prescribed rules to Bhavānī, one obtains sons, wealth as desired, fame, various merits, base metals, and honor.
Likewise,
he obtains basic necessities and wealth other than gold and silver, namely base metals.
Thus ends the Bhadrakālī-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
The King said:
"O Lord of Men, one should worship the maiden Bhadrakālī according to the prescribed ritual."
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvina, O best of men.
Puṣkara said:
In the north-eastern quarter,
one should draw a charming dwelling for Bhadrakālī, the king’s residence adorned with variegated cloths.
[961] O twice-born one, having depicted Bhadrakālī on a cloth, one should worship her there;
the fashioning of Bhadrakālī’s form is shown in that very place:
Bhadrakālī is to be made with eighteen arms and captivating in appearance.
Assuming the ālīḍha stance, she stands upon a chariot drawn by four lions.
A rosary, a trident, a sword, and that which is called the moon;
likewise, an arrow and a quiver, as well as a conch and a lotus, should be fashioned.
The *śruk* and *śruva* ladles should be fashioned accordingly, as should the Vedic mandala;
likewise, the staff and the spear should be made, as well as the spear and the fire.
O highly fortunate one, the hand of Bhadrakālī shall be a mass of stars,
and she shall possess a single vessel made of jewels.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, being self-restrained and pure,
one should worship the weapons, the shield, and so forth, as well as the parasol and the garment, in that very place.
One should worship all the royal insignia as well as the weapons with pure fruits, along with various edible foods and most delightful delicacies.
O lord of the earth, one should likewise keep a vigil there at night with various offerings and spectacles for the public.
Having observed the fast, on the second day the lord of the earth should again worship those [deities] and should worship the entire array of weapons.
In this manner, he should worship the Goddess— who bestows boons, who is affectionate toward her devotees,
who is Kātyāyanī, who moves at will, who possesses many forms, and who grants boons.
O lord of the earth, when she is honored with all necessary offerings, she bestows success upon him;
for it is thus that the lord of the earth honors the Goddess, the foremost in the world, during his expeditions.
A person attains supreme accomplishment from Maheśa, as does any other person according to their wealth and power.

Thus concludes the Bhadrakālī-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Thus ends [this work] composed by Śrī Hemādri— the sovereign lord of all faculties, proficient in all branches of knowledge, and the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Mahādeva.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, within the section on vows (*vratakhaṇḍa*), the observances of the ninth lunar day (*navamīvratāni*) are completed.
[963] Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Now, the vows of the tenth day:
He who has dedicated his livelihood and wealth to the feet of the Moon-crested Lord does not perceive any other object or any obstacle in between.
Satyavrata, the sun to the entire multitude of mountains, the Mountain of Gold, has today proclaimed this collection of vows for the tenth lunar day.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now listen, O brahmin-sage, to the supreme Daśamī vow,
which pacifies all diseases and afflictions, bestows an increase of goodness, and is auspicious.
O one of great intelligence, this vow must be observed by one desiring health;
for it is for the sake of all undertakings that one who wishes to attain long life should desire this.
O observer of noble vows, a fast should be observed here on the ninth day;
then, having performed his ablutions on the tenth day, he should worship Hari, the abode of auspiciousness.
Having meditated upon the Lord of the worlds together with Indrāṇī—
the supreme one who bears the conch, discus, mace, lotus, arrow, and sword—
One should worship with incense, perfumes, flowers, and milk-rice (pāyasa), accompanied by the goddess Lakṣmī. One should place a water-pot filled with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) in front.
In this [lotus], one should invoke the weapons, such as the wheel and others;
with a concentrated mind, one should worship them with red flowers and offerings of rice mixed with molasses.
O Kṛṣṇa, one should have an eight-petaled lotus made of gold and placed upon a black antelope skin strewn with a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds.
One should worship, in due order, the senses with the mind as the sixth, the vital breaths, and the intellect upon the petals; likewise, one should worship Time in the pericarp.
The sense faculties are free from disease, the vital breath remains stable for a long time,
the intellect is untroubled by latent desires, and all things are free from affliction.
May the Lord Hari, whose self is Time, destroy the sin accumulated by me through mind, deed, and speech in birth after birth.
Having thus performed this rite for the king in the presence of the God of Gods,
[he gave it] to a poor brahmin who had a virtuous son.
One should unweariedly give everything to the preceptor who knows the rules for sacrifices and charitable works;
one should also give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor and provide food for the Brahmins.
Afterwards, the preceptor should bathe the practitioner with the water from the ritual jar;
then, with the remaining food, he should do so preceded by the permission of the guru.
One should eat together with one's kinsmen and then relinquish the restrictive observances;
O observer of noble vows, one should abandon even the suffering caused by a disease mentioned in a dream.
Indeed, by means of this vow, once it has been perfected,
a mortal is constantly endowed even with sons, grandsons, friends, kinsmen, cattle, and so forth.
This vow bestows health and long life;
it cures royal consumption, splenic disorders, tumors, abdominal lumps, colic, and fistula-in-ano.
All great obstacles perish for those who observe the vow; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, one who is childless obtains a son and long life.

"One should abandon untimely death; one attains bliss and health. "One should abandon untimely death" means that one does not meet with premature death. This concludes the Ārogyavrata as described in the *Garuḍapurāṇa*.
Now follows the Rājyāpti-daśamī-vrata.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Kratu, Dakṣa, the sage Satya, Kāla, Kāma, and likewise Vasu;
O Brahmin, the Kuravas, Manuja, and Romasāra—these are your ten [sons].
The Viśvedevas are thus declared; the all-pervading Keśava is their tenfold self. O lord of men, his worship should be performed during the bright fortnight.
O bull among kings, O Yādava, beginning from the tenth day of the month of Kārttika,
[one should perform worship] either in sacred mandalas or before images.

Worship (*arcā*) consists of images (*pratimā*), which should be fashioned from gold or other metals as far as possible, using an abundance of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food. At the conclusion of the vow, one should give gold to a twice-born man according to one's capacity.
Having performed this desired vow alone,
one attains their worlds for a very long time;
having dwelt there in the world of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
He may become a king or a preeminent brahmin.
Thus ends the vow for attaining sovereignty on the tenth lunar day as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Now follows the vow for attaining Brahman.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
For Ātman, Āyu, Manas, Dakṣa, Mada, Prāṇa, as well as Havis, Gati, Tasya, Dakṣa, and Pratyak— these are his ten [forms].
A man, observing a fast during the bright fortnight, should for a long time worship the deities named Aṅgirasas on the tenth day according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having performed this vow for a year according to the previously mentioned and immediately following rules,
one indeed attains for a very long time the desired worlds of those [deities].
Having passed that time and attained manhood,
he shall become either a king or an eminent brahmin.
Thus concludes the Brahmāvāpti-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Now follows the Padārtha-vrata.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: On the tenth day of the bright fortnight, a man, having observed a fast,
should likewise begin in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and continue for a full year.

One should perform the worship of the guardians of the directions by means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and excellent food offerings; likewise, one should perform the complete worship of the quarters.
And at the end of the year,
O highly fortunate one, O best of men, he should likewise give a milch cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having performed this vow, wherever a man goes,
there he obtains his desired object and enjoys the fruit of the Putreṣṭi sacrifice.
Whatever is accomplished for a man whose throat is like that of a merchant, as well as for those desiring victory over others,
or for students of knowledge, or for the destruction of enemies; [all that is attained].
This vow is desired as a beneficial matter.
Thus ends the vow concerning the constituent elements (*padārtha-vrata*) in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Now follows the vow of righteousness (*dharma-vrata*).
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight, a person who has observed a fast should worship the god Dharma, who brings happiness to all the worlds.

[968] Then, O subduer of enemies, beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should always perform worship in this manner with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and an abundance of food.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire and honor the Brāhmaṇas therein;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should likewise give a milch cow as a gift.
For this vow has been prescribed as bestowing the fruit of the horse sacrifice;
nevertheless, O best of men, it should be performed during the dark fortnight.
One obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices without doubt;
one attains the heavenly world and uplifts one's own lineage.
And let it be "Dharma" for him; thus the man attains Dharma.
Wherever he may be born, there let him be devoted to Dharma.
By means of this vow, a person devoted to dharma shall become such everywhere;
it bestows longevity, health, and fame, grants a high station, and destroys sin.
A person must perform this duly,
for the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is indeed that Dharma who is to be worshipped.

Thus ends the *Dharmavrata* as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. Now follows the procedure for the *Aparājitadaśamī*, according to the *Ātharvaṇagopathabrāhmaṇa* [Atharvaveda Pariśiṣṭa 18b.2.6–8; 1.27.3, 1; 1.28.2–4; 1.30.1–4; 1.17.1; 1.12.3; 1.11.1–4].

Now, on the tenth day of the Aparājita constellation, during the previously mentioned *vijaya-muhūrta* in the forenoon, the departure-rite (*prāsthānika*) is prescribed. Indeed, these are the departure-rites; these are the eastern gates, and so forth; those which are the paths, and so forth; and the *nakṣatra-homa*. Having eaten curd-rice under the *kṛttikā* stars, one should set out for the sake of success; indeed, he returns again. Having eaten roasted meat [meat of sheep], one should set out under the two *phalgunī* stars; with juices under both [the northern ones]. Having eaten *priyaṅgu* grain, a purifying meal, and various kinds of food under the *hasta* star, one should set out under the *citrā* stars; these are the auspicious varieties of fruit. Having eaten them, he eats abundant milk-porridge and cakes under the two *viśākhā* stars; indeed, these are the southern gates. There, having risen toward the southern direction, he should proceed with a boar’s snout, a net, or something related to fish; he should turn back within a *krośa*. Indeed, these belong to the ritual of the sun; having eaten jaggery under the *anurādhā* stars, one should set out; having eaten rice with lentils under the *śravaṇa* star, one should set out. These are the western gates. In whichever direction he has risen, he should proceed with a bed, a bundle of grass, a stool, a girdle, or a knee; he should turn back within a *krośa*. Within a *krośa*, there is no obstacle for his purpose. Having eaten split pulses with soup under the *śraviṣṭhā* stars, one should set out; with juices under the two northern [stars], having eaten the meal of a householder under the *revatī* stars, one should set out; having eaten sesame seeds under the *bharaṇī* stars, one should set out. These are the northern gates. He rises toward the divine direction. With a drinking vessel, a lump of fermenting grain, or with milk, he should proceed and turn back within a *krośa*. Within a *krośa*, there is no obstacle for his purpose. "Birth of power, birth of fame, birth of luster, birth of splendor, birth of strength, birth of greatness, birth of Brahman, birth of Brahmanic luster. May he be the lord of all worlds, of all Vedas, of all beings, and of all rivers. Therefore, one should act thus under this very constellation. Having placed the fuel-sticks facing east and spread the sacrificial grass, having sprinkled the juices upon the grass and taken hold of the ladle, he should offer oblations into the fire, saying: "The purifiers together with the luminous spheres, Svāhā! Having poured the remnants into the juices and concluded the offerings, he should perform the bathing and consume the portions. He makes these devoid of juice for him; he becomes the progenitor and lord of all metals, of all gods, of all beings, and of all rivers.
They have placed together various radiant lights in the sky, moving beings within the dwelling for people;
Turmiśa, desiring favor, [prays].
The days are to be honored with hymns, reaching unto the firmament.
O Agni, may Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī be easy to invoke; may Mṛgaśiras be auspicious and Ārdrā bring peace.
He causes him to consume the *vāstu*; thus he touches for him the auspicious one who has crossed the oceans.
In *Punarvasū* is truth (*sūnṛtā*); *Puṣya* is beautiful;
*Bhānu* is *Aśleṣā*; *Maghā* is my path to Gaya.
May there be merit; may Sarvaphālguṣa and Anuhasta [the two Pūrvaphalgunīs and Hasta] be here; may Vināśin [Citrā] and Śivā [Svātī] be auspicious for my happiness.
May there be emptiness in Ānurādha, along with Viśākhā and Sahabānurādhā.
O Rādha, Viśākhā, Suhavā, Anurdhā, Jyeṣṭhā— this is a good constellation, with unharmed roots.
May food and flavor come to me from the east, Svāhā! [Aṣāḍhā] **From the east they go upward; may the Uttarās bring them hither.** Grant vigor; may the Uttarās bring them hither.
Having begun with the statement "the departure has been described," there are these verses on that subject as well:
"Adorned [is he], with his circle of servants decorated."
The path for the lofty horses was adorned,
the quarters resounded with the noise of musical instruments, and there was a succession of blessings from auspicious rites.
The king, having departed from his palace preceded by the family priest and having performed the rites for departure, should set out toward the eastern direction.
Having gone to the outskirts of the city, one should commence the worship of the site;
having performed that worship, one should honor the lords of the directions and the deities of the path.
And with all the ancient mantras of the quarters, one should worship the Śamī tree,
which pacifies all inauspicious things and pacifies evil deeds.
I take refuge in the auspicious and blessed *śamī* tree, which pacifies bad dreams;
having constantly offered prayers toward the eastern direction, one should step forward with the *viṣṇukrama* strides.
Having fashioned an image of the enemy, or likewise having meditated upon him mentally,
he is pierced in the vital organ of the heart with an arrow feathered with gold.
The mantras for the conquest of the directions should be recited by the family priest;
in this very same manner, one should perform the rite for the southern and other directions as well.
Having honored the venerable twice-born brahmins for one year, the domestic priest should arrange spectacles and entertainments for the elephants, horses, and infantry.
Then, amidst the sounds of "Victory! and "Auspiciousness!", he should enter his own palace, being honored with highly auspicious lustration rites by virtuous courtesans.
The king who performs this auspicious rite every year attains long life, health, sovereignty, and victory.
"He has neither mental anxieties nor physical ailments, nor does he suffer defeat;
he attains auspicious prosperity and constant victory upon the earth.
Thus it is said. The meaning is that what was stated regarding the departure for a journey (*prāsthānika*) with reference to marriage should also be understood here.
And that which pertains to the departure is as follows:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the departure ceremony (*prāsthānika*). When people are about to go among the folk, there should be drums for him, and lutes should be played; they should be joyful, adorned, and speaking pleasantly. During the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, and having prepared the ritual materials, he should establish the sacred fire at an auspicious moment. Having performed the *śānti* and *pratisara* rites, he should sprinkle the carrier with water. Having caused [him] to apply collyrium, ointment, and unguents as prescribed by others, and having fastened garments, perfumes, and garlands upon him, and having bathed the one standing in front, the performer, taking hold of [the carrier], offers oblations with hymns that grant fearlessness, those containing the word "king," those containing the word "flowers," those providing prosperity, and those containing the words "shelter" (*śarma*), "armor" (*varman*), and "lineage. Having offered for the king with the verses beginning "Itibhā" and "Pragāma," and in many ways with those beginning "Āgacchatā" and "Gatasyeti," and having worshipped Indra with the *sthālīpāka* offering, he should cause [the carrier] to mount the path with the verses beginning "Ātiṣṭha jiṣṇuḥ" and "Anṛkṣarā ṛjevā. He should mutter these: "These two feet," "Yad indra," "Trātāram indram," "Mānavidannabhayam," and "Somo 'haspatir naḥ paripātu paścāt. Having stepped over three strides of Viṣṇu, he should perform the marriage. He should not depart from the joined ground, nor should he joke; he should do it immediately.

In the *Purāṇasamuccaya*, however, the worship of Aparājitā on this very day is prescribed: "Beginning with the bright fortnight of Āśvina, on the tenth day, Aparājitā should be properly worshipped by men, having taken recourse to the northeastern direction (aiśānī) in the afternoon with great care. This [observance] is to be performed on the earlier of two possible lunar days when the asterism Śravaṇā is absent on the subsequent day. Beginning with the bright fortnight of Āśvina, on the tenth day, Aparājitā should be properly worshipped by men.

When the Śravaṇa nakṣatra is prescribed, then that very [tithi] should be observed. As it is stated in the Kalpadruma: "If at sunrise there is a tenth [tithi] and the eleventh is even slightly complete, and the Śravaṇa asterism occurs at that time, that lunar day is called Vijayā."

"O descendant of Kakutstha, since [the journey] was set forth on the full moon day under the asterism of Śravaṇa, men should cross the boundary on that same lunar day and under that same asterism. In all other fortnights, the ninth day (Navamī) should be taken as the time for observance. This has been stated in the *Purāṇasamuccaya*:
On that full ninth day joined with [the asterism] Aparājitā, Aparājitā should be worshipped by men according to the well-known ritual for the sake of security and victory.
The ninth lunar day joined with the remainder [of the previous tithi], when Aparājitā is present on the tenth, bestows victory upon the goddess when worshipped; she is the increaser of triumph.
"Likewise, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, a person should perform worship;
one should not perform the Aparājita worship on the eleventh day. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa as well.
"O King, for that monarch who undertakes a military expedition by transgressing the tenth day,
there shall be no victory whatsoever in his kingdom for a full year.
Thus ends the procedure for Aparājitā-daśamī.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Formerly, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, the highly virtuous wife of Bhṛgu was devoted to her household duties in the beautiful and divine hermitage of Rāma.
She was always one who fulfilled the desires of Bhṛgu’s heart;
and into her, the sage of great splendor deposited the Agnihotra fire.
The bull among sages, having released Viṣṇu— who was filled with terror at the ill-omened sight of the Dānavas— stood by his side in the midst of battle and entrusted him [to the care of the Lord].
Having entrusted all his possessions as a deposit with Divyā,
the great ascetic Hara went to the side of the Himavat mountain to propitiate Hara.
For the sake of the Saṃjīvanī herb, the family priest went daily with his face turned downwards, inhaling smoke from the grains,
for the victory of the king of the Dānavas.
When he had departed, Hari, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, arrived;
having reached that spot, he severed his head with his discus.
Seeing the entire army of the asuras slain by Viṣṇu at that time, it resembled an ocean filled with flowing blood and corpses.
He became endowed with divine weapons and gazed intently at Viṣṇu;
before he could utter a word, his neck was severed by the discus.
He struck off his head, complete with its earrings,
just as that sage was returning after having obtained the Saṃjīvanī lore.
He beheld the Daityas and the sons of Daitya struck down,
and with his face contorted by a frown of rage, he cursed Hari.
Because the universe is characterized by the inevitability of what must come to pass, and for the sake of its welfare,
you have slain the Daityas and protected the Brahmin woman who is my own charge.
Therefore, you shall go ten times to the world of men;
as there is no other ford in the world of men, this is for the protection of the rulers of the earth.
[975] My descent shall be tenfold, occurring again and again in various ways.
O Pārtha, by the causes previously mentioned, I have descended upon the surface of the earth.
Those men who shall worship me, their residence shall be in the triple heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, tell me in detail the vow known as the Daśāvatāra,
together with its mantras and its secret teachings, which destroys all sins.
Kṛṣṇa said:
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Proṣṭhapada, being self-restrained and pure,
one should bathe in a clear body of water and perform the libations for the ancestors and the gods.
O best of the Kuru lineage, having performed this,
a person should return home and take three double-handfuls of grain flour.
One should cook that [mixture] gradually, combined with ghee known as *puṃsaṃjña*,
on that same day for each year, until ten years have passed.
In the first year, one should offer *pūrikā*; in the second, *ghṛtapūrikā*;
in the third, white *kāsāra*; and in the fourth, auspicious *modaka*.
In the fifth year, the Sohālakas; in the sixth year, the Khaṇḍaveṣṭakas;
in the seventh year, the Kokvarasyalakas; and likewise, in the eighth year, the Puṣṭas.
O bull among the Bharatas, one should cause ten Brahmins to partake of it in sequence as prescribed, for oneself, for ten [others], and for ten more.
One half of that half should be given to Viṣṇu, or another half to a twice-born;
having gone to a beautiful body of water, one should eat the remaining half oneself.
Having worshipped the ten incarnations with flowers, incense, and ointments,
the wise man, having sprinkled Hari with water while reciting this mantra, [should proceed].
Matsya, Kūrma, Nṛsiṃha, Varāha,
Trivikrama, Rāma, Rāma, Rāma, Rāma, and Buddha together with Kalki.
I have gone for refuge to the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, the God.
I bow down, O Lord of the World; may that Viṣṇu be gracious to me.
Having cut through the Māyā of Viṣṇu, Janārdana is pleased with her broken [power].
"May he lead us to Śvetadvīpa; may he offer himself to me.
O Pārtha, he who performs this excellent vow according to this procedure, [attains that goal].
Listen now to the meritorious fruit of that which is called the *Daśāvatāra-nāma*. These ten stages of men that are heard of in the world—
Hari cuts them down with his discus-weapons, there is no doubt;
Hari causes them to cross over the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
Pleased by this vow and its observance, he swiftly leads one to Śvetadvīpa;
what could not be attained in this world for him with whom Janārdana is satisfied?
Therefore, O King, I, Janārdana, sporting in the form of Time,
have declared that fearlessness shall prevail in the world of mortals as proclaimed by me, O Pārtha.
Accompanied by her husband and son, she remains for a long time in the world of mortals with steady devotion marked by good fortune, and thereafter is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Those persons who worship the ten incarnations of Puruṣottama, beginning with the Fish, on the tenth lunar days, go from the world of Viṣṇu to the world of Indra, and from there to the supreme state.
Having enjoyed happiness throughout all ten stages of life in the mortal world, they ascend a celestial vehicle and depart for the realms of the Lord of the Gods.
Thus ends the section titled "The Ten Incarnations" from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Now follows the vow of Āśā-daśamī, together with its concluding rite (udyāpana).
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, whose lotus-face is blooming like a fresh leaf on the path,
listen attentively as I describe to you the vow for the fulfillment of all desires.
O lord of the earth, there may first arise a burning heat within those who administer poison;
O King, he who has been defeated by his brother through deceit finds no atonement.
O Indra among kings, accompanied by his wife and a messenger, he went forth with dice to the forest— desolate, terrifying, and filled with the shrieks of flocks of cranes.
Having gone there, he avoided food and water provided by Prītihotra;
then he saw birds with the luster of gold situated in the middle of the forest.
O King, desiring to seize them, he covered them with his own garment;
then, quickly taking hold of the beautiful cloth from the bird nearby, he [acted].
Clad in her garment, she entered a certain assembly hall in great distress;
Damayantī, having reached the hall, was then overcome by sleep.
Having abandoned her out of distress, he went elsewhere to the Lord of Wealth;
but when the son of Niṣadha had departed, the daughter of Bhīma awoke with her face anointed with unguents.
Not seeing Nala, her son, or her husband in the forest, the daughter of Bhīma wandered here and there, crying out "Alas! Alas! again and again.
Overcome by suffering and grief, and longing for the sight of Nala,
she reached a certain thicket in the forest belonging to the city of Cedi.
Beholding the conduct of the people, the mother of the King of Cedi turned about like one mad, surrounded by children agitated with curiosity.
Like a crescent moon fallen upon the earth, illuminating the quarters of the sky, she was taken to her own abode; "O fair-faced one, who are you? he asked.
The daughter of Bhīma spoke with modesty: "Know me to be a *sairandhrī*;
I shall not wash feet, nor shall I eat the remnants of others' meals."
If anyone should now deserve to be punished by you,
O Queen, then by virtue of that promise I shall remain in your dwelling.
"So be it," said the blameless-limbed mother of the king to her;
"thus indeed, O irreproachable one, shall you remain for some time in the house of a slave."
O twice-born one, she dwelt there for half a year; it is said that after a month had passed, Damayantī, having been summoned by her father, went to her father’s house.
Though she was attended by her mother, father, sons, and brothers,
Damayantī nevertheless remained in sorrow, deprived of the King of Niṣadha.
Having summoned the brahmins, he said: "Tell me of a vow or even a gift by which I may have a sudden reunion with my beloved."
Thereupon, the wise Brahmin, skilled in ancient lore, said:
"O blessed lady, observe the tenth day of the lunar fortnight, which grants the fulfillment of your desires."
The slender-limbed lady performed everything that had previously been prescribed by the priest Damanaka, an expert in ancient lore and a knower of sacred narratives.
O best of men, by the power of this vow, Damayantī’s reunion with her husband has been brought about for the sake of happiness and splendor.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Govinda, how and when is this "tenfold hope" (āśā-daśamy) performed?
O Yādava, explain all of this to me, including the months, the asterism Tiṣya, and so forth.
Kṛṣṇa said:
A prince [exerts himself] with the hope of a kingdom; a farmer for the sake of cultivation;
the son of a merchant for the sake of a wife; and likewise a pregnant woman for the sake of a son.
In this world, a maiden seeking a husband does so for the sake of accomplishing dharma, artha, and kāma;
an excellent brahmin desiring to sacrifice does so, and a sick man seeks it for the removal of his disease.
O Hero, when the beloved has gone abroad, she is then afflicted by the heat of longing;
at such times, among these and other circumstances, this vow of hope (āśāvratam) should be performed.
When someone should have a need for relief from suffering, he should then undertake this vow:
having bathed on the tenth day of the bright fortnight and worshipped the deities.
On the tenth day at night, the host of household deities (gṛhīgaṇa) should be worshipped with flowers, red lac, and sandalwood paste,
after having been drawn either with barley grains or with a mixture of flour and red lac.
Those in female form should also be worshipped as presiding deities, marked by their own specific emblems,
just as the god Śakra and others are characterized by their weapons and vehicles.
Having offered the food oblation (naivedya) smeared with ghee, one should separately cause lamps to be presented;
then, having offered fruits produced in season, one should announce the purpose of the rite.
May hopes and desires always be fulfilled; may my aspirations be realized.
By the grace of the Bhavānīs, may there always be auspiciousness.
Having thus performed the worship and given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the brāhmaṇa, one should eat;
by this sequential method, one should perform [the rite] month after month.
Then, as his desire ran full course, he exerted himself further;
and when one month had passed, and six months, and a year, and two years had gone by.
One should have the directions fashioned out of gold, silver, or flour-paste;
having bathed and being properly adorned together with one's kinsmen and relatives.
Having meditated thus, one should worship in the courtyard of the house with these mantra compositions;
Śakra, who is honored by gods and asuras, is present there for you.
O Goddess of the eastern direction, accompanied by the Moon as before, homage to you!
O Preceptor, because of your encompassing of Agni, you are called the southern (Āgneyī) one.
For fire is the supreme power of the waters; become a granter of boons through your fiery nature!
Having approached the King of the Gods, that world shall be brought under control.
Therefore, O Yāmyā, become the bestower of desires upon Saṃyaminī;
may the sword, together with the deformed ones, drink you as nectar.
Therefore, you have always been given the name Nairṛta;
by you, O support of the dwelling, Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, is sustained.
For the sake of accomplishing desired objects, become the source of the Vāruṇī;
and since you have studied [the Vedas], you are once again the giver of vital breath (vāyu) to the worlds.
Therefore, O Vāyavyā, grant us constant peace; salutations, salutations! And you, who are Kauveryā, Śiva, and Saumyā, having attained the eastern direction, you are now the northern one.
O you who have been adorned by Śambhu, the Lord of the world of Pānī, you have immediately granted us unsurpassed desires; therefore, be gracious toward us.
Therefore, O Śivā, manifest your presence; salutations to you!
Though you are served by the Sarpāṭaka clan, you nevertheless remain below.
Do not always be attended by Naga women;
rather, may you always be surrounded by the seven worlds for the sake of auspiciousness.
Surrounded by Sanaka and the others, make the tongues of Brahmā drink [the nectar];
likewise, all the constellations, the planets, and the lunar mansions and planets.
May the Mothers of the Constellations, as well as the Bhūtas, Pretas, and Vināyakas— all of them, for the sake of accomplishing my desired aims, remain forever bowed in devotion.
Having worshipped with these mantras using flowers, incense, and so forth,
and having established [the deity] with water, one should then present the fruits.
With the resonance of the sound of the sun’s rays and the echoes of auspicious songs,
she should pass that night while the women dance and scatter flowers.
Having provided comfort through gifts, honors, and the like, which are as intense as powdered saffron,
one should present all of that to a knower of the Vedas at dawn.
Having thus asked forgiveness for everything and having performed the ritual of propitiation,
he should eat together with his friends, as well as his well-wishers and kinsmen.
O Pārtha, the man who thus observes the Daśamī vow with devotion attains every desire wished for by his mind.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this vow should especially be observed by women;
for the wives of those with meager wealth are always devoted to their desires.
O Great King, I have described to you this unsurpassed vow, which brings merit, fame, and long life, and bestows the fruit of all desires.
Those men who, desiring the desires of the bull among men,
always worship [him] in the ten directions on the tenth lunar days— their hearts are filled to their utmost with special devotion.
Hope is the fruit; it is enough, there is no need for further elaboration.
Thus ends the Āśā-daśamī-vrata with its concluding rite (sodyāpana) from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Now follows the Yama-vrata.
Brahmā said:
On the tenth day, Yama, the lord of death, when worshipped, certainly removes all diseases.
The root mantras and the limb mantras are proclaimed by their respective names.
As before, the Lord of the Lunar Days (Tithīśvara) should be depicted seated upon a lotus petal.

Homage be to him who has five beautiful arms and bestows the boons of the staff and the noose while granting fearlessness; he who stands upon the back of a buffalo and is the noble deity of the supreme gods.
Worship is performed with offerings of perfumes and flowers according to one's ability;
even if performed with deceit or through hypocrisy, it nevertheless yields fruit.
A fire oblation performed with streams of clarified butter, fuel-sticks, curd, milk, rice, and honey,

This is the meaning: this cited prohibition concerns the fast whose occasion is the conjunction of [the weekday] Bhānu (Sunday) and so forth; it does not, however, concern the Ekādaśī fast associated with [the weekday] Bhānu and the rest. For fasting on Ekādaśī is obligatory (*nitya*) and must necessarily be performed. It has been so ordained, and no prohibition of it can be inferred, as that would result in a logical contradiction (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, the *saṃkrānti* and other such occasions do not function as qualifiers of Ekādaśī, because of their association with lunar and solar eclipses, because they are mentioned with different case endings, because of the usage of the words in that manner, and because the injunction for fasting on Ekādaśī applies even when it is joined with a *saṃkrānti* or similar event. The eleventh day (Ekādaśī), whether of the bright or the dark fortnight, should be observed with fasting. As stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Just as a fair-complexioned or a dark-complexioned twice-born man who is well-versed in the Vedas is highly honored..."
Likewise, it is remembered that the two Ekādaśīs deliver the donor.
Just as there is no difference between white and other-colored sesame seeds in their oil,
and just as there is no difference between the milk of a black cow and that of a white cow, both being equally "cow's milk."
Likewise, the merit of both the bright and dark fortnights would be equal to that of the twelfth day;
and the new moon and full moon days would be equal in terms of merit.

In that same manner, the two auspicious twelfth days (dvādaśīs) occurring in the bright fortnights are remembered by the sages as being proclaimed [as meritorious] according to the northern and southern solstices (ayana).
One obtains equal merit on both the twelfth lunar days (dvādaśī). In the Padma Purāṇa it is said:
"Eclipses of the Moon and the Sun are likewise remembered by the sages as meritorious."
Likewise, on the auspicious twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī), which is bright, meritorious, and equanimous according to the Dharma.
Just as Viṣṇu and Śiva are remembered by the sages as worthy of worship,
so too are the two twelfth lunar days (dvādaśīs) of the bright and dark fortnights declared to be most worthy of worship.

Thus it is stated in the *Śukrakṛṣṇaviveka* regarding the recollection of sin. Likewise, in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* and the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "One who kills a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, an ungrateful person, and one who violates the teacher’s bed... [1001] In the *Skandapurāṇa*:
"The killer of a Brahmin, the killer of a cow, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the Guru's bed—
in the *Kālikā Purāṇa* it is said:
'He is proclaimed to be the repository of all sins in this world.'"
To explain this further for their sake,
[the author] cites the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: "And he who, out of delusion, [neglects] the two eleventh days, the bright and the dark, the white and the black..."
Knowing this, one should always observe the twelfth day (dvādaśī), whether it falls in the bright or the dark fortnight;
one should not make a distinction between the two, for by making such a distinction, one goes to hell.
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Whether it be the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, until the dissolution of all beings (*āhūtasaṃplava*).
Furthermore, there is a censure regarding the non-performance of the Ekādaśī vow as spoken by Sanatkumāra:
Whether it be the bright fortnight or the dark, there is no distinction whatsoever;
he who makes a distinction is proclaimed a slayer of his father.
As proclaimed by Sanatkumāra:
"That man who makes a distinction between these two Ekādaśīs— for him I see no deliverance until the dissolution of all that has been called into being."
Now, regarding the censure of failing to observe the Ekādaśī vow, as spoken by Sanatkumāra:
"Indeed, that fool who does not perform the fast on Ekādaśī goes to the Raurava hell, which is shrouded in darkness."
In that same manner, O best of sages, so does he who possesses the birth of a twice-born man eat.
Likewise:
"He who eats [the food of such a person] consumes with every morsel a sin equal to the excrement of dogs and other [unclean animals].
An expiation for a drinker of intoxicants has been declared by the wise in the Dharmaśāstra."
[1002] No expiation has been prescribed anywhere for one who desires food on the eleventh lunar day;
O best of sages, those who drink liquor fall directly into hell.
"One who desires food on the eleventh day sinks into hell along with his ancestors.
In the *Nāndīpurāṇa*:
"He who eats honey on that day eats the sin of the earth."
Likewise: Whatever sins there may be, even those equal to the killing of a Brahmin,
they all reside in food when the day of Hari has arrived.
One incurs those sins by eating on the day of Hari;
for all sins reside within that very day.
He who eats those [foods] out of delusion is not liberated from his sins;
therefore, the Dvādaśī dedicated to the son of Soma must certainly be observed.
He who eats on the day of Hari consumes nothing but impurity.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "A killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a killer of a brother, and likewise a killer of a guru—
whoever eats on the eleventh day shall be fallen from the world of Viṣṇu."

In the Nāradīya Purāṇa, it is said that a widowed woman (raṇḍā) and an ascetic (yatī) incur a specific degree of sin for failing to observe the Ekādaśī vow: "O wise one, a widowed woman and an ascetic who are without the Ekādaśī [vow] are indeed cooked in the Andhatāmisra hell until the dissolution of all beings."
And Kātyāyana says:
"If a woman who is a widow should eat on the eleventh day,
her merit would perish, and she would incur the sin of killing an embryo day after day."
The sin incurred by a woman’s abandonment of a vow has been stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"Having undertaken the supreme Dvādaśī vow according to the prescribed rule..."
Having caused its destruction, a person shall go to the Raurava hell.
Likewise: "He who, having undertaken the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī), commits a breach of that vow,
finds his twelve-year observance of the vow to be fruitless."
Likewise:
"If one has properly undertaken a vow such as that of Ekādaśī and does not complete it, his destiny will be most wretched."
Then, on this day, Kātyāyana said to the authority:
"A mortal who is more than eight years old but less than eighty years of age should fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights."
In the Nāndīyapurāṇa: "Any mortal in my kingdom who, being more than eight years old and less than eighty, eats on the day of Viṣṇu, is a doer of evil."
"He is to be executed by me, punished by me, and banished from my country by me— this is Kātyāyana's view.
For this reason, O Brahmin, one should observe a fast on the eleventh day."
Whether a man or a woman, one may perform [this rite] during both fortnights.
In this secondary alternative (anukalpa), it should be understood that everyone is qualified. As it is said in the Brahmavaivarta:
"O Brahmin, without the Ekādaśī, there is no liberation from saṃsāra."
In that case as well, there is this distinction: it belongs to those who possess the capacity for action.
But the wise do not know the body as being afflicted by a great seizure—
that by which the body is tormented, even by most auspicious karma.
One should not subject it to extreme hardship; rather, that is called "effortlessness," for the body is the primary means for accomplishing Dharma by one who performs great merit.

One should not, out of sheer foolishness, perform asceticism in a casual manner that causes distress; rather, one should practice penance through a hidden grasp of the self, even if it involves personal hardship.
He attains neither success, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
Regarding the incapacity of the qualified person, the Vārāha Purāṇa states concerning a vow that has arisen:
"In the event of physical incapacity when a vow has presented itself..."
Or he should have his lawful wife, or a son endowed with discipline, perform it.
Whether it be a sister or even a brother, his vow is not violated;
hear also of him who fasts on the Ekādaśī dedicated to another [deity].
For whichever Brahmin the rite is performed, it shall yield its full fruit for him;
the performer obtains tenfold merit from this, of this there is no doubt.

Now follows the procedure for the performance of the vow of fasting (*upavāsa*). Regarding that, the general nature of fasting is as Vasiṣṭha has stated: "That which is the dwelling together with virtues after having turned away from sins—know that to be fasting, which is devoid of all enjoyments."

For one who has turned away from evils—that is, desisted from things to be avoided—and who possesses virtues such as the chanting of Viṣṇu’s names and so forth, this vow of fasting (*upavāsa-vrata*) is of two kinds: obligatory (*nitya*) and for the sake of specific fruits. Regarding the obligatory, the avoidance of transgression is achieved by means of the fasting vow consisting of the abandonment of the two meals on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), regardless of how it is performed. And so it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"Having understood this, one must certainly perform the *ekādaśī* vow; even if unable to observe the specific regulations, one should remain abstinent from food for a full day and night."
One who has restrained the senses, is aided by faith, and is devoted to Viṣṇu, is liberated from sins by fasting on Ekādaśī; there is no doubt in this matter.

Kātyāyana says: "Furthermore, O Goddess, if one who observes the perpetual fast should perform the act of eating in the evening and morning when the day of Hari has arrived, [he incurs the sin] of seven births."
Now, regarding the nature of the vow of fasting for the sake of its fruit, he says in that very same place:
"But one who is capable should again observe the rule with its specific qualifications:
in the case of the two days [of the lunar fortnight], at the beginning and the end, [one fasts] in the evening; and in the middle [day], both in the morning and in the evening."
One desiring the fruit of the fast should abandon four meals.

Thus, one who is about to undertake either the obligatory or the optional vow of fasting should perform the cleaning of the teeth after eating on the first *daśamī*. Regarding this, it is said: "Just as one licks the tongue with a tooth-stick on the *daśamī*, so too should one be free from desire for effort, for the sake of the observance of the *dvādaśī*."
With a humble mind, he wipes away that sin even while standing on the bank;
for the sinner who has not yet exhausted his karma indeed goes to the station of Viṣṇu.

[1006] Then, on the tenth night, one should make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the undertaking of the observance (*niyama*). As stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*: "When the day of Hari has arrived, having properly performed the observance at night, one should indeed undertake the Vaiṣṇava vow of fasting on the tenth day."
He states the intention, the mantra, the cause, and the deity:
"O Lotus-eyed One, O Acyuta, having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall eat on the following day; be my deliverer."
Having thus formed the resolve and performed the preliminary rites, one should construct a flower pavilion for the Lord on the day of Ekādaśī.
As it is said in the Brahma Purāṇa:
"With faith and a well-composed mind, one should construct [the pavilion] above the Lord."
O best of sages, with various flowers, he fashioned a variegated pavilion of blossoms.
Having constructed the enclosure, one should subsequently perform the vigil at night;
having thus prepared the pavilion, one should worship the deity during the night.
Likewise, in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"By means of fasting on the eleventh day, one should worship Hari at night;
and that night, according to one's ability, by listening to the Purāṇas and so forth."
The word "having brought" (*nītvā*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. From the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"Therefore, having placed faith foremost and having reached the twelfth lunar day, whether bright or dark, one should worship the Lord Janārdana while observing a fast."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*,
Vyāsa said:
"On the eleventh day of both fortnights, being composed and abstaining from food..."
Having bathed according to the proper ritual procedure, fasting and with his senses subdued.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rule with faith and a well-composed mind,
using flowers, perfumes, incense, lamps, and excellent food offerings.
By means of various kinds of fasts, recitations, burnt offerings,
circumambulations, diverse divine hymns, captivating songs and instrumental music,
prostrations like a staff, and likewise with the most excellent shouts of "Victory! (jaya).
Having worshipped in this manner, one should perform a vigil (*jāgara*). Regarding this very point, it is said: "Having worshipped in accordance with the rules, one should perform a vigil at night.
Regarding this very point, it is said.
A man devoted to Viṣṇu who causes others to hear stories and songs of Viṣṇu goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
A wise person, while meditating upon, reciting, and praising the God, should spend the night performing the narrative of Vāsudeva or even his songs.
Having thus completed the vigil, one should bathe at dawn on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), worship Viṣṇu, and offer the vow of fasting with this prayer:
"O Keśava, for me who am blinded by the darkness of ignorance, be gracious through this vow;
O Lord, be well-disposed toward me and grant the vision of knowledge."

With this mantra, one should resolve upon the fast for the deity; thereafter, one should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*). Likewise, the *Skanda Purāṇa* states: "Then one should perform the *pāraṇa* according to the available path; and this *pāraṇa* should be performed with [food] mixed with *tulasī*. [1008]
Indeed, having observed a fast, he who eats on the twelfth day an offering mixed with *tulasī* destroys ten million sins of killing.

Thus, beginning from the tenth day, one should perform the entire vow, including the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*), in accordance with the prescribed rules. Those rules are stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, restraint of the senses, worship of Śiva, the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*), contentment, and the cultivation of spiritual luster (*tejas*)."
In all vows, this tenfold common ritual action is traditionally taught.
Manu has stated this:
"The performance of what is enjoined, the non-restraint of the senses,
and the indulgence in what is forbidden— these must always be avoided with effort."
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "While fasting, one should avoid bell-metal, black gram, lentils, chickpeas, millet, leafy vegetables, honey, and food belonging to others."
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Bell-metal, meat, lentils, honey, oil, false speech,
physical exercise, travel abroad, sleeping during the day, and the application of collyrium— "
Stone-ground flour and lentils—these twelve are indeed for the Vaiṣṇava.
The word "one should abandon" is understood as the ellipsis. Hārīta states:
"On the day of fasting, conversation with outcasts (patita), heretics (pākhaṇḍin), nihilists (nāstika), and so forth, as well as falsehood, gambling, and the like, must be avoided.
[1009] In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
The recitation of that [mantra], the practice of its recitation, meditation upon it, listening to discourses concerning it, its worship, and the chanting and hearing of its names, and so forth.
"For these virtues resulting from fasting have been proclaimed by the wise. Thus [it is said] in the Viṣṇurahasya.
Brahmā said:
With mind, action, and speech, a man of great devotion and controlled senses should worship the one whose banner is Garuḍa,
performing the three daily ablutions.
One should perform the recitation of Viṣṇu’s names and conversation about Him day and night;
with devotion, one should utter praises of Viṣṇu and avoid false speech.
Endowed with universal compassion for all beings, practicing tranquility and non-violence,
one should glorify Vāsudeva whether asleep or lying upon a bed.
One should avoid recollecting, looking at, smelling, anointing with, or praising [these things], as well as every longing for meats— [all of which belong to] the fortunate one.
One observing a vow should avoid anointing the limbs, anointing the head, betel, and ointments; he should avoid all these and whatever else is prohibited.
One established in a vow should not stay at home nor converse with those engaged in improper acts;
nor should a householder, while standing in a temple, perform a vow.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "During a fast as well as at a *śrāddha*, one should not use a tooth-stick for cleaning the teeth;
the contact of the teeth with wood destroys seven generations of one's lineage."
In the *Viṣṇudharma*: "One should avoid contact with heretics and indeed refrain from conversing with them;
there, men should perform the worship of Viṣṇu while observing a fast."
From the Padma Purāṇa: On the twelfth lunar day, one should avoid these seven things: sexual intercourse, aphrodisiacs, food belonging to others, eating a second time, honey, sesame seeds, and meat.

These observances (*niyama*) must be maintained until the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*), for it is by the breaking of the fast alone that the vow (*vrata*) is completed. Beyond this, one may break the fast according to one's desire and preference, as stated by Kātyāyana: "One may break the fast as one wishes. For one who is unable to observe the vow of fasting, the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* prescribes eating at night (*nakta*) and so forth: "On the eleventh day, one should fast, or else one should perform the *nakta* meal.
The *Kūrma Purāṇa* [also says]:
One who is emaciated, aged, or afflicted by illness may subsist on a single meal or eat only at night;
however, one must not let the twelfth day (dvādaśī) pass without observing the vow of fasting.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: By eating once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only what is unasked for,
by fasting, and by giving gifts, one should not fail to observe the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
The Ritual for the Nitya-Ekādaśī. Vajra said:
"O Brahmin, O best of the twice-born, how is Janārdana to be worshipped during the Dvādaśīs by one who lacks desire? Tell that to me as I ask you."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O wise one, having heard all this concerning the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
the observer of the vow should eat only once every month in this manner for the duration of a year.
The names of Keśava, the God of gods, are each distinct:
Kṛṣṇa, Ananta, Acyuta, Cakrī, Vaikuṇṭha, and Janārdana.
Upendra, Yajñapuruṣa, Vāsudeva,
Hari, Yogeśa, and Puṇḍarīkākṣa are the names of the months in their respective order.
The man who always remembers these [verses] upon rising in the morning—
even his ancestors who have fallen into miserable states shall attain heaven.
He who should daily give twelve sesame vessels to a twice-born man,
and likewise give tawny cows and chant the names for an equal number of years;
The merit of those who fast for a month, of sacrificers, and of those who travel to sacred pilgrimage sites is honored daily by the names of the months belonging to the God of gods.
Every month, one should perform worship, giving, and other rites for Hari under His own name;
the meaning is that it should be done using whichever name is prescribed for that particular month. At the conclusion, a fire sacrifice (homa) must then be performed in the place of that deity.
At the end of the vow,
after the carrying forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana), one should keep these twelve [items] in mind;
one should place them upon twelve leaves of the *aśvattha* tree together with white rice grains.
"Oṃ, obeisance to him; may he protect us"—with these words, one should invoke them separately.
Having then established the fire in the east, one should meditate on [the deities] facing toward various directions.
One should offer the lotus seat, the water for honoring (arghya), and worship with perfumes and flowers;
then, having offered incense, lamps, and garments, one should complete the rite with the remnants of the oblation.
After giving water for sipping (ācamana), one should then present the remnants of the oblation;
having first offered eight sets of eight fuel-sticks (samidh) and eight oblations of clarified butter (ghṛta).
Having offered one oblation of kṛśara and eight oblations of barley and sesame seeds,
one should then perform the sviṣṭakṛt offering with the remains of the deity's portion.

Having performed the concluding oblation (*antahoma*) for the installation of the fire, having offered seats and water for sipping (*ācamana*) to the deities, and having completed the remaining oblations (*śeṣahoma*), one should present the remnants of the offering to the gods and offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with what remains thereof.
For the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the mantra is "That supreme abode of Viṣṇu" (*tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam*).
When the end of the oblation has been performed in this manner, one should give twelve or eight black cows.
Six, four, or even just one milch cow should be given,
with horns tipped in gold, hooves of silver, and adorned with bells, ornaments, and cloth.
Having honored it, one should present to a preeminent brahmin a milch cow with bronze hooves and gold in its various parts, together with its calf.
"May those deities associated with the twelve months be pleased," thus it is said for one who is devoted to Kṛṣṇa, peaceful, knowledgeable in the ritual rules, and high-souled.
Having invoked them with the words, "Lift me up in this way," those vessels are accepted;
and when the sesame-filled bowls have been offered month after month, [the rite is performed] with those jars.
The instrumental case here denotes accompaniment; the meaning is that this mantra is not only for this specific gift, but also for the monthly offering of water jars.
At that time, those jars should be offered with the names of the months.
Since the vow and the merit are the same, one should therefore present the *arghya* offering.
The word "to Sūrya" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
O Earth, when this vow is completed, whatever is desired is obtained;
furthermore, one shall deliver [the deceased] from the hells filled with Mahāraurava.
The son of one's father or his master shall not go to Yama even in hundreds of kalpas;
the destruction of sins such as those of killing a Brahmin or an elephant occurs through horse-sacrifices.
O Earth, this vow excels both one's own meritorious deeds and those performed by one's ancestors,
as well as the horse sacrifice and the śrāddha rite at Gayā.
It is the savior of one's ancestors and oneself, granting all desires;
it delivers those who dwell in hell, as well as those in the womb and those fallen in battle.
Those who, even through childishness, have attained the state of a *bhūta* or *preta*,
and those who do not desire progeny, are liberated from their sins.
By fasting on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, one shall deliver ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself as the twenty-first from among the hosts of the Pitṛs.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇadvādaśī vow as declared in the Vārāha Purāṇa.
Now, regarding the Kṛṣṇadvādaśī vow:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, for what reason has the Dvādaśī not been explained to me? Is it because that day is not dear to you, O Lord, or is it because it is not proper to speak of it?"
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, this unsurpassed secret has not been told by me to anyone;
it bestows great merit and destroys even the most heinous sins.
The vow of the two twelfth days (Ubhayadvādaśī) bestows desired objects upon men, removes sins when heard, and is the most excellent of all vows.
I shall explain that to you; listen with a concentrated mind.
Then, in the afternoon, having offered libations and performed the twilight prayers and other rites, being pure—
Having obtained permission from one who knows the Vedas, desires to teach, is learned in the Purāṇas, and has conquered his senses,
and having worshipped the Lord of the Gods of gods, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth;
And one should take a vow, O Pārtha, in the presence of the guru, the gods, and the sacred fire:
"Having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall [fast] on the following day."
"I shall eat, O lotus-eyed one; be my refuge, O Acyuta.
Having spoken thus, he then bowed to his elders and worshipped Janārdana.
Having conquered anger and abandoned the objects of the senses such as sound, one should sleep on the ground;
then, at the clear dawn, with the mind offered to Keśava.
At that time, one should avoid uttering the word "Keśava" when stumbling due to hunger or similar reasons,
as well as conversation with heretics and the like through sight, touch, or other means.
O Pārtha, one should abandon for three days that which causes a deficiency in the vow;
thereafter, at the time of midday, in the pure water of a river or similar place, [one should perform the rite].
Having conquered anger, one should perform the bath preceded by the five products of the cow;
having performed the bath with a single-pointed mind, one becomes purified in soul and endowed with compassion.
Having paid homage to Āditya and Keśava, the ultimate cause,
one should emerge [from the bath] and put on two garments that are bright and without holes.
Having then offered handfuls of water to the ancestors, gods, and humans,
and having fulfilled his duty according to the golden rule of conduct, he should go home.
There, the wise man should worship Govinda while muttering "Keśava," with flowers,
incense, lamps, and various kinds of food offerings.
One should keep a vigil at night with songs, instrumental music, and recitations;
having placed a water-pot containing jewels and gold within it.
It was covered with a pair of garments, anointed with white sandalwood paste,
provided with perfumes and garlands, and well-adorned in all directions with lamps.
Upon one part of the pitcher, he should place an image of the God of gods, anointed with white sandalwood paste and bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
Having performed the worship according to the rule when the morning had become bright, he,
having fulfilled his duties on the twelfth day, worshipped the Teacher of the World.
One should give a water-pot, along with its accessories and a sacrificial fee, to a brahmin;
having fed the foremost of brahmins, one should also give a gift according to one's capacity.
Having fed his servants and given the daily fodder to the cows,
he should himself consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then eat while remaining silent.
By this procedure, O tiger among men, one should fast on the twelfth day of that dark fortnight, while meditating upon the all-pervading Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Having performed everything as before, one should then present it to a Brāhmaṇa;
having fed that best of the twice-born, one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to them as well.
Restraining his speech, he should afterwards consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the sacrificial fire;
thus, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) in the month of Pauṣa, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
The wise man, while chanting the Nārāyaṇa mantra, should perform all the preceding rites;
likewise, he should perform the bathing, the sipping of water, the giving of gifts, and the eating.
Likewise, O delighter of the Yadus, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins;
then, saying "May Nārāyaṇa be pleased with me," one should ask the preceptor for forgiveness.
O King, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of this very month of Puṣya,
one should worship Vāsudeva according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Then, filled with faith, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born for the God of gods, the Lord of the world, the cause of all causes.
One should first perform the meal as before, and thereafter the giving of gifts, worship, and so forth,
O Lord of Men, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Chanting the name "Mādhava," one should worship Hari as before;
likewise, one should keep a vigil at night with flowers, incense, and lamps.
Having honored the best of the twice-born with the words, "May Mādhava be pleased," the consumption [of the remnants] and so forth is prescribed here according to the previously mentioned rule.
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of this very month of Māgha,
the wise man, reciting the mantra "Pradyumna," should perform all the previously mentioned rites.
O son of Pāṇḍu, one should likewise perform the bathing, the sipping of water, and the giving of gifts, as well as the feeding of Brāhmaṇas and the bestowing of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, a man, self-restrained and pure, should worship an image of Viṣṇu while chanting "Govinda."
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin, saying, "May Govinda be pleased.
One should perform the recitations, worship, and gifts according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Likewise, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, with his senses restrained,
he should perform the rite as before while chanting "Aniruddha" for Kṛṣṇa.
O Pārtha, by that very same rite, which removes all sins,
[one should worship] with flowers, incense, food offerings, and the splendor of perfumes, lamps, and so forth.
One should first perform the offering with oblations and other services;
at the time of giving, one should indeed utter: "May Aniruddha be pleased with me."
O son of Pāṇḍu, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra,
one should bathe with the waters of the five products of the cow and chant the names of Viṣṇu.
A wise person should perform the ritual attendance of the Sun;
for that very deity Bhāskara is indeed proclaimed to be Viṣṇu.
May Viṣṇu, the eternal God of gods, be well-pleased;
with my palms joined in reverence, I offer this salutation to you for the granting of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having recited this and offered a joined-palms gesture (añjali) accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains,
one should worship the deity as before and give gifts according to one's ability.
May the eternal god Viṣṇu, the source of the universe, be pleased with me;
likewise, one should observe the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) of the dark fortnight in this month according to the prescribed rite.
O Pārtha, at the time of bathing and eating, one should indeed recite the name of Puruṣottama; by that very same procedure, one should perform the rites of bathing and giving gifts.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, a man, having performed all the rites such as bathing according to the rules, should worship Madhusūdana.
As before, one should offer incense, flowers, and so forth, as well as fragrant lamps. One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, [saying]: "May Madhusūdana be pleased."
Having uttered this, O mighty-armed one, one should accomplish all of this;
on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of this month, O bull of the Bharatas.
Having performed everything according to the previously mentioned rite, while muttering the mantra of the god Adhokṣaja,
he should worship an image of Viṣṇu with fragrant flowers and sandalwood paste.
Then, O King, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should give sacrificial fees to the twice-born according to the extent of one's wealth, as previously described.
Having performed all the rites beginning with bathing, one should worship Trivikrama at the clear dawn with flowers, incense, and food offerings.
O King, having fed the best of the twice-born with abundant milk, clarified butter,
and various foods on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, as previously described.
Having performed all the rites beginning with bathing, one should worship Trivikrama at the clear dawn with flowers, incense, and food offerings.
Having fed the best of the twice-born with offerings of ghee, milk, and various foods, one should give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), saying: "May Trivikrama be pleased with me."
Having uttered this, O tiger among men, he himself should eat as before;
specifically on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, O lord of the people.
Having bathed according to the previously mentioned rite, one should worship the omnipresent Lord Nṛsiṃha with devotion,
using flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, and offerings of food.
"May the eternal Lord Vāmana be pleased with me forever;
at that time, the observer of the vow should partake of food according to the previously prescribed rule."
O King, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, being self-controlled and pure, one should worship the god Acyuta according to that very same ritual procedure.
Having performed everything as before, at dawn when the sun is clear,
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin, saying, "May Acyuta be pleased."
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
having bathed according to the previously prescribed rite, the wise man should mutter the name "Śrīdhara."
One should worship the Lord of the gods, the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace;
thereafter, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to a Brahmin according to one's capacity.
[1019] At that time, fresh butter should be given to the twice-born, with the thought:
"May Śrīdhara, having arrived, be pleased and may he nourish unsurpassed prosperity."
Having uttered this, O best of the Kurus, one should then dismiss the brahmins;
thereafter, being well-composed, one should eat according to the previously mentioned rule.
Then, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, having worshipped the image of the Discus-handed Lord according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should honor the Lord of Gods with the mantra "Janārdana."
Then, food together with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brahmins;
one should utter these words: "May Janārdana be pleased with me."
Then, O King, he should eat together with his servants as before;
O auspicious one, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada.
One should arrange everything as before and then worship the deity;
having resolved, "O Hṛṣīkeśa," [one should offer] in cases of sneezing, stumbling, and so forth.
One should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability and give them sacrificial fees;
O Pāṇḍava, one should especially honor the deity and offer milk to the Brahmins.
"May Kṛṣīkeśa be pleased with me," he should utter these words;
then, O Pārtha, having offered an apology, he may eat as before, like a householder.
O King, in this same manner, the Kṛṣṇāvrata should be observed in the month of Bhādrapada,
having worshipped the image of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow with the mantra "Upendra."
