O son of Pāṇḍu, being intent on devotion, one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins as before,
for the pleasure of me, the God of gods.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuj, being self-restrained and pure,
one should bathe according to the previously prescribed rite and perform the libation for the deity.
One should indeed worship the image of Hari with the name "Padmanābha," having performed all the procedures such as *jāraṇa* and the rest according to the previously mentioned method.
Then, at the clear dawn, the householder, having performed his ablutions and other rites,
should feed the Brahmins and give them gold according to his means.
Then one should perform a circumambulation, prostrate, and ask for forgiveness;
one should utter these words: "May the Lotus-navelled One be pleased."
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja, a devoted man,
having fasted according to that rite, should worship Hari as well.
O best of kings, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin according to one's ability;
then one should utter this mantra: "May the Lord Hari be pleased with me."
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
having performed all the rites beginning with the bath according to the first procedure;
Wearing white garlands and garments, avoiding conversation with heretics,
the wise man, having entered the house, should perform the rite according to the prescribed injunctions.
One should perform all acts of beautification, as well as the offering of flowers and incense;
and, O Bhārata, a bamboo vessel should be used in all ritual actions.
Having honored the name of the discus-bearing God as "Dāsīdarāya," and having performed a special festival with songs, musical instruments, and other offerings, O King.
Having thus completed the Kṛṣṇā-dvādaśī on that occasion in the month of Kārttika,
she worshipped the name "Kṛṣṇa" of the Discus-wielding God of gods.
O Pārtha, for one who has fallen away [from the vow], no specific rule is prescribed.
In this vow, the twenty-four forms beginning with Keśava are to be worshipped;
here, sixteen names alone are ordained to be offered.
At that time, the primary gifts according to the prescribed rite were the Tulāpuruṣa offerings consisting of one hundred thousand cows, or one thousand cows, or one hundred cows, or even twelve cows.
O best of the Kurus, when the end of their vow has arrived during a solar eclipse at Kurukṣetra, gifts should be given to the foremost of the Brahmins.
By giving a garment of gold on that day, one obtains that very fruit;
O Pārtha, neither Vibhāsa, nor Gayā, nor the nine Puṣkaras are superior to it.
Neither Vārāṇasī nor Prayāga,
O lord of men, nor even the sacred fords (tīrthas) to the east and west of it, are equal to that.
O best of kings, O mighty-armed one, all those [offerings] originating from the northern direction are not equal to those at the conclusion of the Kārttika vow.
O best of men, when there is the conjunction of both twelfth days, one who possesses faith and whose mind is solely intent upon Kṛṣṇa should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
Endowed with universal compassion and other virtues, and firmly established solely in the meaning of the Purāṇas,
one shall uplift seven lineages and attain union with Viṣṇu.
This fruit of both types of Dvādaśī has been declared by way of summary;
O Pārtha, by whom can the merit of one who possesses faith be described?
This merit-bestowing and purifying [teaching], the supreme and highest among vows,
must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who does not wish to listen.
O Indra among kings, this [knowledge] is not for one who is not a Vaiṣṇava; otherwise, one goes to hell.
This is the Brahman for those seeking liberation; this is the goal for those seeking worldly enjoyment.
For that high-souled man, O Pārtha, who hears this or remembers it with supreme devotion,
being freed from sin, shall cast off all suffering.
He approaches the presence of the one of infinite forms.
Thus ends the vow of the twelfth day of both fortnights as spoken in the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
[1022] Now follows the vow of the Fish-twelfth (*matsyadvādaśī*).
Satyavān said:
O Great Sage, who was it that practiced fasting upon this earth? And what were those vows? You should tell this to me.

Durvāsas said: On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one who has restrained the self should bathe, perform the worship of the deity, and carry out the fire-ritual according to the prescribed rule.
Clad in clean garments and with a serene mind, having eaten well-prepared sacrificial food and other offerings,
one should walk five steps and then perform purification once more of the feet.

Having prepared a tooth-stick eight finger-breadths long, produced from a milky tree, one should consume it; then, having carefully performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should proceed.
Having touched the apertures with water and meditated for a long time upon Janārdana—
the one who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, who is clad in yellow garments, and wears a crown— the word *khāni* refers to the sense organs (*indriyāṇi*).
The god with a serene countenance, endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Having meditated and taken water, a person should then offer the *arghya* after beholding Janārdana in the form of the Sun with the water held in the hand.
At that time, O Great Sage, one should utter these words:
"Having become fasting on the eleventh day, on the following day..."
"I shall eat, O lotus-eyed one; be my refuge, O Acyuta.
Having spoken thus, he then remained at night in the presence of the God of gods.
Having himself performed [the rite] on the ground according to the injunctions with the words "Nārāyaṇa," he should then go to a river flowing to the ocean at the clear dawn.
Or else, a man of self-restraint, having brought pure earth from another place, from a pond, or from his own house, [should use] this mantra.
O Goddess, you always provide sustenance and nourishment for all beings;
by that truth, O divine clay, deliver me from sin.
The Mantra for Clay:
"Since the sacred bathing places within the belly of the cosmic egg are touched by your rays, O Sun, they become purified;
therefore, one should apply clay."
The mantra for beholding the earth of the Sun:
"O Varuṇa, all things are eternally and always established in you;
having obtained this earth from you, purify me without delay."
The mantra for sprinkling with earth:
"In this manner, having propitiated the earth, the sun, and the water, one should touch oneself;
having performed this three times, one should indeed draw the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the remaining earth in the water."
Then, having bathed properly with the recitation of mantras and ritual services,
and having performed the necessary sipping of water (ācamana) and obligatory duties, the person should go again to the temple of the deity.
There, having propitiated the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa through great yoga,
[one should worship] the feet with "Obeisance to Keśava" and the waist with "To Dāmodara."
The pair of thighs to Nṛsiṃha; the chest to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa;
the throat to the Lord of the Kaustubha; and likewise the breast to the Lord of Śrī.
"To Trailokyavijaya" [he offers] the two arms; "to the Self of All," the head;
"to the Holder of the Discus," the face; and "to Śaṅkara," the lotus.
The conch is born of water.
And with the mantra "To the Deep One," he should place it upon the waist for the sake of the three forms of the Lotus-Peaceful One.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, the wise man should place four jars before him,
filled with water, adorned with garlands, and smeared with white sandalwood paste.
Those four oceans, filled with jewels and covered by four vessels of sesame seeds, are proclaimed to be the jars.
In their midst, one should place an auspicious pedestal covered with cloth;
upon that, [an image] made of silver, gold, copper, or likewise wood.
If [the prescribed materials] are unavailable, one should fill the vessel with water and then place it there.
"If unavailable" means that in the absence of gold and so forth, one may even make it of wood.
Having fashioned the Lord Janārdana in the form of a fish using gold—
Endowed with the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, it is adorned by the Śruti and Smṛti.
The grammatical connection is as follows: having filled a vessel with water, one should place Janārdana in the form of a fish therein.
There, having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with various kinds of edible foods, fruits, flowers, perfumes, unguents, and incenses, [one should proceed].
Just as the Vedas situated in the netherworld were recovered by you, O Lord,
in the form of a fish, even so, O Keśava, deliver me from this worldly existence.
Having recited this, one should cause a vigil to be held there in his presence,
according to the extent of one's wealth, until the clear dawn.
One should cause four jars to be given to four Brahmins;
one should give [the first] to a Bahvṛca in the east, and likewise to a Chandoga in the south.
One should offer the excellent western pitcher to one endowed with the Yajurvedic branches;
likewise, one should offer it to the Atharvaveda in the north—this indeed is the prescribed rule.
May the Ṛgveda be pleased in the east, the Sāmaveda in the south,
the Yajurveda in the west, and likewise the Atharvaveda in the north.
One should have jars prepared covered with copper vessels containing sesame seeds;
then, indeed, a water-vessel should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has a family.
O highly fortunate one, he should indeed give [the gift], and thereafter he should feed the foremost brahmins with milk-rice; after that, the man himself should eat.
O Sage, he who performs this Dvādaśī once according to the prescribed rite should eat together with his dependents, remaining silent and with his senses restrained.
He attains the world of Brahmā and remains there for that very duration;
among all vows, he who is devoted to Ekādaśī is superior to the observer of Dvādaśī.
That period is the Brahma-period.
Then, at the withdrawal of Brahmā, his dissolution remains for a long time.
Upon renewed creation, he becomes the deity named Vairāja by name.
Even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin,
whether committed in this world intentionally or unintentionally, perish at that very moment.
In this world, whether one be poor or a king fallen from his kingdom,
by fasting according to the prescribed rule, he shall become a lord and a sharer of sovereignty.
She who is a barren woman shall become auspicious through this rite; by fasting, she shall have a son who is supremely righteous, a lord of sovereignty and a lord of fortune.
He who has committed an act of approaching one who should not be approached, whether knowingly or unknowingly,
is liberated from that sin by resorting to this ritual procedure.
By fasting on this day once with devotion, one may obtain the purification of the Vedas, even if the performance of Vedic rites has been neglected for many years.
Moreover, O Great Sage, what is the use of saying more? There is nothing to be attained that is not already attained; for the sinner does not see anything at all.
This ritual procedure must not be given to one who is uninitiated, nor to an atheist;
it should never be disclosed even to one who hates the gods or the Vedas.

This destroyer of all sins should be given to one who is devoted to the guru. For whoever observes the fast according to the prescribed rite, there shall be health, wealth, grain, and excellent women in this very life, as well as various other blessings.
Thus ends the Dharaṇīvrata and the Matsyadvādaśīvrata.
Now follows the Kūrmadvādaśīvrata.
Durvāsas said:
On that meritorious twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Puṣya,
one should perform the formal vow (saṃkalpa) and the ritual acts such as bathing, just as previously described.
Having completed the ritual, O best of the twice-born, one should worship Janārdana, the God of gods, on the eleventh day at night with separate mantras.
Having first worshipped the feet with "Salutation to Kūrma," one should worship the waist of Hari with "To Nārāyaṇa," and the belly of Hari with "To Saṅkarṣaṇa."
The throat for existence, which is free from sorrow for the chest.
With "Suvāhavā" he should worship the two arms, and with "Namo Viśālāya" the head, the discus, and the conch;
and with the mantras of their respective names, using excellent incense and perfumes.
With various kinds of offerings and diverse fruits.
Having worshipped the deity and placed the water-pot before him— its neck adorned with garlands and cords—
and having filled it with jewels as was done previously;
And [one should fashion] the deity out of gold according to one's own capacity.
Having fashioned the form of Kūrma together with Mount Mandara,
one should place it in a copper vessel filled with clarified butter,
having arranged it within a full jar.
But one should indeed give everything to the Brāhmaṇa alone.

The meaning is that one should place a tortoise made of clay upon a copper vessel filled with ghee, set it atop a water-pot, and offer it at dawn. On the following day, having fed the Brahmins and given them sacrificial fees,
one should gratify the God of gods according to one's ability.
Having offered it to Nārāyaṇa according to the Kūrma Purāṇa, one should afterwards eat oneself together with the circle of one's dependents.
When this is done, indeed, the threefold evil is destroyed; there is no doubt about this.
Having abandoned the wheel of saṃsāra, one becomes pure.
But he attains the ancient world of Hari.
The sins accumulated over many previous births are destroyed through devotion;
moreover, a person shall obtain the fruit described previously.
Nārāyaṇa immediately attains satisfaction.
Thus ends the Kūrma-dvādaśī-vrata within the Dharṇīvrata. Now follows the Vārāha-dvādaśī-vrata. Durvāsas said:
O most virtuous one, listen now to another meritorious account concerning Vārāha, who took his stand upon the earth on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Having performed the ritual resolve and the ceremonial bath according to the previously mentioned procedure,
and having worshipped the Lord on the eleventh lunar day, the wise man—
Having worshipped Acyuta with flowers, food offerings, and perfumes,
a person should thereafter place a jar filled with water before him.
The priest [should worship] the feet with "To Varāha," the waist with "To Mādhava," and the belly with "To Kṣetrajña," [and then] Viśvarūpa.
One should worship Vaikuṇṭha with the mantra "to the Omniscient One," the head with "to the Lord of Creatures," the two arms with "to Pradyumna," and the Sudarśana discus with "to the Divine Weapon."
And the conch for the source of nectar; this indeed is the procedure for the worship. Having worshipped thus, the wise one should place [the deities] within that jar.
A wise person should have an image of Varāha made of gold, silver, or copper, [holding] the earth—
with its mountains, forests, and trees— lifted up by the tip of his tusk.
[He saw] Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, who had assumed the form of a boar,
[seated] upon a vessel containing all seeds, which rested atop a jar filled with jewels.
One should install the supreme deity Hari, made of gold, covered with a pair of white garments; or, in the absence of that, [an image] made of bamboo.
Having established [the deity] and worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, various food offerings, and fruits,
and having fashioned a flower-mandala, one should perform a vigil there.
There, the wise man should recite and cause others to sing the accounts of Hari’s manifestations;
thus being praised, at dawn when the sun has risen.

Having bathed and become pure, one should worship Hari and present [the offering] to a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), who is of virtuous conduct, and who is wise.
One should especially cause it to be given to a Brahmin who is a devotee of Viṣṇu;
having thus given according to this procedure, one offers to Hari in his form as the Boar.
And one should give that to a Brāhmaṇa; hear now its fruit:
in this very life, there shall be good fortune, prosperity, splendor, and contentment.
One who possesses knowledge shall become wealthy; one who possesses wealth shall become an enjoyer of pleasures;
and even one who is childless shall become possessed of sons.
Thus concludes the Vārāha-dvādaśī-vrata within the Dharaṇī-vrata.
Now follows the Nṛsiṃha-dvādaśī vow.
Durvāsas said:
Likewise, in the month of Phālguna, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight—
Having observed the fast according to the prescribed rule, the wise man should invoke Hari.
One should worship the feet with "Salutation to Narasiṃha," the belly with "Salutation to Govinda," the waist with "Salutation to Viśvabhuj," and likewise the chest with "Salutation to Aniruddha."
The throat [is offered] to Śitikaṇṭha, the head indeed to Piṅgakeśa,
and likewise to Asuradhvaṃsana, who is the soul of the bearer of the discus.
Having thus honored the conch with scents, flowers, and fruits,
one should place a water-pot before it, covered with a pair of white cloths.
There, above that, one should place a golden Nṛsiṃha in a copper vessel;
having fashioned it from gold according to one's means, or even from wood or bamboo.
The form of Nṛsiṃha is described in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"With thick shoulders, hips, and neck, a slender waist and a lean belly,
seated upon a throne, possessing a human body, clad in blue garments, and endowed with radiance."
Standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, adorned with all ornaments,
his face surrounded by garlands of flames and his circle of hair like blazing rays.
Tearing open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu with his sharp claws, he,
possessing the luster of a blue lotus, should likewise be depicted as accompanied by the deities.
"This Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu is surely concealed here"— thinking thus,
he placed him in a jar filled with jewels and worshipped him according to the prescribed rites.
On the twelfth day, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas;
when this is done, the fruit that was obtained by the king in ancient times is attained.
O great sage, I shall now declare that to you by the name of Vatsa;
at the conclusion of his vow, the Blessed One Narasiṃha was pleased with him.
"He gave him a discus that causes the destruction of enemies in battle.
With that weapon, that best of kings conquered his own kingdom.
Remaining in his kingdom, the lord performed a thousand horse-sacrifices;
and at the end, O best of men, he attained the station known as the world of Brahmā.
O Sage, this auspicious Dvādaśī that removes sins has been described to you;
having heard it with diligence, do as you wish.
Thus ends the Dharaṇīvrata-Nṛsiṃhadvādaśī-vrata. Now begins the Vāmanadvādaśī-vrata. Durvāsas said:
In this very way, O Sage, having made a resolve on the twelfth day of the month of Caitra and having fasted with devotion, one should worship Janārdana, the God of gods.
One should worship the feet with "To Vāmana," the hips with "To Viṣṇu," the belly with "To Vāsudeva," and the chest with "To Saṅkarṣaṇa."

Having worshipped the throat with "Salutation to the Sustainer of the Universe," and the head with "Salutation to Him whose form is Space," one should worship the two arms with "Salutation to the Conqueror of the Universe," and the conch and discus with their own names.
Having worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, according to this rite,
one should place the frontal chamber (prāgvaṃśa) as the belly and the two pitchers in front.
Having placed a pair of garments— a couple of cloths—

along with a golden Vāmana figure made according to one's means, which is short in stature and wears a white sacred thread (yajñopavīta), into the vessel previously mentioned, the wise man [should proceed].
One should place the water-pot at one's side, as well as the small umbrella and the sandals;
and having set down the rosary, one should especially place the staff.
At dawn, one should cause this, equipped with these accessories, to be given to a Brāhmaṇa, while reciting:
"May Viṣṇu, in his short form, be pleased."
Combined with the name of the month and including the designation of the manifestation,
the injunction "may [he] be pleased" is proclaimed as the rule in all cases.

By means of the names of the months—such as Keśava and the others corresponding to the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa—the manifestations are designated as "the one in the form of a fish," "the one in the form of a tortoise," and so forth.
And it is heard in the Purāṇa: "In ancient times, King Haryaśva, the lord of the earth, being childless, performed austerities, desiring a son rich in ascetic merit."
O best of sages, while he was thus performing his desired rites for the sake of a son,
the divine Hari arrived, assuming the form of a brahmin.
He said to the king, "O King, what have you resolved?
and [the king] replied, "For the sake of a son," but he did not answer him further.
"O King, perform this very ritual with diligence.
Having spoken thus, that brahmin vanished in an instant.
Then the king, who was skilled in counsel, did that for the twice-born;
he likewise bestowed it upon the wise Jyotirgarbha, who was poor.
Just as we have attained the status of sons to Diti, who was previously childless,
O Blessed One, by that same power may a most excellent son also be mine.

This very procedure is the Vāmana-dvādaśī-vrata. One who knows the ritual and the mantras—that is, one who knows the mantras beginning with "As Diti was childless..."—[performs] that Vāmana rite. O Sage, by this prescribed method, he became his son, renowned as Ugrāśva, a mighty universal monarch (cakravartin).
One without a son obtains sons; one devoid of wealth obtains wealth;
one who has lost his kingdom regains his kingdom; and having died, he shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
Thus concludes the Vāmana-dvādaśī vow within the Dharaṇī-vrata.
Now follows the Jāmadagnya-vrata.
Durvāsas said:

In this very manner, during the month of Vaiśākha, a person, having performed the ritual bath with clay according to the prescribed rules of resolve (saṃkalpa), should then proceed to the temple of the deity.
There, the wise one, having propitiated Hari with devotion by means of these mantras,
[should worship] the feet for Jamadagnya and the belly for Sarvadhārin.
[1033] He should worship the waist with "To Madhusūdana," the chest with "To the wearer of the Śrīvatsa," the arms with "To the Destroyer of the Kṣatriyas," and the throat with "To Maṇikaṇṭha."
Having thus worshipped with his own name the conch and discus, and [the deity] who bears the cosmic egg upon his head,
the wise man should, as before, place a water-pot in front of him.
One should place it, especially covered with a pair of cloths,
and one should install Hari within that using a bamboo vessel.
Having fashioned a golden image in the form of Jāmadagnya,
one should place it before that deity, with an axe held in his right hand.
Having worshipped with all kinds of perfumes as well as various sorts of flowers,
a capable man should then perform a vigil before it.
"May Madhusūdana, who has assumed the form of fire, be pleased"—this is the mantra.
At the clear dawn, one should present the sun to a Brāhmaṇa.
Now learn from me the fruit that accrues to one who is thus engaged in this observance.
There was once a highly fortunate king named Vīrasena, possessed of great strength;
being childless in former times, that mighty one performed intense penance.
While he was performing that formidable austerity, the great sage Yājñavalkya,
a master of yoga, arrived there either by chance or by design to see him.
The king said:
"O twice-born one, how indeed may I have a son with little effort?
O Blessed One, please tell this to me out of affection, for I am bowed before you."
Thus addressed by that illustrious monarch, the Sage recounted this twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha.
For that king, desiring a son especially according to the prescribed rites,
having fasted, obtained a son named Nala, who was endowed with auspicious marks and supremely righteous.
"He who even today is celebrated in the world as the best of kings, Puṇyaśloka—
this indeed, O Great Sage, is the incidental fruit of this vow."
A good son is born endowed with wealth, learning, and likewise fame;
what wonder is there in this world? But hear from me concerning the next world.
Having dwelt for one eon in the world of Brahmā with hosts of apsarases, he sports there;
thereafter, upon renewed creation, he is born as a universal monarch.
He is born for thirty thousand kalpas; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Jāmadagnya-dvādaśī-vrata within the Dharaṇī-vrata.
Now follows the Rāghava-dvādaśī-vrata.
Durvāsas said:
Having made such a resolve according to the prescribed rite during the months of Jyeṣṭha,
men should worship the Supreme God with various kinds of auspicious flowers.
One should first worship the feet with "Oṃ, obeisance to Rāghava"; the hips with "To the one who is the triple-liberation"; and the waist with "To the one who wears the garment."
He should worship the chest with "To Saṃvatsara," the throat with "And to Saṃvartaka," the two arms with "To the bearer of all weapons," and the two lotus-like palms with their own names.
Having worshipped the thousand-headed one, the head of that Great Soul—
the lotus and the discus, the conch and the wheel—
having thus worshipped according to the rule, one should prepare a jar of clarified butter.
As before, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were covered with a pair of garments and made of gold.
The nature of these two is from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is distinguished by the primary marks of royalty;
'maulī' means wearing a crown (*mukuṭa*)."

"Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna the archer must likewise certainly be made [as images], but they should be devoid of crowns. Having thus honored those two according to the prescribed rite, at dawn he gave them to a Brāhmaṇa.
However, these two should indeed be given by a person who strives according to his heart's desire.
In former times, when King Daśaratha, who was childless and desirous of sons, questioned Vasiṣṭha, the latter spoke to him according to the ultimate truth.
The twice-born one explained this very procedure;
however, having perceived the king's secret intention, the king performed this.
O great sage, by virtue of his satisfaction, Viṣṇu himself was born as his son named Rāma, the slayer of Madhu, though he is but a fourth part of Viṣṇu.
For this very matter concerns the world beyond; therefore, listen to it.

Abiding in heaven, he enjoys divine pleasures for as long as fourteen Indras [pass]; then, when that time has elapsed, returning once more to the mortal world, he is born as a king who performs sacrifices. "Fourteen" is the meaning of "ten times two.
And the sins of that man are destroyed.
One obtains desires according to one's striving;
but one who is free from desire, having performed this very vow, attains the fruit of nirvāṇa which is firmly established.
The meaning is: even after performing this very vow as another means for attaining *nirvāṇa*.
Thus ends the Rāghava-dvādaśī-vrata within the Dharaṇī-vrata.
Now follows the Vāsudeva-dvādaśī vow.
Durvāsas said:
In the month of Āṣāḍha as well, one should likewise perform the rite after making the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the prescribed rule.
One should worship the supreme deity with perfumes and flowers according to the prescribed rite.
To Vāsudeva, however, [he offers] the feet; to Saṃkarṣaṇa, the hips;
to Pradyumna, the belly; and indeed to Aniruddha, the chest.
One should worship the two arms with "O Cakrapāṇi," the neck likewise with "O Bhūpati," the conch and discus with their own names, and the head with "O Puruṣa."
Having thus worshipped, the wise one should place a water-pot before it as before,
and then he should place a pair of garments upon that.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, the eternal four-armed Vāsudeva made of gold, in due order.
As before, one should give [the gift] to a Brāhmaṇa who speaks like a god and is firm in his vows;
hear from me the merit that belongs to one who is thus endowed with these observances.
Vasudeva shall be the king, the increaser of the Yadu lineage;
Devakī was his wife, who practiced vows equal to his own.
She was a virtuous daughter of Atri, devoted solely to the duty toward her husband;
after a long time had passed, Nārada came to her home.
Honored by Vasudeva out of devotion,
he who knew the dharma spoke these words to Devakī and Vasudeva.
Those two also performed this rite with devotion, endowed with faith;
Viṣṇu himself, being pleased with them, indeed became their son.
Thus, this Dvādaśī is remembered as the remover of sins and the bestower of sons;
by fasting on this day, one obtains sons, as well as knowledge and wealth in this world.
Indeed, by her who was brought down upon the earth through her disposition, Keśava restored the kingdom to one whose kingdom had been lost and brought about the destruction of the sins of sinners.
Having died, he rejoices in the beautiful city of Viṣṇu for as long as time lasts—
thirty-six Manvantaras— and thereafter, when that period has passed, he returns once more.
In this world, he shall become a king for seventy thousand years;
as a donor, a performer of sacrifices, and one endowed with forbearance, he shall thereafter attain nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the Vāsudeva-dvādaśī vow within the Dharaṇī-vrata.
Now begins the Vṛddha-dvādaśī vow.
Durvāsas said:
In this very manner, having made a formal resolve on the twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
one should worship the Supreme God with offerings of perfumes and flowers.
Having worshipped the feet with "Salutation to the Buddha," the waist with "Salutation to Śrīdhara," the abdomen with "Salutation to Padmodbhava," and the chest with "Salutation to Saṃvatsara."
One should worship the throat with "To Sugrīva," the two arms with "Viśvavāhana," worship the weapons as previously described, and the head indeed with "To the Supreme Self."
Having thus worshipped, the wise and discerning practitioner should place a golden jar before it as before, having fashioned a Buddha image therein.
The nature of the Buddha is described in another Purāṇa:
"The Buddha, however, should be depicted with two arms, his eyes fixed in meditation.
Having worshipped him in this manner, one should present him to a Brāhmaṇa.
By this rite, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) was previously observed as a fast.
Śuddhodana became the Buddha himself, O Janārdana;
endowed with sons and grandsons, he attained great prosperity. Having enjoyed the splendor of sovereignty, he then departed for the supreme state.
Thus ends the Dharṇīvrate Buddha-dvādaśī-vrata.
Now follows the Kalki-dvādaśī-vrata.
Durvāsas said:
In the same way, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
having made a formal resolve according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
Salutation be to Kalki as the feet; to Hṛṣīkeśa as the hips;
to the destroyer of the Mlecchas as the thighs; and likewise to the embodiment of the universe as the belly.
One should worship the throat with "To Śrīkaṇṭha" and the two arms with "Khaḍgamāṇi."
Having likewise worshipped the conch and the discus with his own name, as well as the head of the Universal Form,
the wise man, having thus performed worship, [should place] a water-pot before it as previously described.
Having installed the golden image of the god Kalkin there, one should cause it to be broken.
Regarding the form of Kalkin, according to another Purāṇa:
"Kalkin should be depicted with a sword in his hand and mounted upon a horse."
Having covered it with a pair of white garments and adorned it with perfumes and flowers,
one should present it at dawn to a brahmin who is most learned in the scriptures.
Formerly, there was a very powerful king named Viśāla in the city of Kāśī;
having observed the twelfth lunar day, he indeed became a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Having worshipped with various sacrifices, he attained supreme nirvāṇa;
he is worshipped in the form of a fish by those desiring omniscience.
He who assumes the form of a tortoise is worshipped for the sake of uplifting his own lineage;
he who assumes the form of a boar is worshipped by men who are submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.
A wise person should worship Vāmana for the sake of deluding others, Jamadagni’s son for the sake of wealth, and the son of Daśaratha for the destruction of cruel enemies.
A wise man desiring a son should worship Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa; there is no doubt about this.
One desiring beauty should worship the Buddha, and one desiring the destruction of enemies should worship Kalkin.
Thus ends the Kalki-dvādaśī vow within the Dharaṇī-vrata.
Now follows the Padmanābha-dvādaśī vow.
Durvāsas said:
In the same way, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja,
having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should worship the eternal Lord Padmanābha.
One should worship the belly for Sarvadeva, the chest for Puṣkarākṣa, and likewise the two arms for Avyagra; one should worship the limbs as previously described.
Having worshipped the head for the sake of prosperity as before, one should place a water-jar in front;
therein, one should install the golden image of the deity Padmanābha.
Padmanābha, however, should be depicted holding a conch, a lotus, and a mace in his own [right] hands, beginning from the lower right hand.
Having worshipped that God of gods with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order,
one should present him to a Brāhmaṇa when the night has turned to dawn.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a powerful king named Bhadrāśva;
after his name, the region came to be known by the name Bhadrāśva.
O King, Agastya once came to his house and said,
"I shall dwell in your home for five nights."
The king, bowing his head to him, said, "Please remain.
His wife, named Kāntimatī, was most beautiful.
Seeing her thus endowed with beauty and splendor, Agastya said:
"O Pārtha, O Lord of the World, all these wives of mine, out of fear, are doing what is auspicious; 'Excellent! Excellent! [they say], 'The woman is a Śūdra.'"
Having spoken thus, Agastya danced exultantly in the presence of the king.
The king said:
"O Brahmin, what is the cause of your joy, that you dance in this manner?"
Agastya said: "This queen was formerly your maidservant to a Vaiśya named Haridatta in the city of Vaidiśa, and you were indeed her husband."
He had a Śūdra servant named Vidhya;
that Vaiśya, being self-restrained and pure, [observed the vow] on the twelfth day of the month of Aśvayuja.
Having gone yourself to the abode of Viṣṇu and worshipped Hari with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, you may depart for your own home; may you two protectors grant us protection.
O Mahāmati, having set aside both lamps for the purpose of lighting them,
when he had gone to that house, they remained intent upon kindling those lamps.
O best of men, until the night dawned, they remained free from deceit;
then, after a long time, both husband and wife passed away.
By that merit, you were born in the house of Priyavrata,
and this wife of yours was born as the daughter of a Vaiśya servant in the past.
Furthermore, the merit of one who, having worshipped Viṣṇu with his own wealth, lights a lamp,
cannot be calculated.
Thus ends the Padmanābha-dvādaśī-vrata within the Śrī-Dharaṇī-vrata. Now follows the Yogeśvara-vrata; then the Dharaṇī-vrata. Agastya said:
Listen with devotion, O King, likewise to the Ekādaśī of Kārttika,
by fasting according to which procedure one may obtain the fruit of them all.
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the previously prescribed rule, one should likewise perform the bath and worship the stainless Lord Nārāyaṇa, worshipping Him in reverse order.
Having worshipped the head of Hari with "Obeisance to the thousand-headed one," he should worship the two arms with "To the Puruṣa," and the throat with "To the one of universal form."

Having worshipped the weapons with "O you whose self is knowledge," and likewise the chest with "To the Śrīvatsa-marked one," he should worship the belly with "To the one who dwells within the universe" and the universal form with "To the one whose form is the universe."
Having taken up the waist, one should worship the feet of the God;
having worshipped the Lord of Gods in the forward order (anuloma), the wise one [should proceed].
One should worship Hari in all his limbs with the mantra "Namo Dāmodarāya.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should place four water-pots before him.
One should place the Ratnagarbha [statues], anointed with white sandalwood paste,
their necks bound with garlands of flowers and draped with white cloths.
O best of the twice-born, these four oceans have been fashioned from copper vessels filled with sesame seeds and adorned with gold.
In the center of that, one should place an image of Hari made of gold according to the previously prescribed method— an image of the Lord of Yoga reclining in yogic sleep, clad in yellow garments.
Having honored him in this manner, one should cause a vigil to be held there;
one should perform the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice and chant the name of Hari, the Lord of Yoga.
When a sixteen-spoked wheel has been fashioned with many colored powders—
on this sixteen-spoked wheel, the "wheel of the chariot"—
having done so, one should then bring five Brahmins at dawn.
There are four pitchers for the four deities, and one for the fifth;
being restrained and pure, he should offer a golden one.
What is given equally to a Veda-studying priest is doubled when given to one who knows it.
To a teacher of the Pañcarātras, it shall be a thousandfold;
for he who provides this [text] together with its secrets and its mantras.
A rite performed for such a person with devotion indeed yields a result a crore times greater;
yet, if a wise man, while a worthy recipient is present, should instead worship another who is merely nearby, [he incurs great fault].
He falls into an evil rebirth, and what is given to him is fruitless;
yet, having given in this manner according to the rule and having truly worshipped Viṣṇu, [the result is otherwise].
One should provide food for the Brahmins and give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability;
indeed, having formerly performed this Dharaṇī-vrata, Prajāpati [attained his goal].
In ancient times, the royal sage Yuvanāśva obtained progeny as well as liberation through this very method, and he attained a pure and auspicious Brahminhood.
Māndhātṛ obtained the supreme, eternal Brahman;
likewise did Kṛtavīrya, the descendant of Haihaya and lord of men.
She obtained Kārtavīrya as her son and the supreme, eternal Brahman;
and Śakuntalā likewise, O great sage, having observed such a vow.
He obtained Śākuntala as his son, the universal monarch Duḥṣanta;
by this method, supreme sovereignty was attained.
In ancient times, this vow was performed by Padmā in Pātāla even before Dharaṇī;
therefore, it is called by the name Dharaṇīvratam.
While this goddess Earth was asleep, Hari, assuming a playful form, lifted her up out of satisfaction; even now she is supported by him like a boat upon the waters.
O Sage, this has indeed been proclaimed by me as the Dharaṇī-vrata;
that best of men who hears this with devotion and he who performs it [shall attain the highest state].
Freed from all sins, one shall attain the same world as Viṣṇu. Even a single one among these bestows a kingdom in times of adversity;
how much more so these twelve, since there is nothing supreme that they do not grant?
Thus ends the Yogeśvaradvādaśī. Thus ends the Dharaṇīvratam as declared in the Vārāha Purāṇa. Now begins the Bhīmadvādaśīvratam. Pulastya said:
Once, while sitting in his own city, the exceedingly radiant Kṛṣṇa listened as the ancient stories related to dharma were being recited.
In the course of their conversations, the powerful Bhīmasena questioned him regarding a righteous man who, despite his virtue, was unable to fast due to the intensity of his digestive fire.
May Vāsudeva, the soul of the universe and the teacher of the world, determine for me some vow that is superior to all other vows without exception.
Bestowing the fruit of all sacrifices without exception, destroying all sins without exception,
subduing all the wicked without exception, and worshipped by all the gods without exception.
The purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of auspicious things.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Bhārata, if [one performs this] on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the twelfth lunar days..."
"You are not even capable of fasting on other days or under other constellations."
Then, having fasted according to this rite upon this meritorious Bhaimī, which destroys all sins, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
When the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha arrives,
one should perform an anointing with ghee and carry out a bath with sesame seeds.
In the same manner, having worshipped Viṣṇu with "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa," one should worship the feet with "To Kṛṣṇa" and the head with "Salutation to the Soul of All."
One should worship the throat with "Salutation to Vaikuṇṭha," and the chest with "To the bearer of the Śrīvatsa";
likewise, one should worship [the arms] with "To the holder of the conch," "To the holder of the discus," "To the holder of the mace," and "To the Giver of Boons."
In this manner, all the arms of Nārāyaṇa are to be worshipped in sequence;
the belly with "To Dāmodara," and the penis with "To Pañcaśara."

Salutation to the Lord of Good Fortune for the thighs; salutation to the Sustainer of Beings for the knees; salutation indeed to Nīla for the shanks; salutation to the Creator of the Universe for the feet.
Salutation to the Goddess, salutation to Peace, salutation to Lakṣmī, salutation to Śrī;
salutation to Nourishment, salutation to Contentment, and likewise salutation to Tuṣṭi, O beloved.
Homage to the Lord of Birds, to Vāyuvega, to Pakṣman;
one should constantly worship Garuḍa, the dispeller of poison.
Having thus worshipped Govinda, as well as Umāpati and Vināyaka,
with perfumes, garlands, incense, and various kinds of edible offerings;
Then, having consumed *kṛśara* prepared with cow’s milk along with clarified butter while remaining silent, the wise man should walk one hundred paces.
Then, a fire-oblation (homa) should be performed by four Bahvṛcas facing north,
and the recitation of the Rudra-mantras by four who are devoted to the Yajurveda.
And one should cause four masters of the Sāmaveda, together with a group of auspicious attendants, to recite the Vaiṣṇava Sāmans all around.
The *Ariṣṭavarga*: the two Sāmans produced from this [verse] beginning with *tapo mūṣu vājitaṃ*—
in this manner, one should worship those twelve Brahmins with garments, garlands, ointments, rings, bracelets, and golden threads.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, he should pass five nights wearing garments suitable for pacification, accompanied by the sounds of songs and auspicious chants.
Furthermore, everything for the preceptor is indeed double that amount;
then, having risen at dawn when the sky is clear, [he offers] thirteen [oblations].
O best of the Kurus, one should also give cows that yield milk, are well-behaved, and are provided with golden mouths and bronze milking vessels.
With silver hooves, covered with cloths, and anointed with sandalwood;
having then given them those [horses] along with heaps of various kinds of food and edibles.
Having indeed provided all the Brahmins with various kinds of jewels,
and having himself eaten food that is free from sourness and salt, he should dismiss them.
Having followed for eight steps together with his son and wife,
let Keśava, the Lord of Gods and destroyer of afflictions, be pleased here.
Viṣṇu is the heart of Śiva, and Śiva is the heart of Viṇṇu;
since I perceive no distinction between them, may he who bears the wind-weapon grant me well-being.
Having thus addressed those jars, as well as the verses and the propitiatory rites,
the wise man should cause all the garments to reach their respective homes.
O Bhīma, in the absence of many beds, a householder should give even a single bed that is well-prepared and provided with all necessary furnishings.
O tiger among men, he who desires abundant prosperity should pass that day by having the Itihāsas and Purāṇas recited.
Therefore, relying on your courage and free from envy, Bhimasena,
properly observe this vow which I have spoken as a secret out of affection for you.
"O hero, this which has been performed by you shall bear your name;
for this auspicious Dvādaśī is indeed Bhaimī, the remover of all sins."
She who was known in former kalpas by the name Kalyāṇinī.
Having bathed previously, he likewise entered that mandala consisting of splendor, which is the body of the Veda;
and on this auspicious lunar day, Vivasvat [did the same].
The thousand-rayed one [shines] with a thousand streams.
Indeed, this was performed here by the Vasus headed by Mahendra, as well as by tens of millions of Asuras and gods; truly,
the fruit of this cannot be fully described.
If there were ten million tongues in each mouth, |||
"Therefore, O Indra, you shall proclaim this [teaching] which destroys the impurities of the Kali age,
so that even all your ancestors who have gone to hell may be reached."
It is sufficient for one who performs it right here to uplift [the self].
Thus ends the Bhīmadvādaśī-vrata in the glorious Padma Purāṇa. Now begins the Bhīmadvādaśī-vrata.
Kṛṣṇa said:
The illustrious lord of Vidarbha and other lands was formerly a venerable and most righteous man on earth;
he was the father of Damayantī and the father-in-law of Nala.
He was habituated to speaking the truth, devoted to protecting his subjects,
delighted in the duties of a warrior, illustrious, and unconquered in battles.
While he was ruling the kingdom according to the actions prescribed in the scriptures,
the highly fortunate Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, arrived there.
The glorious procedure for omniscience [is taught] in connection with the pilgrimage;
having seen that extensive [work], which is the stainless source of the Veda.
Having risen, the king offered him his own desired seat;
he himself presented to him some water for the feet and water for honoring with the arghya offering.
Having offered his kingdom along with himself, he stood with palms joined in reverence;
and being permitted by him, he sat down upon a seat.
He asked about his welfare and inquired concerning his asceticism and Vedic study;
having been answered with "So be it," the sage spoke to that king.
Pulastya said:
"O King, it has been told that all is well with your treasury, your provinces, and your city;
and since your mind is ever fixed on righteousness, O ruler of the earth, you shall continue to prosper."
Bhīma said:
"O Brahmin, all is well with those for whom you desire their welfare;
I have not been burdened by your arrival, O wanderer among the company."
Having always acted thus, even when conversing with one another,
they would speak to each other with stories concerning their former lives, ending with the various aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*).
Then, at the conclusion of the discourse, O Indra of kings, Pulastya was filled with wonder;
the Lord of the World questioned him for the benefit of all the world.
O Blessed One, all living beings dwelling in the midst of the ocean of saṃsāra are seen being tormented day and night by various sufferings.
In hell and in the womb, through diseases and likewise through epidemics,
as well as through sufferings such as separation from what is desired, which arise from poverty.
O bull among sages, there are many such sufferings as these, involving the loss of strength and the subsistence upon others through oppression.
These are indeed the decrees of fate; my mind is deeply distressed by the misfortunes that have befallen these living beings on this earth.
Speak that which brings benefit out of a desire to favor me;
with very little effort, a truly great fruit is produced.
Pulastya said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the best of all vows—
that vow by fasting upon which a person does not become a vessel for miseries.
The twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha is remembered as purifying;
by fasting on that day while one's garments are wet with water, one shall become a partaker of happiness.
Bhīma said:
O tiger among sages, how is that Dvādaśī to be observed as a fast?
By what procedure, O lord of brahmins? Tell me that in due order.
Pulastya said:
Listen attentively, O King, to this vow that destroys all sins;
because of your service, I shall undoubtedly recount it to you.
It must never be given to one who is uninitiated, nor to one who is not a disciple;
rather, it should be given only to one who is devoted to Viṣṇu, peaceful, and firmly established in dharma.
O Great King, this must be told by you to anyone else:
even a slayer of a Brahmin, a murderer of his teacher, or likewise a destroyer of Soma or a woman.
O King, even an ungrateful person, a betrayer of friends, a thief, a base man,
or one who has broken his vows is liberated from all sins by means of this vow.
On an auspicious lunar day and at a favorable moment, one should likewise have a pavilion constructed,
measuring ten cubits in size, on ground that slopes toward the northeast.
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar five cubits in size;
having carefully fashioned the altar from white earth mixed with clay.
There, a Brahmin endowed with Vedic knowledge, a devotee of Viṣṇu who has conquered his senses, should draw the maṇḍala according to the procedure of the five colors.
One who knows the twenty-five principles and is likewise devoted to his own proper conduct should prepare eight or four sacrificial pits there.
With that [mantra], one should employ auspicious Brahmins learned in the four Vedas;
and then, Janārdana should be placed in the pericarp in the center of the mandala.
O subduer of enemies, one should place the four-armed deity facing eastward;
the wise practitioner should worship him according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods with perfumes, flowers, incenses, and various kinds of food offerings, the preceptor, together with the Brahmins, [should proceed].
Thereafter, one should place two pillars made of neem wood;
one should arrange them there upon the pedestal facing the deity.
A square measuring thirty-six finger-breadths on all sides is the best;
there, one should take hold of a stone that is perfectly round, very firm, and new.
Listen to me regarding the kind of jar one should place there:
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
One should fashion it with all its characteristics complete, very firm, and free from defects;
it may be made one hundred thousand times, or even more.
Or, according to the custom of one's own family, one may make a single opening on the side;
then, having placed water and a cloth upon the ground nearby,
one should also prepare auspicious *palāśa* fuel-sticks for the purpose of the fire-oblation.
Indeed, sesame seeds, ghee, milk, and śamī leaves—
on the north-eastern portion of the altar, one should prepare the pedestal for the planets.
There, all the planets are to be worshipped according to the ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the planets;
one should diligently perform the worship of Śakra in the eastern direction.
Then one should present an offering of fruits and unbroken grains to Yama in the south, to Varuṇa in the west, and likewise to Kubera in the north.
Having thus gathered the necessary materials and wearing white garments,
he should remain alert, holding darbha grass in his hand and anointing himself with auspicious fragrances.
Those best of the twice-born should cause the patron to ascend the pedestal;
the patron, too, being restrained and pure, should face the deity.
Having sat down and recited the mantra, listen to this which was spoken in the Purāṇa:
"Salutations to you, O God of gods; salutations to you, O Lord of the world."
Protect me by means of this vow; O Supreme Self, salutations be unto you!
May those streams of water mixed with sesame seeds be offered at each junction of the day (saṃdhyā).
One should bear it silently upon the head with devotion and with inner intent;
thereafter, the Brahmins, being fully dedicated, should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in all directions.
They should recite the chapter on pacification and those hymns known as the Viṣṇu-stotras,
accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments and the sounds of conchs and songs.
One should cause a great festival to be celebrated with cries of "Auspicious Day! and "Victory!", mingled with the sounds of the Vedas and accompanied by auspicious hymns of praise.
An excellent Brāhmaṇa should cause the entire account of the high-souled Keśava, the God of gods— including the Harivaṃśa and other sections— to be recited.
Then, someone skilled in exposition, standing before them, should recite the narrative of Suvarṇika as well as the narrative of the Mahābhārata.
Having passed that night by this procedure which increases [the merit],
the wise sacrificer should proceed until the rising of the sun.
And the Brahmins, O lord of the earth, should spend that night performing rites for the sacrificial fire with divine Vaiṣṇava mantras.
O King, one should pour a stream of milk or clarified butter there upon the head of Vāsudeva; this bestows all perfections.
Then, at the time of dawn, O best of kings, the sacrificer, together with the twice-born,
should perform his bath in a river or in a lake.
Alternatively, however, a sacrificer who is lacking in means should,
after bathing with warm water and putting on white garments, remain firm in his vows.
Having offered the *arghya* to the Sun according to the prescribed ritual, one of serene mind should worship Puruṣottama with flowers, incense, and food offerings.
Having offered oblations with devotion into the fire and then having given the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should honor all the brahmins who have been appointed as officiating priests here.
O Bhārata, the teacher is to be honored here with beds, parched grain, gifts of cows, garments, and ornaments— even with one's entire possession.
Or rather, one should act in such a way that satisfaction is produced, since the Guru is equal to a deity;
for he may be devoid of the power of wealth, yet endowed with the power of devotion.
To the poor, the helpless, and those distinguished by merit, as well as to the bards who have assembled,
he should give food and gold with a pure heart.
Having thus honored the brahmin and fed him as desired,
one should afterwards eat while maintaining silence, according to the extent of one's means.
Food fit for oblation should be prepared with care, and likewise, sesame seeds that are not fit for oblation should be avoided;
this sacrifice, O Great King, which has been proclaimed to you, has thus been described.
By performing which one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter—even those who perform the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices for a hundred years [do not attain such liberation].
Know that all those do not equal even a sixteenth part of this sacrifice;
[it bestows] good fortune, long life, health, and prosperity for seven births.
By fasting according to the prescribed rules on this twelfth day, one attains it;
upon death, such a person goes to the city of Viṣṇu and rejoices together with Viṣṇu.
Likewise, O King, he who assumes the form of Viṣṇu remains for thirty-two yugas in the world of Rudra for exactly twelve yugas.
Likewise, after three [lifetimes] in the world of Brahmā and three in the world of the Sun during a cosmic age,
he returns here upon the exhaustion of his merit and becomes a righteous king.
The illustrious lord of the earth, victorious over his enemies and possessed of great majesty,
has observed this vow in the past, as did the high-souled Sagara.
By Aja, Dhundhumāra, Dilīpa, Yayāti,
and by others who protected the side of the earth here on this world.
O King, it was always frequented by women, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras desiring merit,
as well as by hosts of sages such as Bhṛgu and by Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas.
O lord of men, having been questioned by you, I have related that;
from this day forward, it shall attain renown upon the earth.
And this twelfth day is called Bhīmā; since men achieve all their goals through it, O joy of the Kurus, it was thus described by the sage Pulastya.
And whoever, permeated by devotion, should perform this [rite] as it has been described with diligence,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O Pārtha, even one who is poor should avoid stinginess regarding wealth;
a devotee of Viṣṇu who fears the terrors of saṃsāra must perform this rite.
He who practices correctly goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Somadvādaśī vow as spoken in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the supreme vow of Viṣṇu known as Vibhūtidvādaśī, which is adorned with all ornaments.
In the month of Kārttika, or Vaiśākha, or Mārgaśīrṣa, or Phālguna, or Āṣāḍha,
on the tenth day of the bright fortnight, a man should eat light food.
Having performed the evening twilight devotions (saṃdhyā),
the wise man should undertake the vow on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), remaining without food after having worshipped Janārdana.
"O Madhusūdana, may my meal, which I shall take together with the twice-born on the twelfth day, reach fulfillment without any obstacle."
Then, having risen at dawn and performed his ablutions and recitations, being pure,
he should worship the lotus-eyed Lord with white garlands and unguents.
Salutation to Vibhūti for the feet; salutation to Vikośa for the knees;
salutation to Śiva for the thighs; and salutation to Viśvarūpin for the hips.
Salutation to Kandarpa for the penis; salutation to Āditya for the hands;
"to Dāmodara" for the belly; and "to Vāsudeva" for the chest.
"Salutation to Mādhava for the chest; salutation to Viṣṇu for the throat; salutation to the longing one for the neck;
salutation to Śrīdhara for the face; and salutation to Keśava for the hair and the teeth."

"To the one who holds the Śārṅga bow, to the bestower of boons upon those who hear [his name]; with their own names, [the deities] hold the conch, discus, sword, mace, and the gesture of granting boons in their hands."
One should worship with the words, "O Brahman, salutation to you, the Soul of All," having fashioned a golden fish, fully blossomed, according to one's ability.
One should place before the Lord a water-pot,
along with a vessel of molasses mixed with sesame seeds and wrapped in a white cloth.
One should keep a vigil at night, listening to the recitation of Itihāsas and other stories;
then, when the night has turned to dawn, [one should give gifts] to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a family.
One should present the deity together with a golden lotus and a water-pot;
for indeed, O Viṣṇu, you are always invoked by all forms of prosperity according to your names.
In that same way, O Sage, deliver me from the mire of this entire cycle of existence filled with suffering,
by means of the forms of your ten incarnations appearing in their monthly sequence.
Likewise, the images of Dattātreya and Vyāsa, accompanied by Utpala,
should indeed be fashioned every month out of gold.
Having placed it upon a golden lotus, one should worship it with flowers,
incense, and other offerings, as well as with food offerings consisting of various kinds of eatables and drinks, together with lamps.
With garments and ornaments, according to the extent of one's wealth,
one should keep a vigil at night with men engaged in song, dance, and other such activities.
Then, at the clear dawn, having performed the rites of bathing and so forth,
all this that has been gathered together should be given to the instructor.
Every month, [the rite should be performed] by those learned in the Purāṇas who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
then, at the end of the year, a special ceremony should be performed according to one's capacity—
according to one's capacity, preceded by an abundance of wealth.
Having fashioned it and worshipped it, together with a mountain of salt.
The procedure for the gift of a mountain of salt is to be found in the section on gifts (Dānakhaṇḍa).
The lord of a country should give an excellent bed with its furnishings and a cow equipped with its accessories;
likewise, the lord of a village should give a field.
Having thus honored such a guru with the essence of his wealth— offering a field, a house, and abundant prosperity— [he should perform] the rite of return.
Having also gratified other excellent twice-born ones to the best of one's ability, and having adopted the highest disposition toward [giving] such things as clothing, food, cattle, and gold;
Wherever there is a being who is exceedingly steadfast and devoted to Mādhava, Hari undoubtedly attains satisfaction toward him.
He should perform this for two years according to the prescribed rite of flower worship.
From the Padma Purāṇa:
"In the final [part], cows should be given; in the middle, excellent land;
and a maiden with gold should be given—this is remembered as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)."
The first has Brahmā as its deity, the second likewise belongs to Viṣṇu, and the third has Rudra as its deity; thus the three gods are established within the three.
From the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Whoever performs the Vibhūti-dvādaśī vow according to this procedure shall be liberated from sin and shall deliver a hundred of his gurus."
That mortal shall attain supreme glory for seven births;
he shall never again become a vessel for disease, misfortune, or sin.
And may he have devotion toward the Lord of Sacrifice in birth after birth;
by the grace of Acyuta, may he attain the imperishable station of Acyuta.
This Vibhūti-dvādaśī must be observed without interruption by men;
it pacifies all sins and bestows such fruits as these.
Thus, whoever always recites or listens with devotion to this *Kaluvavidāraṇa* for the sake of people,
shall also attain an intellect in the world of the gods.
He dwells for a long time and is honored by the immortals, free from all evils.
Thus ends the vow of Vibhūti-dvādaśī as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Vajra said: How is Viṣṇu worshipped on the Dvādaśīs by one who has observed a fast?
O knower of dharma, tell me that in truth: what bestows sovereignty?
The student, the householder, and even the forest-dweller who is not a mendicant—
all these, when protected by the king, are able to practice their respective duties.
Though possessing a human body, the king bears a divine form;
even as a kṣatriya, he is worthy of worship by the great-souled brahmins who are among the virtuous.
For that prosperity which exists without a kingdom is considered dependent on others;
therefore, they praise sovereignty, for in it ignorance is destroyed.
O Brahmin, among kings who possess bodies of equal elements and maintain equal limbs, they move upon the earth like gods among men.
Therefore, you ought to tell me about the Rājyadā Dvādaśī,
by fasting on which that twice-born man indeed obtained a great kingdom.
Markaṇḍeya said:
Listen attentively, O King, to the auspicious Dvādaśī that bestows sovereignty;
by fasting upon which a man attains a kingdom free from thorns in this world.
O lord of men, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, being restrained and pure, one should perform a bath preceded by anointing the body with oil.
Eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya) and with a tranquil mind,
one should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the fast to be observed on the following day, preceded by the cleaning of the teeth.
In the courtyard of the gods, he should sit upon the earth strewn with *kuśa* grass and covered with a single upper garment;
there, self-restrained, he should pass that night.
On the second day, one should then perform a bath with water without weariness;
and the worship of everything should be performed by means of all that has been released.
Camphor, sandalwood, jasmine, white yūthikā,
white jāti flowers, and indeed kunduru incense should be offered, O King of kings.
Lamps provided with white wicks should be offered with ghee;
likewise, rice cooked with ghee, curd, milk, and *paramānna* (milk-rice) should be given.
One should offer sugarcane or its products to the God of gods;
one need not concern oneself with roots, fruits, or leaves that grow out of season.
That gift should be given according to what is available, or preferably something pure;
and thereafter, O King, the oblation should be performed with *paramānna* (milk-rice).
The sacrificial mantra is declared to be "tad viṣṇoḥ param," and this twelve-syllable mantra is prescribed for women and Śūdras.
Then, having performed the fire-oblation and honored the twice-born according to one's ability,
the beautification of the ground in the divine abode should be carried out with white lime.
O King, one should keep a vigil at night, performing song and dance for the God of gods,
as well as listening to his sacred deeds.
On the twelfth day, the Eternal One should again be worshipped according to this rite;
a royal insignia should be given as a single sacrificial fee to a Brahmin.
"Thereafter, O best of kings, one should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya);
just as the Ekādaśī, O monarch, stands between the two baths."

The phrase "it should be eaten" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. By the force of the dual number, the bathing after a single meal is drawn in. This is the meaning: when the eleventh day has not yet arrived, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin; once it has passed, one should break the fast (*pāraṇa*). The mention of "bathing" is for the purpose of excluding it from afar.
Entire silence and mental recitation (*japya*) must be performed on all the twelfth days, especially those that are bright (*śukla*).
This procedure has been prescribed for you; one should perform it thus with black cows.
I shall now declare the specific details regarding them; listen as I speak.
The worship of the deity should be performed according to the prescribed ritual with a red cloth;
and red offerings of food, flowers, perfumes, and ointments should be presented.
Lamps colored with great silver should be lit with sesame oil;
wicks should be placed in those lamps, and likewise, a fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with sesame seeds.
And the ground should be beautified with red pigments, O protector of the earth;
having worshipped the Lord in this manner for a year, O King.
When the full moon day of Kārttika has passed, on the twelfth lunar day of the dark fortnight,
at the conclusion of the vow, one should cause a great wick-lamp to be offered.
A cow accompanied by a complete set of garments and a vessel of ghee for milking made of bell-metal should be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
Cows with horns tipped in gold and hooves in silver, adorned with ornaments on their faces and tails,
provided with upper garments and accompanied by wealth according to one's means, should be given as gifts.
By staying for one year in a mountain cave, O King,
a man becomes a lord of a province through the merit of three years.
Likewise, by twelve meritorious acts, one becomes an earthly king;
O Vasiṣṭhas, this Dvādaśī, which removes sins, has been described by me as the bestower of sovereignty.
Having cast it upon the surface of the earth, the lord of men becomes invincible in battle by the hosts of his enemies.
Thus ends the Rājyadvādaśī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Ambarīṣa said:
O best of sages, how is the Lord worshipped on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) with the names of the Sun?
O Keśava, he is worshipped in the mortal world by those who seek the fruit of liberation.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen with a focused mind, O King, to the auspicious Sunāmadvādaśī,
which removes all sins, leads to heaven, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And those best of men who even mentally desire to observe the twelfth day do not again behold the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
O best of kings, among all the vows of the Vaiṣṇavas, the first is that which must be performed by men;
it is the supreme means for bringing satisfaction to Viṣṇu.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the bright fortnight, a man who has restrained his vows should first undertake the Dvādaśī fast according to the prescribed rite.
Completely purified in the activities of mind, speech, and body, with his senses conquered,
he should bathe and bow down to Janārdana on the tenth day with firm resolve.
Having taken food consisting of sacrificial offerings (haviṣya) and having become pure, one should be a practitioner of the vow;
in a clean, secluded place, one should brush the teeth.
"O Lord, having properly observed the fast on Ekādaśī and having worshipped Janārdana,
I shall eat on the following day, the auspicious Sunāma-dvādaśī."
Having thus formed this resolve and undertaken the vow, and having prostrated before the one whose banner is Garuḍa,
he should eat but a single meal on the tenth day and spend the night in self-restraint.
Then, on the morning of the eleventh day, with a one-pointed and concentrated mind,
he should first worship the Sun and thereafter worship the God.
To the god Viṣṇu:
Homage to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; homage to you, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
Homage to you, Bhāskara; homage to you, Ravi, the shining one within the sun.
Homage to the divine Sūrya; homage to you, the seven-times-seven!
Homage indeed to you alone, who possess a single face and a single-wheeled chariot.
To the eternal lord of the luminaries, the taker of all splendor—to you, O Divākara, let there be salutation; to you, O Prabhākara, let there be salutation.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules with flowers, incense, and unguents, as well as lamps, garments, and food offerings, one should then proceed to the temple of Viṣṇu.
One should worship Acyuta with devotion, offering profuse *mālatī* flowers;
one should offer incense of *guggulu* mixed with clarified butter and a lamp day and night.
One should offer to Hari an oblation consisting of a collection of milk-rice, cakes, parched grain, honey-mixtures, and so forth, along with fruits, sweetmeats, and molasses.
One should bow down again and again with songs and musical instruments dear to Hari;
having thus performed the worship of Hari, [one should honor] the twice-born who bestows knowledge.
One should worship [the deity], for there is no difference between a Brahmin and Keśava;
then, having prepared the vow, one should take a new jar with sandalwood paste.
One should place a vessel filled with water and adorned with garlands in the presence of the deity;
it should contain a diamond known as "deep blue pearl" (sunīlamauktika), along with gems and gold.
One should worship Keśava there, with his embryo placed [within] and clothed in garments.
The image of Keśava, however, starting from the lower right hand and proceeding clockwise, should be made of gold and bear the lotus, conch, discus, and mace;
it is by whose radiance all clouds and venomous serpents are held in check.
The oceans reside within his belly; he is the Lord of the World who inspires both fear and awe;
he is the divine essence of the lord of forests, the most excellent among all fragrances.
May this incense, mixed with ghee, be accepted;
[it is offered to] Keśava, the slayer of Keśin and the destroyer of the wicked demon Kaṃsa.
"May that God, the bestower of all desires, dispel my sin.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness.
Having bathed Mādhava here on the twelfth lunar day with fragrant water,
one is liberated from all sins and attains a body belonging to Viṣṇu.
Having performed his ablutions, the meritorious man, having duly worshipped Keśava,
should likewise present a cow that has recently calved to a Brāhmaṇa.
May the god Keśava, the slayer of Keśin and possessor of great splendor, be pleased;
and may that Blessed One, being gratified, grant me my desired wishes.
Having thus performed the circumambulation, hear also what the fruit of that is:
having destroyed the threefold sin committed over thirty years, that man [is purified].
For sixty thousand years he rejoices in heaven like a god;
when, by the lapse of time, he returns here, he shall be a possessor of the wealth of Dharma.
Alternatively, a person may provide ten cows as the measure for that [gift];
indeed, that fruit is specifically prescribed, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's ability.
One attains the fruit through devotion; indeed, devotion alone is the cause here for the man who acts in this way during the month of Pauṣa.
O King, with a concentrated mind, the bestower of the essence indeed declared:
"The waters are called *nara*; the waters are truly the sons of *nara*."
Therefore, he causes the path (ayana) to proceed; thus he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
May the god Nārāyaṇa, who is always dear to men, be pleased with me.
May that [deity], who eternally grants desired objects, remove my sin;
then, having performed a circumambulation, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for that sacrificer:
whatever sin he has committed over sixty years, whether it be small or great.
By giving [this] on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one attains an auspicious heaven for ten thousand years.
For he who, having become pure, with a single-pointed and concentrated mind,
constantly performs the rite of *tapana*, the worship [of the deity], and the satiation of Brahmins, shall indeed [attain success].
O tiger among kings, at the time of giving [the gift], one should recite this mantra:
"Mahālakṣmī, who formerly went to the Enemy of Pura (Śiva), is the sister of the Moon and his younger sibling."
O Mādhava, granter of all desires, may you also be her husband;
may the God of gods, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, be pleased with me.
May the slayer of Kaṃsa and Keśin dispel my sin;
now hear the fruit of merit for one who indeed performs this act in such a manner.
Having destroyed all evil committed throughout one's entire life without exception,
one dwells in heaven for sixteen thousand divine years.
One who gives a cow made of molasses in the month of Māgha, having come here, shall always be happy,
free from disease, and endowed with all prosperity, O King.
There, becoming devoted to Viṣṇu, one shall gradually attain liberation;
on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, being self-controlled and pure.
Having worshipped Hari according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should then, with great devotion, give a sesame-cow and also a bull.
"O Indra among kings, by this mantra may Govinda be pleased:
'You are a devotee of cows, the Lord of cows, clothed in cow-hides, and one who has made his abode for the sake of cows.'"
May he, who eternally grants all desires, dispel my sin;
thereafter, having performed a circumambulation, hear the merit as it truly is.
O King, one who draws the yoke for ten thousand oxen does not obtain that fruit which is attained on the twelfth day.
He dwells in heaven like a celestial being for thousands of divine years.
O best of kings, the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra should be observed as a fast.
Having bathed according to the previously mentioned procedure, using either cow’s urine or cow dung, one should worship Viṣṇu, who moves within the worlds.
Having bathed [the deity] with nectar and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should thereafter worship it with perfumes, incense, and ointments.
Thus, with auspicious garments and by means of this mantra, the wise one,
ever-virtuous and blessed, performs the rite of entry for the sake of protection.
In this month, Viṣṇu is the conqueror of those of evil conduct;
therefore, may Viṣṇu be pleased with me—Viṣṇu, the eternal God.
"For the destruction of all sins, may Viṣṇu be pleased with me.
[One should offer] a honey-cow, or in its absence, a vessel according to one's ability.
Listen now with a focused mind to the fruit one obtains by giving it:
whatever sin has been committed in all previous births, as well as that which has been committed in this present birth.
Having destroyed everything, he abides and is glorified in the heavenly world;
one should worship Madhusūdana during the month of Vaiśākha.
O King, having installed a golden image of Madhusūdana according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should worship it with a water-pitcher while reciting this mantra.
O Hari, in the past, when the waters were a single ocean, the Vedas were destroyed by Dhātṛ;
he too was slain by him [Viṣṇu] who is therefore called Madhusūdana.
May that eternal God of gods be well-pleased with me;
may Madhusūdana be gratified for the removal of all my sins.
Then, having given clarified butter and food, one should feed the Brahmins;
thereafter, having performed a circumambulation, one should likewise give the cow as a gift.
Now hear the merit of one who guards it in this manner:
he who is endowed with devotion attains that same fruit which results from the perfect gift of a thousand Kapila cows; of this there is no doubt.
He remains there for as long as Indra dwells in heaven;
specifically, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Having fasted, one should worship Trivikrama with devotion according to the prescribed rite; then, being self-controlled and pure, one should give a water-cow to a Brahmin.
Having struck down the Daityas who consumed their share of the sacrifice by means of three strides, you have thus traversed the three worlds;
therefore, you are Trivikrama.
I propitiate Trivikrama, the Lord of the three worlds;
then, having performed a circumambulation, I shall give sacrificial fees to the Brahmins.
Having given [these], one should feed them; hear now, O King, what the fruit of that is, as if a Vājapeya sacrifice had been properly performed.
A mortal obtains that fruit and shall become happy in the hereafter,
having diligently observed the fast of Vāmana in the month of Āṣāḍha.
On the twelfth day, one who observes dietary restrictions should worship Vāmana there,
just as Āditya is the granter of desires for the welfare of all the gods.
"O Lord, may you likewise become for me the Dwarf who bound Bali;
then one should give a sesame-cow, saying, 'May Vāmana be pleased.'"
Having bathed the Lord of Gods with these [waters] from the abode of Indra, from the lake, and from the mountain peaks, one should offer auspicious gorocana.
Then, however, water-pots should be offered according to the rules, well-adorned, joined with *jātī* sprouts, provided with fruit, and containing gold.
With the sound of the "Auspicious Day" Vedic recitation, with the resonance of lutes and flutes,
and with the sweet voices of the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards.
Having thus established Govinda, who has been well-anointed and well-adorned,
one should worship him with fine garments, flowers, and saffron.
