With fragrant incense, beautiful lamps, and abundant milk-rice pudding,
as well as with gifts of jewels to one's mother, meritorious fire-offerings accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Brahmins should be honored with garments, pleasing ornaments, cows, horses, and even elephants; for they are the primordial, excellent embodiments of Viṣṇu.
While Viṣṇu was asleep at night, having entered Dāmodara, you were born from the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa); thus you are remembered as Dāmodara.
"O Viṣṇu, let Dāmodara himself accept this cow in the form of a brahmin; for she is your eternal Prakṛti."
In this way, O best of kings, a person obtains the fruit from the gift of earth;
indeed, having given a great cow made of gold, one attains the highest boon.
Having indeed destroyed all evils throughout hundreds of previous births,
one attains the world of Viṣṇu for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
O Lord of Men, when this vow is duly observed here, the Blessed Viṣṇu bestows a fruit that follows one for seven births, and ultimately grants liberation in due course.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion, even with various kinds of food, both superior and inferior;
then, having performed a circumambulation, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability.
One should cause twelve water-pots to be given to the Brahmins—
[pots] whose necks are encircled with vajras and which are adorned with the interior of the fire-oblation (homa).
O King, one should offer many such items combined with curd and milk, along with their constituent qualities;
one should give according to one's capacity, for devotion alone is the essential factor here.
O King, that man who observes the Sunāmadvādaśī even as a casual act becomes a partaker of merit, just as Bali became by making his offering.
O King, the man who thus observes the Sunāmadvādaśī shall obtain a fruit even greater than that of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Whatever merit is found in all acts of giving, whatever merit is found in the forest of asceticism,
and whatever merit is found in all sacred fords— that merit is said to be [attained here].
Twelve cows, pairs of garments, and gold should be given;
or, in the event of not obtaining these, at least one cow and a vessel joined with gold.
Or, in brief, since life is thus fickle,
one who practices the Dharma should avoid many obstacles so that no lapse occurs.
Having understood this, the wise person should strive diligently in the pair of vows;
let there be no greed for wealth in him, for Keśava is to be won over by devotion alone.
The man who, by this rite, observes the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) for a full year,
goes to the supreme, painless world of Viṣṇu.
This is the Sunāmadvādaśī, the most excellent of all vows;
it should be performed first by men who seek to gratify Janārdana.
And the man who recites this meritorious Dvādaśī, or hears it—both of them go to heaven; the performer shall go to Viṣṇupura.
Thus ends the Sunāmadvādaśī vow as declared in the Vahnipurāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, [one should observe the vow].
Whether it be a man or a woman, having duly worshipped the Lord of the World...
O lord of men, chanting the name of Hari with devotion seven times while rising and while sleeping,
one should quickly glorify Hari alone.
Therefore, on the twelfth day at the clear dawn, being self-restrained, one should bathe, duly worship Hari, and give a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin.
One should perform an oblation of clarified butter into the fire dedicated to Hari,
and having prostrated before the Lord of the World, one should utter these words:
May Vasudeva, who established the earth within the netherworld and granted my heart's desires even now, grant me my heart's desires.
Having worshipped him, Diti attained all her heart's desires;
and having worshipped him, the Lord of the World, the Lord of the Gods was deprived of his kingdom.
"Having swiftly attained his desires, may he grant [others] their desires.
Having thus honored him and completed the worship, one then takes [the deity] away.
Having fed his guests and dependents with sacrificial food (haviṣya),
a man, restraining his speech and free from envy, should eat himself while meditating upon Hari.
O King, Phālguna, Caitra, Vaiśākha, and the month of Jyeṣṭha—
by these four months, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) shall be accomplished.
One should perform worship with red flowers for four months;
one should burn guggulu incense and, furthermore, apply the cleansing of a cow's horn.
Let the food offering consist of sacrificial grain (haviṣya), and let that also be my own meal;
now listen to another rite to be performed beginning with the month of Āṣāḍha.
Jāti flowers and incense made from sarjarasa resin are recommended;
having consumed darbha-water here, one should also offer śāli rice.
One should eat that oneself and perform the remaining rites as before;
during the months beginning with Kārttika, cow’s urine serves for the purification of the body.
One should offer fragrant incense according to one's desire, as well as worship with a *bhṛṅgāraka*—
where *bhṛṅgāraka* means a mango tree—
and here one should personally consume the *kāsāra* as the food offering (*naivedya*).
And likewise, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to a Brahmin every month.

At each completion of the fast, when the time for breaking the fast has arrived, one should perform the propitiation of the God of gods according to one's ability, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
Govinda attains unsurpassed satisfaction through sincerity alone;
for this reason, Janārdana should be propitiated at the conclusion of the fast.
Having caused a very beautiful image of Viṣṇu to be made at the end of the rainy season, he grants all desired objects on earth without obstruction.
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa a mace adorned with a conch and a sword, covered with a pair of white garments, and embellished with gold according to one's ability.
Having fed twelve Brahmins there, one should ask for their forgiveness;
twelve jars containing rice, water, and unbroken grains (akṣata) should be offered here.
O best of men, together with umbrellas, pairs of sandals, and sacrificial fees,
cows yielding milk should also be given here to the preceptor.
Equipped with all necessary utensils, accompanied by calves, and endowed with good character—
this meritorious Dvādaśī removes the sins of those who desire its fruit.
O best of kings, she grants all desired objects of longing,
for she fulfills all the heart's wishes through devotion.
Therefore, this twelfth day is renowned in the world as Manorathā;
by fasting on it, Indra indeed attained the three worlds in ancient times.
The Ādityas obtained their desired sons, Auśanasa obtained wealth,
Dhaumya obtained the fruits of study, and others likewise attained their cherished results.
One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth shall obtain wealth;
one overcome by disease attains health; and a maiden finds a virtuous husband.
By fasting on this day, one obtains reunion with those who have gone abroad;
having died, one attains all desires and rejoices in heaven.
By observing this vow, even a mortal who is dominated by women is born neither sonless nor destitute, neither separated from his kin nor devoid of virtues.
O lord of men, having enjoyed for thousands of years in the heavenly world all desired pleasures that are longed for in heaven, he remains there.
In this world, a king free from all diseases is born in the homes of meritorious men who are wealthy and of virtuous character.
They do not observe the fast on the twelfth day known as Manoratha,
nor do they worship Puruṣottama, the primordial god;
they neither bow to nor honor cows and brahmins.
How do those who desire them obtain what their minds long for?
Thus ends the vow of Manorathadvādaśī as declared in the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Bhīṣma said:
[How can one overcome] the multitude of sorrows arising from separation from what is desired?
Enough with fasting or vows;
they merely produce worldly prosperity on this earth,
yet they do not even destroy the fear of existence for men.
Pulastya said:
This is most desirable; it is dear even to the gods, for it is great and difficult to attain.
And so, for you who possess devotion, I shall likewise declare this vow, which is secret even among the gods and dānavas such as Indra.
In the auspicious month of Āśvayuja, there is the Viśoka-dvādaśī vow;
by performing which, a man shall not become a vessel for sorrow or misfortune.
On the tenth day, having eaten light food and performed the cleansing of the teeth at night,
facing either north or east, he should utter this speech:
Having fasted on the eleventh day and having worshipped Keśava as well as Śrī, the prosperity of the worlds, one should resolve: "I shall eat on the following day."
Having thus declared this rule, he who has conquered his senses slept during the night;
then, at the clear dawn, he went to a body of water at midday.
One should perform a bath with all medicinal herbs and with water consisting of the five products of the cow;
then, wearing white garlands and garments, one should proceed to the house.
One should worship the Lord of the worlds, the beloved of Lakṣmī, with blue lotuses:
likewise, one should worship the knees with [the mantra] "To Keśava," the thighs with "To Jalaśāyin," the private parts with "Salutation to Kandarpa," and the hips with "Salutation to Mādhava."
One should worship the belly and the sides with "Salutation to Dāmodara," the navel with "Salutation to Vipula," and the heart with "Salutation to Padmanābha" and "Salutation to Manmatha."
Salutations to Śrīdhara for the chest of the Lord, to Madhughātina for the two hands, to Cakrin for the left arm, and to Gadina for the right.
He offered his nose to Vāsudeva for the destruction of grief,
his two eyes to Vāmana, and his forehead and eyebrows again to Hari.
Saying "for the sake of subduing Alakā," [he worships] the crown for the one of universal form;
saying "salutation to you, the soul of all," he should worship all the limbs.
Having thus worshipped Govinda with perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) out of clay in front of that pavilion.
It is square on all sides, three cubits in height,
fine and pleasing, and in front it is enclosed by two ramparts.
The type of embankment:
the embankment should be three finger-breadths high, and its width two finger-breadths;
above the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), however, the wall should be eight finger-breadths [in height].
One should place an image of Lakṣmī made of river sand in a winnowing basket;
having placed the basket upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the wise person should worship her as Lakṣmī.
Homage to the Goddess, homage to Peace; homage to her, homage to Fortune. Homage to Contentment, homage to Nourishment, to Creation, and to Rain—homage, homage!
May Viśokā, who destroys suffering, be a granter of boons to you;
may Viśokā be for my progeny, and may Viśokā be for the attainment of all perfections.
Wearing white garments, one should worship the Sun while encircling him with fruits,
various kinds of edible offerings, and likewise with a golden lotus.
O Bhīṣma, according to one's means and avoiding stinginess regarding wealth,
they always praise darbha grass and water at night during this vow.
The partaking [of the food] and the vigil, likewise with singing, dancing, and so forth,
should be performed when three watches of the night have passed, provided with all necessary implements.
And having approached, he should honor the couples of the Brahmins—
three or even one— with garments, garlands, and ointments according to his ability.
The places where [the Lord] lies down are to be worshipped; "Homage be to Him who reclines upon the waters!
Then, at the end of the night, one should desist from singing, instrumental music, and the like.
At dawn, having fulfilled his duties, he should feed the couples according to his ability, O best of the Kurus; thereafter, he himself should eat while remaining silent.
On the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), one should avoid these seven things: sleeping during the day, food from others, eating a second meal, sexual intercourse, honey, oil, and meat.

Therefore, after the breaking of the fast, one should pass that day by means of listening to the Purāṇas and other such activities, as well as by the sounds of success (siddhināda) and other [auspicious sounds].
By this rite, one should perform everything month after month;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a cow made of molasses.
O King of kings, one should present this auspicious [image], complete with a pillow for rest and provided with garments and ornaments, to the best of Brahmins while reciting this mantra.
O Lord of Gods, just as Lakṣmī never remains having abandoned you,
so may health, beauty, and freedom from sorrow be mine forever.
Just as Lakṣmī is never born without the Lord,
so may I be free from sorrow and possess supreme devotion to Keśava.
According to this procedure, one who desires his own prosperity should give that entire winnowing basket in its entirety to a knower of the Vedas.
The blue lotus, the oleander, and likewise the amaranth flower;
the water-pot plant, the sindhuvāra, the jasmine, and the fragrant pāṭala.
One should worship these auspicious flowers: the kadamba, the kumuda, and the jasmine.
This is the Viśokadvādaśī, which destroys all sins.
Having fasted with devotion upon this [vow], a person shall partake in auspiciousness and good fortune;
having enjoyed all desires without exception, he shall attain remembrance [of the deity] at the end.
"By remembering Acyuta at the time of death, one ultimately attains a state equal to Him.
He who recites this thus, he who hears it correctly here,
and he who beholds the worship of the Enemy of Madhu, Mura, and Naraka— [attains the same].
Even he who sets his mind upon the deities dwells in the world of Indra, always being honored by the gods and others.
Thus ends the vow of the twelfth day (Dvādaśī-vrata) as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Dālbhya said:
It is perpetually most terrifying, consisting of the syllables that bring fear of weapons and fire;
how is it that one does not go to the hells? You ought to tell me this.
"Alas! How extremely painful is the state of hell, the ripening of sins, which is experienced by men, O Brahmin! Therefore, O best of beings, tell me of liberation from it."
Pulastya said:
O best of the twice-born, the ripening of meritorious action is indeed merit itself;
it is experienced by men dwelling in heaven for the sake of transforming their minds.
In the very same way, the ripening of sins is experienced in its entirety by those men dwelling in hell for as long as their sin has not reached exhaustion.
Just as this twelfth day is praised for men of virtuous deeds,
by fasting upon which, O best of the twice-born, a man does not go to hell.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna,
O best of the twice-born, one should worship Madhusūdana on the twelfth day.
Rising on the eleventh day, one should, with a well-composed mind, perform the recitation of Viṣṇu’s names and the worship of Vāsudeva.
One should recite the phrase "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" day and night,
and one should avoid anger, evil, envy, as well as hypocrisy and greed.
Desire, anger, intoxication, pride, and even power—
all this must be renounced by one whose mind is devoted to Viṣṇu.
And meditating upon the worthlessness of this worldly existence in saṃsāra,
a twice-born man should likewise perform the recitation of the names on the twelfth lunar day.
From the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"O Pāṇḍava, there should be vessels made of gold, copper, or even clay."
Having placed them in vessels of barley, one who has fasted for each respective month [should offer them].
One should recite the three names in their entirety for two days every month,
and likewise chant them on the twelfth lunar day as prescribed.
Having bowed to Hṛṣīkeśa and performed worship, one should propitiate him:
"O Viṣṇu, salutations to you, the progenitor of the world; salutations be to you, Śrī Vāsudeva."
May Nārāyaṇa be my dharma; destroy my evil entirely!
May there be the destruction of all my evils through great meritorious deeds.
May the merit generated throughout many births— during childhood, youth, and old age— increase, and may all evil be brought to destruction.

May there be the increase of peace for that [being], and the fivefold destruction of evils regarding space and the other elements, sound and the other objects, the ear and the other senses, and the mahat-tattva and the others.
And by means of both primordial nature and the person, one attains the realization of Brahman;
for Vāsudeva alone, the Self of all, is established as the one reality.
By that truth, may my sin, which brings the suffering of hell, be destroyed;
and may there be for me an accumulation of days of virtuous deeds.
"Having thus recited, 'May there be the destruction of evil and the attainment of unsurpassed merit,' and having given [the gift] to a Brahmin, it has been explained to you."
O twice-born one, having fulfilled his duties, he should eat when the time for breaking the fast has arrived;
and at the conclusion of the fast, he should gratify the deity according to his ability.
One should perform [the rites] and avoid conversation with all heretics;
thus, at the end of the year, [one should offer] a golden image of Hari.
Having performed worship with garments, flowers, and a vessel of clarified butter,
one should, with a concentrated mind, give a black cow along with its calf to a Brahmin.
And even if the recipient should happen to appear by chance after a delay,
food must be given on that very day without restriction.
Thus, O Dālbhya, has been described this [twelfth day] which brings victory through meritorious deeds;
by fasting upon it, a mortal does not behold hell.
Neither fires, nor weapons, nor birds with iron beaks,
nor the hells afflict him whose mind is fixed on Janārdana.
By the mere utterance of Viṣṇu’s name, the accumulation of sins is destroyed;
for one whose evils have been cast away, how could there be a journey to hell?
One should here proclaim, "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva!";
that mortal, with all his sins completely exhausted, does not go to hell.
Therefore, by not associating with heretics and by fasting on this twelfth day which accumulates merit, a man does not go to hell.
Thus ends the Sukṛtadvādaśī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Pulastya said:
"The man who, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Phālguna..."
"Kṛṣṇa," with devotion, repeat again and again the name of the Lord.
Having performed one hundred and eight offerings to the gods, one who is pure should recite this;
likewise at the time of bathing or setting out on a journey, upon rising, when stumbling, or in times of decay.
One should not speak with heretics, those who have fallen from their caste, or likewise with those of the lowest castes;
rather, one should worship the deity endowed with faith.
And one should recite this mantra, fixing the mind upon it with single-minded devotion:
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, you who are compassionate, be the refuge for those who have no refuge."
"Be gracious, O Madhusūdana, to those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having thus propitiated [the deity] and observed a fast with a restrained mind, [he should proceed].
On another day, having consumed cow products only once during the forenoon,
and having bathed and performed worship, he should again proclaim the name "Kṛṣṇa."
One should likewise sprinkle three streams of water upon the feet of the deity during the months of Caitra and Vaiśākha, and in the same manner, one should worship during the month of Jyeṣṭha.
O Dālbhya, a man indeed attains the highest state in the world of mortals,
and likewise obtains the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa at the time of death.
In the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada,
and likewise in Āśvayuja, a person [should worship] the God according to this rite.
Having fasted and performed worship, one should likewise utter the name "Keśava";
purified by consuming cow's urine, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
At the time of death, one shall likewise attain the remembrance of Keśava, the Great-Souled Lord of the worlds, who has been propitiated.
The consumption of milk is most excellent when performed according to this prescribed method as it has been declared;
one should practice it for four months, beginning with Kārttika, in accordance with the rules.
O Brahmin, by that very same rite, one should glorify Viṣṇu there;
he goes to the realm of Viṣṇu and remembers Viṣṇu when that [life] ends.
Every month, one should give gifts to the twice-born according to one's desire;
and when the Cāturmāsya period is complete, there should be the meritorious hearing and recitation [of sacred texts].
One should cause the stories of Vāsudeva, or even his songs, to be recited;
in this very way, through the proclamation of the gods, one attains the most excellent goal.
If one should perform the *pāraṇa* rite that you have described for four months,
by that means a human being attains sovereignty and divine enjoyments.
By the second [vow], a person likewise attains the enjoyments of Indra;
by the third, he shall likewise attain the breaking of the fast in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus has this supreme procedure been fully explained,
O tiger among the twice-born, which leads to the attainment of the [highest] state and bestows satisfaction upon Kṛṣṇa for human beings.
Any man or woman who, with faith, observes this Sugatidvādaśī fast, attains the threefold goal.
This [river] is auspicious and the remover of sins; thus, it is eternally worshipped for the propitiation of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods, who is praised by the virtuous.
Thus ends the Sugatidvādaśī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"It is said that a man is born indeed encumbered by three debts."
A man shall be released from the three debts by the sight of a son.
Because a son protects his father from the hell named Punnāma,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself.
Those devoid of merit do not behold their own son, though he be naked, shameless, matted-haired, and grey with dust, just as they fail to see Gaṅgādhara himself.
Therefore, for the sake of obtaining a son, one should undertake this vow.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Having bathed on the eleventh day of the month of Āśvayuja and observed a fast, one should worship Hari.
One should worship a cow at night and give the daily fodder to a cow that has a calf.
On another day, having worshipped in that same manner, one should eat at night while restraining one's speech;
furthermore, month after month, one should chant these names of Hari.
He is the unconquered, he whose enemies are unborn, the much-invoked, the destroyer of citadels;
he is the ever-increasing, the lord of the gods, the long-armed, the master, and the all-pervading one.
One should utter the names Subhūti, Sumanas, and Supracetas;
thus, one may complete the vow in twelve mixed months.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should offer oblations of ghee and milk-rice to the deity while reciting its names;
thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins excellent food for as many months as the vow has lasted.
Month after month, according to your ability, perform acts of giving and prayer,
so that you may become like Diti’s son— eternal, imperishable, and infallible.
"O Lord, may it be so that you become my son in birth after birth;
may Surabhi, the devotee of Viṣṇu, who is honored by the gods and by Brahmā, be my mother."
"Accept this ball of rice offered by me, which is the root of freedom from debt;
one should gratify the Brahmin preceptor with gifts of clothing, ornaments, and cows."
Thus ends the Govatsadvādaśī vow as described in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Having destroyed the terrifying sin that causes the destruction of the earth—"
Having prostrated at your feet, O Govinda, I question you.
"Tell me some unsurpassed vow, more secret than the secret,
by which I may cross the ocean of the slaughter of Bhīṣma and Droṇa, which is a flood of sins."
Kṛṣṇa said:
In ancient times, there was a man named Kuśadhvaja in Vidarbha;
he was peaceful, possessed many sons, and ruled his kingdom with unwearied diligence.
Deluded by fate, he too struck the ascetic in the great forest while engaged in hunting; thinking him to be a deer, he killed the brahmin without negligence.
Due to the ripening of that karma, at the end of his life he then became a gavaya;
there, because of falling from a height, he was severely tormented by a fierce horse.
Therefore, a mortal who comes here would become a fierce serpent;
yet even he, O Indra among kings, beheld a brahmin at his feet.
While performing his devotions, he met his death and attained the state of an elephant's offspring;
having perished there, he then became a most terrible lion in his second birth.
Having had his mouth torn open, he became a fierce creature named Sattvabhayaṅkara;
at the end of that life, he was reborn as a preeminent kṣatriya who had gone out on a hunt.
Then, struck down by many weapons by the people of the world,
the king became a tiger once again in his third existence as well.
By the strike of his sharp toe-nails, he destroyed a lineage of deer;
by him, moreover, a certain Vaiśya was brought to his death within a thicket of creepers.
Due to his well-known act of causing the downfall of people,
that Rākṣasa was born as a source of torment, feeding on creatures struck by his claws while covered in a mass of worms and water.
If he kills a dog belonging to a Caṇḍāla, he shall meet death;
in his fifth birth, he will be born as a terrifying crocodile in the ocean.
At dawn, in the presence of Śaṅkara during a lunar eclipse at night, he killed a young woman who had come there desiring to bathe.
Even there, having set a hook, people would deprive him of his life;
then, in his sixth birth, he becomes a flesh-eating piśāca.
Cruel, intent upon finding flaws, base, and a taker of human life—
he has descended as the one named Aṅga, belonging to a certain man.
By means of a mantra perfected through the power of *pūya*, he was rendered lifeless by a practitioner of *vātika* magic;
yet in his seventh birth, he was born again with an exceedingly hideous form that was difficult to behold.
With cruel fangs and a terrifying mouth, feeding on flesh and blood,
naked and dwelling among the stars, this was a Brahmarākṣasa belonging to the lineage of Vasiṣṭha.
King Somadatta, the enemy of the Rākṣasas, having attacked, rendered the entire kingdom— including its cattle and elders— desolate amidst poison and calamities.
Having been struck down by the Brahma-weapon upon his raising his bow in battle,
he shall again become equal to a tiger on earth in his eighth birth.
While roaming in the forest, he was struck by a hungry tiger; however, that elephant was killed by a skillful hunter named Jabhalla.
Even though he was born as one of the five, Pāñcāla was exceedingly terrifying;
with ears standing erect and eyes deeply red, he was short-statured yet firm in birth.
The wicked Rākṣasa Dharmadhvaja, who wore divine ornaments and garlands,
was indeed suspended from the top of a tree by Daṇḍapāśika.
In his twelfth birth, that Pulkasa was born again as a vessel for afflictions;
while clinging to food out of greed, he was struck down by a hunter.
In a previous life, he had performed the Tārakadvādaśī vow;
by its power, even though he was born again and again in a wicked womb, he [was eventually liberated].
He quickly met his death in the ocean of worldly existence and was once again born as a most righteous king in Vidarbha.
Furthermore, by him the auspicious Tārakā was nourished for twelve years;
thus, witnessing the greatness of the vow, she was born again and again in birth after birth.
By the power of his vow, having enjoyed a kingdom free of all obstacles in this world,
he attained a station in the city of Viṣṇu that lasts until the dissolution of all things.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, how is that Tārakadvādaśī vow to be performed,
by the power of which even the sinful Kuśadhvaja attained a virtuous state?
Kṛṣṇa said:
Having undertaken the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī-vrata) during the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should perform a bath in natural water in the afternoon.
Having bowed with devotion to the Sun and likewise performed the worship of the deity,
one should remain in silence until the sun sets.
Then, with pearls, flowers, perfumes, incense, and ointments,
together with water, unbroken grains of rice, gold, and auspicious fruits;
Having placed the vessel for the *arghya* offering upon his head, he should kneel on the ground with both knees at the onset of evening, facing east, in a beautiful vessel made of copper.
Having made a circular mandala on the ground marked with cow dung,
and having smeared it with sandalwood paste, one should place the Dhruva [image] and the deer and ox faces.
O best of the Kurus, having meditated upon the Teacher of the World on the ground while reciting the *Sahasraśīrṣā* mantra,
one who has conquered his senses should offer the *arghya* oblation to the stars.
Having sprinkled water around the fire and offered incense, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin;
having performed everything in due order, one should eat the meal at the arrival of night.
In Mārgaśīrṣa, with various cakes and auspicious flowers;
in Māgha, with sesame-rice and *kṛśara*; and in Phālguna, with sweetmeats filled with jaggery.
In spring, one should offer divine sweetmeats (modakas); in Vaiśākha, sugar-coated cakes;
in Jyeṣṭha, vessels filled with parched grain flour (śaktu); and in Āṣāḍha, those filled with molasses.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa with fried cakes (śaṣkulī), in Nabhasya with milk-rice (pāyasa),
in Aśvayuja with honey-filled cakes (ghṛtapūra), and in Kārttika with sweetmeat balls (kāsāra)— in this sequence.
O Pārtha, having fed the twice-born with these twelve kinds of edible foods, one should eat oneself while restraining speech; afterwards, one should ask the Brahmins for forgiveness.
When the vow is completed, having fashioned a cluster of stars out of silver or flour according to the previous procedure, one should worship them and ask for forgiveness.
Twelve water-pots, filled with water and accompanied by sweetmeats, should be given;
as well as garments for the Brahmins, along with rubies and bodices.
Having given a white cow, sandalwood, a sacred thread, saffron, collyrium, and betel to a Brahmin, and having given these to women, one should ask for forgiveness.
O King, the man who performs this vow according to this rule,
or the woman who is devoted to her husband, or even a widow adorned with virtuous conduct;
He proceeds to the world of the stars in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun,
accompanied by auspicious hosts of apsaras, gandharvas, yakṣas, and vidyādharas.
Enveloped in intense radiance, he is honored even in heaven until the end of the eon;
this vow was formerly practiced by me, along with Queen Śrī, on her deathbed.
That [story] which was [told] by Sītā, Damayantī, Rukmiṇī, and Satyabhāmā,
as well as by other women and various kinds of men.
O Pārtha, this vow, when practiced, removes the fear of all sins;
it burns away even the misdeeds committed in other births, and it secures the application of one's merit day after day.
There is no sin committed by men that the one named Tārā, who is like a firebrand to the cotton of great transgressions, does not consume.
Thus ends the Tārakā-dvādaśī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
"The laws of Manu have been heard by me, and those of Vasiṣṭha have also been heard by me;
O Dvaipāyana, you ought now to speak of the Vaiṣṇava laws as they were taught."
Vyāsa said:
"The laws of Manu have been heard by you, and the Vedic laws have been heard by me;
however, O lord of men, those can indeed be practiced in the Kali age."
I shall declare to you that which is an easy means, requiring little wealth and little effort, yet yielding great fruit— the very essence of all the ancient [teachings].
One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight;
he who does not eat on the eleventh day does not go to hell.
Having heard the words of Vyāsa, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena trembled like a leaf of the holy fig tree and, filled with fear, spoke these words.
Bhīma said:
"O Grandfather, I am not capable of performing a fast;
therefore, O Lord, tell me of even a single vow that yields great fruit."
Vyāsa said:
When the sun is situated in Taurus or Gemini, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight occurs in the month of Jyeṣṭha;
that day should be observed with great effort by those who abstain from water.
During ritual bathing and sipping water (ācamana), a wise person should consume nothing other than water; otherwise, there would be a violation of his vow.
Avoiding water from sunrise until sunrise, a wise man who observes the Dvādaśī vow on the twelfth day attains the merit of twelve Dvādaśīs through his diligent effort.
Then, at the clear dawn of the twelfth day, one should begin the ritual bath,
having given water and gold to the twice-born according to the prescribed rite.
Having fulfilled his duties, the self-controlled man should eat together with the Brāhmaṇas;
hear now, O Bhīmasena, what merit is gained when this is done.
Just as there are Ekādaśīs in the middle of the year, one obtains the fruit of those; of this I have no doubt.
Thus Keśava, the wielder of the conch and mace, spoke to me:
"O Janārdana, tell me the merit that belongs to this vow."
O Vṛkodara, listen to the fruit one obtains by fasting on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, even without water.
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving,
and whatever merit is found in all fire-offerings— that is obtained from fasting on this day.
O Vṛkodara, all the bright and dark fortnights of the year have been observed as fasts on Ekādaśī; of this there is no doubt.
O tiger among men, I tell you this as the truth: those who observe these fasts bring wealth and grain, merit, and likewise bestow sons and health.
The messengers of Yama are massive in body, with terrifyingly black forms;
fierce and bearing staffs and nooses, they come within the range of vision at the time of death.
O tiger among men, by fasting on the eleventh day, they do not go [to hell],
but instead become gentle beings clad in yellow garments, holding discs in their hands, and possessing the speed of thought.
At the time of death, Viṣṇu leads the Vaiṣṇava in this manner to the city of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, by fasting with all effort while abstaining from water,
and likewise by giving a water-cow as a gift, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the vow of the Waterless Ekādaśī as declared in the Śrī Mahābhārata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, please explain correctly to me the vow of Dvādaśī; calculate it for me."
Together with the ritual tasting, together with the fasting, together with the secret teachings, and together with the mantras.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O son of Kuntī, that vow which was formerly performed by Sitā while she resided in the forest, according to the words of Rāghava, as spoken by the sage Agastya—
In the abode of Lopāmudrā, all the wives of the sages, who had many children,
were fed and gratified by everyone with all kinds of food provided for the body.
O Pārtha, listen with a one-pointed mind here to this Araṇyadvādaśī;
on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, at the break of dawn.
Having bathed and observed a fast, a man should perform worship to Janārdana with perfumes, flowers, water-offerings, incense, lamps, and by means of keeping a vigil and other such rites.
Having passed the night, at dawn, in a most beautiful forest region that was provided with water and in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, [he saw] one who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Having fed [the guests] with food consisting mostly of fruit, he himself should eat while maintaining silence;
or else, on that day, he should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having completed the full year,
one should undertake the effort in the month of Śrāvaṇa, Kārttika, Māgha, or Caitra.
The observer of the vow [should offer] jars filled with cooked food, cakes soaked in ghee,
savory and well-cooked rice, and various sweets such as sugar-candies.
O Pārtha, it was provided with various kinds of foods endowed with the six flavors, along with side dishes, leaf-vegetables, and exquisite dried and fresh delicacies.
With refreshing drinks, fragrant leaf-essences, sweet and cool,
and with all fruits produced in season, according to one's own means.
O Dhanañjaya, having gone to that forest devoid of people and possessing sweet water,
[he saw] there pure brahmins seated comfortably, facing the northeast.
Having performed the rites of worship and other preliminaries, one should feed twelve [monks];
in the absence of eminent ascetics, one may also feed householders.
Addressing the god Govinda with twelve distinct names, [one should honor] those who have virtuous wives, who follow good conduct, who maintain the sacred fire, and who are fond of merit.
Vāsudeva, Hṛṣīkeśa, Viṣṇu, Dāmodara, Hari,
Trivikrama, Govinda, Padmanābha, and Janārdana.
O King, one should worship the twice-born with the names "Govardhanadhara," "Kṛṣṇa," and "Śrīdhara" in succession, preceded by the syllable Om and followed by salutations.

O Pārtha, having fed those of good conduct with auspicious foods along with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, out of devotion— with one's own self purified by that devotion— one should give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, having prostrated and dismissed these [deities], saying "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me," he should thereafter eat together with his servants and kinsmen.
O Pārtha, whether by those dependent on him or by common supplicants, he who, with speech restrained,
duly performs the Araṇyadvādaśī in this manner—
At the end of his body's life, seated in a celestial chariot and surrounded by divine maidens,
he shall uplift his ancestors and go to Śvetadvīpa, the beloved abode of Hara.
There, the inhabitants have yellow garments and dark bodies, possess four arms, hold conches, discs, maces, and lotuses in their busy hands, and are adorned with the Kaustubha gem.
Seated upon Garuḍas, wearing crowns and adorned with divine earrings,
their chests were graced with garlands of blue and great lotuses.
The Yādavas— possessing the splendor of Lakṣmī, the complexion of clouds, and adorned with armlets and bracelets— stand equal to Viṣṇu until the dissolution of all beings.
Having enjoyed pleasures there for a long time and beholding the eternal Viṣṇu,
he returned to the earth due to the remainder of his merit, O Lord of the Earth.
He shall become a sovereign king, endowed with prosperity and honored by other kings;
even there, he shall again observe this auspicious Araṇyadvādaśī.
Devoted to Hari, he undergoes exactly twelve births;
at their conclusion, liberated from kinsmen, he goes to the eternal Brahman.
In the forest, the best of the twice-born observe the vow on the eleventh day known as Sitāsaraṇyā;
they are like the Sādhyas' wives, adorned with pure conduct.
Viṣṇu bestows grace and grants liberation.
Thus ends the vow of Aparā-dvādaśī as spoken in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yājñavalkya said:
Listen now to the attainment of Dvādaśī in the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa.
Having fasted upon which, one attains all of one's heart's desires.
Avoiding conversation with heretics and others, devoted to Viṣṇu,
one should, being self-restrained and single-minded, worship the infallible Lord.
The breaking of the fast at the end of Pauṣa and so forth, concluding with Jyeṣṭha over six months, is prescribed;
in the first [month], the name of the Lord Puṇḍarīkākṣa is chanted.
In the second month, however, it is named Mādhava; in Phālguna, Viśvarūpa;
and then in the fifth, it is called Puruṣottama, known as Acyuta.
In the sixth month, one should proclaim the secret name of the god as "Jaya.
During the first six months, sesame seeds are used for both the ritual bath and the consumption ceremony.
In the months beginning with Āṣāḍha, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed;
both bathing and consuming the pañcagavya are indeed recommended.
One should worship the lotus-eyed Lord again with those very same names,
having performed the worship of the deity every month according to the prescribed rite.
One who possesses faith should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin according to one's own capacity;
at the conclusion of the fast, one should perform the propitiation of the deity with devotion.
One should always perform worship of Govinda according to one's ability;
furthermore, a man should eat at night, avoiding oil and alkaline substances.

Having thus fasted on the eleventh day, one should then eat either at night on the twelfth day or during the day; such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). Thus, throughout the year, he gives pleasure, being full of joy.
A cow, clothing, gold, grain, food, and a seat.
One should give a bed to a Brahmin, saying, "May Keśava be pleased";
having fasted according to the rule on this day, one should be intent upon pleasing Viṣṇu.
One obtains all desires and is liberated from all sins;
for one attains everything that one wishes for with the mind.
Then, indeed, that which is renowned in the worlds as Saṃprāpti-dvādaśī was undertaken by those intent on ritual action after they had formed a desire upon seeing it;
and when remembered day after day, it fulfills all desires.
Thus ends the Saṃprāpti-dvādaśī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
When the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) in the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa coincides with the Viśākhā nakṣatra,
a person, having fasted, should worship Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rites on that day.
Month after month, one should worship the Lord of the World according to the prescribed rite with fragrant flowers, food offerings, and various garments and ornaments.

For the sake of purifying the body, one should consume the *prāśana* [substances] in monthly succession; having first rinsed the mouth with water, one should then intentionally consume cow’s urine, water, and ghee.
Then, with a ladle, [he should offer] curd, rice, sesame seeds, and likewise barley,
as well as water heated by the rays of the sun, darbha grass, and milk.
On the twelfth lunar day, the observer of the vow should feed the Brahmins with rice mixed with curd, milk, and jaggery;
having properly performed the rite, he should give gifts to the Brahmins according to the sequence of the months.
Ghee, sesame seeds, rice, barley, and gold combined in a jar;
a pitcher joined with sweetmeats, an umbrella, and milk-rice.
Molasses, sandalwood, garlands, and fragrant scents are the sacrificial gifts;
this vow is of great merit, bestowing both visible and invisible fruits.
This vow should be performed by those devoted to dharma and intent on the worship of Viṣṇu;
having performed this vow, a man [is born] into a preeminent family of brāhmaṇas.
He is born with a noble birth, wise, and a master of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas;
free from affliction, possessing infinite happiness, and likewise a destroyer of enemies through that very bliss.
A wise man shall have many sons and wealth equal to that of Kubera;
as it is for a man, so it is for a woman who should observe this vow.
Having attained supreme prosperity in this world, upon death she shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
Thus is described the Mahāphala-dvādaśī vow as stated in the Viṣṇurahasya.
On the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), one should feed the Brahmins and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). On that same lunar day every month, one should provide daily fodder for cows to the cattle.
The observer of the vow should eat from an earthen vessel, combined with cow’s milk, or curd, or ghee, and it must be free from alkaline salts and salt.
Having fasted for a year on the Govinda-dvādaśī,
a man should again give daily fodder to cows according to his ability.
Having fasted according to the rules on Govinda-dvādaśī,
a man who gives [gifts] according to the rules obtains that fruit which results from giving a thousand cows.
Having observed this highly meritorious Govinda-dvādaśī,
one attains the world of cows, which is overflowing with curds, milk, and ghee.
Having enjoyed there for a long time excellent pleasures and the fulfillment of his heart's desires,
he shall thereafter attain the world of Govinda, where his face is ever smiling.
There he shall dwell, free from fear and filled with supreme joy,
by the grace of Govinda, for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Thus ends the Govinda-dvādaśī vow as declared in the Viṣṇu-rahasya.
Nārada said:
"O Grandfather of the worlds, you have duly described the Dvādaśīs."
Tell me the fruit of the ritual action for those who are devoid of its performance.
O Grandfather, please describe according to the rules the commencement and conclusion of the twelve Dvādaśīs, as well as the fruit of the practice of these vows.
Brahmā said:
Listen with a focused mind, O Brahmin, to this auspicious account that brings pleasure to Viṣṇu;
the vow of Dvādaśī is the most excellent among all meritorious vows.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the bright fortnight,
a man who has restrained his vows should first undertake the twelfth day (dvādaśī) according to the prescribed rite.
And one should have the sacrifice for Hari performed by the preceptor and others according to the rules;
having worshipped Hari there, O twice-born one, and then obtained his permission.
Having seen Hari at Cakratīrtha, and Keśava in Mathurā,
having seen Viṣṇu in the Aśoka grove, and Janārdana at the edge of the bower;
One who is pure and purified in the actions of mind, speech, and body, and firm in their vow, attains that fruit by fasting on the twelfth day.

Then, having bowed down to and obtained the permission of his kinsmen, elders, and Brahmins, a man desiring righteousness should perform these *kṛcchra* penances himself; he should not have them performed by others.
Having obtained permission from his teacher, he should chew a tooth-stick there;
then, taking water with unbroken grains of rice, he should prepare for his vow.
Having observed the Ekādaśī fast for Viṣṇu for as long as a full year,
may the accomplishment of this rite proceed without obstacles through your grace, O Janārdana.
Having thus made this vow and bowed to the one whose banner is Garuḍa,
with senses conquered and mind tranquil, he should spend the night on the tenth day.
Then, on the eleventh day, having performed the morning bath according to the prescribed rules,
one should bathe the Lord of Gods with honey, curd, milk, ghee, and other offerings.
With jars filled with all medicinal herbs and water, adorned with sprouts and sandalwood,
saffron, ushira-root, and camphor, and beautified by garlands of flowers;
There, one should worship the deity stationed there with devotion using auspicious *mālatī* flowers,
and offer incense prepared from *vāguru* or *guggulu* soaked in clarified butter.
One should offer a lamp day and night to the God of Gods,
along with milk-rice, cakes, barley-meal, and parched grain mixed with curds, together with fruits.
Karambha consists of parched grain flour mixed with curd.
One should offer this food offering (naivedya) to Hari with devotion according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having performed singing and instrumental music to the best of one's ability, one should pass the night.
Having thus performed worship of Hari, one should likewise honor a brahmin;
provided there is a worthy person, one should not instead honor another who is merely nearby.
He falls into an evil rebirth and brings his vow to ruin;
having gone to hell due to the ruined vow, he remains there for a hundred kalpas.
O divine sage, when the worship of those residing in the sacred sites has been completed,
the wise man should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru according to his capacity.
There, the Guru should diligently perform the recitation (japa) over the water-pot with the single-syllable mantra, and he should consecrate that water with it.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should install the Sun in the form of water;
in whose every hair-pore the clouds reside, and in all whose joints the rivers flow.
Having thus assigned the oceans to the middle of the belly and all the sacred fords (tīrthas) to the feet,
one should place Viṣṇu in the water and remain there speaking [his names] throughout that night.

The syntactical connection is: "Speaking thus, place [it] in the water. On the twelfth day, the Guru should bathe that disciple with that water, O Nārada, according to the rule and purified by mantras.
Furthermore, may all the sacred fords and all the gods, together with Indra,
sprinkle me today with water for the sake of liberation from all sins.
Completely liberated from all sins, that meritorious soul, having performed the ritual ablution and duly worshipped Keśava, shall indeed attain a body belonging to Viṣṇu.
One should feed the preceptor, who bestows knowledge, together with Brāhmaṇas;
having fed them, one should then present sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should worship the best of the twice-born every month;
listen now to the names that should be recited month by month.
One should worship the one named Nārāyaṇa in the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Puṣya,
Mādhava in Māgha, and likewise Govinda in Phālguna.
O Sage, one should worship Keśava Viṣṇu in Caitra, Madhusūdana in Vaiśākha,
the god Trivikrama in Jyeṣṭha, and Vāmana in Āṣāḍha.
In Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the one named Śrīdhara; then Hṛṣīkeśa in Nabhas;
Padmanābha in Āśvayuja; and from that, likewise Dāmodara.
Having thus proclaimed these twelve names in their proper order,
one should then say, "May Hṛṣīkeśa be pleased with me," and bow down.
Then, for the sake of pleasing Kṛṣṇa, one should give a milch cow with her calf to a peaceful brāhmaṇa; thus, this vow shall reach fulfillment.
He gave sandals, garments, a signet ring, and a water-pot;
jars the size of earthenware vessels, filled with water and accompanied by sweetmeats.
And who, according to this rule, should fast on the twelfth day, giving twelve [cows] along with sacrificial fees to twelve Brahmins;
Having worshipped Hari, they go to the painless world of Viṣṇu;
for this, O Sage, is the Nāmākhyadvādaśī, the foremost among vows.
These three should be practiced by men to satisfy Janārdana,
just as the syllable Om is recited at the beginning of all the Vedas.
Whoever recites this with devotion or listens to it endowed with faith,
being liberated from all sins, that person goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
When this has been performed, the fruit that one obtains is now described:
one becomes proud, wealthy, and endowed with knowledge, born into a preeminent brahmin family filled with riches and grain.
Having cast all suffering aside through discernment, he attains birth with unimpaired faculties.
Therefore, you too, possessing unfailing knowledge, should perform this worship of Nārāyaṇa with vigilance;
make Viṣṇu your lord.
And being propitiated, depart from [granting] fruits.
Having spoken thus to the Creator, he then became silent, being honored by those words;
this concludes the vow of the Twelve Names as declared in the *Viṣṇurahasya*.
Agastya said: Listen, O highly fortunate king, to this unsurpassed and auspicious vow, by which Viṣṇu is attained through auspiciousness alone; of this there is no doubt.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, from the first year onward,
one should practice eating a single meal during the bright fortnight until the tenth lunar day.
Then, having bathed at midday on the tenth day, one should worship Keśava;
having eaten as before according to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should do so on the twelfth day with a pure mind.
Having worshipped Hari with the mantra "O Keśava," one should,
being self-restrained, offer sesame seeds along with gold on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight for his pleasure, O King.
Having stayed there in this manner, one should give barley to a twice-born man;
at the time of giving, the oblation, and likewise during worship, Hari should be addressed as "Kṛṣṇa."
Then, O best of kings, having thus spent the four-month period,
one should again, being restrained and pure, fast in the same manner during the months beginning with Caitra.
One should cause vessels of parched grain along with gold to be given to the Brahmins;
likewise, one should worship Govinda during the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa.
Having spent those three months in this manner until Kārttika arrives,
one should likewise pass that month as well, remaining restrained and pure on the tenth day.
Having worshipped Hari with devotion according to the name of the month, using the mantra beginning with "Priyadatta," the wise man,
having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), should perform the rite with devotion on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) while his senses are restrained.
O King, on the eleventh day, one should devoutly have a golden model of the earth fashioned,
complete with its seven underworlds and the principal mountain ranges.
One should establish her before Hari according to the ritual procedure for the placement of the elements (bhūvinyāsa),
covered with a pair of white cloths and provided with all the seeds.
Having worshipped [the image] with the five fragrances while reciting "O Priyadatta," the wise man should keep a vigil there; then, at dawn, he should again [honour] the twice-born.
Having addressed them by number, O King, and by their twenty-one names,
one should cause a cow and a bull to be given to each of them individually.
And for each [deity], he offered a pair of garments, a finger-ring,
a golden bracelet, and an ear-ornament.
The king, as the bestower of sovereignty, shall grant each one of these a village;
then, according to the extent of his wealth, he should cause a cow to be given.
And even a poor person, if unable to perform [the rite] in full, should do so according to his own capacity;
having fashioned the earth out of gold according to his means, he should likewise provide a pair of cows.
One should then give a pair of garments, or even a single one, according to one's financial capacity; in the event that a pair of cows is unavailable, everything should be performed with gold alone.
Having done so, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, in this very same manner,
one should likewise fashion an image of the earth out of silver, according to the extent of one's wealth and power.
One should likewise give food to the Brahmins,
as well as sandals, wooden shoes, and an umbrella according to one's ability.
In this manner, may Kṛṣṇa Dāmodara grant it to the knower of the Vedas;
may Hari, the universal form who is the god of all, be pleased with me.
The fruit that one enjoys from giving and feeding [the hungry] cannot be fully described even in a thousand years.
O lord of men, that ruler who performs this meritorious auspicious vow shall attain all prosperity and thereafter proceed to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the auspicious Śubha-dvādaśī vow as declared in the Vārāha Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Listen, O highly fortunate King, to this most excellent and auspicious vow.
And in the month of Āśvayuja, O Brahmin, when there is proximity to the Lotus-born One.
From the navel of the Lord of the worlds, the wielder of the discus,
there emerged that which occurs during that delightful and auspicious time known as Śuka-ekādaśī.
In that [state], one should worship Viṣṇu correctly by means of that through which the fragment is fulfilled.
The meaning is: by that worship of Viṣṇu, the incomplete fragment becomes fully complete with dharma and the other [aims of life].
[One should worship] with flowers, leaves, or even fruits endowed with fragrance and color.
And with all medicinal herbs, as far as all that exists among stationary beings.
Ghee, sesame seeds, rice, barley, gold and other precious metals,
gems, pearls, corals, and various kinds of garments.
And the flavors— sweet, sour, astringent, salty,
and bitter— should be offered, provided that they are indeed unbroken.
For the sake of worshipping that Great-Souled Keśava, this should be offered,
by which an unbroken full year is established in the home.
O divine sage, having observed the fast, on the second day he should bathe everywhere with that same bath by which he has indeed kept the year unbroken.
Anointment with either white mustard seeds or sesame seeds is prescribed;
one should likewise perform the ritual bathing of Padmanābha with clarified butter.
O best of the twice-born, that very same [rite] has been declared regarding giving according to one's capacity;
then, one should worship Keśava with flowers, beginning from his feet.
One should offer incense according to the prescribed rite by which [the merit] lasts for a supreme year;
one should worship that Teacher of the World with gold, jewels, and garments.
One should offer savory, liquid, and edible sacrificial foods (*haviṣya*).
Whatever substance was used to accomplish the rite on the first Ekādaśī, with that very same substance must another rite be accomplished on the subsequent Ekādaśīs.
Then, having fully worshipped Padmanābha, the Lord of Gods and Teacher of the World—
O best of sages, O observer of excellent vows, one should understand this by means of this mantra.
Homage be to Padmanābha, the bringer of the lotus, of great splendor!
May dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa be unimpaired for me.
O Keśava, whose eyes are like the petals of a blossoming lotus, just as you are unbroken in every respect, by that same fact may all [virtues] such as Dharma remain unbroken for me.
Thus, when the year is complete, O Brahmin, having fasted and subdued his senses, he should indeed conclude the vow with an unbroken offering of all items.
When this vow has been performed, Mādhava is clearly pleased;
and virtue, wealth, pleasure, liberation, and so forth, arise according to one's own will.
Thus ends the vow of Akhaṇḍa-Dvādaśī as declared in the Vāmana Purāṇa.
The sages said:
O best of sages, tell us of the Kumbhikā-vrata.
Just as there is wakefulness in that state, so indeed is the worship of the gods.
"O best of sages, tell me what deity resides in that [vow] and what its fruit is.
Śaunaka said:
"This vow is exceedingly meritorious, pure, and a destroyer of sins."
One should cause the Lotus-eyed One to be heard, who is difficult to attain even for the gods.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should perform [this rite];
thereby, one shall deliver oneself entirely from the hells, beginning with Kumbhīpāka.
With great effort, they perform a vigil before Viṣṇu during the month of Kārttika,
and especially worship on the night of the very bright Ekādaśī.
Having smeared a square area with four gates using cow dung,
one should adorn it with four colored powders made of rice and wheat.
Having bathed, worshipped Nārāyaṇa upon a sacrificial mound or in images, offered oblations into the fire,
and given the bali-offering to the quarters, one should observe the prescribed ritual procedure.
Then, one should worship [the vessel] adorned with a garland of lamps with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
by meditating upon the water-pot as being composed of the deity, one is liberated from all sins.
The one named Kumbhī is well known;
when the Kumbhī endowed with Sukumā is the destroyer of impurity,
Viṣṇu is situated at its root and the Grandfather (Brahmā) is above it.
Rudra is established in the trunk, and Tripurāntaka at the end;
likewise, the sages are situated upon the branches joined with Indra and Vāyu.
The gods are said to move in its leaves, and the Maruts are said to dwell in its roots;
she is remembered as one who is to be saluted by all the gods and as the fulfiller of all vows.
She is remembered as one who is to be saluted by all the gods and who performs all vows.
Therefore, with every effort, the Kumbhikā vow must indeed be performed;
one should always keep vigil preceded by dance and song.
O Madhusūdana, the garments for the couple and the worship should be performed;
likewise, a sin-destroying sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's capacity.
Whoever performs this auspicious Kumbhī-jāgaraṇa in such a manner should worship the Kumbhī with the mantra; [this is] the auspicious Kumbhī-jāgaraṇa.
Having fashioned a creeper out of gold, with silver flowers,
golden filaments, and provided with various fruits.
A wise person should have an image of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa made of gold and worship them with supreme devotion near a *kumbhīkā* plant.
O Goddess, you were sent by the deities in the past and have now come to this world; accept this worship, may it be auspicious for you, so that all your purposes and goals may be accomplished.
The mantra for worship:
With fruits, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, water, camphor, and sandalwood,
one should diligently offer the *arghya* oblation in a silver vessel or a conch shell.
Accept this *arghya* from me, O Goddess, you who destroy all sins;
this *arghya* is offered by me to you—homage be to you, O Kumbhīkā!
The Arghya-mantra:
You are the mother of all beings; you alone are the Supreme Goddess.
You are the knowledge among supreme knowledges, the subduer of all beings.
The Goddess, who bestows the fortune of sons and desires the welfare and happiness of all, [should be worshipped];
having worshipped the feet for Matsya and likewise the thighs for Kūrma.
Having worshipped the waist with Varāha, likewise the chest with Nṛsiṃha,
the throat with Vāmana, and the two arms with the two Rāmas.
One should worship the eyes with the name Rāma, the fortune (śrī) with the name Buddha,
the hair with the name Kalki, and everywhere with the name Vāmana.
The worship mantra:
Victory, O Viṣṇu! Victory, O Ananta! Victory, O you who assume the form of Vāmana!
[1108] [I offer] the auspicious cow, together with her calf, clothed in garments and wearing a sacred thread.
A cow with golden horns, silver hooves, and a copper-colored back, adorned with a bell,
accompanied by a bronze milking vessel, and smeared with white sandalwood paste.
Having released the divine garland of fruits resting upon the gold,
one should first cause the gold to be recited over and then present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Nandā, Upanandā, Suśīlā, and likewise Surabhī.
"May cows be in my home; may cows, the mothers of the world, be mine.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should either eat at night or observe a fast.
One should keep a vigil at night; one shall obtain the entire fruit, O Grandfather, including sons, cattle, and jewels that are inexhaustible.
For seven thousand and seven hundred kalpas,
one who performs this Kumbhīvrata is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Kumbhīvrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Dālbhya said:
"O Brahmin-sage, O Lord, [is there a way] with little exertion or with a small gift?"
You ought to explain that by which the pacification of evil comes about.
Pulastya said: Listen, O Dālbhya, to the supreme, meritorious Dvādaśī that destroys all sins,
by fasting upon which one endowed with faith shall attain the highest merit.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, if the moon should be in the constellation Āṣāḍhā,
or if it is the twelfth day of the dark fortnight under the asterism Mūla, one who is firm in his vows [should perform the rite].
Listen to me as I describe that procedure which bestows the fruit of merit:
having bathed well, being self-restrained and pure, one should worship the God of gods.
Having worshipped [the deity] with the name Kṛṣṇa on the eleventh day, the high-minded one,
having fasted, should worship Keśava again on the second day.
Having praised him repeatedly by that very name called "Kṛṣṇa," one should give sesame seeds to a Brahmin, saying, "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me."
O Sage, black sesame seeds are likewise recommended for the ritual bath and the consumption [of food] when the annual fast is concluded with mantras that please Viṣṇu.
Black jars, together with sesame seeds and cooked food,
accompanied by a parasol, a water-pot, and a pair of sandals, are wrapped [in cloth] and filled with jewels.
These should be given to the Brahmins according to the prescribed manner and with the expenditure of wealth:
and a black cow, wearing yellow garments, yielding milk, [should be given] to a Brahmin.
One should give a pair of umbrellas and sandals, saying, "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me.
O twice-born ones, as many sesame seeds as grow from the sesame planted in the field, for that same number of years [the merit endures].
For that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world;
moreover, in birth after birth, he is born ever free from disease.
Having observed this twelfth day known as Tiladvādaśī, a man does not become blind, nor deficient in limb, nor afflicted with leprosy, nor contemptible.
Upon the completion of the year-long fast with the recitation of the mantra for pleasing Viṣṇu,
one should perform worship for the Brahmin and likewise give sesame seeds as a gift.
By this method, O Dālbhya, through the gift of sesame seeds,
a person is undoubtedly liberated from all sins without effort.
O best of sages, for the pacification of all sins, there is no requirement for great wealth nor for physical exertion of the body; rather, it is charity, ritual procedure, and likewise faith.
Thus ends the vow of the Tiladvādaśī as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Yudhiṣṭhira questioned Bhīṣma, who was lying upon his bed of arrows.
By that meritorious vow, the world of Yama is not seen.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, they do not experience grief at all;
tell me that, O Knower of Dharma, Grandfather, and show me your compassion.
Bhīṣma said:
"Observe the Ekādaśī known as Vaitaraṇī; by doing so, you shall become happy, you shall not behold the world of Yama, and you shall find no sorrow."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By what procedure, O dear one, should that rite of great fruit be performed? O Grandfather, O Lord, tell me that procedure."

Kṛṣṇa said: O King, when the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) of the dark fortnight occurs in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a pure man, having reached that time, should properly undertake the religious observance (niyama).
The eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) in the dark fortnight is auspiciously named Vaitaraṇī; I shall observe that vow for a year, remaining devoted to eating only at night during the bright fortnight.
At midday, having bathed and regularly completed his daily rites,
a man should bring a fragrant black cow at night and worship her according to the prescribed rule.
Facing east, one should describe a black cow upon a smeared ground;
she is to be worshipped starting from her forefeet and ending at her two hind feet.
Having reached Gopuccha, perform the libation for the ancestors;
thereafter, worship should be performed according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures.
Endowed with faith, one should likewise anoint a cow with sandalwood paste;
having devoutly washed its two horns with scented water, one should wash its feet as well.
Then one should worship with devotion using flowers, perfumes, and scents,
employing the mantras proclaimed in the Purāṇas, according to the proper place and according to the prescribed rite.

In this regard, the mantra for worship is as follows: "Obeisance to the two front feet of the cow; obeisance to the mouth of the cow; obeisance to the two horns of the cow; obeisance to the two shoulders of the cow; obeisance to the tail of the cow; obeisance to the two rear feet of the cow; obeisance to all the limbs of the cow. With a pure mind, one should scatter perfumes upon these various parts.
Afterwards, one should cause incense to be offered, saying: "May Gaurī accept the lamp."
Through your grace, I shall cross the terrible [hells] such as Asipatravana and likewise the Vaitaraṇī river; O Mother of Cows, salutations, salutations to you!
Since the Vaitaraṇī river is certainly crossed with ease by means of it,
therefore, having observed the Ekādaśī, it shall be known by the name Vaitaraṇī.
O Goddess who brings joy to all the world and is ever beloved by the gods, you are the cow; protect the universe, O Mistress of the World! May this lamp be accepted.
The mantra for the lamp:
One should give a covering that is perfectly pure and spotless to the cow.
Through this gift of cloth, may the Supreme Goddess be pleased; may she, who is fragrant, be gratified.
The mantra for the clothing:
"For four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, one should subsist on alms-food;
and for another four months, one should subsist solely on barley."
During the four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, one should eat milk-rice (pāyasa);
three parts of that food are for cows and the Guru, and one part is for one's own sake.
"May the fragrant food offering (naivedya) given by me please [the deity]," he should say;
he should give the second portion to the guru, and the third himself.
One should perform the vow month by month for twelve months;
then, when the year is complete, one should always perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
A bed with a cotton mattress should be prepared for the couple as their bedding;
furthermore, a black-colored milch cow with her calf should be provided.
One should worship the golden image with the previously mentioned mantras while endowed with devotion;
then one should give everything to the guru and ask for forgiveness therein.
Whether a woman or a man, by the power of this vow,
having enjoyed various kinds of sovereignty, is glorified in the heavenly world.
A load of iron, measuring one *droṇa*,
should be given and prepared for a Brahmin householder in order to reach the completion [of the rite] at the Vaitaraṇī river.
Thus ends the Vaitaraṇī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord, when the sky is shrouded by clouds and the rainy season has arrived, [what should be done?]
Abounding with the croaking of frogs and resounded by the cries of peacocks.
What vow should be performed there by women or even by men?
Tell me that, along with the fast, all the names, and the mantra.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Prakṛti, having become pure and composed in the month of Śrāvaṇa during the dark fortnight,
one should bathe on the eleventh day with water containing all medicinal herbs.
O King of kings, one should prepare a hundred *indurikās* with powdered black gram (*māṣa*),
as well as five *modakas*, along with a pure *prastha* of clarified butter.
Then, for his own benefit, he went to a reservoir of water that was free from wicked crocodiles and filled with waters abounding in lotuses.
On that very beautiful sandy bank at the water's edge, having fashioned a circular mandala with cow dung and other materials, one should worship it with flour-cakes and similar offerings.
Having adorned it with fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, and auspicious unbroken grains of rice,
one should draw the Moon there upon the ground together with Rohiṇī at its side.
One should worship with devotion for the sake of auspiciousness with this mantra:
"O King Soma, salutations to you; salutations again and again to you, O Rohiṇī."
"O Great-minded One, O Great Goddess, fulfill my desire!
Having thus worshipped her, one should offer consecrated food (naivedya) before her.
And one should give that very [gift] to a Brahmin with the words, "May Soma be pleased with us.
"May she be pleased," O Goddess; Rohiṇī is dear to the Moon.
Having recited thus and offered that, one should personally enter that water,
reaching it up to the neck, or merely up to the knees, or even up to the ankles.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading King Soma together with Rohiṇī;
staying right in the water, one should consume a hundred drops of moon-nectar.

"Five sweetmeats"—the remainder [of the sentence] is "from a prastha of ghee. When all of that has been eaten, having eaten it and standing on the bank, the recitation should be performed after making the offering; then the meal should be given to the Brahmin.
O Pārtha, one should give the garment for wrapping along with a sacrificial fee according to one's own capacity, with supreme devotion and free from stinginess regarding wealth.
O King, whatever man, woman, or maiden performs this Rohiṇī vow according to the prescribed ritual every year, [attains the fruit].
O Pārtha, having remained for a long time in this world— which is abundant with wealth and grain— in the auspicious stage of the householder, endowed with sons, grandsons, and so forth;
Then, having attained death at a sacred ford (sutīrtha), one shall go to the city of Viṣṇu;
staying there for a hundred divine years, one shall enjoy unsurpassed pleasures.
And having come here, that king is born beloved by the people.
O lord of men, hear the reason why Rohiṇī was taken away by the moon-bearer for his own benefit:
it was because of those hundreds of small moon-shaped figures made from well-ground māṣa beans.
That very fruit, when thrown into water with jaggery and ghee, [produces the same result].
A ball of jaggery is the *modaka*. Thus ends the vow of Rohiṇī-dvādaśī as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

O Lord who holds the conch, discus, and mace in hand, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, and who has Garuḍa as your vehicle, please tell me of the twelfth day known as Malladvādaśī: what is its ritual procedure and what is its fruit?
Kṛṣṇa said:
"In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, served by gods, sages, and ancestors,
when I delight at the Baṇḍīravaṭa on the bank of the Yamunā."
At that time, for the sake of slaying the demon Kaṃsa, I was eight years old and sported playfully among the cattle-herds in the grove on the banks of the Yamunā.
In the form of cowherd boys,
those very same wrestlers and cowherds, together with Bala, were exceedingly powerful in the forest.
Subhadra, whose cheeks were like those of a mandu bird, sang songs that increased the joy of heaven, while they clapped their hands and danced like the gods in the third heaven.
One should also understand the names of those [leaders] in Gokula, such as Pakṣendra-bhaṭa and others,
as well as the names of the principal gopīs.
Gopālī, Pālikā, Dhanyā, Viśākhā,
Viniścikā, Gandhānugandhā, Sīmābhā, Tārakā, and likewise Daśamī.
Having thus seated me upon an excellent seat with these and other such words,
I was honored with auspicious flowers, as well as curd, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains of rice.
Three hundred wrestlers worship me with flowers,
performing dances upon the stage with various colorful movements.
With various kinds of wrestling matches featuring intoxicated and eminent wrestlers,
and with foods, edibles, drinks, and meals consisting of curds, milk, and ghee.
Through acts of affection, mutual attraction, laughter, and playful tugging with one another—
thus twelve [deeds] should be performed and remembered by those who are well-composed.
Wrestlers, and especially others as well, should perform these with devotion;
they worship my very forms in due order month after month.
O Pārtha, one should worship [the deity] by the names of the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa;
at each breaking of the fast, one should give jasmine flowers to a twice-born man.
One should observe a vigil at night with perfumes, flowers, and likewise lamps, with enchanting songs and instrumental music, and with various forms of wrestling.
"Through the separate gifts of ghee, the gifts of milk, and the gifts of curd, may Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the God of Gods, be pleased with me in every way."
In this very manner, the ritual procedure has been declared, accompanied by the bestowal of the mantra;
even now, I perform this Dvādaśī for the sake of increasing strength.
Since this [rite] known as the "Twelve Mallas" bestows victory upon wrestlers,
it should therefore be performed by wrestlers who desire victory in wrestling matches.
O son of Kuntī, for others as well, this [mantra] bestows victory in all matters;
by reciting it, one is liberated from the multitude of sins—of this there is no doubt.

O best of the Pāṇḍavas, because food was given by them to one another in the forest in due order, this is known as Araṇyadvādaśī; O Pārtha, it is this very same vow that is undertaken by men in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
The Dvādaśī is renowned by that name throughout the three worlds;
by its power, O King of kings, [the region] became crowded with cowherds and herds of cows.
With an abundance of wealth consisting of goats, sheep, cows, buffaloes, and so forth, as well as grain,
the king celebrated this meritorious twelfth day known by the name Pāpaharā.
To those devotees of mine who shall perform this, I will grant what is in my heart:
health, strength, sovereignty, and the eternal realm of Viṣṇu—
by those great ones assembled at the foot of the Bhaṇḍīra tree.

On that very lunar day when he was instantly honored by wrestlers with wrestling bouts that displayed unimpeded strength of arm, that twelfth day (dvādaśī) thereafter became known on earth as Valamallasamjñā.
Thus ends the Malladvādaśī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"O Mahāmati, regarding whatever deficiency may occur in the vows of fasting..."
Tell me, what kind of ripening results from his performance of the act of giving?
Yājñavalkya said: Listen to me regarding the kind of deficiency in results that arises from the deficiency of sacrifices, fasts, and vows for one who has undertaken a vow.
Others likewise attained sovereignty and wealth through fasting and other such means.
Furthermore, men who have fallen from their conduct become destitute;
likewise, even after attaining an excellent form, they do so due to the fault of deficiency in their vows.
Those men become one-eyed, humpbacked, or even blind;
likewise, by fasting, a man [loses] his wife, and a woman her husband.
Due to the deficiency in their vow of lifelong separation,
those who maintain the sacred fire with true wives as well as others who maintain the fire with truth alone obtain both [results].
Those of immoral conduct dwell in noble families, while those of virtuous conduct dwell in low-born families;
the former are destitute of clothing and ointments, yet possess great beauty, whereas the latter are adorned with ornaments.
And those who were of ugly form as well as those endowed with the qualities of adornment—
all of them, due to a deficiency in their vows, came to a state of deficiency in their results.
Therefore, in a vow, as well as in giving, in a sacrifice, or likewise in fasting, one must not allow any deficiency; for through deficiency, the fruit becomes deficient.
Maitreya said:
If, somehow, a deficiency should occur regarding the fast or other observances,
tell me what should be done therein so that it becomes free from flaw.
Yājñavalkya said: Listen as I describe this Akhaṇḍadvādaśī, which is equal even to all other rites and is capable of pacifying any deficiency in them.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the bright fortnight, on the twelfth day, being self-controlled and pure,
and having observed a fast, one should worship Janārdana, the Lord of Gods.
