Having bathed, he says "Nārāyaṇa"; likewise, while eating, he says "Nārāyaṇa"; while eating, he says "the god Nārāyaṇa," and again, while sleeping, he says "Nārāyaṇa."
Having bathed in water mixed with the five products of the cow, meditated upon Viṣṇu, and subdued his senses,
he should devoutly give a vessel filled with barley and rice to a Brahmin.
Afterwards, one should recite this in the presence of Lord Hari:
"Whatever incomplete vow has been performed by me throughout seven lifetimes,"
O Blessed One, by your grace, may that remain unbroken for me here,
just as you alone are the entire unbroken universe, O Supreme Person.
Likewise, may all my vows indeed be unbroken;
thus, by your power, may the fulfillment of my desires be attained right now.
Thus, the rule for the four castes is prescribed month by month;
indeed, the first breaking of the fast is prescribed after exactly four months.
Furthermore, one should perform the propitiation of Hari at every breaking of the fast;
however, the breaking of the fast occurs only on the fourth lunar day of the months beginning with Caitra.
Therein, endowed with faith, one should offer vessels of parched grain;
the breaking of the fast occurs during the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa and ending with Kārttika.
There too, one should give vessels of ghee to a Brahmin according to one's ability;
a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay is prescribed.
O King, according to his own capacity, he should have palāśa leaves prepared;
thus, at the end of the year, [he should honor] Brāhmaṇas whose senses are restrained.
One should indeed feed twelve invited guests with ghee and milk-rice,
and after bowing down, one should ask for their forgiveness by giving gifts of clothing and ornaments.
One should also worship the teachers and gurus according to the prescribed rites;
O best of kings, having given a cow and prostrated, one should ask for their forgiveness.
Thus, having fasted correctly and according to the rule for the unbroken Dvādaśī, a man enjoys the fruit of that unbroken vow.
Since the Akhaṇḍadvādaśī [vow] makes complete and unbroken whatever deficiency of the vow was committed at any time throughout seven births.
Therefore, O lady of virtuous vows, men and women who desire the fruit should properly observe the vow of Akhaṇḍa-dvādaśī with great effort.
Thus ends the vow of Akhaṇḍadvādaśī in the Viṣṇudharmottara. The concluding rite (udyāpana) as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
Kṛṣṇa said:
"In ancient times, Nārada [inquired] of Viṣṇu regarding the vow of Akhaṇḍadvādaśī."
Being asked about the procedure for the concluding rite (udyāpana), he spoke; listen to that.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, Supreme Puruṣa of antiquity, I ask you a certain doubt; please explain it out of compassion, O Lord.
Regarding that Akhaṇḍadvādaśī which is described in the Purāṇas—
is it said to be for the sake of fulfilling all fragmented vows?
O Lord, although the deficiency of all vows is thereby fulfilled,
you have not correctly explained the procedure for its formal conclusion (udyāpana).
There is no one to answer that question, nor is anyone who has heard it even very rare.
Viṣṇu said: In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the bright fortnight, one who is pure in his vows—
On the tenth day, having worshipped Keśava and subsisted on food prepared with sacrificial oblation (haviṣyānna), [one should proceed].
Having concluded the evening twilight rites, he should take the tooth-cleansing stick;
having sipped water according to the rule, he should utter this mantra:
O Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, Keśava, destroyer of afflictions!
I shall undertake the commencement of this vow for a period of three days.
Having thus prayed to Govinda with the mantra at the beginning, one should then go to sleep.
The mantra for undertaking the vow:
Then, having risen at dawn, one should perform the vow as prescribed;
O best of the twice-born, it is said that the breaking of the fast occurs after four months.
Indeed, the breaking of the fast is not [permissible] except by the rite of giving that vessel;
thus, O Lotus-born One, having completed twelve Dvādaśīs.
Then, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana), preceded by the prescribed ritual and mantras;
on the eleventh day, the observer of the vow, having bathed and become pure, shall wear white garments.
O Lord, may all the merit found in every sacred ford and all the fruit found in every sacred ford belong to me through the water from the lotus of your feet.
Thus ends the mantra for bathing.
Having performed the bath, one should then worship the Lord who has Garuḍa as his banner—
the Sovereign Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, perfected in a single form.
One should fashion [the image] out of gold, adorned with jewels, according to one's ability;
one should bathe it with fragrant water while reciting the Sahasraśīrṣā mantra.
One should bathe Hari with honey using the mantras beginning with "madhu vātā";
thereafter, one should bathe him with milk using the mantra beginning with "yathāryaman."
Thus, when the bath has been performed, one should thereafter begin to perform the worship;
one should honor [the deity] with sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, saffron, and other such substances.
Having anointed Hari with devotion by means of those [substances], one should then recite the mantra:
"O Lord, according to my ability, You have been bathed and anointed by me."
May Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa forgive all of that, whether deficient or excessive.
The mantra for the ointment: Then, having brought an excellent pair of garments, one should have him put them on—
whether they be yellow, red, white, or variously variegated.
O Lord, this garment has been offered to you according to my ability;
may Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa forgive all that is deficient or excessive in it.
Thus ends the mantra for the lower garment.
Having clothed the deity with various beautiful flowers and having covered him with flower garlands, one should recite this mantra:
O Janārdana, you have been worshipped even with flowers according to our ability;
surely Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa will forgive all of that, and even more.

Thus ends the mantra for the flower offering. Having performed [the ritual] according to this procedure, one should likewise offer a bed provided with a cotton mattress and a frame, along with coverlets, pillows, and bolsters.
Having established there the auspicious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gods, who is mounted upon each foot and firmly established on all four feet;
Offerings such as food oblations, along with various kinds of edibles—
things to be licked, swallowed, sucked, and chewed.
Having diligently gathered all those beverages, in whatever manner they may be found in that place, one should offer them to the deity.
One should offer fragrant fruits and cooked foods;
having thus offered all that with devotion, one should recite the mantra.
O Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, please accept with devotion this offering of wealth as it has been presented by me according to my means.
Thus, one should devoutly perform the offering of food (naivedya) to the God;
one should first designate the head of the God and afterwards the feet.
Then, in the position of the head, one should place a beautiful water-filled jar,
joined with a crab, containing gems, and adorned with cloth.
Having placed that water-pot down, one should then recite the mantra:
"O Keśava, having eaten and drunk, and having likewise sipped this water,
O God, being yourself well-satisfied and gracious-faced through my devotion and affection."
This is the mantra for installation.
One should offer everything pertaining to the service of the bed,
from the commencement of the worship until its conclusion, including the bathing, the offerings, and the meal.
One should burn guggulu resin mixed with ghee before the deity at night;
then, having invited an auspicious brahmin together with his wife.
Devoid of all inauspicious marks and endowed with all primary and secondary limbs,
he was one who had completed his Vedic studies and vows with the ceremonial bath, and was honored by those born of his own lineage.
Then, at the edge of the deity’s [pedestal], one should place a pure and stainless Brahmin together with his wife, facing the east; thereafter, one should worship him with devotion.
O Nārada, what is the use of much further talk?
Just as one worships the God, so too should one worship the Brahmin.
One should never entertain the notion of difference between Viṣṇu and Brāhmaṇas;
thus, those in whose hearts this is ever present, the eminent ascetics, are truly worthy of worship.
With a pure mind, one should bathe the Lord seated upon his throne with twelve other jars filled with pure water.
Likewise, he should place twelve cows with their calves, along with bronze milking vessels,
possessing milk and being of good temperament, in the presence of the deity.
Alternatively, in the event of a lack of wealth, a man may establish the three lineages;
however, he should give [the offerings] properly to a devoted person, for there is a lack of capacity in that regard for one who possesses [only] what is necessary.
Even a single gift of his, endowed with supreme qualities, becomes twelvefold; for whatever a person is able to give according to the power of his own wealth, [it yields great fruit].
One should present all of that, including household utensils, gifts, umbrellas, shoes, and sandals, in the presence of the twice-born and the deity.
One should perform all acts of giving, such as the counting of cows and so forth, for that [deity];
when, through such giving, a single cow is empowered by one's capacity.
She, together with the calf, should be worshipped and made complete;
she should have horns of gold, hooves of silver, and be adorned with bells and ornaments.
One should worship her, dressed in garments of that same color, together with the calf;
having thus completed the rite according to the prescribed method, including the bathing, worship, and other ceremonies, all at once.
Out of devotion to the gods and the Brahmins, one should then ask forgiveness from the Brahmins:
"O Lord, O Brahmin, please accept this along with my wife."
Having thus invoked that brahmin, one should offer everything to him;
for both the recipient and the giver are Viṣṇu, just as they are when observing a vow.
"O best of the twice-born, please accept all this which has been given by me."
The mantra for giving:
"The giver is the Blessed Viṣṇu, and ultimately the recipient is that very same Viṣṇu."
Therefore, all this which was given by you has indeed been accepted by me for the sake of merit.
This is the mantra of the Brahmins:
"At that time, [gifts] are given according to one's ability even to others—to the poor, the blind, the wretched, and so forth; that is remembered as having inexhaustible fruit."
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; thus one shall obtain the full fruit. This is recorded as the ritual for the conclusion of the vow of unbroken observance.
I have told this to you, my child; now hear the fruit of that merit.
As long as the world, with its oceans, mountains, and earth, exists, so long does his lineage continue to enjoy the fruits of merit;
for that long, he does not turn away from the abode of Viṣṇu.
And at the end, it goes to dissolution in Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self.
Thus concludes the procedure for the observance of Akhaṇḍa-dvādaśī;
for that merit is difficult for men to attain, yet it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
having been obtained in former times by Nārada from the presence of the Discus-wielder (Viṣṇu).
And the supreme *vyūha* vessel was spoken of by the Lord himself;
therefore, tell that to me, O Guru, and grant me your favor.
Markaṇḍeya said: In ancient times, Viṣṇu, residing on Śvetadvīpa, was propitiated with devotion by the gods, asuras, and sages for sixty million years.
Being pleased with that celestial sage, the wielder of the conch, discus,
and mace appeared and spoke these words to Nārada, the best of sages.
Speak, O Nārada, divine sage; I am the granter of boons to you, O sinless one. Whatever boon has been long desired by you from my presence, [ask for it].
Nārada said:
O Lord, the Vedas, the Śāstras, the Vedāṅgas,
and the Dharmaśāstras have been thoroughly studied by me in the presence of the Lotus-born One.
Indeed, I have never heard that in the worship of the gods, this is not the most excellent;
nor have I heard of the extraction of the principles (tattvas) and likewise the worship of the limbs (aṅgas).
O Lord Kṛṣṇa, if you have compassion for me, O Master, then tell me of that sacrifice and its power which bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation within the sacrifice itself.
The Blessed Lord said:
First, O Sage, listen with a focused mind as I describe the pavilion (maṇḍapa),
entering which a person goes to that supreme abode of mine.
If someone’s auspicious fortnight falls on the eleventh lunar day, having fasted thereon,
he should perform the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice when there is a conjunction with a male asterism and a favorable lagna.
My worship should be performed on the bright fortnights of Phālguna and Āṣāḍha, on the full moon of Kārttika, during an eclipse, on the Ekādaśī, or on the two Saṅkrāntis.
And just as one [should teach] a disciple who has approached, who is faithful, whose senses are conquered,
who seeks the welfare of all beings, who is devoted to the Brahmins, and who has been well-tested;

A sacrifice that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation should be performed only for one who is devoted to Śiva, whose mind is steady, who is non-violent, and who has conquered the self— not for one who is fickle-minded, violent, or of unsubdued soul.
My sacrifice must not be given to anyone who merely requests it;
rather, for the sake of the sacrifice, one should first examine the ground to ensure it is endowed with good qualities and slopes toward the northeast.
One should first consecrate her with mantras, and thereafter construct a pavilion;
[the ground] which is crowded with charcoal, husks, hair, bones, anthills, and worms.
One should carefully avoid ground that is thorny or saline;
indeed, one should reject soil that is blue, yellow, red, or black in color.

An Ācārya who is a Vaiṣṇava and a knower of Yoga is worthy to perform the sacrifice. One should abandon from afar all such teachers who are attached to other doctrines, who are Śūdras born of mixed castes, who are deceitful, and who perform improper acts.
Then the preceptor, having donned the Vaiṣṇava armor that bestows fearlessness, should properly construct the pavilion that grants liberation.
First, one should draw a square city within the image;
it should be provided with four doors and auspiciously marked with the syllable *khāṃ* at the center.
In its center stands a circular lotus with eight petals;
it is golden-yellow and adorned with red filaments.
One should color the city-gates white and the corners red;
one should place four smooth conch shells at the corners of the lotus.
One should fill the space between the city and the lotus with red flowers;
then, remaining restrained in speech, the man should draw the weapons of the lords of the directions.
One should assign the vajra, śakti, staff, sword, noose, banner, mace,
and trident to the lords of the directions in their respective quarters.
One should place the imperishable principle known as Vāsudeva—
the great Lord, resembling pure crystal— within the pericarp, along with the [syllables of] the colors and so forth.
In the aforementioned interval, there resides on the eastern petal the red-colored syllable,
which is the principle (tattva) of Saṅkarṣaṇa, worshipped throughout all the worlds.
One should point out that [deity] on the southeastern petal, joined with the first vowel (A) and the Bindu, possessing the luster of pure gold, and facing the east.
Likewise, the first [syllable] with the visarga, joined with *bhinnāñjana*;
and the seventh letter from the letter *kha*, adorned with a bindu in the southern direction.
One should place the reality known as Nārāyaṇa on the petal in the south-western direction;
it is the all-pervading reality consisting of Brahman, red in name and having the luster of a flower.
And on the northeastern petal, one should worship Vāmana, the imperishable reality;
these nine forms, O ascetic, end with the word "namaḥ."
The nine principles are well-known and designated as the "Ninefold Array" (Navavyūha);
O best of beings, these are the primary limbs of this Navavyūha.
One should properly assign the enjoyment of vehicles and weapons as directed;
[and likewise] Vainateya, Garuḍa, the unsurpassed king of birds.
One should assign the two doors of the pavilion in the east and likewise in the west;
[with the syllables] *taṃ*, *thaṃ*, *raṃ*, *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, one should assign the wheel venerated by the three worlds.
One should place the great hero Sudarśana on the south of the pedestal;
[the syllables] Khaṃ Dhaṃ Phaṃ Yaṃ Kṣaṃ represent the goddess Gadā, and Maṃ Śaṃ represent the invincible Śakti.
One should place [the deity] at the northern gate, and likewise at the eastern and western gates,
[visualizing him as] the powerful Mahāśaṅkha, with the luster of a lotus stalk or silver.
In the western part of the pedestal, one should designate Pāñcajanya;
[and] the goddess Śrī with a lotus in her hand, accompanied by the utterance of Svāhā and adorned with a lotus.
One should place this Parākāntī on the left and on the right of the pedestal;
and [one should construct] the pavilion which bestows the strength of the vigor of the sixty-four beings.
One should place the eternal shadow of Gaṇeśa to the north of the pedestal;
and this excellent garland of blossoming flowers is for my adornment.
One should place in the western part of the pedestal, in my presence:
*kṣataṃ*, *kṣatraṃ*, *vavaṃ*, *rukṣaṃ*, and the Kaustubha, which is my ornament.
O best of sages, one should place there in the west that great serpent Maṃ,
Yaṃ, Śaṃ, who possesses great enjoyment and is adorned with the jewels of his hoods.
One should also point out that he is the support of all the worlds;
these nine limbs of mine are with form, according to their sequence.
O best of beings, one should properly worship the ninefold array (navavyūha) and likewise the limbs (aṅga) within the center of the pedestal and outside the lotus, as previously described.
Above, a canopy was adorned with banners,
and two mirrors were decorated as beautifully as possible with garlands of flowers.
Having thus worshipped me there, the preceptor, surrounded by his disciples,
should then proceed to the blazing sacrificial fire-pit accompanied by the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having settled me [within himself] and having honored his disciples and the sacrificial fire,
he should offer oblations of sesame seeds soaked in rice and ghee with the root mantra.
O Sage, having offered one hundred and eight, a thousand, or even a hundred oblations for the sake of purifying the bodies of the disciples, [one should impart] the Vaiṣṇava samaya.

Having offered one hundred oblations for each of the personified forms of the Navavyūha and for each of the limbs in their respective order, he should further offer eight additional oblations for each individually.
Having offered either one hundred thousand or one thousand oblations according to the eightfold ritual procedure,
one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), especially at the conclusion.
When the great sacrifice is completed, for the sake of pleasing the inhabitants of the three heavens,
one should then perform the *vasordhārā* rite in the brightly blazing sacrificial enclosure.
With the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, and the tones of mṛdaṅgas and paṇavas,
people skilled in narration should keep watch throughout the night.
Having completed the sacrifice according to the rules and having accumulated a great store of wealth,
he should then worship with devotion his guru who bestowed the initiation.
O Sage, he who reveals the partless, vast wealth of knowledge is indeed to be honored as a guru, just as I am.
Having properly received initiation from a guru, or having attained knowledge that reveals Me,
he who does not bow down to the guru is a sinner and shall go to hell.
Therefore, having bowed with one's head, one should offer a teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā),
consisting of land, water, a cow, gold, grain, garments, and ornaments.
Having offered everything— himself, his wealth, and his home— to the guru,
he should likewise act in such a way that mutual affection for the guru is produced.
When his guru is well-pleased, I am pleased; of this there is no doubt. But when the guru is deeply insulted and greatly enraged, I too am insulted.
Then, O sweet-spoken one, grains, food, and edibles should be given without restriction to cows, buffaloes,
and those in the fourth stage of life out of devotion.
The man who causes my sacrifice to be performed, the devoted person who knows [this],
and he whose soul is purified by seeing [it]— he goes to my abode.
O son, this sacrifice, which is of great merit and the destroyer of great sins, as well as the Ninefold Array (Navavyūha), has been taught to you; it grants liberation from saṃsāra.
Having entered that sacrifice which consists of the ninefold array from its very beginning,
the man who has become purified dissolves into me, [freed] from the flood of suffering of birth.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus, O Kapiñjala, this most secret knowledge of the ninefold manifestation was spoken by Vāsudeva to the high-souled Nārada.
Those men are beasts in this world; what fruit is there in their lives, by whom initiation has not been received or Janārdana has not been worshipped?
In this most terrible saṃsāra, crowded with the diseases of birth,
he alone is truly fortunate who worships Janārdana.
He alone is successful in this world, and by him the lineage is truly adorned—
he by whom Viṣṇu has been propitiated, the support of all the worlds.
Thus, those men on earth who perform this great sacrifice to Viṣṇu go to the eternal, supreme state of Viṣṇu’s bliss.
Thus ends the worship of the nine manifestations as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Skanda said:
[I shall describe] Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods, Janārdana, seated in Vaikuṇṭha.
Having bowed his head with devotion, Prahlāda, the best of the Daityas, [spoke].
O Vāsudeva, Lord of the World, bestower of boons upon your devotees;
for I have indeed been questioned by men regarding the auspicious and inauspicious destinies of the worlds.
O Lord of Gods, by what karma do some men become fortunate while others become unfortunate; how is it that some possess beautiful forms while others are devoid of beauty?
When all of them questioned me thus, O Janārdana, Prahlāda, the best of the Daityas, bowed his head with devotion and said: "I do not know."
O Vāsudeva, Lord of the World, bestower of fearlessness upon devotees!
Having taken leave of all people, I have come into your presence.
Thus, all that belongs to people as well as to me itself comes from that.
The Blessed One said:
"O dear one, formerly in the Kṛta age, there was no splendor in the fire-god;
his body had been disfigured by the curse of a Brāhmaṇa."
Then all the hosts of gods, together with the ṛṣis and kinnaras,
tormented by that grief, went to Brahmā for refuge.
The gods said:
"O God of gods, Creator of the world, Great-grandfather of the worlds!
Because of the curse of the twice-born, the Eater of Oblations is no longer offered oblations in sacrifices."
Brahmā said:
"In former times, there was a vow known as Antilāhī;
by means of that vow, O Lord of the Gods, you must impel the Fire-god."
"By the power of this vow, the sacrificial fire shall be offered with oblations.
Having said, "So be it," those gods caused Agni to undertake the vow.
From that time forward, he was offered oblations in sacrifices as before,
and Brahmā himself appointed him to the status of a world-protector.
Even so, Tiladāhī alone is celebrated among the deities in heaven;
likewise, O Lord of Daityas, you too should go quickly among the people.
Prahlāda said:
By what rite should this most excellent vow, the "Burning of Sesame" (tiladāhī), be performed? In which month and on which lunar day should it be observed, and by what procedure should it be done?
The Blessed Lord said:
On that auspicious eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of the dark fortnight in the month of Pauṣa,
one should fast, perform ablutions, and then chant the name of Nārāyaṇa.
Having gathered cow dung under the Puṣya asterism,
one should fashion balls mixed with sesame seeds and meditate upon the Lord Janārdana.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to one's ability with mantras originating from the Agamas;
and one should have a mandala of Viṣṇu constructed, having placed water-pots (kumbhas) in the four directions.
To the north, one should place seven types of grain, garments, and fruits;
and upon a measure of sesame seeds, the deity together with Śrī, fashioned from gold.
One should place Nārāyaṇa on the feet, Viṣṇu in the form of the knees; one should place Trikrama on the thighs and Trailokyamūrti on the penis.
One should meditate on the god Śrīdhara at the hips, Padmanābha in the region of the navel,
Narasiṃha on the abdomen, and Vaikuṇṭha in the region of the throat.
One should recognize the Universal Commonality in the two arms, the Manifest Form in the face,
the Lamp of Saṃsāra in the eyes, and likewise the Soul of All in the head.
Having thus performed the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should fashion the mantra-body;
having performed worship according to the rules, one should then offer and worship the water of honor (arghya).
O Lord of Daityas, endowed with fruits and jewels, and perfumed with flowers, incense, and the like, I then brought you satisfaction by means of this mantra.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, you are compassionate, the destroyer of the flood of all sins;
grant me beauty and good fortune, and grant me heaven and liberation.
"To those men who perform the vow known as 'the burning of sesame seeds,' I am always the granter of boons; I bestow upon them abundant prosperity."
Having thus heard this and paid homage to Janārdana, the lord of the Daityas went to where he stood upon the ground in the midst of the thronging people.
The worlds said:
"O Lord of Daityas, tell us what occurred as it was related by the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu),
when you were questioned by him previously for the benefit of the worlds, and likewise here."
Prahlāda said:
"O people, alas! For your sake I went where Keśava was;
my most terrible and dreadful suffering was crushed by the wielder of the discus."
I shall relate the decision as it was instructed by Your Majesty;
thereafter, the Danava indeed gave a detailed exposition in the world.
By the power of this vow, manhood is produced;
one is born there free from old age and does not experience suffering.
Their desires are perfectly fulfilled, and they are endowed with sons and grandsons; among the people, women always enjoy freedom from widowhood and the quality of chastity arises.
In this way, she attains complete nirvāṇa through oneness with her husband;
first, this was accomplished by Śacī, the virtuous wife of Indra.
This entire vow was likewise performed by Anasūyā and Arundhatī, as well as by Sītā;
and by Draupadī, it has been observed throughout her entire life.
Happiness, health, sovereignty, and the granting of beauty, good fortune, and intelligence—
all this was accomplished by the princess of Pañcāla through her recitation of the Sandhyā hymn.
Then that illustrious wife of Viṣṇu asked all of that:
"O auspicious one, O friend of virtuous vows, tell me about the Tiladāhī vow."
"Tell me truly the ritual procedure and the concluding rite as well.
Draupadī then related the sequence of the ritual for this vow.
Likewise, on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of the dark fortnight in the month of Pauṣa,
one should fast and then perform a ritual bath according to the prescribed rules.
Having resolved upon silence and having meditated upon the Ancient Supreme Person,
one should then perform worship with mantras originating from one's own tradition.
Having offered the *arghya* according to the prescribed rite, one should offer praise again and again.
O virtuous lady, listen with a focused mind as I describe the procedure for the concluding ceremony (*udyāpana*).
One should worship the maṇḍala of Tilaprasthoparideva, who possesses glory and is born of gold, with garments, ornaments, and fruits.
Four jars, together with cloths, should be placed outside the pavilion;
seven kinds of grain should be placed in the north, and one should cause the fire-oblation (homa) to be performed in the east.
One should worship the teacher, together with his wife, with flowers and other offerings,
as well as with garments, ornaments, flowers, and various kinds of excellent fruits.
O auspicious lady, O fair-hipped one, whoever performs this— whether a woman or even a man—
should give a cow along with a sacrificial fee every single year.
Those men who properly perform the Tiladāhī vow attain incomparable good fortune and are born with beautiful limbs.
Whoever always performs this vow in detail, together with its concluding rite, with devotion, shall indeed go to the city of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O blessed lady, whether it be a woman or even a man who performs this,
he shall attain the supreme state, which is enriched with all desires.
Thus ends the vow of the giver of sesame seeds as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Maitreya said:
Listen, O Indra among kings, to the procedure as it was observed by the wise sages;
one who has fasted on the eleventh day should perform the prescribed observance exactly as stated.
Having first taken up a tooth-stick, with speech restrained and senses controlled,
one should fast on the occasion of Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī and [worship] Janārdana.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, I shall eat on the following day;
one should bathe at the confluence of rivers or wherever the mind finds delight.
A new, flawless golden water-pot, twelve finger-breadths in height and joined with red [threads],
should be wrapped in beautiful yellow cloths.
One should prepare the vessel for the *arghya* offering with a golden bowl,
containing curd, unbroken grains, and fruits, together with gold and sandalwood paste.
Salutations to you, O lotus-navelled one; salutations to you who recline upon the waters. I offer this water of honor (arghya) to you, who assumed the forms of Bāla and Vāmana.
Salutation to the wielder of the discus, who is clothed in pure garments yellow as the filaments of a lotus,
and who bears the discus upon his shoulder like that of the great enemy of Hara.
Salutation to Vāmana, who holds the Śārṅga bow, the sword, the conch, and the lotus in his hands;
salutation to the sacrifice, to the Lord of Sacrifice, and to the instrument of sacrifice.
Salutations again and again to Vāmana, the enjoyer of sacrifice and the giver of its fruits;
salutations to the Lord of gods, the Divine One, who brings about the manifestation of the gods.
Salutations again and again to the dwarf who is the source of all the gods;
salutations to him who takes the forms of the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, and the Man-lion.
Salutations again and again to Vāmana, who is more delightful than Rāma and even to Rāma himself;
salutations to you, Śrīdhara; salutations to you, whose banner bears Garuḍa.
"O Four-Armed One, homage be to you; homage to you, O Supporter of the Earth!
Having thus worshipped according to the ritual with garlands, sandalwood, and other offerings, the man [attains his goal]."
One should keep a vigil at night before the Lord who reclines upon the waters,
having assumed the watery form of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods.
May that Lord of the World, the master of illusion, the dwarf, the glorious Lord, whose belly contains the cosmic egg presided over by the great elements, come here.
Having thus performed the worship on the twelfth day at the rising of the sun,
one should continue to worship for a full year, providing a garment along with a water-pitcher.
"May Vāmana accept; I, being Vāmana, give him back.
One should offer Vāmana, who is auspicious in every way, for the sake of victory."
Likewise, O King, one should give a water-cow, as well as an umbrella and sandals;
along with gold, garments, a cow, or an ox.
Whatever is given there at that time conduces to infinity,
having worshipped the one whose banner is Garuḍa on the occasion of the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī conjunction.
Having given gifts to the twice-born, one should then perform the breaking of the fast during the separation [of the eclipse],
when the sun is situated in Leo and the moon is in Śravaṇā.
The Śravaṇa-dvādaśī should be known as not occurring outside of the month of Bhādrapada;
that lunar day on which the tenth overlaps with the eleventh is one that must be observed as a fast.
But that auspicious [tenth lunar day], when conjoined with Śravaṇā, grants all desires;
the meaning is that even that tenth day joined with Śravaṇā is to be observed as a fast.
However, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) occurs on the twelfth day when there is an increase in the lunar day (tithi), due to the disappearance of the constellation.
If [the asterism] increases, one should perform [the fast-breaking] on the thirteenth day; no fault is found therein.
When the asterism is equal in duration to the twelfth day, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is on the twelfth, meaning that if it extends further, it is on the thirteenth.
Thus, O King, this [observance] regarding the twelfth day and the Śravaṇa asterism has been described.
That [practice], which bestows fruits both in this world and the next, should be performed with diligent effort.
Thus ends the Vijayā-dvādaśī vow in the Agni Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the procedure for the Dvādaśī [conjoined] with Śravaṇa has been declared.
It pacifies all sins and bestows all happiness.
When the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) is conjoined with the Śravaṇa nakṣatra, it is declared to be Vijayā; that lunar day bestows victory upon devotees.
In ancient times, Nārada, together with Viṣṇu, Candra, Agni, and Anila, was entreated by all the hosts of gods assembled there seeking a boon.
The powerful Daitya named Bali, possessed of great strength, was conquered;
by him, all the hosts of gods were deprived of their celestial abode.
You are the refuge of all the gods; deliver us quickly!
O mighty-armed one, slay the Daitya Bali, the foremost among the powerful.
Having heard those words of the gods, which portended a terrible outcome, Viṣṇu,
the knower of speech, spoke these words out of a desire for the welfare of the gods.
I know Bali, the son of Virocana, who is a thorn to the three worlds,
yet whose self is purified by austerity, who is peaceful, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses.
My devotee, whose life-breath is dedicated to me, who is true to his word, possessed of great strength,
equal to Prajāpati in renown, and a doer of what is pleasing to all creatures.
Indeed, his virtues cannot be described by anyone on this earth;
therefore, one must certainly partake of the fruit of austerity until it is fully realized.
And at the end of his ascetic penance, after a long time, it will come to pass;
then, after a great deal of time has passed, that Aditi shall become pregnant.
In the ninth month, she gave birth to a son who was Hari in the form of a child—
small-limbed, small-bodied, with a large head, and a mere infant.
Seeing that he had become a dwarf with thin hands, feet, and belly, and with two small thighs and necks, Aditi’s mind was struck with wonder.
Fear arose among the Daityas, while joy manifested among the gods;
for his birth-rites and other purificatory ceremonies were indeed performed spontaneously.
And the wise Kaśyapa, endowed with the nature of Prajāpati,
acted as the staff-bearing ascetic for those wearing the sacrificial thread, having girded himself with a waist-belt.
Wearing kusha grass, skins, and deerskins, and adorned with a water-pot,
he went to the extensive sacrifice of the powerful Bali.
Seeing Bali performing the sacrifice, Vāmana approached him at that very moment and said:
"O Lord of Sacrifice, I have a purpose; let the earth be given to me."
"Indeed, you stand here for the purpose of recitation by means of the measure of three steps;
the sacrificial offering has been given, it has been given," Bali said to the best of the twice-born.
Then Vāmana, of infinite prowess, began to speak,
planting his feet upon the earth and covering heaven and earth with his head.
At his navel he saw the worlds beginning with Indra, and at his forehead the station of Brahmā;
he found no third station, whereupon the inhabitants of heaven raised a shout.
Beholding that great marvel, the Siddhas and other sages, filled with joy, praised the Lord of Gods, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Then all the hosts of Daityas, having conquered the three worlds and brought them under their control, said to Bali: "Go below, along with your army and your mounts, and dwell there in happiness."
There, protected by my arm, you shall enjoy all desired pleasures;
and at the end of this Indra’s term, you yourself shall become Indra.
Thus addressed, Bali departed after paying homage to the Supreme among Men;
having dismissed Bali, he spoke to the guardians of the worlds of the gods.
"Go to your own abodes and remain free from anxiety.
Thus addressed by the Lord, the gods, having honored Vāmana, departed filled with joy.
Having spoken thus, the Creator of the World vanished right there;
all this occurred on the eleventh day, O lord of men.
Therefore, O King, this very day in the month of Phālguna, conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, is entirely victorious for the God of Gods.
The virtuous declare that Vijayā is superior by millions upon millions of times;
this very Ekādaśī of the bright fortnight is considered supreme.
On the eleventh day, one who has observed a fast should worship Hari at night.
Either in a vessel made of silver or gold, or even one made of wood or bamboo.
Having covered the bowl with unwashed garments and fruits,
and with a leather strap and perfumes, out of devotion or according to one's capacity.
Those with abundant wealth should offer an *āḍhaka* of sesame seeds, or a *prastha*, or even a *kuḍava*;
in their absence, it may be made with barley, wheat, fruits, or white sesame seeds.
One should worship Hari with flowers, perfumes, fruits, and incense appropriate for the season,
as well as with various kinds of food offerings, both solid and soft, and rice mixed with jaggery.
According to one's own means, one should have it made along with gold;
for one who possesses the mantra, it is a hundredfold [meritorious], and through devotion, it is a hundred-thousandfold superior.
Endowed with devotion and the qualities of mantra, and possessing millions upon millions of superior virtues,
one should worship the one whose banner is Garuḍa there with these mantra-words.

O best of men, having become pure and composed, [worship him] with offerings: "Oṃ! Salutations to you, O Puruṣottama, whose body is like water, whose face is born from the water, who bears the conch, and whose very nature is the mass of waters."
Homage to the one whose navel is a lotus; homage to you who recline upon the waters;
homage to you, Keśava, Ananta, Vāsudeva; let there be homage to you.
The bathing mantra: O Supreme Lord, accept this [bath] offered by me— produced in Malaya, rich in fragrance, and most enchanting.
The Sandalwood Mantra:
O Supreme Person, accept this flower offered by me, which has arisen from the Lord of Forests, rich in fragrance and most enchanting.
The Flower Mantra:
Homage to the Wielder of the Discus, whose garment is as pure and yellow as the filaments of a lotus,
and whose discus rubs against the shoulders of his enemies in the great battle.
The worship mantra:
I worship Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Paraśurāma, and Kṛṣṇa; salutations, salutations!
This is the mantra for worship:
"O Lord of the gods, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, this is incense; first there is the worship of the feet and so forth, then the head, and thereafter the worship of all limbs."
O Acyuta, O Ānanda, O Govinda, O Vāsudeva, homage be to you!
The incense mantra:
You alone are the earth, light, wind, and space;
you alone are the light of lights—may this lamp be accepted.
The lamp mantra:
"O God, O Supreme Lord, be gracious; this fourfold food, endowed with the six flavors, is offered by me."
May Agni, Yama, and Vaiśravaṇa destroy my sin, which is inexhaustible.
The mantra for the food offering (naivedya):

May Janārdana, the beginning of the world, whose form is the world, who is indeed without beginning, the ender of the world, and the source of the world and the reservoir of waters, be pleased with me.
The mantra for propitiation:
I bow to Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, who dwells in Mathurā, who destroys the persistence of manifold karmas, and who reclines upon the waters.
Homage to you in the form of the Dwarf; homage be to you, O Trivikrama!
Homage to you, Maṇibandha; O Vāsudeva, homage be to you!
The mantra of salutation:
*Namaḥ*, obeisance to you, O Govinda, O Vāmana, O Lord Trivikrama!
Having brought about the destruction of the multitude of sins, be the granter of all desires.
The prayer mantra:
Salutations again and again to the all-pervading Lord of all gods, the bearer of Śrī, the abode of Śrī, to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe, who reclines upon Śrī.
The mantra for the resting place:
O best of kings, on the eleventh day of the night, one should worship everything;
there, one should perform a vigil with the sounds of songs and musical instruments.
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is the supreme tithi for those engaged in the hearing of the *Yāśrava*;
by bathing at its confluence, one is liberated from all sins.
Having thus made this vow, O King, when the morning has become clear, the gift should be bestowed according to the mantra upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the scriptures.
And the Brāhmaṇa, knowing the mantras, should accept it with the mantra;
the giver is Vāmana, the bestower of intelligence, while the recipient himself is Vāmana established in the sacrificial materials.

[The mantra: "O you who accept from Vāmana, may this be for Vāmana. [1144] *Oṃ* to the secret place; *Oṃ* to the head. One should offer all these—flowers, incense, and food offerings—according to the ritual procedure of worship.
Having thus fasted on the eleventh day according to the rule, accompanied by mantras.
And according to the previously mentioned procedure, the counter-measure is likewise terrifying.
One who is a donor of elephants, horses, and chariots, an enjoyer [of such gifts], and free from envy,
shall be endowed with beauty and good fortune, long-lived, and victorious.
Surrounded by sons, the living soul shall live for a hundred autumns;
this is the reward of Ekādaśī that has been declared to you by me.
The twelfth lunar day conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism has already been fully described;
having fasted on the eleventh day, one should subsequently fast on the twelfth as well.
And in this case, there would be no omission of the prescribed rule (*vidhilopa*), because Hari is the deity for both [Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī].

Whether on Ekādaśī or Dvādaśī, or on either one joined with the Śravaṇa asterism, by fasting on that which is joined with Śravaṇa alone, the fulfillment of both vows is achieved. The meaning is that the "omission of the rule"—which consists in fasting on a different lunar day after first fasting on one vow and subsequently not performing the concluding rite (*apārana*)—does not occur when the deity is one.
[Furthermore,] Dvādaśī joined with Wednesday and Śravaṇa is *saṅgamodaka*.
Bathing, curd-rice, and fasting properly constitute the supreme rule.
O Indra among kings, Sagara, Kakutstha, Dhundhumāra, Gādhi,
and these and others have observed the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) according to their desire.
That twelfth day, joined with Mercury and occurring together with the Śravaṇa asterism in the month of Nabhasya, is declared by the sages to be called Jāyā;
having fasted upon it with devotion, a man attains immortality.
O Pārtha, he attains that which is endowed with the qualities of aṇimā and the rest.
Thus ends the vow of Vijayā-dvādaśī and Śravaṇa-dvādaśī in the glorious Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
On the eleventh day, as prescribed, the Viśvedevas were duly worshipped.
They bestow progeny, cattle, wealth, grain, and likewise land.
The root mantra is proclaimed by its own names as the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra).
As before, the Lord of the Lunar Days (tithīśvara) should be placed upon a lotus petal.
In this rite, the Viśvedevas are the lords of the lunar days (tithīśvara).
Worship is prescribed with offerings of perfumes, flowers, and food according to one's capacity; indeed, even if performed with deceit or hypocrisy, it yields fruit.
A fire-oblation performed with a stream of clarified butter, fuel-sticks, curd, milk, rice, and honey,
while the mind is tranquil, yields the same results as those previously described.
This vow is to be explained like the Vaiśvānarapratipad-vow. Thus ends the Viśva-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa:
"Having committed very great sin, whether knowingly or even unknowingly..."
For the sake of pacifying that evil, what gift should be given, or what vow should be undertaken?
Brahmā said: O child, I shall proclaim to you this great vow, which destroys all sins and bestows happiness, fame, and wealth.
When the twelfth day of the bright fortnight coincides with the Puṣya asterism,
it is declared by Vāsudeva to be the destroyer of all sins.
Those men who, having fasted, worship the god Janārdana there with devotion,
are liberated from the sins born of a hundred lifetimes.
Whatever evil has been accumulated through action, mind, or speech—
that Govinda washes away when he is duly worshipped on that lunar day.
O Govinda, when he is duly honored on that lunar day, it washes away [all sins];
whether it be bathing, recitation, or fire-offering performed with Janārdana in mind.
Whatever is performed by men on that [day], its fruit shall be final;
for it destroys the sins of a living being arising from hundreds of births.
Therefore, the Ekādaśī falling on the Puṣya asterism is declared to be the destroyer of sins;
thus indeed did Bhānu formerly speak to his charioteer.
Bhānu said:
"Or else, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) that is joined with the Puṣya asterism of the Sun is superior;
indeed, this sin-destroying twelfth day should be observed with diligent effort."
The twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna joined with the Puṣya asterism was indeed declared by Viṣṇu himself in the past to be that Jayā-dvādaśī.
Whatever gift is given or austerity performed on that day yields millions upon millions times more merit. One should remain without food on the eleventh day and worship Viṣṇu on the twelfth.
In a vessel made of silver or gold, or even one made of wood or bamboo,
having covered the vessel with unwashed, well-examined cloths;
Success shall be achieved through paths and even through the urethra, depending on one's capacity;
by those with abundant wealth, it may be done with a *droṇa* of sesame seeds, or with a *prastha*, or even with a *kaṭaja*.
In the absence of these, the primary fruit is obtained through wheat; it may also be achieved with sesame seeds.
One should worship Hari with flowers, incense, fruits, and fragrances appropriate to the season.
One should keep a vigil there with various kinds of sacrificial offerings, foods to be chewed and eaten, and rice with molasses, accompanied by the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
When dawn has thus become clear for this person who maintains the observances,
one should cause [the gift] to be given with devotion or according to the extent of one's wealth, together with gold.
O Brahmin, O lord of sages, O sky-traveler, learn from me the merit that accrues when a vow is completed: it is equal to seventy-one cycles of four yugas.
For that long, he sports there in Viṣṇu’s city for imperishable time.
Thus ends the vow of Vijayā-dvādaśī as declared in the Āditya Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
When Punarvasu occurs on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, [that is the time for this vow].
By name she is known as Tijayā, the most excellent among all lunar days (tithis).
O King, he who gives a prastha of sesame seeds three times a day for a year,
and he who, having come there, observes a fast on that same day— these two are equal.
In that [place], Hari, the Lord of the universe, the God and Sovereign of all worlds, becomes manifest before one's eyes; therefore, it is remembered that the fruit there is infinite.
By Sagara, Kakutstha, Dhundhumāra, and Gādhi,
Kṛṣṇa was propitiated on that [island], and he granted them the entire earth.
Thus ends the vow of the Ekādaśī of Ativijaya as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:
"O Janārdana, regarding the twelfth days (dvādaśīs) of the dark fortnight alone—"
O knower of Dharma, from what time onwards, and by what rite, should one worship?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, once the full moon day of Māgha has passed, this vow should be observed by one who has fasted on whichever twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) follows thereafter.
And on the dark twelfth days (dvādaśīs), one should proclaim the name of Kṛṣṇa;
with that very name, one should likewise perform the recitation (japa) and the fire-oblation (homa).
The offering should be made with sesame seeds, and likewise the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with sesame seeds;
this is when the full moon of the month of Pauṣa has passed and the twelfth lunar day of the dark fortnight occurs.
At the conclusion of that vow, O protector of the earth, one should give sesame seeds, gold, and likewise red garments to the twice-born.
O bull among men, having observed this vow for a year,
one does not fall into the womb of an animal but goes to the heavenly world.
O best of men, he who, being composed, observes this vow for as long as life lasts, does not experience the suffering of hell.
Where the Vaitaraṇī river is difficult to cross, with razor-sharp edges and mountains,
and where it purifies the wicked— there he shall not go.
Her hosts are of terrible strength, most fierce, with faces made formidable by fangs and hands grasping sharp weapons;
they are the ones who put to flight the men who commit evil deeds.
They do not follow the path of that vision today.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇadvādaśī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:
"By fasting on a single Kṛṣṇadvādaśī according to the prescribed rite, a man..."
One obtains great fruit; tell me that, O Mārgava.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the month of Mādhava has passed, that twelfth day of the dark fortnight which is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism is called Tiladvādaśī.
One should perform the ritual bath with sesame seeds, the fire oblation with sesame seeds, the food offering with sesame-sweetmeats,
the lamps with sesame oil, and likewise offer water mixed with sesame seeds.
O King, sesame seeds should be given to Brahmins on that day;
O King, on the day of fasting, sesame seeds should likewise be offered as oblations.
Having fasted, on the following day one should especially offer oblations;
likewise, O sinless one, fuel should be provided to the Brahmins.
Having then offered a prastha of sesame seeds while fasting and with senses subdued, one does not fall into an evil rebirth; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
That supreme, eternal mantra of Viṣṇu is proclaimed as the Soma-mantra;
likewise, it is joined with the Puruṣa-sūkta and the Śrī-sūkta.
Then, O Indra among kings, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed for Sāvitrī, the Supreme Self.
This has been declared for the twice-born; now hear what applies to women and Śūdras.
O lord of men, two twelve-syllable mantras have been proclaimed for those great-souled ones;
they are beneficial and are the best of mantras for the twice-born.
Indeed, there exists no mantra anywhere that is superior even to those.
Vajra said:
O sinless one, tell me the two mantras consisting of twelve and eight syllables—
those which are meritorious, purifying, auspicious, and destroyers of all sins.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Om, salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva; Om, salutation to Nārāyaṇa.
These two purifiers have been recounted by me to you.
They were masters of mantra, destroyers of sin upon the earth, the supreme refuge for all ascetics, and the most excellent of the excellent,
eternally so throughout the worlds.
Just as this guest of yours is endowed with the hearing [of the dharma] in the month of Māgha as described by me,
so too should she be treated with special care by the king.
In the purifying yoga of the one called Saritā.

Thus ends the description of the Tiladvādaśī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharma. O Bhārgava, best among the upholders of dharma, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight in the month of Phālguna, worship should be performed for the deity of the Vedic meters.
By this [lack of worship], the god becomes devoid of qualities, so that he does not obtain such pleasure from one possessed of virtues; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the vow of Kṛṣṇaikādaśī as spoken by Dharmottara.
Having likewise reached the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, one should worship;
having worshipped that most fortunate one, one attains the auspiciousness of the home.
"Tam" refers to the deity of the sacred syllable (*chanda*).
This concludes the vow for the "White Ekādaśī of Non-Widowhood" as described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Ahaṃkāra, Sūrya, Nirṛti, Vāpageśvara, Havaṇa,
Veśvara, Mṛtyu, Kapālaka, Kaṣa, and Kiṅkiṇī.
In that regard, he who, fasting on the eleventh day, likewise worships Soma along with the eleven gods who are the lords of the three worlds;
The excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense,
and food should be maintained from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa for as long as a year.
At the end of the year, he should give a milch cow to a Brāhmaṇa;
having performed this vow for a year, O King, a man attains the desired state of Rudra.
Having dwelt for a very long time together with Rudra,
one attains desires that are delightful to the mind.
Likewise, one should joyfully worship the all-pervading Rudras everywhere;
thus one attains all desires that are omnipresent and unconquered.
Thus ends the vow for the fulfillment of all desires as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Sanatkumāra said:
"If, in the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, there occurs a day sacred to Hari..."
And there, the conjunction of Mercury and Śravaṇa is attained and honored.
Vāmana grants all desired objects that dwell in the mind;
this lunar day is called Vijayā, which brings delight to Hari.
At that confluence, the union of all sacred fords occurs;
the Śukla [confluence] in the month of Bhādrapada leads to heaven, while the Kṛṣṇa [confluence] brings about the destruction of impurities.
In the month of Phālguna, one attains liberation and even the realization of Brahman at the meritorious confluence of the rivers Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Narmadā.
O twice-born one, at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the Aruṇā which destroys all evil,
or at Brahmavalmīka, Sābhrāma, or Saptadhāra;
At other confluences as well, the dwarf (Vāmana) comes of his own accord;
there, being duly worshipped, he becomes the bestower of liberation from the state of a preta.
One should cause a water-vessel filled with curd-rice to be given, saying:
"Worship the Lord of the World; may Vāmana be pleased."
For this Vijayā lunar day at the confluence is indeed the bestower of great merit;
by fasting on it, the destruction of all sins certainly occurs.
Having undertaken the vow, one should go in the morning to a confluence of rivers or similar places and fashion an image of Vāmana out of gold, or even with a single gold māṣaka.
Having installed the Lord of the World upon the water-pot according to one's ability,
and having bathed him in the vessel of fullness, one should worship him with these mantras.
Oṃ, one should worship Vāmana at the feet; Dāmodara at the waist; Śrīpati at the thighs; and Kāmadeva at the private parts.
One should worship the belly of the Lord of the worlds as "to the Sustainer of the Universe";
the heart as "to the Lord of Yogins"; and the throat as "salutation to the Lord of Śrī."
"Salutation to the face resting upon the lotus, and salutation to the head, the soul of all.
Having thus worshipped the Teacher of the World and having clothed him with garments, [he should proceed].
One should offer the respectful water (arghya) with great faith using coconuts and other fruits, [reciting]:
"Oṃ, salutations, salutations to you, Govinda, known by the name Budhaśravaṇa."
Having brought about the destruction of the flood of sins, become the bestower of liberation upon the preta.
This is the mantra for the purpose [of the rite]:
"One should give the gift of an umbrella, a pair of sandals, food, and a water-pot, especially to the foremost of the twice-born, saying: 'May Vāmana be pleased.'"
They praise the gift of a cow at the confluence of the world-protectors,
specifically at the junction of the sacred river, dedicated to the beloved of Kamalā.
They say there are three supreme gifts: cows, land, and Sarasvatī;
one who gives them here purifies even his lineage to the seventh generation through the knowledge of the Vedas.
One should cause gifts to be bestowed upon the foremost of the twice-born according to one's ability;
one should keep a vigil and perform songs accompanied by the sacred scriptures.
Endowed with supreme faith, gazing at the night with unblinking eyes, one should feed the Brahmins at dawn; thereafter, the breaking of the fast occurs on the twelfth day.
One should perform all three with faith, and everything shall attain fruition;
thus, when this Vijayā-vrata is performed on the day of victory (Jayā-dina).
Nothing whatsoever is more difficult to obtain in this world or in the next;
for men, victory is difficult to attain, and meeting with it there is even more difficult.
Faith in the worship of Govinda there is even more difficult to attain;
it flows like the confluence of all sacred fords at their most abundant meeting point.
On the day of victory, at the gathering of all the gods upon the earth,
there is also here the sin-destroying confluence of the Ramyodaka.
The fruit of this confluence of rivers cannot be fully described;
it is proclaimed as a secret in all the Purāṇas.
By worshipping Vāmana at the confluence, one does not become a preta;
the fruit of this vow is said to be the supreme deliverance of the gods and ancestors.
One attains liberation even after six months from [this practice] which uplifts one's lineage;
nothing purer than this is spoken of here.
Whatever else is obtained as equal to the Vijayā-vow consists of a left-handed consort (vāmā),
a dwarf (vāmana), a water-vessel, and four cows.
O dear one, by giving here at this confluence, one attains the same world as Viṣṇu;
through the performance of hospitality toward the gods, one becomes free from debt, even if done out of delusion.
Even while performing [the rites] for humans and ancestors according to the vow of victory,
whatever is done, given, or practiced as austerity is rendered fruitless by being performed without faith.
It becomes fruitless neither here nor after death;
faith is the daughter of Dharma, the goddess, and faith is the supreme means of accomplishment.
This person consists of faith; he who gives with faith is truly himself.
He who attains the goal through yoga reaches the same goal that is reached through the path of Sāṃkhya.
Whatever state one attains through sacrifices and charitable works, that same state is attained in the Kali age by worshipping Vāmana;
furthermore, his ancestors—both on the father’s and the mother’s side—are liberated from their lineage.
No states of existence as a preta arise in that lineage;
this is the supreme secret, the most purifying, proclaimed by sages within the collections of Purāṇas.
The virtuous, who are established in the Supreme Self, declare that the specific rite called Vijaya is [the means].
Thus ends the vow of Vijayā-dvādaśī as declared in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
The Goddess said:
"How is this Vaiṣṇava vow, which is dear to Viṣṇu, to be performed?"
One should perform a night vigil; tell me by what ritual procedure that should be done.
Īśvara said:
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
one should bathe in a river, a pond, a tank, a well, or even at home.
Having gone to a mountain or even to a forest where that auspicious one may be found;
for when the Ocean of Milk was being churned, a tree emerged.
O King, because it crushed the Daityas, that deity is remembered as Sāmalakī;
O King, Lakṣmī always resides in this tree, as if in her father’s house.
The tree in which Śiva and Lakṣmī reside is served by the best of gods;
indeed, that tree has been made Vaiṣṇava by all the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
Having gone there, Hari is to be worshipped at the foot of a tree, or else Śivā is to be worshipped with auspicious flowers; men should observe a vigil at night.
One should perform one hundred and eight circumambulations of it with fruits;
having thus circumambulated, men should then eat the fruit.
A water-pot filled with water should be prepared along with a vessel;
sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) should be prepared, and a lamp should be offered according to the prescribed rite.
Thus should vigilance be maintained by those intent on hearing [the teachings],
so that embodied beings are liberated from the sins born of the Kali age and produced by the body.
Those men who previously [performed these acts] are honored at the end of the body's life in the abode of Hari.

Thus concludes the Āmalakaikādaśī vow as declared in the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa. Now, O Sage, by what ritual procedure and with which mantras for milking cows do men quickly worship Hari so that He becomes pleased with them?
O Sage, in former times, while the Ocean of Milk was being churned by the gods and asuras,
five cows were born, who are the mothers of all the worlds.
For the sake of benefiting all the world, for the gratification of the gods,
for the successful completion of sacrifices, and likewise for Hari and Hara.
The six products of the cow— cow dung, bile, milk, urine, curd, and ghee— are pure and likewise bring about spiritual accomplishment.
O best of sages, by offering a tall hollow tree and cow dung, one obtains prosperity there;
for that reason, it is called the Śrīvṛkṣa (the tree of fortune).
From *gorocanā* were born the auspicious ones who fulfill all desires;
from cow’s urine was then born *guggulu*, which is of auspicious appearance.
Whatever vigor exists in the world, all that originates from milk;
everything born of curd is for the sake of accomplishing auspicious purposes.
Since the production of nectar from clarified butter is certainly dear to the gods and the asuras,
one should therefore bathe Hari well with milk, curd, and ghee.
One should burn guggulu resin with horses while reciting ancient mantras,
accompanied by various kinds of food offerings, lamps, and most beautiful garments.
Having thus performed the worship according to the prescribed rite, one should then gratify the Brahmins with munipuṣpa flowers for as many lunar days as there are here.
For as many thousands of aeons as there are syllables [in the mantra], he is glorified in the heavenly world;
thereafter, he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which he does not return again.
Those who are his ancestors, even if they have fallen into the ocean of hell,
having reached heaven, rejoice, freed from all suffering.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, O bull among sages, one should bestow upon the Brahmins, according to their order, a cow endowed with all excellent qualities, as is the custom.
According to this rule, for five days ending with the autumnal equinox,
a man should eat only one meal per day, consuming light food at the end of the day.
By giving water, clarified butter, honey, a cow, as well as sesame and gold,
one obtains merit that cannot be attained even by all the great sacrifices.
Whatever he does correctly while observing this supreme vow of great growth,
he is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
In this [work], having proclaimed the various deeds, there are mortals of great intelligence;
for those who desire a good rebirth, expiations have been prescribed.
O Sage, having committed sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, sexual intercourse with forbidden women, theft, or the drinking of liquor, one is liberated through [his] grace.
O Sage, by performing this pure vow after having sold sesame seeds or cows,
one is immediately liberated from the sin mentioned, simply through its recollection.
Or likewise, having fasted for twelve months on the eleventh day (ekādaśī),
whatever a wise man of purified soul performs, he shall become one who has fulfilled his purpose and be happy.
The Sunāma-dvādaśī should be honored with twelve names;
twelve cows should be given as gifts, for Hari grants all desires.
In heaven, the gods together with Indra, having performed manifold deeds,
subsequently propitiated Hari here by means of pure vows.
Thus ends the Śuddhivrata as declared in the Vahnipurāṇa:
"One who fasts on the eleventh day and worships Puruṣottama through the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa on the twelfth day shall go to the supreme abode."
This lunar day, belonging to the bright fortnight, is indeed sacred to Viṣṇu;
on that day, one should diligently worship the Lord Janārdana.
Thus ends the Dvādaśī vow as declared in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
By fasting on the eleventh day and worshipping Janārdana,
one is liberated from great sins on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
Thus ends the Dvādaśī vow as described in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"In the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), Viṣṇu was born as the Fish (Matsya) of great majesty; therefore, this lunar day is always dear to Him."
Having fasted on the eleventh day at the outset, one should recite the account of the Fish Incarnation;
then, while listening and having caused the golden mantra to be performed, one should speak as follows:
In the Viṣṇudharma: Having said, "May the Fish be pleased," one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa;
he who gives it, having become happy, shall go to the auspicious world of Viṣṇu.
In the month of Pauṣa, during the bright fortnight, on the twelfth day, that Blessed One was born in the form of a tortoise; therefore, this lunar day is always dear to him.
Having fasted on the eleventh day at the outset, and while reciting the *Kūrma* and *Tāraka* [mantras],
or listening to them, one should have a golden tortoise fashioned and say this:
Having said, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me, O Tortoise," he who gives [this] to a Brāhmaṇa becomes happy and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
That mortal who, especially on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
having fasted with devotion, worships a boar fashioned from gold;
On the day of the Boar’s birth, one endowed with faith should give and recite the supreme *Vārāha-carita* to a Brahmin.
Having encountered this [teaching], one rejoices for imperishable time;
and one attains the true pleasure of Viṣṇu as Varāha and of the Lord Kūrma, exactly as they are.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, one who is pure and observant of the vow should fast and worship Nārasiṃha with devotion on that day sacred to Nārasiṃha.
Having fashioned a golden image of Nṛsiṃha according to one's ability,
one should give it to a twice-born man while listening to or reciting this account of Nṛsiṃha’s deeds.
Having conquered his enemies here and attained prosperity, that best of men eternally reaches the underworld and heaven, accompanied by the women of the Nāgas and Daityas.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra,
one should worship Vāmana, the Supreme Person, on that day of Vāmana.
The man who gives a golden Vāmana image, or who recites this with devotion,
or who listens to this account of Vāmana while fasting for a long time, [attains the supreme goal].
Endowed with wealth, having enjoyed human pleasures here on earth,
he who is devoted to the Name attains the world of Brahmā and gains knowledge.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one who is pure should worship Jāmadagnya Rāma and give a golden [image] to a Brahmin.
And on the birth anniversary of Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, a twice-born man should either hear or read this account of Rāma’s life.
He who gives a golden image of Sītā and Rāma to a brāhmaṇa on the twelfth lunar day, while listening to or reciting this account of Rāma’s life;
By the very grace of Rāma, he attains the world of Indra;
in this world, he obtains fame, wealth, sons, and long life.
The twice-born who, having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āṣāḍha,
worships Rāma, the son of Rohiṇī, who possesses great strength, on the twelfth day;
On the excellent lunar day of Rāma’s birth, the son of Rohiṇī,
one should give a golden image of Rāma, together with a water-vessel, to a Brāhmaṇa.
He attains the world of the Nāgas for as long as fourteen Indras endure;
here on earth he enjoys the pleasures of women, becoming powerful and free from disease.
O twice-born one, he who, having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
worships the pure Kṛṣṇa together with Rukmiṇī on the twelfth day, [attains great merit].
Having fashioned an image of gold, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa;
and being pure, one should recite the life-story of Kṛṣṇa on the day of Kṛṣṇa’s birth.
Or whoever, O Supreme Person, should hear this in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
shall be liberated from this saṃsāra after having enjoyed supreme pleasures.
But he who, having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
should worship the golden Viṣṇu, the Imperishable Kāla;
On the twelfth lunar day, which is his birthday, Kalki Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods,
shall bestow that [fruit] upon a brāhmaṇa with joy through the performance of devotion.
One who recites this account of Kalki Viṣṇu or listens to it thereafter attains Janaloka and obtains birth in the Kṛta Yuga.
On that very day, however, let all the gods worship the incarnation of Viṣṇu; thus they shall be worshipped forever.
Thus ends the vow of the ten incarnations as described in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Furthermore, he who eats only at night on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) and offers whatever [food] he has—
The word "viprāya" (to a Brahmin) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Having fashioned a golden [image] for Viṣṇu in this mortal world, he shall attain the station of Viṣṇu.
This is known as the Kṛṣṇavrata; it brings about the attainment of happiness until the end of the kalpa.
Thus ends the Kṛṣṇa-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Agastya said:
On the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), one should diligently observe the night-fast (nakta) according to the prescribed rite.
The wise one should begin at the start of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
That vow, when performed here for the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), bestows riches.

Thus concludes the Dhanada-vrata as declared in the Vārāha Purāṇa. Thus ends [the section] composed by Śrī Hemādri— the sovereign lord of all sciences, master of all faculties, and illustrious king of kings— who is himself the Great God (Mahādeva).
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the section on vows (*vratakhaṇḍa*), the vows of Ekādaśī.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Next, the vows of Dvādaśī.
The devotees of Viṣṇu, such as Sūri, Hemādri, and others, now set forth the vows established on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī),
by performing which living beings transcend [all obstacles].
Him, the far shore of this saṃsāra whose torrent is difficult to resist.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
Rāma said:
"For those who are unable to fast, what would constitute a single day of fasting?"
O Mahādeva, tell that which yields great fruit to me who asks you.
Kṛṣṇa said:
That Dvādaśī which is joined with the hearing of the Rāmāyaṇa is indeed great;
having fasted on that day, bathed, and worshipped Janārdana, [one attains the fruit].
O knower of dharma, by making an effort on that day, one obtains the fruit of twelve *dvādaśīs*; on that day, one should give to a brahmin a water-filled jar accompanied by curd-rice.
Having given a parasol and sandals wrapped in cloth,
one does not fall into an evil rebirth and attains a preeminent birth.
One attains the imperishable state; there is no need for deliberation on this point, provided that Wednesday coincides with the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī conjunction.
That twelfth day is proclaimed by the name Atyantamahatī;
on it, one should perform bathing, recitation, giving gifts, fire-offerings, ancestral rites, and the worship of the gods.
O descendant of Bhrigu’s lineage, one who bathes on that day at any confluence whatsoever attains everything in its inexhaustible form.
O Rāma, one undoubtedly obtains the fruit born of bathing in the celestial Gaṅgā;
for in the month of Śrāvaṇa, all confluences always bestow supreme nourishment.
It is especially meritorious when joined with the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), and particularly so when conjoined with Mercury;
likewise, the twelfth lunar day is declared to be most excellent when combined with the Śravaṇa asterism and Mercury.
And likewise, O knower of dharma, the third lunar day is proclaimed to bestow the fruits of all desires; so too is the auspicious fifteenth day.
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
"If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) occurs in the month of Phālguna,
conjoined with the pure Śravaṇa asterism, that conjunction is known as Vijayā."
The gift of a water-vessel accompanied by curd and rice,
as well as the worship of Vāmana, shall prevent one from being born in the womb of a preta.
By him the lineage was uplifted; he has been liberated from his debt to the ancestors.
From the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Puruṣottama, for those who are always unable to observe fasts..."
O sinless one, having fasted on those twelve meritorious twelfth days, [one attains my state].
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In the month of Bhādrapada, the twelfth day of the bright fortnight conjoined with the Śravaṇā asterism is meritorious, granting all desires; it yields great fruit through fasting.
Having bathed at the confluence of rivers and fasted on the twelfth day,
one attains the fruit of twelve Dvādaśīs.
In this case, the injunction for fasting is specifically on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), due to the force of the scriptural statement.
Furthermore, it is said in the Viṣṇurahasya:
"The fast is here on the twelfth day, while the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is on the thirteenth day."
"Even that which is forbidden must be performed; such is the command of the Supreme Goddess."
If that same twelfth day should coincide with the lunar mansion Śravaṇa and the weekday of Mercury, it is exceedingly great; whatever is performed on that day here becomes inexhaustible.
O descendant of Bharata, when the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) coincides with the Śravaṇa asterism,
one who bathes at the confluence of rivers obtains the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā and other sacred waters.
One obtains the merit of fasting; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Then, the wise man, having placed a jar filled with water, [should proceed].
Having placed Janārdana, well-fashioned and endowed with the five jewels, wearing a sacred thread, and well-honored, upon his shoulder;
According to one's ability, having bathed according to the prescribed rite a golden image adorned with a conch and the Śārṅga bow, anointed with white sandalwood paste,
covered with a pair of white garments, and provided with an umbrella and a pair of sandals;
Oṃ, salutation to Vāsudeva; with this one should worship the head. Likewise, one should worship the face with "Salutation to Śrīdhara" and the eyes with "Salutation to Vaikuṇṭha."
Salutation to the Lord of Śrī for the face; salutation to the bearer of all weapons for the two arms;
salutation to the Pervader for the belly; salutation to Keśava for the stomach.
One should worship the penis of Hari with "To the progenitor of the three worlds," the shanks with "To the lord of all," and the feet with "Salutation to the soul of all."
O King, according to this procedure, one should worship with flowers and incense;
thereafter, an offering of food cooked in ghee should be presented before him.
One should offer fresh sweetmeats and jars according to one's ability, as well as a priestly fee;
having thus worshipped Govinda, one should keep a vigil there.
Having bathed at dawn in the clear light and having worshipped the one whose banner is Garuḍa with flowers,
incense, and other offerings, as well as food offerings, fruits, and beautiful garments;
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should utter this mantra:
"Homage, homage to you, O Govinda, known by the names Budha and Śravaṇa!"
"Having brought about the destruction of the flood of sins, become the bestower of all happiness.
Immediately thereafter, O Brāhmaṇa who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, [he spoke this].
One should cause it to be given according to the rules, especially to one who knows the Purāṇas, with the thought:
"May Janārdana, the Lord of the gods, be eternally pleased with me."
O best of men, by this very method on the bank of a river,
one should cause everything to cease, even while being devoted to eating only a single meal a day during the period of the crops.
Kṛṣṇa said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history;
O protector of the earth, hear that which occurred in a vast forest.
There is a region named Deśoraka; in its western part lies the district of Ativāja, which strikes fear into all living beings.
The ground consists of scorched sand where great serpents have been ploughed up;
it is strewn with trees offering little shade and teeming with dead creatures.
O Pārtha, it was filled with śamī, khadira, pālāśa, krīra, and pīlu trees,
as well as excellent-winged and fearsome trees, and thick with sturdy thorns.
In some places, the ground there is seen to be crowded with swarms of fragrant creatures;
O bird, the earth is uneven with unexpected heat and covered in grass.
And whatever is seen there is like a blazing fire;
nevertheless, living beings continue to live, bound by all their karmas.
The clouds there do not release water, nor do they bring blue lotuses;
yet at times, birds are seen floating upon them.
O King, some who had gone into the interior together with certain thirsty children said, "We see those whose lives have been taken and whose excellence has been destroyed."
Leaping again and again with great speed, that deer has reached a sandbank;
it can indeed be destroyed by the waters, just like a sandbank.
In such a region as that, a certain merchant, by the power of fate,
having strayed from his own caravan, entered a desert wilderness.
Having spoken thus to Malina, the son of Triśaṅku wandered for three months with a bewildered heart, emaciated by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, while observing the earth.
"I shall go today, tomorrow, or in days to come; I am not like a fool," he thought, yet he saw how his senses were agitated by thirst.
