With bones bound together by sinews as his feet, running here and there,
he saw one of wondrous appearance mounted upon the shoulder of a *preta*.
He saw him approaching calmly, surrounded on all sides by many spirits,
preceded by sounds of praise.
Having gone to the earth where the heaps of the deceased lay, he approached his presence;
having saluted the eminent merchant, he spoke these words.
"How did you come to this most terrible place?
To him the wise merchant replied: "I was lost in the forest with my caravan."
My entry here was due to the conjunction of fate and my past actions;
yet, O caravan leader, thirst afflicts me, as does this intense confusion caused by hunger.
My vital breaths have reached my throat, O King, as if my speech were failing me;
I see no means of obtaining food by which I might live, O King.
Kṛṣṇa said:
When this had been spoken, the ghost addressed the merchant with these words:
"Abandoning this male name, wait for a moment."
"O King, you shall be born after I have performed the rites for guests; [wait] as you please.
Having been addressed thus, that merchant, tormented by greed, did exactly so.
When midday had arrived, he then came to that place;
there was a beautiful water-vessel, its water cooled by the shade of a nearby tree.
Then, having descended with curd-rice prepared together with a *vardhamāna* vessel, he offered the foremost portion for the sake of the sacrifice.
By giving food to them, the merchant attained satisfaction;
in an instant, he became free from thirst and free from fever.
Then, from that [food] intended for the deceased, he took a portion;
through the curd, rice, food, and drink, the departed spirits attained supreme satisfaction.
Having satisfied the guest and the entire realm of the departed spirits (pretas),
he then himself ate the remains of the meal at his ease.
When he had finished eating, his parasol and water became inexhaustible;
then the lords of the pretas spoke these words to the merchant:
"This is a supreme wonder to me, appearing so exceedingly bright in this forest: from where does this excellent supply of food and drink come to you?"
With such a small amount of food, you sustain so many individuals;
how is it that they are satisfied in reality, their bellies neither fleshy nor distinct?
Furthermore, how can there be affection for me when my offspring have perished?
Who are you, O crane, with hands rendered powerless, tormented in this waterless forest?
And yet you are thirsty; how is it that even you have become one who seeks a mere morsel of food?
Who are you, that you take such delight in this most terrible and utterly futile slaughter?
"Therefore, cut through this doubt; my curiosity is great.
Thus addressed by the merchant, the ghost spoke these words:
Listen, O noble one, I shall declare my own evil deed:
in the beautiful city of Śālaka, I was a man of very wicked mind.
O sinless one, in former times, a merchant named Kāla was attached to my vehicle;
he lived in the beautiful city of Sākala, belonging to that wicked-souled nihilist. [1169]
Out of greed for wealth, I never there made a distinction regarding my riches;
nor was alms ever given to a mendicant by me, who was like a rain-cloud to craving.
There lived a virtuous Brahmin who was my neighbor;
it was during the conjunction of Śravaṇa and the twelfth lunar day in the month of Bhādrapada.
Accompanied by me, he went with me to a river named Toṣī,
at its holy confluence with the Candragangā.
There, at the most enchanting confluence where the waters were cool with ascetic penance, flowed the Candrabhāgā, the daughter of Soma, who delights the Sun.
Having fasted accordingly on the occasion of Śravaṇadvādaśī,
he bathed and drank deeply from jars of water from the waters of the Candrabhāgā.
Together with vessels full of curd-rice,
along with an umbrella, a pair of sandals, a garment, and an image of Hari, according to the prescribed rite.
The great sage, who knew the secret, bestowed it upon that foremost of brahmins;
and for the sake of protecting his wealth, it was then [bestowed] by me as well.
Having fasted, she then gave that most beautiful garment,
adorned with flowers, to the Brahmin at the Candrabhāga river.
Having done this, I returned home; then, after some time, having met my death through atheism, I fell into the state of a preta.
O sinless one, you have likewise seen in this terrible forest these wicked men who,
having stolen the property of Brahmins, have entered the state of ghosts.
In this most dreadful land, some are devoted to the wives of others, others to betraying their masters, and some to betraying their friends.
“O sinless one, these calamities have come upon me for the sake of food and drink;
yet the Blessed Viṣṇu is inexhaustible, the Supreme Self, the eternal.”
That which is given in dedication to someone is proclaimed to be inexhaustible;
being deprived of me, what reality do you perceive in this most dreadful forest?
O illustrious one, out of a desire to show me favor, you shall experience for them a terrible suffering born of their own karma.
You may take all the various names and lineages in their entirety;
moreover, you possess a beautiful casket that has come from the Uccā family.
Likewise, having reached Himavat where the treasure is sought,
go from there to Gatyāśīrṣa and perform the śrāddha rite, O high-minded one.
Then, addressing each individual preta one by one according to their pleasure,
he who shone with the luster of refined gold spoke thus to them.
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, that merchant departed from here to the heavenly world;
and in heaven, by the power [of his merit], he gradually became the lord of the pretas.
Having recorded their names and lineages, he departed for the Himalayas;
having reached that place, he took the treasure and deposited it in his own home.
Taking his share of the wealth, he went to the banyan tree at Gayāśīrṣa;
there, day after day, he performed the śrāddha rites for the deceased ancestors in their proper order.
Whichever faithful merchant performs his duty on that day according to his devotion,
he always reveals his own form to him in a dream.
And by your grace, O illustrious and sinless one, I who was observing a vow have abandoned my state as a ghost and have attained the supreme goal.
Having honored the pretas with hospitality and having obtained wealth,
the merchant returned to his own home there in the month of Bhādrapada.
Having worshipped Janārdana on the conjunction of the twelfth lunar day with the Śravaṇa asterism,
and having given gifts to the Brahmins while fasting and with senses subdued;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having attained such a state of vision, he then performed the ritual giving according to rule every year at the confluences of great rivers.
He attained the supreme abode, difficult for all human beings to reach;
there, the trees yield fruits according to one's desires, and the rivers have mud made of milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having reached that region, which possessed cool, pure water and was delightful with flowering trees, the high-souled merchant,
his limbs adorned with highly polished gold, arrived there.
For an entire eon, he remained always joyful together with his beautiful women and his friends.

On the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) conjoined with the asterisms of Budha and Śravaṇa, at the waters of the Saṅgama, the offering of curd-rice is prescribed; this is the rule for one intent on fasting.
O Indra among kings, by Sagara, Kukutstha, Dhundhumāra, Gādhi,
and by these and others as well, the Kāmadā Dvādaśī was performed.
That twelfth day in the month of Nabhasya which is joined with Wednesday and the Śravaṇa asterism is indeed called Jaya by the sages;
having fasted upon it properly and with devotion, a person—
One attains perfection endowed with qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
Thus ends the Śravaṇadvādaśī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
O Goddess who traverses the three worlds, may Lakṣmī always be dear to you;
may the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) be yours, and may you become capable of assuming any form at will.
This is the speech addressed to Hari:
"Whoever, devoted to Him, should eat ghee on the twelfth lunar day—
whether a man or especially a woman— let that person become a dweller in heaven."
Thus ends the Harivrata as declared in the Vārāha Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In this world, one who is born in Bhārata is indeed of noble birth and a virtuous person.
He is the sacrifice, the head of all, splendor, and the eternal flow of truth.
Prasava, Avyaya, Dakṣa, and likewise Dvādaśaka;
these are designated as the twelve gods worthy of sacrifice, known by the name Bhagins.
One should perform their worship according to the rules on the twelfth day,
with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food offerings.
And at the end of the year, one should give a milch cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having observed this vow for one year,
one attains the very same world as those [deities].
Having dwelt there for a very long time, the human being—
He may become either a king or a preeminent among the twice-born.
Thus ends the Bhṛgu-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Manomana, as well as Prāṇa, Nara, and the valiant Jāta;
Vīti, Hayanagha, Haṃsa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa.
The Vibhus and the Lord himself are proclaimed as the twelve Svādhyās;
one should worship them during the bright fortnight, beginning from the twelfth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having observed this desired vow for one year,
a person attains the very same world as those [deities];
having dwelt there for a very long time, that human being—
He may become either a king or a preeminent among the twice-born.
Thus ends the Sādhyavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Śakra, Aṃśa, Varuṇa, and Bhaga.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, and likewise the twelve [Ādityas].
Having fasted during the bright fortnight, one who is firm in their vow should worship the twelve Ādityas,
beginning from the twelfth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
O hero among men, at the conclusion of the vow, the man who gives gold attains the worlds of the Sun;
having returned to human birth, he becomes free from disease.
He who has conquered his senses and is endowed with wealth.
Thus ends the Dvādaśādityavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Pulastya said:
In the month of Pauṣa, during the bright fortnight, on the twelfth lunar day under the constellation presided over by Śakra (Pūrvaphalgunī),
one should first worship Viṣṇu when it is in conjunction with that asterism.
From that time forward, O best of Brahmins, one should worship Janārdana every month while fasting, until a full year has passed.
I declare that on that lunar day, month after month, one should give gifts according to the prescribed rule;
and one should consume [the food] duly, according to the ritual, in the proper sequence.
Understand all of that as it is being told.
Ghee, rice, barley, gold,
barley-food, water, chickpea-food and drink,
an umbrella, milk-food, molasses, and treacle— these are [the gifts].
Fine sandalwood and clothing in successive order.
Each gift is mentioned by a single word:
cow's urine, water, ghee, raw vegetables,
dūrvā grass, curd, rice, barley, and sesame seeds.
Water heated by the rays of the sun rises up from the clouds.
Milk, administered in monthly increments, along with water boiled with darbha grass and kuśa roots,
[leads] to a family preeminent and filled with wealth and grain.
Possessing discernment, [she dwells] where all suffering has been stilled.
He attains birth with unimpaired faculties, and becomes free from disease, wise, and happy.
Thus ends the Sujanmadvādaśī vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Bṛhaspati said:
"How did that sovereign king, established in fortune and superior to all the worlds, [attain this]?"
And how, O Lord, did he attain divinity and union with Viṣṇu?
How was Umāpati, the lord of all the gods, pleased with him?
Brahmā said:
There is the twelfth lunar day known as Bhāgyarkṣa-dvādaśī, which bestows all fortune;
having performed the worship of Hari there and having offered lotuses according to the prescribed rite, one attains prosperity.
The great sage Aṣṭāvakra, having mastered his senses, should install both: the image of Hari, endowed with all auspicious marks, and the half-form of Śaṅkara belonging to the Supreme Person Hari.
"Half of Śaṅkara [belongs] to Hari," and so forth; the meaning is that one should install both forms, Hari and Hara—namely, half of the person Śaṅkara and half of the person Hari—in this manner.
Madhusūdana, worshipped with devotion and all offerings within the circle of dust on the twelfth day by means of the first Cakrarāja [yantra], [is thus honored].

The King was pleased by that, and through it he attained good fortune. O best of the twice-born, the mantra of the Great Sudarśana, the sovereign of wheels, being satisfied, the God of gods granted a boon.
From now on, my child, you shall become equal to me.
O dear one, the worship of that [deity] should be performed on the twelfth day of the constellation Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī) or on the eighth day.
One should perform the worship, the offering of water (argha), and the sacrifice within the mandala dedicated to Hari;
gold, cows, land, sesame seeds, and other such gifts should be bestowed upon the preceptor.
Through the excellence of the sacrificial fee according to one's wealth, Hari purifies [the donor] from the ocean of hell;
by the power of their fortune in the age, Hari bestows the fruit.

"By the power of the fortune of the age" means by the power of the karma of the age, such as the Kṛta and so forth. O twice-born one, just as even a single courtesan, having gone to the right time and place, attains a hundredfold increase, so it is with the age of fortune.
O best of the twice-born, one should know that the nature of the Bhāgya, Pauṣṇa,
and Vāsava nakṣatras is identical on the twelfth and eighth lunar days.
The constellation Bhaga is Bhāgya (Fortune), Pūrvaphalgunī has the deity Bhaga, Revatī belongs to Pūṣan, and Dhaniṣṭhā belongs to Vāsava.
When these are favorable, the Lord of the Gods of gods, whose crest is marked by the crescent moon, is pleased;
Janārdana bestows sons, long life, sovereignty, and good fortune.
And that mortal who, month after month, performs the worship of Hari and Hara upon a lotus endowed with auspicious marks and adorned with all colors;
Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, whose hand bears the discus, is pleased with him.
Thus ends the Bhāgyarkṣa-dvādaśī-vrata as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
The Puṣya-rkṣa-dvādaśī is meritorious and the destroyer of all sins;
by whom was it performed, O Śakra, with the offering of vessels of ghee and other gifts?
Then, Janārdana, the God of gods, beheld before his very eyes his own auspicious body, yellow-hued and four-armed.
Thus ends the Puṣyārka-dvādaśī-vrata as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
Brahmā said:
By worshipping Viṣṇu on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) here, one shall always be victorious.
And he is to be honored by all the worlds, just as the Lord of Rays is honored by the rays of light.
Gopati is the Sun; he whose rays are directed toward the cows (the quarters) is Gopatikarā, who is Viṣṇu.
The root mantras and the limb mantras are proclaimed by their own respective names.
As before, Tithīśvara should be visualized as situated upon a lotus petal.
Worship is performed with offerings of perfumes and flowers according to one's ability;
even if performed with deceit, worship bestows its fruit.
A fire-oblation performed with a stream of clarified butter, fuel-sticks, curd, milk, rice, and honey,
while the mind is tranquil, yields the same results as previously described.
This vow, however, is to be explained like the Vaiśvānara-pratipad-vrata. Thus ends the Viṣṇu-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O delighter of the Yadavas, tell me of the Aviyoga-vrata;
what is its procedure, what is its merit, and who is the deity therein?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen attentively, O Pāṇḍava, as I describe this [vow] known as Aviyoga-vrata, the most excellent of all vows.
In the month of Śukla-proṣṭhapada, having fasted on the twelfth day,
one who is pure, wearing white garments, and having bathed in a clear body of water, [should proceed].
Having made a very beautiful mandala with cow dung on the edge of water,
one should place Janārdana together with Lakṣmī in its center using wheat flour.
Having anointed Hara and Gaurī, as well as Sāvitrī together with Brahmā,
and the Sun, O King, who illuminates the three worlds, along with the monarch;
One should worship with devotion using perfumes, flowers, incense, and food offerings;
O Pārtha, being intent upon that, one should perform the Aviyoga-vrata with this mantra.
With a firm mind, free from separation [from the goal], one should place Keśava,
Śaṅkara, the lotus-born Brahmā, and Ravi, the ornament of the sky, within the heart.
One should recite this, O Pārtha, having placed "namas" before it and preceded by the *praṇava*:
"The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, Padmanābha, Janārdana."
The sage Vyāsa, the teacher Kapila, the Blessed One Puruṣottama, Nārāyaṇa, Madhuhā, Viṣṇu, Dāmodara, and Hari.
Mahāvarāha, Govinda, Keśava, Garuḍadhvaja, Śrīdhara,
Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Viśvarūpa, and Trivikrama.
Upendra, Vāsava, Rāma, Vaikuṇṭha, Mādhava, Dhruva, Vāsudeva,
Hṛṣīkeśa, Kṛṣṇa, Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Acyuta.
May the great yogi Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Ananta,
as well as Śrīkaṇṭha, the slayer of enemies, be forever well-pleased with me.
Umāpati, Nīlakaṇṭha, Sthāṇu, Śambhu, Bhaga, Ariha,
Īśāna, Bhairava, Śūlin, Tryambaka, and Tripurāntaka.
Kapardin, Gopati, Liṅgin, Mahākāla, Vṛṣadhvaja,
Śiva, Sarva, Mahādeva, Rudra, and Īśvara of the hosts of beings.
May Śaṅkara, together with Pārvatī, be ever the bestower of happiness to me;
may he be Brahmā, Śambhu, the all-pervading creator, the nourisher, and the Great-Grandfather.
Hiraṇyagarbha, the knower of the Vedas, Parameṣṭhin, Prajāpati,
the Creator, the four-faced one, the Maker, the Self-born, and the Lotus-seated One.
May Viriñci, the lotus-born, always be the granter of boons to me;
[and likewise] Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Sūrya, Arka, Savitṛ, and Ravi.
Mārtaṇḍa, Maṇḍala, Dyota, Raśmimālī, Grahāgraṇī,
Prabhākara, Saptasapti, Taraṇi, Dyumaṇi, and Khaga.
Divākara, Dinakara, Sahasrāṃśu, Marīcimān,
Padmaprabodhana, Pūṣan, Jagaccakṣus, and Dyubhūṣaṇa.
May the twelve-fold one of great splendor, Mitra, the destroyer of Time, Hari,
the god beloved of Nikṣubhā, be forever well-pleased with me.
Lakṣmī, Śrī, Kamalā, Padmā, Vibhūti, Harivallabhā,
Pārvatī, Lalitā, Gaurī, Umā, Śambhupriyā, and Satī.
Gāyatrī is the primordial nature (prakṛti) and the creation; Sāvitrī is esteemed by the gods. Rājñī, Bhānumatī, Saṃjñā, Nikṣubhā, and Bhāskarapriyā [are her names].
Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā, as well as Amoghā and Vidyuti— these are [the goddesses] according to their forms.

Thus is his essential form to be known. Sūrya, however, should be depicted with a beard, four arms, holding two lotuses in his upper hands and a flower-garland in his two lower hands; on his left side, Nikṣubhā should be made with a golden lotus in her hand. Having thus fashioned Padmanābha, Śaṅkara, Pitāmaha, Arka, and the others together with their consorts, and having given gifts to the preceptor at the conclusion, one should go home. The person who has performed this vow, being imbued with devotion, becomes famous, a possessor of wealth, endowed with progeny, and free from affliction. Having enjoyed vast pleasures in the worlds of Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Prabhākara in due order, he then becomes liberated and perfectly blissful. This applies whether it be a pair of man and woman, or if some man alone, or a woman, having observed this vow, should go forth protecting [the precept] of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Aviyoga-dvādaśī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Eighteen akṣauhiṇīs have gone to their destruction for the sake of the kingdom of Madra."
Because of that evil, a profound sense of loathing arises within my mind.
There, the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and others were slain, as were Bhishma, Drona, the King of Kalinga, and others, along with Karṇa, Śalya, and Suyodhana.
The sin resulting from their slaughter cuts into my vital organs;
O Lord of the World, tell me some dharma that might wash away this evil.
Kṛṣṇa said: "O Pārtha, O mighty-armed upholder of the Pāṇḍavas, there exists the Govinda-dvādaśī vow, which generates very great merit."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Janārdana, regarding this [vow] known as Godvādaśī, what is its procedure? How did it originate, and at what time?"
Tell me all of this, O Hari; deliver me from the ocean of hell.
Kṛṣṇa said: O Pārtha, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, ten million sages assembled on a mountain and performed extensive penance, observing various vows.
Filled with great joy and longing for a vision of the gods,
they went to the highly meritorious Jambūmārga, which was adorned with various sacred fords (tīrthas).
O King, on the beautiful Pāripātra mountain, at the delightful Badarikāśrama,
on the supreme peak renowned as Ghaṇṭāravī.
The incomparable forest of ascetics, adorned with divine groves,
was frequented by Vasiṣṭha, Śukra, Aṅgiras, Kratu, Dakṣa, and others.
The circle of Bhṛgu’s hermitage was clothed in bark garments and deerskins,
frequented by various herds of wild animals, and filled with troops of monkeys.
A forest where lions and deer were at peace, filled with trees extending everywhere,
dense yet devoid of undergrowth, beautiful and crowded with rows of palm trees.
It was adorned on all sides with various lions, tigers, elephants, deer, hares, antelopes, boars, and birds.
O Lord of the Earth, while those sages were performing austerities there, desiring a vision [of him],
the one whose eyes are half of half of twelve (the three-eyed Śiva) assumed a disguise.
There was an old brahmin, his hair white with age,
his skin loose and his body hunched, holding a noose in his hand and trembling all over.
O Pārtha, hear what kind of cow-form Umā assumed,
which was produced from the waters of the Ocean of Milk during the ancient churning for the nectar of immortality.
O Pārtha, there are five auspicious cows who are the mothers of the group of five:
Nandā, Subhadrā, Surabhī, Suśīlā, and the virtuous Bahulā.
For the sake of benefiting the world and for the gratification of the gods,
Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Śiva, and Gautama [composed these works].
Then the gods, having given five wish-fulfilling cows, received from them the cow-dung,
the bile-stone, the urine, the milk, the curd, and the clarified butter of the cows.
The six limbs are pure and effect complete purification;
the glorious Bilva tree, beloved of Śiva, has arisen from cow dung.
The goddess Śrī, holding a lotus in her hand, dwells there; therefore, it is known as the Śrīvṛkṣa (the auspicious tree).
Furthermore, the seeds of blue and white lotuses are produced from cow dung.
Gorocanā is auspicious, purifying, and the accomplisher of all goals;
born from cow's urine, it is fragrant and pleasing to behold.
Food is the sustenance for all the gods and especially for Śiva;
whatever exists in the world, that seed of the universe should be known as originating from milk.
From curd all auspicious things were born for the accomplishment of goals;
from clarified butter nectar was produced, which is the cause of satisfaction for the gods.
The Brahmins and the cows constitute a single family divided into two parts:
in one part reside the sacred mantras, and in the other resides the sacrificial oblation.
In cows the sacrifices proceed; in cows the gods are established.
In cows the gods are fully contained, along with the six Vedāṅgas and the Pada and Krama recitations.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu are eternally stationed at the base of the horns of cows;
at the tips of the horns reside all holy places, both stationary and moving.
In the center of the head is Mahādeva, the cause of all causes;
Gaurī is stationed on the forehead, and Ṣaṇmukha is in the nostrils.
The two Nāgas, Kambala and Aśvatara, reside in the nostrils;
the two gods, the Aśvins, are in the ears; and the Moon and the Sun are in the eyes.
All the Vasus reside in the teeth; Varuṇa is situated in the tongue;
Sarasvatī is in the syllable *huṃ*; and Yama and Yakṣa are in the two cheeks.
The two twilights are in the two lips, and Purandara is in the neck;
the Rākṣasas are in the belly, and the two goddesses are stationed in the heels.
The entire Dharma with its four quarters always stands upon his shanks;
the Gandharvas are in the middle of his hooves, and the Pannagas are on the tips of his hooves.
The Rākṣasas are established in the hindquarters of the horse;
the eleven Rudras are on its back, and the Vasus are in all its joints.
The ancestors reside upon the slopes of his hips, and human beings in his armpits;
the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, rests within his belly.
The four oceans are filled with the milk yielded by cows;
Parjanya [the rain-god] is present in the streams of milk, situated as a mere drop within the clouds.
The Gārhapatya fire is in the belly, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire resides in the heart,
the Āhavanīya fire is in the throat, and the Sabhya fire is situated in the joints.
The mountains are established in his bones; the sacrificial rites are established in his marrow;
likewise, the Ṛgveda, Atharvaveda, Sāmaveda, and Yajurveda are established there.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the colors of cows— white, red, yellow, and black—
are established according to the shape of their noses among the Surabhis.
Listen, O King of Dharma, to how the goddess Gaurī, relying upon that [mantra], instantly transformed her body into one resembling the sun.
One with six elevations and five depressions, frog-eyed, possessing a beautiful tail,
with a waist situated on copper-colored thighs, pleasant-voiced, fair-faced, and well-proportioned.

Having touched a cow in the form of a woman— one well-behaved, affectionate toward her calf, yielding excellent milk, with full udders, and possessing a beautiful face— he should provide lodging for his master there.
Delighted in his heart by the conduct of Mahādeva,
O Pārtha, the great ascetic, assuming the form of a brahmin, proceeded slowly and steadily.
Having given it, O son of Pāṇḍu, one of great splendor should offer his own body at the side of Bhṛgu, the lord of the lineage, among all those ascetics.
He gave him a cow as a formal deposit, saying, "Let her be protected for two days,
until I have crossed from here by way of Jāmbū and returned here."
"We shall fulfill this sacred vow made by the sages;
otherwise, O Lord, you who were like a deer would once again become a tiger."
He has claws like a vajra-wheel, holds a ladle, and has blazing tawny eyes;
his mouth is terrifying with its tongue, and his tongue reaches out as a tail to seize [his prey].
With a roar, he terrified the sages stationed in all directions, as well as a cow with her calf that was yielding the fruit of the stages of life (āśramas) and their perfections (saṃpads).
Even the sages, being overwhelmed, let out cries of distress;
some cried out loudly, "Alas! Alas! while others uttered sounds of lamentation.
Seeing an exceedingly terrifying tiger, some gave out loud claps;
a cow, along with her calf, leaped up and caused her master to become afraid.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for the sake of pleasing Hara, let this Kapilā cow, afflicted by the fear of a tiger and fleeing, rest for a moment amidst these rocks.
There, the salutation of Vyāghra and Vatsaka by the gods and kinnaras is seen very clearly; I do not grant [the gift of] a quadruped.
That Śiva-liṅga with its water is the supreme sacred site (tīrtha) of Śambhu;
O Indra among kings, he who touches it is freed from the sin of killing a cow.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, having bathed there at that great sacred ford on the Jambūmārga, one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa; of this there is no doubt.
Then those sages, filled with rage, struck the great-sounding bell given by Brahmā,
which had been presented by the gods and was capable of filling the mountain caves.
At that sound, even the tiger released the cow along with her calf; thereupon, the brahmins gave him the name by which he became renowned as Ḍhuḍhugīr.
Those Rudras drank for the purpose of consuming the remainder; of this there is no doubt.
Then, Maheśvara, the god, was visibly the most excellent among them.
The wielder of the trident, the destroyer of Tripura, the one attained through desire, firmly established upon his bull,
accompanied by Umā, the bestower of boons, together with his Lord and Vināyaka.
Hara was accompanied by Sanandin, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, and Bala,
and was surrounded by Vīrabhadra, Cāmuṇḍā, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and others.
Indeed, by the hosts of Mothers, by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Guhyakas,
and by gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Munis, Vidyādharas, and Uragas.
Having prostrated before the God of gods together with their wives,
the cow in the form of a cow with her calf was likewise worshipped by the celibate students (brahmacārins).
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, through the Nandinī-vrata,
O King of kings, he descended from there onto the surface of the earth.
Listen now to how this vow was performed by Uttānapāda:
there was a lord of the earth, a kṣatriya named Uttānapāda.
He had two wives, renowned as Ruci and Śrughnī;
from Śrughnī was born his son Dhruva, who, while still a child, was unwavering in his devotion to the Lord's feet.
"O friend, this Dhruva has been entrusted to Ruci of Śrughnā; let him be protected.
In the meantime, I myself shall always personally attend to my husband's service."
In the home of Savitṛ, a vow toward a heroic man is constantly born;
Śrughnī, ever devoted to her husband, performs service for her lord.
Perhaps, having been provoked to anger by that co-wife,
I myself shall strike him down, for his body has been made pale and mottled with white spots.
Then, at the time of eating the meal, one perfected being himself would place that well-prepared body into a vessel and present it to the king.
Having told her husband that the meal contained meat, she indeed ate it;
then, at the time of the meal, Dhruva regained his life.
And in that very manner, with a serene soul, he came to rest upon his mother's lap;
seeing this great marvel, Śrughnī was struck with wonder and questioned him.
Tell me this account: what was that deed by which this result was obtained?
Was some vow performed by you, or was a gift given, or likewise an oblation offered?
Truth, truth, and again truth: by this your son lived—he, a mere child, was slain and cut to pieces while sleeping upon his bed.
Cooked by himself in a pot along with curries and foods,
how did he obtain life again while remaining as a remnant?
Has the auspicious great vidyā, the reviver of the dead, been mastered by you?
Or the jewel, the great gem-jewel, the collyrium of yoga, and the great medicine?
"Tell me, O illustrious one, the truth, the absolute truth; you are my sister.
When she had been addressed thus, she explained to her the vow of Vatsaka.
Just as it was performed in the past on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
by the power of this vow, my son shall live again.
At the time of my calf’s return, my mind again dwells upon the object of my desire;
and even for those who have gone abroad, there is a reunion through their vows.
Thus has this Godvādaśī vow been explained to you according to its true meaning;
at some time, all of this—whether auspicious or inauspicious—will indeed come to pass.
Thus, having performed the vow as prescribed, the sons of Ruci were endowed with happiness;
and when their lives came to an end, they were established in the abode of Dhruva.
Ruci, having lived with her husband Brahmā, the creator, remains joined with ten constellations; that Pole Star (dhruva) is visible even today.
"When the world is seen by Dhruvarkṣa, it is liberated from sins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Janārdana, tell me what that ritual procedure is like."
O scion of the Yadu clan, that which was done by Ruci at the request of Śrughnī—
Kṛṣṇa said: O best of kings, when the month of Kārttika has arrived, during its bright fortnight,
on the twelfth day, having made a formal vow and bathed in pure water, [one should proceed].
Whether it be a man or a woman, having formed a resolution in the mind at night,
one should then perform the worship of the deity and other rites at the time of midday.
Intent on meditating upon cows, he should wait with devotion for the arrival of a cow that has a calf, is of the same color as himself, is well-behaved, and is full of milk.
Having anointed [the image] with sandalwood and other unguents, one should worship it with flower garlands,
with saffron and lac, and with fragrant incenses, perfumes, and lamps.
Then, having placed [the offering] in a copper vessel, [he should worship] with flowers, unbroken rice, sesame seeds,
sandalwood, saffron, fragrances, and likewise with seasonal flowers.
O Pāṇḍava, it should be placed at the base of the foot with this mantra;
"pātā rudreṇa" is the mantra proclaimed by the twice-born.
O mighty-armed one, this mantra has been proclaimed for women and Śūdras:
"O you who were born from the ocean of milk, O you who are saluted by gods and asuras!"
O Mother, who embodies all the gods, accept this arghya; homage be to you!
Having offered the arghya, one should place that meritorious water, together with unbroken grains (*akṣata*), upon the head.
Then, from the first month onwards, one should offer well-prepared *vaṭaka* cakes—
five, seven, ten, or one— according to one's own means.
O Surabhi, Mother of the World, eternally established in the station of Viṣṇu,
you who consist of all the gods, please accept this auspicious morsel today.
Having offered the *arghya* and the food offering (*naivedya*), having performed worship and being well-restrained,
the wise man should join his palms in *añjali* before the victim and pray for blessings.
O Goddess who embodies all the gods, adorned by all the Vedas,
O Mother, O Daughter of Joy, make my desire bear fruit.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules and given the cow its daily fodder,
and having sprinkled it with water, one should then bow down with devotion again and again.
On that day, O Yudhiṣṭhira, having offered a *sthālīpāka* prepared by the Tāyikas,
along with cow’s milk and cow’s ghee, one should present curd and milk.
If one should eat black gram and rice at night out of desire, yet remain free from malice,
sleep on the ground, and observe celibacy— listen to what fruit he shall obtain.
O descendant of Kuru, for as many days as there are hairs on the bodies of cows, he rejoices, honored by the immortals in Goloka.
Or if a woman ever performs this vow, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
she attains the delightful eastern eightfold region of Meru belonging to Indra, Agni, Yama, and the Rakṣasas.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, Goloka is above Varuṇa, Anila, Rudra, and even Rudra himself; there that observer of the cow-vow goes.
For those who, at the end of the *ūrja* month, on the tenth day, worship a cow with her calf using *vaṭaka* cakes and pleasing flowers,
they shall partake in the abundance of all desired pleasures and enjoyments.
And the king’s children have remained in the mortal world for a very long time.
Thus ends the Govatsadvādaśī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"In ancient times there was a royal sage known as Ajāpāla."
He was brought by the subjects for the sake of dispelling all suffering.
"O Lord of Men, dispel this manifold disease!
Thus addressed, he meditated for a long time and, having subdued the hosts of diseases, [he spoke].
Delighted, he protected [the flock] and thus became Ajāpāla;
by him this propitiatory rite was created, known among people by the name Nīrājanā.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, listen as I describe the characteristics of that [city]:
the king, together with his domestic priests, having performed the rites according to the injunctions, [should enter].
At that time, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
resided in Laṅkā and directed the hosts of gods to their respective duties.
He made the full-orbed moon his royal parasol;
he appointed Indra as his commander-in-chief and Vāyu as the sweeper of the dust.
He appointed Varuṇa, who presides over the act of binding, as the giver and protector of wealth;
Yama, for the restraint of enemies; and Manu, for the purpose of counsel.
The trees shed their blossoms as if with longing for wisdom,
while the Seven Sages and other Brahmins remained there, intent on rites of propitiation.
Yama is in the first enclosure; the Gandharvas, intent on song, are in the second; the eight Apsarases are in the third for the sake of spectacles; and the outermost is surrounded by the Vidyādharas.
The Gaṅgā and other rivers abide in his drinking water; the domestic fire resides in his sacrificial fire; and kings stand before him, performing service as if they were his city.
Shining with radiant jewels and ornaments from his palace,
Nārada saw him and spoke to the excellent doorkeeper.
"Turn back and, in my stead, say who has arrived here.
And the night-stalker Daṇḍapāṇi, having bowed before him, spoke.
Among these were Kakutstha, Māndhātṛ, Dhundhumāra, Nala, Arjuna, Yayāti,
Nahuṣa, Bhīma, this Rāghava, and Vidūratha.
"These and many other kings sit here;
they are performers of service, yet Ajāpāla has not come here because of his station."
The enraged Rāvaṇa said, "Dispatch a messenger immediately.
When this was said, the Rākṣasa named Dhūmrākṣa was sent as a messenger.
"O Dhūmrākṣa, go and speak to Ajāpāla on my command:
'O King, come and perform service for Kabandha.'"
"Otherwise, with my sword Candrahāsa, I shall make you headless like Rāvaṇa.
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, Dhūmrākṣa became like Garuḍa.
Having reached that beautiful city and entered the royal palace,
he saw a certain Ajāpāla tending his flock of goats.
With disheveled hair and loosened armpits, having eaten many times, with both feet together,
with a staff upon his shoulder, covered in dust, and surrounded by diseases.
Having inscribed their names upon the earth— which slays the tigers that are enemies and destroys all calamities— they utterly destroy the hosts of their foes.
Having seen the mantra— which had been bathed, eaten, and rendered effective in an auspicious place— Dhūmrākṣa, with a joyful mind, spoke what Rāvaṇa had commanded.
Having been thus addressed with reproach, Ajapāla also sent Dhūmrākṣa as another messenger; then he established the truth.
Having summoned Jvara, the lord of the earth spoke thus:
"Go to the abode of the Lord of Laṅkā and act as is appropriate."
Commissioned by Ajapāla, the King of Fevers departed;
having gone there, he caused the Lord of Rākṣasas, along with his retinue, to tremble.
But Rāvaṇa, unaware of that most terrible fever, said: "Let the king remain; I have no need for him."
Thereupon, that king, the younger brother of the Giver of Wealth, became free from fever;
this peace was composed by that wise Ajapāla.
It pacifies all diseases and destroys all calamities;
[it should be recited] on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika at the beginning of the night.
When the god Dāmodara had likewise arisen from sleep,
at the conclusion of the Vidyā, he was surrounded by garlands of men and women in a delightful place near the women.
Having generated a new Viṣṇu and having offered oblations with mantras by the best of the twice-born,
[he worshipped] the sacrificial fire with lamps adorned with *vardhamāna* flowers.
Having performed this, all the people should slowly perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Hari;
they should worship the Lord with flowers and anoint him with sandalwood paste.
With jujubes, karvara fruits, trapusa gourds, and likewise with sugarcane;
with perfumes, flowers, ornaments, garments, and honored jewels.
One should likewise worship Lakṣmī, who is approved by him, as well as a Brāhmaṇa,
Caṇḍikā, Āditya, Śaṅkara, Gaurī, a Yakṣa, Gaṇapati, and the Planets.
One should perform the lustration (nīrājana) in due order for mothers, fathers, and cows;
one should perform the lustration of the cows and the ritual circle (maṇḍala) for the queen and others.
One should cause them to whirl and terrify them with sounds, the ringing of bells, and coverings;
for those cows that have milked, there is likewise pain and disease for them.
With the tips of their horns adorned with vermilion, lowing loudly along with their calves,
the cowherds follow you as they traverse the forests.
With their limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste and wearing red, yellow, and white garments,
[the attendants gathered] when the fivefold tumult arose during the lustration ceremony (*nīrājanotsava*) of the cows.
Having brought forth horses endowed with auspicious marks and well-honored elephants,
as well as all the royal insignia, into the courtyard of his own house;
The king, seated upon the throne together with his domestic priests, preceded by ministers and servants, was accompanied by the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, wealth, lamps, and ointments.
This worship of horses and other animals is to be observed during the Mahānavamī festival.
Therein, a woman endowed with auspicious marks—whether a courtesan or a lady of noble family—[should perform the rite].
And she should whirl it three times above the head of the lord of men.
May there be peace through sacrificial fuel, by the twice-born, or by the sound of the Vedas;
thereafter, one should cause the army, teeming with elephants, horses, and chariots, to be sprinkled with water.
Thus, O son of Pāṇḍu, this great peace known as the *nīrājanā* is proclaimed among people; it should be performed in whatever kingdom, city, or village, O joy of the Pāṇḍus.
Their diseases come to an end, and there is always an abundance of food;
in the light of the peace-offering lustration, all diseases are dispelled.
Having increased the lifespan of the worlds like one who wanders as a cowherd,
he acted out of a desire for the welfare of those beings who were afflicted by diseases and other miseries.

"The Śānti-nīrājana should be performed every year. Those who perform the lustration ceremony with horses and cows for Hari— who resembles a fresh cloud and acts for the welfare and benefit of cows and Brahmins— [attain great merit].
By the word of Ajapāla, they become free from all diseases, accompanied by servants, and long-lived upon this earth.
Thus ends the Nīrājanadvādaśī vow from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, the asuras were slain by Hari.
Afflicted with grief for her sons and grandsons, she departed for the highest world of mortals.
At the holy site of Samantapañcaka, on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī,
she performed severe austerities, devoted solely to the propitiation of her husband.
Then Diti, the mother of the Daityas, assuming the form of a seer,
subsisted on fruit and performed severe penance, including many Cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
For more than a full hundred years she remained overwhelmed by old age and grief;
thereafter, having been tormented by her ascetic penance, she questioned Vasiṣṭha and the other sages.
"May you tell me, sirs, of a vow that destroys grief for one's son and bestows the fruit of good fortune both in this world and the next."
The sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha, described the Madanadvādaśī vow,
by the grace of which she became free from grief for her son.
The sages said:
"I wish to hear from you the Madanadvādaśī vow,
by which Diti formerly obtained forty-nine sons."
Sūta said:
Listen now from me to that very same excellent account which was previously told in detail by Vasiṣṭha and others concerning Diti.
In the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnight, on the twelfth day, one who is firm in his vow should place an unblemished jar filled with white rice.
Likewise, it should be provided with various fruits and accompanied by stalks of sugarcane;
it is covered with a pair of white cloths and anointed with white sandalwood paste.
Equipped with various kinds of food offerings and accompanied by gold according to one's means,
one should place a copper vessel filled with molasses upon it.

In the absence of that, one should perform a discourse on Kāma and Keśava without [using their actual names]. One should remove the image by the name "Kāma" and bathe it with water mixed with jaggery.
One should worship Keśava with white flowers, unbroken rice grains, and sesame seeds;
having worshipped the feet for the sake of desire, one should worship the shanks as the bestower of good fortune.
"Recite 'to Ūru' for the thighs, 'to Manmatha' for the hips,
'to Stambhodaya' for the belly, and 'to Anaṅga' for the chest of Hari."
One should worship the face with "Salutation to the lotus-faced one," the two arms with "To the five-arrowed one," and the crown with "Salutation to the Self of All," thus worshipping Keśava.
Having thus kept a vigil, the observer of the vow, adorned with white garlands and garments,
should then present that water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa at dawn.
One should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability and eat together with one's kinsmen;
having eaten, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and recite this mantra:
May the Blessed One Janārdana, who can assume any form at will and who is designated as the Self within the hearts of all beings, be pleased with this.
By this procedure, one should perform everything month after month;
fasting on the thirteenth day, one should worship the immutable Viṣṇu.
Having consumed a single fruit on the twelfth day, one should sleep upon the ground;
then, in the thirteenth month, [one should give] a cow together with ghee.
One should give a bed, complete with all its furnishings, to a preeminent brahmin,
as well as a golden Kāmadeva and a white, milk-yielding cow.
Having honored a Brahmin couple with garments and ornaments according to one's means,
one should offer all types of perfumes and other gifts, and utter the words, "May he be pleased."
One who knows the Dharma should perform the homa with white sesame seeds while reciting the names of the desired objects; likewise, he should do so with cow’s ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should give food to the Brahmins, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
furthermore, one should offer stalks of sugarcane and flower garlands according to one's ability.
Whoever performs this Nandana-dvādaśī according to this rite,
being liberated from all sins, attains identity with Hari.
In this world, one obtains excellent sons, good fortune, and happiness—
he who has called to mind Smara, who is Viṣṇu, whose nature is bliss, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
One who desires happiness should worship that Lord of the Universe with a form according to one's desire;
having heard that, Diti wandered everywhere without exception.
Kaśyapa, having arrived out of the greatness of his ascetic vow, with supreme joy,
again made her beautiful and endowed with youth, yet not harsh.
She covered him with boons, and she chose as her boon a son;
then, through the greatness of her vow, she conceived an unsurpassed embryo.
Once, when she had gained access to Diti's womb because of their enmity,
Śakra entered it alone and slew her after dividing her into forty-nine parts.
As many as those hairs were, so many more cried out, having reached death;
then indeed the slayer of Vṛtra reflected, "What is this?"
Behold the majesty of Dharma! These very people have been restored to life;
surely this woman must have observed the Madanadvādaśī vow.
By his grace, people live even when they have been struck down;
surely that worship has now reached its fruition.
Even if struck by a thunderbolt, they would not meet with destruction;
for even though the embryo was destroyed, it attained multiplicity from being one.
Oh, how great is the majesty of this Madanadvādaśī vow,
by which a woman is born with living sons and many children!
Thus ends the Madanadvādaśī vow as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Bhadrāśva said:
O twice-born one, who should be propitiated by one desiring the arising of spiritual knowledge?
How indeed is he propitiated? Tell me this, O twice-born one.
Agastya said:
Viṣṇu alone is the great sacrifice and the Lord even of all the gods;
I shall declare the means by which he may become the bestower of boons.
The secret of all the gods and likewise the highest of the sages is that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme deity; by bowing down to him, one does not suffer.
And it is heard, O King, that in ancient times the high-souled Nārada recounted this nourishing vow of Viṣṇu to the Apsarases.
In a former kalpa, Nārada went to Lake Mānasa as an arrow;
there, for the sake of bathing, he beheld the entire host of Apsarases.
Seeing him wearing a crown of matted hair, reduced to nothing but skin and bones, and carrying a parasol, a water-pot, and a skull-bowl, those playful women [were struck with wonder].
Those beautiful-faced women, desiring always to witness the strife between the gods, asuras, and humans, questioned the son of Brahmā, who was devoted to asceticism.
The Apsarases said:
"O venerable son of Brahmā, O twice-born one, we desire a husband;
tell us how Nārāyaṇa may become our husband."
Nārada said: A question preceded by a salutation is auspicious in every respect;
yet that was not done by you out of pride born from the intoxication of youth.
For thus has the auspicious Hari, Viṣṇu, the god of gods, been glorified by you with the name "Bhartṛ" (the Supporter), saying, "May he become your husband."
By the mere utterance of his name, everything is accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
Now he related the vow by which Hari himself [was attained].
One obtains excellent teeth and attains the status of a master on that auspicious twelfth day of the bright fortnight which occurs in the spring.
Having fasted on that day according to the prescribed rules, one should worship Hari along with Śrī;
having prepared a couch for reclining, it should be provided with various coverings.
There, having fashioned an image of the God together with Lakṣmī out of silver, one should present it;
then, above that, the wise man should have a pavilion constructed adorned with flowers.
One should cause a vigil to be held there with dance, instrumental music, and song;
one should worship the head with the mantra "To Manobhava" and the waist with "To Anaṅga."
One should worship the root of the arms with "To Kāma," the abdomen with "To the Flower-Arrowed One," the feet with "To Manmatha," and everywhere else with "To Hara."
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods with flowers such as mallikā and jāti,
he should then take four very beautiful stalks of sugarcane.
O King, bowing down, one should place [the image] of that deity in the four directions;
having done this, at dawn, one should cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having fed Brahmins who are wise, possessed of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and complete in all their limbs, this vow is concluded.
Then, at the conclusion of the vow, Viṣṇu will certainly become your husband;
however, O beautiful ones, you asked out of pride without having first offered salutations to me.
"By means of this vow, having obtained the Lord of Gods as your husband out of self-conceit,
you shall suffer humiliation and abduction by cowherds."
"The god shall become the husband of the maidens who have been carried away. Having spoken thus, the celestial sage Nārada departed in an instant.
For this reason as well, Hari himself performed this vow for their sake when he was pleased;
thus is described the *Bhartṛprāptivrata* as told in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, a man [should perform it].
One should worship the Lord who reclines upon the waters with offerings of food, perfumes, flowers, and other articles.

And having bathed, a wise man should recite one hundred and eight times the mantra "ananta" while focusing on those men who perform improper acts, heretics, and those who have fallen from their status.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, eating, waking, or when stumbling or sneezing,
one who is afflicted by pain should always remember the Infinite One with mind and speech.
A man should perform this vow according to the prescribed rule for one year;
thereafter, he should feed the Brahmins and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability.
When a full year has passed, having worshipped Janārdana according to one's ability,
one should cause singing and dancing to be performed with lutes, flutes, drums, and other instruments.
Having worshipped Hari with devotion and having performed a vigil accompanied by song and instrumental music, one obtains infinite fruit; so it has been declared.
Non-violent, pure, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of all beings—
a man who observes this vow is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Anantadvādaśī vow as declared in the Viṣṇurahasya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By performing what is a living being liberated from the five great sins?"
Likewise, it delivers the ancestors who have become ghosts due to the five great sins.
The maker of night, the nourisher, the deity of the full moon—
these are the Lord of the World, the upholder of the earth, the sovereign of the gods, and the son of Devakī.
Four-armed, mace in hand, bestower of fragrance, with beautiful eyes;
omnipresent, discus in hand, heroic, and destroyer of the asuras.
And Śrīśa—these twelve deities are thus proclaimed;
[they are worshipped] with these names in the dative case, accompanied by the utterance of *svāhā*.
The observer of the vow performs the worship of the deities at the beginning of the month of Śrāvaṇa;
indeed, it is proclaimed that one should perform it specifically on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) of Śrāvaṇa.
On the full moon day, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) to the gods;
then, on the new moon day, one should offer sesame, mung beans, and rice with jaggery to the deities.
For the pacification of the five great sins, one should offer the five jewels to the deities,
along with a golden image of the fivefold form accompanied by the five nectars.
O King, one should feed Brāhmaṇas in the number of five or twelve;
by performing this, the Subduer of Pāka was liberated from the slaughter of Vṛtra.
Bṛhaspati [fell] from the sin of consorting with Ahalyā; Soma from drinking liquor; and Bali from violating the wife of his preceptor and from stealing gold.
By other rulers as well, such as Dilīpa, Sagara, and others,
they were liberated from the defects born of great sins (mahāpātaka) as well as the minor sins (upapātaka).
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, you too should perform this auspicious vow,
which the great king desires for his own attainment of the state of Śākha.
Thus ends the vow of the Dvādaśī that destroys the five great sins, as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa. A man who, having completed twelve such Dvādaśīs by means of fasting,
should then devoutly honor a cow-calf, gold, and Brahmins.
One attains the supreme state; this is remembered as the Viṣṇu-vow.
Thus ends the Viṣṇu-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Varāha said:
Those men who indeed observe a fast on the twelfth day,
being solely devoted to me, attain unto me alone.
Having observed the fast and having taken a handful of water,
one should gaze at the sun while reciting "Namo Nārāyaṇāya."
For as many drops of water as fall from the hollowed palms,
for that many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world.
In that same manner, having performed the ritual on that twelfth day according to the rules,
with white flowers, refined perfumes, and incenses;
One should also hear of the destiny of whoever causes such ground to be prepared;
having placed flowers upon the head, one should recite this mantra:
Having uttered "Oṃ," the mantra is:
"O best of gods, O support of the earth! Having accepted this flower with a well-disposed mind, may the Blessed One, the Lord of Ambikā, be pleased with me."
With this mantra, one should offer a flower. The mantra for incense is stated as follows:

*Oṃ namaḥ tubhyaṃ svasti vidhyukta-sugandhaṃ gṛhāṇemaṃ maṅgalavate Viṣṇave*. (Oṃ, salutations to you; may there be well-being; accept this fragrant [incense] prescribed by the rules, O auspicious Viṣṇu.)
With this mantra, one should offer perfumes.
Even without having heard the scriptures, whoever should cause me to be worshipped in this manner shall go to my world and be born with four arms.
Śyāmāka and ṣaṣṭika rice, as well as excellent foods and their qualities; likewise, various condiments, śāli rice, barley-meal, and similarly boiled nīvāra grain.
But whoever, devoted to my ritual service, should consume these,
he shall be marked with the conch and the discus, and bear the plow, the mace, and the club.

The vow consists of fasting, offering an oblation (arghya) to the Sun, worshipping Viṣṇu, and breaking the fast with śyāmāka grain or one of the other specified items. This is the Viṣṇudvādaśī vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
On the twelfth day, having worshipped the Guhyakas with offerings of meat and unbroken rice grains,
one devoted to fasting should indeed give gold to a Brahmin.
This indeed is declared as the auspicious Guhyaka vow, which removes all sins.
Thus ends the Guhyakadvādaśī vow as described in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods, the Sovereign of Waters, on the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī), [one should perform the rite].
One obtains Puṇḍarīka and Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures.
Thus ends the vow for attaining the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Having worshipped Śakra, the chariot of the gods, and likewise Nara,
one obtains all desires and goes to the heavenly world.
Thus ends the Śakra-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. [1205] Umā said:
O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, I wish to hear about the supreme marvel.
It should be spoken with sincerity, if there is any friendship toward me.
O Lord, by what means and by which vow is this deformity destroyed,
and by serving whom is supreme good fortune attained?
"Tell that to me, O Lord of Gods, which bestows my supreme desire.
Īśvara said:
"Listen indeed to this supreme secret, an auspicious vow that removes all sins."
The twelfth lunar day named Surūpā is the destroyer of great sins.
She is the bestower of beauty, likewise the increaser of good fortune,
the enhancer of the lineage, and the giver of all happiness.
Listen with diligence, O sinless one, as it is being told by me:
in ancient times, at the end of the Dvāpara age, Viṣṇu, the slayer of the Daityas, [appeared].
It is said that the Lord of the World of Mortals was born in the family of Vasudeva;
by him, moreover, was wedded the daughter of Bhīṣmaka named Rukmiṇī.
Exceedingly beautiful and devoted to her husband,
she indeed does not experience even the slightest happiness without Kṛṣṇa.
Devoted to her husband, she performed the salutation at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law;
however, due to some fault in her past actions, her mother-in-law, the mother of Kṛṣṇa, was angry with her.
He did not quickly placate her, but desired a rival in affection;
thereupon, a wrath that strips away all virtues arose within the queen.
She spoke angrily to Kṛṣṇa: "If even your own mother were to do so, she would still be considered an outsider—ugly, devoid of virtue, and inferior."
"O upholder of the lineage, you ought not to act contrary to my word.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"I cannot bring myself to abandon the sinless Rukmiṇī for the sake of an auspicious story."
He who abandons his wife while her body remains unimpaired.
That dull-witted person incurs misfortune extending to seven generations;
he attains deformity and finds no happiness anywhere.
Or else a disease arises in the world that is censured by embodied beings;
how then could I, even through inference, speak such words?
Devakī said: "O child, among all gifts, the gift of one's mother—such as providing for her needs at sacred sites and so forth—is most weighty; who would disregard her word?"
How could there be any wickedness in carrying out my word?
O delight of the Yadus, in this world the mother is honored, not the wife.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"I shall not abandon my beloved, the mistress of my life and wealth.
Thus Keśava, seeing his mother humiliated and silent, spoke.
He fell into deep anxiety, wondering how happiness might be attained;
at that very moment, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived.
He approached suddenly, and seeing Viṣṇu filled with wonder,
he honored him with supreme devotion and offered him the guest-offering (arghya).
[1207] When he had sat down according to custom, Nārada inquired after his well-being:
"Why are you so overcome with distress? What is the cause of your agitation?"
Why does what you desire not become pure? O best of the Yadus, abandon your agitation.
Kṛṣṇa said: "O best of the twice-born, O lord, commissioned by my mother to marry,
take as your wife whichever maiden you choose, even if she be ill-favored."
"In this matter, the mother's command has been honored with due respect.
Nārada said:
"Listen, I shall relate the ancient account with care."
O Lord, in former times, you were sporting with Lakṣmī in the Nandana grove.
Then the blessed Durvāsas, the best of sages, arrived there; and he was honored according to custom, preceded by the rising from one's seat.
Upon seeing his loathsome form, the goddess then broke into laughter;
he, however, blazed with great fury like the fire Vaiśvānara.
Filled with rage, the evil-minded sage cursed Lakṣmī:
"O foolish girl, you laughed at me while looking upon your own form!"
"O evil-minded one, become deformed! Have you not indeed recognized me?
Having been addressed thus by that goddess, she was properly pacified.
Being pleased, he spoke these words: "My curse shall not be in vain;
through another birth, this ugliness will attain fulfillment."
She indeed descended as the daughter of Gotraka;
she was Satyabhāmā, with deformed limbs and likewise an ugly appearance.
By the power of that [act], her ears and nose became extremely deformed;
likewise, her hands, feet, hips, and neck—all exhibited the characteristics of deformity.
"O great wise one, he will give his daughter to you.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Blessed One, how shall I constantly behold a face that is deformed?"
Having married that ugly woman, how shall I attain peace?
Nārada said: O delighter of the Yadus, it was solely by the grace of Rukmiṇī that he attained an excellent form, supreme good fortune, and the highest happiness.
Indeed, a mother must be honored by one who desires dharma, pleasure, and wealth;
for in this way, having transcended [the ordinary], such a relationship was ordained of old.
You must carry out the words of your elders as a great command;
it is sung in the Vedas that on this earth, the mother is the most venerable.
The Lord said: Having spoken thus to the Great Goddess, Nārada departed for heaven;
and Kṛṣṇa said to his mother, "Let the marriage indeed be performed."
Then, O Goddess, according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas for the conclusion of a marriage,
he had her brought forward and showed that bride to him.
Look at her; speak according to my words: "O lady of pure vows, you have been wedded;
go forth toward the supreme cessation [of suffering], and be supremely gracious."
Having spoken thus and having looked upon her, Kṛṣṇa, the one of great strength, bowed down to his mother and departed to perform the tasks of the gods.
Seeing her, the mother of the gods shone forth, deeply overcome with grief:
"How shall I conceal such a deformed and hideous appearance?"
Thinking "this is my concern," his mind became exceedingly agitated;
yet he did not tell anyone else of that deformity born of his own body.
Then, what did Rukmiṇī do at that time before you?
Having first paid homage to her mother-in-law and then touched her feet, she then inquired after her welfare.
He spoke these relevant words, full of devotion and bringing joy:
"I desire to behold the power of you, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa."
"And may they show me [the child] quickly; let your favor be well-granted.
Devakī said:
"O fortunate one, I am indeed your mother-in-law; do as I say."
O fair-browed one, let the beautiful vow of the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) be granted quickly.
[1210] "He bestows this mental vision; you shall behold it.
Rukmiṇī said:
"How is it that dharma and even a most difficult vow are bestowed?"
How can I bestow upon her that fruit which is so difficult for even the gods to obtain?
The Goddess said:
"Let half be given to her, or else half of that;
or again, a fifth, a seventh, a sixth, or even a sixteenth part."
The goddess said:
"I do not wish for even half a sesame seed's worth of the merit of the Śrūpa-dvādaśī,
much less a sixteenth part from a co-wife of such wicked intent."
Having spoken thus, that lady of beautiful eyes then went to her palace;
yet, with a bow, she questioned them again out of indignation.
O Goddess, I ask you: this master of mine has been told [by you] but does not act;
how shall I see that slender woman, my newly wedded beloved of Kṛṣṇa?
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O fair-browed one, you shall see your mother—fie on her beauty! She is slender-waisted, yet her ears and nose are deformed; she is misshapen and has a distorted face."
But I cannot bear to look upon such a form, O lady of pure smiles;
it is the fruit of the deeds of men, involving the uncertainty of both auspicious and inauspicious results.
Thus, after a long time had passed, by the power of the gods,
Satyabhāmā was sent to the queens' quarters and introduced there as a female disciple.
I pray that those who strive shall quickly attain the fruit of the Surūpa-Dvādaśī vow,
which indeed yields even a sixth part more than [the merit of] sesame seeds and even more than that which issues from fire-offerings (homa).
She went into her presence at the door of the wedding chamber,
and that Satyabhāmā of pure vows spoke to Rukmiṇī.
O Goddess, daughter of Bhīṣma, grant me even a single oblation;
or grant me half an oblation, for I have immediate affection for you.
Rukmiṇī said:
"What is this delusion of yours regarding the beautiful Dvādaśī?
I shall offer an oblation of sesame seeds; open the door!"
Having spoken thus, she quickly bathed, offered a single oblation of sesame seeds, and gave away a sesame seed; by that very act, she became superior in beauty.
Seeing her, she was overcome with wonder and asked the beloved of Hari:
"Tell me, who are you, and for what purpose have you come here?"
Satyabhāmā said: "O blessed lady, I am your sister; I am the wife of Kṛṣṇa according to dharma.
My name is Satyabhāmā; I bow at your feet."
Having heard these words, her eyes wide with wonder, Arcangī said nothing at all; she was utterly amazed.
And at that very moment, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"O you who are devoted to the vow of truth, by the power of your generosity—"
[1212] "The merit of the twelfth day (Dvādaśī), O beautiful one, is difficult even for the gods to attain.
The Goddess said:
"By what rite should it be performed? Tell me, O Kumāra, the proper conduct."
Let a rule, a fire-oblation, a gift, and a favor be duly ordained.
Īśvara said:
Having reached the month of Pauṣa, one should thoroughly purify oneself under the Puṣya asterism;
on that night, with a restrained mind, one should meditate upon the eternal Viṣṇu.
A white cow of uniform color— its dung is to be taken as it falls from the sky— while he remains pure and observes silence.
Having performed one hundred and eight oblations for her with sesame seeds,
those devoted to fasting should await the eleventh day of the dark fortnight.
Those who are joined with self-restraint should especially cultivate their practice with disciplined minds;
having bathed in a river or a pond, they should then contemplate Viṣṇu alone.
Having fashioned a golden image of Hari— or one made of silver according to his means—
one should place it upon a vessel of sesame seeds within a water-pot containing the ritual ingredients.
Then follows the worship of Viṣṇu.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite with flowers, incense, and sandalwood paste,
[one should offer] an oblation mixed with sesame seeds and various kinds of fruits.
Having employed the *arghya* mantra, one should recite a hymn of praise before him:
"Homage to the supremely peaceful one; O Virūpākṣa, homage be to you!"
"Accept this *arghya* for the destruction of all impurities; salutations to you!
This is the *arghya-mantra*.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should offer oblations of cow-dung into the fire.
[1213] Sesame seeds joined with oblations, accompanied by mantras of the Thousand-Headed One.
Having meditated in his heart upon the eternal Lord of Gods accompanied by Lakṣmī,
he meditated upon the god Janārdana, who holds the conch, the discus, the mace, and the shield.
O best of the twice-born, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should perform a Vaiṣṇava śrāddha;
having given them food and performed a circumambulation, [one should depart].
Having spent that night there awake, engaged in listening to the Dharma,
one should present that Kumbha, the form of Viṣṇu, to a Brāhmaṇa.
Whatever is deficient in mantra or deficient in ritual action, one should seek forgiveness for all of that therein.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess, listen to me regarding the merit of that man or woman who thus performs the Surūpā-dvādaśī vow.
His misfortune, even that acquired in other births, is destroyed;
moreover, through some other cause, he comes into contact with the earth.
For him also, there shall be no suffering or deformity in his birth,
nor separation from kinsmen due to being parted from those he loves.
One’s lineage increases, and one becomes renowned on earth;
one attains the recollection of past lives and shall reach the state of nirvāṇa.
Whoever listens with devotion and a concentrated mind to this as it is being recited constantly attains merit and is glorified in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the vow of Surūpā-dvādaśī in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
[1214] Māndhātṛ said:
O Great Brahmin, Ekādaśī bestows the fruit of great merit.
But tell me, O Lord, when they are conjoined with the lunar mansions.
Vasiṣṭha said: Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Pāpanāśanī—
this [vow] which removes all sins must be performed by those who desire its fruit.
When the asterism Punarvasu occurs on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, that lunar day is known by the name Jayā; it is the most excellent among all lunar days.
Having observed the fast, the observer of the vow is liberated from sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
That person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
When the Śravaṇa asterism occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
that is declared to be Vijayā, the most excellent among all lunar days.
A person who bathes in that [river] has bathed in all sacred fords;
likewise, their gift and their purposeful merit become multiplied a thousandfold.
One shall obtain the fruit of thousands of oblations, recitations,
and fasts when Rohiṇī occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
That lunar day is called Jayantī; it removes all sins, whether the sin committed over seven lifetimes be small or great.
Govinda washes that [image] with devotion after worshipping it there,

Then she was described as possessing exceedingly great merit and as the destroyer of sins;

One undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a thousand Ekādaśī fasts through bathing,

Whatever is performed in this [rite], all of that shall become inexhaustible;
therefore, those who desire its fruit should perform it with diligent effort.
O King, a special distinction has been declared for the month of Phālguna:
the meritorious Āmārdakī vow, which bestows the fruit of the world of Viṣṇu.
Having gone down to Āmardakī, one should perform a vigil there;
by performing a vigil for Viṣṇu, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Māndhātṛ said:
O best of the twice-born, when indeed did this Āmardakī come into being?
Tell me all of this, for my curiosity is great.
Why is this [rite] purifying, and why is it the destroyer of sin?
Why, by performing the vigil, does one obtain the fruit of a thousand cows?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O illustrious one, I shall tell you: I would go to the earth where there is the great Āmardakī tree, which destroys all sins."
In the past, when a single ocean had arisen and all things mobile and immobile had perished,
when the hosts of gods and asuras had vanished and the serpents and rākṣasas were utterly destroyed;
There, the eternal Supreme Soul, the Lord of the lords of gods,
meditated upon the supreme Brahman, the imperishable state of the Self.
Then, as he was reciting the sacred prayer (*brahman*), a drop endowed with saliva fell from his mouth— resplendent like the moon— and dropped upon the ground.
From that drop was born the great tree Dhātrī itself,
with its many branches and twigs, bowed down by the weight of its fruit.
And he is proclaimed as the origin of all trees;
at that very time, however, he created various kinds of progeny.
He created the Brahmins, and by them these creatures were procreated:
the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas.
And having seen them, O fortunate one, they were struck with great wonder,
even as they reflected from all sides that these trees were not of this world.
As they were thinking thus, an incorporeal voice arose there,
belonging to Viṣṇu, intended to awaken the sages.
The Blessed Lord, the God, created the sages and likewise the immortals;
and here, where the stream originating from Viṣṇu flows, they remain unconquered.
This mountain Āmardakī is indeed preeminent and renowned throughout the world;
born from the spittle of Viṣṇu, it is truly the most excellent mountain of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always serve Āmardakī;
she is declared to be the remover of all sins, belonging to Viṣṇu, and the destroyer of evil.
Viṣṇu stands at its root, and the Grandfather (Brahmā) indeed at its top;
and on its trunk resides the venerable Rudra, the destroyer of Tripura.
In the branches are all the rivers, and in the twigs are the deities;
in the leaves are the Vasu gods, and likewise the Maruts in the flowers.
All the lords of creatures are established in the fruit;
for this Earth has been described by me as consisting of all the gods.
Therefore, she is indeed most worthy of worship by those who are solely devoted to the service of Viṣṇu.
The seer said:

Vāc said:
"He who is the creator of all worlds and the fourteen realms, whose body is the form of the bodiless one (Anaṅga)— having beheld him, I am that eternal Viṣṇu."
Having heard those words spoken by the god, the brahmins stood there,
their eyes wide with wonder, overcome by supreme amazement.
They began to praise the God who is without beginning or end:
"Oṃ, salutations to the Self of all beings, to the Being who is the Supreme Self."
Salutations ever to the Unmanifest; salutations, salutations to the Infinite.
Salutations, salutations to Dāmodara, the Pure One, the Lord of Sacrifice.
Homage to the Great Soul, the sustainer of the world concealed by the veil of Māyā;
homage ever to Acyuta, and repeated homage to Ananta.
Thus praised by them at that time, the Blessed Lord Hari was pleased;

The sages said:
"If the Blessed One is indeed pleased with us out of a desire for our welfare,

This meritorious vow bestows wealth and grain, grants satisfaction to the self,

"O Lord of Gods, by what deed is one glorified in the world of Viṣṇu?

One should not speak with fallen thieves, nor with heretical men,
